_childDocuments_.review: The current state of the game is completely unacceptable, to take a year hiatus from the beta that was generally well received to return with an objectively worse product in almost every way is almost commical. Theyve slowed the game speed by roughly 15%, the camera is so zoomed in you are literally incapable of seeing the entirety of the moves your characters are doing. Not to mention how theyve basically tripled the grind needed to unlock characters from the beta, theyve removed the ability to play all the characters offline and the ability to play the game offline in general, killing the local scene. Then theres the removal of not only a majority of the accessibilty settings, but also there being a ton of stuff missing from your locker, items you paid for during the beta are completely missing and even if you contact PFG they WILL make you wait weeks and then it might not even end with you getting your items. All of these issues and I havent even commented on the actual gameplay loop, in which they have also, unexpectedly ruined just like a majority of the game. The balance of the game is maybe the worst its ever been, with the strength disparity of the weakest to strongest in the cast being possibly worse than even the beta was at its worst. With both doubling the sizes of the characters and not changing the blast zones for some ungodly reason, while ALSO increasing the strength of multiple moves it results in an incredibly mashy game in comparison to the beta that very heavily relied on confirms and precise reactions. Undeniably worse than the beta but even if it was on par or better as one would expect, they removed ranked and free for alls entirely making the game modes available incredibly dull and repetitive. No skill based matchmaking either, so you are rarely fighting someone of your skill level as well, and most of your games will either be against someone who is clearly new and inexperienced with the genre and when you find someone of your skill level to have a fun challenge they will more often leave after one game. TL;DR The game is in a rough spot right now, a very rough spot and if they do not get their ♥♥♥♥ together immediately it will not last. The patches theyve been doing have been trying to put a bandage on a severed limb and everyones patience is already wearing thin. With no info on when crucial modes like ranked or new content people enjoy like a character drop are releasing people are leaving on masse. The game has a lot of potential to be good, but potential doesnt matter if the game is bad.

_childDocuments_.review: Game felt way better in the beta, you were able to chain together attacks seamlessly and move around quickly. Now the game feels slow, clunky, and way too floaty. The same day I started playing, I already bought the most expensive founder pack (which claimed to be there for a limited time) and continued at this pace of playing almost all day for a week or two, adding up to 120 hours of gameplay at the end. But what started to discourage me in the game was, first thing: repetitive maps and classes clearly too OP's. Some character combos are clearly broken, and it's something that I as a player understand is very difficult to balance (maybe impossible).Smash games have this constant problem, developing a game like Multiversus is asking to work , because with each new character to be released, ALL the others will be affected and their gameplay, skills, combos, timings will have to be readjusted, and that is at least hell for those who are developing.So, the expected happens, the characters are completely broken, and the randomness of the character selection doesn't help this to work well, as we can fall against a team with two robots and I'm, I don't know, bugsbunny. Can you win? Maybe. Do I need skill for this? No, just luck. And this lucky is discouraging, because no matter how much you know how to play, you are at the mercy of losing to someone who doesn't even know how to play but uses a stronger character.Not only that, but the INEXISTENCE of a ranked mode makes the game completely meaningless, as you click to play and you can fall against both a person who has just created the account, and someone who has already played 250 games on closed beta (happened to me), and obviously you can't have fun playing against someone extremely stronger than you, obviously. Do some kind of integration with the steam workshop, give prizes to winning maps, or something similar, just like CS:GO has its workshop tab for you to make skins, use this feature to add multiple maps (Speed​​Runners also do something similar). name: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara
detailed_description: Join series favorite Koa and her friend Napopo on an action-packed journey through the world of Mara! Traverse wild islands, dodge cunning traps, and defeat the pirate bosses in this loving tribute to classic platforming adventures. Eight worlds to discover and explore. Each level has its own theme, traps, and bits of story. Sail through the ocean and upgrade your boat to reach every corner of Mara. Full of memorable characters. Meet all kinds of characters and help them. Discover all kinds of hidden secrets, challenges, and collectibles! Upgrade and customize the city of Qälis and get a lot of new skins and backpacks for Koa. Unlock an archipelago piece by piece. From sandy beaches to bubbling volcanoes, there’s no shortage of charming and colorful islands to visit, each one chock full of secrets and collectibles. Each level offers beautiful visuals rich with detail and depth. Relax and unwind - or knuckle down and challenge yourself! From newcomers to speedrunners, Koa and the Five Pirates is a buccaneering adventure for all.

short_description: Join Koa and Napopo on a 3D platformer adventure through the islands of Mara! Outwit traps, explore the ocean, maneuver dangerous environments, and have fun in 8 wild worlds on their quest to recover stolen pirate loot.

_childDocuments_.review: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is  latest game, set in the same universe as  and  This time, it is a basic 3D platformer that pays homage to the classics of the genre. It is extremely similar to the developer’s previous titles but fortunately, it is short and sweet - a stark contrast to  previous projects which are known to be filled with bloated content.Playing once more as Koa, a young girl which is seasoned from her action-packed adventures in the previous games. She now sets out alongside her trusty friend Napopo, determined to bring back stability to Qalis after pirates have stolen all objects from the island. They must travel to the neighbouring islands to defeat the pirate challenges, retrieve the lost pieces of the map and bring back the stolen goods. Although the story is very minimalistic, characters do remember Koa from her previous adventures and already think of her highly. This could be confusing in the beginning if you are not aware of the Mara universe, but it is not essential to understand. The narrative is just like all  games that I have played, an afterthought.  It is not awful, but it is plain and dry, perhaps meant for a younger audience to enjoy, but still lacks any sense of flare or individualism. The developer’s seem to trial out a new genre with every game they release, which seems unusual, but I do enjoy the variety so I cannot complain about that! Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is a 3D platformer with simple controls and gameplay. Koa can roll to increase speed, smash objects after jumping and only perform a single jump (interestingly, no double jump). Koa travels from island to island to complete levels and the traversal is done via boat in a small area. The whole game is designed with speed running in mind, and every level will award you a bronze, silver or gold medal depending on the time you made. Of course, there are collectables to be found in each level which will typically go towards cosmetics, boat upgrades and facility upgrades to the town. Levels are very quick, generally ranging from only 2-4 minutes and are very fast-paced, making the game a breeze to play. Adding onto this, but it is also very easy as well. I did not find any part of it challenging, and I would recommend this game for young children, or for parents to play alongside them.Each different island is categorised by a different biome such as a volcano, icy glacier, underwater etc. Each will have different levels leading up to a small boss fight The game also introduces new gameplay to keep things interesting and maintains the pacing well. Some levels are races where Koa zooms through speed pads while collecting shells (the game currency), dodging obstacles and so forth. Others are more generic such as just running to the finish line, jumping up different ledges, using objects to power up a bridge and so forth. Given that the levels are rather short, it never felt too monotonous as the gameplay was constantly changing and swapping through its diverse style of levels.Annoyingly, the camera angle is static, and many times it moved far too slowly for my pace, resulting in unnecessary deaths. This was typically noticeable in “race” levels where Koa has to keep up with something else that is moving alongside her, yet it moves so slow that I have to try and intentionally slow down so I do not get my view cut off. The game is also much shorter than  or  where they became frustrating and too repetitive towards the end. Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is quite the opposite and maintains its speedy pacing from start to finish. However, although the genres are changing frequently, the game feels too familiar with its unchanging artstyle, overlay, characters and so forth. Even in  everything feels eerily analogous to all their other games. There is not much depth to Koa and understandably, more focus is given to the gameplay, but I hope to see the next game stepping away from this IP and introducing a new story with new characters and to freshen up the aging overall style.Visuals are cute and vibrant and succeed in being rather eye catching. Unfortunately, as stated above, these visuals are beginning to lose their radiance to me as everything is replicated from the developer’s previous games. Sound is minimal, with a relaxed soundtrack playing in the background of each level. Dialogue is once again, copy-paste from previous titles and characters are not voiced, but they will repeatedly make the same grunts, hmms, or eh sounds when conversing with them. I do not mind this as a stylistic choice, but once again, given that this is exactly what I have played in at least two of their other games, I am yearning for something to change to feel fresh.    Around 4.5 hours Yes Yes, for speedrunners / achievement hunters.Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is a fun little platformer, made for players looking for an easy, casual adventure and do not need much of a story. The gameplay is fun, and the fast-paced levels are made with speed running in mind. Whilst I enjoyed my time, the world of Mara is beginning to wear thin. I am hopeful for the next game to finally showcase something different, and not just with the genre, but with the story, characters and style.

_childDocuments_.review: is set in the same universe as  and . While the three games belong to different genres and can be played independently of each other, they share a common set of characters and the same setting. Being a rather challenging action-platformer game,  brings new energy to the trilogy, which is otherwise oriented more towards casual players.You will reprise once more your role as young Koa whose help and assistance are required in a little town plundered by pirates. They looted all available goods to enhance the obstacle courses that they built for entertainment. Koa will be tasked not only to retrieve these goods but also to test all these trials and compete in all races.The game is built linearly, with a new area made accessible only after you complete all the trials from the previous one. These are also unlocked sequentially, ending in a boss fight or a notably harder level after you complete the three or four stages included in that area’s batch. Each of these levels has set timers that award gold, silver and respectively bronze medals for speed-running, but they can also be completed in a leisurely manner, allowing you to take your time to explore and collect every little shell (the main currency used in-game). Aside from shells, each level also has between one and three collectibles that you can gather which, in combination with the shells, allow you to purchase cosmetics for your character, boat or rebuild the town. There is no option to upgrade your abilities in any way (aside from some minor boat upgrades), therefore gathering all these is entirely optional. contains a very varied set of levels, both in terms of biomes used (ice, lava, temple, hills, water), but also regarding to the mechanics. Some are parkour levels, others involve swimming underwater. Some boss fights take the form of competing with the boss in a race to reach the finish gate first, while others will require you to directly fight the boss and fend off their attacks. Each of these levels is pretty unique in its own way and new mechanics are introduced every two or three levels.The controls are well-implemented and responsive. Instead of double jumping (which doesn't exist here), most of your time will be spent alternating your jump with a roll which has to be timed exactly when Koa lands from her jump. This makes her advance very fast (walking is extremely slow otherwise) but it also means that you will need an increased level of precision and pre-planning to perfectly chain these together so that you land on stable ground and not somewhere in the void between two platforms. It becomes like a fast-paced, yet rhythmic dance that you have to interrupt every so often to overcome traps or other obstacles and ultimately an exercise in alternating quickly between the adrenaline rush of the speed and tempering yourself to not mess up the jumps.On the other hand, I had real problems with the camera perspective. The game uses a static camera that follows the main character’s movement, but it switches perspectives rather unexpectedly and this caught me off-guard many times. Aside from keeping up with the fast movement of the character, my mind also had to continuously (and quickly) re-adjust to the new perspective. There is no way for the player to control the camera themselves. Additionally, some levels contain a chase sequence in which the camera moves at a set speed and with a set orientation. If you don’t keep up with it, you lose the level by not being in the frame anymore.Regarding the difficulty, I’d say that the levels range from moderate to high-intensity exercises (or at least above average), culminating with a rather brutal end-boss. Even if the game can be played in a non-speedrun mode, the chase sequences can seem really tight and frustrating for new players, and there is also a considerable amount of precision jumps, timed jumps and sequences in which you have to carry an object without being hit by anything. On the positive side, the levels are split into different stages, with checkpoints in-between, and reaching a checkpoint will replenish your lives back to the maximum of three. Also nice is the fact that you won’t lose the items collected if you die, neither the coins / door keys picked up from the beginning of the level, nor the collectibles. The game offers two difficulty modes, with the difference between them being the number of checkpoints encountered in a level.  is certainly a well-made game, even though it doesn’t add anything new to the genre. Completing one playthrough takes around six hours if done in a relaxed way (or four hours in a more rushed way), but if you aim to obtain 100% completion it will take you several more hours. For this, you’ll need to obtain all gold medals, win in all races against the NPCs and buy everything from all the shops which essentially means gathering every collectible. Due to its classic 3D platformer style,  can definitely scratch that itch if you’re nostalgic for games like Nintendo’s Super Mario 64, PlayStation’s Crash Bandicoot, A Hat In Time and it’s perhaps most similar to Kao the Kangaroo.

_childDocuments_.review: In Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara, players take control of Koa and Napopo, who must make their way through eight different worlds in a new island paradise in Mara. The pirates have stolen or destroyed a number of items from the town Qälis, and now they want to challenge Koa and Napopo with a variety of tasks and trials. As an adventurer with a thirst for redemption and conservation, you will set out on your ship to visit these colorful biomes and return what was once stolen to its rightful home. From magical temples to temperamental volcanoes, players will assemble a group of brave friends in pursuit of a band of mischievous pirates who have turned the city of Qälis upside down. Now it's up to you to rebuild the town, get new outfits for Koa, help clean Mara's waters to protect its wildlife, and most importantly, discover if you're a fearless little pirate.Influenced by games like Super Mario 3D World, Crash Bandicoot, and even The Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker, Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is sure to appeal to those who grew up playing platformers and those looking for a simple, but fun summer adventure. The game is all about moving quickly through colorful environments, avoiding traps and solving puzzles to progress through each stage. Thankfully, Koa's boat is still around, and you'll be able to collect seashells that can be used to buy new items, clothes, and even upgrades for the main town hub. In-between levels, you can explore a town with shops, have people to talk to, and you can do sidequests.Like Mario 3D Land/World, Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is basically a linear 3D platformer with a fixed camera perspective. The game focuses on having a smooth and responsive control scheme for the gameplay, and it succeeds somewhat in most aspects, but falls flat in a few. For example, you can sprint, jump, and you can roll on landing, which gives you a much bigger speed boost. There is also a grab button that allows you to throw objects such as bombs into certain obstacles, but that's about it. This is all Koa can do, which is not a bad thing in my opinion, but there could have been a lot more interaction. Instead of spending most of the game jumping and rolling once I hit the ground, I found myself longing for a Super Mario-style dive, a double jump, the ability to roll without jumping, or even a sidehop to give me some different choices.Structurally, each level has a few alternate paths for any collectibles you might need, but otherwise it's a straight shot to the end. The speed with which you complete a level earns you either a gold, silver or bronze medal. So it's better to take your time, collect all the collectibles, and then replay the level to get the best time. The levels were generally not designed to stand out, but overall they were fun to play. There was a basic platforming idea in each level that was executed in a straightforward manner. I had a lot of fun when the roll-jump was a perfect fit, and it is a really good feeling to be able to complete a level without any mistakes. Once a level is finished, the microsecond celebratory pose of Koa and Napopo is comically undersold compared to Mario’s – now rather overblown – twirl when collecting a star.Koa's adventure is therefore all about her overcoming fun trials/challenges; it's not about her having deep conversations with anyone. As you can see in the two prequels that take place in the same universe, Summer in Mara and Stories of Mara, she has already experienced a lot. She is held in high esteem by every character from the very beginning, which can be very confusing if you haven't played the other games. Sadly, Koa fails to be both wholesome and to have meaningful dialogue throughout the plot. This means that each person is completely forgettable. What's more, three of the four kids from the intro cutscene quickly disappear from the main screen. They all stay on the hub island, occasionally taking part in a race where they fall behind drastically after a second.A full playthrough will, at most, take six to eigth hours for casuals to complete, including the hidden collectibles. It's a rather short game, so don't go into this for length. Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is like a delightful evening meal with your parents: a perfect experience for the few bites it takes and the hours it lasts. In fact, the run time is more enjoyable particularly because it doesn't really overstay its welcome. The game knows what it's about, lays out what to expect and then lets players come to a fitting conclusion, before the whole gets too stale. Although I have to admit that in my personal experience the game loop got a little bit monotonous towards the end, which is why I'm glad that it's not that long.For the price, especially if you have kids, Koa is a nice platformer for a game night when you want to do something casual and wholesome. It's a little too easy, and most players will be able to complete 100% in two or three sessions. It is an experience that is sure to leave you wanting more in terms of gameplay, but what we have here is pretty good. The protagonists are neat, the graphics are vibrant and colorful, and it's a lot of fun to bounce around the levels. With a little more range of motion or even freedom of movement, as well as a more meaningful dialog, Koa could have been exceptional. So if you're in the mood for something wholesome, this will no doubt do your gamer's heart good, if only for a short while.

_childDocuments_.review: Koa is a decent 3d platformer. It has good movement, decent story and progression, but the fixed camera and platforming can be suboptimal, and the frequent game-pause-camera-pans within gameplay are quite disturbing. It doesn't get my general, active recommendation, but if you like 3d platformers, it can be worthwhile, or enjoyable if you're less bothered about some things than me.+ Decent implementation of cute characteristics and child-wonder/adult-supported-child-adventure story+ Good movement with caveats (more below)+ Decent variance in level design, level and gameplay mechanics, and environment themes* 4-gameplay-style mix of mostly 3d platforming, but also auto-running-platforming sections, swimming, and partly boat-navigating-hub-world* ~4.3 hour story playthrough; has additional optional side-missions, collectibles, and unlockables- Level-design/-implementation seems [only] acceptable- Solving a [part] objective locks the game, pans the camera, even if you're mid-jump etc, leading to frequent gameplay and sometimes problematic control interruptionMost of the game is a 3d platformer. Some sections are auto-runners and swimming. Each area has a boss battle. The hub world is a mix of 3d platformer in the explorable home-island, and boat navigation (on one hand simple, on the other with abilities and upgrades).Good movement. But you always run anyway, keeping the run button pressed. Roll-jump can give additional speedup, with an opportunity for going fast or speedrunning, but often makes it much harder or infeasible on platforming sections. The roll-jump controls felt unintuitive at first, but you can internalize it rather quickly (no forgiving pre-ground-roll-input acceptance). The suboptimal platforming environment (the combination of placement, hit detection, movement, …) can make it not a clean, intuitive experience. In earlier levels, there seemed to be more opportunities for shortcutting.Dialogue is text-only. Characters are voiced minimally, mostly with noises only. By the end, I skipped dialogues as well. I wasn't invested in the story, and it was quite predictable and always the same.Maybe because of not having taken notes, but maybe because it's diffuse, I'm somewhat dissatisfied not being able to write down negatives here to warrant not recommended. Either way, overall, to me, it felt only acceptable. I like the movement, but it nor anything else stood out significantly. And with some things irritating me, it does not get my recommendation. Still, if you like platformers, it's not necessarily a bad fit.
_childDocuments_.name: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara

_childDocuments_.review: "Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara" seems like a cutesy platformer set in a tropical archipelago, but unfortunately, that's just the first layer. After a very simple tutorial, you encounter the first real levels, and the difficulty level quickly ramps up. The times to complete stages are very demanding, and combined with the difficult, unintuitive controls and lack of clear indication of where Koa will land, the whole experience quickly becomes very frustrating.There is a "Relaxed" mode, and it is much more enjoyable to play.I recommend it, but only if you are not put off by a high level of difficulty. And when it's discounted.
_childDocuments_.name: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara

_childDocuments_.review: A fun little game, but ultimately rough around the edges and often pretty frustrating. Koa's default speed is way too slow and makes most jumps impossible, so you'll want to be running all the time. This means holding down the run button for the entire game like it's Mario on the NES except that same button is what you use to perform rolls and long jumps, which frequently results in accidentally vaulting off ledges. The game expects and encourages you to go fast all the time, which sometimes leads to getting hit from something coming on-screen faster than you can react to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game, it's just a tad better than mediocre. The briefest way I can describe the experience is that it feels like a properly completed and polished final college project for Game Design. Simple, and mostly too easy, so easy that I basically only died by letting my guard down at how easy it was and getting lazy. The dialogues were pretty lame too, though the characters themselves had an interesting charm with their designs. The things this game gets very right are the art style and the classic Mario-like jump and run mechanics. The performance is also great. Still, I would probably only recommend for kids.
_childDocuments_.name: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara

_childDocuments_.review: Fun platformer, not hard but does have some levels that I thought were tricky so it's not easy 100% which I think is good. I think the controls worked well and plays great on the Steam Deck. If you like Mario, A Hat in Time, then you might like this one. For the price it's not bad and the collectibles are easy to obtain.

_childDocuments_.review: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is a respectable high-cute-factor platformer for the casual gamer, but I think Chibig missed the boat here by situating it in the Summer in Mara universe. As someone who loves Summer in Mara, I have to consciously ignore some things to enjoy it, in a way that I wouldn't need to for a standalone title. I loved Summer in Mara for its depiction of island life and values, for the way it depicted the natural world, and faithfully captured the heart and spirit of village life as seen in places like the south Pacific. This title has a quite different mood and aesthetic. It has a toy-like polish to the environment and characters that does have a sort of charm, but it's a very different charm and not what I was looking for in another title in this universe. (In fairness to Chibig, this was clear in the trailer, I just thought I could look past it a little more readily than I really could). The aesthetics are closer to Kirby than Summer in Mara. The bonus things you can earn are things like t-shirts that take the look further and further from island life. There was a bit of that in Summer in Mara too, but it wasn't particularly presented there as something to aim for if it didn't interest you. Here, it's a form of street cred with the antagonists.More gratingly for me is the dynamics between the characters. When you strip away the cute trappings, Koa is essentially taking part in a rigged race and scavenger-hunt game put together by the local bully kids to get the town's belongings back (a town full of adults who, by the way, could probably retrieve or replace their own things given half a chance - the same glaring plot hole that plagues Innchanted, another title drawing on real-life Pacific lore). Plenty of games have flimsier premises than that, for sure, and I could look past it if it was mentioned once in the beginning and then forgotten. But Koa is routinely subjected to the stakes being changed and hidden gotchas by said bullies, which they revel in the telling, uncomfortably and frequently recalling real-world childhood bullying, at least for me. I reacted negatively to them in a way that I don't to the more-fanciful foes found in most games. Koa is a normally smart and sassy character,  and I kind of wanted to shake her and tell her that she doesn't have to buy into their sh*t. She literally has her own boat and island to go to, which she regains control of in the very first level, at the end of which I just wanted to leave her there. I'm sure eventually Koa will prevail, but it's a game she doesn't have to play at all. And from an adult's point of view, she's rewarding them by playing even if she prevails. Precisely because the antagonists are so small and ordinary, because we've all actually met people like them, rewarding them leaves a really sour taste in my mouth.I don't know whether I will play the game any further. It is enjoyable in that low-stakes casual way of colour and sound. But there are better examples out there, and they don't require me to put aside in-universe disappointment and a sinking feeling as someone who genuinely  Koa, as an intrepid and self-possessed little orphan taking care of herself and her island, and doesn't really want to see her in this dogfight even if she wins in the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara

_childDocuments_.review: Cute and colourful platformer game. Reminds me of Super Mario 3D World but I never played it. Levels are short and simple but controls are sometimes a problem.You see, since it's a game where you want to gain most momentum while running, you have to do long roll jumps (à la Super Mario 64) but the jump button is also the ground pound attack (which shares with RS button) and the roll action at the same time. So, I often end up killing my momentum or even plunging into the void.Beside this point, I get a lot of A Hat in Time and Shantae vibes from the game. It's good and chill.

_childDocuments_.review: You can view my 3D in VR gameplay here: Yes, you too can play Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara in 3D in VR as long as you have the right setup. It's actually very easy to do. Mainly, you'll need to download the free, open-source Unreal Engine 3D fix using the Geo-11 3D driver. Just look for it. Also, you'll need a way to view 3D in VR and VR Screen Cap is one way to do it that is completely free as well (just look for it too).The 3D visuals are great. This anime / cartoon style just pops in 3D in VR. Really, the visuals are excellent. The only issue I found is that the geo-11 3D driver for some reason interferes with the roll on gamepad. I did play this game in Non-VR and I could easily roll, but that wasn't the case once I went to 3D. It really doesn't effect gameplay too much since you can still run, but it may make some sections harder than they need to be.Other than that, I would say it's a near perfection conversion to 3D in VR. It's like looking at a 3D movie at a 3D movie theater. I wish this game had native VR support though. Even with just a 180 screen, it makes the game look that much more beautiful than the 2D normal viewing.

_childDocuments_.review: This has been a lovely platformer focused on collectibles and speedrunning. The style is cute, there's lots to do and it's just plain fun once you get used to the controls. The controls are similar to mario games in the sense that you have to create momentum with button pressing. But it's a bit more challenging to get right when you're required precision with higher speed. Also kudos to the achievements. They're focused on random fun that is easily achievable, collectibles and finishing the story. It took me less than 9 hours to get 100% on everything. There are some minor flaws:1. I'd have liked quick teleportation to the town hub. 2. When you're shopping, the icon on the objects you're selecting is white. It's easy to lose track of what you were looking at because the background is white as well. A more prominent icon would have been better.3. Sometimes the game lacks a bit of life due to the lack of animation/movement. This is mainly apparent in the town hub and the result screen when you clear a level. In the town, the NPC are kind of lifeless. There is no motion and it's pretty apparent. In the result screen, Koa suddenly stands still. The transition is very sudden. It's a bit jarring.4. There are some light feminist and LGBT elements through some dialogues, characters and the last upgrade for your boat (pink blue). I'm mentioning this for the folks who are sensitive to this. It's definitely worth playing if you're looking for a 3D platformer focused on collecting stuff and similar to classic platformers from the past.
_childDocuments_.name: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara

_childDocuments_.review: This is just perfect for a few hours of relaxing and feel-good platforming. The controls are very responsive and simple to pick up and play. There are no hidden or overly difficult mechanics, and the progression feels good enough, so I wanted to get all the achievements. There are a few not-so-easy levels that serve the purpose of giving you a nice sense of pride, but that's it!
_childDocuments_.name: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara

_childDocuments_.review: Being a huge "Summer in Mara" fan, I was really excited about this new game. However, I can't help but feel a bit let down. The graphics don't quite match up to the previous game, which was my cozy escape on tough days. The vibrant world and lovable characters in "Summer in Mara" had me completely hooked. Sadly, this new game falls short in capturing that same level of magic. While I do appreciate the sentimental value it holds, there's a certain charm and depth that seem to be missing. I had hoped for an experience that could replicate the warmth and familiarity of the original, but this new game doesn't quite hit the mark in the same way.
_childDocuments_.name: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara

_childDocuments_.review: When I decided to buy this game despite my horrible coordinations in platform games, I was guided by a thought "oh it seems cute", "I'm still in a Submerged funk" and "People says that the achievements are easy, it means that I do not need to sweat about it" (because yeah, while I don't play games for achievements, I love from once in a while to have one nearly handed into a silver plate). Mara is an unknown universe at this point, before a friend of mine informed me that it's the same girl as in Summer in Mara, which is not my type of game. You know, farming ressources, feeding animals, yada yada.But here I am, playing with a controller and trying to understand everything. I'm not rushing the game though, first, it's exploring before getting that gold medal (beating a set of time). But well, first, I'm learning about the plot: Qualis, an island on Mara, has been robbed by the pirates: Awan, Caleb, Noohoo, Taka, Pilly, Tilly and Milly are quite deseperate to see their jobs threaten by these thieves. Mayo, a wannabe pirate, and her friends are explaining to Koa, a young explorer, and Napopo, a living seashell, that if they want to restore everything, they have to take part into a course to become a pirate. Koa and Napopo are ready to take the challenge. Beating each pirate should be easy right? Well... You don't expect Taima to be so kind, you don't expect Ereti to be so mad or... well, in reality, yeah, you should be expecting that because if you played Summer in Mara, these characters are themselves (keep in mind that I have no idea of the universe).So, the goal is to grab a piece of a map from the pirates, to go to your next destination (weirdly enough, it's like you're discovering Mara again). The currency is the seashells you can collect along to unlock new backpacks and new shirts, you have the main island to collect them but also little islands to do it... or to find gears to upgrade your boat. Each level have secrets: fabrics to keep unlocking new clothes, trash to keep unlocking new backpacks and pearls because Edegan, the banker, is a jerk as he will act as the one between the pirates and yourself to restore what the islanders lost. Also, you have diving places, though this time, it's Napopo on a grappling hook for the sunken treasures. It should be easy to jump, roll and go fast? Well.... if you consider that it's a platformer... you will have to avoid spikes, tiles falling down once you set a foot on it and other traps that I have cursed around. In other words, yeah, it's pretty to get a golden medal once you have mastered the controls AND found one or two nice shortcuts and explored casually the level so that you can get the hidden secrets and plan your strategy. Oh and if you want to fully explore Mara, you have also to beat Mayo and Co in a race. Strangely enough, Mayo is always second behind you, Sandee (?), claiming to be the fastest, is the third and Boohoo (who really doesn't want to be there) is the last one. And like I've said, knowing one or two shortcuts is helpful.The one downside? The last level where you really need to be as perfect as you can be because you have so few checkpoints (I've played in Normal but after a while, I've lowered the difficulty of some levels to Easy, and the last one was among them), mess one leg and you can ask for restarting the level. I'm accepting responsability because I made some ridiculous jumps at a bad moment but my already bad coordination isn't explaining all as it took me 3-4 hours to speedrun the level when I was cruising some levels that were as hard as this one.Also, I don't know why and sometimes, I died without falling down, without touching any trap... just literally lost my three lives in one go... in an already hard level in the temples. Yay!The levels are varied enough: your own island is relatively easy, compared to traps in the Marine Base or even in the temples. All the characters are nice enough with you (apart Ereti, who is always mad anyway - you really shouldn't have broken into her sanctuary) and are familiar faces from Summer in Mara.Anyway, I loved this game so much that I've bought (and finished) Summer in Mara, as it's as chill as this platforming game. I love the cuteness of the graphics, I loved the soundtrack. True, the achievements are easy... but you already know that the one with all golden medals was hard as hell with the last level. If you're familiar with Mara, then, you'll catch references with the universe, if you're not, I strongly advise you to play Summer in Mara and Stories of Mara (though I have to still play this one).

Impossible to play and not smile from ear to ear! So yeah, a big recommendation, specially if you're into 3D Platformers. You'll have a blast!!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty fun when it sticks to its strengths, but sadly tries to shake things up a bit to much a bit to often in ways which absolutely kill the fun I'm having with the quite solid movement. Sure I get it that games like these can benefit from shaking up their gameplay with the occasional underwater level, auto scroller and auto runner, but having all 3 of those within the first 10ish levels isn't an attempt to shake up stale gameplay, its an, in my opinion unwarranted, lack of confidence in what seems to be the core gameplay of this game. Having played 117 minutes of this game, I'm not that sure if I want to play the rest of it.Also, a fair warning to people expecting this game to be a collectathon, in the style of M64 or Banjo Kazooie: Its not one of those. _childDocuments_.review: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is a level-based 3D platformer with a fixed camera. Of course there is running and jumping, but there is also a roll-jump that is performed by pressing the run button right after landing a jump. So any roll-jump needs to be planned ahead. Koa's island has been invaded by pirates, well kinda. These pirates did steal a bunch of stuff from the island that Koa needs to get back, but the pirates are generally friendly. Koa even helps to set one up on a date. In addition to the platforming levels, there is also the ocean area that acts like a hub world where you sail a boat around to different islands. The explorable area is restricted so that you have to beat levels to gain access to more levels. There is a coin currency found in both the levels and the ocean area that can be used to buy things in town like outfits.The movement is unique with the roll-jump that doesn't take too long to get used to. I don't even think the roll-jump is mandatory to use to beat the game, but it is great for speed-running. There is the mandatory goal of reaching the end of each level, but there is also one to three collectables hidden in each level. The game tells you upfront how many before starting each level. There is also a time trial challenge for each level to get gold, silver, or bronze. Grabbing the collectables unlocks things in the town like outfits for Koa or upgrades for the boat. The game is also plenty long, taking me about 10 hours to do everything. It may be shorter if you skip the optional stuff.I think the vibes are a bit weird because there is the serious issue of the pirates stealing a bunch of stuff from the island, but they are also friends with Koa before and after she retrieves the stolen property? Each level has the time trial challenge, which I like, but then there are also racing challenges against a particular pirate in just a handful of levels, which feels redundant and filler.The game is a bit on the easy side without any end-game or post-game super challenges.I do recommend this game even though I found it a bit easy, it was still fun to find all the collectables and get a gold time on all the levels.This game is good for beginners. The fixed camera means there is no difficulty surrounding managing the perspective, the camera won't get stuck on level geometry. More games like this:;Super Mario 3D World

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes you just need a good 3D platformer as a fun palette cleanser after a grueling at time at work - that's where Koa and the Five Pirates comes in, as a charming little level-based platformer that doesn't overstay its welcome, and packs just enough variety in to stay interesting, but not enough to really climb into the realm of idiosyncrasy. Think Lucky's Tale: Short levels without a ton of precision involved and minor collectibles. Though, what does add an additional sprinkle to joy to Koa is none other than the roll-jump.Koa's levels are pretty straightforward: You navigate the basic biomes with a mix of walking, jumping, ground-pounds, rolls, and the occasional throw. There's no real enemies, just environmental hazards with decently generous checkpoints and no lives. Each level has between one and three collectables, depending on the type of level. What adds an additional level of fun is replaying levels with time challenges, opting the player to learn how to effectively use the roll-jump. Most levels can be completed in under a couple of minutes, and being able to blaze through them with additional precision makes Koa an even more enjoyable experience.Completing levels opens up minor benefits, such as costumes, ship upgrades, or cosmetic upgrades to the main town. Koa's narrative revolves around pirates coming, being pirates, and Koa going through trials to be integrated within them. It doesn't make a ton of sense, but don't think too hard about it: It's a children's level narrative without any real villains at the helm. There's a group of pirates that you get to race every now and then, and these levels provided a fresh take on an existing stage. I wouldn't say there's much of a challenge to Koa, whether that be boss fights, races, or time challenges, but there's a healthy variety to the mix. Though, the levels with fixed cameras were the worst, and outright ruins one of the ending challenges in an early level.Koa plays well across the board; I played it on my Steam Deck and was overall really satisfied with the smooth 60 FPS performance. What did annoy me was that the final two achievements would not unlock, despite the conditions being met; I am hoping they will randomly unlock, as a couple of others did, but I am not holding my breath. Just a disappointing way to finish off the game.Koa and the Five Pirates can be beaten in well under eight hours, fully completing all components of the game; it's a charming experience and a great introduction to platformers if you don't have much experience with them. It's a soft recommendation - it won't steal much of you time, but roll-jumping through perilous moving platforms certainly makes for a good way to spend one's time.

_childDocuments_.review: Koa is a well-made 3D platformer indie game. It's exactly what is has to be, no more, no less. It took just over six-hours to get all the achievements, and I feel more than satisfied with my purchase. All levels have three different motivations for tackling its obstacles: getting to the end (progresses the story), finding the three hidden collectibles (unlocks customizables), and racing against the clock for gold medals (purely for joy/vanity). Koa is a delight to control. She is easy to move with well-communicated gravity and momentum. Her speed roll after jumping combo'd into a long jump is the best mechanic in a 3D platformer in recent memory. It makes speeding through levels necessary, fun, and just the right level of challenge. The amount of polish here is surprising for a dev team of this size. The game's assets, the lighting, the transitions, and menus all look great. The character art is wonderful, creative, and charming. The VO is cute as heck, save for the constant underwater gurgling as you mash maneuvers underwater. I adore the idea of improving Qalis as the game progresses, making you feel like your actions matter in the world. The aesthetics of the different islands were tastefully disparate, if not a little familiar. Navigating the overworld map on your boat is just fun enough and offers you a sense of space that makes otherwise disconnected platforming levels belong to the same world. The music is unfortunately forgettable, at worst failing to match the vibe of what Koa's doing. The writing also doesn't shine much; the cute visuals do infinitely more to set the vibes than the 'too cute for its own good' dialogue does. A lack of reward for getting all the gold medals was also a bummer, but it was still a fun and manageable challenge. The game is very well paced; coming back to Qalis between the major islands was a great break, getting to see what new cosmetics are unlocked, and having a race against my pirate 'friends' across familiar levels. That, and the tasks outlined by the levels themselves range from escaping a giant colossus in the snow trying to crush you to speedrunning a nap on an island of pigs. Really lovely stuff. I feel it also important to note that I experienced exactly zero bugs, glitches, or game-breaks whatsoever, a feat that should be celebrated.Koa hits the mark exactly, breaking zero no ground while also never floundering for a moment. It's a tight, charming experience that should be a standard for small-budget indie games. You can feel the care from the dev team in every stitch. And I mean, there seems to be a lil more map to clear, DLC perchance? :eyes:

_childDocuments_.review: A polished and playable 3d adventure platformer, suitably challenging for younger players. It isn't very long for longtime gamers, I was able to 100 percent within about 6-7 hours, but its structure, length and available tech would make for a good speed running challenge if you were so inclined.Challenges are nonviolent as a rule. Stages have physical obstacles and hazards rather than enemies, and even aggressive enemies take the form of races rather than fights in most situations. There are 4 boss encounters which might constituted a "fight" but each involves dodging attacks until bombs can be thrown back at, or buttons pressed to shut down a machine. Consider for relevance if a pacifistic stance on children's entertainment is desired.5 islands, each with 3 stages and a boss, plus a handful of single stage mini islands and rush challenge reworks of each island, gives about 25 stages all around, so none of the stage gimmicks (you've played platformers so you likely know what to expect for several examples) overstaying their welcome, but more islands and stages would be a welcome addition. In many ways it feels like if a 3d mario game was a 5-6 hour game instead of a 20 hour affair. But it comes in at a lower price point and an indie studio, so I'm happy to endorse it. Perhaps a future project might represent "this, but more of it" and that would also be a good buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara

_childDocuments_.review: I would give this an "OK" rather than a "recommend".  I could see this game being fun for speed-runners, but it's also very basic when it comes to movement.  I love a good platformer, and this one was a short and breezy sort of outing (most stages can be completed in under 3 minutes- many under 1 minute).  I appreciate that there aren't invisible walls preventing you from skipping across bits of level geometry to cut past potentially large parts of the stage. The jump-roll is fun sort of "risk/reward" ability to move faster and jump farther, and it grew on me quite a bit over the course of the game, but I wish Koa had a larger set of abilities than that.  Mario 64 has taught us that a good 3D platformer aught to provide many optional movement abilities so that the player can experiment and express themselves- and make their own fun in early stages that are too easy for them!  There is WAY too much talking, and basically none of it is important.  A button to instantly skip entire conversations would be very, very welcome. I would also have loved an option in the menu to disable the "would you like to make this stage easier" prompt that pops up after a few deaths.  Let me test the boundaries in peace! (Also sometimes it's faster to jump off a cliff and re-spawn at a checkpoint than to retrace a path after hitting a switch or retrieving a collectible.)Performance on my PC was much worse than aught to be expected for a game that looks like it aught to be able to easily run on my phone.  I hope the devs intend to bring several performance patches to the game so that others will have a smoother experience than I did at launch.
_childDocuments_.name: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara

_childDocuments_.review: At the beginning, I won't lie, I wanted was falling asleep. I closed and re-opened the game a few times but the speed of Koa was so slow I couldn't bare it. Buut, I love a good 3D platformer so I put the game on mute, played some video on my 2nd monitor and blasted through the main story in about 2.5 hours for credits to roll.This game has its ups and downs. It manages to justt balance the good and the bad for me to continue playing.PROS:- Pretty & classic art style. Colourful, lots of variance in the levels/islands. Main selling point for me.- Unique mechanics. Ice, bombs, fun bosses, boat system.- Its QUICK, Each level is max 2 minutes on average. With many even being in the seconds. Made the progression much more enjoyable for me.- Races feel balanced, they were pretty fun and did the back to back once unlocking all of them. Only the ice level really made me struggle as Koa's jump height while on ice is very specific, vs the AI which knew the perfect line up.CONS:- The story/characters I could not care for 1 bit. I know its wholesome & chill but I honestly just skip spammed all the dialogue and still had my fun. This would be a good introduction to 3D platformers for new gamers I think.- Koa's speed isn't "smooth". When roll jumping, all is well, lots of momentum, peak game design. But her normal speed even while "running" has no momentum on the jumps. It feels like you are JUST reaching the platforms if not roll jumping and feels really infuriating. I wish the jumps went a little further when sprinting cause it almost feels like rubberbanding.- Some controls were not working at all/wrongly assigned? To pet dog it says "F", however, "Q" worked instead. There were a few of these errors, or holding shift and pressing every button to skip dialogue and it just not working? Not game breaking but just gives it a lack of polish.Overall, if you like Mario Odyssey or Hat in Time I reccomend to give this game a try. It's not a masterpiece, or has any big lore, the bosses/levels are all relatively easy and I died most of the time for rushing or not paying attention. 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good-enough-to-play linear 3D platformer with hidden collectibles, speedrun goals, and speedrun leaderboards. Both the overall gameplay and level design don't really bring anything new to the genre, but the levels are generally enjoyable and the movement is quick and satisfying, thanks to a fast-roll / long-jump mechanic that has you rhythmically tapping the run button before landing after a jump rather than holding the run button constantly.In between levels, there's usually some cutesy unvoiced dialogue with characters who seem like they're supposed to be familiar from a previous game. My biggest complaint so far was that it just took too darn long to get through the initial dialogue and into the game. I can tell that the game wants me to care about these characters and remember them from previous games, but neither the characters nor the story are deep enough to merit all the dialogue in the opening. At first, this feels like a game aimed at a younger audience because of the low initial difficulty and kiddie writing, but with there being so much dialogue at the beginning, and it being unvoiced, I think young players are likely to get bored in the opening, even more than I did.But the difficulty does ramp up to around the level of your typical Mario game ... ish ... and the text boxes do lay off a bit once you get into the game.Basically, my verdict is that this is a good but not amazing 3D platformer, but a pretty darn good game for speedrunning.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT - So I went back to play some more, and my leaderboards completely stopped showing up, even after restarting Steam. I don't know if this is a widespread issue, but it has sort of ruined the post-game speedrunning for me.The game is fun, but very,  easy. The platforming is solid and the physics feel great, but most of the fun for the platforming elite will be to increase your rankings on the global leaderboard for each level. The collectibles are fun, sometimes placed in tricky spots but usually placed at the end of an obvious split path. For casual gamers there is a relaxed mode that offers more checkpoints, but I honestly can't imagine anyone needing it. The story is cute and simple, I actually enjoyed the personalities of all the pirates, and Koa is very charming. I'm assuming these characters are from the two other games based in the Mara setting, but as a person who didn't play them I had no trouble following the plot at all. Achievement-wise, they are simple but rewarding. Get a gold medal for time on all levels, collect all collectibles, buy all upgrades and cosmetic items. That's pretty much it. Despite my game time, a 100% playthrough only takes 5-6 hours. I just happened to leave it on while afk for a bit.Overall, the game was amazing, but honestly made me wanting a more challenging experience. I wouldn't be against a DLC with platinum medals being added, for more challenging time trials. Nevertheless it was a lot of fun, and I'd recommend it if you are even slightly into platforming.

_childDocuments_.review: Watching a Review is a whole lot easier ❤️: We'll break it down into sections...Story: Pirates have pillaged and thieved...In Koa, you play as… Koa. A little girl who’s keen on saving the Islands of Mara from Pirates, who seem to be a bit bored with nothing better to do… soooo they decided to put on a challenge to find the next pirate, but that involved wreaking havoc on the locals, and now, it’s up to us to restore some sense of peace. All while simultaneously becoming the next Pirate? No spoilers here, so you’ll have to play if you want to find out.  I have to compliment Koa on its ability to not only offer great gameplay but also an engaging story. For a level-based game such as Koa, it’s hard to deliver the story through much more than cutscenes and text lines from NPCs, and that is how most of the story is received, but it was far more polished and playful than most titles. The characters you meet along your travels are all unique in their personalities and art, and the overall storyline you follow not only flows well but makes sense with the world around you. There were no awkward moments of ‘Why did they write it that way?’ or ‘How is this relevant to the game?’ the way I’ve felt with a few titles lately. I’m a big fan of less is more, but also, too little is not enough, and finding that balance in a storyline can be tough, but paired with a genre that isn’t story-driven to begin with it becomes even more of a challenge. Koa truly took it a step further than most titles in the “level-based” Platformer Genre as they baked the level system into the game in a way that doesn’t create a lack of immersion. Being someone who’s played Super Mario 3D World in its entirety, I was glad to not be following a little line to the next level bubble, then hitting “okay” to start it. Nope, Koa presented the levels as Islands you had to sail to, just so they could keep the story immersion intact. Kudos to them for caring that deeply because they honestly probably could’ve gotten away with just a level select system, the gameplay is tons of fun, but they chose not to, and for that, I say thank you.Gameplay: Island Hopping & Trash CollectingI want to say that my favorite thing about this game, despite the fact that it is a level-based 3D Platformer, is that the gameplay doesn’t reside in just the levels. Some of my favorite moments were going back to the home Island after finishing a few levels and checking out what new things I’d unlocked in the shops, and doing my civic duty throwing away the random bags of trash on the island. They’re simple things, but they add a level of depth to the game that makes it feel cohesive, as I mentioned in the story section. The even better part of it is that the graphics are cute and comedic so it’s enjoyable wandering around and sight-seeing, meeting our neighbors, and spin-jumping accidentally off a cliff and into the ocean. Let’s talk about the levels, and I’ll start by saying that I adore how different they all are. Koa revolves around visiting different islands and completing a set of levels, then returning to your main island with a new map fragment that will unlock more. The best part is, each island has a distinctly different theme around the levels, allowing for enough diversity that I didn’t find myself getting bored or feeling as though the levels were just assets being re-used. From rocky lava-filled mountains you have to sprint through delicately, to luscious tropical paradise levels that have you swinging from coconut trees. They were all so vibrant and well-made that I didn’t find myself disliking any of them. Sure, some are harder than others, but that’s what I’d expect, especially as you get later into the game.I do stand by what I said in my original review of the Demo, this game is a speed runner's dream. The amount of level decorations that you can use to hardcore parkour your way to a secret shortcut is ridiculous. I’ve seen a few runs on social media and it’s insane the routes people have found. So, while I’m nowhere near skilled enough with a controller to do speed running, if that’s something you enjoy, this one should be on your list of games to pick up.Aside from your main island and the level islands, there are also smaller islands and sunken treasure spots to find when you’re out sailing. These provide some extra unlockables and fun things to do and I admittedly wound up completing all of them, so you can expect a Full Walkthrough from us that features where to find them. Check out the YouTube channel for details on that.One of the last things I want to talk about in this section is the sheer amount of replayability Koa has. Each level offers a Gold, Silver & Bronze time, so if you’re an achievement chaser, get ready to join the Koa Olympics. As I mentioned previously, there are also plenty of collectibles and you’ll need to find every item around the world to unlock all of them, so get ready to be diving for treasure chests and aiding the spirits.Visuals & Audio: Playful, Nostalgic & FunTouching on the Visuals & Audio, we’re happy to report we didn’t run into any performance issues during our playthrough and for that we’re glad, because we got to fully enjoy the vibrantly fun graphics and playful soundtrack. Koa currently holds my makeshift award for 'Game with the soundtrack that remained the loudest'. It’s so fun and reminds me of all the old Nintendo soundtracks, so it sparked nostalgia that just feels good to the soul. If you’ve seen a few of our reviews you’ll know I rate a game based on if it earns a mute or not, so maybe you’ll see why this award was a big deal for me (lol). The world and level design, as well as the character art, were all brilliant. Exactly what you’d expect for a title such as this, so if you’re a fan of this graphic style, rest easy knowing it’s something to look forward to. The Bad, Broken & The Boring: Placeholder TextI always prefer when this section is more of a placeholder in our reviews, but it does keep us humble and forces me to think about things I truly didn’t like about the game. That being said? There’s honestly nothing I didn’t enjoy about Koa. I can say that it’s not a game I can play all in one sitting. I find my time limit for any platformer game is about 2 hours per session, but I always wanted to come back to Koa until I had finished it, so it’s how I know it was a good one. I give up on the Platformer genre the most out of any other genre as it frustrates me more than any other gaming experience, that being said, there wasn’t any of that for Koa. Even when I got frustrated because I was failing at a certain jump or movement combo, it was due to my own lack of ability and not the game's challenge level.Adding on from this perspective, I suppose I can say that the races against the NPCs on the main island, which get unlocked after you complete each new set of levels, are definitely what I found to be most challenging. There aren’t any checkpoints or restart portions, so if you die, you’ll have to completely restart. This, ironically, wasn’t a problem for me as I found myself able to take first in all of them within the first 5 tries, which is significantly less than it took me to complete the boss portions of Ori & the Blind Forest, so I was nowhere near my “limit” of patience either. Positives:-Engaging & Cohesive Story-Story & Gameplay Fluidity -Fun & Beautiful Visuals-Level Diversity-Speed Running Potential-Plenty to Do-Replayability-Collectibles-Great Soundtrack-Character Art-Not Overly Frustrating-Keyboard/Mouse + Controller Support-Difficulty Feels BalancedNegatives:-Not Bingeable

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay:The game is reminiscent of the classic platformers Crash Bandicoot, Super Mario 64, Sonic, Banjo-Kazooie, Psychonauts, and SpongeBob: Battle for Bikini Bottom without limited lives and Game Over screens.To join the pirate team, Koa needs to explore the islands and complete the pirate challenge.Each island contains a series of platforming trials and boss fight.These platforming segments can be completed at any rate (you don’t have to acquire a specific score to continue), but you’ll be graded based on your completion time, how much of the seashells and collectibles you managed to gather. The cartoonish animation style is lovingly crafted gives the game an incredible personality and charm that is completely endearing. Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara does its job well, even while suffering from the camera issues that 3D platformers are often known for.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought Mara day one because it was cute but was ashamed to say I never finished it. I really liked the visuals and the characters and this brings that back, while altogether being a solidly built (but easy) speedrunning platformer. The levels are designed pretty well, and the limited movement makes speedrunning a level surprisingly satisfying. I think it speaks well to the art direction that the levels referencing the original, which I haven't touched for like... 4-5 years now, still feel familiar. Also I like that unlocking different shirts changes your character portrait, that's such an unnecessary detail that most games wouldn't bother with. They sprinkle in just enough variety to stop the game from getting boring before you finish the second world, which is a thing a lot of games just don't do, and all of the side objectives are well done, even if they don't ever evolve beyond distractions.My biggest critique is I think the cutscenes for doors opening majorly break the flow and are so sudden that I think the game is crashing every time it happens. Also you can't seem to play as the other three characters even though they already have the moveset of the main character. Maybe I'm missing something there, though. I just want to play as the catgirl.I actually think this would be a good game to iterate off of, build more challenging worlds and maybe add one or two moves to the character. I would enjoy that. Also I distinctly remember Mika being in the demo of this game, I'm sad to not see her in the full release. I was hoping to unlock her or something.

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game from backing it on Kickstarter. Did not get to actually finishing the game until recently due to prior backlog. I don't know anything about the previous Mara game, but I backed this only due to it looking cute and wanting to play more platformers. The final product is pretty good. There's not much of a story as it is seems to be a last minute addition. As for the main importance of gameplay, I find it is pretty fun and responsive though I do have one major complaint. The default walk speed is too slow to do anything useful so you will always be running, and having the timed roll for speed running be on the same button as running seems very stupid considering that there are many available buttons to use. You end up getting use to it though as the button is right next to your jump to just press together. The aesthetics and music both fit its very positive, good feels environment it has going. It doesn't have anything particularly memorable in terms of music but it does its job. The stages themselves look pretty good though that and its level design do follow the generic "Worlds" game design, but it's not really an issue for the genre imo. You get ice slippery levels, hot lava level which has the Mario jump disappearing platform mechanic, and some other worlds. Koa is not a hard or long game, but has a atmosphere of lighthearted cheerfulness to just spend the night getting through. It's a pretty cheap game too looking at its current price, but if you want a chill game and have time to wait for a sale I recommend picking this up.

_childDocuments_.review: Great casual game. There's a reason I sunk 8 hours into the demo. It only featured 3 or 4 of the levels contained in the final product yet it made me completely obsessed with speedrunning. Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is designed very well and its structure (collectibles, gold medal times) should be immediately familiar to players of Mail Mole. Koa's movement however feels soooo much better, and there is a stronger cast of supporting characters as well as more polished graphics.The most enjoyable levels of Koa are without a doubt the auto-runners. Chibig/Talpa/Undercoders really know how to make those addictive. I wish there were more of them. Navigating the open sea to travel between worlds was also a nice Wind Waker-esque touch. Gameplay isn't very challenging overall (even if you're going for all gold medals) when compared with the stricter requirements of Mail Mole, but there are still a couple of levels that will test your mettle (Temple of Life, Grant Loom's Lair). Adrian Berenguer has composed a joyous, energetic soundtrack that gives Koa such a fresh vibe. It's a shame tracks are repeated in some stages as I would have loved to hear additional unique melodies. My favourites were the generic underwater themes and the one for 'Grant Loom' - tons of Monkey Island goodness in that.I'm excited to see more cute and wholesome games in the Mara universe. Mika and the Witch's Mountain looks very promising although I'm not yet sure which connections it will share. This dev team has unlocked something truly special with this formula.

_childDocuments_.review: Koa is a cute-like-heck platformer that is worth to kill some time with.Difficulty ★★★★☆☆☆☆☆☆* visuals and artstyle look nice* skins affect the look during hand-drawn cutscenes as well (devs put in some extra work)* gold speed medal times are very fair measured* controller layout was weird first, but worked out pretty well during speedrunning if mastered* hitboxes of some objects are weird* some moving platform flicker when you are standing on them* no native PS controller support* no coop / competitive multiplayer mode (for example couch-coop splitscreen) * auto-scrolling elements work against the speedrunning principles as you cannot vary your speed anymore* in some scenes you run against the screen with a fixed camera position, this is annoying* mostly very repetitive gameplay* only 8 hours of playtimeThe game does a lot of things pretty good, with minor issues I can live with. The biggest problems are the repetitive gameplay and the missing of a coop mode in my opinion. But still Koa was totally fun to play.

_childDocuments_.review: My review video: This game felt like a palate cleanser to me. I play a ton of games and enjoy them, but sometimes, it's nice to just have something that's not too long, not too hard and just wholesome throughout. That's what Koa is. If you like 3D platformers like Super Lucky's Tale, you'll recognize a lot of what this has to offer, including a bunch of collectibles to pursue as well as time trials. Getting 100% will take a decent amount of time, but if you just want to play through the story, it'll be only three to four hours.This is a non-violent platformer so there's no combat. Koa is a cheerful and happy little girl who ends up making the best of every situation and is able to turn adversaries into allies. It's one of those games that just keeps a smile on your face and never feels like a chore or a grind. It's a rare title that you could give to a young kid and they could still complete it, but it also has enough appeal for adults as well. Co-op would have been cool for parents to be able to play with their kids, but as a single player experience, it's also great.This type of "palate cleanser" game isn't something everyone wants or needs, but I appreciate the occasional one and really enjoyed my time with this. I hope it succeeds and allows these talented teams to make something bigger in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is a really good 3D platformer where you play as Koa on her quest to retake what the pirates stole from her town. While not revolutionary, it's still a fun take on the genre with solid level design, great art, and an interesting mechanic in explore islands on a boat. And while I haven't played Chibig's other games, I like how it's part of a bigger series of games.

_childDocuments_.review: A few years ago i enjoyed Summer in Mara a lot, which is a mix of casual farming sim, adventure game and visual novel. This is set in the same universe, but it's a completely different genre. Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is a 3d platformer, not too casual and not too difficult. And i liked it. I met all the characters i liked in Summer in Mara, visited a lot of the locations and had a good time doing all kinds of jump & run challenges. And for those looking for a real challenge there are lots of optional collectibles and time trial challenges in the game.Good game for Summer in Mara fans, but even without having played that before Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara is still a fun little 3d platformer. And i love the music and the atmosphere in these games, that's clearly influenced by Studio Ghibli movies.

_childDocuments_.review: Koa and the Five Pirates of Mara was a short and fun platforming adventure. Loved the colorful summer vibes. Koa as a character has such positive energy and a ret-to-go attitude; it was cute seeing how she interacted with every character in this story. The plot is very light(honestly I was skimming most of the dialog, but was till able to follow) and the music is not really anything special(I started just listening to Spotify while playing after world 3), but for what it was, I enjoyed myself. As a seasoned gamer who has been playing platformers since I was a kid this was very much on the easy side for me and I rolled credits in only 5 hours, but for what it was, Koa was a decent time. Would recommend for younger players or fans of 3D Platfomers in general.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay video: Short version: 100% recommend this game to anyone that's a fan of 3D Platformers.  Fantastic level design, wholesome experience, speedrunner's dream, and tons of unlockables.So what do you get here?  Quality levels spread over 8 different islands, great graphics, sound effects, and music.  Each island has its own theme, and every single level has a certain level of distinct quality to it that you rarely see in games today.  It's a pretty straightforward platformer with a goal of getting from the beginning of the level to the end, with the occasional trek off the beaten path to find a hidden treasure.There are boss levels, which are relatively varied and fit the setting they're in.  They aren't difficult, and really there's not much of the game that might be considered difficult.  If you do have a hard time you can always turn on a mode that gives you more checkpoints which should help you finish through the levels with no issues.Hidden treasures consist of Cloth, Plastic, Pearls, and Gears.  These unlock new outfits, backpacks, boat upgrades, and restore certain areas of the main island.  If you miss them during the first run through of a level you can always go back to collect what you've missed.As you play you'll gain maps that unlock new islands to explore, and it progresses the story very naturally.  Aside from the main islands used for gaining maps you will find additional islands that you'll find hidden treasures on - so they're worth exploring.Overall the game will probably take you around 4-5 hours to play depending on if you're attempting to find all of the unlockables.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty straight forward game and even a complete gaming noob like me can get his name on the leaderboard so perhaps you can too. Final stage is a pretty good challenge to test your mettle.Overall This game is short and fun and it has just enough action to not overstay its welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great platformer! I'd call it moderately challenging and never unfair. I was initially skeptical when I found out that there are no enemies, but other hazards keep the gameplay challenging and interesting. The difficulty curve fit me very well over the course of the game, but I'm not a hardcore gaymer anymore, so others may find it easier. The controls are very responsive, and the camera is nearly flawless—and that's a stunning feat for any 3D platformer, to be sure.I didn't enjoy many of the features outside of the platforming, meaning meaning things like cosmetic customization or upgrading the boat used for overworld travel. Fortunately the level design is good enough on its own to carry the rest of the game. In plenty of other platformers that I've tried, replaying levels to collect hidden trinkets often feels like a chore. In Five Pirates, for me it was just fun to replay and explore a bit more, even though the cosmetic rewards weren't much to write home about.I'd recommend skipping dialog whenever possible, because it is entirely nonsensical. I'm not sure that whoever wrote this game has ever met another human being. The premise of the game involves pirates ransacking the island where everyone hangs out and constantly putting the protagonist in dangerous situations, yet all dialog is exceedingly friendly. I am baffled by the complete lack of conflict in a scenario like this, and I think it's good that there is a dedicated button to skip any conversation.I played this in full on my Steam Deck. Currently there is no official word on compatibility, but the game worked just fine for me. Occasional framerate stutter and a broken intro video (that I could still play out or skip) were the only problems I experienced. With a patch, Five Pirates should be a flawless match for the Steam Deck.The cloying dialog makes me hesitant to look into the other games in the Mara universe, which aren't platformers, but the gameplay here is good and leaves me hoping for more platformers from these developers. Mail Mole, another platformer from Talpa and Undercoders, looks very similar. That may be what I check out next.
