_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately this is a big thumbs down for me. I do not have VR and this game is close to unplayable with a controller or K/M. The character moves around WAY too slow and the game gets really fiddly with your block placement on puzzles.If the game was top down 2D or maybe just swapped between a couple of views, it might work. But that's the real problem. The puzzles are super easy, you're fighting the camera and jank of the game, not using your brain power on the puzzles.Could have been an excellent game.
_childDocuments_.name: Tin Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Works on Reverb G2, except for Menu button.This is a neutral review.Tin Hearts looks and sounds amazing in VR steadily maintaining cozy atmosphere, but it's way too slow even by pretty low puzzler standards.Some of the later levels are too big for their own good: even with fast forward button it takes a lot of time for toy soldiers to march through them and even more - for player to teleport back and forth moving around the pieces. I gave up in the 3rd act after just looking at a giant room filled with 3 vertical layers of gizmos. It just felt more like a chore than fun. But, to the game's credit, it happened after 5 hour mark - most of other VR puzzles would be over by that time.
_childDocuments_.name: Tin Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful! From the details in the art to the music to the story. There is not a single thing I would change in this game. It is perfect as a puzzle game with a heartfelt story. The game progresses in difficulty at a casual pace and there is no real reason to rush through the game. It's just gorgeous and I cannot wait to play it in VR.
_childDocuments_.name: Tin Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Very endearing puzzler game. A lot of love and heart has been poured into this little gem, it's full of character and spirit, and the art style is without doubt nothing but wonderful. But what does it play like?The puzzles start easy enough but get more involved and tricky soon. One by one, you're being introduced to the many play elements to get your tiny tinners from their starting point to their goal safely. While the game mechanics are very solid, the controls can be a bit finicky at times, but they're serviceable and once you're used to them, they pose no obstacle to getting the job done. You're not being rushed anyway and can pause the relentless march of your little soldiers anytime (or even rewind time), so any misplaced element can be sorted out.What you get out of the game really depends on your expectations. Adrenaline junkies will know better than picking this up, but if you're anything like me and on occasion like to take a break from slaying monsters or sniping the enemy, this game is perfect to wind away a few minutes or hours. It's great for achievement hunters too, as there are many hidden around the levels. I'm not far into the game but already know I'm picking it up every so often and will complete it - eventually -  between more hectic gaming sessions.For the price tag, it is definitely worth it - even more so if you find it on sale. Do yourself a favour, pour yourself your favourite tipple and ponder over these puzzles!
_childDocuments_.name: Tin Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: I found this one on my discovery list one day and I have to say it's a little gem. It reminded me of the Lemmings I used to play looooots of years ago, but I think this one is better! The art is lovely, the puzzles are intuitive but will increase in difficulty and length the more you advance. I found myself repeating a level 5 times in Act 3, but once you complete that puzzle that gave you a headache is so rewarding! You can also use hints if  you need help which is a nice adition from the devs in case you're not that patient! I loved the sountrack, it's very relaxing and dind't feel repetitive at all.And the story? The story is a beautiful journey that had me playing one level after another because I wanted to know what happened in the end.I strongly recommend it, so give it some love!
_childDocuments_.name: Tin Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game I would just like to know if you can change FOV because currently I get insane motion sickness so I start sweating and feel ill.If a dev could reach out and maybe tell me if there is a config I can change?So this is a recommended for me but only if you are not sensitive to closer fov.
_childDocuments_.name: Tin Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: It's a cute little puzzle game, in the style of something like Lemmings, where you guide little toy soldiers around obstacles in a Victorian era toy maker's home. Some of the best levels so far for me have been the ones that use entire rooms in ways you can't necessarily predict when you start a level, where they open up and you have to explore options as you play them. My only major annoyance with the game is that the controls can be a bit frustrating. It sometimes feel like you have to fight both them and the camera to get blocks and other puzzle pieces correctly aligned in the world. I also don't think the tutorial section really does the game justice. I at least was initially turned off by how restrictive the controls were and how much it hindered my ability to interact with the levels. It was only after unlocking the ability to move freely that I really started to enjoy the game. I understand gradually easing players into a game and its controls, but I think the developers might have taken things a bit too far in this case.I'd suggest giving this game at least an hour and do the first 10-15 levels before deciding if this is something for you. The game only really begins to open up at that point.
_childDocuments_.name: Tin Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very nice puzzle game, while the early levels are fairly simple, once you start doing Act 2 levels, then the difficulty of the levels start to ramp up. This also tells a story, but you need to play deeper into the game, to start seeing cut scenes in the levels themselves. They are can be triggered by either getting the toy soldiers to a place, or over a letter. As for the game itself, you have to use blocks to make the toy soldiers go where you want. Some of the blocks might have a symbol, so can only be placed on a place that has the same symbol, or in some levels, a block that can be placed anyway. Also, as you progress, your ghost character can acquire new skills, like been able to interact with objects. or unlocking a box that might have extra blocks. Then on top of that, there are hidden collectables to find and kick. (on those levels, you can take control of one soldier. ) With the music, the story (which takes a while to get into) the puzzle design. If you like puzzle games, then give this gem of a game a chance.
_childDocuments_.name: Tin Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Guide squads of tin soldiers to safety through this magical toy filled world. A beautiful VR puzzle game with a heartfelt story. Are you guiding the soldiers or are they guiding you?

name: Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn
detailed_description: Digital Deluxe Edition The Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn Deluxe Edition includes the base game and three customization packs for Nor. · Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn – Noble Outfit · Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn – Champions Outfit · Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn – Vanguard Outfit About the Game From games studio A44, makers of Ashen, comes an explosive Souls-lite, where Gods and guns collide in a battle for the future of humanity. The Door to the Great Below has been opened unleashing the Gods and their armies of the Dead. The lands of Kian are besieged, the city of Dawn is on the brink of destruction. It’s time for the Coalition army to fight back. Embrace vengeance, gunpowder and magic as you embark on an epic journey to defeat the Gods, close the door and retake the world. Kill all gods. Your battle begins now. Step into the boots of Nor Vanek, an elite member of the Coalition army, joined by Enki, a mysterious fox-like companion, in their quest for vengeance against the Gods. Guided by Enki who shares his knowledge of the world with you, your combat skills and traversal capabilities will be imbued with his magical powers making you a duo to be reckoned with. Flintlock retains elements of the souls-like genre and infuses it with rapid mobility resulting in dynamic and explosive combat. Weave in melee, gunpowder and magic in rhythmic battles where combos chain together to create a deadly dance. Use Nor's gunpowder abilities to exploit verticality to your advantage and deal death from above, or quickly recover from danger. Unleashed upon the world, the vengeful Gods are on a rampage, intent on causing chaos and the downfall of mankind. Traverse the ravaged landscape of Kian, utilizing Enki's magic and portals to soar through the skies while confronting hordes of the undead. Discover new equipment, strengthen your weapons, and upgrade your gear in anticipation of the ultimate showdown against the Gods.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely not terrible, and entirely acceptable for the price, but leaves a lot to be desired. I'm a bit conflicted.It's a beautiful game with a familiar dynamic and engagement, and some good features. But it feels unrefined, a bit bland, often just a lot of empty space with sparse enemies, and occasionally clunky. This is certainly anecdotal, but I was streaming this for six hours today and was regularly asked if it was in early access. The consensus seemed to be that it looked incomplete, like a good skeleton for a game that wasn't fleshed out yet. (And, for whatever reason, the audio balancing is all out of whack. I turned down sound effects so I could hear the dialogue, but certain attacks blasted at full volume and most of the dialogue from anyone but the main character was 30% lower than it should be.)
_childDocuments_.name: Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn

_childDocuments_.review: One thing i have to point out before: I have fun with the game.But! Unfortunately i cannot recommend the game without remorse. It feels like the Developer ran out of money in the end. The audio is not balanced out (loud NPCs, quiet NPCs, no spatial sound for NPCs talking next to you) - The core systems has potential  - Movement, Fighting, SkillsystemAnd there are quite a few things that are fun to play - shooting the musket, change between ranged and close combat immediately, traversing the world.But Number 2! Overall it just feels not finished (and i´m not talking about "polished"). There are a lot of parts and mechanics in the game, where you realize that they are not implented well or were put in the game just to fill the space. _childDocuments_.review: Some reviews are really strange (not to say RIDICULOUS). How can someone review a game with 30 minutes of gameplay? How can someone say that the game won't run on their PC, when they have a PC from the 90s?At the time of this review, I've played the game for 3.5 hours and so far, I haven't had a single crash. The game has its own peculiarities and this sets it apart from other games with the same style.I'm playing in Possessed mode and I haven't had any major difficulties.Later, when I finish the game, I want to leave my final impressions.To be continued... (3 days later)Having finished the game, I'll leave my impressions...I played for 30 hours. During that time, the game performed perfectly. I had no freezes, no fps drops, no crashes, or anything that compromised my gameplay. I had a bit of difficulty with some bosses because I played in POSSESSED mode.I read some reviews where people complained about the character's movement and controls. I noticed a certain delay in the shooting command when I was in combat, but nothing that severely compromised my gameplay.I would like to emphasize once again that you should not expect smooth gameplay if you do not have a machine that is suitable for such a task. Therefore, saying that the game does not run well is untrue.One thing that bothered me a lot, and this will help anyone looking for an opinion on the game and who will play it later, is in relation to the crafting items (wood, iron, and sulfur). They are very scarce in the game and this was one of the reasons why it took me longer than usual to finish the game, as I explored every possible corner in search of these resources to upgrade my weapons and equipment.If you play for the ACHIEVEMENTS, I strongly recommend upgrading only one weapon and equipment from each class before going out and leveling everything, as there are achievements related to this, otherwise you will have difficulty obtaining the achievements.Another important tip... after the last boss and the credits, you can't return to the game, unless you load the last save point. Use this to do remaining tasks and side quests. For example, I was unable to discover a camp and complete a mission, so I used this trick to do them.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels unfinished. The store page describes it as "Souls-lite", and that's what it is - in the worst possible ways. "Lite" on the build depth and variety. "Lite" on the difficulty. "Lite" on the content and length of the damn game! I completed the main story, including all side quests, all "Enki feathers" and all shrines... in 11.6 hours. I played on normal, so maybe the hard difficulty is more of a challenge, but the big bosses were trivial. Even the final boss fell over pretty quick. And the story is nothing to speak of. Oh, and the game kept crashing for me. Thankfully the game seems to save its state before exiting, even on a crash, so I never lost any progress.Don't get me wrong, I had some fun. I wouldn't have spent 11.6 hours on it if there was no fun to be had. It's particularly satisfying to switch between melee and ranged combat relatively fluidly. Or to shoot a suspiciously-well-placed explosive barrel to clear a pack of enemies. But that fails to make up for everything the game lacks.Overall I think this game is criminally undercooked. The concept and world had decent potential, and the combat isn't terrible either, so given a few more years of development, I could see this game being pretty good. Sadly what we got was just mediocre on almost all levels. I wouldn't suggest you pay much more than $10 for it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is not terrible. It looks great and I've had no performance issues. However, I can't recommend it because the balance is simply terrible. The game can't decide whether it wants to be Assassin's Creed or a Souls game, so it veers wildly and unexpectedly between difficulties in way that I found persistently irritating. Most of the time the game is Assassin's Creed, a fun game that requires little technical gaming expertise. In Flintlock, you follow the quest marker, parkour over obstacles that are clearly marked in white or zip through rifts that give you an infinite amount of time to choose your direction. If you wander around, you find resources or hidden treasure chests. The game might be more like God of War, but the writing in Flintlock is so dull that I don't want to make the comparison. Flintlock's writing is dull like Assassin's Creed Valhalla is dull. But, from time to time and without warning, the game turns into a Souls-like game. The parkour in the Black Powder factory, for example, is not really difficult but if you haven't fallen to your death 1,000,000 times in Elden Ring to get the Thumbprint Shield, you might not be used to missing your jumps. The game does not prepare you for the first boss fight, for example, which has 3 phases and requires good parrying skills. That's not a bad thing if the rest of the game had the same vibe. But it doesn't. I loved the Parade Master fight in Lies of P, it was engaging and taught you about the game you were about to play. I don't like the swings in difficulty in Flintlock. The combat in its open world is from a different game than the boss combat. And I'm not an impatient player, it took me 2 days to learn to dodge and beat Consort Radahn, and 4 days to learn to kill the Nameless Puppet. But Flintlock doesn't inspire me to put the time in because the game, as a whole, doesn't inspire that kind of commitment. If its gameplay were more cohesive or its story more interesting, I might feel differently. Perhaps the devs will retune the game in an update.

_childDocuments_.review: I know I really haven't play much of it, but as a game marketed as a souls-like or souls-"lite" (I'm unsure what it really means by lite either), I wouldn't recommend it to people that are looking to cover the souls-like itch. This game probably a lot of fun for a lot of people, but I think it's worth pointing out why not all souls players may not enjoy this. HOWEVER! Try the game for yourself please, as I do think there are a lot of good aspects to this game, but it just doesn't click for me.The Good: - The core game mechanics are cool, it's a well thought out combat system. Gun for countering red attacks, dodging is always viable, and parrying will always be fun. - You are more mobile than most souls-likes- Ran very well- Visually looks goodThe things that turned me away personally:- The enemies feel very generic, and feels like there is no difference in the factions presented early on. This however could change with more game time.- Parrying just doesn't have the "umpf" that I would like out of a parry, and is way to easily rewarding as well. That's a personal preference, but it's worth mentioning.- Red attacks (for how punishing they are) come out way to fast. The gun is supposed to be a counter measure, but when the enemy flashes red for a half of second I'm barely even pulling the trigger yet.- Enemy placement is actually ridiculous. Each encounter I faced had 3 enemies at the same time, and the game doesn't give you the tools to really deal with that many enemies at once. Maybe it doesn't feel as bad on lower difficulties, but on an encounter to encounter basis the enemy placement feels unbalanced for the highest difficulty. It's like Dark Souls 2.

_childDocuments_.review: Not worth it at full price. Game is "OK", but not good. Combat is loose and never feels precise. Traversal is equally loose feeling like you're never sure if you're going to miss your jumps. Story is uninteresting, but who plays for that anyway. Voice acting is ok, but the audio is produced poorly, so your characters voice is loud while many NPC voices are super quiet. Performance is ok on my system, but overall the game is kinda bland and boring. Mostly trash enemies with unpolished combat. Its the kind of game that you buy on sale when you don't have anything else to play. Its the kind of game that isn't even worth trying to get good at because the combat is boring and unpolished, so you just set it to story mode and button mash through it till another better game comes along. Also, Just had a boss bug out on me. Mid fight he just started standing there in the arena motionless. Had to quit and reload. This game is cheaply made. One final annoying thing, parrying is a core mechanic which I like, but 75% of the time enemies do their unblockable attack which you can't block or parry and have to dodge. Lots of enemies do unblockables almost exclusively so it takes the fun of having a parry machanic right out of the game. Its kinda stupid. One more final thing, visually the game looks terrible in some areas, like unplayable terrible. No matter how you set the gamma control, the game looks either too dark or completely washed out or both. The game looks you set the contrast control on your system all the way down, so all the blacks look medium grey. It washes the game out visually making it super hard to see. Some areas are worse than others. Needs an immediate fix, I actually can't even play the current zone I'm in cause it looks so bad. Seriously don't buy this game till its patched and on sale for like 5 bucks. Update: After finishing the game and giving it a solid chance, I have to say that its complete crap. Most games get better as you play them, but this one just gets worse. Its a real stinker. Gameplay is comically bad. I initially said the gameplay was "ok", but now I can confidently say that its just cheap trash. I spent my whole playthrough laughing about how terrible it is.

_childDocuments_.review: After a rough start (about 20-30 minutes?) I started getting into the rhythm of this. So here's a breakdown of what I liked and what I didn't.PROS:- Movement here feels really great, with both a double jump and a blast forward that let you really blow across the landscape and makes for some solid platforming sections.- The dodge/parry system is pretty standard here, but it feels great. It's clearly riffing on Bloodborne (you parry with a gun), but it works well.- The story/writing is better than average! I liked Nor and Enki a lot, and rescuing old comrades and bringing them together is satisfying, with each character being well-written and having their own story and relationships.- Speaking of Enki, the magic system here is SUPER basic but it works. You select a type of effect (poison, for example) and while you fight, you can have Enki doing minimal damage and applying status effects. As you level up, you can give Enki a wider variety of attacks and some really nice passive abilities, too.- The level up system here is simple but really effective. There are more than enough points that you don't need to specialize in which abilities/bonuses you take, but it's almost impossible to get ALL of them in one playthrough, so you still have to pick and choose which higher level ones you build towards.- I really like the Equipment here. There are basically five 'sets' of armor. Each piece of armor offers an ability rather than defense, so if you're leaning into a gun-based build you would want a different set than you would with a magic-based build, with a bigger overall bonus for the full set. Because the selection is limited, the bonuses feel more noticeable/meaningful and could definitely affect my playstyle.Cons- The variety of enemies is SUPER limited. This includes bosses. A LOT of bosses are basically the same armored guy with slightly different strength or attack patterns. Only maybe 4-5 bosses really stand out, and none are particularly difficult.- It is not well-optimized. On the Steam Deck, it starts on the highest graphical settings. It also starts at what looks like 5 FPS. To get it to run relatively smoothly, I had to drop it to the lowest graphical settings. Once I did, I got a PRETTY stable 60FPS, but even then I had a few jittery moments.- The locales aren't as distinct as I'd like. While you're traveling across two large maps and two small ones, only the two small ones really stand out as distinct locales. The rest of the world is a pretty indistinguishable ruin.Overally, way more positive on this one than negative. I hope the team gets a chance to make a follow-up, because with slightly more polish, this could become something truly great.

_childDocuments_.review: Is Flintlock an ultra-polished triple-A GOTY? Answer no. Is Flintlock a fun double-A game that was worth the 17 hours I spent with it? Answer yes. It's super fun to play, but beyond that, simply *being* the main character Nor is a enjoyable experience. Strong attacks have a weighty, satisfying feel. Well-timed parries tear enemies apart. Magic lights up the screen with flashy visuals. That sort of thing.As a souls-LITE it strikes a good balance between providing enough challenge to keep things interesting without the punishing difficulty when you're in the mood for something lighter. Honestly there's few major problems, mostly just little things lacking depth or polish that may or may not bother you. In 2024 other games have done everything here better.Dialogue does let the team down. While the scriptwriting is mostly fine, unfortunately this is one of those games where you'll get tired listening to the same 2-3 stock lines every time you collect an item or defeat an enemy. Also volume equalization is a total mess. Some characters are too loud, others too quiet, and dialogue overall is much quieter than other sounds.

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to approach this review outside of my normal style and give you more of my raw experiences with it after reaching the end game. What honestly holds this game back besides some design choices truly is the price tag. So I would recommend this game on a deep sale. Let me go into a few details as to what worked for me and what did not. The story, while not extremely deep, was overall enjoyable. I really like the main character Nor and their Fox-like sidekick Enki. The voice work for both characters was very well done, especially Enki. The conversations and remarks were not overdone or constant but just inserted at the right moments to further the narrative along. So you play as Nor, part of the Coalition army, who has taken it upon herself to stop the Gods and their armies of dead from destroying what is left of the city of Dawn along with Enki, who has his own personal reason for helping you destroy them. Technically the game played well for me, no crashing and no bugs causing any quest progression. What stood out to me as a definite frustration was the progression system.Reputation is this game's currency but also its xp.  It is earned from not getting hit in combat, rewarded for quest completions or playing and winning hands of Sebo). With everything pulling from the same currency pool (and things are expensive) you have to choose between upgrades to this or that and cosmetics. I spent some reputation on cosmetics and I would have loved to collect them all but reputation is not earned easily. You also require crafting materials to upgrade your weapons (which is also scarce). Also in a game that is open world I would really like to understand why developers do not fill the world with interesting things to find like rare loot and currency. I want to be rewarded for my time and effort in going into areas that are off the beaten path.  There is a mini game called Sebo. Think this game’s version of Gwent but not as fun. In the beginning I played it to gain reputation. But it gets old fast. And the only reward is reputation, no special loot. And each game has two stages. You start off attacking and then defending when it is your opponent’s turn. If you fail one stage you have to start all over again. You can collect special coins you can use in the game as you progress (found at wells in the world) that mix up gameplay. Opponents you meet will vary in their difficulty as you progress. The music in this game is well done. I really enjoyed the soundtrack. But the audio… (credit to hearing George Takei’s voice). It is pretty bad at times. I heard conversations between settler npc’s long after passing them by in a hamlet. I would be entering a fight and hearing a conversation that I overheard miles back. Audio in this game is definitely a low point. But the voice work was on point. As I mentioned above Enki and Nor were voiced really well. Their conversations are full of emotion and intelligence. Enki had some interesting insights into humans as well. So shouting out a job well done to the voice actors who voiced Nor and Enki (Olive Gray & Alistair Petrie). I really liked the combat personally in this game. Parrying could be a bit rough but dodging, running, and flying through the rifts was enjoyable. It is your typical formula for a souls lite game but not as polished as say Lies of P or the Dark Souls series. The main boss fights do have multiple stages and the majority of enemies you meet in the world do get a bit repetitive and samey after a few hours but still provided a challenge for me (especially the archers in higher ground). There is a lot of platforming in this game. I have heard others say it feels off and floaty. Myself I had no real issues with double jumping or reaching longer ledges. I did not get frustrated at any point with not being able to do a jump or climb a ledge. I also enjoyed sliding down the odd spot like I was surfing then to double jump at the end to a ledge. Flying though the rifts once you unlock them is fun. Some offer a means of quick traversal out or into an area and some are for getting to secret locations to find a health shrine or chest. Visually I loved this game and it is what sucked me in to try it besides an interest in the main characters. I love the idea of fox-like God as a sidekick. Photo mode is a great addition to this game and I used it a lot to capture some great screenshots. I will share a few below. I did not care for the filters and all images are just in-game naturally how they look. The filters are nothing special or varied (your usual sepia, black and white etc.). You can choose to have frames or not, and play with the depth of field. Overall this game is an enjoyable experience with a price tag that is too steep for what it is. I recommend it on a deep sale. I did not purchase the dlc (cosmetic pack) so I cannot comment on that. However the in-game cosmetics were nice, I found some pieces I liked. I had a good time and enjoyed the story and the game’s conclusion left me on a high note. ✨

_childDocuments_.review: Not every game needs to be a masterpiece in order to be an amazing fun time. If you're looking for a entertaining action game, with some challenge and "Souls" elements, give this game a chance!I rarely write review on games, but with this one I felt compelled to do it. There's a whole discourse surrounding this game that obnubilates what's really important in video games: HAVING FUN.First of all, let's adress the elephant in the room, the "SBI thing": There's no politics in this game, there's no forced inclusion. There's nothing to hate about the game being woke or bigot. Nothing. This is a "popcorn videogame" in the best possible way. It takes itself serious enough just to avoid those Josh-Whedon-like jokes.The combat is a mix between Bloodborne/Lies of P and God of War, clearly less polished than these, but with a way better designed companion mechanics than the latter. You parry with block or gun, depending on your enemies attacks and resource management, and you're encouraged to sinchronize your attacks with Enki (the fox companion) for boosts and benefits. There's also some lite character building that emerges from armor/weapon/skills synergy.If you want to have the "Souls" experience, the hard mode is very well balanced to what veterans are used to. You can not brute force through the enemies, you will need to be strategic about combat. There is some jank here and there, particularly in the plataforming, but the movement in combat is very well polished. Progression is also well acomplished, you might have to "farm" to unlock all skills, but the gameplay changing ones are very low in the tree.Overall the game si solid fun, IMO well worth the AA price asked for it.

There are some bits that seemingly don't gel as nicely as one might hope, the setting is dope, trench warfare against the undead and some really nice locales and people that aren't standard fantasy fare absolutely rocks, but the storytelling around the setting is lacking. _childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed this game, though I can admit it is not without some flaws. As a whole the game played quite smoothly, I enjoyed the combat loop, the exploration, and the narrative. This game might not brave many new frontiers, but what it does aim to do I think it accomplishes quite well. The action felt like it was  appropriately labelled as "Souls-lite," and I quite enjoyed that approach. The best way I can sum up my thoughts is that this is the exact kind of AA game I wish there were more of.The playtime is not overly long, but it feels largely to fit smoothly with its systems of progression and exploration. I loved finding my way into each nook of the two main maps, and though I might have enjoyed one more full map to explore, the game as a whole is definitely one that does not overstay its welcome, and I am very happy to have had the experience and support the dev team. That said, I really loved most every second navigating my way through the world, noticing small side-paths, searching for secrets/collectables, and generally platforming my way around the world. That platforming also allows for subtle choices in approaching enemies, coming from above, sneaking around, picking off stragglers/snipers, etc. The combat felt enjoyable most of the time., While it is not the most varied in the moment to moment, the progression through the skill tree helped to provide new options and new perks to the mix. One big point I appreciated was that the skill tree was not simply a list of "do X% more damage when", but rather each either expanded your capabilities or added entirely new moves or powers. Having easy access to a variety of melee, ranged, and quick-shot (think Bloodborne off-hand guns) options allowed for a nice variety. Though the combat on normal difficulty never hit Souls-level trial and error, I found that to be more because of how well equipped I felt than because the game lacked difficulty. I'm sure that if you want a more punishing experience though that the higher difficulties are what you will want.I really loved the main art direction for the game, and this was one of the main aspects that pushed me to buy it on release. There were some moments of the environmental art that got me to pause and appreciate what I was looking at, and some of the boss designs are quite gorgeous to behold. That said, there are some aspects I wish they had leaned more into their more innovative designs--and oddly the bosses were one of those. The first/last boss has a very engaging look to it (imo), and while the others were still well thought out, I wish they had leaned more into the bizarre or outlandish visuals that could have been possible given that they are, indeed, gods. Your companion is both a recognizable fox-like being, but the subtleties in his design made his model really gorgeous, and the same is said for Uru. Though  individually I like the designs for the 3 other main bosses, I with that there had either been more visual variety in them, or in the mobs, that leaned more into the fanciful possibilities that the models for Enki and Uru embraced.Honestly I think this game is an enjoyable experience as long as you aren't expecting a Dark Souls or Bloodborne level challenge. It doesn't even say it's aiming for that. I took this game at its word and was grateful, as I enjoyed the entirety of my 19 hours with it.

_childDocuments_.review: What drew me in about Flintlock was the interesting duo, Nor & Enki, and its wild combat. The demo had me hooked and looking forward to more - and the final release did not disappoint! As I said, Flintlock's strongest feature, to me, is its addicting combat. It's fast-paced and dynamic. You have a gun and an axe and let's not forget, a tiny, fox thing - err, God! - with you, who can dish out some neat magic spells! I pretty much stuck to the weapons I got from the Deluxe Edition all game, upgrading them as much as I could. I shamelessly played on Story Mode and had a good time fighting my way through the hordes of the Undead. With the Undead comes my first, tiny complaint but nothing that took away from the fun. The enemy variety isn't very big, nor very versatile. But the bosses more than make up for it, in my opinion. Further, I found it a bit much that even for the weapon upgrades you had to use Reputation. Which you also need if you want to develop new skills. It would have been enough to let you upgrade the weapons via the numerous resources you find throughout the world - of which there are plenty! Something else that felt a little pointless after a while was, perhaps, the exploring since you could have a LOAD of resources but, in my case, rarely enough Reputation to upgrade anything with (since I focused more on the Skill Tree). Still, I very much enjoyed the different landscapes and level design and catapulting my way through it all via gunpowder made for fast, fun exploring indeed! What I also found refreshing was the fact that side-quests, while simple enough, all had a story to them. They gave you a better picture of the world and its inhabitants and the grim war they faced. In general, the story was put together neatly. It's nothing ground-breaking but I had a good time with it and especially the ending was, in my opinion, phenomenal! It felt a smidgen rushed but was the perfect length for a game like this. Not too drawn out and not too short, either. Flintlock gets a solid 7/10 from me and is a game I will definitely play again in the future and I would love to see more content for (NG+ and DLCs for example). Definitely recommend giving this a try!

_childDocuments_.review: The combat is so smooth! The action is fast paced and varied with the impressive amount of enemy and weapon types that feels fluid and fun! The bosses in Flintlock were, for the most part, pretty damn good! Their designs were unique and interesting, but I found that near the end the bosses felt a little too easy (I played on 'Normal'). There were a few repeat bosses but they weren't repeated enough to be a problem to me. Each boss felt fair and beatable which is always a good thing!The story of Flintlock is pretty good! while at times it can feel somewhat generic and predictable, I found myself not caring about that because Nor and Enki's relationship and banter kept me engaged. The voice acting would slightly vary in quality for the other characters, but Nor and Enki were awesome through the whole game! The other characters were interesting too and the side quests were very enjoyable! Side Quest Spoilers: The open world aspects of Flintlock were perfect for me! The world felt big enough that I could explore and get some cool armour or weapons, but it wasn't too big that I felt lost (like a lot of games have had recently). The activities around the world were fun and rewarding and I enjoyed every minute of exploring it!The performance was general pretty good (I averaged around 90 fps with max settings) but I did notice that in some areas the fps would drop significantly, but after a few seconds it would fix itself. I also noticed that the audio would sometimes be weirdly quiet in comparison the the rest of the audio but these will most likely get fixed in an update!Overall, I found Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn to be an extremely enjoyable and highly polished indie action narrative game! The game felt similar to some AAA games like God of War (2018) but still managed to feel unique and stand on it's own legs!

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my top picks for games of this year, but I will say outright, I think it's a modest but not perfect game. Firstly, I'd like to focus on the obvious aspects of the game that players immediately notice. This game features a female protagonist that is a person of color and even a supporting cast that is mostly people of color. I think that's pretty cool, considering how that is not a commodity in Western or Western-inspired (i.e., European and North American) media, which  is understandable to one extent. But perhaps to the other extent such a convention is not so understandable in the current age of these societies in which the racial/ethnic demographics and cultures are so diverse now. [This is just a fun fact, but I think the studio that created this game is in New Zealand, if I remember correctly.]Continuing, I also appreciate how the environmental settings are so drastically diverse with certain areas even appearing to be inspired by Northern African lands and containing inhabitants that resemble people actually from these places in a positive light where they are just living their daily lives. There's your dose of open-minded realistic fiction. I did find it quite amusing to hear voice acting with characters from these places having more of a New Zealander accent than perhaps an accent closer to what a person from these inspired locations might have possessed. I think that would have personally sold the character experience more for me if they did the latter, but I figured it's OK not to get TOO nit picky and just let the fiction be what it will be in this right. It may have been more cost effective for those making financial and creative decisions for the game to utilize whatever local vocal talent that was readily available for production of voice-recorded audio assets rather than try to find proper fits for all the roles. You could regard it as laziness or frugality or cultural sensitivity ("playing it safe") or even a combination of all three reasons. I think that's an opinion you'd have to make for yourself, but perhaps I'm going a bit overboard for assuming the reasoning behind anything here. Only the creators will know why they didn't make that extra effort in this situation. I recognize that I lean towards giving more of unique cultural vibe to different ethnic groups of people even if they are just fictional characters in a fictional world where there are no rules, meaning anything is possible.Furthermore, I think this game proves a unique ranged/melee/magic hybrid combat system that I have never seen before. The Prime ("Curse of Death") mechanic -- which involves filling up a secondary bar above enemy heads in order to land a guaranteed critical hit -- is definitely an interesting twist I have never experienced before. I have been told this game plays similarly to God of War: Ragnarok with its own unique twist via the Prime mechanic. I have never played the latest God of War game, but I heard good things about it. With that said, I'd dare say comparing it to God of War in that right serves as both a compliment in one way and a criticism in another way. Nonetheless, Flintlock has its own quirks within the design of its combat system.Lastly, I will say that, since you can CC chain stun enemies (including bosses) to death, I don't find this game to be very challenging, personally, but I find this game does excel at providing you with a lot of power and a variety of options to use that power within their own combat system. Additionally, I also think this game stays true to the linear design it takes you through both narratively and gameplay-wise. In conclusion, I think a culmination of all the aspects I discussed previously about the game gives Flintlock a branding that allows it to rest within its own niche. It's not a very challenging experience, but it's definitely a fun, short, and concise experience.

_childDocuments_.review: At its reduced price point I think it's fair to say that this game's a solid recommend; it's a "Souls-lite" set in a flintlock-themed fantasy world where that trusty pistol at your hip is never not useful, and never not satisfying to use. I enjoyed Flintlock, particularly for its aesthetic riches, but it can feel like a contradiction to itself at times, and in certain respects it's pretty hollow. The issue isn't so much that the game needed some time in Early Access (it's too slight for that), but that its entire design document is trying to fuse together disparate pieces that actively conflict with each other in play. I think the most damaging thing, for me (I'm primarily in it for the flintlock setting), is that the game's narrative and genre do not mesh well at all. Much of the game world is crafted to conform to the Souls-lite experience of slugging it out with enemies who are always in the same place after every reset. Souls-like principles inevitably create a timeless artificiality to their environments, which can make for a weird, haunting atmosphere, but that requires a particular type of liminal narrative (like in a FromSoft game), and Flintlock is trying to tell a story more upfront, about a civilisation desperately trying to hold off against a divine onslaught. There are soldiers, and armies, and populated towns, but all this intriguing world feels relegated to poor set dressing, especially as the story is told in a detached way that even goes as far as suggesting -- in sketched, Diablo 3-esque vignettes bridging the acts -- that character development is happening off-screen. The game can feel unaware of itself, or of obvious bridges it could make between gameplay mechanics and narrative. When Nor dies (which isn't too frequently; the game is a fun, surmountable challenge on Normal), there's a loading screen, and she respawns at the last obelisk she used. She keeps her skill progression and equipment earned in her last life, and can go back to the site of her death to recover her Reputation (a misnomer for XP currency). These mechanics aren't incorporated into the narrative, despite the fact that Nor's companion is a literal fox-god (and more besides, as the story reveals halfway through), who could easily be written as having resurrected her. I would have preferred, and I think the game would feel more natural as, a straight-up action game in the vein of a Ninja Gaiden or maybe one of the more recent God of Wars. Because it's painful how badly a unique setting like this one, together with some pretty solid voice acting from the main cast (Nor and Enki in particular), have been attached to a game that can seldom uses them well. Which is not to say there aren't virtues to the moment-to-moment play: exploration is nice and intricate, especially with the rift traversal mechanic, though a game that claims to have "rapid mobility" and allows you to reach such vertical heights really shouldn't also include roofs you slip down from as soon as touching them. Having finished the game, I'd definitely play more if there was an expansion or DLC, but it frustrates me to see a game end up so below its own potential. Even so, I still recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not bad by any stretch of the imagination.  It's actually really good.  The combat is fun and engaging.  The skill tree is one of the best I've seen in a game.  Sure it's not huge but nothing is included that feels useless.  For a AA studio the amount of enemies they put in this game is very impressive.  Nor's voice actress is fantastic.  She has a sweet, caring tone and has a sense of humor.  Enki's voice actor is also great.  I'm 10 hours in and I'm having a blast.  Good job, Devs of A44.I take back what I said about the skill tree.  It's actually a pretty good size.I've since beaten the game and I want to add a few things I didn't like. 1. The cameraIt can be annoying at times.  In my opinion, this game's camera should've taken aspects from the new God of War games.  In those games, the camera stays to your back and you choose which enemy to fight with your thumb stick.  Lock on in those games is optional but in Flintlock it's a necessity.  If you don't use the lock on Nor swings blindly.  2. The Final boss fight.  The camera is too close.  The final boss is big, so you can't even seen what it's doing because most of its body is out of frame.  Other than that, I enjoyed the fight.3.  The Ending.  It felt premature.  I've seen this complaint a lot.  It's not a bad ending but I was just expecting a little bit more.  4.  The Audio.  It needs some work.  Even after turning the music slider down to half it's way too loud during boss fights.  The background music often muffles what the characters are saying.  I wouldn't have even known they were talking if subtitles weren't on.  I was really invested in the story so not being to hear the characters talking was annoying.  I'm still happy I bought the game.  I want to make that clear.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. Combat wise, it plays a lot like modern God of War does. The parry and dodge requirements for enemy encounters does take time to "click", but it is immensely satisfying when it does. Combat is made more robust with an excellent skill tree. The three disciplines of Melee, Gun & Magic each have meaningful unlocks that overlap and synergise with eachother, adding more power and opportunities in combat. Exploration is the game's next biggest strength - Exploring is highly incentivised with the variety of impactful rewards like new armour, weapons, Maximum health upgrades, or crafting materials to improve the gear you have already unlocked. The level design is certainly souls-like inspired - with a lot of vertical platforming and fun new "magical zipline" shortcut mechanic which made traversing new and previously explored areas A LOT of fun.Performance was pretty consistent until lots of visual effects were on screen, where I would experience frame dips momentarily. I also experienced one hard crash on the final boss. While inconvenient, these issues did not impact my enjoyment of the overall experience.I think this is a solid AA game and definitely worth checking out. I think it's perfectly placed for newcomers to the soulslike / action genre, but also very enjoyable to people familiar to those games as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Aptly named soulslite that explores some new ideas. Doesn't have the polish or price of AAA games, but plenty to enjoy here. I beat the game in 15 hours on medium difficulty. To it's credit, it doesn't fit neatly into any existing boxes which is why I think people are saying it struggles with identity.CombatPlayer plays like GOW, enemies play like dark souls. Overall it works. Lots of fun weapons to use (rifles, cannons, mortars). Lots of height variations/verticality, making encounters feel quite different to other games, but introducing a lot of jank, e.g. lots of melee enemies which can be killed from height. Fighting feels visceral, impactful and the sound design is great.Instead of managing stamina or magic, you manage powder charges and Enki charges. Resource management felt good, and the gun adds a really nice dimension to gameplay. Enki felt poorly balanced:  early on he really doesn't do much, but when he can CC things he's very strong. Curses felt mostly superfluous, and Witherings (like an Ultimate) didn't really add much I feel.EnemiesDecent amount of enemy variety, but most do the same/similar things. Some cool ideas (grenade throwing enemies, exploding enemies, an enemy that can parry you) but they aren't explored much. I wish enemies broke the rules more: The ones that did really stood out.There are some clever encounter ideas: The arena fight was great, and the undead horde battles offered a solid opportunity to use heavy ordinance. I also enjoyed the "no powder" restricted battle. Enemies are placed around corners and sometimes ambush you!BossesThe game has plenty: four major bosses, a minor repeated boss, a secret boss, and lots of unique/elite regular enemies. All major bosses looked great and had creative visual designs. First major boss is particularly good in all areas, but they rest feel like they needed a difficulty boost to match the player's increased abilities. Secret boss was cool, but felt like it needed a slightly bigger arenaUnique enemy mini bosses were great and all felt quite different to fight. The teleporting one who sends wave attacks was particularly good, and actually warped onto a roof to rain attacks down on me. The stone enemy near the start of the game was perfect.I was a bit disappointed by the final boss: It had very awkward movement, and flew out of sight constantly. Dodging its attacks felt very random, I mostly just facetanked it. Phase 2 changes up some core mechanics a lot but gives you no indication as to how/why.Balance/DifficultyEarly game has a great difficulty, but once the player scales up enemies do not scale to match. Not much progression in terms of mechanics. Lategame you just ignore mechanics with powerful skills. Some enemy kits not well thought out, e.g. Early shield enemies seem designed to be parried, but throw mostly unparryable attacks.The gunshot interrupt skill is very overpowered and can be used against all enemies in the game, even the final boss. Most skills seem to be designed to allow players to ignore mechanics, as opposed to strengthening tools they enjoy using.ProgressionNew gear and equipment upgrades are few but meaningful. Instead of arbitrary stats, they offer passive abilities. Really well designed, and you don't feel like you're constantly swapping out for newer better items. Aside from the very strong Judge's hammer, there isn't a strong temptation away from the default axe and pistol.Skill tree looks slick and has an interesting layout. Skill balance is questionable, some are overpowered, others minor upgrades. Lots of Ultimates/Big attacks which can be unlocked, they're fun to use in the short term but they make the game significantly easier. Some upgrades feel essential (like gunshot interrupt and charge attack).ExplorationThe world isn't too big, but has lots of verticality and a decent amount of pickups to get. There are some areas which felt a bit empty (cities, in particular). getting around using the triangles is fun, the platforming element is a nice addition.Breaching could be a bit annoying, as the barrels look similar to others and are frustratingly hidden sometimes. Shooting the flags is an odd one: I liked looking for them, but actually landing the shot wasn't easy. They should have a lock-on point to make it simple.Given how many  decently-refined systems exist relating to exploration, there wasn't actually much of it. I got the feeling the game cut a lot of content for release.StoryI have a lot to say here, as it feels like a lot of time/effort was put into the story with this game. I don't think the story for this game necessarily needed to be great (gameplay feels like the big selling point with Flintlock)Solid effort put into cutscenes but overall the story was weak. I didn't feel like I knew (or cared about) any of the side characters. Story beats felt rushed. There's a moment where a character reveals they did something terrible: Everyone forgives them in a few minutes. There is a moment where a character laments the death of a relative, but we didn't know they were relatives, and only just met them, so we don't feel sad.Nor is poorly done, she feels like this hot-headed badass that comes in, kicks ass, and leaves. She never shows any vulnerability. There is a some dialogue where she talks about raising a bird when she was young: This is the only characterisation she gets outside of wanting to kill gods.There was never a moment where I felt like I really cared about what was going on with the world. After we kill our first god, we don't see the results of our actions. Did the world change at all because of what we did? The dialogue between Nor and Enki was nice as you explore the game. The ending was pretty good, although I wished we could see more of the impact on the world from the outside.Bugs/IssuesThere was definitely some issues with AI where enemies would stand still. Lots of jank around vertical combat encounters, but also I'm not sure how to fix that. Performance was good, but occasionally it would drop severely for a moment. There was a spot in Sybil where it tanked to almost 5fps. Final boss bugged out for me and vanished for around 30 seconds.It has bugs, but nothing that really affected my experience too much.Final Thoughts?Good game! No, it's not Elden Ring, but is by no means bad and is worth checking out. The 7/10 scores are about right. It's an interesting exploration of souls-like gameplay. I wish there were more games like this, pushing genres forward and trying new ideas. Some of the ideas work and some don't, but it's fun to see them regardless. I do think its a lot better than their previous game Ashen. The story shouldn't put you off playing. A balance pass could do wonders. Improving the difficulty of the 2nd half of the game. Power up those bosses. And re-think some early enemy kits: Start with enemies that can be parried reliably, then introduce unparryable ones. More enemies that push boundaries and break rules.

_childDocuments_.review: I came to Flintlock as a huge fan of the developer's previous game Ashen. This game is very different from that, despite both having soul-like elements in their design. Where Ashen was an open-world game with a huge focus on exploration, and coop. Flintlock is closer to the modern God of War duologies with how it designs its semi-open world areas. It has no multiplayer, and is much lighter with its souls-like elements, properly calling itself a Souls lite. Its combat is closer to an outright action game, and I am all for it. Your movement is incredibly smooth and fluid, with one of the best-feeling triple jumps I have used in an action game. I find myself trying to use it when playing other third-person games it's so natural to use. Its mixing of guns and melee is very impactful, with both allowing for fast-paced defense with parries. I am very glad they did not try to use a stamina system, as between magic and guns being restored over time and from melee hits respectively, there is little downtime in combat. The gear and skill trees give you some personalization with your playstyle, but you are far more limited than a traditional souls like. You *will* use a mix of magic melee and guns if you want to succeed. The story is not amazing, but still good and much more cinematic than the subtle storytelling of Ashen, with good performances from all the actors. Nor and her magic fox companion Enki, along with her crew of Sappers make up a good cast. With side quests for each of your camp members that will feel familiar to anyone who played Ashen. The game is short, a normal run only being around 15 hours, with my extra time coming from playing about half the game on hard and replaying it to get all achievements, as well as spending a decent amount of time on the Sabo minigame. I have seen some hate for this mini-game online. But I miss when games used to throw in a mini-game just for fun. And it's easy to ignore other than its strangely brutal achievement. I would take it over a hacking mini-game that is forced into gameplay any day.Overall Flintlock is everything I want from an AA game. Its combat could easily hold up a much larger AAA game, even if its other elements show its lower budget and the small size of its developer.I think games like this, Stellar Blade, and Black Myth: Wukong show you can take elements of souls like combat, but use them along with more traditional action systems to great effect. I highly recommend Flintlock to action game fans, and souls like fans if you know what you are getting into.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all the game plays fine with mouse and keyboard if you're used to them. You can rebind the keys too. Performance wise I have an RTX 3060 and it's pretty smooth at 60 fps and 1080p with DLSS on and set to quality. There's an ocassional stutter but nothing major. In terms of gameplay Souls-lite is pretty apt. There's grindable respawning enemies, the "soul" collection and retrieval mechanic, limited healing, but there is no stamina bar. Your ability to attack or dodge depends on timings, speed animation and recovery, not a limited, regenerating amount of moves. You can sprint as much as you want too.It's a mechanically pretty rich game. There's the basic attack, block, parry and attack interruption with your gun but all of these can develop new variants and functionalities via the skill system and can potentially interact differently with specific opponents like parry being capable of yanking shields out of opponenets' hands. Your fox god companion can perform a number of actions both passively (taunts, interruptions) and actively via spells and debuffs that need to be charged or synchronized with your attacks to work. While you do have guns you can't just shoot everyone to death because replanishing ammo requires getting into melee which is a bit immersion breaking but works well as a gameplay mechanic. Guns and melee have to work in tandem. Rifles also take time to reload and there's a "perfect reload timing" mechanic that provides bonus dmg. Naturally there's also the usual like gear, different weapons/armor, upgrades, cosmetics, consumables like grenades, etc.Personally I think the theme of the game is really cool. I like the idea of being an army engineer in a "pike & shot" type of setting. Axe, guns and explosives (and some dark magic) vs. gods, posessed and undead. There's a fair amount of verticality and you can double jump as well as dash through the air and grab onto ledges to climb. If you become proficient with the controls here, including those for rift travel, movement and exploration can be pretty stylish. Flintlock's a mid-budget game, some might call it Euro-jank. Visually it's a bit dated and voice acting is decent to good but the recording quality's iffy with characters often sounding muted or like they're not at the distance they're at. Animations are quite good, especially the various special moves and finishers though you'll probably always have a bit of a feel that things are janky. If you like Spiders games, stuff like Greedfall, and don't mind a bit of a lower production value I think Flintlock's well worth it, especially with a 40$ base price. I think ACG was a bit too harsh on the game but I'm also someone who enjoys that peculiar charm and "odor" of AA gaming. Or, you know, you can just go back to playing Elden Ring. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

_childDocuments_.review: a short but solid action game. most of the "souls" elements are pretty meaningless and I kinda wish it had been marketed as a straight action game instead. the combat is pretty rewarding with the right armour and skill setups but there's definitely not much variety in how you approach it.the big draw for me was the movement, it kinda feels like a slower, weightier version of bloody spell with a double jump and air dash plus a "grappling" dash system for its version of a souls shortcut. I wish they'd done more with the movement for boss encounters, there was really only 1 encounter that required the use of double jumping and air dashing to avoid attacks. the story had some genuinely interesting elements that kept me interested enough to keep playing, but there needed to be a more substantial introduction to the world before Nor unleashes the gods as it comes across very paper-thin. however the star of the show is certainly Enki who is a very novel interpretation of a god curious about the world they effectively serve and the consequences of that curiosity. he pairs very well with Nor and helps elevate the story and writing above what it otherwise could have been. my biggest gripe with the story is simply that there is not enough: I want more gods, more time with Enki and Nor (ESPECIALLY in the transition from Three Peaks to Wanderer's Rest) and a more detailed look into this world.one of my biggest issues is how expensive all the upgrades and skills are. I did quite a lot of exploration and ended up with only enough materials to fully upgrade 2 pieces of gear out of the possible 8 you can be using at once (2 melees, 1 pistol, 2 rifles, 2 grenades and 1 helmet) which was only possible because the equipment I fully upgraded didn't share any materials. the skills themselves are all pretty well costed (though the trees are not particularly balanced) but when you can permanently lose your primary currency for both skills AND upgrades everything is needlessly expensive and losing any significant amount of reputation is extremely punishing in a way that is not enjoyable. Comparatively, in a souls game losing your souls/runes/blood echoes does punish you but the primary cost of upgrades is in the materials you use and the currency cost is quite low, and missing out on a level or two is a very small loss of potential power.I really enjoyed my time with flintlock but a lot of small issues makes it hard for me to recommend at its full price, but at a 40-50% discount it is a solid experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good fun. I've never been a big souls-game player (although I do own Dark Souls 3), but I can say that this game's combative focus is very enjoyable. There's been plenty of uniquely different weapon types & means for upgrading equipment that makes the experience more diverse than a spam-the-attack-button simulator. The relationship between black powder (ammunition), your melee attacks, & disrupting enemy attacks, is a beautiful mechanical design that tickles me in a similar way to how card games do, & I love card games. Dodging can feel a bit inconsistent in its effectiveness, but overall is not too problematic. My only other notable mention in regards to combat would be that melee attacks feel very heavy, & as such, they are very difficult to cancel out of quickly without certain weapons that attack faster or certain upgrades to help you maneuvor. As a person who really likes to play reactively, this isn't a big problem; I only need to better pick my window to attack. But, if you're a fan of more offensive & rush-down combat, that may be hard to replicate or do effectively in this game.The story thus far has been quite engaging, & I do genuinely like the main cast of characters. When I was reading through some comments on posts of this game on a few different sites, it seemed like a lot of people were concerned or sure that the game would contain some political agenda in its writing? I didn't look into the reasoning for that all too much, but I can assure any reader that, at least to the point in which I've played, there has been no sliver of an indication of that.This game is great, & I intend to see it through to completion. The game has difficulty options if you're worried about difficulty, but I've been playing on the normal setting, & I've found the game to be rightfully challenging without being absurdly tedious or stressful. It does seem like this game has some optimization issues; I had to reel back the graphical settings a bit to keep the frame rate higher, but the game still looks good even with lowering the notches a tad. I recommend this game to anyone who finds the combat potentially interesting. And the gun-play is a lot of fun, I mean: seriously!
_childDocuments_.name: Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn

_childDocuments_.review: Im gonna keep this brief but i want to preface this by saying that i do really WANT to love this game. Its got a lot of interesting aspects and its a fresh installment into a genre that is typically very crudely made and lacking in invention.That being said, this is functionally only 2/3rds of a game. The story is rushed and crudely executed, the dialogue .... could be better. The gameplay is a little crunchy but once you get the hang of it, it can be very satisfying. The world is interesting and brimming with potential, wasted potential, but at least its there. Im just so torn because its almost a stellar game, if it had just been properly finished it might be in my top 5 games of the decade but god nothing quite like wasted potential. Im gonna say thumbs up because i want to see the studio do more (and better) and i do think there are a lot of good things happening here, but im hoping that we see some major improvements in future games.

_childDocuments_.review: Flintlock is a solid souls-like. _childDocuments_.name: Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, absolutely needed more time in the oven though, The core combat loop is really fun, you have loads of flexibility and you dont really have to worry about consumables/resource hunting since potions and ammo restock either through combat or retsing at campfires. Jumping around and bashing enemies with your axe is really fun, and the few boss fights you get are great, theyre really fun and the boss designs are sick. However, you can really tell the devs didn't have enough time to polish the game, exploring normally only reveals resources for armour upgrades which is useful, but obviously not as fun as when you get new weapons. The art and voice acting is great, and the knew what they were doing putting in a photo mode - my steam screenshots library isfull of pictures of Enki being a little goober. You can tell his animators/artist had fun. Seriously, the beastie design in this game is super fun,I love all of them. For sure the kind of game I'd get the artbook for if/when that eventually releases. Plot is simple but good, and theres some fun side-quests. The one where you go to your comrads old mansion is pretty neat! I like the little details you see too - Baz playing the banjo at camp, enki scampering around when you're idle. I can tell a lot of love was put into this. I beat the game in about 20hrs, and got most of the achievements. For sure will come back for another playthrough/finish the platinum atleast if they do some big updates over time. Random aside, but its a shame the game isn't doing that great, in the past games like this wouldn't potentially cripple the studio, and probably wouldn't've had culture war ♥♥♥♥ stirring up negativity for no reason. If the studio ever release a sequel I just know/hope it'll improve on this by a lot.I think if you've played a lot of AAA games this might not really be up your alley, but I do't play them often so it was pretty fresh. Pretty decent intro to soulslike games too, if you want to ease yourself into those mechanics + it has an easy mode.  Also, it ran fine on steam deck for me, I could get about 40fps - but I beat the game before the performance patches so its probably better now.
_childDocuments_.name: Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn

_childDocuments_.review: Very rough around some of its edges but overall very entertaining.pro:-Decent Story-Great voice acting (when you can hear it)-Interesting Combat system-Good looking environment-20 hours run time with most side quests made sure it didn't outlast its welcome-Gunpowder double jumps + dodging in mid air felt greatBosses are fair and funcon:-Sound design is terrible. Music keeps being too loud. Most of the time I cant hear the characters talk which is a shame because the actors are quite good.-Climbing while it works most of the time feels very off. Character slides sideways against platforms before latching on making it feel like you're nearly missing the jump a lot.-Too few bosses (4 I think) At least they were all good. I know people will say there are more but most games would call the others elite enemies.-Crashes once a hour or so. Most often in menus and resting places. Often you can feel it coming 5 minutes away like there's a memory leak or something. Luckily the game saves a lot.As a side note. A lot of people complain you don't get enough experience points. I didn't have this issue. I was able to upgrade my main weapon and armor and unlock almost all skills without having to grind a single time.
_childDocuments_.name: Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn

_childDocuments_.review: The combat is fairly classic souls with a small splash of Sekiro in the form of two different styles of parry. There's a mix of guns and melee that felt pretty novel, and different enough from other similar games with both like the Remnant series. There's a couple bosses that I was able to get into a nice flow with both the gun and axe parrys, and while still no where close to something like Sekiro, I did get the slightest hint of that battle flow vibe. One thing worth mentioning though, there's about 5% of enemy attacks that come out way too fast to react to. It's not egregious or frequent enough to be a huge problem, but did serve as a source of frustration a few times.The environments are well crafted if not slightly generic. One of the main locations you explore feels like it could be from literally any European style fantasy setting, slightly disappointing given the unique lore and fantasy elements present. Similarly, the enemy variety was a bit lacking/generic as well. If you're going to go fantastical and give me giant spiders and scorpions get crazy with it and give me some other interesting fantasy enemies, not just 10 various flavors of human. The gods you fight though are all unique and interesting fights, I really wish there was more of them, and that they were a more core aspect of the gameplay like in Sekiro though. Overall would recommend if you like souls-likes and have played through the more famous and well received games in the genre. It's not going to hold a candle to the greats, but if you need something new and aren't expecting a masterpiece you'll have a good time.
_childDocuments_.name: Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my time with this game, overall flawed but really fun experience. The VA work really helped sell the characters despite them being fairly underwritten imo. The art design was beautiful, the sound design had some really weird issues of voices and actions sounding really far away even though they were close to the protagonist which was odd. The gameplay itself was fun, getting a parry off and blasting an enemy in the face with a shot was really satisfying. I enjoyed the reputation system. saving up the percentage and being rewarded with how well you played with more was a really cool feature. Having limited resources to upgrade weapons and armor was something that should have been communicated to the player more effectively. The ending and overall story once again did feel really underwritten, not quite complete. Maybe there will be a dlc to flesh out more of the world overall but who knows. A recommend from me.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay for what it is though 4 hours in i'm over alot of the core open world offerings. The map is flooded with boring very "video gamey" collectibles that break any sense of immersion you might get. Going off the beaten path just to find a stack of wood or some stupid npc that wants to play the in-game board game with you feels beyond disappointing. Overall I haven't felt too rewarded for exploring. The skull/fox teleports feel out of place and an odd addition to the game. The story seems to have been written by a sixth grader for a school project. The character is as bland as they come. This being what I hoped would get me through the game is quite disappointing. I'm a huge fan of flintlock fantasy and this being such a dull entry to this genre is such a letdown. The combat is okay and has some cool mechanics to it. Def ran into more then a few odd hitbox issues with my weapon doing no damage and the enemy attack hitting me when it was miles away. That in collision issues plagued me quite too often so far. When it works though it can be rather fun! It offers enough build choice and options to deal with encounters how you see fit. Its good enough to the point where I will least attempt to finish the story.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game; I want to start with that.However, this does seem like one of those games that is 95% done and should just need some cleanup. For instance, the fighting and movement are really good, but there often seems to be an overlap between the mechanics, and it is fairly annoying. Plus, your character seems to move faster than their legs, creating this weird sliding effect. Climbing is also really off. You will jump to a ledge but will not quite clear it's like the ledge catches on your knees or sometimes your ankles, and instead of tucking your legs or rolling, you are required to watch your character almost fall to their death before they catch the ledge with their fingertips and pull themselves up. It causes a little panic attack, so often I will try to redirect and go for a more accessible ledge, and then I screw it up and miss all the opportunities to go where I want to and instead fall.Beat the game. not bad. 7/10

Enki is decent and not annoying at all. The best part of the game was the ending. (It was decent and i found it touchy)Content 4/10  the lack of variety of npcs, most of exploring feels unrewarding  all u can find is some crafting materials and from time to time some  wepons.Music 8/10 The music in this game is well done. I really enjoyed the soundtrack, specially the ending track is amazing.Audio 3/10 It is pretty bad at times. I heard conversations between settler npc’s long after passing them by in a hamlet. _childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed my experience with the game, especially the exploration. It's a souls-lite, not a souls-like so just like with roguelites it takes only some aspects of souls games. You'll find bonfires and animation priority-based attacks but it eshews stamina for more action oriented combat. World is fun to explore with many alternate paths and side stuff to find. Zooming around in the air makes backtracking not an issue if you want to go back for collectibles but be aware there's a hard ending and you can't visit the open world after beating the game. Audio's a weird one here because mixing seems weird at times and characters standing next to you can sound muffled. Music on the other hand is absolutely fantastic and I hope we get a soundtrack release on Steam in the future. It's not flawless by any means. I encountered some small bugs like enemies getting stuck, visual issues during cutscenes but nothing game breaking and I'm sure things will get patched up in the future. For the money I think it's a great buy.

_childDocuments_.review: UPD: After Beating the game. Took me 27 hours to beat the game with almost all achievements. Only some grindy stuff left. Possesed difficulty. In general, it's a 12-20 hours on normal.What can I say. A hidden little gem. Don't expect Elden ring level of quality, it's a very solid AA game.1) Combat. If you are familiar with GoW4, Evil West and a bit of souls - this is it. The game has some time to get going, after purchasing some defensive perks it clicks.2) Gear. Not so much, however the game isn't very long either. 5 sets, multiple weapons for different styles.3) Visuals. It's UE4, but enviroment is surprisingly detailed. It's not 10/10 cyberpunk married hellblade level of visuals, but very good for what it's worth.4) Gameplay loop. Classic linear experience. You move from one area to another, some side activities here and there, then boss. Shortucts included.5) Story. Nothing mindblowing, but at least you get it in a nice pace. Though, I'd love to the continuation.PS: side note for the controversy. The amount of woke lies around this game is enourmous. The game has none of it.So far so good. Combat - if you combine Evil West with souls-lite - you get this. The game is pretty solid with an interesting and rewarding mechanic in combat of being aggressive.Visuals are nothing unreal, it's fine. I'd say, it fits the game. Considering the optimisation is there (with only a minor issue) - again, it's solid.All-in-all, a fun AA game. We need more of these. Straight in my collection with Mad Max, Evil West and RoboCop.
