_childDocuments_.review: Hm... So is it a turn based tactical thing? Yes. But for these game there are a couple of really important things that this game is currently lacking (and some are pretty screwy in my opinion). 1) Cover for you and the enemy works fairly good. I propose (if you decide to buy) you use the detail panel to see how it calculates because it WILL show you like 73% chance to hit. Which typically can mean 3% to hit and 70% to grace. Yes. That *IS* a pretty silly UI thing and this stuff matters - a lot - when playing these games. 2) What does not work at ALL is the fact that after a while you realize everything on the map pretty much means nothing. You can move into and out from ANY kind of obstacle from any angle without much happening, but more so - you can actually shoot trough it all. In other words. Yes. An enemy gun can absolutely sit behind 6 blocks of houses and (magically) shoot a straight shot at you. Which is reflected in a bit of retardedness like mortars shooting OUT of houses etc. But at least the rules goes for both parties. 3) ... Which would be fine except the game *BLATANTLY* cheats by knowing where all your units are. And yes it WILL sit miles away and pound them with artillery, cannons, etc (trough a ton of stuff) because it magically knows where you are. This. ♥♥♥♥. Got. To. Stop. Yes- the system will have a sort of "reveal" when you DO use a unit to shoot, and if you do not move it after - they will get spotted and retalliated against on the enemy turn. We are not talking about this. We ARE talking blatant bad cheating AI. 4) ... speaking of retalliation. Oh joy! No matter f you have a spotter that can sus out an enemy unit there is *ABSOLUTELY NO WAY* for you to get a first shot at that unit other than with distant weapons like mortars and such. If YOU can see them (aka - a unit can spot them) - they can spot you. And guess what? Ta daa - they get first shot because they are usually on overwatch. Again - EVEN if you know they are there. The only way to close assault is to shell them, to get them demoralized and then you can run right up and torch them with a flamethrower for good fun. Heck. You can flame them twice!5) Speaking of odd retaliations and such. Your scout has snuck trough the hedgerows, and spotted an enemy mortar team! Aha you think! Time to relay the info to the sniper team that bellies closer, lines up a shot and unloads a bullet in the night. ONLY for the MORTAR team to quickly say "it came from there" and launch a MORTAR SHELL back at the snipers. Guess what. Your snipers die. In one shot. A LOT of the time. Whoever cooked up that piece of code deserves employee of the month award. 6) At least you get commandos that.... Well. Are absolutely useless because they have to get close to a car to use their anti-tank weapon which for some reason is a german grenade even if your playing as the brits. So it goes a bit like this. "Dilbert! Attack that panzer with our commando anti-tank weapon! A sock with a bit of gunpowder in it! Tally ho chaps!""Sure thing sir! Let me first run at the tank in a straight line! ♥♥♥♥! ♥♥♥♥! It is fiering on me!""Whatever you do - do NOT return fire! You are a commando! A special unit! take it on the chest like a man!""Ok - I am moving another square closer! ♥♥♥♥ IT IS FIERING AGAIN!""Well chaps. we are just one man left - but at least we are close enough to toss our socks at it now"*You have 13% chanse to hit*"Drats"It is then the enemys turn. Enjoy biting two rounds of Machine gun bullets. WHO comes up with this???7) So should you buy this? I don't know. I really want smaller teams to succeed and support devs that try to give us new options in the genere. But at the pricepoint you quickly figure out that it has a lot of nice features like skill-trees and you can buy equipment between missions etc. I love a lot of the stuff WITH the game. But.. It has some CORE shortcomings that I suspect wont be patched away, and really should NOT have made it into the game. Sort of stuff that you know are embedded deep in the entire battle thing. Being a programmer myself - I am just guessing here - but I suspect they were unable to code an AI that was good enough to navigate a map with building features and plan attacks and such. As a result they just sort of made it into a big 2D map with lots of squares that all have cover bonuses each direction but dont really adhere to angles of attack, much of lines of sights etc. Once you see past the "magic" of it and notice these things the magic quickly goes away. You are not in a town. You are sort of just playing a flat chessboard with some bonuses. Your strategy makes for very thin options compared to what it would be with a bit more adhering to structures etc. They ALMOST got there. But - they didnt. And riding on a cycle with one pedal is still sort of a ♥♥♥♥ experience. So I would say. If you love WW2, and you LOVE Xcom type games -and ARE looking for something. This is a good pick. It is a tad pricy, but I would support the devs and hope they learn. If you are short on cash - wait for a sale. It is not worth full price right now I think (and my heart bleeds to say it). And - if you get frustrated by cheating AI, stupid map events (Hey this one enemy that fired one bullet killed my 4 man team hidnig inside of a seaside bunker) type of stuff.... Then I would just avoid it and save the blood preassure. HAVING to give a thumbs up or down. I am giving a down as a warning. But - as said - it is good'ish if you LOVE the genere. Cheers!

_childDocuments_.review: I am really on the fence about this game.This game has a lot of good things and a lot of bad ones.I am a "game mechanic".  I look for the way the game works then use the game mechanics to beat it.  For instance- in the this game, snipers make better scouts then the scouts and destroy infantry and towed guns better than any other units with a cost of not being able to ID enemy units and some view distance.The good -Game play is easy to understand and very smooth.Graphics are pretty good and excel in places.  When the game goes to a self-generated cut scene, the cut scene portrays the game almost perfectly.  I just wish they weren't so short and not block the view just because the game has a bush in the way.AI is decent most of the time - single player.  Don't know about he generated scenarios.  More on the AI later.The bad is more specific than the good.One of the biggest problems is Line-Of-Sight.  For the player, it is enforced with a few glitches.  For the AI, the ground seems to be flat with the buildings sometimes there and often not.  I had to quit playing when the AI shot through two buildings (with no LOS through them shown for my unit) to hit me in the side.LOS will also get you when the AI kills your hidden units.One good thing about the LOS, you can click on the enemy unit and see their LOS - if it was working right.The Ai is rather stupid at times.  You can drop arty and dive bomb units and they never move.Easy to sucker the AI into moving by moving a unit it can kill into it's LOS then moving back.  Often the AI will move out to attack you.  Typical AIOver all, I'd give it a 7/10.Fix the LOS problem and I'd rate it 11/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Feels like a turn based Company of Heroes (the original one), sort of a WW2 X-Com.  I like it, a beer and pretzel game.  This is tactical level stuff where core units follow you through missions, but you are not penalized if they get destroyed, they show up again next mission.  Those core units improve.  You can slowly modernize your force as better units are introduced.  The points spent on upgrading units or improving your commander can be refunded with no penalty.  That means you can customize your core units and your Commander's bonuses to tailor them to the upcoming fight.  Nice.  So nothing revolutionary but a nice basic turn based war game.

_childDocuments_.review: HQ:WW2 a fairly quick-playing, lightweight war game with nice graphics. I enjoy the combat animations and the general ease of how a turn plays out. It is not a difficult game, and the challenge level isn't especially high, though my unit choices and how I utilize them could have something to do with it.There are three campaigns, each with nine actions (27 total scenarios). I played the tutorial two or three times and have completed about six scenarios in the first campaign. With around 12 hours of game time, it's taking me about an hour per scenario.The game provides you with core units—you never get an empty slot, as it always gives you a unit of some sort. If you want something else, you pay the difference in costs and switch it over.The units can gain experience and up to three new skills. If a core unit gets wiped out, the game returns it to you at full strength. I'm not sure what happens if you lose two core units. I like this choice because it negates the tendency for save scumming that some games like this are know for, and the penalty of no experience is probably a sufficient price for failure.There are 'hero' units in the game. You attach them to a unit, granting that unit new special abilities. I won't spoil anything by naming names, but it's pretty cool and a nice feature.Beyond leveling up units and attaching heroes, you can also buy skills for classes of units (e.g., infantry skills, armor skills, artillery skills). This makes it easy to focus on a style of play that you enjoy.  For those who don't like turn limits, this game does use them, but trust me, they aren't tightly arranged. I usually have about a third of my turns remaining when a scenario ends. If you don't buy trucks or half-tracks and walk everywhere, it might feel tighter, but there is all kinds of time to turtle across the map.  However, the scenario might present you with a new secondary objective that is on a much tighter timer - something like 'Stop the Germans before they destroy the port facilities' - and you are given a dozen turns to accomplish the goal.**Negatives**:Once you understand how the game works and figure out how to optimize the order of unit actions, it can feel less challenging. I think this is aimed more at entry-level war gamers, which is fine, but you should know this when making your purchasing decision.When the computer opponent has a lot of artillery, it will target a single unit until it's gone. Fair enough, that's what I do too, but it can make it difficult to keep a core unit alive.Sometimes the menus don't make a lot of sense until you play around with them. And occasionally, there's a lack of highlighting that makes it feel more like a leap of faith than it should be.**Overall**:I like HQ:WW2 - I hope they keep tweaking it and add some more units or nationalities.  It isn't going to over tax your noggin, but it still will have some tense moments that will hold your interest.

_childDocuments_.review: I always liked the polish and passion of Starni’s previous games but never liked that specific Panzer Corps style of abstraction. So with the new game having less abstraction and actual individual units, I thought I just give them the benefit of the doubt. But what can I say? I couldn't bear more than 30 minutes. This game is so much worse than I expected and it's clear that this is not a finished, full version of the game but rather Early Access. And so I’m gonna be strict. They made enough games by now, and for the first time had a renowned wargames publisher at their side, so there is no excuse that this game is such an unpolished, badly thought-out product.  1. Skirmish: I set up a game with 4 players (3 AI and me) and 2 teams. My teammates were not moving  at all. The enemy was moving sometimes, sometimes they didn't. And this was not a tactical decision on their part, they simply refused to do anything with their numerous units. Their overall tactic, however, was to just form a long line with as many vehicles as possible and shoot at me every other turn. This was on the beta branch, by the way, which already included 2 major bug fixes for the AI. 2. The game is a blurry mess. I had already disabled Motion Blur and set Post Processing Effects to a minimum. Yet the game is just blurred. And when the "action camera" sets in, the whole affair gets even blurrier! 3. Stutters and constant dips below 60 fps! And that with an RTX 4070 and a Ryzen 5600x on an SSD with 16GB Ram. Skirmish ran a bit better but the first campaign mission of the Americans was just awful. Every explosion, every transition to the action camera, every fast movement with the camera resulted in stutters. 4. Tanks have health bars! Meaning that even if your caliber can't penetrate the  enemy's front armor but is strong enough to  destroy the tank, you just have to shoot it long enough for the health bar to deplete and it will magically explode. Similarly, my Sherman apparently fires HE or even incendiary shells against other armor because with every hit there’s a bright, fiery explosion. 5. The game is a constant succession of overwatch and fire and counterfire. You walk up your troops and trigger overwatch. You fire at enemy troops and trigger counter fire. Enemy walks their troops up and triggers overwatch. Enemy fires at my troops and triggers counter fire. I get what they were trying to do but it simply doesn’t work. It’s just tedious and makes your actual actions less impactful.  6. Some sounds are clearly missing. During the Omaha Beach mission artillery hits the ground all around you, yet, magically, there is no sound. 7. The narrative is as cringe as it gets. War's a breeze and at the same time a serious affair for manly man, for sure. Now get off that beach soldier and kick some German/American/British butts! (Germans speak proper British by the way.) 8. The map is so cluttered, you can barely navigate it with your brain. They really went hard to make this game look "beautiful" but it just comes across as fake and is overall a mess. The camera navigation certainly doesn’t help. You can actually zoom out quite a bit, yet you won't get any overview because nothing stands out. 9. I guess the devs knew this, so they made spotted yet not identified enemy vehicles shine bright red like a toy car.  No, not like a toy car. It's literally a shiny toy tank. It figures that when you take out a AT gun with small arms fire, that the thing just explodes. Again, there’s a lot of magical energy in this game. 10. The UI is horrendous. Some things are way too tiny (the spreadsheet of hit chances and probabilities) while other things are way too big (unit symbols, portraits of the personnel of your vehicles??), yet gives you no relevant information. 11. Numerous other things: tanks are rotating completely in the direction they want to fire instead of just moving the turret 30 degrees; when vehicles retreat they do so by turning around instead of moving in reverse (which is odd because you can reverse most vehicles manually); the animations are too slow but you are able to skip them with a mouse click but that might be too fast, there is no middle ground. So my critique is obviously twofold. The design choices and flow and ruleset of the game simply don’t gel with me. It’s basically a turn-based , albeit with a gingerly increased degree of realism. You won’t see an MG take out a Sherman in this game but a lot of other silly stuff. Much graver though is the fact that this game is very unpolished. I am very tired of this new trend of either just skipping Early Access or rushing Early Access to 1.0 while the game is clearly not yet finished. People seem to have fun with the game and that’s great, really. I wish Starni success, still. But if the points mentioned trigger you as much as they trigger me, keep away and buy  instead. I myself just found out that  surprisingly dropped a new DLC only a few hours ago and I’m sure as hell gonna buy it together with the other latest DLC as soon as I get a refund for this one here. At the end of the day, I like wine and steak better than beer and pretzels, if you get what I'm saying.

_childDocuments_.review: Review is for mid June 2024. Long rant for broken saves not loading, now on mission 6 of American campaign. Will either have to abandon or wait until the save game issue is fixed, if it will ever be. If you like UFO enemy unknown and UFO terrors from the deep (yes I am that old) then this game is for you as it provides the same level of realism. Might as well locate it in WW3 on Mars. You command a mix of armor, artillery and infantry units with randomly programmed values - infantry squad of 5 eg. Looks like Close Combat series had a way more accurate depiction of battlefield action, but that was in the mid-late nineties. Even on harder levels it's relatively easy to play, basically send scouts up front and wipe everything out with artillery. Other people complain about inaccurate stats during engagements, cannot confirm, as the AI is very predictable and passive in nature, rarely did I lose a unit during the 6 scenarios played. To sum it up:- Ahistoric scenarios - mixing in 101 airborne and random historic battle names won't make it historic.- For purely entertaining values - units stats and sizes don't make sense.- Combat physics gave it a try, but came very short, a pile of hay has same defensive value as a brick building.- no fog of war, making scouts the most important unit of the game, together with the artillery.- Catchy scenario names - Caen, St Lo, with little background or explanation how a mixed arms unit got there to begin with.- Will grant the benefit of the doubt until the early release stage passes, for no cannot recommend.For someone that is a history buff and enjoys reading memoirs and history books from the era, a big disappointment. Honestly, I don't see how it can be fixed. That being said, played 6 scenarios, and would have plaid more if the save game wouldn't break. Cudos for trying, way more work ahead.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun and scratches a lot of those turn based strategy games itches but not without a couple of glaring issues.Balancing is my biggest issue so far as the German armored units are essentially invulnerable to most allied anti tank tools which is contrary to reality. The Sherman Firefly not being able to penetrate Tigers and Panthers was the straw that broke the camels back for me and I'm disappointed that I had finished the US campaign only to realize that the UK units were nearly identical in stats to their US variants (Firefly having the same AP value as the Hellcat and 76mm sherman conversion for example).There's also the ridiculously low AP values for artillery and air support despite the relatively high top armor values on most German vehicles (Why the ♥♥♥♥ can't the Sexton or Priest gun motor carriages pen certain tanks even though their AP value exceeds the top armor value of said tanks???).As it currently stands, there are too many immersion breaking experiences for me and so I would not recommend this game to others as a consequence. If you like arcade style turn based games though, this is definitely for you.

_childDocuments_.review: In my opinion this is Starni's best game so far. As with their other games, reconnaissance is KEY! if you don't scout properly you will get obliterated and you won't know where you got it from. Infantry scouts are great in cities. With only 1 promotion level (can't remember the name of the promotion) for extra stealth, you can get to an adjacent enemy infantry unit without being spotted, as long as you remain in the building and that unit isn't a scout.P.s. do NOT forget to remove their over-watch ability if you have some of your friendlies behind you that are exposed because when the AIs turn comes and the enemy reacts, an infantry unit might come from nearby and your scout will over-watch him exposing your position...and there is a fairly good chance your scout will not survive that fatal mistake.A recon vehicle is also great for open spaces as it scouts big areas and even if it does get spotted (keep an eye on the stealth icon on-top of the unit) you can retreat.The same applies for snipers & paratroopers.Keep paratroopers in buildings & as long as they have their 1st promotion for stealth you can creep up to an infantry scout unit & use the assault option.No need to talk about snipers....they are human artillery pieces :) & great scouts also.And finally I love that I don't have to burden my self with aeroplane units.So find your enemy before he finds you and outmanoeuvre him. That's where your tanks come to play.I only wish it did not crash on me so many times, I have sent several feedback reports. Though I have started suspecting that something might be up with my laptop as well.Awaiting more DLC's...many more :)

_childDocuments_.review: Save your money, Play Battle Academy 2.I hate to write this because Headquarters WW2 has some potential, and maybe this will eventually change, but as of now, this is not a $40 value game or a game that I could see myself putting any time into. 1. The User interface needs a lot of work. The UI design is very bulky and covers 1/3 of the screen ingame, but there are also a lot of weird scaling issues where text overflows out of text boxes. The UI makes the game feel very "indie" and not polished. 2. The camera angles and zoom are really terrible. The default zoom has you looking very closely at the game world, really just a single vehicle or two - when you attempt to zoom out, you are put into a very tight overhead view. Overall, it's just very difficult to see the map and plan what you're doing. The developers picked a very odd design decision with zoom, which I suspect is linked to performance issues, which is #3....3. The game seems very poorly optimized. There are oddly long load times, specifically the editor takes about 120+ seconds to load (even on a gaming rig) and there is some clunkyness with FPS and graphics that just makes the game feel very unpolished. 4. The editor is odd. You cannot modify terrain (hills, valleys, etc) and can only place objects and terrain types (grass, flowers, etc). The problem is that doing anything in the editor is extremely clunky. Tiles are placed in a single direction and changing them is 5 key-clicks per tile. It's very clunky and cumbersome. 5. The AI seems VERY passive - as in, not very intelligent or having the ability to do anything but sit idle. There are some players reporting that the AI in skirmish mode will not react at all (Steam forums) and it's just another "thing" that brings the game down.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good WW2 squad level tactical game. Not quite as shallow as Battle Academy, but not too mechanically heavy (for better or worse), and very similar to the Troop, but lacking that game's meticulous tank mechanics. I like that it gives you all the modifiers that are being calculated for chances to hit/kill. Also, I like how each space can have different cover values for each side of the square, and the game will display that with icons. And some squad members serve different roles and losing them can negatively impact the squad is various ways when they are killed. Oh, and building destruction.There's a few disappointments, such as an uneven UI sizing--they give you options to scale it, but some sections become way too small to read (when <100%), while others are fine, so it never feels "just right." Similarly, there's no option to adjust the size of icons that are above the units. Also, the AI isn't great, but not terrible--it could use some improvement.There is a random map generator/editor, which is great (though no Workshop support yet, sadly), but I'd very much like to see a dynamic campaign generator--linked random maps which utilize the skill/leveling system of the standard campaigns. Or at the very least, a campaign editor so we can make our own, manually. The RMG/editor is what The Troop lacks, and the dynamic campaigns is what HWW2 lacks.In some ways I like The Troop more, however there are some things I like about HWW2 more...so I think I'd have to give them a tie. If their powers could be combined, it would be amazing, haha.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, Insurmountable difficulty is not insurmountable at all, since AI is non-existent. Unless you uncover your position intentionally to lure enemies into a prepared massacre — they just sit and suffer, inciting you to value range and spotting over anything else.You can use the scout plane to uncover all enemy positions one by one via reloading, remember them, and they won't ever move, unless you expose your units nearby or they retreat. Loading is quick, which is a good thing, but difference between save and load menu is nigh, and there's no confirmation, so you have to pay extra attention not to do the opposite of what you intend.Secondly, attack rolls are pre-determined: you always get same effect of each particular unit attacking another. This renders certain attacks to be either overpowered or useless, all you need is to remember the outcome, reload, do this, don't do that, rinse and repeat. That's pretty much all the gameplay you can expect.Units skip-move to destination, spotting spot or objective if you click again, but you simply can't switch to another unit while they do, or move in formations, so don't expect to enjoy the show of animations (and I turned action camera immediately, since it breaks the grasp of the battlefield). You move units one by one only, and animations are mighty flawed. Sometimes mortar impacts land when they are shot, not when the projectile reaches target, german mortar vehicles hang when returning fire, and so forth.Feature that units movement and action pools don't overlap seems good, but frankly I don't get how they regain hidden modifier if they move to the side, and get back to their exposed location afterwards on the same turn.Reinforcement on the spot is a dumb feature. Carpet ship artillery fire looks cool, but does negligible impact. Ammo and fuel are unlimited. Good thing infantry does not expose its location if it can do no damage, but all in all it's an non-sophisticated arcade strategy.P.S.Let an old veteran tell you a story about a game called M.A.X. (Mechanized Assault and eXploration).I bet none of modern developers ever played it, and therefore they re-invent the wheel that knows no improvement...

_childDocuments_.review: Starni Games Headquarters reminds me a lot of the BBC Battle Academy games. Only in a nicer way.Turn-based battlefield tactics.Challenging.Rudimentary battlegroup management.Do you know those little model building diarams in which a scene is captured? Headquarters feels a bit like that. The battlefield is presented in extreme detail. I almost want to say lovely. Unfortunately, this is in contrast to the units' Pinochio-like animations. It seems a bit as if the developers ran out of time. This impression comes to mind when it comes to all game mechanics.I think the idea of ​​installing the individual squad members in the groups and vehicles as mechanical parts (shooter gives additional aiming accuracy, driver gives additional movement points, etc.) is great. How nice it would have been to give them characters too. Biographies, a character point system, etc.All units are granted enormously detailed perks over time. Starni Games always does that. I find it difficult to keep track. On the other hand, due to the level of difficulty, hardly any squad survives long enough to advance.The actual battle is classic, turn-based. There's nothing new here. I miss the flow. Everything is a little wooden. The cutscenes tire me out quickly and only slow me down.But even though I've criticized more than praised it, I still play for hours at a time. The fun is there and the product works.

_childDocuments_.review: Headquarters: WWII is a fantastic turn-based strategy game. Missions allow plenty of turns for completion, making it crucial to carefully plan and execute your strategy. I’ve found it immensely enjoyable, though there are a few minor adjustments I’d suggest to improve the experience.Firstly, I would introduce a system where units that are destroyed lose their accumulated experience. This way, when they’re reintroduced in subsequent missions, they would lack the veteran status they previously held. The same concept could apply to heroes, who could be permanently killed if lost in battle. This would add a layer of realism and increase the stakes during missions.Aside from these small tweaks, the game has been a lot of fun to play. While it’s not as detailed or comprehensive as Steel Division 2, it feels like a turn-based counterpart, albeit with slightly less emphasis on deep strategy and fewer units. That said, the game still rewards creative and enterprising play, and its roster of units delivers a distinctly WWII atmosphere.So far, I’ve completed the German campaign and have now moved on to the British campaign. With over 90 hours invested, I can confidently say it’s been a rewarding and engaging experience.

_childDocuments_.review: First Impressions Review:Pros:There's lots to like here. Great graphics, the textures and maps look amazing even with a grid-based system (I prefer free movement but it's fine). I LOVE pop-up numbers. Voice acting is well done, they clearly put effort into this and it shows. The best pro is they give you full unit, stat, and combat calculation detail right there in very easy to read (and suppress, as needed) pop-up windows. You want crunch? YOU GOT CRUNCH. Terrain modifiers, varying armor values for a lone unit, and the overwatch system are really fun to micro manage. Successfully setting up your turn order is very rewarding and saves unit lives, scout unit mechanics make scouting important, plus you get limited mid-battle heals and airstrikes and fun abilities. This is a turn-based strategy player's dream.It's not just for grognards, though. So far, the campaign missions are really thematic, and I expect a lot of replay value with different factions playable for each campaign. The ability to change difficulty on the fly makes this an all-comers game for sure. Stats are deep but not critical if you just wanna move tanks around and shoot stuff. There's something for everyone here. In my two hours, virtually bug-free experience, so A+ developers.Cons: Overall, the performance was not as good as I had hoped. I've got top-of-the-line graphics and processor and still seeing frame drop at times, which seems odd. AI takes a while to churn as well, sometimes up to 2 seconds per unit. Hopefully we'll get some fixes there. The camera system feels confusingly old at times; the free camera is fixed first-person (head-on-a-swivel) rather than fixed map point, which is silly, and can only be used at certain zoom levels. Not useful at all. Thankfully the core camera system is great, with zoom and rotation. The "autocam" animations are fine but they get old very, very quickly and I turned them off within the first hour. Feels bad because it seems like a lot of effort went into these, and they just slow the game way down, even with the ability to speed them up (which didn't seem to really do anythnig?). It's great that you can fast-track unit turns by double clicking to skip movement and shooting animations, but unfortunately it also skips all non-action events, like overwatch fire results. The game really needs a combat log so you can just skim what happened if you don't want to sit and watch the pop-up numbers. Sometimes combat results are confusing: you get a "grazed" result, which is 1 damage, and often your units complain about barely hitting them, but if it was it's last point of damage, it destroys the unit. Kind of a mismatch.On damage: every unit basically has 5 hit points, represented by crew. It's cool that units get weaker in effectiveness as they get more damaged, but the damage system is not very clear. Lots of percentages and numbers going into calculations, but it seems like everything has the same 5 hit points and that's all that matters. A "grazed" result is in fact 20% loss of HP--was the unit really "grazed"? Hard to tell if this is all false crunch or not, because 5 hit points for every unit is the opposite of the granular stat system the game seems to have under the hood.I'm also not convinced of the post-combat campaign system yet. Probably not a lot of army building in this game, pretty simple level up system.Minor quibbles include a tutorial that is well-written but a little hand-holdy (just let me skip quickly through stuff as needed). But it's quite comprehensive so can't complain too much. UI is solid but at times hard to find what you're looking for. Partially mitigated by nice options to modify it in minor ways.Overall, this is a fun one. I don't know that any one thing is done better than other great strategy games, but the inclusion of a combat and terrain system deeper than most games gets my two thumbs up. Definitely a 20-hour single player experience with enough options to add replayability for die-hards. Skirmish and co-op will obviously add even more time if your friends are into it. Add on the included level editor and there's so much here. I think it's worth the $40 price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I don't like square based map layout for games like these. It doesn't make much sense in terms of movement and positioning. I understand that in terms of map layout with houses, roads and whatnot it makes things easier, but there are good counter examples with hex based layout.I like that movement and action points are not linked, so you can do such maneuvers where you move out from cover, shoot, then reverse back with a tank unit.I like the system of losing different crew members has different effects to your unit. That mostly applies to tanks to be fair.Some units like the flamethrowers seem to be absolutely useless. Never used them for anything. They are slow, and have a very limited reach. So by the time you get to an enemy unit with it, they will be mowed down with machine guns.AI seems to be very stupid. Once you expose them without you giving away your position and you bomb, shell and shoot at them, they're going to sit there and just take it. They're not going to move at all. Like a chimp falling in to deep water. Sitting at the bottom waiting for the grim reaper to arrive.In campaigns there is no randomness of events. Everything is working like clockwork, so you're not going to get surprised by AI acting randomly, or certain secondary objectives coming up randomly. Everything is laid out in a given order and nothing can change that. This means that you can easily save spam and cheese the game. It also takes away any replay value. Once you finish a battle there is no reason to go back.Yes, you have skirmishes, but that's a one off battle and there is no campaign mode for it.Reinforcement is dumb, but at least it's not available every turn. Just select the unit and magically it will be full again. I don't know what crazy technology they use to teleport new crew members in to a Sherman, but hey, it works.But my biggest gripe is really that we are covering the Western Front, yet again especially D-Day.I just had enough of the damn D-Day! It was done so many times that it's just not fun anymore.There were so many battles, skirmishes on other parts of the world. Pre-war, early and late stage as well. Why can't we have those?Spanish Civil War.Poland.Winter War.Continuation War.Campaigns in the Balkans.France.The Whole Damn Eastern Front!Italian Front.Battles with Vichy France.And let's not even mention the other side of the world. Where there where countless amounts of battles on the same damn time!At this point I would take a "what-if" scenario any time of the day.For a guy who plays these games alone, it's just not fun. Gives very little content and what it gives is not that good.Maybe the multiplayer side is booming, bit for Single Player Generals it's a letdown.

_childDocuments_.review: Headquarters: World War II:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Operation Overlord was launched on June 6, 1944; to this day, it remains the largest amphibious invasion in military history. However, it was not just about the naval aspect of the operation. It was also about dropping a large contingency of soldiers behind enemy lines to secure key infrastructure points such as bridges so the Allied could liberate France and advance toward Germany. The airborne occurred first, and thousands of British soldiers were dropped behind enemy lines to take their objectives and hold them until the American forces took over the beaches and caught up with them. You are about to relive the accounts of these events from the American, British and German perspectives in Headquarters: World War II.Headquarters: World War II is a turn-based strategy game developed by Starni Games and published by Slitherine Ltd. on April 12 2024, on the Steam platform. The game consists of three campaigns, one for each force with nine missions each. The American campaign will start on the beaches of Normandy, as will the German campaign. The British campaign will be behind enemy lines. You can play a skirmish game and have an online mode. You can join the online mode through Steam or Slitherine accounts. However, you cannot enter tournaments or play via email if you log in with your Steam account. I haven't played a skirmish or an online game, so I can't comment about these modes, but I have played up to the last mission for the American campaign and two German and British missions. Before the start of each mission, you'll be at your headquarters, where you’ll have information about the upcoming mission and can access the management unit's interface. You can swap units, upgrade them or assign a hero to one of your units at the headquarters. While assigning a hero doesn't cost anything, swapping units will cost prestige points and upgrading your unites will cost skill points. When you start any of the three campaigns, you'll only have six units available, and because you have not earned any prestige or skill points yet, you won't be able to do anything before the start of the second mission of each campaign. You'll start with a combination of seven infantry and motorised units, which includes a tank and a car. From the second mission, you can attach a transport vehicle to any of your infantry, depending on how many prestige points you received at the end of your previous mission. But don't worry; prestige points will accumulate from there on. So, you'll be able to swap units easily as you progress within the campaigns. When you launch a mission, you'll have an excellent narrative introduction with a good voice-over outlaying the primary and secondary objectives. New objectives will be added in most missions as you complete the initial ones. The English narration voice-overs are great, but there is no German accent for the Nazis either in the narration or in-game voice-overs, which is a bit disappointing. The battle interface is what you would expect for a tactical, strategic game. The map is displayed at the bottom left of your screen, and you'll have access to several options, including the settings. The bottom centre of your screen will display all your units, and on the right side you’ll see the unit you currently selected. Just above that, you'll have three to four additional perks you can use during battle. These perks are artillery, flight reconnaissance, bombers, morale boost, and reinforcement. Refilling these perks will take several turns before you can re-use them. The number of turns left to complete your mission will be displayed on the top right of the screen, and the countdown will start at 40 turns.  As mentioned, I mostly played the American campaign and enjoyed all the missions, but I struggled in several of them, including the last one, which I haven't been able to beat. The German tiger tanks don't take on any damage from front shots from my tanks or artillery, and getting a bazooka unit close to these tiger tanks was quite tricky. I like the fact that you can destroy buildings and that tanks and trucks can remove destroyed vehicles from their path. In terms of actions, each unit will have a specific movement and action points. As units take on damage, their movement and action points will decrease. You can use the reinforcement perk on one unit, but it will take at least four turns to refill that perk. When you play the American campaign, you will have ongoing reinforcement. For example, new units will arrive on the beach on their first mission at every turn. But when you play the British Airborn campaign, there is no reinforcement available in the first two missions as they are behind enemy lines. I haven't played the other missions yet. I thoroughly enjoyed the tactical tank-versus-tank battles but lost many of them. I mainly tried to ensure that my tank unit, with a hero and upgraded skills, was as healthy as possible. Because if they were taking out the fight, they would be replenished but within their skills. This is the case for all infantry, vehicle and artillery units. And let me tell you, it is a pain in the bum when you lose a bazooka, sniper or tank unit when they reach their third skill level. I had one mobile artillery unit in most missions I played so far. These units have a more extensive range of attacks and can severely damage anti-tank canons, infantry, and enemy-mobilised artillery units. It is vital to keep them as far away as possible from enemy artillery units but close enough to the field of battle. If they are destroyed, it will become a struggle for the rest of the mission, and if they are too far from the action, you'll probably suffer heavy infantry and light vehicle casualties.I also like the fact that infantry units can launch an assault on enemy units that take cover in buildings. However, it would be best if you disturbed their overwatch stand before launching such an assault, especially if the unit you sent the order to has already received skill upgrades from the previous mission. You don't want to lose too many men from that unit.   Regarding issues, I encountered several crashes to the desktop, which was pretty frustrating. But the game autosaves every turn, so you can quickly reload and rejoin the fight. Everything looks great on 2560 X 1440 resolution, but I experienced constant shading issues on higher resolutions, which affected the buildings more than anything else. Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Great graphics and voice-overs+	Three campaigns with nine missions each+	Multiplayer and skirmish modes+	Accurate replica of German, British and American units+	Good difficulty progression+	Autosave after every turn+	AchievementsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	Several crashes to the desktop-	Issue with shading on resolution above 2560 X 1440-	No  trading cards as yetRelive the events that took place on June 6, 1944 from the German, British and American armies in Headquarters: World War II. An excellent tactical strategy game.7/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

There's a little watch/clock that appears on the screen with the AI is taking it's turn and I swear to god that on one of the axis campaign missions, I sat for over 20 minutes waiting for it to process the entire AI turn. My computer is not slow, this is a failure in AI programming somewhere. I'm not patient enough for that and it really turns me off from the game.I fell in love with the demo campaign mission but found that most of the full campaign missions lacking the same excitement. Mostly missions are, capture this point BUT DON'T DESTROY THE BUILDING. Repeat, and repeat. The first German mission says you can blow up the oil storage but that's the only time I've run into an objective you're actually allowed to destroy. Seems like a lack of creativity to not have more destructive objectives and just repeat the same "don't destroy building" one over and over again.A couple suggestions:+When the enemy player is making engagements it would be nice to see a couple mini thumbnails of which enemy unit is engaging which allied unit. The camera is kinda panning my units when they're getting attacked so you can see the damage but half the time I'm not sure which enemy unit is actually doing the damage.+Split out the Combat results menu into a per round log with more detailed information about the engagement like which unit it was killed by and how.

_childDocuments_.review: 6.5 out of 10.This is a fun and challenging Turn-Based Game, set in WWII. There are some quirks to it, as I am sure that you will read from the whiny posts or the entitled kids "demanding" this and that in the game. Is it perfect? No, not in the least. There are some AI issues, and the AI seemingly teleports or something weird when they suddenly appear next to your troops from time to time. Despite all of the flaws, it is a good and fun game with a ton of customization options.Is it worth $40 USD? That is for you to decide, but I say no. The entire game (all three campaigns) can be easily finished in less than 20 hours. I have finished it in 14 hours.. and I stepped away to cook a meal in between turns. I have seen some great $20 USD games that keep you going for double or triple the time.Overall, I can recommend the game with no regrets... but I would wait until it is on sale. $2/hr for a game is extremely excessive and should not be the norm.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought because I like tactical games and WW2 and this looked interesting. Started playing a skirmish just to see how it was. 90 minutes flew by as I was cursing the enemy tanks and cackling in self-satisfaction as I managed to take the enemy artillery from the back after a long march. This is fun.  Recommended if you like turn-based war games; many units, lots of customization, a random map generator and a nice editor, three campaigns. Eager to play more of this.UPDATE: Having played for more than 12  hours I can confirm my initial positive impression, this is a must-have for fans of WW2 turn-based games. Flaws? I tried multiplayer thrice, and thrice it eventually froze. You can't save MP matches, so that's rather frustrating. Hope they work on that. Single-player is strongly recommended though. A pet peeve is that the campaign missions automatically end when you complete the primary objectives, cutting you off from the secondary objectives and their rewards. Sometimes you do not have complete control over when you complete the primary objectives, so that's annoying.For example one British mission ends when you destroy 12 German units. I deliberately did not push forward when I was close to the end so I had time to crawl to a nearby building and complete a secondary objective, but enemy units kept swarming me and triggering my tanks' overwatch and dying, so the victory message was greeted by my loud cursing as I was inches away from completing the secondary goals too. I am not a completist, "must get every achievement" guy, but I did find it irksome.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo of Headquarters: WWII at Nextfest and wasn't really feeling it during the tutorial because the mechanics felt a bit clunky and rigid. But after the first few very positive reviews here I am glad I gave the game another shot. Played a few missions of the American campaign so far and the translation of historical WW2 combat to this turn based systems works really well. Scouting and covering fire is extremely important and if you just blindly run forward you will have a bad time. That being said the AI itself is not very aggressive in normal difficulty which strikes a nice balance for me. Between missions you can upgrade your units and change your composition and unlock new "commander abilities". There is quite a bit of build variety here and overall this would probably help with replayability. Even if a soldier or vehicle gets destroyed in combat, they get replaced after after every mission while keeping their experience, I personally loved this small change because it stops you from reloading every time you lose a unit like in XCOM because otherwise you would just run into the more difficult missions with fresh troops. And when you unlock new unit types during the campaign, you can swap them with existing ones and also keep the experience. It might not be "realistic" but it allows you to experiment with unit composition. During missions you also get one-off units to play with which is a cool feature to test other kind of troops. Long story short, great little WW2 game.

_childDocuments_.review: I like HQ WWII a lot, it has some initial quirks and kinks, though I'm hoping in due time these are ironed out.+ Great infantry, some of the best of I've seen in this type of game.+ Good mix of units, for each side, 25 in total for each army, US, UK and Germany so 75 units overall.+ Map editor-maker, very simple, easy to use, I can create a custom map and be playing on it in minutes.+ Ability to custom your units, camo, insignia, etc., are nice, a bit basic though still cool.+ TBS is a nice change for WW2 game. - AI is essentially brain dead at the moment.- Graphics are too sharp, need an ability to change it some. - Unit colors, on the units, very unnecessary, IMO, takes away the immersion. - FMV of unit actions are cool, though they often hang, you can unstick by crl-alt-del, and come right back to the game, though it's happened on several occasions.- A little overly simple at the moment, this is mostly due to the AI, IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: An enjoyable game. If you liked the old Panzer General series or similar games, you fit right in.The game currently has 3 campaigns, each having 9 scenarios. You can play the German, British and American forces. No doubt more campaigns will be added in the future (or so I hope).Every scenario starts at the army management screen with the objectives and a map. Here you can manage your army, which consists of 8 (later 9) core units, which will always return to your roster even if they are destroyed in battle. You can freely exchange these units for others, whatever you will need for the scenario. If you replace a unit, they keep their accumulated experience so that is a great feature.The units can be renamed and camo customisation is also a thing. You get, during a campaign, officers which you can attach to certain units. Furthermore, you earn medals in the scenarios for whichyou receive officer points which you can use to upgrade three types of units (armour, infantry and artillery).The scenarios are all based on real-life events and during a scenrio, usually there will be additional objectives which will pop up while playing , and can cause your well laid out plans needing a revision.Units have overwatch and a certain amount of attacks each turn and artillery can freely move and still shoot, if you have the movement available. Each unit has a certain amount of soldiers which makes up the hitpoints. Losing hitpoints impairs your unit. For instance, a tank is hit and its driver and gunner are killed (-2 HP). The unit now moves slower and loses one attack. To heal the units you can use HQ commands which are on cooldowns. These commands also give you the option to use recon planes and bombing runs. Morale is also a thing and when a unit is hit too many times, it will break and flee. This also can be negated by HQ commands.The unit graphics are detailed, and look extra great when the small cutscenes trigger when a unit attacks or kills. The title screen changes with every campaign you are playing, which is a nice feature also. Soldiers and vehicles are well detailed and you can instantly recognise the different tank units on the battlefield.There is a scenario editor and skirmish mode. Multiplayer is max 4 players and you can either use a Slitherine account (for the soon to be released leaderboards), or just use Steam for multiplayer maps. There are only  a few skirmish maps, but hopefully that will change.A bit of a hidden gem, well worth buying and playing. I am having a blast personally.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid WW2 strategy game that is both historically accurate and fun to play. Set during the Normandy campaign of 1944 it allows you to play campaigns for the British, US and Germany. I only play WW2 strategy if British and Commonwealth forces are included as I disagree with the false rewriting of WW2 seen in so many games these days that point to once the Americans arrived in Europe they did everything whilst the Brits stayed at home with their feet up drinking tea! I'm currently playing the British campaign and the missions follow what really happened historically very well. The graphics are good and it's challenging on higher difficulty settings, but the enemy is not OP like in some games of this genre. There are many difficulty settings and this can be adjusted between scenarios. There is a wide range of troop and equipment types and the devs have obviously done their homework on this.  There is a skirmish mode as well as the campaigns. The voice acting is good and sets the scene in the time period well. I like the mechanics of this game a lot and there are some features not seen before in turn based strategy games. All in all its a very competent game and I sincerely hope the devs add further campaigns .

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game but extremely sparse campaign. There is about 30 missions, 10 for the USA, UK, and Germany. According to a devlog I read, actually add more single player content to the game seems to be their lowest priority and it could either be paid DLC or free expansions.Now that I'm writing this I've come to the opinion this game is way overpriced if you're only in it for a single player offering. Not only is there little content, there is absolutely no replay value and the way missions are formatted often create situations where enemies will just spawn in front of you. Today I was playing a USA mission and several German tanks just spawned in a field all facing my exhausted troops halfway through my turn and I had nothing available to even survive the next turn so I quit because they could just return fire if I attacked and overwatch if I retreated. I think the devs consistently expect me to have made less progress than I have when I finally reach an objective and if they're reading this I would suggest not putting enemy spawn points in the middle of open fields and instead next to bases or the edge of the map. Not that they always teleport enemies on top of you, but if you played the tenth German Mission you will understand just how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ insane and unreasonable the situation can get because you didn't do the bare minimum.Last 2 complaints are there doesn't seem to be a way to arrange your deployment before you begin a mission and they added a functional anti air system that's never used by you.You can change the composition but I consistently end up with my recon units at the back of the column which forces to painstakingly reorganise a traffic jam or drive my armor into ambushes.There are anti air units and sometimes the game even gives you some as auxiliaries and not once have I seen an enemy plane in this game. They're still useful for shooting infantry but they'll never serve their primary purpose as far as I've seen. Also why bother not revealing the location or artillery or anti-air when they shoot if you can physically see where the shells are coming from on the map?So basically it's fun, especially when you're playing flawlessly, but it's not worth the full asking price currently and it doesn't look it will be anytime soon in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: some quick corrections on grammar and the response from the developer being acknowledged. Added a few extra thoughts to help with my reasons for the verdict.I feel like the initial wave of reviews are disingenuous. Perhaps some of them are legitimate, perhaps some of them are generated by the publisher/developer. Who knows.What I can say is the following from within an hour of play upon initial release:- Graphics feel dated and very archaic. It detracts from the ability to draw attention to important details, making unit/terrain/game information and actions murky at best when it comes to dissecting tactical options. I've seen better from games older than a decade ago. I do not like the UI, the units and animations seem extremely dated or just outright lazy. If anyone is familiar with Nintendo games like Fire Emblem or Advance Wars, you would probably find the animations or display of info much more engaging and interesting (hint: 20 year old games hold up better).- Gameplay is hard to grasp from the get-go, especially with the aforementioned issues. I started the game on the first campaign mission with US but did not notice any sort of dedicated tutorial (it appears the developer pointed out you need to find it under "load game" which is a weird spot to place it, cannot confirm since I have already refunded the game). The first mission feels like an attempt at a tutorial... of sorts... but it does not explain key gameplay fundamentals which made me a bit frustrated with the unintended effects of my choices from the very first turn. I restarted the first mission a few times as a means of compensating any errors and trying to learn from them. Unfortunately, the game fails to help you understand the game's rules or implications of your movements -- WHICH IS CONTRADICTORY TO MANY REVIEWS LEFT HERE THUS FAR. Yes, I know with time you could get the hang of the game but this is a legitimate critique of making a game accessible for all audiences.- The sound quality is "meh" at best. I have seen better samples of sound quality in Company of Heroes (any of them), XCOM, or most FPS/strategy games (WW2 or otherwise).- Quite frankly, I had high hopes seeing a WW2 turn-based strategy game coming out this year. Unfortunately, all of my expectations fell short of the end-product that is available. Many other titles out there, whether they be simpler or more ambitious with complexity, are worth your interest over this. I am a huge fan of 4X, turn-based or real-time strategy games no matter the scale or flavour; at the very least, take this from a seasoned fan of the genre that you should see some genuine reviews with recorded gameplay to verify before purchasing.Conclusion: Please hold off on this purchase until this game and its developers show better promise.

_childDocuments_.review: It's times like this I really wish Steam had a Mixed review option, because I don't think it's a bad game at all. I quite enjoy it a lot, as it's a different take on what most Lego games do. I'm just gonna get some stuff out of the way so you can know what you're getting since it doesn't tell you on the steam page or the trailers.First off, not every franchise gets an equal amount of treatment, and I think it's disingenuous how they label all of these "hand crafted worlds." You get access to a hub world that not only gets bigger as you progress, but the hub world is unique to you and your save file depending on which worlds you want to go to in what order. It's a really cool idea, and brings a bit of varied gameplay, making sure your playthrough is unique. The biggest problem with this however is that there are actually only 7 worlds to play through, which are:Jurassic WorldScott Pilgrim VS. The WorldThe Umbrella AcademyMasters Of The UniverseHot FuzzThe Thingand Battlestar GalacticaEach world consists of 5 unique levels that cater to the style of that franchise, and imo they do a really good job of capturing the essence of each one. The Thing makes it feel like you're playing a horror game, Battlestar Galactica feels like a third person shooter, and Scott Pilgrim is just you playing through the movie with a lot of easter eggs and nods to specific things. (My favorite part was when you had to melee kill a guy when you needed a password, which happens in the movie) Some levels are definitely harder than others, and although order doesn't truly matter, if I would have known how easy (and costly) it is to die, I might have chosen my worlds in a different order. Each world has a unique unlockable that can be used in other worlds, and some vary in use tremendously. I'm not gonna get into spoilers, but with some worlds being so combat focused, some unlocks are better early than others, but you can still manage.Now, with there being only 7 worlds to choose from, how do all the other "worlds" come into play?Well, every world I haven't mentioned has either a single level or no level at all. Characters like Megaman and Megan are unlocked by completing multiple puzzles and challenges throughout all 7 main worlds. Once done, you have the character unlocked and you can play as them when replaying missions. Other franchises get a bit better treatment by giving you a single level to explore a bit. Once finished, you usually unlock a character, which is alright, but it's frustrating that this system isn't explained anywhere in the promotional material. In the Steam Page, is says:"Play with some of your favorite characters from across TV, movies, games, and comics, and explore handcrafted worlds inspired by Jurassic World, Back to the Future, JAWS, The Thing, Chucky, Battlestar Galactica, Hot Fuzz, The Umbrella Academy, Five Nights at Freddy’s, Masters of the Universe, Invincible, and many more!"Only 6 of the 7 main worlds for the hub worlds are in the description, and they aren't even the first ones mentioned, and you won't be able to access a lot of these worlds until you usually finish the first level of each hub world franchise. People who have watched the first trailer 1010 Games put on Steam would probably think that Back To The Future and Invincible are important in the game, but they aren't. They give you no indication at how long it will actually take to unlock all the characters they showcase in the first 30 seconds of the trailer, which I imagine would bum some people out if their favorite franchise was given as little treatment as something like Megaman or Chucky. Something that adds a final straw to it is that the characters aren't THAT different from eachother. The game plays very much like a Lego game, in that most characters have the same moveset and there are a handfull of characters that have a unique ability that you'll have to use, but the variation of characterization just isn't there. Characters have different firing speeds, movement speeds, charged melee attacks, and a few have unique abilities other than a dodge roll.I'll be honest, it has plenty of issues when it comes to bugs, some people are claiming they are losing their save files with updates, not having an option to change the cut scene volume kinda sucks, the hub world can get annoying to traverse the more worlds you unlock, and the actual character variation feels very much like Lego but worse. I wouldn't recommend this game to many people, especially at the price tag it's selling for. The price you're paying is strictly for the ips and that's really it. At the same time, however, I really enjoy the game. I enjoy seeing all these characters I know and love being together, I enjoy using Megaman to fight through the Scott Pilgrim Movie (even though the character you chose never gets put into cut scenes, which kinda makes sense, but it would be funny to have them replace one character). I enjoy the simplicity of it on a base level but the varied gameplay of each world. No matter what, I think this game is a little gem to keep in case you want to see a cool proof of concept, but really nothing else. Get the game if it ever goes on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure: I actually bought this game and refunded it at first, because I really disliked it.  But then I reconsidered it, gave it another shot, and played it to 100%.  So here are my thoughts.It is not a perfect game, but it has some pretty fun combat, a mixed bag of puzzles, and some really great IPs (particularly if you are an Edgar Wright fan).  Some of the puzzles can be tedious, most of the boss fights are pretty fun, and I think the comedic bits hit pretty well.The IPs are great, at least to me, but your mileage may vary.  If you are not into the IPs that are featured in the game, then you will probably not like the game.  The characters and settings are 100% the draw of the game -- as it stands, I don't see anyone playing Funko Fusion solely for the gameplay.Some of the puzzles are genuinely clever.  There are a fixed number of printable gadgets and character powers that you can use to solve the puzzles, but they mix and match them enough that solving some of the puzzles can be a challenge.The visuals are fantastic -- if you like the Funko Pop! aesthetic, you will love the visuals.There's a lot to collect -- between the cameo characters and the weapons, there's a nice variety of stuff to grab on the levels.  It would be nice if some of the variants were also collectible rather than purchase-able, but there's still a decent range of stuff to grab.Some of the boss fights are pretty great.  Not the Eddy battles, which tend to be pretty tedious, but the mini-boss fights on the Scott Pilgrim level can be pretty great, or the mini-boss fights in the MOTU levels.  The minion combat is OK.  Not great, just okay.  The gameplay is focused on shooting, as shooting is, without exception, better than melee, and you generally only resort to melee when your shooty weapon has to be reloaded.  Some of the characters have better shooty weapons than others, and some characters have a shield (useless) versus a dodge, and that defines your choice of character.  There's really no situationality to the combat.The Eddy battles are...fine.  There are some high points (the Battlestar Galactica Eddy battle is pretty good), but most of them resort to blasting stuff off of Eddy until you can summon a giant boss friend to finish the battle.  Sometimes, there are minions to deal with, but the battles are generally pretty blah.Some of the puzzles are just...fine.  Kind of one-note.  For example, every level has a "race to pull four switches before time runs out" puzzle.  They are occasionally interesting, but these puzzles are usually just a thing to do.  Like, every level has one of those, a combat challenge (which is not very challenging), and a collectibles challenge.  So that's three of seven puzzles that are exactly the same on every level.The collectible weapons are...meh.  They generally don't feel significantly better than your default shooty (depending on which character you are playing).  It would be cool if you could use the printable weapons to shore up the weak points in your selected character's fighting style, but the frequency of character switching and the lack of real pros and cons between characters discourage this.There are definitely some bugs.  Like, a couple of puzzles that can't be solved without doing some weird, glitchy stuff bugs.  And I experienced some really weird lighting bugs where, for some of the levels, I needed to mess around with my video settings in order for the entire level to not be pitch black.Some of the puzzles just suck.  Like, every level has a chest to unlock where you need to collect anywhere between 5 and 10 blinky things on the map.  These blinkies range from enormous and obvious to tiny.  So a lot of play time is spent running around the maps looking in every nook and cranny for some a tiny funko pop that may or may not be blinking.  That definitely gets old quick.  There is also a "hunt the timed, random minion" type of puzzle that is just kind of repetitive and frustrating -- I feel like those would be better as a specifically coded minion so that it doesn't spawn, say, behind a door that you can't open until a fair ways into the level.There's no keybind customization built in, and the default keymap sucks for mouse and keyboard.  I installed a keyboard re-mapper application to reconfigure my keys to something sane, and I was much happier with the game after doing so.  The game is, at its heart, a shooter, so playing with a controller feels typing with boxing gloves on. I assume they'll add keyboard customization at some point, because it's egregious that it's not in there.

_childDocuments_.review: Who is this game for: 13+ year old's to pretty much anyone interested in the main story franchises (Jurassic World, The Umbrella Academy, The Thing, Masters of the Universe, Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, Hot Fuzz & Battlestar Galactica).Who is this game not for: Children (parents should stick to the LEGO games, Funko Fusion can be genuinely hard at times, both in terms of difficulty and things not always being obvious). The game is not for those who have no interest in several of the main story franchises above (other franchises in the game are present to a much lesser extent).Pros: This game made me watch The Thing for the first time and finish watching The Umbrella Academy, which I had previously abandoned watching. It also made me re-watch other content prior to playing it in the game, which really added to the experience, seeing how well 10:10 Games took scenes and re-created them in video game form. I am not that familiar with Masters of the Universe or Battlestar Galactica, though still found this content enjoyable enough to play.If you really like games that are heavy on collecting like the LEGO games, you should enjoy Funko Fusion. The licensed music for some of the franchises is really catchy and you don't need to be big on collecting Pop Vinyl's to enjoy the game.Cons: The game is not yet 100% bug free, though is definitely playable and 10:10 Games does seem to be making a genuine effort with updates. Some parts of the game are almost too hard (at least compared to what casual gamers may expect), though patches have already been released to better balance things. Purchasing real Pop Vinyl's to get Funko Fusion characters in the game is a thing, though this thankfully appears to be limited to variants of characters, you don't feel like you are missing out too much if you want to avoid this.Pay full price or wait for a sale? I have personally gotten my value out of the game, having paid close to full price. I have played just over 28 hours at the time of writing this review (taking my time, trying to find as much as I can), with 1 and a half of the main franchises left. I have barely touched the cameo content (other franchises) in the game yet. I however wouldn't blame people for waiting for a sale/for more of the bugs to be ironed out.In summary, the game is not perfect, though I think some of the industry reviews were a bit on the harsh side. Give the demo a play and make up your own mind (keep in mind that the progress does not carry over to the full game). I don't regret picking up the game at launch and am excited to see what the future holds for the game and Funko video games in general.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5)I wasn't sure what to expect from Funko Fusion, but it turned out to be a surprisingly fun and quirky game! If you’re a fan of Funko Pops or enjoy light-hearted action-adventure games, this is a cool little title worth checking out.The gameplay is simple but really enjoyable. You run through different levels based on popular franchises (Back to the Future, Jurassic World, etc.), smashing enemies, solving puzzles, and collecting studs (yes, like a LEGO game). The levels are well-designed with a nice mix of platforming, combat, and exploration. There's a good amount of variety and some cool Easter eggs for fans of the franchises.The highlight of the game is definitely the roster of characters. You can play as iconic Funko Pop versions of famous characters from all kinds of movies and TV shows. Each character has their own unique abilities that help you solve puzzles and progress through the game. It's always exciting to unlock a new character and see how they play, and the fact that they're all Funko-ified adds an extra layer of charm.For achievement hunters, there’s a solid selection here. Some are straightforward (like completing levels or unlocking characters), while others require a bit more work, like finding all hidden collectibles or completing certain challenges in the game. It definitely keeps you engaged and adds replayability, especially if you’re a completionist.Graphically, it’s not pushing the boundaries, but it’s exactly what you’d expect from a Funko game: bright, colorful, and super cute. The environments are cartoonish and stylized, which fits perfectly with the Funko aesthetic. The character models are awesome, and it’s fun to see your favorite heroes and villains as little Funko figures.Overall, Funko Fusion is a fun and lighthearted game that’s perfect for casual players or fans of the Funko brand. It’s not a super challenging or deep game, but it’s full of charm, humor, and a sense of nostalgia for pop culture fans. It’s worth picking up, especially if you’re into collecting achievements or just want a game that’s easy to jump into.Would recommend if you’re looking for a fun, laid-back experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has such massive potential but I cannot recommend Funko Fusion at this time.I love these developers, I love their work. And clearly, this game has a lot of passion and heart behind it, made by diehard fans of both well-known and more niche pop culture IPs. I find myself remembering my disappointment of the Lego Skywalker Saga. What I wanted out of that game was a classic TT Games experience: good linear fun with a buddy, all completely unique characters that are encouraged to be used again for different levels than their own, references to the source material that is both faithful and includes that TT charm. The Skywalker Saga was not a bad game by any means, however, it made many questionable decisions that took me out of the whole experience even before Episode 3 rolled around (I only completed Episodes 1+2 fully). The game introduced character classes with very slight diffences in characters (mainly all of them shared the same passives and equipment depending on the class), and the game became a fully open world collect fest with meaningless collectibles that don't contribute to the overall goal for me: obtaining every character and vehicle in the game. There were some that did this, but the overall pace of the game felt like one big fetch quest without meaning. That is why when I first heard about this concept, a game like the old Lego games but in Funko format that included franchises like The Thing, Hot Fuzz, Shaun of the Dead, and Scott Pilgrim, I was already sold. Those are arguably some of my favourite films of all time and being able to experience them in a TT-esc format was a dream come true for me. Then the game came out...While not all bad, this game feels more align with an early access model rather than a full priced product. I also would like to add that in terms of content offered, the way the game functions, and the objective types, this game should at least be half its price. Right off the bat I've had 3 game breaking crashes in the span of less than two hours of game time, two of which completely reset progress on levels (one of which reset progress on the final level against the last boss in Hot Fuzz). Paying this price to receive crashes like this is not acceptable for me. I understand the team intends to work on the game further with coop implementations and more expansions, however, releasing a game in this state just doesn't sit right with me. I would also like to add that so far (although I've heard this is a common criticism across worlds), the bosses are not great. They mainly consist of "fight this kaiju version of a possessed character in the franchise, collect ooze from that character by shooting them, use it to summon a kaiju version of your helper, then shoot the boss while the two kajius duke it out". That's it. I believe most bosses follow this format which is so disappointing to me. You use to have such creative boss fights like the complete saga anakin vs obi wan mustafar fight (which saw one player vs another player in combat), the maul fight in naboo, and grievous fight, and so on. Those are just lego star wars bosses off the top of my head, but TT has made several bosses from all their past lego games that have been unique, with different mechanics that require you to think for a second. The bosses here are very rinse and repeat, enemy types as well. However, like I said, not all is bad here.For one, I loveee how authentic the whole experience is. The sets are jam packed full of references, music from the movies, little niche jokes that hardcore fans would get, and finally unique characters to select from the films that have unique traits. Nicholas Angel has his duel wield pistols from the final confrontation of Hot Fuzz and can roll slightly better than Danny Butterman, Doris Thatcher has a button that toggles a riot shield she used from the last battle, and Tony Fisher always makes comments during crime scene analysis about "what he said". Details like these are small but make diehard Edgar Wright fans like me smile with joy. It's wonderful, and being able to experience these levels in a "Lego" style is absolutely amazing. I've only just begun gushing but they really did a great job of separating each character uniquely, introducing unique mechanics for combat and puzzle solving, and so much more.That's why I'm 50/50 on this one. I like a lot about it, but with the current enemy variety, boss variety, and state of the game with god awful bugs that completely delete progress, I would say wait for a sale. Unfortunately, I'll be refunding this one, you should not pay (at least for the steam version of the game) this kind of price to receive a game that barely functions properly. Once they fix the game and bring the price down slightly, I'll be getting that again and changing it to a positive review.
