_childDocuments_.review: Let me just clarify by saying: I DO NOT agree with the things that the Funko company itself are doing. I don't support their business practises, I don't support NFTs, and I just really hate FunkoPops as a whole, as I see them as the pinnacle of utterly useless and worthless merch.Buuut... I very surprisingly enjoyed Funko Fusion.Being created by the same developers who brought us the LEGO games, I was shocked at just how well the LEGO game formula translated into a world without plastic bricks. As someone who LOVES the LEGO games so much, it was a welcome style for me to get right into.I have only completed two campaigns so far (The Thing and Hot Fuzz), but I was impressed with what I saw and played... Kinda?First, let's fast forward a bit and talk about the bad. I'm gonna list them for your reading pleasure.- The extra lives system is incredibly stupid, especially since LEGO games were designed to be accessible to everyone of any gaming skill level.- The character rosters for each IP are lacking quite a bit. For example, despite Freddy and Foxy being playable, you can't play as Chica and Bonnie. Or despite Doc Brown and Marty McFly being playable, you can't play as Biff or Jennifer.- Enemies need to be nerfed, badly. One too many times I've encountered enemies spawning endlessly or enemies getting cheap hits off of me.- Boss fights need serious work. You are barely given hints on how to damage bosses, but only sometimes... I got stuck on The Thing's final boss fight for an hour due to how I was given no hints on where to hit.- Bugs, glitches, the usual suspects. This game suffers from poor optimisation too. My PC is just slightly under the recommended specs, but even on low settings the game struggles to maintain a decent framerate.- The story is pretty poor too, unlike LEGO Dimensions, each IP doesn't really correlate with each other. You won't be seeing MacReady interacting with He-Man, or Scott Pilgrim interacting with Heavy, which is a little disappointing. Instead, you get more straight forward adaptations of these films and shows, just with game's main villain added into their final levels.- I wish this game had voice acting, man...Buuut... Aside from that- I genuinely enjoyed Funko Fusion, and I hope that the issues I've listed here will be fixed in future patches and content updates.Overall, the game is a solid 7/10 for me. It's good and enjoyable, but it needs just a bit more time in the oven.

_childDocuments_.review: I am not a big puzzle or single-player gamer, but I am a Funko fan and have been having a great time in my first 12 hours of playing. Is this GOTY? Of course not, but it is the perfect game to kill some time with and I think that enjoyment will be multiplied tenfold once co-op releases. There are bugs and gameplay can get repetitive at times, but if you're a fan of puzzle games, the LEGO games, Funko in general, or any of the featured IPs you're going to enjoy yourself. I have not gotten very far in the general overarching story of the game, but the levels I have played so far loosely follow the events of the IP they're based off of with cute gags and Funko-fied cutscenes. I've enjoyed all the levels I've played, but especially the ones from the movies or shows I have personally watched. The game is rated T for a reason. Can't say I'd recommend younger kids playing the game, at least not the levels of the more mature IPs. The game also doesn't hold your hand, like at all. There were several times where I had no clue where to go or what to do and had to figure it out myself. Was a fun change and I liked not being able to Google the answers or be spoon-fed the solutions from the game itself. I can see how that might be frustrating for some people though. There's also a LOT of side quests/collectibles to find in each level, so if you're someone who enjoys hunting for every single piece of "loot" and likes to 100% games, the game will certainly keep you busy. In short, the game isn't some incredible singe-player experience with cutting edge graphics, voice acting, or life changing narrative, but it IS a fun time and feels like a love letter to the fans of each respected fandom. You can tell that the team behind the game genuinely enjoys the worlds and characters that they were given access to. This feels like a game made for fans, by fans.

Idk if the DLC downloaded automatically but I have no option to download them and they don't show up in game... I wish the objectives were more direct, would make life easier. _childDocuments_.review: Contrary to what other reviews mention, the characters shown such as Chucky and FnaF "Freddy" ARE in the game. They are just not MAIN levels, they are cameo characters/levels. Over all enjoying my time with the game, you can definitely feel the Lego team DNA. although I'm maybe not in love with all of the IP choices (personally I don't care about the thing, hot fuzz, Battlestar Galactica... I would much prefer full levels based on invincible, etc) and they didn't necessarily evolve the formula from the latest Lego Star Wars game, it's still a fun sandbox to play with the IPs we know and love. I'd probably recommend waiting for a sale, but I'm certainly not unhappy with my purchase so far. Never thought I'd be playing a Lego style Scott Pilgrim or invincible game, so that's a win in my book 😁

name: Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin
detailed_description: Ultimate Edition Purchase the Ultimate Edition of Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin now to receive: 'Deluxe’ Profile Customisation Set, a selection of customisation options for your in-game profile, including a unique avatar, avatar frame, banner, and banner image. 4 Alternate Hero Skins Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin - The Celestial Spear and The Mouth of Mork Hero Pack About the Game A real-time strategy game from Frontier, set in the iconic Warhammer universe. Become a warlord and lead four unique factions to conquer the wild and savage Realm of Ghur in tense and tactical battles: • Cinematic campaign – Enjoy a rich, character driven story of desperate conflict in a savage realm, co-written by acclaimed Black Library writer Gav Thorpe. • Comprehensive multiplayer – Dive into 1v1 and 2v2 cross platform multiplayer matches with any mix of human and AI teammates/opponents, and climb a 1v1 competitive ladder. • Eternal conquest – Battle across procedurally generated wildlands in a single player experience, as you fight towards the final enemy. • Endless creativity – Build, share and compete on your own maps or other people’s, paint your own armies, create beautiful dioramas to show them off. Explore the nature of war from the perspectives of righteous champions and villainous warlords. Battle for survival and dominance across a campaign featuring four major factions, including Stormcast Eternals, Orruk Kruleboyz, Nighthaunt and the Disciples of Tzeentch! Experience a cinematic plot, penned in conjunction with acclaimed Black Library author, Gavin Thorpe. Challenge warlords from around the world in online cross-platform multiplayer modes. Build your honour in casual play or put your strategy to the test and crown yourself as the one true ruler of Ghur in ranked, competitive play. Compete 1v1, or 2v2 with up to three AI – or play co-op with a friend. A single player challenge mode played over a procedurally generated campaign, that pits players against a series of unpredictable combat scenarios and maps. Featuring rule-breaking twists that transform the conditions of conflict. Strike forth directly to victory or take on more battles to craft a high score the choice is yours. No two Conquest campaigns will ever be the same.  Become one with the Realms and construct battle maps with a revolutionary Map Editor , which utilises the same tools used to create existing maps in the game. Leave a personal mark in your path of conquest with the Army Livery , a system that allows you to personalise your forces with paint from the Games Workshop's Citadel collection Create spellbinding scenes to share with the community with the Scene Editor , an additional tool that allows you to place and pose characters and props in creatively curated and sharable scenes.

_childDocuments_.review: 4/10+++++I welcome any new Warhammer or 40k games.  The gfx look great, and the game runs well on my system.  The gameplay mechanics are simple and combat animations look cool.  I played up to Chapter 5 so far and the story is pretty interesting.   -----Every mission plays out similarly; capture and battle over points on the map.  There is minimal resource management.  No base building.  No RPG elements.  The controls are wonky.  Units don't always move and attack, they'll often stop and watch as their buddy gets pummeled.  Units move *SLOW*.  Most of the Stormcast units look similar to one another.  The longer I play the game the more likely I'll uninstall it and never play it again.  I wish I could gift it to someone from my library that will appreciate it more because to me it's just plain bad.

_childDocuments_.review: Good things:- general presentation: graphics, sound, ingame cutscence- it's Warhammer and more Warhammer is always good :DBad things:.. where to start..- lets begin with the worst: Unit balance! The game introduces a rock-paper-scissors kind of unit balance. But the balance clearly favors ranged units. Especially ballista-type units are way to strong. Most melee units just die before reaching their ranged attackers, even the ones countering them. Some melee units dont have gap-closing abilites as well. You only need 2-3 melee units to block stragglers. The melee damage units are very underwhelming and basically useless.- locked combat: once a unit is melee attacked, it is locked into melee combat and cannot receive any commands other than to retreat or special abilities which trigger some kind of aura or buff. Though this design is "realistic", it is very annoying and deprives you from having any influence in the current state of the overall combat situation.Those two issues lead to the following gameplay:You get 3-4 ranged units and let them rain down on the enemies. If some come close to them, you just engage with a melee unit to lock the enemy in combat. Your ranged can finish them without any trouble. But this is not always necessary: Even if the enemy reaches your ranged units, only one is locked in melee combat. The others still can finish the attacker.- campaign difficulty: Some of the 18 chapters are ridiculously easy, while others are way to hard (played on "normal"). - cutscence during a mission are not skipable.. very annoying! Don't forget to save!- UI: The UI is not very intuitive. I often had the feeling of not being in control, accidentally ordering a retreat or opening the wrong panel. In addition selecting a specific unit during combat can be tricky if the icons overlap.- and the final thing: This is not an RTS! There is no base building, so I would rather sort it into the real-time tactics genre, like World in Conflict etc.So if you really really want another Warhammer game, go for it. But expect a lot of fruststration due to the lack of balance and the campaign difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: Sluggish, unresponsive and feels almost mobile game inspired. How did we get Dawn of War so many years ago but have only regressed since.Don't bother right clicking an enemy unit with multiple of yours selected, most of the time your units will wander on past, the pathing makes Total War Warhammers look perfect!Seriously needs some stances, aggressive, defensive etc as I would actually like my shields in front of my bows to ENGAGE the enemy so they don't just walk around to the archers without having to babysit the units.The graphics are great, the voice acting is very good, combat animations are okay but for such a small squad-to-squad style especially with the insistence that squads must lock into combat, there's no sync kills??The objectives in the campaign are just skirmishes with some cut scenes, hold X till their points are 0, riveting.Once again in modern game fashion, it's half done and especially so for the Warhammer franchise.If patches increase unit speed, improve the AI, add stances so they don't stand still like melons while the enemy runs past, it'll be vastly better.

_childDocuments_.review: Realms of Ruin makes all the same mistakes that Command and Conquer 4 made almost 14 years ago. It takes the maps and concept of a multi player game format and tries to rap a single player RTS around it. It wasn't fun then and isn't fun now, if you've come here looking for a good single player experience you will be sadly disappointed. It lacks any innovation and throws the excellent work done on character models and environments right under the bus.It's your typical take and hold command points with very limited, slow moving characters who take forever to build. On these points you can build either defensive, resource or base buildings which in turn can be upgraded as can your units. each map seems to descend into running around in circles trying to defend all your points against relentless enemy hordes, even on the easiest mode they just never let up.It just becomes an joyless relentless grind, merely a trainer for the multiplayer portion of the game, with a dry boring story.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a lot of fun, with a good campaign and some interesting mechanics+ beautiful graphics, especially in an age when fantasy/sci fi RTS seem to all be cartoony warcraft stuff or soulless Supreme Commander style pawns -- everything comes to life and has a lot of personality+ good cinematic campaign with fun missions+ unique mechanics - units getting "stuck" in melee means that you have to be really careful about positioning; ranged units are all fairly powerful but have to "set up" to shoot, which means positioning them is also crucial. really fun game of maneuver.+ the counter system is pretty good, but not too strong - with clever positioning and unit combos you can beat far superior forces, because of this focus on maneuver, which i find really satisfying- baffling absences, like the lack of free-for-all, or even a "random" faction option for skirmish mode- the story and setting are not explained at all!- no campaign missions for the nighthaunt (ghosts)? why no cavalry units, everything acts like infantry! so much room for variety here which would make the game even better.It might not be worth $60, just because there's not a TON here, but its a fantastic casual RTS which you can play in 30 mins or so, and is a really good looking game. Definitely pick up if on sale for 50%+ off. Easily a $30 game though in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game at the last minute for a few reasons: - some recent controversy of the PC Gamer review more focused on trash talking the AoS setting rather than reviewing the game. I figured to get it to see for myself since the ♥♥♥♥ writer can't get over an 8 year old decision (you're getting your old setting back, let it go)- I heavily play Age of Sigmar on the tabletop since 2E in 2018 and have a fun time with it, especially since 2 factions I use to play are in the game.- I figured the game would play similar to Dawn of War and I've always enjoyed RTS games, even though I'm not the best at them.Downloaded it yesterday, played through the entire story 'til 1 today and slept to get my thoughts ready.And...wow...this game is rough.First, gameplay is more akin to Dawn of War 2, where that alone is more like Company of Heroes as I understand. There's no base building, instead you SLOWLY amass resources by gathering troops around the map at certain points. Said points can then have a structure built on them that can range from healing troops outside of base, more resource gathering or defensive structures. Thing is, resources take a while to gather. The buildings take quite a few to just get started as does EVERYTHING, even abilities. So if you're not careful and need to use a certain hero ability but used it to que a new unit, can't use that ability and vice versa.And that's just part of the problem. Units will get "locked into" melee combat and you can't get them out unless they win, die or retreat them all the way back to main base with, yes, an ability that cost precious resources. Units, in general, are slow and clunky. Trying to select a unit to attack is horrible as the cursor doesn't change when I move over a unit to attack and doesn't seem to register a hit box that well. Ranged units I kept getting into melee accidentally since they require setup and issues with said attack selection. No unit stats to see, basic rock-paper-scissors counter system, lots of abilites for units I kept forgetting to use and honestly didn't care to use, HORRIBLE UI system of menus and mass unit selection (I could barely see their icons at the bottom of my screen or who's who). I could find other problems but that would require me to play the game more (not interested) or others have already mentioned them.Now the story... is pretty decent! I won't go into spoilers for major events but for the most part it's well written enough for a Warhammer tale and gets pretty grim by the end (proper considering WHR in general). However, and this could just be me being bad at RTS' like I said, but by the third mission on normal I thought the AI was somehow ramped up. You have to hold 3 points for 2 minutes, but when you leave one area the AI will naturally take it back. So it's a lot of back and forth running about or leaving smaller squads to get wiped by a surprise force of the enemy and on top of that, if you lose your only base, game over (learned that the hard way first time). With how everyone moves slow, it's kinda hard to lock everything down in time, WHILE also making sure the AI just doesn't flank you (somehow) and make you lose. I dropped down to easy, only had to hold for 1 minute, passed and moved back to normal for the next mission. Then I got to the mission after that, which is literally just multiplayer map battle and somehow got stomped again and just switched over to easy for the rest of the time. From here, it varied on what missions were good or not. There's 'almost' a solo hero mission where you can find allies to help...which I failed to save the last one somehow 'cause the side objectives are marked horribly on the map, a neat boss fight where you get to use your new power you unlocked...and only ever use on side objectives out of reach since it's pretty niche, a  fun sabotage mission, which I think might be my personal favorite...but THEN EVERYTHING TURNS BELLY UP AFTER THAN IN THE FINAL FEW MISSIONS (save for one) BECAUSE THEY'RE MULTIPART MISSIONS AND IF YOU FAIL, YOU START ALL THE WAY BACK AT THE BEGINNING! NO CHECKPOINTS! And once again, with how slow units move, resource management, etc. it just becomes a chore, even on easy! The final mission I thought I wouldn't get through and probably would've just quit after a 3rd attempt. You need to grab two points, while still defending your base (almost what you've done throughout most of the game) and after that just kill the final boss, WHO'S SURROUNDED BY DAMAGING GROUND AOE, HAS HORRIBLY WORDED OBJECTIVES AND I JUST CHEESED IT WITH A WELL PLACED SAVE LAST MINUTE TO RELOAD FAILS AND SUPER LONG RANGE UNITS!!! ALL OF THIS ON EASY STILL!!!Tried Conquest, wasn't interested in gameplay loop still. Tried map editor, felt glitchy as certain objects would want to be placed in super sunken/raised terrain (and I'm not super creative or skilled enough for that stuff). Army painter, pretty good as you can customized individual units but limited in colors (oh and the Knight of Shrouds/Lord Gloam are literally the same if you don't have variation for $15 DOLLARS EXTRA).My overall conclusion of this game is simple: it's a slow, clunky mess that relatively looks nice. And I'm sad to say that since I really was getting excited about this one. But it just feels so bad. I wasn't that big of a fan with DoW 2's change in gameplay and having that mirror here but worse is agony. The story is interesting enough as you play through both Stormcast and Kruleboyz (with a little Chaos) but that's mostly it and it still felt like a chore after a while. I know I'm not getting my $75 back. If you're looking at this for AoS, better to try the tabletop or some novels. If you're looking at this for gameplay, try looking at DoW 2 or CoH first and seeing if those feel more polished to try out. The only positive thing I can say about this game is that I finished it and can uninstall for other games in my library of shame.

_childDocuments_.review: Right now, it's a mechanically poor console port of a console focused RTS game.TL/DR: It's a copy of the worst Dawn of War game (3,) but worse.It's a tremendous amount of polish on what amounts to a pretty simple rock-paper-stone kind of game, where engagements in multiplayer are won in the first few minutes of a match and anything after is just spraying in the wind. Fights revolve around unit composition but not ability to use said units. At times it feels like the game is just dressed up auto-battler.I don't understand why a designer would make a game so similar to one of the least liked entries in the Dawn of War saga and RTS games generally and then go about reinventing the wheel multiple times and changing how very straightforward things within games should work. AI is exceptionally poor although I bet you could ask a designer and they will tell you its functioning as intended. Aggro ranges are poor. Melee units will regularly just stand and be attacked from a few feet away by a ranged unit. Apparently these amazing reforged warriors are dumb as rocks after a few resurrections. Meanwhile Total Annihilation from 1997 has customisation of AI for each unit fielded with a unit count that's an order of magnitude greater.The interface is poor throughout the product with simple things like a map not having a preview of the terrain biome to be encountered, just an overly designed layout with pretty icons is provided. You can't even see what colour of troops you've picked. The in game interface doesn't make much sense. Functionality is missing so you can't click a unit when its on the selected unit bar. There isn't quick select icon for your heroes so you can jump to them quickly, you have to fish them out of a mob of similar looking, similar coloured units once you've selected a quick group.With the campaign demo being reasonably polished and the talk of improvements to the speed of multiplayer I purchased the game despite my previous gut feeling and regrettably I feel burned. I hope they fix the game but Frontier don't have a great track record of support in recent years and with this likely to bomb, I don't think any overhauls or many fixes will be forthcoming.4/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is getting review bombed, primarily by classic RTS players and trolls who are mad at it not being Old Warhammer Fantasy.The game is very centered around good control, it will seem that it has a Rock-Paper-Scissors balance, and in principle it does (Early tier units especially fall pretty squarely into "Tank", "Tank Hunter" and "Archer" categories) but that does not mean that tank hunters are going to lose every fight to archers, or Tanks are going to lose every fight to Tank hunters. How you go about your engage makes a load of difference. Good charges on your sword units and using actives at the right time can absolutely clutch fights. The combat is simple, and more methodical, but definitely feels satisfying when you start to make it work. The big challenge is that the game wants you to split your forces and tackle multiple objective simultaneously, and that's a tall order for a lot of people, hence why old school RTS fans are having a ♥♥♥♥♥ about the game right now.The story is pretty good, all the characters are pretty well characterized, our good guy cast consists of a seasoned and dutiful, but slightly detached, Veteran commander Sigrun, her Bannerguard, Iden is is more hot-blooded, though never quite feels rash, and comes off as a genuinely likeable individual, and a Celestial Battlemage Demichrius, who is more bland on account of being a pretty straightforward example of what one expects a mage to behave like. None of the cast particularly stands out, but that's not really the point of the story. In the grand scheme of our adventure they are relatively average examples of people in their position, making decisions that are competent within their role, but not perfect in their execution. The Orruk and Chaos characters are also more-or-less archetypical, but that's hardly a problem. All of this might sound like a scathing criticism, but there has been scant few Age of Sigmar stories released that treat their cast as merely average example of their positions, and it's refreshing to have a core cast whom are ultimately so normal, especially given the relatability of it's characters has been a major narrative block for Age of Sigmar since it's release.Big criticisms I have have to be the sound mixing and control schemes. Many of the control elements are going to be unfamiliar RTS players familiar with the genre, selecting one unit out of a herd can become a chore when moving a large group as the game will keep the whole stack selected when you click on a unit that is part of that group, so if you pick up the game you will have to get very used to deselecting by clicking the ground and then selecting individual units to perform more complicated commands like splits. The sound isn't unmanageable, but the base sound balancing wasn't great for me, I ended up swapping to the nighttime/quiet mode setting and that fixed much of the issue for my device.Overall I have enjoyed the experience, I bought in during the winter sale for roughly 40.00 USD, and I would say that's a good value. At the full price I would only grab it if you are a big fan of Age of Sigmar and Relic-style RTS. I think the campaign is a good length, I'm near the finale and have put a solid few afternoons over the winter break playing through on hard. I would recommend taking the difficulty down a peg for most sane individuals, as even having a decent grasp of the system from the open beta I found I still had to restart on several missions.I would give it a 3/5 Stars, solid foundation but could use some work. Personally I hope the game sees some expansion content, though I'm not holding my breath at this point for anything more than a bit of polish.As an aside, I find it odd to admit, as someone who has been interested in Age of Sigmar as a setting for a long time, that I did not particularly like the Stormcast Eternals until seeing them in action in this game. The cutscenes, especially early on where we see more of Iden and Sigrun together, really do some work for reminding that although SCE are the best of the best, they are still human in the ways that count, and by no means inured to pain, doubt or emotion. The VO and animation here are top-notch, and I love to see it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, so I played through the 18 level campaign, and a single skirmish match against the bot.  I played on easy mode, because I suck.Disclaimer:  I know very little about the Warhammer Sigmar universe.  I'm a bit more of a 40k person, but still typically like 40K games and love all the other RTS 40K games excluding DOW3.The good:- The engine is amazing.  Great graphics, great textures, great animations, just looks great- The sound is great.  Good voice work, good acknowledgements, sounds great.- The story is pretty decent, and though cheesy at times, its good- You get 4 races to choose from- It had a lot of polish and I do not think it was rushed at all.  It felt complete, just a little light, and ran very smoothly.- The missions aren't just all "kill the opponent", which is nice.The bad:- Its pretty darned simple.  You get close to points that let you build a building on it that lets you do various things.  So there really isn't any base building, and you only get like 4-6 total building options and most are not all that remarkable.  It gets old, and fast.- This game uses the whole triangle thing, where a defensive unit beats a sword unit that beats an arrow unit, or something like that.  Its kinda boring too.- You get maybe 6-10 upgrades you can do for all your troops.  Many are a choice between 2 drastically different things.- You get maybe 10 units per race, a couple heroes in there and some troops, but it doesn't really feel like much variety.  No builder or medics for example.My recommendations:- Your heroes don't have an icon on the screen to find them easily.  They can get lost easily if you don't hot key them.  Add icons for each hero, you have at most like 3.- Since you only get 1 building that can build units, its silly to need to click on it to set its waypoint.  Should just have a waypoint button on the screen all the time.- Also add icons on the screen for all your buildings to show their type/damage.  There are not that many, and its nice to know when one is getting damaged.- Need an engineer that can build things and a medic that can heal things.- Give some ability to build turrets or walls or *something*.- if it doesn't have amazing mod support, add it, as the engine is superb and mods could make this game go from a 4 to a 9 easily.  Far too much work done on making a good engine to have it only live a short life.I will recommend this game, but just barely, and only if its moddable, it will be amazing and totally worth it.  If you can't mod it, it'll get old, and I can't recommend it then.I suspect there will be DLC for it if it sells ok, which may introduce additional races, campaigns, and so forth.  Not sure it'll ever have base building or any form of harvesting though, which may hurt it long term.I do hope to see more for it in the future, especially in regards to mods, but I won't touch it again after the campaign unless I hear about updates to the amount of content.

_childDocuments_.review: I gave this game a try for over 15 hours.. it feels awful, just went back to other RTS like Dawn of War and it feels like night and day. I can also only say how it felt playing Stormcast in MP.Campaign:While I love Warhammer for the "ez" way in, like everyone will tell you to pick an entry point and it may or may not hook you and doesnt matter which IP (40k / Fantasy / AOS) from there you develop your love for it yourself. But this game is... ♥♥♥♥ at this. While you have in Vermintide a cast of heroes that go about the endtimes you are in for the fun ride right from the start or DOW 1 where you get to know Space Marines (Gabriel) and Inquistors and three more faction a bit more with a neat story to boot, this is bland in only the first few missions. These games make me want to get to know the IP more but this attrocity has bland characters, don't know where we are and what they are talking about is a giant question mark. Maybe AOS folks know whats up, but as an entry point for someone with no knowledge it is awful.I just stopped playing, since it became frustrating, having a jumbled narrative, bland characters, cutscences that play out of nowhere and that ♥♥♥♥ up your cooldowns too and a difficulty (played on highest) that was so retarded due to the mob spawn and slow moving units that I just installed DOW 1 instead.. :DThe RTS Elements:There is no real depth to structures / unit upgrades period. Structures => When we take a MP match you have at the start 2-3 nodes were you can build a structure of your choice, 2 generate resources (that you need to build stuff), one gives you a healing point and another a turret. You can upgrade all of these once thats it, they give you small extra boni but nothing that branches out. Units => While you have a few units depending on your upgraded main building, some of them have an upgrade "choice", yeah rather than having the options to research everything for more fun you have to pick one over the other, lets say the Huntsman can either have stealth or more defense. So basically you have 1 upgrade for a unit if any... and no other form of enhancing except the healing structure that gives when upgraded 1 more unit? I think. I also love the upgrades that say "increase defense for all damage".. how much etc. doenst matter, why would I want to know if I have to choose between upgrades am I right???Combat => There is a rock / paper / CROSSBLADES approach to combat, but who thought that combat locking is a good idea? What if you want to kite? Doenst work. You want to disengage from a fight? Doenst work except for full retreat back to base. And since you units are quite slow you will learn to love all the backtracking!At times it feels more like a tower defense game at times where you send units down one of three roads and hope for the best. The most fun I had was managing stuff at one end while I hoped my units will at least try to survive without me for a second and when I went looking two units just idled a meter away form a unit that got obliterated... yeah just great! But wait there is more!Remember the good old RTS times, where you could give units stances or formations? Like defend position, free attack, aggressive advance? ♥♥♥♥ that who needs autonamy on the battlefield at times NO ONE! MP => 2v2 games (quite a fan of multiple folks fighting) will become quite rare in the future I guess, waited for 1 game over 7min and disconnected after 5 from the queue a second time. The playerbase is quite low looking at steam db so who knows how MP will look in the feature. I also agree with many folks here that there needs to be more modes than capture the points.I am always happy when I see a Warhammer game, even if it aint all that good. But this one was just frustrating if anything. Maybe it will get better I can't recommend it like this and will update this review when there is the first DLC or when I come around it again.

_childDocuments_.review: A review of this game can't really do it justice. A review only focusing on the game itself fails to showcase the situation surrounding it. If you are looking for my 2 cents, 100% get this game if you enjoy RTS with RTT mechanics and if you were a fan of the DoW 2 mechanics. Disregarding that, oh man is this game divisive. Hundreds of reviews with less than 5 hours clocked on the game, judging it quickly for mechanics that the game doesn't have instead of actually trying the game for what it is. If you are a die hard OG RTS gamer that still creams his pants at the thought of SC brood war or DoW dark crusade this game might not be for you, even though this game was marketed as a RTS to RTS audiences it set up expectations to a community that is already cynical of new warhammer RTS titles, and it shot itself in the foot with those same expectations.I recommend you give this game a chance regardless of if you are a casual, competitive or new RTS player, simply consider that the game is not your usual RTS format. There is much more depth and time you can spend in this game than you can initially guess. It is not a simplified RTS for new audience, it isn't a MOBA and it isn't DoW 3 with an AoS skin over it. Have a nice day reader!

_childDocuments_.review: Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin : By Triple F“Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin” is an ambitious real-time strategy (RTS) game set in the sprawling, high-fantasy universe of Warhammer’s Age of Sigmar. Developed by Frontier Developments, it aims to capture the grandeur of massive, factional battles while staying true to the rich lore of Games Workshop’s Age of Sigmar tabletop game. With a focus on faction diversity, tactical combat, and visually stunning representations of the Mortal Realms, “Realms of Ruin” brings the immersive and often chaotic world of Warhammer Age of Sigmar to life. It strikes a balance between deep, strategic mechanics and accessibility, making it appealing to both Warhammer enthusiasts and RTS newcomers.The game’s story mode follows the forces of Order, specifically the Stormcast Eternals, as they engage in a brutal campaign to secure the lands of Ghur from the encroaching Orruk Kruleboyz. The campaign weaves together the lore and high stakes of Age of Sigmar, offering players insight into the internal and external struggles of the Stormcast Eternals as they fight not just for territory, but for survival in a realm teeming with monstrous threats. The narrative is more character-driven than many RTS games, with dialogues and cutscenes that deepen the personalities of faction leaders, bringing a level of immersion that fans of the lore will appreciate. This story mode is divided into several campaigns, each with unique objectives and challenges that cater to varied strategies and keep players engaged.One of the highlights of “Realms of Ruin” is its faction system, offering players access to multiple factions with distinctive playstyles and units. Each faction whether it’s the resilient Stormcast Eternals, the sneaky Orruk Kruleboyz, or other iconic Warhammer forces, each have unique unit rosters and mechanics that impact gameplay strategy. The Stormcast, for example, are powerful, heavily armored warriors capable of holding the line against formidable foes, while the Orruks emphasize speed, surprise, and overwhelming numbers. The faction diversity not only stays faithful to the tabletop experience but also allows players to experiment with different strategies, lending the game a high level of replayability.Combat in “Realms of Ruin” emphasizes tactical positioning and unit synergy, with the game blending elements of traditional RTS with mechanics inspired by tabletop wargaming. Units have strengths, weaknesses, and unique abilities that make them effective in certain roles but vulnerable in others. For instance, ranged units can support melee troops from afar but are weak against flanking maneuvers, while heavy units like Stormcast Retributors can absorb damage and disrupt enemy formations. Terrain also plays a role, as certain areas provide cover or positional advantages, encouraging players to think critically about where and when to engage the enemy. This blend of strategy and tactical depth captures the spirit of Warhammer battles, rewarding careful planning over brute force.The visuals in “Realms of Ruin” are nothing short of impressive, with an art style that brings Age of Sigmar’s fantastical landscapes and armies to life. Each battlefield in the realm of Ghur feels alive, from dense jungles filled with monstrous flora to desolate wastelands scarred by previous battles. Units are meticulously detailed, with armor glinting under sunlight and magical energy coursing through weapons. The Stormcast Eternals, in particular, look as powerful as they are described in the lore, with auras of energy surrounding their thunderstrike armor, while the Orruk Kruleboyz are grungy, fierce, and distinctively intimidating. The dynamic animations of spell-casting and melee combat further enhance the sense of immersion, making every skirmish feel like an epic clash.Sound design is another strength of “Realms of Ruin,” with a score that captures the grandeur and danger of the Mortal Realms. The orchestral soundtrack complements the high stakes of each battle, enhancing tension during combat and underscoring the somber tone of the story. Voice acting is equally compelling, bringing personality to key characters and adding depth to the campaign. Environmental sounds, like the clash of steel and the distant growls of lurking monsters, immerse players further into the war-torn realm of Ghur. These audio elements work in concert to bring the dark, mystical world of Warhammer to life in a way that few games achieve.Multiplayer mode in “Realms of Ruin” is a key feature, offering competitive and cooperative play that lets players test their skills against others or join forces for a tactical edge. Multiplayer skirmishes are intense and demand quick thinking, especially with each faction’s strengths and weaknesses on full display. Frontier Developments has implemented a ranked matchmaking system that pits players against similarly skilled opponents, fostering a competitive community. In addition to ranked matches, casual play options allow friends to team up or face off without the pressure of rankings, making the multiplayer accessible for both casual and hardcore players alike. The ongoing balance adjustments and potential updates promise a continuously evolving experience.In conclusion, “Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin” is a robust and immersive RTS that successfully brings the fantasy of Warhammer Age of Sigmar to digital form. With a rich narrative campaign, meticulously crafted factions, tactical combat, and a stunningly realized world, it provides a fulfilling experience for both Warhammer fans and strategy gamers. While some may find the complexity of unit management and faction balance challenging, the game offers enough guidance and accessibility to accommodate various skill levels. “Realms of Ruin” stands out as one of the most compelling Warhammer RTS titles, capturing the essence of the Age of Sigmar universe and delivering an intense, rewarding strategy experience in the process.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game. I'm a big fan of Warhammer, and especially Dawn of War. It wouldn't have taken much, but this game managed to massively fail to reach even the lowest bar.The game plays a lot like DoW 2, which is a great game. Except that it's not simply a re-skin with new units; they also managed to break numerous things. Pathing is entirely messed up, and barely works. There's no ability to micro during combat (or even to move away). There's no real way to defend points you've captured; resource generating buildings don't provide vision. And so on. It's simply baffling that anyone actually playtested this game and said "This is fun."The campaign story is even worse. It's not interesting. It makes no sense. The voice acting is horrible. And you can't skip cutscenes. For some reason an obviously male character is repeatedly referred to as "she" - it's unclear if this is some attempt at a political message, or just the same gross incompetence that suffuses this entire game.TL;DR: Don't play this game. It's bad. Replay DoW (or just about anything else) instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: This game is not to be taken as an RTS like Starcraft 2 or Warcraft 3.It's the other kind of RTS, Dawn Of War 2 or Company of Heroes. A game focused on a smaller amount of units, with a push and pull, tug of war aspect.With that all of the way, I would recommend this game heartfully.Realm Of Ruin is a game based on Age Of Sigmar, an universe of High Fantasy where gods and immortals are walking among the mortal. It's based on the tabletop game of the same name by Games Workshop.And first thing first, it shows. It's a love letter of the game with the quality of the animations, sounds, abilities or even the feel of the units on the battlefield. Even more than the tabletop game, they feel right.The campaign is interesting and challenging, maybe even a bit much sometimes. The normal IA is equivalent of an hard one somewhere else and it will kick your ass more than once.Conquest mode is a procedural generated maps with twist on the different battles you can have. Play with the latest tech, only one point to capture, half life of your units. It changes the way to play when you have interesting twists.About the gameplay.As I said above, it's a RTS that does it's own things. The goal is to capture critical points on the battlefield to deplete the opponent victory points. 4 races available (like W3 or DoW backin the days) and asymetrical.Unit abilities cost ressources. They are extremely powerful, but due to the cost, slow down your tech acquisition. So do you want to spend now to win engagement, or bank it to get higher tier units faster?Units are locked when a melee occurs and can only fight. A move action will be a retreat to the base. You need to know if this is a fight you wnat to take, and you want to be able to catch your opponent off guard with bad engagement.It means that even with a relatively low amount of units (between 10 to 14 units on the maps) you need to be active on the majority of them and mobile. There is not much APM needed, but you always have to make decisions to not get caught off guard.Matches are intense and with roughly equal levels, you can expect comeback and fights that finish with only a few points left on both side.All of these points are here for a good reasons. It's not like the majority of RTS. It should not be taken as such.It clicked for me pretty quick as DoW2 was one of my favorite games, but for themajority of people, I think it needs to be taken with a curiosity to try something new. Not Starcraft 2, something different.Lastly the Dev are really active on the discord and are pushing fixes and enhancement each week.I hope it will keep on as there is a lot of potential in new units/maps/armies with different way of playing.If you play, don't hesitate to go on their discord if you have question. There is a small community that can help you with the different aspect.Have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: In attempt to put a dent in my backlog, I've played and reviewed a lot of really good and really bad games this year. However, this game is such a disaster that it's earned the title of "The Worst Game I've Ever Finished", dethroning the previous title holder released back in 2000. Realms of Ruin has terrible basic game design issues, limited/missing controls, minimal HUD information, and is still suffering from launch gameplay bugs while still receiving DLCs. Some bad games are fun to play as an oddity or to laugh at with friends (like Shaq Fu), but this is just bad bad. This game wants to be Dawn of War 2 with an Age of Sigmar skin, but it fails at properly implementing RTS game elements even from the 90s, never mind its inspiration. Unless you're really into painting AoS minis, this game has no redeeming value and should be avoided.Let's get the most glaring gameplay issue out of the way: once any unit is engaged in melee combat, . The only way to break them out of combat is by issuing a retreat command like in DOW2, except you have to spend Control resources to do so. There's only two resources in the game for all factions, with Control being your basic "Gold" resource for buying all tiers of units, and Realmstone being used for unit abilities and advanced units. The cost to retreat also increases for higher tier units and costs are charged per unit; if a stack of units get stuck in, it might cost you half a building's worth of resources just to save them. Not like it matters half the time though because regen from your home base is abysmal... It's usually better to just let low tier units die and repurchase them than wait several minutes for them to heal. Even if you can save units, pathfinding is terrible and is per character model; There were several missions where I was basically given -1 unit cap because a single entity was stuck on terrain and couldn't even be selected thanks to the retreat order. Game balance in general is frustrating because of the simplistic rock-paper-scissors balancing system and units getting stuck in. Early game this balancing doesn't matter much, but T2 shield units can easily tank several ranged units even while pinned down by another melee unit. Other balancing issues plaguing the game include: home base upgrades (unit cap, unit tier) being cheaper than any other buildings, Arcane Conduit buildings having the normal control point buildings being split into four mutually exclusive buildings (damage, sight, regen, resources separated), and poor unit balancing with ballista and single entity monsters being obviously overpowered. Endgame battles seem to come down to who gets their unit abilities off first, followed by who can keep their ballistae protected. Of course, I only played through the campaign so I didn't have the intended E-Sports experience, but that would be hard to given the 28 concurrent players.The campaign is 18 missions, jumping between all of the factions, and is riddled with poor game design choices. I could probably write a whole review about the issues with each mission... Mission 3 has you holding three control points to stop a ritual, but the bar starts almost full and the enemies get infinite free units from spawn camps around the map (like Gauntlet). Mission 4 has you intercepting an undead leader, but you have to build mission-specific towers that can only damage him, and then he "died" with 1/3rd health left anyway. Mission 17 was a special kind of nightmare, with a bug that prevented me from recruiting more units after the halfway point. However, RTS campaigns are usually a warm-up, so how's the skirmish mode? It's absolutely barebones with only 1v1 and 2v2 maps with no team composition options. Where are Free For All, 3v3, and 4v4? Where are alternate victory conditions? DOW2's AI suffered from focusing on backdooring control points and this game suffers from that too... I don't see myself touching Skirmish mode, even if they improve the other issues with the game.Realms of Ruin at its core feels like it was designed for mobile and upscaled to PC with minimal knowledge about how actual RTS games work. There's a serious lack of information and controls on the HUD: characters have health bars but no health numbers or percentages, units have no visible stats (despite upgrades providing stat bonuses), and units have no stance options. Attack-move was apparently added post-launch but it doesn't work well either; your units seem to only engage units directly in their marching path, regardless of their attack range, when in most games an attack-move would give them the freedom to attack anything they encounter in their vision (another thing fixable by stances). There's also almost no tooltips provided for the minimal HUD outside of the overpowered unit abilities... Good luck finding out what all those buffs and debuffs on units are and where they came from. Units can be thankfully grouped but there's no way to remove units from a group unless you completely remake the group. Lastly, the default controls are bad, but the camera controls are especially frustrating and there's no way to increase the panning speed with a key press (most isometric games use Shift for this). If it was a movie on Best of the Worst, it'd be one of those generic monster movies where they get lost in the woods for half the movie, have a five minute big name actor cameo so they can put a famous name on the box, and use box art for the monster that doesn't match the monster's design in the movie. This game is a mess and isn't salvageable. Age of Sigmar is a hideous, Marvelized half-breed between Warhammer Fantasy and 40k, but reskinning this wouldn't do anything to fix the terrible gameplay. This is a slow-paced, poorly controlled mess that was designed to be watched and not played. The only positive things I can say about it are the graphics are okay and the cutscene animations and rigging are fantastic (I hope you guys can get better jobs). It's a travesty that Warhammer Fantasy died for this. A true abomination and a waste of money, both by myself and the developer's investors.

Look, it's got some frustrating issues but has enough potential that  things are fixed would easily give players a fairly competent PvP RTS. Units can be really unresponsive and often just refuse to move or get stuck on map terrain. Your agency to micro/take good engagements is ripped out from under you over and over again. combined with the overall sluggishness I usually walk away feeling as tho I wasted my time. I cannot recommend the game as is.. but I have hope it will move in a positive direction. when it works it is legitimately fun, given time and effort it should become an experience I will enjoy coming back to

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start by saying that I've never been a hardcore RTS player. I dabbled with Starcraft and played quite a bit of Dawn of War/DoW2 back in the day. Also had plenty of time with the Halo Wars games. I'd say that this feels a lot more relatable to the DoW series, in that it doesn't seem to focus much on base building and masses of units. The campaign up to this point tells a solid story, and it's not too difficult to follow in a narrative sense. The gameplay focuses on tighter knit groups/heroes that move slow, and hit pretty hard. The game follows a fairly simple rock/paper/scissors with unit types, which admittedly limits some of the more advanced tactical potential that you may find in other RTS games, but as someone who isn't a hardcore RTS person this felt great to me. I haven't delved into multiplayer so I can't say whether or not it's alive and well or not, but the conquest mode has some replayability to it. Ultimately not a bad game. It's also very pretty to look at and makes me really want to play the tabletop more.

_childDocuments_.review: Realms of Ruin isnt actually a bad game, it depends on what you expect from it.The slow pace of the game and relatively low amount of units and factions is great for getting into the game pretty quickly and is especially great for beginners in RTS genre. Factions have unique and beautiful design, the whole setting is interesting and the game has one of the best map editor I have ever seen. Being able to paint your faction is also nice. But here comes the ,,but".The game is surely not worth the full price, so if you cant get it cheaper, dont buy it. Also, dont expect it to be the game where you can spend houndreds of hours, at least not at this state.Campaign is relatively short, multiplayer is pretty shallow, as matches are too short and there is no way to increase victory points or change victory condition (to annihilation for example), maximum size of a match is only 2v2 and the game doesnt offer any campaign/conquest coop (at the time of this review).This game still needs a lot of work, but sadly, that is the ,,modern plague" of almost all games nowadays. Anyway, to summarize it, Realms of Ruin might be great game for beginners in RTS genre, for Warhammer fanatics or for players looking for occasional fun. But for RTS veterans, it wont bring anything new and will be mostly likely even a downgrade, compared to other RTS games.

_childDocuments_.review: If 2 hours is enough for negative reviews on other games, then it's enough for a positive review on this game.This game isn't groundbreaking. It's not reinventing the wheel. It's a rather simplistic, what you see is what you get, RTS. However, I don't think that is a bad thing, at all. We still have options, even within the Warhammer franchise, if we want something a little deeper and more complex in Total War: Warhammer. This is not that, but what it does offer is fun.I haven't even attempted the story campaign yet, as I am not too much of a fan of story campaigns in RTS games. The mode that has piqued my interest is the Conquest Mode, which is a series of skirmish battles that all lead up to a "final boss", so to speak. It's something of a rogue-like game mode, and so far it's been my preferred mode.The gameplay is standard RTS fare, just without the base building. You gather resources, use them to build units and research upgrades. Since there isn't base building, your goal is not to wipe out your opponent's base, but rather to hold objective points to win. It leads to a fast paced experience where you need to strategically decide which locations you should target, and which you are willing to sacrifice. There are also resource locations that are available to capture and defend as well. In my time playing so far, the AI is actually pretty challenging, which I see as a positive, because it will give me something to continue aspiring towards. I haven't played multiplayer yet either, but given the nature of how the game plays, I think the multiplayer will end up being a really fun mode that I will likely sink a good amount of time into as well.Add in all of the creation and customization options this game has as well, and I think that overall, we have a winner.I think this is a great "pick up and play" sort of game. I probably won't binge hours at a time on it, but for short bursts, it certainly hits a note. I bought this game simply because it's part of the Warhammer franchise, and the concept was interesting to me. I certainly don't regret my purchase.Again, it's not reinventing the wheel. I haven't seen anything in this game that really stands out as novel or innovative, but I don't think a game necessarily needs that to be good. The elements that it does use, it uses well. It won't redefine the genre, and overall, it's rather simplistic in its mechanics, so I wouldn't go into it looking for a deeply complex RTS experience. It will satisfy for a very basic urge to crash units into each other in a fast paced rumble.

_childDocuments_.review: Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin" promised an epic foray into the rich and vibrant universe of Age of Sigmar, aiming to captivate fans with strategic battles across the fantastical realms. Unfortunately, the game falls short of expectations, delivering a frustrating and monotonous experience that fails to capture the essence of the Warhammer universe.Firstly, the absence of base building is a glaring oversight. In a genre where strategy and personalization play pivotal roles, the inability to construct and fortify a base feels like a missed opportunity to deepen gameplay and engage players in their war efforts.Moreover, the game is plagued by an AI system that leaves much to be desired. The AI forces appear unlimited, turning what should be strategic battles into tiresome, never-ending skirmishes that feel more like a war of attrition than a test of tactics. This imbalance makes victories feel less earned and more like the result of sheer persistence.The decision to impose a limited unit cap further exacerbates the game's shortcomings. Such restrictions stifle creativity and strategy, forcing players into repetitive gameplay loops that quickly lose their appeal. Instead of crafting diverse armies and experimenting with various tactics, players are pigeonholed into using the same units and strategies, draining the game of variety and excitement.Finally, the game mechanics themselves are a letdown. What could have been an engaging exploration of the Age of Sigmar universe is reduced to a series of boring, repeating tasks that offer little in the way of innovation or challenge. The gameplay quickly becomes a chore, with each mission feeling indistinguishable from the last.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really want to like this game. I have hundreds of hours in DoW titles and other RTS.  I also don't have the Sigmar-phobia that most players have because they love WHFB memes...Before I get started, I will say that the campaign is enjoyable, and is fairly long, so thumbs up for the storyline/scenarios there.Now the bad:The pathfinding is trash, actual trash, how did this make it out of the door? Units are often  just spinning in circles or moving 180 degrees away from their assigned target.The unit's lack responsiveness to hotkeys, so that in competitive matches I am literally begging my units to retreat as they stand in a torrent of fire, turning circles, neither fighting nor running. This is not a cooldown management issue: the button is lit, the resources are there, and still they just stand there until about twenty keystrokes which is too late.I bought this because I thought, after some of the absolutely terrible games  Games Workshop has licensed recently (looking at you Fatshark, Relic) that this would be a game with some polish, a little pizzazz, maybe even an enjoyable play experience.... and it is, if you don't mind your multiplayer matches being ruined by poor quality control.That's before we get to balance on larger maps, which can feel like an absolute drudgefest when playing as the stormcast. I get why they should be slow infantry, but come on, you cant balance 6 slow units in the early game against 8 or more opposition units with 50% faster speed in a game of region control, especially when objectives are taken at the same speed regardless of unit value. A nighthaunt unit that costs 40% less than a stormcast unit is expendable for realm control and is one eighth of population cap, vs a much slower unit at one sixth of pop cap and a higher resource cost, limiting your options for larger battles as 1/6 of your army isnt there because he/she is babysitting a point. I started playing as the nighthaunt to try to enjoy some of that speed and fear cheese, but its not even enjoyable as I know exactly how I'll abuse my enemy when I see they are playing stormcast.I might feel better about this if I could see some actual stats for a unit, and could maybe figure out what nuance I am missing, but instead I get nothing more than the Combat Triangle and a pat on the back. If you're going to treat us like children who don't care about the numbers, at least ship me some juice boxes and orange slices for after the game.I feel like simple issues like these shouldn't be enough to ruin a game, but tell that to my poor Knight-Vexillor being crucified time and again because he is confused which way home is.TL:DR Looks Pretty, Quality of life is doo-doo

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so this game, in my mind, is a shiny turd, you can guild it in gold, polish it to a mirror shine, and place it in a velvet lined mahogany display case for all to see. It's still ♥♥♥♥.The UI is doing everything it can to be minimalist and just ends up being very clunky as a result, I just end up lost on what's actually happening in the game, micro just ends up with me confused on what units are doing what, especially when they're in battalions. Some simple things like model health bars and some clear numbers on the screen (damage taken, damage dealt, a unit card that shows total hp and general statistics) shouldn't really be a big ask for an RTS at this price.The game feels very Halo Wars console RTS, not particularly fluid or clear on what units are selected, no great range of options, and the double click to use abilities that are self-cast, as well as what feels like significant delay on that same cast is just a ball ache. Having a mouse cursor feels like an afterthought, everything except movement on mouse and keyboard is done in the same amount of space on your keyboard as the average coffee spill, and unit selection is stickier than the average teenagers bedsheets. Also attacking a specific unit is like sewing a button with parkinsons, instead get used to attack moving everything and just hoping your units get the right idea.No clear range of engagement for abilities like Charge, and what feels like a very restricted camera angle makes this a bit hard for me to love, I do like being able to tie down units but honestly there's a real lack of 'chaff' to make it feel meaningful, the rock paper scissors unit triangle is pretty uninspired, just having some really simple cheap paper towel units to tie stuff down would be so much better to make use of that mechanic.The economy makes no sense, trying to work out the ratio of economy point buildings to have a fluid economy induces the same mental haze to an NFT bro gaslighting you in to investing all your cash in to an inebriated lion with a colourful scarf.Ultimately the price point is just a bit too high for me to really warrant this game if it only offers 4 flavours of rock paper scissors viewed through the field of view of toilet roll binoculars and the information feedback of a shopping mall race car ride with no quarters to spend.And as a bit of a gripe, and this largely comes down to GW and just how they've structured AoS armies to be so thematic, but jeebus is is hard to visually determine between your units as Stormcast Eternals. Especially prosecutors when they're landed, that's a needle air dropped in a wheat field.

_childDocuments_.review: The game involves capturing points; I was expecting something similar to Dawn of War Soulstorm, but it seems like those RTS games are not coming back... _childDocuments_.review: When I first came across this game, I asked myself: How hard could it be to copy a Dawn of War Dark Crusade, a 17-year-old game? For God's sake! You have the super popular franchise,  just replace units’ skins from WaHA 40k to Fantasy Worlds and here you go.Well, I was wrong. This game doesn't have anything as a good strategy would have: base buildings, a careful calculation of strategy, or gameplay variety.Gameplay is as simple as it could be: you have to capture and hold 3 strategy points. The first thing AI does is just spawn waves and waves of enemies from the first second of the game that are running toward strategic points. The only countermeasure is to start spawning your waves. Which is a game perfectly designed for. There is no such thing as resource management because capturing resource points does not bring considerable strategic advantage. All units are the same with AI worse than good old Warcraft 2 from 90th. Sometimes swordsmen stay still while another unit is attacked in front of them and you need to give them the command to attack. And here we come to the final thing is complexity which is caused not by a complex strategy but by a ton of micromanagement you should do because of poor design and constant rush. I think that game was initially developed for smartphones with the same principles when you push one button to produce the same units and then just move them to the right points on the map. In any case, spending over $20 for such a game is a ridiculous thing to do, and would highly recommend spending money on something which gives a more pleasant experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The core design of the game is there and it's a compelling world that the devs have created with visual fidelity to match, unfortunately it's marred by a very basic combat system and poor QOL. I personally would've preferred units to have been more generalist or more specialised instead of being a flat scissors paper rock scenario that echos through all tiers of units with the exception of the hero units. Perhaps if abilities were made less costly and there were more emphasis on their use and timing their use - perhaps the basic SPR combat could be redeemed.On the subject of QOL, units not fighting back when engaged by other units or having some form of a "guard stance" to attack approaching/nearby enemies is certainly an odd choice. Not being able to talk or type to allies in multiplayer games is also another questionable choice. There's more other small issues sprinkled throughout, but I'm sure in time these can be ironed out.Now as for the positive recommendation, the game itself is sound, it can be fun frantically trying to micromanage your units across the map, ensuring you're building the right buildings on your points and making "manoeuvres" that get the better of your opponents. The ability to customise your units paint as well as build your own maps is a welcome feature set and the campaign is pretty enjoyable with some really well done in-game cutscenes. Overall it's a decent game, just maybe not yet worth the price tag and requiring some more time in the oven for balancing and QOL.

_childDocuments_.review: I approached this game with an open mind, tried the various game modes including the campaign. I got it very cheaply, and my initial impression was that it is a decent game, but simply not worth more than 20 or so euros. At this stage I don't think it's worth your time even if you can get it for free.Out of all the RTS that I have played, I think DoW2 comes closest to this one. Both the scale and the overal design philosophy feels very similar. Unfortunately, it had none of the quality and nuances that DoW2 had. As such the game just fails in almost every category. This is the first AoS RTS I have tried, and probably the first AoS RTS on the market. I think for that reason, the developers tried to play it as safe as possible and not rock the boat by coming up with new and fresh gameplay mechanics, hoping to hook people into the setting more than the actual game. For example, You could not been more rock-paper-scissors than this game, it is basically spelled out to you during the initial stage of the campaign. Defenders beat archers, archers beat attackers, and attackers beat defenders. You then have three 'tiers' of unit who all fall into any of the three aforementioned roles. Some units can fly, most unit have some special ability or the other, but that's... it really. Even the heroes don't really feel that special, and many abilities are copy-pasted, with a slightly different visual effect.The combat has one crucial aspect I didn't like, and that's being locked in melee the moment you get into arms length of an enemy unit. You can forget about controlling your unit. It would have been less of an issue if we actually had formations, and the pathfinding of groups and multiple units was better, but as it stands your precious ranged units will get stuck in combat, unless you order them to retreat... Which, for some absurd reason, costs resources. The result is that combat isn't fun or interesting, when combined with the combat triangle above, what you are left with is a situation in which you can easily predict how a fight goes, and besides retreating or activating one ability, there's not much tactical depth as to what you can do next. No micro or better positioning to outplay your opponent. At that stage combat becomes less of an interesting gameplay feature, and more of a major annoyance. Unit preservation isn't really key here either, units regenerate lost health and models ridiculously slow, and there is no veterancy. I don't understand why they bothered with a retreat mechanic at all. It's just best to let your units die and replace them.This game does look good though, almost as good as some RPGs from ten years ago. For some reason it reminds me of Dragon Age: Inquisition. But the overal design and atmosphere feels very bleak, and the color palette isn't varied. They did a great job at the modelling of the units, but then watching them in action is a bit of a let-down. It's cool for the first few battles, but there are no gory sync kills which the DoW series was so well known for. The models of units look good, but the buildings look terrible, and their size feels out of place with the rest of the game world.Like with DoW2, you can expect basebuilding to be very minimal, and it is. You have a 'main base' that contains only headquarters, from which you can recruit and upgrade units. Across the map there are capturable points on which you can construct all of 4 different building types. This usually means a building that can generate a blue resource, a building that can generate an orange resource (dow 2 anyone?) and then usually a watch-tower of some kind, and and a structure that can reveal the fog of war. This is true for all 4 of the factions, with some minor differences here and there. Lack of faction diversity doesn't end there. For all the three unit types, across 3 different tiers of units, you have about 9 units per faction. It doesn't help that factions don't have unique army abilities or faction mechanics either. All is tied up with how they look and their units and that's it.I will say that this game feels well optimized, and the menus look good and thematic. I do believe that this game had potential. I mean, it never was the next milestone in RTS history mind you, but a game designed with this scale could have worked better if the combat and pathfinding was good. That at least to me, seems fixable at this stage. Then they could have introduced better mechanics later on.The campaign is ultimately what made me stop playing. At one point, you had a scenario in which you could control only one hero, and you basically have to avoid combat altogether in order to win. You also have to move through a corridor-like map. That particular scenario reveals so much at what is wrong with the game, because if your hero dies you lose. Then you have the locking-in-combat mechanic I described above... see where I'm going? The cutscenes are also cringeworthy. At one point your hero dies in a rather dramatic way, and we have to pretend to care about this particular character even though she had 5 minutes of screentime. Then another cutscene feels very drawn out, involving two orcs plotting what they'll do next. It had me alt-tabbing. I don't know, I feel like game takes itself too seriously. Finally, there are strange difficulty spikes, which makes me think that the AI doesn't play by the same rules as I do, I mean the enemy can suddenly replenish a lot of units and deploy more units than I can, inflating the difficulty in ways that can't be described as 'fun.' The only thing the campaign did well, is that you get to play from the perspective of all the available factions, so at the start you'll be playing sigmarines, but at one stage you get to play as Tzeetch and then as the orks. Good idea, but unfortunately since the rest of the game is so weak, this feature cannot save the campaign, or the game for that matter.This game is devoid of soul and substance. You can save yourself some time and skip this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a love letter to the tabletop version, which is both good and bad at the same time.The campaign is pretty good (haven't finished it all yet), voice acting is great and cinematics are very pretty.There are few complaints out there that units are not responsive. I think this mostly comes from the design choice of mimicking the tabletop melee rule set.Once your troops engaged in melee they can not break out of it unless you retreat them. I think when ppl get used to this it can deepen the tactics and how you approach encounters.Melee units are not very keen to engage in a fight unless you tell them to do so.This one is interesting, not sure if the aggro range is too small or when if you send them with move command they end movement with stand guard mode. This not indicated anywhere, so one can only guess. Range units will only fire in the arc you positioned them.This is again a design choice mimicking the tabletop.It will force you to position your troops better.Some say that this game is slow... I don't think it is true... Definitely feels sticky due the above reasons mentioned, but also micro heavy because of the unit abilities and the fact that you will need to baby sit your troops.This is not a base building strategy in the classic sense like what you would expect is SC or AoE, but also not like a CoH game where your base is just there to unlock new troops.Here buildings can be built across the map on set points which are also resource nodes and some of these building come with functionality as well apart from just providing resources.For example you can heal your troops.The game also includes a map editor and an army painter which both are very welcome.To sum it up, I think this is a very well made game and the future potential is great.What remains the question is how well the multiplayer gonna be balanced, and whatever units will have use in lower tiers as well (eg not just racing top tier... first wins)

_childDocuments_.review: I definitely recommend this game. It is definitely simpler than most other RTS games, but the chief complaint (locked combat) is how the tabletop works; you have to force engagements and be tactical knowing a unit will only be able to retreat after it has been engaged.Personally, I don't need a carbon copy of Age of Empires; I already have the best version of that kind of game. I want something that fills a different niche, and this delivers. It nails the theme and setting, has very immersive units (the small roster is not a big deal considering the attention given to what is provided), and delivers well on the campaign.That said, it would benefit from a cover system and currently has some very frustrating bugs that cause inconsistency when trying to use a mouse and keyboard. Frankly, the controller is pretty comfortable to use. It's just less efficient, and efficiency is king.

_childDocuments_.review: In period of RTS famine, the game will still allow RTS and Warhammer aficionados to enjoy themselves.The game is clearly a meat grinder, (at least in single-player) you spam units, sending them off to die, until you slowly gain the upper hand.Pros:-Atmosphere-Graphics (for an RTS)-Soundtrack (voice, music, ambiance...)-Combat feeling ==> eally good-Non-stop actionA scripted campaign, pretty cool cutscenes (well, we're happy with them at a time when 3/4 of all games ignore single-player).Cons :-Limited content (not enough units per faction, 4 factions "only")-Units that die too quickly (this is more personal)-The campaign... Why didn't they apply the 30% speed boost to the campaign?-A few details (can't skip dialogues, UI, not enough explanatory info...)-The micro and unit response...It feels more like a total war than a classic RTS. And this can be surprising at first (once your units are engaged...You can only disengage them by sending them sprinting back to base, which is...surprising.)I'm hopeful that the content issue, the UI problems and a few equlibration points will be resolved, then the game will be very good. _childDocuments_.review: An excellent RPG with even more potential.The map and objective system play a lot like Company of Heroes 2, but very well executed in a high fantasy setting.The unit rosters are consistent across all four initial factions leaving a lot of potential for the remaining AoS factions. The combat system is fair (ranged has advantage against swords, which has advantage against shields, etc) without any single unit being an absolute answer to the other. If you're outnumbered or facing a more elite unit, these advantages don't make you crumble and allows for thought into lore as much as strategy when considering what units to invest in.The factions themselves are diverse in what they specialize in and allows fans of the tabletop and books to utilize approaches that veterans of those factions outside of this game will come into just as comfortably as players new to the AoS IP.People who are new to AoS will get a good introduction to the lore. People familiar with the lore will appreciate the homework the writers did in the campaign. The custom army painter uses the GW paint line (2023) which will allow ease of understanding if you plan to use your custom scheme in your tabletop army.I only give it a 9/10 because everything that could make it complete remains to be added in the very very near future.
