_childDocuments_.review: I'll start by saying the game is absolutely not worth its price tag, the "deluxe bonus" take this to a sick joke, the heroes dlcs add insult to injury for they are not only not worth it but a very scummy practice, especially at this price tag.This being said, there is a lot to enjoy here though among many flaws.Everything pertaining to the artistic domain is great, this being graphics, sounds, music and writing. Perfectly on-point adaptation of the Age of Sigmar universe, good characters and story, good and faithful visuals, nice musics and sound effects. For fans or afficionados of the universe, you're going to love this rendition.Gameplay-wise it's a bit more complicated.Core mechanics are solid though maybe a bit too common with a triangle of units (shield units beat bow, bow beat sword, sword beat shield, at least in theory for in practice it gets more complex), ressource nodes to capture and build a building of four varieties upon (two different ressource mines, automated turret, healing area), buildings that can be upgraded along your base camp that'll also unlock more units and upgrades for your units, units and upgrades that'll be useful to seize more nodes and victory points that you must keep under your control to score victory.The controls are globally elegant, the game is reasonably simple to learn and navigate but the map is made in such a way it is really hard to keep track of your units and what is happening on the board, espacially given you must micro manage everything for your troops are not much more than dummies without orders most of the time. It will still create a very interesting environment for strategy for the way you position your units and have them move around the map is absolutely paramount to victory.The campaign adds various twists and objectives to the formula each chapter and have you play with three of the four factions present in the game. Which keeps things new and interesting all along but also create a lot of chaos for events you couldn't foresee will totally mess up your strategy, regularly obliging you (at least me) to play again, this time planning forward for the scenarized turns and added objectives along the ride.About objectives, the lack of tactical pause is sorely missing in the campaign. Often I found myself completely overwhelmed, not having time to decipher the map and make sense of the various markers, especially when new ones keep spawning along with new objectives. The problem mostly disappear when you replay a chapter and I could complete many of them on my first try on normal difficulty still but sometimes it really dulled the pleasure of discovery. Same thing for discovering new units and upgrades which I just had not the time to reflect upon nor even read before the situation escalated again.The various obstacles and objectives of the campaign are still quite interesting and the challenge very satisfying to overcome but sometimes going in blind is also very frustrating at times.Overall I enjoyed the story and faithful rendition of the universe a lot, in fact I love it and I want my Realms of Ruin Stormcast minis.The gameplay of the campaign though is a mixed bag as I explained above. It has great moments though and I really liked beating all those chapters one after another, triumphing of things I first dimmed impossible to overcome.What is easier to recommend though is the conquest mode. A mode where you'll fight various encounters with all sorts of modifiers with your faction of choice against the other three. Gameplay-wise it is much more enjoyable though less diverse and cinematic than the campaign for it is "just" you playing the game versus an opponent, without scenaristic events suddenly changing the course of the battle and on equilibrated maps.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend if it's on sale. Full price is a bit much.I think a couple things would make this a truly good game.1. Larger units. It's more visually fun when you have units of 10 running around instead of 4. This opens options for the reinforce system as was done in Dawn of War.2. Retreat system redone. Before a unit dies you can have them retreat to heal. Generally good. The problem is that the unit will run all the way across the map to your main base. If it was set up so that they retreated until they were a certain distance away from all enemy units it would be far more effective. With large maps sometimes it's better to just queue up a few units and let the ones across the map die. The timeframe for the retreat, then healing, then running all the way back across the map is just too long. Summoning another unit takes maybe a third of the time.3. No tactical pause. Even an experienced RTS player can recognize that especially early on when you are learning the game it is good to be able to really delve into the micro instead of playing a chapter four times in a row.4. Scrolling. Some people have a differing opinion on close-screen like in Starcraft. Personally, it really helps to be able to see more of the map at once. Helps a lot with both micro and macro.TLDR; Fairly fun with systems (like retreat) that desperately need a rework. They should take a look at the standard features of other RTS (they could learn a thing or two from Dawn of War 2) and it would greatly improve the overall quality.

_childDocuments_.review: Following in the foot-steps of its obvious inspiration, ,  seems like it could actually be a really good game. At least to a Warhammer and RTS fan craving more of each. However, do not be fooled by the visuals. It’s a terrible game and certainly not worth its asking price. I’m not even sure I’d recommend it on sale. While it looks pretty, the game is ultimately shallow and a chore to play which results in more frustration and tedium than any semblance of fun. If you had a choice between playing this game or cleaning your bathroom you should choose cleaning your toilet 100% of the time and you’d still be exposed to less ♥♥♥♥ than if you played this game.The story mostly follows the Stormcast Eternals faction, Warhammer Age of Sigmar’s fantasy version of Warhammer 40K Space Marines. There is just a small battalion left on a crusade against Orks and the campaign follows the various grand battles, sieges, and skirmishes that take place between the two factions. Interestingly, the story shifts POV several times and even follows the Orks for a time, allowing the player to see firsthand how they become a threat to the Stormcast Eternals. While most missions take place between these two factions there are two other factions in the game: the Nighthaunt – pretty much the undead – and the Tzeentch chaos faction. While the Nighthaunt doesn’t get a POV in the campaign, they’re an enemy in quite a few missions. Tzeentch on the other hand is a playable faction for a few missions in the campaign, however it is told in story as a vision being watched by the magician character.Anyways, the story isn’t really all that special, but it at least seems Warhammer enough with some twists here and there. The story was never really the driving force to keep me going but It at least had something there for a reason to fight in each mission.Although where the game and story overlapped was one of the first areas that made me hate the game. In-game cutscenes. The actual cinematics are fine (when they didn’t crash on me, more on that later). But whenever there was a scene in the middle of a mission using in-game models I contemplated uninstalling the game and never seeing it again. First – the game actually continued while it forced you to watch the scene play. This meant a battle can continue happening beyond your control and by the time the scene ends your unit may be dead since you weren’t able to deal with the battle. Secondly – while the cinematics are skippable, the in-mission scenes are not. If you have to restart because of some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like the above, a timer, or some other reason for a failed mission then have fun watching the scenes again because you can’t skip it!Game looks fine, I’ll give it that. Part of what made me want to play it was that visually it looked interesting and reminded me of  but with a flavor of Age of Sigmar, Admittedly, I do not know much about Age of Sigmar and played only one other game with it, so I wanted to know more. But unfortunately, it does not have nearly the same kind of staying power as . At least I got to see what various Age of Sigmar units look like? is a real-time strategy game where the strategy revolves around unit caps, composition of the army based on these caps, and map placement to hold various strategic resource points all while completing objectives. On paper, this sounds good. Even the units are described as having a sort of rock-paper-scissors dynamic of melee, ranged and shields.This last point is also where things immediately fall apart. The game balance absolutely does not reflect this triangle. Instead, ranged is simply king and will beat literally everything: melee, shields and other ranged. What is the point of melee and shields if the ranged unit will just obliterate them before they ever reach it? Oh yeah, unit speeds (at least in campaign, I did not bother with other modes) is also pretty slow, just more icing on the cake.The ranged units are actually kind of fun and pretty satisfying to use – especially the chaos flamers and horrors. At least when you’re actively using them. All too often I will have units just stand around doing nothing while an enemy is in range because they’re looking slightly to the right. Worse, sometimes they could actively be shot and still just stand there instead of pursuing the ranged unit attacking them. There seems to be a lack of any kind of guard mode and playing defense is just very frustrating and unresponsive. And you will definitely have to play defense, way more than you want to. Many missions involve holding several points at once which is like a terribly unfun game of whack-of-mole. You take a point, leave to take the next one. And already the enemy respawned double your number and take the point back. So you absolutely have to leave squads at your points and hold them while you send another to actively take new points. With the unit cap, this can even seem impossible at times. This was never clearer than the first mission against the nighthaunt – I believe it was mission 3 or 4? The enemies spawn endlessly with no way to shut them off while you’re supposed to simultaneously hold and defend three points. It was painful.A tip for any poor unlucky soul who actually plays this game – focus on upgrading your HQ over anything else. That raises your unit cap. The game is actually playable when you have enough units to defend multiple points. Still absolutely tedious and annoying though. Don’t expect any kind of blitzkrieg assault here. No, the campaign is a slog where each mission will feel like you’re slowly crawling to victory via a war of attrition as you scramble your units across the game of whack-a-mole. I will admit there are some cool moments or ideas here or there. But every time I want to praise the game, I’m immediately hit by another reason to be like “oh that’s right it’s still crap – just a polished turd.” I think it’s poor design when sometimes it’s just actively better to ignore the mission you’re given. For example, there is a “boss” encounter where you are meant to capture several locations to weaken it. I tried to do that and it just became an endless battle where the enemy was able to overwhelm me and take it back. So I looked up online and saw other people had the same problem. They all recommended to ignore that objective and to just attack the boss at its’ full strength instead. I did that and had a much better time. Amazing. I was just happy to no longer play the game.The game crashed to desktop on almost every cinematic for me. Actual game ran fine and I could watch the cutscene once I loaded back in.Operating System: Windows 10Processor (CPU): Intel Core i5-3570K CPU @3.40GHzGraphics Card (GPU): NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070Memory (RAM) 16 GBGAME BAD. Absolutely not a full-price game, what the hell were they thinking with that price point? I’m aware I kept playing it even though it’s a bad game. But I certainly do not recommend anyone else doing that. It was just a mixture of sunk cost fallacy and a desperation for Warhammer RTS content with a curiosity for Age of Sigmar. Well, my curiosity was satisfied. But at what cost? Sixty dollars and some wasted hours. Not the end of the world but figured I might as well help someone else save their own money on this mediocre title. What’s truly disappointing is that it could have been good with just some effort on making the game actually fun to play, but oh well.

_childDocuments_.review: Enormously satisfying RTS game with fast, frantic gameplay. Expect to lose, even on normal difficulty, until you get the hang of it, which can take a little while as your brain adapts to the way it is played. It isn't like age of empires, with base building and peasants gathering resources. It's about expanding and holding strategically important territory and deciding what to do with it (gather resources, defend, heal, etc).The apparent "con" of this game is the fact that your units won't attack, even if being attacked from range. The reason for this is because units become battle locked and so the game wouldn't want your units wandering off and getting locked into battle without your commands. Thus, it is important to keep a close eye on what is happening as you zoom around the map attending to this or that node and the units guarding/fighting for it.People are saying it's like Dawn of War. No idea, since I've never played that, so for me, this is an entirely new RTS experience and well worth the money. It's a clean, polished game with an addictive gameplay loop that will keep you engaged.Each non-campaign scenario shouldn't take you more than 30-40 minutes, so it's good to play in small bites as needed and doesn't NEED to be played for hours on end.To help get you started, here are 5  tips that aren't immediately apparent, nor are they covered in the otherwise excellent tutorial:- Nodes are CAPTURED at 1%. It does not need to be at 100% to be owned by you (or your enemy). By standing your unit(s) in the control zone, the control zone expands. As it does, not only does its radius expand, but its power expands (ie, a resource node will net you more resources the more it is expanded).- The retreat command appears to have a global cooldown, NOT a unit cooldown IF you have a whole group selected (if the units are separately selected, it appears to be a single-unit cooldown).- While being upgraded, nodes (or your base) will stop working (ie, they will stop healing units or gaining resources for the duration of the upgrade).- Tier 1 units become obsolete as the game goes, and by mid-game it is better to let them die to make room for your bigger units- Commands you give units are NOT automatic and take a second to "kick in." So if you are waiting until the absolute last second to activate a shield, for instance, you will probably lose that unit. Anticipation is important, so activate your abilities in good time so as not to activate it, spend resources, and then lose the unit anyway because it didn't activate fast enough.That's it! Have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: The game has definite potential:The 4 factions stand out and have their own playstyle.Visually, it's beautiful.However, there are some serious shortcomings that would make it pass as a small independent game. The price of 60 euros reminds us that this is not the case:Balancing is completely absent. You can control the map, fortify points to strengthen your economy, but you will still lose if your opponent reaches tier 3 where 3 units are enough to destroy your army. It's stupid, frustrating, and above all, not at all strategic. One wonders if balancing tests have been done.In multiplayer, you cannot communicate in writing with your ally. Yes, you read that right. You can't chat. There aren't even ping options.The maps are dull. They all look the same, and the map design deserves significant improvement.Some point fortifications are useless. Literally. There are points where units can heal. But they can't decide to make it their retreat point. Points meant to defend the conduit are ridiculously weak and can be easily breached for a cost that corresponds to more than 4 Tier 1 units.Multiplayer modes are sadly few. 1v1 and 2v2, and that's it.In short, like Darktide, this game can really improve, and I sincerely hope that the team will offer a roadmap worthy of the name to correct these issues.Without that, I can't decently recommend this title. If you're hungry for a good RTS like me, reinstall Dawn Of War 1 or 2 or go play Company of Heroes. But steer clear of Age of Sigmar.

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes a game appears that keeps us glued to the screen for hours with great graphics and a fantastic gameplay experience. And sometimes a game is released that we talk about with our friends for weeks to come. With Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin, however, a game was finally released that rekindled my long-lost love of analog tabletop gaming. That is a real rarity. Positive things about Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin+ Greatly written characters that fit perfectly into the Age of Sigmar universe+ Tactically very challenging game mechanics, especially on higher difficulty levels+ Various entertaining game modes that require tactical mastery of the game's tactical mechanics+ An army editor AND a map editor! + A fantastic soundtrack, probably one of the best this year+ Brilliant sound design and perfect voice acting + Exciting story that fits very well into the Age of Sigmar universeNegatives about Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin- The army selection is sufficient with 4 starting armies, but not a good representation of the massive variety of the Age of Sigmar universe- Base building is even less than in games like Warhammer 40 000: Dawn of War II- For even more tactical depth, units need more functions, positions, formations, etc.- The multiplayer aspect of PvP, PvE and PvPvE can be expanded. Examples such as 3v3 and higher or 8 players all against all are still missingIn conclusion, I can say that Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin is the perfect introduction to the tabletop hobby of the same name and the incredibly gigantic lore of the Age of Sigmar universe. Veterans can lead new armies across the digital battlefield for their next project and try out new color schemes with the army editor. Let your creativity run wild! A BIG thank you to the developers at Frontier Developments for adapting the Age of Sigmar universe into a digital strategy game with unparalleled love and respect for the original.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid base game with incredible potential.Realms of Ruin is a gorgeous forray into fantasy Warhammer. The game is played out in a series of strategic skirmishes that rely more on meaningful decisions than on digging through upgrade trees and menus (not that those types of things are missing). Once you understand these decisions the game becomes very fun - but it does not do a great job of teaching you initially.The game's tutorial is composed of a few missions that cover some of the basics. It's an arguably slow introduction with very little decision making that spikes in difficulty on the third map. The first time I played it I lost and it felt bad. I had spent two missions diligently doing as I was told, just to be dropped in the deep end. Then I replayed it using what I had learned - and it felt great! I wish those first three maps had all been like smaller versions of the third, each with more decision making related to an aspect of the game, like resource management, troop composition, building types, etc.Once you are out of those first missions the gameplay opens up and you get a variety of objectives that range from tower defense style "stop the enemies", to controlling points on wide open fields. Missions will have primary objectives, extra bonus objectives, and usually some surprises along the way.There is very little hand holding, aside from your leaders occasionally reminding you about what needs to be done. If you want to go brute force you can. If you want to try and scout things out first, by all means. But if you choose to run a unit to its death because you ignored the game's "rock-paper-scissors" style mechanic the game is as unforgiving as it is happy to let you try (and maybe you have a strategic reason to try?...)A unit committed to combat is "stuck" in combat till they die or retreat. This type of mechanic is very common in tabletop games such as the one this is based on. Retreating has a cost, and should be treated like losing the fight and trying to salvage some resources. While this seems harsh on the surface, this mechanic is strategically huge and means you can tie up enemy units with combat as well. If some massive threat is heading for a victory point even the smallest goblin in his way can give you time to respond.Overall it's a fun game with incredible production value. It's not perfect, and could be clearer in explaining many of its important aspects to you before you learn them through trial and error. It's got great characters and a solid story in an interesting universe. And while it can feel punishing at times, it's also very rewarding and gives you a lot of freedom.As an aside: Having played in both the private and open Beta, as well as early access - I have seen this game grow by leaps and bounds. Feedback has been implemented, the game has run considerably better every time, and quality of life has grown as well. I hope the game continues to grow, because it would not be hard to erase my complaints of the game just communicated a little better.

_childDocuments_.review: As a Warhammer fan who has been playing Warhammer Fantasy in various iterations since the 90s I felt compelled to check this game out. My very first impressions of this game could be summed up as "Wow, this looks and sounds great but the combat feels a bit slow, where are my base building options?" But after pouring 30+ hours in this game I can say it's pretty damn good and I'm really excited to see what they do with it down the road. I'm glad I stuck with it and learned to appreciate the different and nuanced approach to the RTS genre. I was a bit disappointed at first, but in the course of playing many matches with friends I came to really respect and appreciate the approach that Frontier took with this game. The game makes tactical management of each engagement very interesting with it's various skill shots, importance of positioning your units as well as your overall army composition. At first I felt the game was a bit light on upgrades but then I realized how significant some of these choices can be - the ability to make a unit a stealth unit, or maybe just give them more damage and defense - it might seem small at first but combined with the grander vision of the game some interesting strategies emerge. Each engagement, at higher difficulties, becomes crucial in terms of long-term strategy. Positioning your troops feels more like tabletop when engaging in combat. Don't listen to the Age of Sigmar haters, the game is solidly built on a good RTS foundation that is really solid and fun in it's current iteration. It's not Age of Empires or Starcraft, and it's not trying to be. This, I believe, is ultimately a good thing. Frontier sets out to capture the feel of the world and the spirit of the table top game combat, and I think they did those things very well. I'm personally looking forward to seeing where they go with this game, would love to see additional factions for the 4 alliances.

_childDocuments_.review: My experience with Realms of Ruin left me feeling like it straddles two genres without fully embracing either. It features the combat rules, unit counts, and slow movement typical of a pure tactics game on a map scaled for an RTS, yet it lacks depth in tactics or strategy. It harkens back to strategy games from the early days before they were refined in the 90s. The gameplay feels simplistic, akin to a game of rock-paper-scissors where each move is predictable with only one counter available. Considering its premium price tag, I expected more depth and polish, especially with superior Warhammer strategy games already available. Like its lengthy title, Warhammer: Age of Sigmar - Realms of Ruin feels somewhat overwhelming and could benefit from significant refinement.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly disappointed by this game. While the visual of this game are fantastic and quite stunning it does nothing to make up for the lack of quality of life features standard to any RTS game. To provide specific examples: units in this game have no auto engage feature, meaning that your units will not move from their position to engage enemy units regardless of circumstance. This includes sustaining ranged damage, witnessing friendly units become engaged in melee, and watching as enemy units walked right by. This coupled with the fact that the game also has a poor auto alert system to inform you of units taking damage means that a player can become distracted or focused on other engagements. I experienced an incident during the campaign where I was battling the orks across 3 victory points. While I was playing and microing between 2 separate engagements a powerful enemy unit attacked my third group of warriors. As I was distracted I did not notice this fact until I happened to glance at the map and saw a giant red triangle next to my strong point. curious I panned the camera up there to witness one of my heroes and one of my ranged units torn apart in two separate engagements all while my prosecutors stood there helplessly. This was a frustrating experience because together my army would have been capable of winning the fight but they were defeated in detail. The reason this frustrates me so is due to the fact that many other RTS games feature units with stances. Stances that allow for some degree of autonomy or some form of auto engagement range. The typical stance includes moving withing a reasonable distance to engage enemy units that are spotted or to respond aggressively to ranged damage. Had a feature like that been implemented then a lone enemy unit walked into my battle line would have resulted in death and not a victory. That was one example of many concerning features that other, older RTS's possessed. Even if the QOL features were present the game still fights itself in many ways. Heroes play a vital role in the game for their damage dealing capabilities and durability for a single model. Heroes achieve this through skills and abilities, all of which are active abilities. That means that the player must push a button in order to benefit. This is standard to any RTS however, this game features one of the most frustrating and poorly designed UI's I have experienced. There is a very small unit hot bar that displays abilities for a single unit that is currently selected. This means that in order to cycle between abilities you must cycle through units. The game does feature use of the tab button in order to switch between selected units but even that doesn't work most of the time. Due to the games poor optimization and general slowness I have noticed that many times I will press the tab button and one of two things will happen. Either nothing will occur or I will swap between 2-3 units all in one go. This makes managing hero abilities difficult and reduces overall army effectiveness. Considering that every unit in the game has an ability further complicates the issue. On a different note the game is heavily miss-marketed and does not feel like an RTS, it feels more like a MOBA or some form of squad based hero game like Dawn of War 2. While that is not inherently bad the games execution of this design is poor and lacking. Dawn of War 2 featured a fantastic UI with easily accessible hot keys and the game kept the player very well informed of what was happening at all times. Dawn of War 2 also featured wide open RTS themed maps. Realms of Ruin features MOBA themed maps with a heavy emphasis on lanes and tower construction. Continuing on to the single player experience, the first few missions of the game were interesting, they all possessed unique objectives that severed to introduce the player to basic core mechanics. Following the first 3 missions the game abandons that formulae and instead replaces it with generic skirmish based objectives. "Here go play tug of war for the third time for 20-30 minutes against a brain dead AI that will give up halfway through the match." All in all I feel that for the price the developers are asking for the game falls incredibly short of the mark. While a great multiplayer experience can be had with the right people all other aspects of the game-play are lacking and yield frustration.To surmise I do not recommend this game for a few reasons.1. I feel that the game was marketed as an RTS when it is more like a MOBA.2. The UI and lack of QOL features present in many other RTS games make the experience poor and frustrating.3. The game is poorly optimized for how little occurs and how slow it happens.4. For the price point of $60.00 the single player experience is lacking and heavily inflated with un-fun and boring skirmish missions.

_childDocuments_.review: Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin promised a strategic experience set in the rich, immersive world of Age of Sigmar, but it falls short of expectations, especially when it comes to gameplay depth.The most glaring issue is the overly simplistic gameplay. Strategy games should reward careful planning and tactical maneuvers, but Realms of Ruin leans heavily on basic, repetitive mechanics that leave little room for real strategy. Unit variety is limited, and the combat feels unchallenging, with simple commands and straightforward objectives that don’t evolve as the game progresses. This leaves experienced strategy players with little to keep them engaged, and even newcomers to the genre might find the lack of depth disappointing.While the game visually captures the feel of the Age of Sigmar universe, this isn’t enough to make up for the shallow mechanics. Battles lack intensity and feel more like routine skirmishes than epic confrontations. Additionally, the lack of meaningful customization options for units or strategies means each battle can feel almost identical to the last, making it difficult to stay invested in the long term.The storyline has potential, but it fails to elevate the experience when paired with such lackluster gameplay. Instead of a gripping narrative that drives players through the game’s campaign, the plot feels secondary to repetitive missions and uninspired encounters.Overall, Realms of Ruin feels more like a missed opportunity than a worthy addition to the Warhammer universe. For a game set in such a rich world, it fails to deliver the depth and challenge that fans might expect. Unfortunately, it’s hard to recommend this game to anyone looking for a satisfying strategy experience. I’d give it a 4/10.

_childDocuments_.review: So despite some of the bad reviews, I decided to try this game. So far it reminds me of Dawn of War 2...as there is pretty much no base building, you have hero units and the goal seems to be to keep your units around so you can upgrade them. Also, as noted by others the units move kind of slow. If you want Starcraft 2 clicks per minute...you will be dissapointed. If you want a slower paced, and more tactical game, then I would say this scratches that itch. That said the story seems like hot garbage and the main character is sigrun who is a female space marine...who basically looks like a guy but has a womans voice. Like...this is a stupid addition to the game that does not make sense lore wise, nor does it make sense physically. Wokeness is seriously infecting video games at this point..and the voice actor sounds as bored with the story as I am...this is not a space epic...this is a moldy sci fi comic with half the pages unreadable...(so if story is your thing then avoid this game). IF you just wanna go out and kill some orcs and other enemies though...it is pretty decent. Would I pay full price for this game? Not really. It is polished, the graphics are nice, and all and I do like the gameplay...but 80 bucks? no. With a huge discount though, this game is amazing for 15 bucks. I spent some of the money I saved on the DLC pack characters for 12 more dollars. This is my main issue with these Warhammer games...they release a half-baked game for full price and then nickel and dime you with DLC. My practice now is to wait a year and buy everything for half the price of the game upon release (DLC included) and then you get your value for money. All in all, this is a good game and I recommend it but only when heavily discounted because we should not reward their predatory business practices and buy it new for way more money than it is worth. Yes I get that I am supporting the dev with my purchase...but only for what I believe the game is worth and only a year after it released. Caveat emptor regarding the story/woke inclusion of female space marines...but otherwise a fun game.

Its mostly about the decisions you make, BEFORE you start fighting ie have you put your soldiers in the right place, do you have enough of them, are you ready to counter what the enemy will probably bring. There are also a bunch of abilities etc to change the tide while in the scum of things. This positional nature can lead to frustrations when units will sit around watching the fighting. _childDocuments_.review: DON’T think RTS. DON’T think MOBA. That’s the perspective you need to 'click' with this game. A few things have changed (all for the better), so I thought I should quickly update (original review below)- Recent changes mean units/gameplay *much* more responsive.- Retreat mechanic now works instantly, and is much better for it.- DLC content is excellent.- IMPORTANT - DLC are *side-grades*, not upgrades - you have to select them in place of something else.- Frontier have stuck to their word: fixed bugs, produced patches, some initial balancing and overall game play improvement. More to be done, but looks like they are committed.TL;DR - Its still a great game and keeps getting better.  There are many, many games with Warhammer IP. Most are just Game X skinned with Warhammer IP. RoR is the first time I’ve felt a game is 'Warhammer First'.  I’ve logged over 50 hours now, enough for a helpful review. And I’m glad I waited because it didn’t really ‘click’ until I’d spent about ten hours playing.  This game takes time to get into.  So, The Good, Bad and Ugly.  This feels like you’re playing Warhammer but in real time. It’s easy enough to jump in, but quite quickly, you discover there’s a lot of strategy to figure out. The depth is there but is not where a typical RTS might focus. All factions are unique (thanks, GW), but the balance is pretty good. Some dominate early games, some late, and each has a distinct idiom, but there is no dominant faction. Units are fully fleshed out (and very close to their TT counterparts). There are exciting synergies and various tactics that will feel natural for a WH player. Important:The game uses some noteworthy mechanics – Lock in (or retreat) combat, no ‘stances’ or other auto-behaviour. You must commit to your fights and closely watch the mini-map. Fog of War, space, position, timing, distance from retreat point, etc. All factors in every decision to fight. There is more strategy going on than first meets the eye. These ‘features’ surprised many RTS fans (judging by other reviews), but Warhammer players will ‘get’ it. It *adds* to the game rather than take anything away. At first, it feels frenetic, but soon, you find it’s not APM-oriented. There’s plenty to do, but a player won’t get a massive advantage through multi-button-click-ability.  Strategy > Mechanical Skill, which is *exactly* what a WH game should be. The art design is fantastic; however, that’s not surprising as it’s mostly the hard work done by GW... But... that’s fine. Animations, visuals, audio, etc... all AAA. The campaign is fine (and quite challenging) if you like that sort of thing – but the multiplayer is where the real game shines through.  Every game feels different. The map editor and army colour scheme stuff is great – potentially, they could do more, but it’s really nice stuff to have in a WH game. I’ve had no crashes or serious bugs, although I’ve seen that some people have. The game length is also perfect at 20-30 mins. Re-playability – the more you play, the better it gets. There’s some frustration at first, but after the initial ‘hump’, the fun starts to snowball.  There’s not a lot that is outright wrong. The price, perhaps. Consoles, I understand (licensing and all that), but £50-60 is a touch steep for a PC. Now, IF a lot of future DLC is going to be free, ok. But with no roadmap announced, am I faced with another £10 for every new army? What’s my total investment likely to be? It looks like the pricing model is very similar to fighting games, a la Street Fighter.  I’m price-insensitive, and the game has proved to be brilliant. Others may feel differently. Money is a very personal thing. There’s only one game mode. It’s good, but I’d have expected a bit more variety, certainly for casual games. A point-based ‘annihilate’ mode seems an obvious miss. Performance is good for me (I have a top-end rig), but it still seems to be getting the old fans blowing, if you know what I mean. For a game that’s essentially a top-down RTS, Minor update: I tried it with DLSS/DLAA on, and it works very well - if you have an Nvidia card, I'd highly recommend trying DLSS - game seems more responsive, and notably increase in performance. This game has a few warts in its current state. It’s nothing game-breaking and all fixable, so it’s in this section. More audio/visuals for various events. Like if something comes under attack, etc. The UI default settings are not optimal – you can change the sizes of things, and I suggest you do. Bigger mini-map, smaller announcement banners (which frequently get in the way). There’s no ‘reconnect’ timer. A minor network glitch will kick you out, and you cannot get back in. A few maps are meat grinders and could do with some tweaking. The Battletome section isn’t well organised and could benefit from having all the in-game data available. The mini-map is ok but could be more detailed. Auto routing could be better in some cases. Even with manual movement, it’s tricky to have units avoid certain kinds of terrain. Just clipping it even slightly slows them down. There could be a better way to select a specific unit from a roster. The battalion creation feature is confusing. AI skirmishes –  AI improvements have improved this mode. In Summary Great game. It’s got an ‘opinion’ about what a Warhammer game should be, and I agree. I enjoy it more each time I play. Haven’t regretted spending the money.

_childDocuments_.review: Such a promising Gem of an RTS.Perfect launch, outstanding presentation & artistry, a true passion comes through all the features that are not gameplay.But it suffers from the greatest Sin of all recent big RTS imo: no Game Modes variety:- no annihilation mode- BFME style build-able but even more limited- no terrain corruption payoff for Controlling a part of the map, which can be very satisfying when other parts of gameplay are lacking. Paint the map is always fun.I dropped the game 2 weeks after launch, played the open beta & bought on Day1, I saw the potential and it was glorious.And now I'm coming back to play it, it is a good but lacking RTS.The Dawn of War vibes are strong with this one, and I wish it had gone the more creative route Relic always entertained with build-able defenses.I wish the devs had stuck with it, and developed it into a deeper, free-er style of gameplay like how Relic kept fixing the very rough Company of Heroes 3 post-launch.Sometimes, you just got to stick with it until it works.So unlike Company of Heroes 3, we can't follow the greatest development adventure and say "Yes, it's worth 60€". But it is a very solid game.I am recommending it because:1. I love RTS, and I want to see more.2. Realms of Ruin is one of the best RTS of recent years despite gameplay shortcomings... Realms of Ruin 2 or Big Faction Expansion better be a thing, otherwise such a waste of talent!Frontier, one advice: Stop going for dumb down gameplay. They throw you into a new army, having never played them, and give you a seemingly impossible task of killing this NPC before he reaches the end of a trail. I've almost killed him numerous times, but it always seems to have me fail the mission.I've watched a ton of videos and streams of people playing it, but I can't seem to do it myself no matter how well my units are set up.The only way I've actually won a match is playing 2v2 against 2 easy AI with a medium teammate.I give the game a 5/ 10 overall. If it weren't for the difficulty spike being so high, the game might be more successful and enjoyable for new players. But the high difficulty of the AI, even in the storyline, makes this game borderline unplayable in certain aspects if you don't know every hot key and have quick micromanagement skills.I don't recommend this game at all, even on a massive sale.

I also had several instances where units would stop short of where I'd clicked/needed them to go to trigger an action. I believe this is partially due to melee combat having a sort of vortex that will suck in nearby units even if they're not engaged.-Nearly all range units use a fixed arc of fire and act like stationary artillery pieces, this ends up with instances where they're unengaged and completely ignoring enemy units coming in beside them. This makes sense for the actual artillery pieces but not bow/crossbow/ranged magic units.I feel bad for the developers care was put into shaping the game and from a functional perspective it's in better shape that most new releases. _childDocuments_.review: This game is very reminiscent of DoW 2 and as someone who loves that game, that is a massive plus. The focus on combat and battles instead of building is very DoW 2 like. Some people are upset due to the lack of base building, which is understandable, to a certain extent. You ARE able to build a few things, ie. upgrades for control points (damage enemy units in your zone, command point gain increase, mineral increase and regen/replenish units.) There are also mass upgrades for units at the main command building where you can recruit units and purchase said upgrades. You must also upgrade the tier of your main base to access better units and better upgrades. This is VERY DoW 2 the only exception is that individual unit upgrades are gone. So your commander wont have 3-4 upgrade slots like DoW 2.The only couple of negative points I have, if they could even be considered negative, maybe more personal opinions. 1- Once your units engage in melee with another unit, they are unable to move until either one of them die. If they engage with 2 enemy units, both enemy units have to die before being able to move, or you knock them back far enough to allow freedom of movement. I say this because some units have MASSIVE damage aoe abilities and you cant micro manage the unit to dodge out of the way, its a guaranteed hit on that ability. 2- For some people the campaign will be EXTREMELY unfair and difficult. For story purposes some missions will be very unfair for the player, I've seen people in discussions complain about this constantly. On veteran at least, some missions take 3-4 tries minimum to get down since 1 mistake can escalate into a massive loss.  Side Note: Many players don't manually save during a mission and will lose causing you to start the ENTIRE mission over again. There is no checkpoint system, if you lose, you start the entire mission over. Just manual save and it will be fine.9/10 Final Verdict

_childDocuments_.review: So, I finished campaign and played couple of AI matches (yeah, good luck trying to find a match with a human being...) and... I stand exactly where I stood with the original review.It's not even an rts, it's more like MOBA with SOME rts elements but it's much closer to Warcraft Rumble than Company of Heroes.First things first.1) Story lacks introduction. There's no world setting as if creators made an assumption that everyone knows what are the realms, factions, how magic work and where the heck are we. I am a Warhammer 40k veteran and do know a thing or two about Age of Sigmar but... I felt a little lost at the beginning. I Imagine someone who knows less will be very, very lost.2) It's like Warhammer 40k: Down of War 3 just much worse. You are forced to play all the factions, the story is warhammerish and quite good but pacing and repetetive missions (capture points and hold them, yay) make it boring like hell. There's a lot of nuance missing from the game.3) The game's very uneven. Some missions are easy peasy, others are a challenge even on "normal" difficulty settings. That's because one must micromanage troops that die like mad due to awful lack of AI.4) Retreat... MAKE THE KEYBINDING DIFFERENT. It's one of the skillbuttons and it caused me retreat troops by accident...5) Lots of gameplay issues:- Enemy units spawning behind your lines- one troop can turn off your conduit as they don't defend themselves- Oversimplicity - you can beat any missions with two or three tank units and lots of ballistas- Enemy has unlimited amount of resources and thus will push wave after wave against you and You can't even replenish troops- Healing? Forget. Build a tower and run back every couple of minutes.Positives are the world as a whole, story is ok, so far, voice acting, models and all - huge plus.Anyway... _childDocuments_.review: It's a really good simple RTS, it brings me right back to the old Dawn of War days when RTS was really popular. Realms of Ruin really captures the "miniatures" vibe really well and when playing it feels like my hand painted minis have come to life and are battling it out! There is a lot of potential here with this game, currently Disciples of Tzeentch are very over powered, but once balanced I think they'll be a fun opponent to deal with, a lot of the complaints I see about the game are units being dumb and not attacking when attacked, I have had a different experience as I utilize the F + Left Click when moving my units around the field, this will cause them to attack anything in their path on the way to the destination. I also would really like to see a ping system or some form of communication with your team mate as currently as far as I can tell there is none, I would like to also see there be a shift towards multiplayer match stability as more often than I would like a match lobby just disconnects and the game is over. The graphics and attention to detail is immaculate and everything looks and sounds VERY Warhammer, I think the game is great, but a bit over priced for whats available at this time. This will be on to watch over the years!

_childDocuments_.review: I think I've never played a game that captures the tabletop experience in a real-time way as well in any game.  This is NOT RTS.  This is not Dow2, where keeping units as as This is RTT and I think it's that at its finest.  The reviews on this game are clearly not understanding what is going on or how the game is actually playing out.   It's much faster than total war, and you have fewer decisions that you are actually making during a total war game, but also the match length between 13-25 minutes is pretty refreshing.  The Nighthawk(a ghost race) are all about map control and using abilities with 3 heroes(they only have 1 ranged unit), the SCE are an elite army (similar to massing stalkers for sc2 players) are a tactical race like protoss about saving units and getting value, The tzeech are a tanky race which really hit hard with a punch with timings, the Kruleboyz are about hiding, setting up traps, ambushes and they have a good coverage of the types with no big weaknesses and no real early or mid timings..  They have monsters, can summon a wretch at tier 4, and they have the strongest tier 1 hero.  I love how the pvp games interplay.

_childDocuments_.review: So I give it an 8/10.My background:Thousands of Starcraft 2 Laddering matchesWarcraft 3 ladderingBrood war light ladderingDawn of War 3 hundreds of hours team games + 1v1'sOther Dawn of wars light ladderingTotal War: Warhammer 1,2,3Bit of company of heros 1 & 2.I've also played through the campaigns of most of these games.I would say I'm more of a multiplayer player. Review======The Good:It's a beautiful RTS -- great models and animations.The units are interesting the factions are asymmetrical, and fun. The heros and abilities are cool, with dragons lighting up 5 or 6 squads at a time. It's glorious.I love how the heros play.The 1v1 ranked mode has enough players to get games in >1 minute most of the time during normal hours. It seemed to dry up a bit around 1 am.The campaign is voice acted, and cool. I have a sense of urgency / purpose. It doesn't feel like, "go capture a point." It feels like, "Oh shoot I need to go save my scouts that got nabbed!" I like the writing.I played the first couple missions and started laddering, but it's a fun campaign.Neutral Things to Know:It plays like company of hero's 2. So when units get engaged in melee they don't break until you give them a retreat order.It' s a bit counter intuitive to just clicking away, but they get locked in melee unless you give the retreat order.Cons:====The execution needs to be better when giving orders to units in multiplayer. I need to be able to seamlessly send a charge command to my 5 units of chain rasps and have full confidence that the ability will fire.There feels like a missing piece of artillery. There isn't a form of artillery to batter down victory points. It's monsters, calvary, ranged, shielded, sworded.Summary:========I like the game. Will everyone like the game? No.If you need that immaculate polish of an old school blizzard title, that's perfectly responsive, you'll get frustrated.I think if you liked company of heros 2 or dawn of war 2, you'll probably like this game.If you're looking to try a new RTS this is a good one.The laddering system does work and has plenty of active players. The campaign is also great so far.I'd recommend it. I hope they polish it up more. It has a ton of potential. I love the game, and will keep playing. I also understand it may not be for everybody.8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough one. I love Warhammer, love Age of Sigmar, love strategy games. However, I have never been good at all with RTS games and Realms of Ruin has its issues. Immediately upon diving into this game I had flashbacks to Dawn of War 2 (To which all comparisons with this game are completely valid. They feel very similar) where I logged dozens of hours but never really knew what I was doing; I just liked watching Orks run around and shoot stuff.So moving through the early stages of the campaign was very frustrating for me. I felt constantly lost, like I just could not keep up with the AI. To my credit, the general consensus seems to be that Normal difficulty is a bit too difficult, so I don't feel like such an idiot. However, it's no fun to feel several steps behind at all times. And the game does not assist you much at all - it's hard to micromanage your units and they also aren't very smart. There have been many times where I saw one unit getting crushed while another unit stands by and watches. So that sucks.But when I swallowed my pride and knocked the difficulty down to easy, I found myself enjoying things a whole lot more. It's still a lot to keep up with at once, but I am getting better with the controls and (more importantly) I'm enjoying going through the story.Multiplayer is fine, but not really my cup of tea. I love the "create" options - that's a real big bonus for the game.So, long story short, I can recommend this game if you don't expect too much and the price isn't too high. That goes double if you're a fan of the setting. It's a treat to see the Mortal Realms come to life, especially da Kruleboyz. However if you want a game to change the way you think about the RTS genre, or give you a mind blowing story, or give you a nigh-infinite amount of depth and replayability, this ain't it.

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe I was hoping for something more dawn of war inspired, instead it has no real base building. The 'lockup' mechanic feels bad. The game at least for me, is simultaneously too fast and too slow. I generally prefer a defensive playstyle but there is no such thing in this game. You are on the attack constantly, you are having your troops be a revolving door from base, back to one of the points. It plays almost like a MOBA. Hero units with abilities that cost resources to use seems like a great way to make sure there is no comeback mechanic. I would've preferred longer cooldowns on them instead. I don't want to punish someone for doing well, but if you have the upper hand you can make sure the enemy feels it with little issue. Could be it's just not my style of game and I should stick more to SC2 or AoE, type of games. I just really wanted this one to be good and it doesn't feel as such. I would hate to see yet another Warhammer attempt at a strategy game just flop. (barring total war) I want there to be more strategy games but..not this constant moving about the battlefield. If your units get into contact with others you can no longer move them, your only recourse is to retreat all the way back to base. It feels like a poor knockoff of Ancestors Legacy, with all its problems but none of the redeeming qualities that made it fun. If there was an option to lengthen the game time for my single player experience. It might be a fantastic game, but I'm locked into a very (for me) mediocre experience. A stance setting wouldn't go amiss either so that perhaps units who I imagine have some will to live..don't just stand there taking arrows from off map while I'm busy moving other things around or recycling the next wave etc. I also experienced a few bugs where ballista in particular would be recruited and then just..not move. Like they were stuck in the spawn. I've lost a few games because of this with wasted time and resources.

_childDocuments_.review: Its about time, we got an RTS in the world of Age of Sigmar.I tend to play lots and lots of strategy games. And to be honest, I enjoy playing this one. TL;DR:If you are a Dawn of War II player and an AoS fan:  Go on and purchase it, if you may.The game has potential and even though I enjoy it, there is lots of space for improvements and of course more content (this is Frontier after all) and factions!!  Gameplay:The game is fast-paced with lots of micromanagement and victory point capping going on. And it can get much more punishing than dawn of war 2 at times. As others said, you will forget to blink. Your units when engaged in combat can't be pulled away, only fight or retreat back to the HQ which reminds me of Ancestors Legacy. You have to master strategic retreats and/or unit sacrifices. And you have to attend your units. They don't react on their own. Which I equally like and despise based on the occasion. I believe there should be an aggressive / passive behavior toggle button for our units.Also, there is no actual base building, its only your starting HQ and a number of choices when fortifying points on the map. Don't expect to build a base like in Age of Empires or StarCraft or DoW1. It plays exactly like Dawn of War II only with a more extensive point fortifying system.Visuals:Plain and simple, the graphics are jaw-dropping. The units are awesomely looking and the animations are decent. The environment of the realm of Ghur is finely designed and depicted as well.Audio:The sound system is well-designed.The voice overs are fine and cool.The music is thematically fitting.Controls: The controls seemed clunky to me at first, but I got used to them after a few matches. It does feel like the controls were made with console controllers in mind.Campaign:Despite some sudden spikes of difficulty at times, the campaign seems pretty enjoyable with lots of chapters and some nice twists.Yes, you get to play with most factions in the campaign. Also, some in-game cut-scenes are some of the best I have seen in this genre since ages.Multiplayer / AI Skirmish:- In multiplayer and AI skirmish, the four factions currently in the game (Stormcast Eternals, Kruleboyz, Nighthaunt, Disciples of    Tzeentch) are asymmetrical and thus play differently. - The number of maps available for multiplayer / AI skirmish is decent as well.- Victory conditions and match adjustments are lacking. There is the classic "Capture Victory Points" condition like it is in CoH and DoW2 games or "annihilation" if you manage to destroy the enemy HQ.I hope that we get to see the match settings expanded with new options like extended population caps, resource generation rates, an option for free for all, or more victory conditions like a standalone Annihilation mode etc.Conquest: The conquest mode is fun but its not Total War: AoS fun, don't have this expectation. You get to play a long chunk of games in skirmish maps with random buffs / debuffs for both you and / or your AI enemy. Conquest mode could have been much more. Hopefully, the developers will expand more on this in the future.Army Painter:As a proper Warhammer strategy title this game does indeed have one and its awesome!Map Editor:As a proper strategy title this game was launched with a map editor and its cool if you are the creative type!Profile leveling system:It is expected nowadays, yes, the game features a profile leveling system which provides the user with new cosmetic rewards like profile banners, portraits, frames etc like AoE4.Bugs and Crashes:I encountered only a graphical bug in the mission where you get to play with the Kruleboyz for the first time. In general, for the vast amount of time, the game seems to be bug-free.Also, up to this moment, I encountered only a crash in the campaign where you set a trap to a particular undead Lord.Overall, the game runs just fine and I have everything on max settings in a three years old laptop. Kudos for a well optimized title.Interface:The menu interface is fine.The in-game Interface is clear but it lacks a section that let's you see your currently recruited unit squads, their health points, their combat status, grouping number etc at all times. Instead of not having such an interface section at all, the devs could have given us the option to toggle it on or off. I don't know why the developers omitted this altogether. In Conclusion:RoR has potential. And I find it fun. The DoW2 vibes are strong and I play that game to this day. I find it interesting how they translated AoS in a DoW2-like game.I am looking forward to competitive play and ranked matches, new maps, match adjustment settings, heroes and of course more factions!!P.S: By Sigmar, If you read all this, you are a little hero yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very good. It could actually be fantastic, that depends on the level of quality in the campaign. I have only played 4 hours of campaign and 3 hours of skirmishes against AI and players in the beta. So far the campaign is pretty great, the missions are challenging, they are varied, the storyline is engaging enough for a single player RTS (miles above DOW and close to SC2 level in quality).The game is clearly better than the reviews suggest. This might be a case of review bombing. A small minority in the Warhammer community has a very vocal, negative online presence about Age of Sigmar. This game also has a female leader figure in the main campaign. Some people dislike this sort of thing.Yes, it's a micro heavy MOBA-like RTS. It could possibly work on a mobile device, but it's clearly not a mobile game. The UI and the responsiveness is a bit different than what you would expect but it only takes a bit to readjust to the changed pace and focus. It's a bit strange that units don't auto-attack when under fire. This is arguably one of the worst criticisms of the gameplay.The game is challenging, there is depth in map control and unit choices. It follows a Rock-Paper-Scissors system with complexity added by heroes, special abilities, upgrade options of control points and army composition. The decisions in tactics and map strategy matter. I prefer this style of smaller, more fluid decision making as opposed to the very rigid decision making in SC2 build-order modifications.It's an improved version of an old-school RTS style game. People's tastes might have changed, and the genre is not as well-liked as it used to be but this game is actually quite well-designed. A lot of RTS suffer from unnecessarily huge tech trees, too many units without no differentiation. The design here on the other hand is quite focused. The abilities of each unit are quite important, the cooldowns and global resource costs of abilities are finely balanced. This is simply just good design. The game allows the players to have significant impact with strategic and tactical choices while also not overwhelming players. In my experience this is a hard thing to balance but they succeeded here.I hope the game gets more positive recognition.

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played the campaign so far, but overall, I very much like the game. The campaign so far is interesting. If you're going into it thinking it will be like Warcraft or Starcraft, you're in for a surprise. The game doesn't have large expansive maps, instead it has smaller, rather linear maps. These make the combat slower, but more intense. There is a retreat button that allows your units to quickly return to your base and heal your troops. There are some small nitpicks about the game that should be noted:1) You can't skip cut scenes. Cinematics can be skipped, but cut scenes in the game cannot, so if you have to replay a bit, you have to go through the cut scenes all over again.2) There is no auto save. If you're like me and get distracted and mess up, you're going to lose scenarios. And if you're also like me, you get invested in the game and forget to save. Meaning that you'll have to restart the level from the beginning (and watch the cut scenes all over again.)3) There really isn't base building. Instead, you have arcane points that you can take over and there you can build resource harvesting buildings, healing buildings, and so on. Unless you actively build defense towers, those buildings will not be protected unless you leave troops there.4) You have a small population limit. This is normal in RTS games, but in this game (so far) the maximum population is 12. And your heroes take up a slot. So if you have 3 heroes, you can only build 9 units. The problem is, the AI doesn't have this limit and can send out waves of troops to attack the control points as well as your arcane points. This makes it hard to defend anything as the Ai can attack 3 places at once. If you can get used to the way the game is played, it is overall enjoyable and you will get invested.

_childDocuments_.review: The look of AoS is utterly nailed.Sound-wise, no complaints. The soundtrack evokes a grand battlescape and everything from the grunts of Orruks to the clatter of Sigmarite as folks walk around pulls you in.The controls take a few minutes to get used to, but the opening few campaign missions set down everything you’ll need. Once everything started to make sense I found them really intuitive.Get ready to get micro. Succeeding in any battle will need you to get in on your micromanagement. Once the rock paper scissors-style damage triangle gets into your head, it all starts to make sense. Don’t expect to make a big lump of 19 liberators and win. A single assault unit will cause merry havoc among them.Don’t expect to just leave something somewhere to fight your battles. Units don’t really ‘engage’ unless you tell them to. Be active. Be mobile. Don’t spread yourself too thin.Oh and it’s hard. Been running through the campaign on Veteran and started hitting walls on chapter 3. So I dove into Conquest mode, and there I’m having such fun.Multiplayer works well and is fun both 1v1 and 2v2. Queue times are medium, takes 1-2 minutes to get a game but I suspect that will improve now that the game is officially released.Will it set the world on fire? Too early to say. Kinda. But does it tick the AoS boxes? Yep.

_childDocuments_.review: "Do not buy this game!" was my initial impression to the game, after having played about half of the campaign. Now I say: Grab it on sale, but get your expectations right. Do NOT compare it to top RTS games like StarCraft, Warcraft. MAYBE to Dawn of War, Company of Heroes. It's not simple to learn if you come from these games and it is even more difficult to master - but it's great once you get the hang of it. It really is a STRATEGY game, giving you all the tools to make meaningful decisions and correct choices. It's not about building a cool army and simply rightclick on the map to win.Pro's:+ Strategic play+ No downtimes+ GraphicsCon's:- Steep learning curve- Unit Triangle too opaque- AI campaign is ridiculous (hard)On the positive site, the game looks fantastic. Great graphics, 1:1 unit adaptation from AoS and amazing cutscenes. Sadly, the gameplay during the campaign is very lackluster and seldom providing much novelty.About RTS: this IS different from mainstream games, be aware of that. Don't hate it, accept it - or walk away. Understanding the mechanics and using them correctly can be very rewarding. Every unit you build matters. Every skill must be timed correctly. You can't spam an army and walk over the map and clear everything (unless late game). Understand your army and unit composition. Learn each role and the game changes dramatically.In MP or Conquest games, the AI is always pushing, leading to no downtimes at all. You don't queue buildings or units, wait 5 min and go. You go right away.But the learning curve is very steep. The worst part of the game, besides the uninteresting campaign gameplay, is it's tutorials. The games does NOT teach you the game via the campaign, but rather via hidden menues and text boxes. It also just covers the basics, the advanced stuff is up to you to figure out.There is a unit triangle in the games, which means that every army has basically 3 unit types (plus heroes and monsters later). Every unit type is strong against one type and weak against the other. That's the basic. The advanced part: faction units differ in unit sizes, strengths, hit points and armor. You don't know at first if my unit can defeat another one just based on the rock-paper-scissor mechanic. And what about rock vs rock? Who's gonna win that? It's all up to you to figure it out.It really takes time to learn the game and having no ongoing online community makes it even more difficult (you can't find build orders or many matchups of Yt). But if you spend some hours and accept the mechanics like they are, it really is a great strategy game.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game as part of the humble Bundle. It'd been on my radar for a while, but 60 dollars is a hard price tag to give it a try for. Glad I didn't. 60 dollars is too much for this game. Comparing it to other RTSes of the same price tag, there is just not a comparable amount of content. 4 races and 9 or 10 units each is just not 60 dollars worth.That said, for 20 or even 30 dollars, we have a good game here that's easy to recommend. It has it's flaws, but otherwise this is a solid RTS.The flaws- Controls are clunky at times. There are stealth missions in the campaign, but your character will shoot as they are moving and alert things.- Once a unit is in combat they're in combat till they die or you retreat them. means combat doesn't have position micro- Only one map type. DoW got away with 1 map type, but it also had A LOT more faction content than this game.- All races follow a similar formula for what units are available. Everyone starts with a melee and ranged unit, everyone will get a ballista unit. That type of stuff.- Outside of the campaign, there is a giant gap between easy and normal. Normal was fien for me in the campaign, but conquest and skirmisher got very difficult. The computer is very smart, even at easy. The computer knows which units work best against what you are building and will actively build your counter. Even on Easy. I think the difference between difficulties is resource generation. You need to know your faction strengths and counters before going into a normal skirmish or conquest.The Good- Army Painter. I wish every Warhammer RTS had army painter. It feels good in this game and does what it's supposed to.- General balance feels really good. Aside from the AI on the computer being overtuned, there isn't a unit that just felt too good or units that felt useless. Solid overall balance.- There are enough units to create builds and compositions, and there's reason to change your build depending on what you're fighting- Units are interesting. Though every factions starts with a melee and a ranged, units all play differently and either start with or can gain abilities through upgrades.- Terrain matters. THis is a hard one for RTSes, but the terrain factors into the game in a healthy way.-True to the source. I'm not big on Age of Sigmar, I'm a End Times or Age of Reckoning guy, but this does seem to be true to the AoS source material which is good.Lastly, the fun factor is good. I beat the game, have done some skirmish and conquest, and plan to do more cuz it's fun enough. However, all of this would have been marred if I had to drop 60 dollars on the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Its a stripped down version of an RTS. No base building, workers, or resources. Unit and upgrade variety are very low for each faction. Combat is also an overly simplistic rock paper scissors system. You can barely field any units to the battlefield. Because of that, it feels less like a strategy game and more like micromanagement. You have to constantly micromanage your army composition while also spreading out your units over an entire map, because resources are based on controlling nodes. So you're running in circles to constantly defend your stuff. Lose a command point, go take it back, which takes 5 minutes. In the meantime, another control point got taken so you run back to retake that one too, and then you just lost the one you rebuilt. Rinse and repeat. Its a very tedious back and forth tug-of-war situation that makes matches feel like a slog.I think what they were trying to do is make an RTS that's more thoughtful. Less focus on maximizing APM, predefined build orders, and massing units into a mindless death ball and attack moving like SC2. That's why the units move and fight a lot slower. And I totally respect that goal, because SC2 combat is lame. However, slowness does not make a thoughtful RTS game by itself. It can certainly help, but its only one piece of the puzzle. Without bases and other RTS elements, all you're doing is micromanaging the units, making the slow speed of the game a detriment rather than an advantage. If there was more stuff to do in your base, more of an emphasis on macro-management, this would actually complement the slower paced combat very well. But since the combat is all there is, it gets very finicky and boring, fast.Another problem is there only being one match type, which is control all the objectives. I always hate this in RTS games because its such an abstract victory condition. If I have a much better economy and army strength than the AI, and more control points captured, obviously my forces would eventually win, so why does the enemy still win because a lone orc was scratching its ass on some random rock that the developers decided was important because reasons?The story is nothing great either. Maybe if it was on par with the quality of WC3 it could have supported the shallow game-play, but its nothing special.

_childDocuments_.review: Foreword: I really really wanted to like this game.Most strategy games have a variety of missions in a single player campaign, focusing on different things, then multiplayer. Realms of Ruin has exactly one mode you play on every single mission, or in multiplayer.  There are several nodes (little circles) on a map, one being the enemy HQ node, one is yours. You can upgrade your HQ when you get enough resources, of which there are two kinds that you steadily and automatically collect. You can order a very small selection of units (about 9 for each faction, total, across all tech levels). All the nodes in-between you can move a unit onto to capture, then can build one of four structures on. One increases money, one increases special tech currency, one heals your units, and the last acts like a turret out of a MOBA. There are then between one and four victory point nodes on the map that you cannot build on.You pick your small number of units, who move very slow, and take these nodes, and wait. This is the entire game.Realms of Ruin has atrocious to nonexistent unit AI. The attack move function is locked to a key bind, not a click. Units will not react in any way to a ranged unit shooting them. They will not move unless directly ordered to. When you select a group of units, you cannot issue an order to just one in the group you have to go go click the ground repeatedly, deslecting all the units, then click the one unit you want. Basically, this game is running behind RTSes from 20+ years ago in terms of UI and AI. Realms of Ruin feels like the team at Frontier looked at Dawn of War 3 (the one that killed a franchise and underperformed) and made an Age of Sigmar game. Only, DoW3 was made by a veteran team with years of experience. It may have had bad design decisions, but it WORKED smoothly. This doesn't. They made bizarre choices when choosing the factions, with the default Stormcast, but then the Kruleboyz (new, less popular, swamp orks), Disciples of Tzeentch (least popular chaos faction), and Nighthaunt (very monotone in appearance ghost faction). The game feels sluggish and bad to play. The story is okay. It is told in very small and bland cutscenes uing the in game engine between missions. Spoilers for those who care. It is a fairly cookie cutter and predictable affair with characters you are rapidly shown, and thus don't care about, stumbling upon an artifact they apparently need to save a city from... well the original threat isn't really ever expounded on. You take the artifact from Nighthaunt who ominously warn about a prophecy. The artifact is tainted by Tzeentch. A group of Kruleboyz start out just trying to kill the Stormgitz, and want the artifact. This ends badly for everyone involved. At no point is any character fleshed out with a background or any relationships. The Kruleboyz end up being the most likeable by dint of being the only entertaining faction, where everyone else drones on.I was really hoping this game would do and be for Age of Sigmar what Dawn of War was for 40k, or Total War was for Warhammer Fantasy. It isn't, and I am sad I spent $60 on it.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is getting a bad rap...No it is not like many other Real-Time Strategy games on the market. There is no base building, your units are locked into combat once they are in melee, it is much more of a MOBA/Lane based approach with two players starting on opposite sides of a mirrored map...But the game is clean, responsive, has tactical depth and enough units and factions to create a variety of approaches and is a nice change of pace for the Genre. Every unit has or can be upgraded to have abilities, all of which are useful in different situations and branching choices for how to play them. There is a lot of micromanaging with individual units across the field needing different forms of attention, but if done correctly you can have an incredibly close tug-of-war with your opponent. I'm enjoying the game very much, it's unfortunate that not many people are available to play multiplayer with... but with the recent steam sale and humble bundle it's possible the numbers will go up for a time.In addition, it has a very enjoyable Age of Sigmar based campaign in a setting not many casual Warhammer fans may know too much about, there's an army painter, map maker you can publish online, and a single-player procedurally generated rogue-like mode. There's a lot here if you're willing to learn a new type of RTS! I think it might even be a good entry point into the genre for many!

_childDocuments_.review: After about 3.5 hrs of gameplay, I know this game is not for me, I would not recommend it, and I am going to put it down for now. AoS:RoR presents boring concepts and underwhelming gameplay in a very shiny package. It has some good aspects, but games should compete for your time, and this one is not up to snuff. I think AoS:RoR suffers from a lack of inspired combat mechanics. Its calls itself an RTS but toes the line between being an RTS and an RTT. It has rudimentary research and unit upgrades, no base building, and the most basic rock, paper, scissors style strategy mechanics. Its feels like an RTT, with the emphasis on a small number of beefy units that require constant attention instead of macro-focused economy and large-scale warfare. All 4 missions and one skirmish I played had map design focused on lane combat. They almost felt MOBA-like, with me worrying about which lane needed reinforcement and which lane to push in. I didn’t find this type of gameplay appealing. All this to say, I didn’t find much to like in its strategic offerings. And honestly, RTT games are best when they have cover systems and primarily ranged combat. Think of your favorite RTT games, Company of Heroes, Dawn of War 2, Sudden Strike, etc. They feature unit variety, cover systems, and the like. The combat in AoS:RR has primarily melee units fighting melee units. Ranged units are there but feel like an afterthought. Watching melee units slug it out is cool at first, but doesn’t make for exciting RTT combat.Much like other RTT games, the gameplay centers around capture points that you can then build on. You have choice of like 4 or 5 buildings which can boost resource income, provide defense, and other support abilities. It’s a bit underwhelming. Just give us base building and have these capture points be resource and pop cap boosters like DoW.Props to its high-quality graphics and sound design. I might think the game is mid but credit where credit is due. The game also has great customization options, I like how there is a map editor! If I enjoyed the root gameplay, I’m sure I would enjoy making maps as well.    I don’t think AoS:RR is bad, but it is disappointing and not for me. I decided to play longer than the refund window to give it a real shot, but I sure am glad I bought it on sale.
