_childDocuments_.review: As far as Real-Time-Tactic/warhammer games go, Realms of Ruin offers a rather polished experience. I've played so many hours of Dawn of War 2 (the most direct comparison to this game) and Company of Heroes, and to be honest, this games feels very close in quality, if not more so, to those games, especially if you would compare those games' release states to how RoR released. I've played a lot of warhammer games since Dawn of War 1/2 were released, and relatively speaking, this game blows the warhammer game competition out of the water with it's amazing attention to detail in voice acting, visual effects/models, and strong faction themes to give us that glorious asymmetric gameplay. As a veteran RTT player, the game offers a fresh take on combat with the "locked in melee" mechanic (this prevents units from moving away from melee, they must finish the fight or retreat (and occasionally have access to abilities to use). This core mechanic can seem awkward at first if you're coming from more traditional RTS. I've always found it weird units could run away from melee so easily and consequence free (and thus, makes melee units somewhat weaker than they should be), and I like how this games squad-based combat has a sort of Total War-esque feel: committing units to combat is an endeavor, and once there combat is not easily broken. It rewards forethought and careful planning of formation/flanks vs. the endless dancing you would have to micro your units with in order to scoot-and-shoot. Instead, the skill expression looks a lot more like a MoBA, as each unit has powerful abilities that can change the course of a fight in one move, where the value of using these abilities rests in the player's careful decision making, timing, and positioning. This ability-based combat gives the game great moment-to-moment gameplay, as you are always trying to set up good use-cases for your abilities while avoiding giving the enemy a great set-up for their own.As a note: the unit ai is, well, much more straightforward than your standard RTS. Essentially, units do exactly what you tell them to do and no more. This quirk of the mechanics means that units will not react to being hit from range, will not "auto engage" close targets, etc. It can take some getting used to, but the upside of these unit ai mechanics is that the game behaves extremely predictably when you understand how movement/attack orders work. No getting stuck on terrain during a retreat, not weird pathing decisions (hello DoW tanks doing donuts). In this respect, I consider the game smooth and polished. If you try to apply your previous RTS expectations of unit behavior to this game, I can see how it may seem "clunky." Adding stances à la Dawn of War could help give players more agency over their units' behaviors when you are not baby-sitting them.Most of my review comes from a Multiplayer perspective, a that's where i've focused 90%+ of my time. I think that experience is phenomenal in terms of technical gameplay mechanics for an RTT game. However, the game suffers from some connectivity issues (some have been fixed, some not) which hinder it from being a flawless experience. The balance is honestly the best I've seen coming from playing DoW2/3/CoH2/3/AoE4 - the triangle of counters this game implements helps prevent certain units from completely overrunning the meta. It has far more maps at release than any Relic title I've played too. And with a map editor included at launch, we already are seeing some community maps as well. The campaign is a solid experience with a good warhammer story driven by quality in-game cinematics. It does lack replayability. That's where conquest mode comes in, which I think should be the core driver of the game, but is the one part of RoR that feels somewhat undercooked. The skeleton is there, but it lacks meat. And a variety of meat. Its procedural-generated nature should lend itself well to replayability, but some of its random features are simply not catching enough to keep you engaged endlessly. It should also have co-op added, considering 2v2 is already in the game. I know a lot of warhammer fans love fighting hordes of baddies with your buddies.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. The aesthetic is very well done and feels very Sigmar. The units, the animations and cinematic are all great to watch and the abilities are very nicely done. The AI is surprisingly sturdy and holds up quite well. If you leave it an opening, it will abuse it. The game play itself is reasonably fast paced and call fall out of hand quite quickly.Though not a base builder, this is definitely a decent strategy game with the traditional triangle system for units, Defence beats ranged beats offence beats defence, though this isn't strictly the case in all scenarios, you can use your head to beat this like most strategy games. Having multiple tiers to this allows you to create a reasonably dynamic force along with an upgrade system that can let you change the roles of certain units. Its a capture point system for resources which is fairly common so not hard to learn. The heroes are cool little centre pieces but not absurdly strong. They will die if you leave them unattended.One complaint is that there is no unit stance system so units will stand still and get shot unless you tell them to move and the alerts could be louder to help the player combat this issue. Campaign wise you get to play a multitude of factions throughout the one campaign which is kind of nice, I will admit is annoying if you have no interest in the faction for that mission. So having multiple smaller campaigns focusing on one faction at a time would of been a bigger win for me here. However that said, the campaign is quite long for a modern RTS on a story driven game. The conquest mode I think I'll be spending most of my time on is quite fun and the missions have different twists, changing up the game play here and there, though I wish it had more mission variety.Also has an army painter. Though we're not spoilt as much as earlier Warhammer games as far as colour palette goes, its decent enough for my needs. Overall - Pretty decent game, I've not encountered many bugs and nothing game breaking and will likely be stopping back on this ones conquest mode for a while. If you like a more fantasy version Dawn of War 2, this a good purchase for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall this is a pretty fun Warhammer RTS with a pretty decent campaign. The overall atmosphere and story telling of the game is fantastic. The voice acting is also well done. Micro management mostly comes in the form if using abilities at the right time, and point management. On the hardest difficulty, most of the main story missions offer a good amount of challenge. Several of the maps require using flying units, or fast units to sneak points from the enemy rather than directly engaging. This gives a good amount of challenge and micro management strategy needed to complete each mission. The game is not without its issues. The game desperately needs a patrol function that you can command units with. Right now there is only move and attack move. On that note, your units require a TON of micro management. They will often require you to target enemies that are 2 feet in front of you. Often times an enemy unit will be shooting one of your idol units literally doing nothing until you give it a direct command. The AI should be smart enough to attack units firing on them or their allies right near them. I'm assuming the developers didn't do this because of the combat lock function, but retreating is easy enough. Some of the missions can be a bit ridiculous. Enemies seemingly have endless amounts of resources and waves on units that spawn from caves or similar unattackable structures. Even stealing victory points or arcane structures doesn't seem to slow down the enemies capacity to spawn units from the corners of the map. Killing an enemy stronghold also won't stop units from spawning. I don't think we need a full base building mechanic in this game, but enemies shouldn't be spawning unlimited amounts of units with no way to stop them. It feels like this was a bit of a lazy way  to design the campaign rather than introduce proper mechanics to stop enemy production. There was often times where I basically had to bunker down at my main base or maybe one additional resource point until I unlocked the base tiers high enough to actually make progress against the endless waves of enemies. While still very much doable, it's not nearly as satisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Age of Sigmar (I mean REALLY like AOS) then you'll probably tolerate this game.  If you don't like AOS or don't know what it is, then this game's flaws will ensure you don't bother with checking out the rest of the franchise.The best part about this game are the aesthetics and cutscenes which are generally well done and mo-capped well.  But nearly everything else is like most other reviews have said: a very poor. sluggish imitation of the Dawn of War II / Company of Heroes style RTS.  The difference is that Relic's COH engine was far smarter on pathing, formations, and responsiveness.  Beyond there being essentially no cover mechanics to speak of, this game will see troops blob up to melee or barely capable of performing the most simple of Move-Attack commands while inputs of adorable little special abilities get eaten or delayed by precious seconds.Thankfully the game's currently 80% off on Summer Sale, which is sad that it needs to be that low to justify a purchase as it's generally a good looking game - the cutscenes hit almost all of the aesthetic and the models are so very very very close to their tabletop originals that it's really the first time AOS has been done some justice in a game visually.  We'll probably never get AOS in Total War, but it's disappointing that the aesthetic of this game is so on while the gameplay is so bad.Buy it if you like AOS or are willing to suffer through the game's many flaws to see what AOS could look like when rendered well.

_childDocuments_.review: wish there was a "neutral" review option. However, i also got it on sale (80% off) and still want a discount, so i guess that speaks for itself. i just barely went over the 2 hr limit (at 137 minutes at time of review) so here's hoping i can still get my refund.TLDR: The cosmetics are there, but the game is off. Like Dawn of War 3, Total War, and Poke'mon (Rock Paper Scissors / counter-mechanics) had a child with an identity crisis. It's not "bad" but definitely "weird" Pros: Graphics. Factions. Small scale. uniqie in the turrets, sort of. Graphics are gorgeous. The factions feel pretty well done and diverse (With the limited unit count). And it's nice to have small scale, reminds me of DoW 2. 6-16 units is the avg team size (6 at start, 16 at end). Really like the concept of upgrading and determining your resource or defense from a capture node. -Amazing voice acting. Cons:-It's just ... off. hard to describe-The units are "Tank, Range, Melee" archetype. literally. you get 3 units to pick from, then you get a t1 - t3 variation. 9-10 units (2 of which are heroes). while, this, in and of itself isn't bad, it just feels, off, probably because of the "rock paper scissors" mechanic of the game. -Rock, Paper, Scissors. Rather than each unit bringing x to the table, the game is about counter building (which, i'm fairly common with, i play, and love, "wargame: red dragon"), if you see enemy with Tank (shield icon), you need to counter with melee swords.-No stats. I don't know how much dmg one unit does compared to another, what the multiplier is, how much health someone has (as a raw number) ... there's no raw data. how much better is a t2 unit vs a t1? etc. **i wish i could see the more in depth game numbers. is there a multiplier for swords vs shield? because melee swords SHOULD beat ranged in melee. the neutral:-the maps are very small "lane" style with corridors, so this means u can defend with range, but, ofc, can be countered. which isn't bad. -Fairly micro heavy. -"Locked In" ... so, if a unit engages, you can't control that unit (u can use skills, but can't make them move) except to retreat. they are "locked" in melee. it's an odd mechanic. not "bad". just weird. so stays in neutral. it's like.... DoW 3 and total war had a child that wasn't sure what it was. Hopefully it'll get better? it's not even a year old, so, fingers crossed. but again, the graphics are gorgeous, and the units feel very true to their faction.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary of my notes from playing skirmish mode match and the first half or so of the campaign missions. Solid gfx, audio, and overall presentation. Excellent sound design as expect from Frontier(if played Elite and fought/been hyperdicted by thargoids before, you know what I mean), performance is good, maxing it out at 4k, no issues. (6900 gpu + 5950 cpu for reff). Like TW Warhammer, visually this is "table top comes to life" feels.Standard "second gen" rts as I call them(which I guess is a "RTT" as recently learned), ie post Company of Heroes design. Capture points, not much in way of base building but do have research tree and match tiers like DoW. Has the classic AoE matches triangle balance for units, some care been given to bring over TT rules like how charges work and retreating. Slower pacing though, this is not a blitz rts like SC or DoW2, in this category reminds me of something like Battle for Middle Earth tbh.Heroes, but havent seen anywhere where they level up or anything, so really like DoW 1 heroes if anything.Decent skirmish AI, whooped my ass first match but can see if I practice it's not insane. Campaign missions can be little unforgiving but usually trying something diff, or learning from mistake etc will be the trick to the second try. Writing isnt terrible for the dialogue so far, and honestly want to play out campaign just to keep watching what happens to characters, which is saying something given theyre otherwise generic stormcasts units.Overall? If you're a diehard rts player thats been desperate for something new with some quality presentation to it(ie, little bit above typical indie fare imho), and/or big into AoS should be worth price tag for ya. If just casually interested, I'd wait for sales and/or some kind of bundle in future, get a feeling going to be some faction pack DLCs etc coming down the pipes if this catches on like we see with the Warhammer total war games.Oh last note. Geez is is nice when boot up a game these days, no sep launcher(need log in for mp tho, but eh, gotta track your stats for match making etc somehow I guess), no game ending bugs, no weird ass glitches or messing around with windows updates etc for half an hour. It just worked. So, that's always nice with any new game these days.

_childDocuments_.review: Mixed on this game, has its ups and downs and while I don't hate the gameplay, I just find it difficult to find a reason to actually play it. It was obvious this game was designed heavily with consoles in mind, but RTS games have NEVER been popular on consoles. It should have been made for PC and then ported for console ease. Here are some additional pros and consPros: - Good voice acting- Army painter is robust and fun to use. - Multiplayer scene is active for now.- Unit designs are very good.- Game runs great for me.Cons: - UI is terrible, probably one of the worst I've seen from an RTS game. Given timings can make or break some games in this game you'd think they'd make everything such as base upgrades, units, and upgrades in the same menu, or communicate you can upgrade capture points (and need to)- Balance is totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Nighthaunt are busted, ranged meta is real and there is next to no reason to not just spam ranged even into shielded counter units. Just blob ranged units with one or two melee units to tie down the enemy and win every fight. Start to lose abuse special abilities. Not to mention stuff like Nighthaunt can get increased recruitment capacity from their realmstone node upgrade, which is literally the only upgrade ever worth taking. - Unit responsiveness and click detection are horrendous in this game. Units feel sluggish in their actions, both in movement, retreat orders, and move orders. It's also insanely easy to misclick ranged units and put them closer or outright in melee. With your total unit count being very important losing a unit because your retreat took 2 or 3 seconds to go off or you accidentally locked a ranged unit in melee is crippling. - Melee locking is dumb for an RTS game in general when positioning and movement are core aspects of RTS games. If two units enter melee regardless of what they are they cannot leave it unless one retreats or dies. Makes ranged spam infinitely stronger since you can use ONE unit to tie down the ENTIRE enemy army and delete the enemies before they even have time to kill that one person. - Prices of things are wonky particularly with the nodes. Given node upgrades SO expensive like 700 unit resources for just the base upgrade, it makes building any of the other node upgrades when you aren't  ahead completely worthless. - Realmstone system should just be changed all together. Make it so nodes passively generate realmstone at smaller amounts increasing the more you have the point captured. Gives a reason to play aggressive and take the enemies nodes, while also being less punishing when an enemy rushes your realmstone building. Also remove the lump sum realmstone upon node acquisition. I'm concerned with recent news about the companies refocus on sims that they might just silently abandon this game, putting in the bare minimum of effort until they drop support all together. They could easily make a high quality RTS it's just not there yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable so far, though does take a little getting used to, with the retreat mechanic among other things, and the fact they have, in response to feedback, increased movement speed in scenarios but not the campaign.The campaign gives you little time to read and absorb info about new units and skills, as it will throw new mechanics at you quite quickly. I found mission 3 bad in this regard, you fight a new faction, get given a new unit, and have a new objective type to accomplish, and are attacked on three sides from the very start of the mission. It is cinematic and feels like an ambush would, as you really do fumble and feel very lost and overwhelmed for the first few minutes. it's particularly painful as the Nighthaunt Units pretty much are all just black ghosts, so you can't easily learn the different enemy matchups that are important to the combat system. I didn't even realise we had a camp and could recruit units until after I thought I'd failed the level the first time, as they either didn't mention you had a base, or I missed it due to being so busy. They could do with a small grace period after the first ambush of the mission to let you take stock, and introduce each mechanic or objective individually.  That said, it is fun and I'm enjoying it so far.

Save yourself the money and just watch all the cutscenes on YouTube. 3/10 cannot recommend (I haven't played multiplayer, and I'm not planning to).

_childDocuments_.review: Been awhile since we've had an RTS that was actually decent on release.Let's just get this out of the way- A lot of people seem to be upset that this isn't a traditional base-building RTS in the vein of Starcraft and Age of Empires. It's not. It plays a lot closer to the Company of Heroes series, with fighting over objective points that must be captured in order to drain the opponent's score and win the match, and others that provide trickles of resources. Buildings are limited to a small selection of upgrades that can be built on these points to increase resource income, provide vision, attack enemies, heal allies, etc. If you come into this expecting a more traditional RTS you will be disappointed here.This is more a game about managing your units- not only army composition, but their positioning, timing their abilities, and when and where to engage. The last part is especially important, because once units are locked in melee combat they cannot manoeuvre or change targets- aside from the use of certain special abilities, they must fight to the death unless given the order to retreat. If ordered to retreat they will flee all the way back to your main base to heal. This makes engagements a very deliberate and tense game of cat and mouse, carefully moving to avoid ambushes, charging the enemy's flanks, and tying up their ranged units in melee so they can't harass you.While some people have been critical of the way units become locked in melee combat and can't be micromanaged, it really is integral to the way the game plays, and is a blessing, because it forces you to focus on the overall battlefield rather than trying to stutterstep to avoid attacks, and trust me the game is hectic enough without that extra level of micro! It also makes the decision of when and where to engage, and with which units, an extremely important one, because you are forced to commit to those decisions and can't simply form a big blob of units and have them all target your enemy's crucial pieces. Instead you must protect your own crucial pieces by intercepting incoming attackers whilst trying to circumvent or create gaps in the enemy's own defence.The gameplay may seem simple on the surface, but there is a lot going on. It's a low skill floor, high skill ceiling kind of game, and I can already foresee multiplayer matches being very intense, with lots of opportunity for clever team plays in the 2v2 mode.Graphics are very nice, and performance has been good even on my older machine. Sound design is fantastic, with excellent performances from the voice cast, well realised atmospheric effects, and evocative music. I was especially pleased to see a robust options menu, with lots of accessibility settings, something that is sadly still lacking in many modern games.While not perfect- I'd love to see more factions, and more game modes featuring higher player counts, this is a game that clearly has been given a lot of love from the developers. The fact that it launched with an army painter and a fully integrated map creator with photo mode, should alone lead to longevity provided by player creativity, and while I heavily stress this is a fully featured and complete game, not something unfinished that has been pushed out the door, I can only hope the developers continue to support it for years to come. With continued love, this could very well become a new flagship RTS title.

_childDocuments_.review: What I have done in-game   Played the Campaign on Hard   1v1'd against my Older Brother useing different factions   Took a gander at map editor   Created a couple scenic pictures   Attempted a ConquestTLDR     It's more in-depth than people think, micro better, git gudNow is the game fun? Yes.    The game is very micro heavy, you need to pay attention to what your units are doing less you enemy pays attention for you. All factions have something they excel at, Stormcast have the most shield unit and are the most armor'd units in the game. Disciples of Tzeentch are stupidly micro heavy.Is the campaign good? Yes.     The campaign has a rendered cut-scene for almost all of it's 20 chapters, the characters and set-up / pay offs are good... barring one but I just think they ran out of time. On hard the game get a CRAZY difficulty spike and the "final" (second to last) level you need to cheese. It is a great campaign with interesting characters who make mistakes.The game has very in-depth combat decisions.      You may see the Rock-Paper-Scissors unit counters and think it is too simplified to be in-depth this how ever is bait. A tier 2 shield will beat a tier 1 sword, it will just take a bit more time without support.      This game has AoE's everywhere if you blob up to kill one unit it's joever as they say. Also if you enemy blobs up get ready for a massive nuke on their face.     Every unit has an active ability and can be upgraded to have more active abilities. so while you disciples of tzeentch cultists (sword unit) will lose to the archers shooting at them if they use their sorcererous bolts ability then an unaware player could lose their archers to a sword unit... at range. Stormcast Eternals have a shield unit that decides it's a sword unit and literally plows through EVERYTHING in it's path dealing MASSIVE damage.The A.I does not mess around. Seriously     The A.I loves to do this thing called split up and backdoor victory objectives. I have fought A.I who are harder to beat than real players. I had a Tzeentch A.I build nothing but Pink Horrors against me so I went heavily into ranged only for that same A.I to get Tier 2 and build nothing but Tzangors (shield unit) so yes I got baited by an A.I.But Snek I don't like micro or I'm not good at micro. Same     I hate micro, it's too much for my itty little brain. THANKFULLY you can reduce the amount of micro you have to have. See when you upgrade units you will most likely get a choice. An active abillity or a very helpful passive ability. So if my swamp archers need to get behind enemy lines and flank enemys then you get the "ov'r der" ability which let's you teleport while in stealth... or you just increase there base damage and range.     Night haunt have a TON of passives they can stack if you don't want to add on more micro. but if you can micro... you should. Synopsis? It's better than you think.     Dodging charges, counter charging, flanking, moving through units because you are unstoppable. Upgrading your Killer bow to chunk heroes. Building a primary fallback point so you don't have to return all the way to base. The abilities, micro and moment to moment decision making are what make the game unique and challenging.      If any of this sounds interesting then I say give it a try because it is a full package deal like the games of old. I didn't even go over the map editor, unit painter, The fact that every animation is playable in the map editor so videos could definitely be a thing. I think it's important to consider that no game has been a complete game in recent years Realms of Ruin is a complete game. Thanks for reading my ted talk...

_childDocuments_.review: Come sit by the fire young one, and let me tell you a tale as to why Realms of Ruin is not worth its going price.... TLDR at the end.The golden age of RTS games, where in those hallowed halls stand the statues of Zero Hour, Red Alert 1 and 3, Dawn of War, Starcraft 2: Wings of Liberty, and AoE 2, has past. RTS players are few and far between, a forgotten niche within a forgotten niche, and so when a new RTS appears, like moths floundering in years of darkness suddenly attracted to a candle flame in a foggy forest, we flock. And we judge, based on our spoiled history, such new titles, to the grand slam whammer jammers that were the elite, and often unfairly forget that these golden titles of long lost yore were not juggernauts to start. Nigh on every single one of these RTS games started off with limited content. Factionwise, Generals had 3. Red Alert had 3. Even Dawn of War started with a mere 4. Any additional factions would come out in later expansions. Dr Thrax and Townes in Zero Hour, the Necrons and Tau in Dark Crusade. As far as content, Relams of Ruin provides what you can expect, and DLC/another expansion is, while I hate to say, an acceptable par for the course. However, the reliquary titles of the golden age provided you with tons of unique maps, which allowed for vast replayability, as well as a randomizer to allow you to be surprised by what the computer would throw at you. This is somewhat sidelined due to the map creator in the game, but it reeks of hot potatoing developer deliverables to the community. Those golden titles of the past had character and charm. Voice lines and whimsy allowed you to sense the uniqueness of the game, from the, admittedly racist, GLA lines (I NEED NEW SHOES), to the resonating rumble of the "Even in death I still serve" of Dawn of War SM dreadnoughts, and in this Frontier delivers. The models look wonderful, and the voice lines are fantastic. Hearing an ork (or orruk for you legal folk) say "Mork's da best...", and then immediately change his mind upon changing direction, stating with conviction "...WE'Z da best!" is a joy, and its these things that often gets lost in the E-sports lineups that have come forward after Starcraft 2's competitive scene success. Props to frontier for getting these elements right. The effects do feel a bit toony, and the animations feel perhaps a bit stiff, and maybe that's why people get the sense that it feels like a phone game. Maybe...While Frontier has a disadvantatge in terms of its candle being held to the roaring fires of the golden titles of the past, the judgement is warranted. So many RTS games have come out, each with a unique spin on the age old classic recipe. And Frontier was spoiled for choice in sampling the delectable dishes that obviously inspired its design. Dawn of war 2 added cardamom to the RTS formula, doing away with base building, instead focusing on smaller scale, unit level, tactical positioning with firing arcs and cover. Company of Heroes 2 refined the recipe, by adding a dash of Quality of Life features, and implementing a balance mechanism to allow for players a chance at redemption even if their opponent had full map control. These are the two titles that best resemble Realms' gameplay, and while it's not your base building butter basted steak avec pomme fritte du paprique, is still just as much a baby back beef ribs with a side of paprika fries: Its still classified as RTS, just not in the classic, in my opinion more satisfying sense. But the meat and potatoes are there. Considering this, it was Frontier's duty to review in utter detail the things that worked and didn't work from at least those two titles. Was the gravy good enough? Or were the units too slow? Is there a need for salt? Or should they instead bake in a way for players to feel like they can return from a loss? And just before a restaurant serves its dish, it needs to check: Is the cockroach in the soup a bug? Maybe it needs to be rectified. Mmm bitter.... the faction selection always default to stormacst, and not the last selected faction. Add some lemon. Is the army truly fully customizeable, as it says on the menu? Or are there specific paints you must use, replacing a full color wheel...To this point Frontier stumbles. It looks like a tasty, yet run of the mill burger and fries, but the bun is squished, and the fries seem floppy. The gameplay is good, but there aren't any creative herbs and spices that really add some zesty character to the gameplay itself, and there are some questionable oversights. I believe were Frontier more diligent in its research of CoH 2 and Dawn of War 2, their gameplay would've at least come up to par with either - a modern revamp and upgrade of an existing recipe, tweaked with the few design choices like sticky combat, and a very strict focus on the rock paper scissors formula. Add in a few more creative elements and designs that would make this game feel unique gameplay wise, and you'd have a best selling RTS in 2023 hands down!!!I'm willing to forgive a few oversights for a developer's first forray into the genre, but its not as excuseable when you have a wealth of resources to research your game. The result is gameplay that conceptually matches CoH2 and DoW 2, but doesn't have unique flavor that makes it say "I'm an Age of Sigmar lamb chops and hash browns, try me and be amazed!"The increase of unit speed as a result of user feedback was necessary, as the game was too boring without that. I found the campaign, where the speed was kept at default achingly slow. Surprisingly, that same speed adjustment breaks AI skirmish difficulty, which while providing an interesting challenge to RTS veterans like myself, would definitely not be classified as "medium diffuclty". The reason why the AI is so challenging is it seems programmed to multi-task and respond quickly to be on par with human input With unit speed increased, that multi-tasking is elevated tenfold, creating a very severe challenge for even the most seasoned RTS fans.In addition, plenty of elements you'd expect in an RTS game are not there: audio and visual notifications of recently built units, or soldiers under ambush, map pings that show you where, keybinds that make sense and are intuitive, clean and effective targeting when right clicking on units, without having your ranged units run straight into combat because clicked 1mm off the model instead of the unit itself, to name a few. Also, the TERRIBLE decision to have online play be linked to a frontier account is HIGHLY questionable! Why do I need an account to play with people? Plenty of games before have added online play without that requirement. Its an unnecessary extra step that players need to take to play with friends, maybe because gathering information on players is the real business of companies, who knows. It's just an absolute dumb thing. Realms of Ruin was on the right path, but some big missteps make it that the value asking price for the game is definitely not worth what you get in return. The game is fine, and it's fun, but 70 dollars US, 80 Canadian it is not. Frontier's gameplay needed to feel flavorfuly unique, in keeping with the setting. They should've added more maps, done their research to implement key RTS features, and been more vigilant against bugs. And whoever thought setting up an account for online play was a good idea was stupid. Had these simple things, easily avoided, been done right, I'm sure this would've taken its place in the vaunted halls of the golden gods.Unfortunately this game is priced like it's wagyu beef, when its actually just an overpriced burger from next door Joe's. Get it at 50% off minimum.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game.- Visually its great, and there was clearly a lot of effort put into making it this polished.- The audio is decent too, the voice acting is stellar, even if the lines are cheesy.- The story is par for the course for a Warhammer game - predictable, but as a backdrop to a game its fine.- I came across far fewer bugs than most new releases in recent years, the only notable one being units getting stuck on some geometry when they are retreating, and since retreating removes control from the character they are on their own to get unstuck, or you just reload a save. This only happened to me twice during my campaign playthrough.But this is a game, and as a game, it feels terrible.- If, like me, you looked at this game and hoped for a kind of WH40K Dawn of War 1 experience you will be sorely disappointed. As others have said this takes all the mistakes of the DoW sequels and packs them into one place, with almost no redeeming features. You have one building, your HQ, that you must defend, gives access to units and upgrades, heals your nearby units and has its own turret to damage enemies. There are capture points that you can build one of 4 buildings on, with slight variation between factions but ultimately they feel very weak and easy to lose, making your units the only thing you really need to worry about. There is a low population cap, most of the map will feel empty most of the time, thankfully this fact is barely hidden by the limited vision range of your units so most of the empty map is hidden by fog of war.- The units themselves get forced into melee engagements with nearby enemies, and you can only pull them out if you press retreat, which sends them all the way back to your HQ. There is an insanely simplistic rock, paper, scissors combat system which would be fine if it was obfuscated by varying stats, unit abilities, strategy and tactics options - but its not (at least not enough, they do have abilities but they feel weak). The combat here is not like Total War, its like TABS. At the very least the campaign does not tell you to go and destroy the enemy HQ 17 times in a row, there are a variety of objectives which at least tie into the story and hold your attention for a microsecond longer than the game would otherwise.- Game balance is poor. Some levels feel insanely easy especially early on in the campaign, to the point where I ramped up the difficulty. Later on the AI cheats so much and you are so limited in strategic and tactical choices that I was forced to drop the difficulty back down. At this point I was also so bored with the gameplay I just wanted to get it over with.- Once you are done with the campaign you have conquest, which IS "destroy the enemy HQ" over and over again with the occasional "twist". I don't imagine people playing this much in multiplayer when you have better RTS games like Total War, and better lane battlers (this does feel like a lane battler with far fewer entities on screen).Overall, its a shame. Its rare to see a game this polished, visually, aurally and in terms of bugs come out at this price point and there was clearly a lot of work put into it. The problem is that ethos was not applied to the gameplay. Its like they had a bunch of talented artists make a bunch of assets and they just slapped them into the simplest game they could justify for a £50 price tag. I wouldn't buy this game, even on sale, because its barely a game, its more of an interactive visual novel and would have done much better in that format.

_childDocuments_.review: I usually leave comments on but already removed my last review due to some some spicy fans out there...To be fair, I didn't explain myself well in the last review so I'm going to try and reword this so the fanboys don't work themselves into a tizzy. But I doubt that will work...I'll keep comments on so let's see how it goes.Preamble: I played and beat the demo (over an hour of content), then picked up my progress from there to play another 90 minutes dabbling in conquest, multiplayer, and the campaign (2.5 hours worth of content played, despite what it says here). I also put the game down for a while to think about my feelings before returning it as I really love the presentation. All that to say, this isn't a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ review, this is my opinion based off over 2 hours of playing every mode available. Say what you want, but it doesn't take 30 hours of gameplay to form an opinion.Actual criticisms: The voice acting and overall design are amazing, really got me excited. Even the demo had me excited. But once you get into the meat of the game, it's boring plain and simple. I don't get how so many people can ignore the fact that this game is BASIC AF. You have a handful of unit types that are re-skins in each army. All of your troops enter battle and become uncontrollable, there is no micro in this game and very little actual strategy when you realize the entire combat is based on rock paper scissors, as others have criticized here. Absolutely no base building, which isn't normally a deal-breaker for me, but in this game just feels like another missed opportunity. Finally, the army painter is a huge let down for me personally. As someone who has painted Warhammer figures, I felt the devs lead me to believe this aspect would be much more in-depth than it actually is. There are only a handful of paints to choose from, and you can only paint a few pieces of the armor individually. I had thought it would be a much more detailed painting process where you could really make your army standout. Some may enjoy it, and some may grin and bear it for the AOS title. That's all well and good, but for me this just isn't worth $60. So before you lay into me in the comments, touch some grass and think about it. Is this really what you wanted from an AOS RTS game? If it is, leave a comment that explains why instead of just calling me a liar because I don't have enough hours logged. If you need longer than 2 hours of gameplay to form an opinion then I don't know what to tell ya.

_childDocuments_.review: AestheticsThe game looks great with high graphical fidelity and visually appealing effects that are not too overpowering or noisy. I feel like it looks like Warhammer: Age of Sigmar (which I play a lot). Animations are generally pretty good, but it's not something I've focused heavily on.SoundI like how the game sounds in general, it's very thematic to the universe. An improvement to me would be to add more unit/model barks and voices during combat, to make combat feel more impactful and realistic.FactionsI really hope new factions are already being worked on, but I know that stuff takes a long time so I don't expect it in the near future. At the time of writing, Tzeentch and Nighthaunt seem like the best factions in terms of balance and unit variety. They are also the most fun to play, where I feel Stormcast is a fairly underwhelming faction in terms of playstyle, units and aesthetics. A bit of the same goes for Kruelboyz.Game feelingStuck in combatCombat is still fairly clunky. If you go straight into it without the campaign, you don't know that it's intended that your units are stuck in combat until one party retreats or is slain. It makes sense on the tabletop that this is the case and it feels more suited there, but I'm not convinced it works in a video game. I feel like it's a loss of agency, which is often not a good thing in a video game.RetreatingI think retreating is still too costly. It is already a big price to pay to give up and retreat with your unit, I don't think it needs to also cost command points. It makes sense for the tabletop, but here you need to retreat much more often and you give up ground to do so all the time. That's still a cost. It took me a while to realize that I need to hold shift + R to retreat all my units at the same time and I'm not sure I like it. I was expecting the ability to retreat all if I have a bunch of units selected.Game informationI gave this feedback during the demos as well, and it has improved a little bit since then. But I still think the game is very lacking in terms of giving the player info and details about unit stats and abilities. What's the reasoning behind this? I want to be able to clearly see what my units do, how worth they are for the cost and how much an upgrade will improve them. I don't know if "increased unit health" or "gain 2 armor" is worth it, if the unit already has a lot of armor, or if the increased health is a lot or not. Please write some numbers and give us unit info. It can even be a toggle on in the settings.ConquestPlease add more depth to this system. It feels extremely shallow and I can't see myself playing this system through more than once, not even for each faction. Each battle just feels like a normal match, and I the conquest map and bonuses are not significant enough. I would like the bonuses and twists to either be more impactful, change the way I play or have some added content in them. Otherwise I can't see myself or many players playing it a lot. It's a cool idea in theory, but it needs content. I think similarly to the campaign, your units need to level up and gain items or at least upgrades that you can choose outside of each battle. Just like in the tabletop game Age of Sigmar's Path to Glory system, your units earn veteran abilities and you can upgrade them. I would want this game mode to be more like that. It's a cool system and you end up caring about each of your units and heroes more. You can even give them names so they feel super thematic. I really really hope you explore these aspects of Conquest mode in the future. Until then I can't see myself playing it.CampaignI hope in the future that your units and heroes gain levels/ranks and find items. The story is cool and all, the voice acting is great. The cinematics are very nicely done, including the animations and other visuals.As a part of this I hope units can gain experience and ranks during ANY battle, even skirmish. This would make me care more about the units and it feels awesome to have units get better over the course of the battle if they survive long enough. This is also fairly common in other strategy games and I hope it gets implemented here as well.I would LOVE to give this game a positive review as I love the setting so much, but I cannot do that yet as I feel it is not finished. It looks and sounds great, but it's not feeling great yet and that's more important to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:1. Visually, the game is pretty well rendered and the animations/VFX are pretty good. 2. The storyline and the voice acting is decent so far. 3. Customization feels good and I personally love all things warhammer, so its a good immersion into the Age of Sigmar. Cons:The gameplay is extremely frustrating.1. Units don't react to having other friendlies attacked near them and once a unit reaches the location of a movement command (normal or attack command) they just stand there even if they're getting shot. 2. Pathing for enemies/your own troops is mediocre at best. 3. The fact that most abilities must be enacted in the moment and most abilities aren't targeted means you have to micromanage one fight and ignore the rest of the map.4. Control groups sometimes work, sometimes they don't. 5. The units move abhorrently slow. 6. Once units are in combat, it seems impossible to disengage without having to waste resources on the "retreat" order... and that retreat order has no way of canceling it. So instead of having a unit back pedal and engage on a different front (like every single RTS in history) the unit engages until it wins or loses or you waste resources on it so it can run back all the way to your base. Who thought that one up?7. Units are extremely expensive due to the fact that everything uses resources. You can't expand, you can't use abilites, otherwise you can't field a large army. If you DO field your maximum amount of units, you're broke. You cannot build anything and abilities can't be used. Expanding your zone of control also feels extremely unrewarding because if you build in other zones of control and keep their aura at maximum, you don't get resources (unless its the secondary resource building), so you can't ramp up resource production to snowball. If you could cut the cost of units by half and increase the retreat cost by double, I'd be fine with it because I would be able to enjoy battles without constantly fretting that half my units have to trot (they don't run) for 1-3 mins of game time all the way back to the base and heal up slowly. 8. Why don't retreat orders adapt to your healing nodes? I build a healing node so that they can run back to it but instead they still run back all the way to the base? It's extremely punishing and frustrating gameplay. The ai gets so many resource cheats to field the armies they have that you can't keep up on some single players missions above the 2nd level difficulty (I'm no Starcraft pro but I can hold my own). I field the maximum unit cap and then micro manage them against half the amount of enemy units (orks vs stormcast in this example) and they still lose, even with upgrades and perfect counters. I don't have the luxury of spamming my abilities like the ai because I'm constantly without resources or holding off so I can retreat them... just so that they can lose again in a couple minutes. 9. The minimap is useless. Games back in 2002 had better minimaps. I get no pings for engaged combat, I can barely see what enemies are near zones of control. Its quality is poor so I cannot use it to identify threats of any kind. 10. Unit formations seem nonexistent. Most games form up units so that you can engage the enemy in the manner in which you built your army. In this game they just do a 180 turn and range are right at the front and your front line has a clumsy and difficult time getting past them to reach the frontline, which becomes infuriating when your range units engage in melee and you can't disengage them without running all the way back to base. If Frontier would invest in improving the gameplay so that it was half as good as BFME2 or C&C the game would change dramatically for the better. Hopefully they'll care enough to improve the depressingly poor gameplay so that the game can shine. I do not recommend it. Go play BFME2 or AoM if you want medieval high fantasy RTS. This game requires a lot of improvement before it reaches an "Acceptable" title.

_childDocuments_.review: The Game is often compared to Dawn of War II. And having played both games I can agree with that statement. It's a squad based RPG in a Warhammer IP with (at launch) four factions. With a focus on heroes, abilities and individual units. Due to the greater focus on Melee combat it doesn't use DoW II cover system but rather a terrain system more reminiscent of DoW I were certain terrain can slow down or in this case even damage units passing through it. The main mode of skirmish in this game is the same as DoW II focused on capturing Victory points. In terms of the DoW II comparison my thoughts on some of the differences:-the faction rosters are about the same size as DoW II at launch though there are only 2 Heroes per faction, which can both be recruited during a game-ability use costs no energy of the unit but rescources-Arcane Conduits (the equivalent of resource points) can be upgraded in a variety of ways-the campaign is a set 18 Missions, with more scripted missions than DoW II, also while the faction is focused on the Stormcast Eternals, the player does take command over other factions during some missions-instead of DoW IIs modular campaign with various generic missions, RoR has a Conquest Mode that can be played with any faction and puts skirmishes on a world map, fighting through missions to reach a climatic final fight. Some of these skirmishes have special twists making the easier or harder. Generally I consider RoR a worthy sucessor of the DoW, especially DoW II mantle, and think in some aspekts it offers a good deal more than DoW II, primarily giving more than just one faction considerable singleplayer content.

Its an RTS without the base building so one has more time to be focusing on their units, which are built from your starting building.Its actually strategic because there are arcane conduits on the map to fight over for resources, and victory points to win the game. One can build bastions (A choice of 3-4 types) on captured conduits which are effected by how much territory the conduit controls (it expands towards its maximum so long as you're the only player with units in its area) which is a great mechanic and unique to this game.If I could have any game I want manifest into existence, its foundations would be this game.On the down side, craventhrone guard seem to be too strong at the moment, but the other 3 factions all have fun matchups. _childDocuments_.review: This plays like a game where the developers were too lazy to program AI. I understand the argument of it being "based on the board game," but we're not playing a board game. Having to chaperone every single unit because they'll just stand there and be shot at is tedious at best, and is one of the biggest gripes I have with the game. The campaign also has a few missions that are incredibly unbalanced, and expect you to scrape by by the skin of your teeth (like mission 5, which starts with the enemy already having map control and you losing tickets before you even move from your base). The game is very poorly optimized, even on a 3070. The game does have its strengths, like unit identity, but that's also where part of the game is at its weakest. Shield units all have a barrier, sword units all have a charge, archers/artillery all have a barrage. The game is basically just Rock-paper-scissors, and is mind numbing in the "I wanna turn this off and take a nap" kind of way. The voice acting is fairly good, but I've noticed several moments where the lip movement is fairly off from the voices, but that's not a voice acting problem. The graphics are very nice, and the sound design is good, nothing crazy, but it's satisfactory. I would not recommend the game to anyone who likes to play RTS games unless you wanna babysit each individual unit like there is not a single thought between their eyes.

Mind you, I've only played the first 4 chapters of the campaign story, and I don't feel a strong desire to continue due to these issues.It's a really gorgeous game, with great vo, but the balance is a serious, serious killjoy at the moment. I'd love to see some balancing patches, but seeing that this game it came out 5+ months before I wrote this review, I am not too hopeful.Buy this game on sale if you REALLY love the setting (I'm new to AoS), and don't mind throwing your head against the wall to accomplish mission objectives. _childDocuments_.review: Realms of Ruin kinda' came out of nowhere to me, as I learned about it when it was announced but haven't followed it since. To my surprise, it's a really interesting take on the RTS genre that already offered me some great moments in online PVP. I didn't play the campaign yet, but I'll try to update the review when I do.It's a small scale, tactics-heavy take on the genre which seems to play like a mix between Company of Heroes, the first Battle for Middle-Earth all the while giving some Myth flashbacks. You do not really build a base, but... You actualy do. Your home base is a pre-built HQ that recruits units, and you fight over control points which can (and have to be if you want to win) be upgraded with specialised buildings. Said buildings, same as HQ, can be upgraded, together with units with researchable upgrades (many of which are mutualy exclusive for added depth). Do not be fooled by the MOBA similarities a passing glance can provide: This is an RTS through and through. You have resource managament, build orders, upgrades, multiple modes of harassment of the enemy, defence structures, varied unit types, all stremlined but in a quite clever way, one that retains a lot of classical RTS' gameplay depth while being easy to learn and fast to get into. However, I believe mastering all the different mechanics for multiplayer can be an interesting challenge.Thus far my games felt like truly enjoyable battles of wits, where army composition, unit counters, placement, build orders etc. allowed for a lot of interesting back-and-forth instead of a brutish spam less thought out often RTS devolve into.The game at launch has 4 different, quite varied in playstyle factions, all with their unique quirks and features, from the elite, thundering Stormcast Eternals (the Age of Sigmar equivalent of Space Marines), through brutal and cunnin' Orks, blue Tzeentch cultist (who I haven't figured out how to fight against yet) and delightfuly morbid Nighthaunt undead (who surprisingly became my favourite faction to play due to amazing voice work and fun, spammy-but-tricky playstyle).On top of enjoyable multiplayer, there's a full-fledged campaign, skirmish, a classic conquest mode, a map editor and an army painter. For the price tag it's a respectable amount of content. The game has a good, enjoyable level of polish, and feels like a AA/AAA title, which is a nice surprise for an RTS in this day and age. The graphics are good enough, with decent environment and really good unit models and animations. The strongest part, so far, seems to be the audio: The sounds of combat are great and the voice acting for unit is exceptional, elevating entire factions' feel from good to amazing. I can't overstate how fun is it to listen to the wailling and rasping of the murderous undead. I also love how the announcer calls out the names of skills you're casting, a great touch. The music, when it plays, is great, and I love the main menu theme with the orchestra over a synth beat. I wish there was more interesting in-game music, as most of the time it is an quiet ambient which, while good, is barely noticable (if it is in there at all and it's not level background sounds).Thus far, the gameplay was smooth, the performance was good (with DLSS on Performance and all on Ultra), and I haven't seen any bugs. Sometimes I wished the units would be a bit more responsive, but it may be due to my lack of knowledge of games' mechanics, as melee units are locked into combat when they start fighting and all skills are put on a cooldown for a few seconds during that time. Some simple basics like unit formations or stances are missing, and while I don't miss them *that much*, they'd be a good thing to add in a patch.Overall, a really damn nice surprise for me at the end of the year already filled with surprisingly good games. I can only hope the game will have a healthy community, because I believe it may deserve it.First impressions are a definite 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not often I bother to write a review. Lots of games I've played, lots of good and lots of bad, but it takes something particularly special for me to actually say something. Realms of Ruin is particularly special.Realms of Ruin is a beautiful game. Deceptively so. The cutscenes are gorgeous. The voice acting is top notch. The maps are lush and full. And all of that is there to hide what is a truely ugly, broken, and hateful game underneath. I picked this game up from the March Humble Bundle to play on my youtube channel as I do every month and initially I was enamoured with it while knowing nothing about the Age of Sigmar setting. And then Chapter 4 happened. Chapter 4 highlights everything wrong with the game. In every other mission the Unit AI is clunky, but managable. In Chapter 4 that becomes a liability. In Chapters 1-3 you're taught how to use the economy. In Chapter 4 they take that away. They give you a faction you've never played, units you've never seen, a map you cannot hope to cross, and a time limit so that you can't even learn what you're doing. It's as if they were taught how to make a tutorial, and then purposefully did the exact opposite of everything. I don't know what the rest of the game looks like or how it plays. I gave up. After three hours and researching tactics online, turning the difficulty down, and doing everything short of God Mode-ing it, I gave up. But if this is a look at things to come then I have to assume that the developers have absolutely no idea how to make a functioning game. As I said at the beginning, it's a beautiful game. Stunning to look at. But the most important part of a game is being able to play it. And this is unplayable.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend Realms of Ruin if you are a fan of similar real time tactics games such as company of heroes or Dawn of war 2. There is no base building as the game focuses more on the combat and positioning of units around the map while holding and claiming objectives. The campaign isn't too bad once you get past the introductory tutorial missions, the AI is competent so the missions aren't a complete comp stomp. The story is a good introduction to the Age of Sigmar and cut scenes and voice acting are top notch.The Conquest Mode leaves something to be desired as it is in essence just a selection of skirmish matches against the AI with various modifiers such as "units have less health" or "there is only one capture point" that sort of thing. It would be nice to see this evolved into something more akin to Dark Crusade's conquest map with multiple factions all trying to claim territory on the map.On the Multiplayer side of things there is a good selection of both 1v1 and 2v2 maps with hopefully a lot more to come from the devs and community due to the inclusion of a map editor. Sadly there are no 3v3, 4v4 or free for all game modes which I feel is a shame. Hopefully theses are game modes that can be added in the near future.Extra marks to the devs for including an army painter, this seems to be something that more RTS/RTT games seem to have been omitting.

_childDocuments_.review: It feels like the mere foundation of a potentially good game, but released as complete, with far too little content, and charging a premium price. The AI can't do anything on its own, and there's hardly any tactical options at all--just a rock-paper-scissors system and a few unit abilities. Everything feels soooo slooooow--except your units dying, that can happen pretty quick, but it'll take forever to spawn more and get them back out (very limited unit cap, btw). And some of these flaws probably won't be fixed, as they are tied to core game mechanics. Namely, the units getting LOCKED into combat, the only option is to retreat, which relinquishes control of your squad as they run back to the "base." So the unit passivity and weird movement options (passive movement, which is default, and attack movement) are to help units manage this odd design choice, I assume.The game certainly looks good, graphically, but who cares if the gameplay doesn't measure up to it? It runs well, and I've experienced no major bugs, so there's that. The campaign is decent, with pretty good voice acting, and okay-ish story. The conquest mode is the only real interesting inclusion, but the gameplay is so slow and bland that it hardly matters.I hope they can improve it with more content and gameplay tweaks, but I'm guessing no significant changes will be made. A good bit of any extra content they offer should be offered for free, or cheap, considering the money they're charging for this on release...unless they pull some magic trick and make this game actually fun to play.

_childDocuments_.review: First off: don't expect Dawn of War when coming into this game. Though it may also be a Warhammer title the two games take very different approaches to the RTS genre and offer different types of gameplay. With that out of the way I want to say I loved my time with this game. The campaign/story is a ton of fun to go through and is incredibly well done and worth the entry. The characters are interesting, the variety of missions is great, the story is engaging enough to keep you wanting more, the voice acting is phenomenal, and the cinematography in cutscenes is better than many many other games. It's not often you get well-framed shots in a game! Serious hats off to whoever was in charge of that.The gameplay itself is also quite a lot of fun but could use some tweaks as other reviews have mentioned. It's not a grand detractor from the game but the pace of gameplay is a bit slow as units physically move a bit sluggish. It's easy to see why that is the case as you play it though as the devs seem to be focusing on small groups/unit gameplay instead of massive hordes/armies. While the game relies on a triangle system for combat (sword beats shield, shield beats bow, bow beats sword) it forces you to move your units into place to best counter your opponent and being able to time that well enough to move quicker than your foe is where some of the tactical aspect really kicks off. Basically, the better you are at telling what your opponent will use the better you can prepare and ambush them. I will say I have not tried the online portion of this game and I'm unsure if I will. For RTS games I typically stick to story/campaign/skirmish/conquest with AI and will likely do so here. I did play a few skirmish games against AI to try out other factions and that seemed to be fun - though I do wish there was a better way to see the map you are choosing for it. Also a minor - but fun - element I havent seent talked about in reviews is the in-game army painter feature. You can customize the look of your whole army or even individual units by picking what colors you want them to be. Not a whole lot of customization outside of that but it's fun!Hope the Devs are able to make a sequel or at least a continuation of the story in some way. I'll be there for the next one.Waaaaaaaaaaaaaaagh!

_childDocuments_.review: Having done two skirmishes to get a general grip of this game's complexity and having watched some videos to see if I missed anything I think I can give a brief review of this. It's a hard-pass from me right now and will likely stay that way for a while.Single playerGo play DoW Soulstorm with mods if you want lots of unit variation in a good single player experience. There are only 4 factions on release with 3 units per tier with 4 tiers leading to a mere 12 units with a similar equivalent of upgrades. This is basically no more than DoW games released over a decade ago now, don't pay more for less. MultiplayerIf you want a competitive RTS, this isn't it, the micro is tedious as most units have abilities which have a small affect that will often turn a 1v1 if on the same tier of unit but ultimately exceptionally bare-bones. The more I play it the more I feel this could just be a DoW3 mod it's so empty. There are good RTS games out there, most are modern (ww2 onwards) and it's a shame that another fantasy RTS is so weak.Conclusion.Even the current sale of 40% is not worth it for this game. I have sunk hundreds of hours in C&C generals, DoW, CoH. This is weaker them all,  and worse yet, has denuvo. Will likely mean any modding will never exist so ultimately will get abandoned if too few people buy it which would be a shame as there could be a good game here if given an awful lot of TLC. For now though I would definitely avoid, give it 2 years and see if Frontier haven't done the CoH2 approach of just chucking new heroes into as a bunch of useless dlc. Truly a shame as I really like Warhammer lore in general and was looking forward to giving this a good try.

Wait for a sale  if inclined but a full price purchase wont kill you if you have the money to spend.

_childDocuments_.review: Realms of Ruin is shaping up to be a great RTS so far.  I'm very much enjoying it.The game is beautiful.  The interface is really pretty and reminds me of Warscrolls from the table-top game.  All the units are rendered beautifully and look exactly like their miniatures.  The maps are really detailed and interesting.I am enjoying the 4 factions present so far.  They have a good variety to them.  I'm still learning their nuances, but there is a lot there.So far the campaign story is interesting and engaging.  The voice acting is really good.  Sound design is also great.  I like the sounds that your abilities make, and the music is good.Combat in Realms of Ruin is slower paced than other RTS games, in a good way.  This isn't like Starcraft where you have to have insanely fast reflexes to win.  Here, you have to think strategically and tactically.  You need to carefully think where to commit your forces and how to set them up.  The game instantly punishes you for making a mistake and sending the wrong force into battle, or leaving yourself undefended.  I really enjoy this tactical thinking versus just making the game about how fast you can click.This game is HARD.  I am a veteran of RTS's, so I set the difficulty to the "Hard" setting when I began the game.  Once I got to the third campaign map, I had to turn the difficulty down!  Since Chapter 3, I've had to replay each map several times to win.  It's awesome to have a challenging single-player campaign like this.  So far each chapter is also very different in terms of how it plays and your objectives.  I've been enjoying that a lot.I'm still getting the hang of the interface.  It is extremely minimalist, more so than I am used to from other RTS games.  So basic things like how to select units to use their abilities or how to produce new units or select upgrades I'm still getting used to.  I need to get accustomed to simply using the hot-keys for this instead of clicking the interface icons.  I've gotten used to using TAB to select unit abilities though.  I think this just takes practice.Sometimes when units are standing near each other, I want to just select a certain couple units and leave one behind to guard.  I end up selecting all three of them too often.  I think this is somewhat related to the "interface" issues mentioned above.There is a lack of detailed information about units, such as how much damage they do, how much damage their abilities do, their defenses, etc.  You get a health bar, and that's about it.  You get a description of your abilities, but until you try them out it's not clear how effective they'll be.  Usually, they're really effective though, so I think the game is trying to tell you not to worry about the numbers, and just use your troops.I'm still learning the game and all the units, but I feel like for Age of Sigmar there is not enough magic represented.  The focus is definitely on melee and ranged troops.  What magic is in the game is very powerful though.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid RTS with a surprisingly challenging (maybe even frustrating) campaign.  Very pretty visuals, good music, interesting campaign storyline, and quite excellent voice acting.  Mechanics are mostly fine but need some tweaking.  For example melee units do not react to getting shot by ranged units and will just stand there until they die.  Retreating to preserve units a fun mechanic but there needs to be a way to set where they retreat too.  Going all the way back to the spawn point and then slogging back up the entire map just takes too long.No base building so if that's what you like prolly give it a pass.  However if you are a fan of Dawn of War 2 you'll like this one.

_childDocuments_.review:
Experience the Mortal Realms brought to life in Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Realms of Ruin, a real-time strategy game set in Games Workshop's expansive fantasy universe. Become a warlord and lead four unique factions to conquer the wild and savage Realm of Ghur in tense and tactical battles.

A CAMPAIGN OF DESPERATE SURVIVAL
Tame the savage Realm of Beasts in a rich narrative, exploring the nature of war and survival from the perspectives of righteous champions and villainous generals. Battle for survival and dominance across a campaign featuring four major factions, including Stormcast Eternals and Orruk Kruleboyz, and experience a twisted plot, penned in conjunction with acclaimed Black Library author, Gavin Thorpe.

AGE OF SIGMAR COMES TO LIFE
Experience the rich lore of Age of Sigmar brought to life by world-class animation and state-of-the-art graphical fidelity. Built in close collaboration with Games Workshop, every unit is precisely modelled after their tabletop counterpart, allowing you to experience an authentic and dramatic vision of the Age of Sigmar universe.

FORGE YOUR ARMIES
Engage in a diverse range of mission types and modes, and rally an army of units inspired by Age of Sigmar Warscrolls, each with their own tactical strengths and weaknesses. Recruit from a legion of unit types from fast-moving flyers to lumbering monsters, mystical wizards and powerful heroes.

DYNAMIC REAL-TIME BATTLES
Secure strategically-located Arcane Conduits in an ever-evolving battlefield to obtain resources, bolster defences, rally new forces and seize victory!
The tides of war ebb and flow with no battle ever being the same – upgrade and specialise your forces with dynamic in-battle tech trees to counter your opponent’s forces… or to strike with the upper hand!

name: Among Us VR
detailed_description: Among Us VR is a party game of teamwork and betrayal. Grab your crew and headset and launch into the VR version of this hit multiplayer deduction game. Play with 4 - 10 players as you complete tasks to hold your ship together. But beware! One or more random players among the crew are Impostors bent on sabotaging and killing everyone. VR-Exclusive Highlights Gameplay : Experience the core Among Us gameplay you know and love, such as tasks, sabotages, emergency meetings, and venting, but now in VR In-Game Voice Chat : Communicate using voice chat (featuring proximity chat) or use quick text chat Minigames : Play old favorites and new-for-VR games, too Customization : Pick your character’s color and hat Comfort and Safety : Adjust your settings for the best experience possible Cross-Platform in VR : Play with other VR users, even on other VR platforms and headsets Locomotion : Choose single or two-handed locomotion options Custom Lobby Settings : 18 settings to customize the game, including ‘Hands Visible’, and ‘Number of Impostors’, resulting in millions of setting combinations Player Safety : In-game reporting, muting, kicking and voice chat moderation Cosmetics : Fan favorites from the original Among Us and VR exclusive hat DLCs In this game, you’ll play as either a Crewmate or an Impostor. Crewmate Mission : Complete all the tasks or find the Impostor. Keep your eyes and ears open since there is always someone lurking right around the corner. Impostor Mission : Kill and sabotage the Crewmates! Be as sneaky as possible and lie, lie, lie. It’s as simple as that! Join our Discord for more Crewmate fun outside the headset.

_childDocuments_.review: Basically just the minimum possible among us vr experience.No cams, missing tasks, one map, no hands in normal play, no lobby settings, etc.You should probably just play the VRchat version, it's free.Edit: A developer has responded explaining that a "year one roadmap" will be coming soon. _childDocuments_.review: Edit: Playspace mover via OVR can definitely grief games. Killing/interacting across the map, moving faster than intended, etc. I won't describe how to do it, I'll just say I've found worse while testing and I hope this gets patched very soon.Ignore the meme reviews. Launch day is pretty rough. A large majority of lobbies lag so bad they can't even start, and when the host leaves there is no migration, the lobby is instead dissolved entirely and you are forced to re-queue. ** There's so many basic features missing and, embarrassingly, a lot of primitive VR jank that's been solved for years now.**I did manage to complete a few games eventually.  When you do manage to get some rounds in, this game is fun. It's just a matter of finding a working lobby.When the window is unfocused, no controls work.Going near the cafeteria doors while in a lobby just blinds you for some reason?Movement is instantaneous, and ridiculously fast, with a vignette as the only band-aid.Some tasks are different, but most are pretty boring. This game is nowhere near as feature rich as the desktop ($4.99) or VRChat (free) versions, lacking any sort of game settings to alter the experience with. Also no camera room. The in-game map/menu doesn't even rotate with you fast enough while using Smooth turn, making navigation incredibly disorienting. Snap turn doesn't have this issue.The "Recenter" button in the gameplay and controls tab is sometimes just invisible? And even when it is you can still click it by aiming your laser in the spot it's supposed to be in lol. Even when a lobby manages to start, there is no guarantee you won't black screen and get stuck hearing random sound effects.The color you choose for your spaceman doesn't matter, it gets randomized when you join a lobby.Your in-game rotation via the stick is not based on your playspace position. This can create very sickening turns when moving irl, then rotating in-game.The art style is cute.Game is very optimized using basic culling techniques.I give it aHost is no longer available or has shutdown / 10. Stick to the VRChat version.

_childDocuments_.review: My name is Walter Hartwell White. I live at 308 Negra Arroyo Lane, Albuquerque, New Mexico, 87104. This is my confession. If you're watching this tape, I'm probably dead, murdered by my brother-in-law Hank Schrader. Hank has been building a meth empire for over a year now and using me as his chemist. Shortly after my 50th birthday, Hank came to me with a rather, shocking proposition. He asked that I use my chemistry knowledge to cook methamphetamine, which he would then sell using his connections in the drug world. Connections that he made through his career with the DEA. I was... astounded, I... I always thought that Hank was a very moral man and I was... thrown, confused, but I was also particularly vulnerable at the time, something he knew and took advantage of. I was reeling from a cancer diagnosis that was poised to bankrupt my family. Hank took me on a ride along, and showed me just how much money even a small meth operation could make. And I was weak. I didn't want my family to go into financial ruin so I agreed. Every day, I think back at that moment with regret. I quickly realized that I was in way over my head, and Hank had a partner, a man named Gustavo Fring, a businessman. Hank essentially sold me into servitude to this man, and when I tried to quit, Fring threatened my family. I didn't know where to turn.Eventually, Hank and Fring had a falling out. From what I can gather, Hank was always pushing for a greater share of the business, to which Fring flatly refused to give him, and things escalated. Fring was able to arrange, uh I guess I guess you call it a "hit" on my brother-in-law, and failed, but Hank was seriously injured, and I wound up paying his medical bills which amounted to a little over $177,000. Upon recovery, Hank was bent on revenge, working with a man named Hector Salamanca, he plotted to kill Fring, and did so. In fact, the bomb that he used was built by me, and he gave me no option in it. I have often contemplated suicide, but I'm a coward. I wanted to go to the police, but I was frightened. Hank had risen in the ranks to become the head of the Albuquerque DEA, and about that time, to keep me in line, he took my children from me. For 3 months he kept them. My wife, who up until that point, had no idea of my criminal activities, was horrified to learn what I had done, why Hank had taken our children. We were scared. I was in Hell, I hated myself for what I had brought upon my family. Recently, I tried once again to quit, to end this nightmare, and in response, he gave me this. I can't take this anymore. I live in fear every day that Hank will kill me, or worse, hurt my family. I... All I could think to do was to make this video in hope that the world will finally see this man, for what he really is.
