_childDocuments_.review: Man, this game could have been a masterpiece. How did it fail so harshly in such critical aspects?I would consider this a stage play first and an SRPG second. This game has easily the worst pacing of any game I've ever played. You will regularly go for 45-60 minute stretches just watching cut scene after cut scene. Then once the cut scenes are finished, time to go "explore" (talk to everyone in town). Then more cut scenes, THEN maybe a battle. The bright side is that the story(ies) in Triangle Strategy are some of the best you will ever experience. A captivating, well-written plot that's easy to digest and keep track of. Nothing gets too far off the reservation. Very few pieces you'd consider cliche. The influence from Game of Thrones is palpable.The choice and consequence is truly difficult to decide on with how much gravitas the choices make. You are almost always tossing someone to the dogs in order to save another. The constant betrayals, playing off the back foot, and absence of a truly moral decision can be exhausting though. This is not a feel good video game.But, even this age-old system is flawed in Triangle Strategy. What's the point of choice and consequence when regardless of what *I* want to do, some NPCs can usurp me and pick a different direction than me? Why tell me my convictions are strengthened every few minutes when i still can't convince them ♥♥♥♥? Think about it, it should be as simple as "Which path will you take?," and instead it's here's a break from the five cut scenes you just sat through, go talk to everyone in town to get evidence on that you'll then have to recite to the party members in an attempt to convince them to select the path you (the player) want. You will fail.Poor design isn't replayability, poor design is *expecting* you to replay the game. You don't have conviction levels high enough to pick certain paths your first time through. Because of this, they actually force you certain ways in decision making during your first playthrough, furthering an already flawed system under the guise of choice.The combat and battle customization are puddle deep. There is no weapons or armor, no classes, and barely any skill variation. The tactics you use at the first battle will be nearly identical to the last. You can tell the "budget" put story first and everything essential to a good RPG dead last.The upgrade system is unbelievably convoluted. Like, who-thought-this-was-a-good-idea-and-fire-them bad. No such simple resource like job points you can use to get upgrades, you instead need a silly amount of materials from an ever growing list of resources and also a ton of currency. Every time you upgrade one piece, the others all get more expensive too. It just makes so little sense I'm getting pissed writing this. It *could* have made sense, but no... they needed to keep you from fully upgrading to drag you along into another playthrough. Grinding for currency and mats doesn't even make sense. I would do the highest level mock battle I could at the time and come away with scraps. There is a huge economic issue where not enough resources are provided or able to be obtained if needed.The OST is soooooo good. Almost every track is an instant classic. Special care was put into each battle theme.Even with copious annoyances, I still kept coming back. Was it for the story? Maybe. Was it to fill the void of being without a a Square Enix SRPG since the DS and PSP era? Absolutely it was.
_childDocuments_.name: TRIANGLE STRATEGY

_childDocuments_.review: Points of note:-The story and characters are nice and likable but fairly generic, or otherwise simple/one-note. -The story has choices that make for real awesome branching paths, but sometimes they can feel limited in that the branches converge back, save in the final act. -The side-characters are cool but often have little to no relevance to the story, and the side stories to fill the gaps don’t add all too much. -The event-to-event pacing is a bit slow.-There are multiple endings but, the golden route/ending to the game, while nice on its own, I think unfortunately can make the other routes/endings feel unsatisfying by comparison. -All things considered, I think the game is actually very good! The main pull to the game is the aforementioned choices that add branching paths to the story. The choices given to you feel as well done as they can be within reason. Often there’s pros/cons and some nuance to each choice you make in the game, encouraging you to really learn details and consider each suggestion before making your choice. Choices primarily change the short-term events of the story and this can change the information you learn in the game, your perception of certain characters, as well as the characters you have available to you. In addition, the cumulative actions and choices you make will influence which of the endings are available to you in the end. This can make for a pretty unique experience imo, and It’s because of this that it felt to me like the choices were incredibly impactful. I went for the golden route but, found myself often looking up what would happen or who I would recruit had I gone down a different path. The choices, and not knowing what might unfold next exactly, is what kept the story interesting and the game overall fun to me at least. The gameplay was also pretty solid, I really like the kudos system and there’s also nice music, graphics, and art to the game. That being said, the combat could be streamlined a little bit to be a clearer and have more/better QOL features. The game has a bit of reading/cutscenes/dialogue, and there are notes and books that serve as additional lore; I personally enjoyed this but, it’s not for everyone.Overall probably like an 8.5/10 I’d say.
_childDocuments_.name: TRIANGLE STRATEGY

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I'm surprised this game isn't rated higher. It's pretty damn well done. My favorite aspect is that no matter what choices you make, there are reasonable costs to them. The typical JRPG/SRPG story seems to have an "everything will be great as long as we work together!!" theme and characters with plot armor all over the story, but not this. In TS, people actually fall, the story takes turns for the worse, and the ending was even bittersweet with some heavy costs to the route I took. Definitely rewards multiple play-throughs. Other pros were good combat, wide range of characters to play, and a cool upgrade system. Classes are set in stone, but that doesn't really bug me much. I like when characters have a clear path.Downside is probably the voice acting. Not bad by any means, but feels kinda stale and unpolished. Story is told well though and I enjoyed most everything else. Definitely recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: Loved it!  Been a while since I played a strategy RPG but I really had a great time with Triangle Strategy.  The story was nothing groundbreaking but I thought it was executed well enough to be enjoyable.  Some of the low res textures don't hold up super well on a larger screen but overall I think the game looks really great and the blemishes didn't detract much from that at all.  Like I said it's been a while since I played a strategy RPG so I don't have much to compare the combat to but to me it was fun.  It was deep enough to keep me engaged and honestly I was mostly in it for the story anyway so it's not as important.  And if you're interested in this game be aware that it is a RPG first and foremost!  Most of the game is dialogue and story with some roaming sections to learn new info to use in the decision making process.  Rather than make the decisions directly your companions vote and it's up to you to sway them in the direction you want the story to progress.  I thought this was an interesting idea and at least added some extra layers to the decisions themselves.  Definitely recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried to like this game but I just can't. I made it around 70% of the way through the campaign before deciding that proceeding farther just wasn't worth the effort. What I liked: The art is great. The characters have a lot of life. The voice acting is solid. The UI conveys the information you need without getting in your way.What I didn't like: First up, gameplay. Maybe this game is aiming for nostalgia I just don't have or maybe it's just misjudged, but I find the battles joyless. Enemies have piles of hit points and plentiful healing, requiring multiple turns to chew through even unarmored support characters. At the same time, they universally hit hard and will punish any mistake on your part, or even just bad luck if the AI gets a good initiative roll or a key dodge. The gimmick here is that attacking from the back does extra damage, and putting characters on either side of an enemy will provide bonus attacks. Which supposedly make this a game about controlling movement, but with few options to actually restrict where the AI moves and reinforcements popping in without warning from unexpected directions, all while being at a significant DPS disadvantage vs. your opponents, the result is to punish any aggressive moves on the player's part. Instead, you're left to turtle up in a corner while slowly wittling down the enemy one at a time. Doing this once or twice feels clever. After that. it's boring.Next, progression. Just playing the main campaign won't provide enough XP and money you need to prepare for battle. So you are forced to repeatedly play the practice battles back at camp to slowly grind out resources. I actually don't mind a bit of XP grinding, but these battles are all overly-complex scenarios which take a long time to play and are not always ideal for levelling more specialized characters. They provide plenty of XP but never enough money. The last thing I played in this game was a practice mission which forces your team to spread out inefficiently. I ended up using 3500 money worth of healing consumables to grind through a mission that only paid me 1700 money. That wouldn't be enough money to buy what I needed anyway, even without the overhead.But really what killed this game for me is the story. It clearly aspires to be an ultra-serious Game of Thrones style political thriller, but it's not nearly clever enough to pull it off and in failing it occasionally drifts into insulting instead. As political extremism rises in the real world, I have little patience for a story that mixes silly reveals of identities hidden behind simple masks and the player being asked to decide whether to sell a racial minority into slavery to benefit their political ambitions. But the final straw was twice being told that my character's actions in defending their homeland were really no different than the actions of the politicians who launched an unannounced war of conquest for economic gain.  Yeah, not thanks.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall it's a good game from Acquire Corp which follows the artstyle of Octopath Traveler, but with a tactical RPG battle system and without an open world.There are some low resolution textures, mainly for the ground, as well as weird background textures outside of the playable square area, which breaks a bit the immersion of the pixel artstyle that is otherwise very solid on Octopath, forcing Anisotropic Filtering to 16x and other settings through UE4 config files does not change  this whatsoever. The game is also locked to 60 FPS for no reason without an in-game setting, needs to be unlocked through UE4 config files by overriding the max FPS setting, other settings such as Bloom also need to be configured manually through the .ini engine files as they are not exposed ingame. Also, as expected from Square Enix, the game doesn't support PlayStation controller prompts, so you need to play with Xbox prompts even if you use a DualShock/DualSense.Some plot points are weird, specially the one at the beginning of Chapter 17, but the story is enjoyable overall. The soundtrack is also enjoyable but there's no track that really stuck on me during the whole game.As for the battle system itself, it is quite unbalanced at best, it almost feels like it's designed to force you to play the New Game +. Just following the story, grabbing the items on the floor - which by the way, sometimes are not possible to spot unless you wander around the whole area spamming X - grabbing the spoils when possible and buying materials to upgrade/enhance your characters is not enough to be on the required level/power for the battles as the game progresses on certain harder battles - and this while playing on Normal. You're expected to grind EXP but the game is not open world and there's no real way to do it that fits the story unlike in Octopath where you can level up between areas. To try to reduce the impact of this, they made it so that if you lose a fight, you can retry it but keep the exp/level that you've earned when fighting the previously lost fight, so you get stronger when retrying fights, which feels like a band-aid game design decision.I think it's definitely worth a try but this game is not worth the selling price of 60€, it's worth 30€ at best, so if you see it discounted go ahead and give it a try if it interests you, but don't go into the game expecting something at the level of Octopath Traveler.Take notes Square Enix: now remove Denuvo from Octopath Traveler 2 if you want me to buy it, otherwise I will continue to ignore it like I did with this game until it was removed.

_childDocuments_.review: Triangle Strategy is a grid based tactical RPG that plays a lot like Fire Emblem. I would recommend if you are into that style of gameplay. Each character is unique and has a handful of passives and active abilities, however, each character has linear class progression and their weapons are upgradable, but locked. I had to rely on certain characters to cheese some of the battles because they are quite challenging. Most story battles have the enemies at 1-2 levels above your current party so doing mock battles for XP on the side was a must for me. If you are a better tactics gamer than me, you'll probably find it a bit easier.In between each story battle, there are lengthy cut scenes which can be a turn off for some. Overall, I thought the story was nothing to write home about. I would recommend if you are looking for something to play while waiting for Tactics Ogre or the next Fire Emblem. With 42 hours in, I'm about 70% done with my first playthrough, though I did hit up the mock battles quite often to get my party leveled.

_childDocuments_.review: Triangle Strategy is currently my favorite entry within the tactics RPG genre.It is a game that is admittedly very heavy on the story, but the story is executed very well from the voice acting all the way to the overall "flow" as you make heavily weighted choices that are felt throughout your playthrough. For comparison, TO:R has 3 routes but there exists a jarring contrast wherein both Catiua and Vyce seem borderline schizophrenic when going from 1 chapter and locking onto a route. In Triangle Strategy, the player can self-insert their own convictions when making decisions while the reactions or consequences affecting Serenoa's companions are written really well (Frederica in Roland's route for example). I was glued to my seat for the major turning points in the game especially since Team Asano made expert use of camera angles and panning (think of the Theater scene in FF6) to keep narration fresh. It wouldn't be a huge leap to say that this game provides a cinematic storytelling experience.As for combat, while some may consider TO:R a bit more hardcore, TS has more variability and diversity in some regard. This may sound weird if you consider that you have a set of 30 unique/usable characters in TS as opposed to the army you can raise from various races and classes in TO:R, but hear me out for a second. TS has difficulty settings that can punish the most hardcore players for making 1 bad decision OR allow those new to the genre to learn the ropes and get a chance to appreciate the game. It's that variability in difficulty that gives me the confidence to recommend this to all of my friends. As for diversity, nearly every single one of the 30 playable units in TS lends to 2 styles of play (aggressive or otherwise). They each have their modestly developed backstory that's told really well through their character stories. I personally prefer this over how things are done in other titles within the genre. The maps also lend to that diversity as you see a broad array of map layouts (that do reappear to some degree) and not just an obnoxious repetition of height-based terrain (looking at you TO:R fortresses). This is a game where choices do indeed matter and this is key to their design choice because it takes a total of 4 playthroughs to platinum TS. Each playthrough is different enough in a significant way (both story and combat) to keep things fresh and you can strategically speed through the common routes/parts thanks to the various upgrades you unlock. I haven't had this much fun hitting up NG+ 4 times over in a long while. You owe it to yourself to experience all the endings and the battles because there really is substance there. I broke down a little bit after completing the golden route thanks to the vivid change on the title screen. So emotional. So epic. Overall the tone of the game (and the slow pacing) reminded me a lot of Gundam Iron-Blooded Orphans except I was the captain of the ship and I was the one making the hard decisions.I treasure the time I spent playing this game and I hope a lot of newer tactics RPG players choose this as their first game. It's a special experience and to anyone who gets the 100%, I'll happily shake your hand in solidarity. Erador best girl.

_childDocuments_.review: Such a great game doesn't deserve such a terrible name. Yes, this is a strategy game. There are three guiding principles that form the core of the decisions you'll make in the game which, more or less, form a triangle. The name is still stupid.Anyway, this is a great successor to the Final Fantasy Tactics games. Each character feels fairly unique in their skills even when sharing the same or similar roles. Resource scarcity forces you to plan who to promote and what upgrades to purchase. It isn't possible to use every single character to their full potential and you likely won't even unlock all of them in the first playthough. In the event that you do want to level everyone, exp is really quite easy to accumulate until you match the level of the enemies on the map. I've noticed many people complain about the length of the cutscenes in the reviews. Boo hoo, go play Call of Duty if you have such a short attention span. There is little that a game in the style of Triangle Strategy can do to share the lore of the world with the player without (sometimes) lengthy dialogue between characters in cutscenes. And if that's such a problem, there's literally a skip button. Replayability is good. New game+ allows you to see other endings and keep your unlocked characters and skills.

_childDocuments_.review: Great story. Far better than I expected it to be. Love the choose your own adventure aspect with the Scales of Conviction and the choices actually mattering. My issue is with the actual gameplay. Felt like another Tactics game that really forces you to grind mock battles to keep pace with the game. Chapter 13 is when I really started feeling like my units were pathetically weak compared to the enemies. I truly despise the upgrade system mainly because the upgrades are so minuscule you don't feel like you gain any power and the cost of materials for the next upgrade in the same tier doubles or triples as soon as you get one upgrade. Leveling up feels empty as well. Think of it like Item Level in MMORPGs where it's just a number to gauge where you are at instead of feeling like you get stronger reach lvl. For those that are hardcore Tactics veterans you will easily love this game. _childDocuments_.review: Great:- Gameplay/battle system. No criticisms here. Character abilities are fun and look good, everything generally makes sense and feels fair. Good incentives/punishment for positioning, and the environment tiles are worth paying attention to especially in regards to the elements, but even finding out that grass gives +10 % chance to dodge was cool to see.Good:- Graphics. Yeah, it's not 3D but it looks great for what it is. Some objects are actually full 3D but then have a 2D texture and it does help make everything look better from other tactic titles like this such as Tactics Ogre Reborn. The ability to easily rotate the camera to any angle and zoom in and out is great, though sometimes the camera will be off when a spell casts or it is an enemy's turn (e.g. Wolfort Castle Town Gates, camera may automatically swivel behind the gates). Spells and abilities look good.- Overall story. There is a lot of story here, which I don't consider a bad thing because for the most part I enjoy it, it's intriguing, and I pretty much always am eager to see what happens next. I think the presentation could be a little more seamless though instead of having to keep going back to the world screen, then put your cursor over the next spot and press a button to transition back into and continue the story. Especially when there is only one choice with no optional scenes available and it is required to continue forward, and it all feels like part of the same act anyways, so why not just continue the cutscenes without the extra transitions to the overworld and button presses which makes the non-interactive parts feel even longer.- Characters. For the most part I enjoy the characters personalities (strengths, weaknesses, convictions, etc). There are times characters decisions, actions, or dialogues don't make a lot of sense though. Biggest example for me is "Chapter 17 - If Griefs Could Passions Move". I've ran through 2 of the options and at least 2 of your supporting characters decisions/actions (either pre-scales of conviction or post) don't actually feel believable to me. But, I don't expect the writing to be an iron-clad, emmy-winning masterpiece. Especially considering what they are trying to do with the conviction system and making decisions feel impactful, there's probably bound to be some imperfection and plot-holes.Bad:The bad for me is the loot system & grinding for materials and levels via mock battles. Mock battles aren't always that bad but become un-fun and a slog after a while. These all affect each other for me so I'll break down each one:- Loot. Picking up loot becomes really tedious. Tactics Ogre got it right in that you don't have to pick up spoils before the end of the battle to claim them, you just have to make sure you don't let enemies grab it. At the very least, being able to claim materials from an adjacent square or having other ways of picking up materials without having to move directly to that square and waste a turn (most of the time), especially for just enemy-dropped loot, would make things less tedious.- Mock battle prep. The above is made worse by not having a way to save team compositions / accessory loadouts. If you want to be efficient, you will be grinding to level up your least leveled characters and trying to catch up on upgrades at the same time. In continuing efficiency, this generally means swapping out your accessories per character nearly every mock battle, on top of needing to re-position everyone. This would be just a QoL upgrade and not one I'd really expect to be included with this genre, but I had to bring it up because it adds to how tedious mock battles become.- Variety of mock battles. I feel like there should be at least 2 different mock battles between battles that you can choose between. Some of the mock battles are far more annoying than they are a challenge (this might depend per-person), and sometimes I'll just skip to the next chapter under-leveled because I really just dislike the mock battle offered and find it really tedious. Again, this probably wouldn't be an issue on its own, but it's usually due to how annoying it is trying to collect loot.Ultimately, I feel like changing the way you pickup loot would make grinding for upgrades & levels suck way less. But as it is, I'm taking more and more breaks toward the end of the game because I'm getting sick of grinding for levels and materials.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great tactical game and I feel a great successor to final fantasy tactics. The most common complaint right off is that there is a lot of story. There is, but the thing that isn't mentioned is that the story is quite good. There are many decision points along the way that present true moral conundrums to balance between what the characters need and what is right. The tactical game is interesting and balanced through NG. I have not gone farther than two play throughs so can't comment on other runs, but so far the scaling does not take anything away nor does it feel like just bigger numbers. Every character feels viable in some way, some are easier to determine their use and feel more powerful right off but with a little bit of experimenting everyone has a strong case to be in the party. Some characters may feel more useful over time as they are leveled up or playing at higher levels as well. At all times it was difficult to not want to take everybody but for some levels with the terrain and start positions some characters really would shine. I am a big fan of tactics game but I do lean hard into needing a good story to make each battle feel good. This game his great theme music for each character and specific places, acceptable voice acting, and just looks great and plays great. I wouldn't let the length of story cut scenes scare you off, if you enjoy any kind of political maneuvering in your story it's a great one that'll will add a lot of context to the battles you are fighting while also getting to play around with some great combat that has a strong emphasis on positioning. If you enjoyed FF Tactics and are looking for something close to it, this would be one of the best modern takes on the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's see, we've got a story driven fantasy rpg in which you take turns moving characters across a grid.  That must mean it's time for more Final Fantasy Tactics comparisons!  It says a lot that people are still thirsty for more over 20 years after the masterpiece was released.  Sadly, this ain't Final Fantasy Tactics.First the good.  The battle system is on point...probably the best tactical rpg battle system since Tactics itself.  The most fun thing about Tactics was playing with overpowered named characters (cough cough Cid), and Triangle strategy wisely chose to just say screw it and make all of your units special characters.  It's glorious.  Every character is very unique, and balance is quite good.  Upgrades are limited, but that's really ok since customization comes from the units you choose to take with you.  Abilities strike the right balance between being meaty enough to feel like you're doing something without being all one-hit wonders, and as an added bonus there are a couple of really powerful combos to discover.  The main battles themselves are all well done and serve the story well.Oh...the story.Well, for the first five hours it's hype af.  I was really invested from the starting bell, and there's a fight a bit in that's absolutely the best "back against the wall" battle I've ever seen done in a video game.  Sadly, the story falls apart shortly afterwards.  Aspiring writers, take note: helpless stupidity and incompetence are not plot devices.  It's not just one instance...there are at least a dozen plot points that could have been resolved easily if someone had just taken second to not make the worst decision possible.Did I mention decisions?  Part of the gimic of this game is that you make choices that influence what type of ruler you are.  Are you an honorable and naive nitwit?  Drunk too much freedom coolaid?  Fancy yourself the next coming of Machiavelli?  No?  Too bad, those are your only choices.  It's interested in theory, except so many times the choices are pretty stark.  Bend over a barrel and nobly take it from behind or murder your mother because she made you eat broccoli?  The choice is yours!  Beyond that, you have to convince your main party to go along with your lunacy.  In theory, your companions have their own moral compass, but you can usually convince them to do whatever you want with no trouble at all.For all the awfulness of the story and how the conviction system doesn't work, however, the game is still incredibly fun.  The story does have its moments and at the end it was satisfying, and even if it weren't, the game would have been carried by its battles.  It's not tactics, not yet.  You can see a compelling foundation to become something greater though.  Here's hoping for Triangle Strategy 2.

_childDocuments_.review: 100% would recommend if you enjoy SRPGs in general. I am still on my first play-through, about 30 some hours in, and it picks up after about 4+ hours. That first set of hours though, its pretty heavy in trying to orient you with the story and setting up things to come. If you can get through the initial setup of the story, it does pay off. I am enjoying the illusion of choice in the game so-far, but again, its just my first play through so that's why I say illusion. I would like to see how different choices impact the re-play value.This game does a better job than most when it comes to force-feeding lore at you. As an adopted model some other games have where you get some lore, but you get more with notes and information collected around the world. You can then (re)consume this information if you want in the menus. Though this game does do a lot of lifting to try and get you immersed in the world, its nice to see there are still bits and pieces I can explore on my own, or completely ignore if I want.I am oddly okay with the way they have the grinding in this game, with the mental battles, it does a better job than most in this respect. For me, this is one of the bigger drawbacks to SRPGs, where there's not enough variance in the battle schema, to allow for a fresh feeling in the grinding between story points. This game does a good job of minimizing it with different objectives and allows for targeting of specific resources ahead of time.So far, if I had to choose anything to improve upon in this game, would be the story choices and their respective alignments. The way some of the story and the choices are laid out, its usually shades of grey VS polar opposites. I either get 3 choices that are almost seemingly the same, or 3 choices that go the entire spread of the scale. It would also be nice to give a little bit of context as to what the outcome might be, but then again, that might actually ruin the story or surprise(s) around the corner. Basically there was one choice that was made and I feel like it had the complete opposite impact on the game than I wanted it to, and I'm not sure how else I might have gone in that direction with the other allotted choices. I will test this out in another play-through. Again, not game breaking by any means!Overall, I am really enjoying the game, look forward to completing its story, and going again through another time around!

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game, if you can even call it that, it's more like a virtual war novel. It's not as good as Octopath Traveler in terms of game play. Octopath was all game play and no story so SE decided to flip the script and do the exact opposite.My biggest gripe with it is that I was seeing more black screens with the word loading in the bottom right corner than anything else on subsequent play throughs.The game's run time is around 30 hours and about 6 of those hours is you watching cut scenes and deliberating amongst your group. I find the lack of actual battles in this game fairly disheartening. Don't listen to other gamers that compare this game to Final Fantasy Tactics and tell you that it's on par or even better than it.. it's definitely not even in the same league... and by that I mean Triangle Strategy is a discount version. The music, plot, characters and game play don't even compare.The meat and potatoes of the game comes in the form of mock battles, which you can engage from your groups encampment. You can instantly fight a set match and grind for materials / XP and items if you're having trouble in the story... there's also 4 difficulty settings if you're having any trouble at all, you'd have to be trying to completely wipe on Very Easy mode.There are multiple paths and 4 different endings but the Golden Ending is definitely the canon classic "fairy-tale" ending that you want... Also it's the longest path through the game and nets you a really powerful character so you might wanna just go for that ending first. Be warned though that the other endings are all flawed in some way with some of them being a down right awful way to have spent 30+ hours playing through this game.You'll have to beat the game a minimum of 4 times through just to net all the achievements. If you don't have a lot of spare time on your hands and also a ton of patience to wad through the entire game again, then this game might not be for you.Not a bad game, I was expecting a little more game play factor out of it but it's a decent purchase on sale for like $30.. don't pay $80 for this. Final Score: 7.5 / 10

_childDocuments_.review: Do you...Enjoy seeing 16 bit characters laying in pools of realistic blood?Cringe every time you hear English voice acting in a non-English game and immediately switch over to Japanese VO with subtitles?Want to hear the mic test (tap-tap-tap) (...) several times times during any given cutscene for the entire game?...Then chances are you will enjoy Triangle Strategy! It's a decent throwback to older FF tactics games among others. Good story, charming graphics and a multi-path "Choose your own adventure" style of making critical decisions during the ongoing war. The best part are the characters you can recruit (20+ worth) and deciding through trial and error what team(s) work for you the best. The cut scenes are a bit long and winded but the story is fairly solid.One gripe is towards the end (no spoilers) where it will be optimal to have every team member trained and maxed up/out. _childDocuments_.review: Just beat the game today after playing it on and off for the past few months. Here are my thoughts:Gameplay wise, this is one of the most satisfying games I've played in a while in regards to the battle system. Instead of the typical Mana system that most other RPGs opt for, Triangle Strategy uses a TP point system for techniques, and TP recovers naturally each turn. This makes for a super-engaging battle system where you'll have to balance using TP points for status inflicting techniques, defensive techniques, high-damaging skills, etc. You'll have to think about every turn that you'll take in every battle; even one turn can turn the tides to the enemy's favor. The characters are all very well balanced as well, you have your fast, nimble characters that can act twice, your tanks that can direct enemy damage to themselves, your magic nukers that can utilize 2-4 TP points at once for big damage, and more. Every character has a use, and each stage has it's own advantages and disadvantages for certain characters. No two battles feel the same, and that's by design. Sometimes, the amount of enemies can get a bit overwhelming, even on the normal difficulty. But I'd rather have a game that's a bit too hard than too easy. All in all, it's a joy to play. The story is also very well written, and being someone who enjoys reading about geopolitics in our modern world, this political take on a fantasy based story was such a breath of fresh air. Each and every character, from the main cast to the bad guys have their own set of convictions and interests, and those convictions often times clash during the story's big moments. Your actions and words hold weight in this game, as your party will be forced to make story-altering decisions at various checkpoints throughout the game, kind of like a direct-democracy approach to moving forward with your plans. If you play through the game as a goody-two shoes, then it will be difficult to convince your party to take the more brutal and unforgiving routes down the road, and vice-versa, due to your prior choices and convictions. That's rare to see in games these days, and I'm glad that Triangle Strategy was able to execute it in such good fashion.What more can I say? The artwork and graphical design is beautiful and crisp. The music is outstanding, especially during those big moments. The voice acting.... could be better, but that's just a small blemish on an otherwise incredible experience. This game has multiple endings, and I'm definitely going to go back and play through a few more times to see them all.A fantastic entry in the HD-2D genre, and my personal Game of the Year from 2022. Bravo, Square Enix. You've knocked it out of the park this time.

_childDocuments_.review: Triangle Strategy is not quite the same as its spiritual progenitors, and it is not without its flaws, but it certainly has a place in the genre. If you are an old school SRPG/TRPG fan, you may have some issues with certain aspects of the game's design & mechanics, and its shortcomings may stick out like a sore thumb, but otherwise it's perfectly fine and certainly above average in terms of quality/polish. It starts out very slow with a lot of dialogue/cutscenes. It’s all skippable if you only care about the battles, but the story is great IMO. There's a lot of political/ethical drama, with little to no contrivances. The exposition and writing is very well done and digestible IF you are into the themes/subject matter that the game plays around with. The music is good enough to the point where it got stuck in my head and I found myself humming along during battles/cutscenes.There is tons of replay value as the game is intended to be beaten at least 4 times to experience all branching paths/battles/endings in the story, and to get all the characters (via NG+). The branching paths are based upon a three-way conviction system (Morality, Liberty, and Utility), which is primarily influenced by your dialogue choices. It's an opaque system during the first playthrough, so a guide is recommended if you want to chart your own course, but it becomes much more transparent during NG+. The biggest letdown is the absence of chapter select, to jump into a specific part of the story, or to a specific battle. Though, there is a catalog with few dozen mock battle scenarios that you can access at any time, which is nice. The lack of customizable classes/jobs is both a blessing and a curse, as it makes the game much more accessible/digestible, but also limits creativity/flexibility. Luckily, the 30+ characters are diverse enough in their own right to allow for some experimentation with different tactics and playstyles either way. I see a lot of people complaining about difficulty or lack thereof, but there are difficulty options, so I don't understand this criticism.  Personally, I cannot stand the English voice acting, but you can play with Japanese voice acting instead, so it's fine. Despite its flaws, I thoroughly enjoyed my 80+ hours with this game. Getting all the achievements and nearly 100%-ing the whole thing was very cathartic. Great game for completionists and achievement hunters alike.

_childDocuments_.review: It has an immense amount of pros that outweigh the cons and is by and large an easy recommend as the closest thing we'll get to another Final Fantasy Tactics but I'd be remiss if I didn't point out those things that annoy me. First off, the voice acting is raw garbage served with a trash garnish. Set it to Japanese because they actually emote. Secondly, there's like 3 parts story broken up into small chunks for every part gameplay. And the gameplay itself is broken up into two types of battle: the story battles that are usually too difficult unless you did some grinding and the "mock battles" you perform in your encampment for a bit of extra kudos and exp that get old way too quick but you're just sick of having Frederica die so quick or Erador being too slow. It's frustrating since the story and writing is actually good but it's just too much at a weird pace and you just want to get some combat going but it's fleeting. Aside from that gripe and a camera that's misbehaving on purpose, the game is a blast. The fighting feels wonderful - you're always looking to get more kudos and take advantage of the terrain - and the soundtrack is absolutely fantastic. Hardly anything is worth $60 lately but I had zero qualms about buying this one again for some achievements. It was killer on the Switch but I think it's a better fit here.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me get straight to the point : TRIANGLE STRATEGY is a GOOD game. And I really mean it as a long-time RPG player. However, compared to a game like Tactics Ogre, it doesn't bring the same level of depth in terms of gameplay and balance between characters which is completely understandable as it probably was meant to be less niche and more accessible. The story felt somehow -and regrettably- cliché and didn't explore all the great ideas and multiple endings presented from the beginning that could have brought the game to higher grounds. Nevertheless, I highly recommend giving it a try because I had a really nice experience overall!

_childDocuments_.review: If you like rpg games, but want extra features not found in RPG maker games, but you crave the 2D aesthetic  look no further. In this beautifully crafted RPG, you play as Serenoa, an on the rise only child of your battle hardened family. Your decisions make a difference in dialogue and story progression! Will you be a SIMP clad in a gentlemen's suit and fedora? Or will you fulfill you desire to finally call it as it is, as a machievellian badass, as you and your waifu bride to be join the bois for some questing of geometric proportions across this world of tactical squares. The game has a multitude of characters to join your party, letting you swap between them before battle for those who want to challenge themselves or swap up the strats. Among a few of these are: The Maid Assasin-Rogue from every one season anime, The Family Buffler (Buttler Buffer), Sandy Subzero ice mage, Nurse Joy, etc. 10/10 would meme again!

_childDocuments_.review: To start off, I have "played" other SRPG's in the past, but I never quite got the hang of them to be honest. However, I was significantly younger and probably just need to go into them now that I can actually understand mechanics and the pro/cons of making certain decisions. An example would be when I played FFT as a kid. It was fun, but I never could grasp the true mechanics and would get steamrolled a lot (which I would eventually just give up the game).With that said, I would say that this game is a very great introduction to SRPG's. There wasn't a huge amount of character customization, but I was honestly fine with that considering I was tackling a style of game I was already uncomfortable with. Although that may seem like a negative to some, it was welcome to a beginner in this genre like myself. There was enough pacing in upgrading where I didn't feel like I was ever TOO far behind, but with a couple mock battles, I was able to catch up some levels and get materials to upgrade characters. People are correct that there is A LOT of story in this. Especially in the first couple chapters. They pretty much throw in every character from the start and the plot just isn't interesting at first. There is no slow build up to caring or disliking the characters you're supposed to so it was a bit rough getting the ball rolling in the "trying to be interested" aspect. However after pushing through to your first conviction voting, the pace began to level itself out and I started getting invested. It was a slog, but if you really don't care too much, you can easily skip the cutscenes and read up about it in your chapter history.There were also complaints of lack of battles in the game. I would agree that this would be the case as well, but after clearing the first ending, I would have to say it is because this game is a marathon with doing NG+ to experience multiple branches and not a race to finish. I am not a super fan of doing a NG+ myself unless I am extremely invested in the game, but with the story focus and the decisions you make to alter the paths you take make sense that this is the case.Overall, I felt this is a great game for beginning SRPG's. This gave me the itch to tackle others that I've been interested in (and even revisit FFT that I gave up on...hopefully we get that remaster ;) ). I wouldn't really recommend for those who are well versed in the genre as it will probably feel like a little empty with the lack of character customization, but it is a visually beautiful game and the battles are definitely fun. The game does what it intends to do well, it just may not be everyone's cup of tea in the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: TRIANGLE STRATEGY

_childDocuments_.review: NO MULTIPLAYER MAKES FOR OBVIOUS OVERSIGHT 25 YEARS AFTER FF TACTICS.This is the spiritual sequel to 1997's 'Final Fantasy Tactics', and the battle/magic mechanics are indeed worthy of FF Tactics. Much better battles than the GameBoy Adv sequels.The Achilles Heel of Triangle is that this game has no skirmish mode or multiplayer....which seems like an obvious mistake as FF Tactics players have been discussing two-controller multiplayer since the original came out in 1997 on the Playstation 1. Single Player Issues - Unfortunately the dev team seems to think we came here to read a novel, and not play tactical rpg battles. I was never into the story of FF Tactics, but at least it was short between battles most of the time. Not the case in Triangle Strategy. I have been skipping the story, using the 'fast read' and 'skip' features. It still takes about 10 or 15 mins of skipping the dialogue between every battle. It would likely take an hour to listen to the voice actors. Some people love a novel, but it needs an option to skip all in one go.Conclusions - if SquareSoft implemented a multiplayer mode, it will sell some actual copies of this game and bring so many new players into the FFT fandom via friend-invites and social media hype. The deeper the multiplayer system, the better the game. But really anything would be better than nothing.

_childDocuments_.review: It was a pretty decent game overall. I enjoyed my time with it, but I don't think it will be one of those titles that sticks around in my head for very long.On the gameplay side, the game is a mixed bag. I enjoyed it a lot early on when I played on hard. Fights were challenging enough that I had to think seriously about my actions without feeling like they were unfair or requiring an absurdly specific strategy. But as the game went on, the gameplay failed to keep pace. Units will level up and their stats will improve, but the way you use them in battle rarely changes. New abilities are rare and more often than not aren't different enough to meaningfully change your strategies. Most unit growth will revolve around making existing moves deal more damage (necessary given how much enemy health pools increase).Most new moves will instead come with the addition of new deployable units who join your party at various points in the story or when certain conditions are met. But since you can't deploy many units in a single battle and unused units will fall behind thanks to their lower level and lack of upgrades, you have to go out of your way to incorporate these new units into your strategies. Some of them are powerful enough to be worth it... but others are either very situational or just not very good.By around the halfway mark, I turned my difficulty down to normal and kept it that way for the rest of the game. Enemies just kept getting more and more health until it would take 4-5 of my units to kill one of theirs, while their attacks could kill me in 1-2 hits. And the levels felt more and more restrictive as if there was a specific strategy I was supposed to take in order to avoid guaranteed defeat. Normal difficulty was still fine, but it was still a shame that I had to back off from the challenge because of the awkward difficulty spike around the halfway mark.As for the story, Triangle Strategy struck a good balance between simplicity and depth. While it is a fantasy world, the game doesn't dwell much on all the big worldbuilding and history. While there are bits and pieces about how the world got to its current state, its not treated a big focus with lore compendiums and infodumps that I've seen a lot of other games waste time on. Rather than concerning itself with history, the conflict in Triangle Strategy revolves more around its characters and their ideals. The game's two main villains represent the extreme forms of each ideal with either total Freedom or total Equality, while the cast of 'good guys' all find themselves somewhere in between but still wanting a way to harmonize the two. Its pretty simple, but I do think the character writing and plot were done well and gave the ideological conflict a fair bit of narrative weight. I wouldn't call the writing masterful by any stretch, but it did its job of giving some sense of purpose behind each character's actions and some impetus for the me to continue playing.Triangle Strategy is far from the best tactical JRPG I've played, but its not a bad bet either. Its good enough to be worth giving it a shot, but you're not missing out on anything amazing if you decide to spend your time on something else instead.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm neither a visual novel fan nor the biggest jrpg fanbut TS is kinda unqiue (atleast for a game i've actualy played)it's very narrative heavy, but that i mean that there's almost as much narrative driven content like you'd watch a series on Netflix (or Amazon). thankfully it's actualy quite a standing out narrative (presentation).the VO and the writing are very, very good and engaging. there's some small, typical, jrpg cringe, but it's relegated to side characters you practicaly can ignore.the main cast and story, aswell as the major side content are very "mature".imagine a FF take on Game of Thrones...the good seasons.it looks pretty, it sounds very pretty, it playes pretty and is very polished.the actual progression mechanics and the combat are okay. they are nothing to write home about, but i found the combat encounters quite fun...it's sorta an Orge Tactics (FF) light, and suitable even for beginners. you can grind, exp aswell as currency, but you realy don't need to apart from wanting to fully upgrade the cast.there's often enough special conditions to the encounters to spice things up...all in all not mindblowing, but fun nonetheless.the element of choice and consequence plays quite a role and what paths you chose can quite drasticaly change what actualy happens in the narrative, which i found pretty great. decide to protect your friend (and the soon to be king) but sacrefice quite some peasants in doing so. the major players will react and you can sorta see the reactions of the rest of the world in mini-side-episodes. when starting out (within the 2 hours steam refund limit) the game might not actualy feel that special, but trust me: keep going.

_childDocuments_.review: It is okay, nothing to write home about.Vandal Hearts 2 probably does political drama and scope better, and any modern turn based tactical RPG is probably better in terms of gameplay than this.The issues are frequent; There's uneven pacing, a storyline that takes place across three nations, but has people jumping between them relatively quickly ~ obnoxiously so. The passage of time barely seems to happen, it is just 'this happens, now this event happens, and now this event happens.'There's no lull where the consequences of events can take its time to sink in. Every other optional story blurb is an almost unnecessary scene that pads out the time but offers little in way of additional drama or value.The game is basically crying out for more minor skirmishes, incidents that go along in the chapter arc that lends weight to the actions of the villains and the heroes. Instead, with basically 1 battle per chapter arc, the events fly forth so rapidly, it's difficult to really care. And isn't helped, by some giant leaps of logic in the story (you're telling me an entire army traversed through a border etc without any alarms being set off along the way? Really? Or that, having surrounded an enemy, when they reveal a potential nation shattering secret, we simply relent and let them 'discuss' the situation rather than exterminating the problem right there and then?)It is a shame really, because the initial premise was quite promising. If the story is a bit meh, then it needs the battle system to save it, but this isn't a particularly unique system, you've seen it before, and difficulty only really comes through by escalating the level gaps. The first bloody fight is a level 2/3 fight, when you're level 1 for gods sake. Eh, by chapter 11-12, the fights don't really offer enough variety, neither do the units (IMO) and the tactical fights aren't that difficult ~ mind you, I grew up on this sort of game style, so maybe it's my years of experience helping.Overall, I thought this was a disappointing game. I'll crack on for the golden ending, but honestly, it's lost its shine ages ago. I'd only pick this up if you're really desperate for a tactical RPG, and are willing to switch off for some interesting logical leaps for the storyline.

_childDocuments_.review: Triangle Strategy is an exceptional tactical JRPG that seamlessly blends the strategic brilliance of Final Fantasy Tactics with the captivating artistry found in Octopath Traveler's HD-2D style. From the very first glance, its mesmerizing visuals instantly captivate, but it's the flawlessly fluid animations of the sprites that truly breathe life into the game's immersive world.At the heart of Triangle Strategy lies a tale brimming with political intrigue, a web of complexity woven between three powerful nations. A more than solid narrative enthralls players, leaving them eagerly anticipating each twist and turn that awaits. The game introduces moments where difficult decisions must be made, amplifying the sense of agency and responsibility. The choices players make reverberate throughout the journey, altering outcomes, unlocking diverse recruitable characters, and unveiling unique character arcs that shape the fate of the protagonists.The gameplay bears resemblance to the renowned Final Fantasy Tactics, yet Triangle Strategy excels in offering accessibility without compromising depth. Engaging in battles on masterfully crafted, pre-designed maps becomes an exhilarating experience. Players must meticulously consider the impact of elevation and intricate geometry on their every move and attack. While it may not delve as deeply as its predecessor, this refined approach minimizes frustration while still delivering a rewarding and intellectually stimulating tactical gameplay experience.One of Triangle Strategy's most remarkable features is its ingenious approach to the class system. Instead of generic units, each character embodies their own distinct class, complete with a rich tapestry of individuality. These characters become living, breathing entities, woven seamlessly into the narrative with their own personalities, engrossing stories, emotional cutscenes, and formidable abilities. This meticulous attention to detail ensures that every member of the party feels like an integral part of the adventure, transcending the boundaries of typical RPG conventions.The soundtrack of Triangle Strategy is so well made surpassing my expectations. While it may not boast an extensive array of tracks, it more than compensates with the profound depth found within each composition. Every track embarks on a captivating journey, beginning with a distinct vibe and evolving into awe-inspiring crescendos, immersing players in a symphony of electric rock or the ethereal melodies of trumpets and violins.Now, One important aspect to note about Triangle Strategy is the abundance of cutscenes that punctuate the gameplay experience. The game is deliberate in its storytelling approach, immersing players in a meticulously crafted narrative that unfolds gradually, carefully building towards a climactic crescendo. However, this narrative-focused design choice means that players will spend a significant amount of time engaged in cutscenes, which may not appeal to everyone. Triangle Strategy prioritizes the art of storytelling and aims to deliver a cinematic experience reminiscent of epic tales found in other mediums. The wealth of cutscenes serves as a means to fully immerse players in the game's world, allowing them to forge deeper connections with the characters, witness pivotal moments firsthand, and absorb the intricate details of the political intrigue. This deliberate pacing creates an opportunity for players to fully appreciate the intricacies and emotional weight of the narrative. However, it is important to recognize that this style of storytelling may not resonate with all players. Some individuals may prefer a more streamlined experience with a greater focus on gameplay, finding the extended periods of cutscenes to be a hindrance to their enjoyment. The game's intentional dedication to storytelling might require patience and a willingness to invest in the narrative.In the end, Triangle Strategy was a really great experience, and I look forward to seeing a sequel that further pushes the IP forward, like octopath traveler 2 did to the first.8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR; JRPG fans who like a focus on story and lot of politics will enjoy this title. Those expecting a Final Fantasy Tactics experience should be warned that there character builds are very limited, and the tactical aspects are very simple.----------Somebody really, really loved Game of Thrones.Perhaps the game should have been named Triangle Politics? The focus of the game is maybe 50-75% on politics, negotiation and branching plot-lines compared to tactical combat. You do not play some adventurer, you play a member of the noble family. That means betrothals to establish alliances, lots of talking, lots of world building and talking to nobles to get a sense of what is going on so you have a good idea what you want to do next. This is *not* a tactics and flexible character builds focused game. For example, there is a mini-game where you have to convince your party members to vote according to your choice whenever there is a big decision to be made. This democratic process is odd considering you are playing a noble lord yourself, but the devs wanted players to experience more negotiation and influence aspects since you are a noble lord.The story combats you get will depend on these choice you make, sorry, these choice you convince your party members to vote for.This is all well and good if you allow yourself to take in the political intrigues which are going on, take note of the key players, and make decisions based on the information available.If you were expecting another Final Fantasy Tactics though, it's not. There are no character builds to speak of. Sure there are a multitude of extra characters who you can take into your party, but these all need to be levelled up separately. And the optional missions which you use to grind out levels for your party members are always the same. No randomization just repeated grind.Oddly enough, I was consistently *underlevelled* for the story missions whenever story missions unlocked. Having to grind out levels in the same optional missions over and again broke my spirit. I could not continue.I can see the draw of this game for some players however, so I can recommend this game. Just be aware of what you are buying.

Buy this game only for the story when it's on sale for like $20 in a year. If you want another Final Fantasy Tactics, just play Final Fantasy Tactics again.

_childDocuments_.review: I was disappointed.Triangle Strategy is a bland SRPG from two companies who have demonstrably proven they can do far better. The Artwork for the game does a lot of the heavy lifting in producing its charm, but ultimately, it can't make up for battle system devoid of many meaningful options and the soul shattering amount of grinding required to gather the resources to upgrade.Nor can it make up for the story and characters being bad. It's not Fanfiction levels of bad, nor something I'd expect the average college student to even dream about writing, but it reeks of an amateur Philosopher/Sociologist writing about surface level personality types and ideals from long dead theorists, while doing its best to make the lead a messiah figure.Nor can it make up for the forgettable sound track. _childDocuments_.review: Triangle Strategy is a game of political intrique. I love the game but it can be pretty hard to know whether a game is for you from just the trailer so I will try to compare it to Final Fantasy Tactics and Fire Emblem.In comparison to Final Fantasy Tactics, TS is...:1) Much more political as the scale system allows you to choose a different story path based on your allies' opinions. You can persuade your allies to align with your own political compass. Consequences of your choices are also pretty substantial as it has lasting consequences and will dictate the ending you will get at the end of the game. TS story is similar to FFT story but without the ability to dictate political choices at every turn.2) Less flexible in terms of character builds compared to FFT. There is no class change in TS. Heroes and allies all come with their own unique skill set and roles. If you want a healer, you pick a character that can heal, no changing of class or roles.3) Also much more story driven. The whole game is very focused on its political state and it takes it time to flesh out the story properly. If you are mostly into the SRPG gameplay ONLY, you might be disappointed with the excessive story cut scenes and dialogues. That said, the story is well written and the political puzzles are great.4) Pretty similar to FFT when it comes to the battle system. So it is no where basic just because it has more focus on the story.In comparison to Fire Emblem, TS is...:1) Much more difficult. The battles even on normal is pretty brutal. You really need to strategize even as early as the first map or risk getting wiped...at normal difficulty.2) More varied when it comes to characters. Although it doesn't have the class changing mechanics of FFT, it also does not go with the role system on Fire Emblem.  So instead of a few characters with different stats having the same 'mage' role, you have different spell casters of different niche, spell master that can cast all 4 basic elements and pyromancer that specializes in fire magic.3) Fun if you love solving political and diplomatic dilemmas.  Also no romance options in TS which is good because it helps the game to be more focused on its theme and story.4) A much more realistic war story. Not so much on big bad trying to end the world but more on greed and corruption; the usual reasons for war in real life.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10, IGN, too much water.In Depth Review:Triangle Strategy is one of my favorite games of all time. It's like the game version of an anime. I've played Triangle Strategy 3 times, twice on the Nintendo Switch and once on PC, probably somewhere between 150-200 hours in total. The defining feature of the game is that the main characters vote on how to progress the story and the player has the ability to influence their decisions. You literally take on the role of the protagonist, Serenoa. Although this is my first review of a game on Steam I hope that you will find it helpful. I think that my video game experience of Triangle Strategy was and is much better than I describe it here. My review will use check-boxes with descriptions after each section.------{Graphics}--------☐ Breathtaking☑ Great☐ Average☐ Poor☐ Hurts to look atThis HD-2D game looks impressive and has great scenery. Although I think that it is great overall, there are a few breathtaking locations, like the Wolffort demesne, the Falkes demesne, and the Crown City (in Mental Mock Battle). I highly recommend disabling Depth of Field in the graphics settings, which is the setting that blurs your screen in exploration environments. The HD-2D graphics can be a little funny sometimes. There is a scene of Gustadolph giving an inspiring and serious speech but he looks so cute and chubby at the end.------{Story}--------☑ Superb☐ Engaging☐ Average☐ Substandard☐ Please endThere is not much to say about the story without spoiling it. I'll just say that it had me hooked from beginning to end, all 3 playthroughs. ------{Music}--------☑ Stunning☐ Quite enjoyable☐ Average☐ It's just there☐ MuteAkira Senju composed a masterpiece! I often find myself humming or whistling Triangle Strategy songs. They fit the story situations very well and cover a diverse range of moods. I think that the music is on level with Dragon Quest and Skyrim, in its own right. Some of my favorites are Yearning for Freedom, Merriment, Pride of the Three High Houses, Arise Warriors, Combat-March, Combat-Subjugation, Combat-Destiny, Combat-Resistance, The Footfalls of War, Until That Day, A Moment of Respite,  and Travis's Thieves. Some of my favorites! ------{Gameplay}--------☐ Phenomenal☑ Well-made☐ Average☐ second-class☐ BoringI found the combat to be fun and strategic. You can choose which direction a character faces at the end of their turn, affecting whether their back is exposed or not. All abilities are vibrant and none lose their use in the game (excluding New Game + maybe). In Dragon Quest XI I was disappointed that so many abilities lost their value or were just bad from the start. A really good game mechanic is suspend, which allows you to save your battle progress and exit. This feature should be more widespread in video games.------{Difficulty}--------☐ Legendary☑ Challenging☐ Average☐ Easy☐ Just press AI have used Normal difficulty (including in New Game+) and Very Easy. Normal difficulty required me to level up every now and then in Mental Mock Battles (a fun rate) while Very Easy allowed me to play casually.------{Characters}--------☑ Nakama☐ Pretty good☐ Average☐ Bad☐ Who are you again?I think the characters are one of the components that makes this game shine. Their dialogue and actions can be funny, smart, serious, soft, or plain ol' crazy. The four main characters are especially well-developed. My favorites are Benedict, Exharme, Frederica, Anna, Erador, Svarog, Avlora Shōgun, and Maxwell.------{JP Voice Acting}--------☑ Wow!☐ Professional☐  Average☐ Disappointing☐ Better if it was not thereAnother strong point of Triangle Strategy, at least the Japanese. I tried English and did not like it, but maybe others do. It has anime style voice acting, where the actors can be very strong and enthusiastic. My favorite voice is Gustadolph's. It fits him so well! What a boss. Takanori Hoshino should get an award for his voice-over work on this game.Minor negatives: • Those who do not like collecting things may be a little disappointed that the game compels players to collect information. I like talking to every NPC in games (e.g. Dragon Quest), so I do not mind. In fact, I like it! • Only 10 save files. • When you promote a class, a character's look changes, not necessarily for the better. The same goes for weapon upgrades. I really like Erador's middle upgrade look, Roland's middle upgrade look, and Serenoa's original look. Conclusion:Try it! Steam has a 2-hour playtime refund policy. Perhaps Triangle Strategy will be one of your favorite games too!

_childDocuments_.review: Are you tired of Fire Emblem games with no difficulty? Have you whaled in War of the Visions? Will Advance Wars 1+2 Reboot ever release? Then look no further than Triangle Strategy. Many games have attempted the Tactics formula but this one hits it out the park. Classic mechanics return like height, back attacks, passives, and special abilities. Triangle Strategy takes it a step further with elemental interactions. Players will have to keep track of the field conditions like frost, wet, fire, and electrified. Similar to Record of Agarest War, units can combine their attacks by pincering their enemies. There are a number of buffs, strikes, and ways to fight your way out when the enemy boxes you in. Character variety is refreshing, and you can never get too comfortable fighting the grueling AI.As for the story, it's brilliant so far. I've been playing on Hard so I haven't gotten too deep into the plot, but the decision and judgment systems are fun to manipulate. Triangle Strategy's world building is enhanced by the octopath traveler art style and wonderful voice acting. The side stories are just as good as the main plot, so try not to skip out on any details (and some characters can be recruited this way as well).VV Playability would be a 4 out of 5 VVSteamdeck: 100% Yes, game runs smoothly and is a blast to play in bed. Anyone familiar with Tactics Ogre or Tactics Advance will be able to hop in.PC: I recommend the game, however be careful when using the mouse to make your selections. There have been times where the mouse placement did not agree with the HUD and turns have been ended prematurely.Looking forward to pushing through this hellish run. Try it out!

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, overall. 7/10, 50 hrs.I enjoyed the political human vs human story quite a bit, kinda like a GoT-lite, which I was very much in the mood for. I enjoyed all of the characters too. The game has the same character artist as OT2, Naoki Ikushima, and I love his work. I feel like he gives everyone so much personality. There's also a party voting mechanic that influences your story path, which I quite liked.The SRPG gameplay was fun. There's an emphasis on flanking mechanics, which I found interesting. Character progression and customization is somewhat limited, which I didn't really mind. (I wasn't interested in figuring out super complicated custom character builds.) Part of the fun comes from having a huge roster, and picking the right characters for each battle. The problem with this is that the game is rather stingy with character upgrade materials, so you end up focusing on just a few characters to upgrade. There are four potential endings to the game, including one true ending that is pretty much impossible to get on a first run. I HATE it when games expect you to play NG+.A lot of people complain about the story-focus of the game. They describe it as a visual novel with some battles scattered in between. As I said, I actually really enjoyed the story, but the pacing was terrible. For example, there was one point after a battle where I unlocked 15 non-related cutscenes at once. Painful, even with fast forwarding, particularly due to the regular standard of dialogue in Japanese games. By the time I hit 40 hrs, I really wanted the game to be over already.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautiful game that you don't get to play.  There is literally hours of dialogue and scene changes and more dialogue going on somewhere else and then back to the original dialogue then more dialogue and a scene change and now there's more dialogue.  Then a battle, which is fun and enjoyable.  Then more dialogue and more exposition and more dialogue.  I am not exaggerating, the amount of dialogue and exposition is just endless.  They even give you a button to fast forward conversations and sometimes skip entire scenes, 2 hours in and I was using them both and had given up on following the long winded story but even fast forwarding and skipping every single scene of dialogue it takes 10-20 minutes to get to the next battle. _childDocuments_.review: As a seasoned player and expert in the realm of tactical RPG's, I can confidently say that this game is a standout title in the genre. From its unique and immersive graphics, to its masterfully crafted storyline and expertly composed musical score, this game offers a level of depth that is rare in the industry.The voice acting is top-notch, adding depth and believability to the characters and their world, while the combat system offers a true test of skill and strategy, providing a satisfying level of challenge on both easy and hard difficulties. The advancement system is well-designed, requiring strategic decision-making and rewarding players for taking their time to develop their party, while minimizing the need for grinding.Overall, this game is a true testament to the developer's skill and stands among the likes of Tactics Ogre and Final Fantasy Tactics as one of my all-time favorite tactical RPG's. It is a must-play for any fan of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Ignore my low playtime, I fully played through the game on switch when it initially released, which is why I haven't played the PC version much.This game deserves so much more love than it gets. I first went into this game with relatively low expectations coming off of the first Octopath, as while I love Octopath conceptually, the constant level grinding and disappointingly bare-bones story (in my opinion) left me with a bitter taste in my mouth. Going into Triangle Strategy (which I decided to try out as a result of there being a switch demo), I was expecting largely the same. Instead, what I ended up getting was a shockingly excellent experience, to the point where I would consider it near flawless in everything it tries to do. It offers a consistently compelling narrative paired with excellent tactics-like game play, great art direction, and an amazing soundtrack. Of course, not everything is perfect. Initially I was gonna write an extremely long review detailing every aspect of the game, including what it does and doesn't do well, but it started getting really wordy and unrealistic to expect a consumer to read, so I'm just gonna make some bullet points summarizing both.The GoodCompelling and well written narrative. Tends to tackle a lot of mature subject matters and handles them all very well. Choices feel like they have real weight to them and are never easy to decide. The character's are all portrayed realistically and their reasoning is always guided by not only subconscious personal biases, but genuine logic as well, giving value to every person's opinion whenever you need to vote in the game. It's also very consistent throughout and every ending is equally compelling and interesting. This is the kind of game that can very easily generate discussions and debates.Great tactics-like gameplay that challenges the player adequately and encourages creative strategy. Map design also tends to be elaborate, making way for fun battles. Because of how Triangle Strategy handles its units, there are a lot of interesting characters given to you to play around with. Difficulty is also generally consistent and I found that I didn't have to seriously grind for levels even once throughout my playthroughs of the game, though because leveling scales, if you need to it also happens to be very easy to catch a low leveled unit up to your other units.Great art direction, HD-2D in Team Asano games always looks beautiful, in my opinion. That being said I think both Octopath games look better.Fantastic score, both extremely fitting for the game and memorable. Not much to say about it, it's just consistently great.The BadThis game could be considered part visual novel. There is a lot of reading. I used to be a big Ace Attorney fan so I personally didn't mind this, but if you don't like reading and just want to cut to the gameplay, don't get this game.There is no traditional job system, which many acquainted with the tactics genre may be used to. Instead, Triangle Strategy opts to make every character their own completely unique job, ensuring no character is the same. I personally think this is cool and lends itself well to the gameplay, but for some it may be a turn off.Emphasis is placed on the narrative first and foremost, not the individual characters. While many characters are very well written (Roland in particular is a standout here) quite a few don't get much focus compared to games like Fire Emblem, which gives each character its own mini-arc through optional side content. I don't consider this an inherently bad thing as, like I said before, the narrative is very good.Voice acting is OK at best. Some voice performances are genuinely really good (such as Frederica), while others feel much more lackluster (Benedict is one of these, in my opinion). I've heard the Japanese voice acting is better, but have not played through the game with it. I believe you can also turn off voices. Regardless, I find the English voice acting serviceable and not something most people will mind, just not particularly standout either.

_childDocuments_.review: For what is more or less my first SRPG, I gotta say I am impressed, although the game is not perfect.The story of this game is quite good, although it's slow to start and ends horribly. For those that played the demo, the first 2-3 hours is the hardest part of the game to get through. Battles are limited, lots of repetitive dialogue and cutscenes. However, this is the portion of the game where most characters are introduced, which sucks, because there are maybe 3 or 4 characters whose voice acting isn't absolutely ridiculous. Seriously. Most of the main party (with the exception of maybe Benedict and Anna), sound like they're voiced by a high school drama club, with almost no expression of emotion or depth. Voice acting isn't something I really look for in a game or care all that much about, it's just really noticeable in this game. Again, shouldn't be a total dealbreaker though.Once you get into the mid-game, and you start getting into 1-3 battles per chapter, the game really takes off in my opinion. Maps and objectives are varied and interesting, giving each character a unique and important role to play. I more or less took the same party all the way through, but there are tons of characters with unique abilities, so there are numerous strategies you can take in each battle.There are some spoilers in this next section, so read at your own peril.All in all, a great game. I honestly hope Square Enix stays afloat to hopefully release a sequel addressing the voice acting and ending.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to give this game a thumbs up, because it's a new strategy RPG IP (my favourite genre) from Square and not another revival / remaster of a classic. Its biggest flaw is how much story-focused the game is. Problem is that the story and characters are BAD. It feels like a poor copy-paste of other fantasy dramas and older video games, filled with all the medieval fantasy tropes you have experienced 1000 times before, so poorly written and voice-acted which many times reach the point of cringe.
