_childDocuments_.review: Triangle Strategy comes from the same company that brought us Octopath Traveler, and boy does it show.  It has a lot of the strengths from that game, but unfortunately a lot of weaknesses to.  The company is still to be praised for putting out another gem, but also denounced from totally failing to learn from their mistakes.First the good:  The story is excellent.  With all the constant back-stabbing, alliance changing, and brutality, there's certainly a serious Game of Thrones vibe going on here, for all the right reasons.  Your own character is basically Jon Snow.  The perfect boyscout who as the game goes on will find it harder and harder to walk the morally upstanding path.  And that's where the game gets really interesting.  It has probably the best command choice system I've ever seen in a video game.  You're choices don't boil down to the simple "do something good or do something evil."  You actually have some very difficult choices where morality proves impossible to maintain in the face of pragmatism, as well as some where there really feels like there's no right answer at all.  And they only get harder and complex as the game goes on.  On my first playthrough, there was one character who always seemed to recommend something bad.  So I was just rejecting him over and over the entire way through, to the point where I wished I could kick him off the team just to stop getting his bad advice.  But late in the game, at the most crucial time where I had to make a decision that would have the most enormous ramifications, he suddenly came up with what I thought was the best plan, against the recommendations of two of my favorite characters who had come up with inferior ones.So I was faced with a devastating decision.  Follow the best plan from the guy I really hate, potentially destroying my relationship with two of my favorite characters and my best warriors (team members can leave at certain story points if you make a particular decision), or accept his advice for the sake of the plot, since I felt his plan would have the best outcome.  I don't think I've ever seen a game that puts so much pressure on the player when it comes to making their plot choices.  Not only does it create an excellent system with real consequences, but it also give good incentive to play the game again so you can see how it goes when you take different paths.As for the gameplay itself, it's pretty good.  There's a lot of different characters with unique spells and abilities, plus all sorts of ways to use terrain and obstacles to your advantage, such as setting grass on fire or hitting enemies with lightning while they are standing in water.  It also has a unique mechanic where if you attack an enemy with an ally on his opposite with side, it will result in attacks from both characters.  This means you can use your sissy mage with his pathetic wooden stick to still deal decent physical damage by using him to activate a warrior's attack who is on the enemy's opposing side.Now for the bad.  The most immediate thing that stands out is that this game suffers from a severe case of main character overload.  There's a ton of playable characters, way more than you can bring into battle.  So that means you're going to be constantly leaving your excess team members on the sidelines with noting to do, especially since they aren't very well balanced.  There are some characters who are just way better than most others, so that really decreases the incentive to be constantly rotating your team members into battles so everyone can participate.  On top of that, some of the classes are just really dumb, like Shieldbearers.  Either no one taught them you can carry a weapon and shield at the same time, or they are just really big fans of the anime "Rise of the Shield Hero", because they only carry shields!  They don't even bother to carry a weapon along with them.  Sadly that shield-only rule seems to apply to everyone who uses a one-handed melee weapon, including your own character, cause they just leave their off-hand swinging in the breeze with nothing to hold.  Also on my first playthrough, I managed to pick up 4, yes 4 different classes of archers!  Why?  Just why would you make 4 different versions of a guy with a bow and arrow?  It makes no sense.  If you want to make multiple ranged-weapon characters, that's fine, but don't give them all the same weapon.  Give someone a crossbow, or a musket, or throwing knives, or a javelin, or a sling.  There's just so many other options, that making 4 different archers was just the height of laziness.  Another frustrating thing is that most of the characters who join your team are optional recruits, meaning they don't participate in the main story of the game at all.  So not only do you have to often leave them out of the combat, but they are left out of the plot as well.Then we get to the main problem of the game:  The grinding.  Good lord the grinding.  It was a major problem in Octopath Traveler, and here it's even worse.  At least in OT, you could grind in a lot of different locations and use the optimal one constantly.  Not so here.  Here you can only use "mental mock battles", basically practice battle where the level of the characters don't change.  So you have to be using the highest one available to get anything worthwhile.  The problem is a lot of the later ones have turn limits you need to complete.  Very low turn limits.  This forces you to focus more on winning than on collecting the maximum amount of XP and items, so you end up having to run them way more often than you should.  Combine that with the fact that experience points aren't shared among the team, and it means you have to be constantly doing extra grinding battles to rotate your "backups" in order to make sure everyone is properly leveled and upgraded.I am not kidding when I say about 80-90% of your combat on the first playthrough is going to be grinding.  And while the game does have a "new game+" feature for a second playthrough, that doesn't change anything since the enemies automatically are bumped up to your level from the first one, meaning unless you want to decrease the game's difficulty on your second run (which kind of defeats the purpose of playing a second time), you'll be grinding like crazy again!Overall this is a good game, but one that forces you to put up with some very frustrating problems that really are unforgivable, not just because they could be easily fixed, but also because they were present in the last game the company released.   It's still worth getting if you're a fan of the genre, just make sure you know what you are getting into.

_childDocuments_.review: I got it on switch years ago and re-bought it. 60% sale was worth it. I was looking for a good turn based tactics RPG that was controller friendly. Some things I like about it is the common experience each player has, meaning everyone struggles with the first mission on hard mode. No, seriously, the first mission is possibly the hardest mission with the difficulty cranked up.  The next is how New Game+ gives you extra info to help the player 'gameify' which characters to unlock next via the 3 paths.  The extra info telling players what is raising morality, utility, liberty is very welcomed. There is a reason to beat the game ~4 times, and that is to unlock every character.  It makes the secret route easier when doing so. I have heard of players unlocking the secret route on their first play through, however I'd really recommend against it. The fun of this game comes in unlocking characters and the game play. It's not the most story driven game, but I enjoyed it.

_childDocuments_.review: My disjointed impressions after beating the game with one of the standard (non-golden) routes: It requires a lot of time to get through the story and ensure you're leveled enough to get through each battle, but it's so much fun. The story was interesting enough that I was excited to see another scene after each battle and the mechanism of making your party "vote" and then choosing what path to take based entirely on the vote. Noting, I never once felt that I couldn't get the party to "swing my way" with the votes, but even still, there are some tough choices, and as some of the situations come to a head you'll wish you had a magic wand to right all the wrongs because you know the world is set up to where you can make a difference but you can't save everyone, do everything right, and that's gonna make you play it over again OR follow a guide to get the golden ending. I did know there was a golden ending, and I thought I should possibly follow a guide to get it, but I was having too much fun choosing my answers blindly. The only painful thing is, as an adult, it's hard to find the time to beat one game that takes 100 hours much less beating it over again, but some gems are worth it! I barely had any playtime with my favorite character (Prince Roland's sister, Cordelia), and I see from the achievements that she's a playable character? Not on my first try, she wasn't! So, of course, I'm going to play it over again. And I want to see the best ending, because now I care about the world and the characters. The story tone is more serious than I'm used to when I think of a typical jrpg, somber, and there isn't a lot of comedy, but it works well for the setting. Yes, I did have some flashbacks to FF tactics, and I think even some of the sprites are from the same pack of 'NPC soldier characters.' hah! I could barely get the name of the game out to my friends "triangle strategy" sounds like a nerdy math game! Eww, what's this a game about Pythagorean theorem?!Towards the end, each time you finish a battle at the required level, you'll see the next battle requires you be several levels higher, which entails more 'practice fights' in your camp to level up. That did get annoying as the story started heating up towards the end - you want to see what happened, not spend 2 hours leveling everyone up! But that's a testament to good storytelling. If you like strategy games and jrpg storylines, give this one a try!
_childDocuments_.name: TRIANGLE STRATEGY

_childDocuments_.review: A great game, and a spiritual successor to Tactics Ogre. I originally played this on Switch (beta and full release), and waited for a sale to replay it on PC. In many ways, it is a flawed masterpiece but a masterpiece nonetheless. If you haven't played Tactics Ogre, or feel its too old but want a similar game, this is probably the best entry point.A disclaimer upfront is that there is a significant amount of controller downtime, and that the game takes roughly ~8 hours to really pick up the pace. So it's worth being prepared for that. Most of the negative reviews I have seen are in relation to the 'boring story', but it really is just the time it takes to pick up speed.Another disclaimer is that the game is also designed to be replayed multiple times. Not just because of branching paths/story outcomes, but through character levelling and unlocks. Trying to do this game on hard and run the secret path is effectively impossible without obscene grinding. It's just a hard fact that you will always be low on materiels. This is frustrating because at higher difficulties you will feel paper thin and like you're hitting enemies with a wet paper towel. Additionally, because materials are so rare in relation to late level skill unlocks, you miss out on a lot of higher level synergy plays. I think that's a misstep because about 2/3 of the way through the game you likely feel ready to do more complex plays now that 90% of the characters are unlocked.As a result, I ended up enjoying my second playthrough far more than my original simply because you can amp up the challenge and actually be able to execute high level plays without getting instantly KO'd.Overall, there is an insane level of detail and thought that went into this game. Lots of backstory and notes are within the game, not to mention you get a free PDF file with lots of artwork from the amazing art team. Additionally, if you meet certain requirements you unlock a hidden chapter that can be freely viewed from the main menu, which provides additional context and a secret finalé scene. It really does show that the developers put everything they had into this, and that really should be respected.In relation to the port, it's basically the best Square Enix port in years. Super low install size, really well optimized, I wish this type of port was the standard.I would say a must-buy at 50% if you're unsure, but for Tactics Ogre/Tactics fans, I would say full price is justified. It's likely you will keep coming back to this game over and over across the years.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very good, but don't go in expecting it to be a new Final Fantasy Tactics, it's not quite that level.The way the story is laid out is interesting, with different paths depending on your choices, selected through a voting process with 7 of your closest friends in the game. You can influence them with conversations before each vote if you wish it to go a certain way, but you won't always succeeed in convincing them.I'm missing the job system of FFT, but at least they have made each character to recruit unique in some way and you can build your army around their abilities. I do wish character upgrates weren't timegated though, requiring material that is drip fed to you over time.The artstyle and general presentation of the game is nice. I wish I could coment on the music but I think it's not been catching my attention enough. Overall, so far, I'd give this game a 7/10. Will see if that changes after I beat it. The fact it has some replay value by going the different routes is somewhat intriguing. I believe there's a New Game + system but I don't know what that entails in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game to scratch the Final Fantasy Tactics itch.Coming back to update after following every path, but I'm gonna have to do a 6th playthrough cause I somehow HAVEN'T FOUND ALL THE CATS (Edit, I found all the cats, there's one hidden in the weeds in the Falkes Demesne)I think Triangle Strategy made a bold choice here to prioritize storylines over battles. By the time I'd gotten to the Golden Run, the imperfect endings really lent themselves to increase the impact of the "true" ending. However, because there's so much story, I often find myself skipping through cutscenes I've already seen, and the way the paths fell back into one another in some ways felt disingenuous to the story. But to be fair, it's a game. There's only so much realism that can be expected here. All in all, this might be my favorite Square Enix game in the last few years. Some of the voice acting was flat (looking at you, Rudolph), but the main characters are strong. The villains are believable. When there's disagreement within the party, both sides tend to have merit. I eventually gave up achievement hunting for this one because Avlora's character stories are only unlocked on the golden route, and I wasn't prepared at this time to go through a 7th playthrough just to get it. Perhaps my child will take up the mantle and succeed where I have failed. Still a great game tho. Highly recommended to any tactics fan.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished my first playthrough and achieved that golden ending. I have to say this game is a total blast. Excellent story, with fantastic tactical gameplay. The decision to remove job system affords player to focus on slowly growing their party and picking up who to bring into battle becomes a vital part of the gameplay. Story is also interesting, intriguing but not convoluting. The first 2 hours can be quite draggy, but past that, you'll find a strategy turn based RPG worthy to put next to Final Fantasy Tactics.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very story-focused tactical JRPG. The combat system's emphasis on positioning and terrain frequently makes the optimal play non-obvious, which is a plus. You can't minmax your party into oblivion FFT style - each character has a unique kit with no real customization aside from upgrades. But just about every character has a use, and there are many battles that will make you reconsider your default roster in favor of the more strange options that get opened up to you later on. Fortunately, grinding a character up to the current level is very easy with the mental mock combats, and you won't often need to do more than one side mission to pull everyone up you the current level thanks to how XP is calculated.You need to either have a strong tolerance for "the kingdom of so-and-so, with a monopoly on the flarb trade, has strong relations with the blah blah kingdom" type stuff in this game. Even with those cliches in place, I found most of the characters charming and a few of them compelling. But bear in mind if you're a strong tactical-head gamer used to something like XCOM or Fell Seal you'll spend a lot more time in story cutscenes than you're used to.

_childDocuments_.review: Perhaps I ought not to write a review, as I stopped after 5 hours due to massive plot holes, but those plot holes were SO massive I wasn't interested in spending any more time on this trainwreck to find out just how bad it would get later.  Rather than write a story in which plausible events shape the narrative, the writers sledgehammer the plot into the shape they desire, never caring whether or not it makes sense.  ***This review will contain spoilers for one early game event, as it's impossible to discuss plot holes without discussing the plot.***Short setting primer: three countries each have something the other two need: One has iron, one has salt, and one has natural resources and is situated on the river for easy trade.  War happens, war ends, the three nations agree to cooperate on a new mine in the trade focused country, with Aesfrost (the iron producer) providing expertise.Something incredibly important is found in the mine by the representative from Aesfrost who writes home, demanding a political appointment to keep it secret from the country the mine is located in.  While a lord and prince from the mine's country are on site, Aesfrost sends assassins to kill their own representative.  On this map, you must keep that representative alive.  Once you do, he jabbers something barely coherent about never thinking they'd go so far (they being his home country, Aesfrost), just enough for everyone else present to realize he'd been hiding something.  He is then immediately killed by an assassin with a single arrow from all the way across the map.  The party which, again, contains high ranking nobility and royalty, is in the middle of being shocked when a herald runs in to inform them that the king's castle is under attack by an Aesfrosti army.  The party tells the herald to handle burying the Aesfrosti mine representative, and rushes off to the castle.  Aesfrosti agents then slip into the mine behind them, kill the herald, and act generally evil.Now:First, A major foreign represenative, responsible for a huge part of the first international collaboration after a war was assassinated in another country.  This is an international incident.  You don't leave one herald behind to bury the guy.  It's a crime scene, and the representative knew something—the characters even said he did.  Attack on the palace?  Okay, you send the rank and file soldiers, MAYBE, while anyone connected to local nobility removes the body to either be handled respectfully, or shipped back for demoralization.  You also SECURE THE MINE, because it's of international importance, and was just the site of an INVADING FOREIGN FORCE.Second: "Phew, cleared the level where the objective was to keep <representative name here> alive.  Go me."  Random assassin kills him with a single arrow from an illegitimate distance (the cutscene plays out on the map, we know for a fact bows don't have that range in game), because reasons?  Kindly don't make the characters morons, writers.  NOBILITY WAS JUST ATTACKED, NO ONE SHEATHES ANYTHING UNTIL EVERY ASSAILANT'S HEAD IS DISCONNECTED FROM THEIR SHOULDERS, OR THEY'RE IN IRONS.Third: Aesfrost attacked the castle, and I quote, with "no warning."  Horse.  Crap.  We've stared at the map over and over again.  The defending country is mostly plains.  You can't march multiple brigades with SIEGE ENGINES across plains unnoticed, and you can't threaten a castle with less than that.  Also, it takes weeks, if not months, for that kind of travel overland.  Nonsense travel time had been foreshadowed earlier, when the prince got from the main character's town to a separate village in less time than it takes to take a bride's measurements for a dress, but that at least was immaterial to the story, so I was willing to tolerate it.  I'm less willing to tolerate nonsense handling of huge international incidents and invasions, all in the name of forcing the plot the scenario writer wanted, without the effort of actually writing that plot plausibly.Moving past the story, and to be clear, the story is the whole reason I quit and requested a refund, there are other issues.  As a PC port, it's mediocre.  Rather than properly supporting mouse and keyboard, there's a weird behavior to the mouse almost like a sticky auto-aim.  This frequently results in difficulty pointing where you want a character to move.  Key mappings are weird in places, with J and L used to rotate the camera.  On the world map, the sticky auto aim is back, but also with weird, floaty movement when you're not close to anything in particular.  Finally, less detrimental but silly enough to hurt my head, are the Scales of Conviction.  In one of the game's actual good ideas, the path the story takes isn't entirely up to you.  Decisions are made by having your companions vote, and you're bound by that, though you can use information you gained talking to people to try to sway your companions toward the result you want.  The ridiculous part is how voting is handled.  The main character hands out 7 coins, and each companion puts them on one side or the other of a scale.  Fancy particle effects, because the scale is magic or something, but... seriously?  It's just weighing the coins.  Most votes wins, and the voting isn't (or wasn't, by the point I was through with the garbage) secret, so you could just as easily call for a show of hands.  It's a whole lot of pomp and circumstance for no good reason, and just feels stupid and pretentious.  Even at half price, I regret paying for this.

_childDocuments_.review: A criminally underrated gem.Triangle Strategy weaves a tale of deft political intrigue and maneuvering like very few games I've played. The character writing suffers in turn, with development kept in reserve for only the absolute key players, but the payoff is well worth the trade. Constantly shifting borders, a balance of honor versus necessity, and genuine consequences for your actions all pave the way for a story that holds its own against the greats of the genre. There are a few flaws, some of which may not irk you depending on your mindset. Firstly, as many other reviews note, yes, this is an incredibly story-heavy game. The early hours especially will see you move through mountains of text between fights. As someone with the patience to go through VNs, I didn't mind this requirement at all, but it is worth keeping in mind before making a buy. Something I can't say I'm as hot on is the practical requirement to grind. By the mid-to-late-game, you will have to spend hours grinding battles on the side to hold any chance in the main story. The only time this *really* bothered me was when the game was on such monumental emotional highs that I couldn't wait to move to the next chapter, only for an increase in three levels to send me back to the tavern to grind and get my characters up to snuff. This could've been offset by being paired with some engaging side stories, but unfortunately, that's far from the case. The only 'optional' stories at all are either auxiliary cutscenes to supplement the main quest, or cutscenes involving the characters you recruit over the course of your journey. They are not tied to battles of their own in any way, passing up a real opportunity to offset the grind at least a little bit.Others have commented regarding the simplification of the SRPG genre in this title. While I'm not fluent enough in its particulars to take to defending this decision as much as I'd like to, all I can say is that I enjoyed the game regardless of these streamlined mechanics. Honing characters into the maximum efficiency terminators per their assigned class was really enjoyable for me, and I loved being able to repeatedly refresh and mix up my lines on the battlefield to see the interplay between these classes. I would've liked a greater emphasis on loot and gear here, but the sparse focus didn't hurt the game in the long term as much as I initially assumed. Without additional playthroughs, I'm afraid I can't comment on how much variability Triangle Strategy has between its routes, but I can absolutely affirm that even if the road I took was the only one available, I would still think it worth every penny. There are a few plotlines and characters that are either seemingly forgotten about or downplayed tremendously when they should have come to the fore, but Triangle never loses its commitment to providing a grounded and bitter narrative. Choices were rarely easy, and good outcomes from them were even more infrequent. The game isn't afraid to pummel you into the dirt, and I loved it for avoiding so many tropes of the genre, most particularly near the end. I cannot recommend Triangle Strategy enough. It was an absolute joy to play through, and my biggest surprise of the year, by far. The game deserves more love, and I pray Square Enix gives it another go in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best JTRPGs! It reminds me of Final Fantasy Tactics and in my opinion it surpasses it in every aspect. Played it at hard difficulty and it was such a blast! You really need to carefully think about each move/positioning and make the most out of it. For example, your mages and healers cannot take more than one hit from most enemies so you have to carefully position them behind your tanks and have your tanks distract your enemies. And usually your opponent's army would out-level and outnumber yours, so you even cannot be too careless with your tanks leaving them being flanked either! There is no useless character and every skill has its own place in the battle. Speaking of skills which consume your character's TP to cast, the game implements a rather fun mechanism on TP management. Again take your mages as examples. They are major TP spenders and they cannot cast their powerful spells continuously due to that. However, if you are clever about your moves, you can make them cast their spells non-stop! For example, the fire mage can gain extra TPs if her attack kills an enemy unit. The frost mage on the other hand can gain extra TPs if he's standing on frosted ground. There are also characters that gain extra TPs if they don't move or move for more than a certain distance.The story is also quite good and this is a game where your decision(not really yours but your companions' as you need to persuade them to vote for you) do matter!

_childDocuments_.review: Good game.  I'll never open it again, however, as after grinding 100% for the past 40 hours of game play I have thoroughly killed whatever tiny replay value this game has. Most of the fun comes from learning the entire lore (which is tedious to do) and stomping on opponents in the most vicious ways possible with zero regard for the well-being of your supporting cast.  Good news is that you can get the achievements on very easy, which just increases your damage and decrease enemy damage, so I played on that for NG+5 and 6.Be prepared to read dialogue.  You have to want the story.  Combat is fun enough to begin but if you're paying anywhere close to $60 for this game you should be doing it to hear the story.  And it's a fairly compelling one with logical branches to most (but NOT all) paths, though the ending is clearly rushed.  Sure, it's voice-acted well, but I would guess that there are probably 8 hours of voice acted dialogue in a single play-through - you'll want to speed read.7.5/10 Play if you like Fire Emblem / Tactics Orge / FFT, Buy for $20.

_childDocuments_.review: I took the work to review some bad reviews and let me clarify you: is the game good? YES yes it is.Is is a visual novel? no no its not, most cutscenes are skippable, you have a fast forward button, and yes the games does goes into great lengths on developing the story, yes maybe too much, BUT, most of it is even optional!Does it have actual tactics?  yes it has, is it easy? no its not, you will loose fights if you dont know what to expect, what are the rules or go slightly under leveled (but the game gives all the info you need, it doesnt make you grind, and it does reward exp freely, but is quite fair and quite permissive if you do loose), and it does get challenging from times to times.Does it has more story than fighting? actually not, theres a ton of optional non history fights to be had (and all serve as grind too!).Is the story amazing? well no, but it is quite interesting and you get hooked by all the twists (some ofc predictable).Anything else is just useless nitpicking and ppl comparing this to their old favourites, criticism does not apply and just dont listen to them; the game is fantastic for us in this niche!totally recommended!!

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game hoping for something like Final Fantasy Tactics. At about 5 hours in, I was frustrated by the many ways in which it was different. At this stage, I appreciate the differences and can honestly say Triangle Strategy is worth playing.The biggest difference that I initially found frustrating was that characters are locked into their class. You can't make the main character an archer, wizard, or ninja. Serenoa is just a swordsman. What changed that frustration into appreciation was that, rather than mostly unnamed companions, the entirety of your party is composed of voiced characters with their own stories. The first bit is still a bit stifling, as your party composition is really limited, but later in the game you get to make interesting choices and have to deal with the fact that you can't stack a single class.It's pretty good!

_childDocuments_.review: I put a lot of hours into the Nintendo Switch version but no where near completion so decided to sell that version and buy for PC. No regrets! The game runs flawlessly. I like being able to use a controller and the steam achievements and trading are an added bonus this time around. Very similar gameplay to Fire Emblem Three Houses but without the added relationship stuff. I love the Game Of Thrones style narrative. It is fairly text heavy in regards to actual time on the battlefield but when the battles do start is a fantastic in depth turn based strategy with some clever puzzle elements like if an enemy hits you from behind it's always a critical hit and vice versa you can also surround your enemy for extra damage and even an extra turn and some levels give you the option to use traps and decide if you want to burn your villagers house for an easier battle but in doing so you your reputation takes a hit which brings me on to another equally important part of the game. It has branching paths which are triggered by you decisions and majorly effect your playthrough it's like a tell tale game only with greater impact from your choices. The characters are also unique enough from each other and each  have a special ability that grants buffs etc .  . Their is also a practice arena if sorts and some exploration on really pretty 3D diaromas with objects like gold and potions cleverly hidden. For me it's the closest thing to a Fire Emblem game!

_childDocuments_.review: During my 30hr journey to complete a first run in Triangle Strategy, I enjoyed everything from the 2DHD pixel graphics, to the music and voice acting, gameplay and story.Triangle Strategy puts you in a land with three main forces whose balance is as shaky as it can get. Without spoiling much, obviously conflict arises and this is the starting point of our story....an starting point that is a bit long to reach, as the game is stroy-heavy and this is specially shown at the beginning. You might only have one battle in your first one hour or one hour and a half of the game, and while the story itself is incredible engaging, compared to Game of Thrones by many (and rightfully so) it takes a while to get there. Characters are not out of place and while the japanes influence is shown with some anime troupes, there is a surprising amount of the cast who is darker and more down to earth than I first expected. And man, does the game get dark at times...As for the combat system, while it's not groundbreaking, it definitely works thanks to careful scenario design. You must be wary of each movement and take into account your party position and weak points, as well as the enemies'. Overall, I enjoyed most battles as they usually come to a quirk to them that made them all the more interesting, specially if you are no overleveld, which is a difficult thing as level progression is heavily tied to your competition, so griding endlessly won't report much benefit, while it's east to catch up if you have an underleveled character.Character progression is a bit poor, though. There is level progression that raises attributes, weapon enhancement and class promotions, but you cannot choose different classes or options/branches for your characters. Thankfully so, there is a good variety of different characters so most of them feel unique, and they will definitely impact the wat you approach battles, such as tanks, mages, healers, archers, rogues...The replay value is also huge. What SE did well in a story-driven SRPG is that there are choices that will influence your route, as the game possesses branching paths. To make it even more appealing, there is a voting system in which you will need to use your wits to convince your party members to tip the scales in the befitting direction. There are four different endings in the game and one go took me 30hrs. While I don't plan to beat the game 4 times, I'm running it once in NewGame+ so I can unlock the True Ending, which is difficult to get in the first go.All in all, while the price tag in this once is a bit steep, I would recommend it. It's a solid 8.5 in my book and one of the better SRPGs in PC right now.

The game got easy after the first play through.The characters are fixed with set moves and not much choice for equipment.  This is kind of boring, but helped to keep the battles from becoming too easy in the first play through.  The battles had a feel similar to FFT, but were more challenging due to not easily being able to over level or chose overpowered classes.  On replays, the unique items and items found on the maps do not respawn which is disappointing.The story has 4 endings.  You can replay after completing so you can get the different endings without needing to build up your characters again.  The enemies also scale on replay so they won't be as week as if they didn't.  The first time through the story, and character's actions and the available choices made sense mostly until things fall apart near the end like every Square RPG story.  I must have been lucky the first time since during every later play through, the story didn't match up well with the choices I made.  The choices available were not logical in most situations and the characters were inconsistent.  The story artificially setup excuses to have the fixed points occur no matter what decisions were made previously.  This is a huge disappointment, but my first play through had a good enough story and I enjoyed the combat, so the poor implementation of choices is not a huge problem for me.The game is expected to be replayed to get the different endings.  However, it wastes time by requiring certain battles to be repeated even though they are the exact same each time.  These should have been skippable.  The is a skip option for most dialog and scenes.  However, you still need to load the scene first.  This is a waste of time for already viewed scenes.  They should have made them skippable at the map or have a "skip to next decision/battle" option.To make decisions, you need to get your main characters to vote.  This is a neat way to get more dialog with the characters which is pretty good.  However, it is very easy to get the vote to go however you want so it doesn't really function as an challenge.  Worst case, you can just reload the save if you don't get what you want.  There should have been an option to skip this and just force the decision for later play throughs.The music was pretty good overall.  Even though they aren't exactly the same, the music sounds like it is reused from other Square games, but most of the music is pretty good.  The big exception is the music in the base.  I hated this music.  It is too loud and super annoying.  I ended up muting the music after awhile due to this.  It is very similar to the music from the town in FF12 which played way too much in that game and is all worn out.  I wish they would have let you select the base music so you could pick one of the good musics.I ran the game on an old laptop so I can't judge the graphics very well.  Since this is using UE, I was able to find instructions to configure the graphics down so that the game ran smoothly and I could still tell what stuff is.  With my settings, the graphics quality was the same as FFT of PS1.  This is what I want for this type of game, so I was happy with the graphics.  I'm not interested in all the BS effects that games push nowadays.  I was able to disable all this nonsense including the idiotic edge blur that wastes screen space and/or will cause vision loss if the user looks at it (don't try to simulate what people's eyes do naturally).  I hope Square gets sued for vision damage caused by this effect so it will not occur in any more games.  Glad that they at least made it possible to disable for this game, but they should still be liable when looking at blur has long been known to cause vision damage.  This is more harmful than the screen flashing that always gets warned about due to affecting the whole population vs just a tiny vulnerable group.

_childDocuments_.review: the english voice acting is so bad, it would be better without it. There is an option to switch it to japanese audio. Personally I miss the days when everything didn't have to be voiced. Voice acting is not a selling point if it's terrible. Less is more.Anyway the fights are fun. Takes a while to get going. Plays out like a choose your own adventure sort of thing, branching story paths, takes notes from ogre battle. I always choose the 'nice' thing, but I also get the sense that the stories with the less nice options are better told. I think that's a classic problem with games that use this kind of narrative structure. If you've played the mass effect games, you probably know what I'm talking about: the narratives give you an option to make a sacrifice that would be gutwrenching to make--or, if you have an option to save everyone and make no sacrifices. Everyone chooses the latter. But the former tells more interesting stories. That's how the moral dillemas play out in this. Do you give up your friend to save your people? Or do you shelter him, and sacrifice them? Or do you simply save him and also not sacrifice them? As a player I want to choose the last. But as someone looking for a compelling story, I'd prefer if you gave me the first. Do you ally with the guy who is scheming to backstab you and lead you into a trap (the guy with terrible, over-the-top 'bad guy' voice acting)? Or do you not ally with the guy who will obviously backstab you? As a player, you don't. As a person who wants to see a story, you do. Freedom of choice can make for compelling stories. Red Dead Redemption 2 was a great example. Give people the choices to follow their conscience or not to--but don't give cop outs for consequences.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good take on the strategy rpg genre. All units are unique and have some good uses and synergies. There are no generics or swap-able classes like TO or FFT. Combat really does feel like it's about positioning and tactics above anything else. Support units tend to be the most powerful, and certain utility can really make a huge difference in more difficult battles.Customization is very limited other than choosing from a very small pool of upgrades to purchase. Though there are limited resources to buy upgrades which does make those choices feel important.The story is fairly grounded with just light supernatural elements for the most part. The story isn't anything special but the characters are decent enough and they take center stage in every part of the game. Their flaws and convictions drive the plot and influence the options available to you.  And you will be forced to make some difficult choices even though only a few of those difficult choices will actually matter by the end of the game. Voice acting is pretty average to bad with a few exceptions but it can be disabled.  There are a lot of cut-scenes, narrated segments and the like so if you tend to be put off by those you will not enjoy this game. It's a fairly short game as far as strategy rpgs go but the game expects you to do a few playthroughs to see all the branching paths and recruit more characters. Almost everything carries over in NG+ and enemies scale to your level. There's definitely enough unique content to justify 2-3 runs of the game.  Though you'll need a few more playthroughs after that if you want to do absolutely everything. Overall if you enjoy strategy rpgs you will likely like this game as well. It doesn't quite reach the same highs as TO or FFT but it's close and definitely a solid game in it's own right. Though if you don't already enjoy the genre with all it's quirks, then this game will probably not win you over.

_childDocuments_.review: Unlike most people who played this game I didn't have a problem with the cut-scenes being long. Long cut-scenes would be fine but the pacing and the writing is very... bad. The writing isn't bad in a "this plot makes no sense" bad. The plot is absolutely great in a broad strokes sense. But the actual *WRITING* line by line is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ atrocious. It's boring. It may seem like an asinine criticism when the game's story is about geopolitical conflicts between states but the game has characters. And these characters do not carry the story. I like each of them in the abstract but every scene is written almost like how someone who isn't familiar with Shakespeare thinks that Shakespeare reads. It is droll and every scene seems really long because they go on for much longer than what's required to establish what has moved forward int he plot and none of the fluff elevates the material. It just feels like time spent.I quit the game in the moment where I chose to turn against a particular character, betraying them as payback for something they did to a party member that you start with. The consequence of my betrayal was not her death, but instead her being upset after the battle and running back to an enemy of mine to tell them what happened. This was extremely infuriating as my betraying her and winning the battle... has the effects that i would expect from betraying her and losing.Gameplay is fine tho. The game itself is just ridiculously frustrating to play because of everything other than gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: It's probably the best Fire Emblem game on PC. Word of warning: the game is more story-heavy than game-play. The combat does have depth, but I would say it's like MGS4, where it's 80% cut scenes and 20% game play. I really liked it, but I know that isn't for everyone.Combat is a good middle ground of strategy, and "Sword go burrr." The Mana/Abilities system is really fun with everything using TP. This way, you never have to worry about mana potions or whatnot. You can also combine elemental spells to make terrestrial hazards like fires, puddles for electricity, and ice patches slow. You can also use items like oil jars to make traps or close off attack directions. Hard mode is brutal and shows no mercy if you aren't used to the mechanics. You can't change the difficulty mid-playthrough, so maybe try normal and then New Game Plus Hard unless you are used to these types of games.As for the story, it's "Game of Thrones for kids." Which is fine. The story is long and does a good job of giving you choices that matter. There are four different endings, which all reward you with new characters and other extra-unlockable battles. It's basically a political thriller with "SALT AND IRON" (if you know, you know). It takes about 30-35 hours for one playthrough between cutscenes and battles.The last thing is customizing. You cannot change classes or equipment outside of two Accessiroes. You can upgrade their class or weapon, which both allow you to pick and choose what you want as long as you have the materials.Performance is great on desktop and runs flawlessly on Steam Deck without any Protons.TLDR: Heavy Story game with 80% cut scenes and 20% combat. It takes about 30–35 hours and is pretty fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game and spiritual successor to FFT. Many optional characters, engaging story, branching chapters, multiple endings and fun battles. NG+ includes benefits for multiple playthroughs, adding new mock battles and being more challenging (but if you want to rush it, like I did, you can still change the difficulty).

_childDocuments_.review: This kind of game design happens so rarely that I forget it exists, then something like Triangle Strategy comes out and I still can't believe it exists. For anyone who loves FFT for the tactical combat, but didn't like the game breaking aspects of it, didn't want to fiddle with all the gear all the time but still wanted meaningful decision-making, this game is better than anything before it. Triangle Strategy sets a new standard by which I will judge all other tactics games past and future. Playing on hard is a joy. Each battle is a well-designed set piece where you try different approaches and manage battle field gimmicks, enemy abilities, terrain advantage, turn order manipulation, one-time per battle global abilities, etc, etc. I can't stop playing.... I haven't even beat it yet but there seems to be a new game + that people say is insane. I believe it.For me, decision-making in a battle goes like this. I pick characters I like who are underleveled and who I simply like for the voice actor or the character, try to make it work, come up with a strategy, for example, to get my old man archer up on top of a mast of a ship teeming with enemies while my invisible ninja blocks the top of the mast so that enemies can't climb the ladder. Getting the two of them there is a feat and a half. Then they send the two flying units I missed seeing up there and sideways flank him in to oblivion.Back to the glorious drawing board of upgrading equipment, thinking of synergies between character abilities, tweaking accessories..... Oh my god, I need to stop writing this review and play more...

_childDocuments_.review: So im about 20 hours in the game so far, and its pretty good!As a fan of games like final fantasy tactics, tactics ogre and the likes im always looking for the a new dark fantasy, heavy politics, game of thrones kind of stuff, and Triangle Strategy has partially scratched that itch.Firs thing first: Gameplay - 9/10  very smooth game play - alot of additions to make tactical combat better - like attack from up top bonuses, double attacks when flanking and more make this gameplay wise great. There's still some improvements possible i feel - for example combo attacks or something, things like morale, and not a huge fan of the TP system  (sort of mana for abilities, u start with 3-4 points and a good skill cost 3, a decent one 2. Not fully sure how to handle this better but bit annoying at times but ok.Difficulty: i play it on hard and its indeed difficult. It becomes necesary to cheese a bit. One of the characters can place ladders, you can block with a character so once you go up or down enemy cannot follow, which seems more or less mandatory, or you need to overlevel a bit - nice thing is even if you die or wipe or retreat you still keep the xp your chars got so its never a full loss.Story: So far pretty good, next to the fact that (i know i wished for game of thrones) but theres ALOT inspired from game of thrones. From the slavemasters of the free cities, to the main protagonist basically being the starks and the white haired elitist naughties that remind me quite a bit of the lannisters/or targarians - and several events are more or less copied from game of thrones circles, which seems a bit low inspiration. All in all they start super nice with ALOT of characters... sadly they kill off most in the first 5 hours, and it becomes quite bland in terms of actors on the main stage. Also a bit cringe how some people escape "randomly" even though we captured them at swordpoint.  They put some nice branched storyline in - but i feel more choices on how to deal with your prisoners and maybe some minor city building (prison for example) would have fitted there very nicely. Also love how there's more and more depth in a lot of the characters and how some of their storylines intertwine.Sound: lovely music , japanese voice acting is great (english voice actiing SUPER bad and couldnt listen to that for more 30 minutes).Gonna continue playing and maybe update later.

_childDocuments_.review: This ain't it.I'm in the final quarter of the game and I'm really just struggling to even force myself to continue.I'm spending the vast majority of my time watching, with glazed-over eyes, as my Steam Deck's screen dims from being idle while I watch unfathomably boring cutscenes. The worst part is, I'm punished if I skip them. You see, you need to talk to EVERY NPC YOU CAN in order to get the information blerbs and invisible stat points you need to convince your lacking lackeys to acquiesce to your requests at various decision points.Particularly frustrating was when, halfway into the game, I am presented with a critical decision that I needed to go a certain way in order to get the "true ending." Since I didn't click enough NPCs or whatever, no matter what I would say would not convince the requisite number of NPCs to agree with me, thus forcing me down a different route. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this might be my favorite game, not even joking.  I love the ♥♥♥♥ out of it, and it does everything I wish fire emblem would do in terms of making battles feel more tactical.  I understand it isn't for anyone, because the story, while VERY GOOD (Like Game of Thrones-esque) is very long to get through between battles, so the gameplay loop if you want to engage with the story is like 1 hour story, 1 hour gameplay, assuming you want to see the story (You can skip dialogue very easily and quickly if you are that kind of player, no mashing the a button here).  But the combat is really fun!  Every character feels unique and special, with abilities from creating walls of ice to block enemy pathways to riding birds to snipe enemies from buildings they can't even get to, the game really does try to encourage you to think, and doesn't just rely on flat numbers for balancing.  Hell, you can even freeze the ground, burn the frozen ground, then electrify all enemies in that water using the powers of conductivity!  There's just so much room for creativity in battling, and it's hard to go wrong with using whoever your favorite characters are even in the hardest difficulty, you just need to be smart about it!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I quite enjoyed my time with Triangle Strategy. I love the 2D-HD graphics. I thought that the story was good, and I certainly felt like I was being presented with dilemmas in the branching narrative that made me think about what I really wanted to do. I enjoyed the cast for the most part. Music is strong. The battles had some interesting quirks here and there which reminded me of Vandal Hearts. Some cons would be that, at times, I thought the game was a bit too exposition heavy. The voice actors are good but I felt like the voice direction (as far as English is concerned) was pretty subpar. _childDocuments_.review: When starting a new game, you will have the option to choose the games difficulty, there are four difficulties Very Easy (for those not very confident in tactical games but want to enjoy the story), Easy (for those new to tactical games and players who prefer to focus on the story), Normal (recommended for those who have played tactical games previously and looking for challenging battles) and Hard (for tactical experts and wish to fully immerse themselves in the trill of battle). The world of Norzelia is divided in to three nations, the Holy State of Hyzante, the Grand Duchy of Aesfrost and the Kingdom of Glenbrook. Glenbrook is ruled by King Regna and there are three High Houses of Glenbrook under King Regna, these High Houses are House Falkes, House Telliores and House Wolffort. The Kingdom of Glenbrook was instrumental in bringing an end to the Saltiron War which raged on for years over the resources of Salt and Iron. The Holy State of Hyzante controls the resources Salt, the Grand Duchy of Aesfrost controls the Iron while Glenbrook sits in the middle of both nations.  For thirty years peace has been welcomed in Norzelia and the three nations have been working hard towards a new mining venture which will benefit all. Part of everyone getting along is the arranged marriage between, Frederica of Aesfrost and Lord Serenoa, son of Lord Symon of House Wolffort. You play as Lord Serenoa and the game begins with you walking around the village in the Wolffort House grounds where you are being congratulated by the village folks. Here you meet Benedict, House Steward and Right Hand to Lord Symon, who tells you that you should head to the port and welcome your bride-to-be. So, you head off to the port, this will open the World Map, this will display markers on the map which will advance the story. There are two types of markers, Red and Green, the Red Markers indicate the main story events, while the Green Markers indicate side events. The side events will disappear from the map as the story progresses so you may want to check the side events before moving on to the main story events as you could miss out on some vital information. You will also be able to unlock your Main Menu now after which allow you access to Roster, Inventory, War Chronicles and System, later you’ll also unlock Encampment. Roster will let you check those who have joined your group, here you can gain information on them, their stats, type and class of character, weapons, abilities etcetera. Inventory allows you to see what items, potions etcetera you currently own. System lets you save your game or load a previous save from here, there are ten game save slots that you can populate for your game saves. War Chronicles here you can read information about the world of Norzelia, the High Houses, King Regna etcetera, although you’ll have to find this information as you progress through the game on notes or through other means. Encampment, here you can visit your encampment and visit traders, blacksmith, tavern and others who will take up residency in your encampment. Other characters who join your group can be found here also and even the characters who run the tavern or other services can join your group allowing you to choose them from the Roster and follow you into battle should you wish to make use of their abilities. The Tavern allows you to play mock battles, this will allow you to grind some characters levels up and each battle will have some sort of reward for completing and you can also gain Kudos for completing certain actions. Visiting the Smithy (blacksmith) will allow you to upgrade and unlock weapon abilities if you have the right materials and pennies to pay for the upgrades. You can increase your Weapon Rank by three levels, each level will allow you to unlock new abilities making your characters more and more powerful. The games story will play out through Events where you’ll read what is said from various characters as they talk about the current situation. After which you may have to enter the combat phase, this will take place over an area and will depend upon where you are currently. Your first battle will take place in the docks and the area in which you can move and fight upon is divided in to square tiles. These tiles will cover a range of heights from sea level and upwards of several times over depending on the current area you are in. You’ll be able to use these height differences to your advantage and some characters will definitely benefit from attacking from a greater height as it will also allow them to attack an enemy at a greater distance than they would if they were attacking from ground level. It certainly helped me after I had played one of my characters upon a roof top out of range of the enemy. I was doing well in battle however; I made a mistake by ending one of my characters turns instead of moving them.  This happened quite a few times where I ended my turn instead of performing an action and this was down to the controls. Using my gamepad for the most part worked perfectly but at times instead of moving the thumb stick up and down I would knock it left or right then I would hit a corresponding button to perform an action only to have changed the action I wanted without realising but it was too late to change. This is what happened with my character, instead of moving my character out of the way and being able to set a trap which was the goal I ended up losing out and I lost the chance to take advantage of the trap.  Because of this I got my botty spanked and before I knew it, I only had the character on top of the roof left. I was able to attack using my bow and luckily the enemy couldn’t attack back as I was out of reach. It took a few turns to defeat the boss but I managed to get through the level which I thought I wasn’t going to do and was thinking I’m going to have to restart this level again all because of a silly mistake and over sensitive thumb sticks being able to select inventory or end turn by going left and right, I think rebinding the buttons to shoulder buttons or something might be best action but I haven’t tried that so far, I guess I’m a glutton for punishment. Combat will have you move about the tiles to confront your enemy and have you use either a weapon or abilities to perform physical or magical attacks along with healing and protection depending on the character. If an enemy takes a physical attack, an ally on the opposite side of the enemy may trigger a Follow-Up Attack. This follow-up attack can take place even if there is a distance between the enemy and the character which triggers the follow-up attack. These attacks are great for reducing enemies with high health although you must be careful as the enemy can do the exact same to you.  Positives  + Fantastic graphics and artwork + Very enjoyable game + Good story with multiple pathways + Steam Deck Verified + Has achievements + Has cards Negatives  - Thumb sticks switching to other options The Saltiron Wars have been over for years but an uneasy balance still lies between the three powerful nations, as Lord Serenoa of House Wolffort along with his trusted allies help to keep peace in the world of Norzelia. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Most people considering this game are likely in the "turn-based tactical RPG" sphere, so this will get looked at through the lens of "so how much is this like Final Fantasy Tactics?" by many people, including myself.The character systems are certainly less robust than FFT. This is OK though, as it's made up for in the sheer volume of different characters (who have different strengths, weaknesses, and advancement customizations). You have far less choice on how an individual character develops, but you have plenty of choice in how to form your party and what tactics you want to emphasize. It's not FFT's system, but it is a pretty good system.The actual tactical battle engine is quite good. It's quite a bit less punishing than FFT, and has less depth than FFT's intricate charge/time system, but is still rather deep and very satisfying. One of the game's primary advancement resources is basically farmed by...playing the game well. So it's satisfying both in action and reward when things go well.The amount of dialogue this game has is...almost tiring. I love the story, and the choices this game makes you engage with start with pretty simple and end up borderline horrifying. But holy hell, it feels like literally half the game is reading. It's a bit much.I overall recommend this game, I think it hits on most marks and misses rarely. Be prepared to read a whole lot though.

Some of the characters are hateable, but none are loveable. This is a pretty significant problem, given the amount of dialogue in the game. Worth it if on sale if you're a TRPG fan, but probably not at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: On chapter 14 of 17 after about 44 hours of gameplay. If you like tactics games like Tactics Ogre, Final Fantasy Tactics, Fire Emblem, etc. then you'll probably enjoy this game. If you have read other reviews, know that people are not joking when they say there's a LOT of dialogue. One nice feature of the dialogue is that it's all voiced (although varying in quality) and you can set scenes to auto-play so you can sit back or walk around (if you are playing on a hand-held device or use a wireless headset) while characters talk and talk and talk. PROS: Combat is fun and doesn't require a lot of grinding. Grinding is very forgiving, as when you lose a battle you can restart it while retaining the experience you gained during the failed attempt. Normal difficulty feels like a good medium with an appropriate amount of challenges. Each character has their own unique class, and there are many different characters that can join your group, so you have lots of options. Character deaths aren't permanent, so it's a pretty low-stress game. You can steer the story in different directions over the course of the game, which leads to several different endings and there's a new-game+ feature to explore the different paths. CONS: The story is good overall, but the lore and many plot points can feel watered-down and lacking in certain ways. A lot of the dialogue is superfluous and there's too much of it. The same story could have been told with 20-30% less text, leaving more room for subtext and giving the player better opportunities to wonder what might happen next; rather than just outright being told nearly every step of the way. Furthermore, everything you do in a chapter or subchapter is recapped for you at the end of that chapter/subchapter. That's nice if you only have a few hours to play each day/week, but generally it just feels like the episode recap of a show you're binging on Netflix (except you can't skip these with the click of a button). Like I said at the top, if you enjoy games like Tactics Ogre, Final Fantasy Tactics, and Fire Emblem then you'll probably enjoy this and I would give it a recommendation. If you're on the fence, or mostly enjoy those games just for the gameplay and aren't big on story and/or lots of dialogue, I'd skip this one. I hope the game did well enough to get a sequel eventually because I really think a Triangle Strategy 2 could knock it out of the park with the right effort.

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics are great, soundtrack isn't memorable but solid. I was worried the plot would be dull, but actually there was a great deal of thought put into it and the many branches and inter-woven threads.I hope this game gets more positive reviews, because this is a step in the right direction for Square Enix after several lackluster releases.  There's just a lot of things this game gets right, compared to goofy releases like Dungeon Encounters, etc.If I had to point out some flaws... _childDocuments_.review: Triangle Strategy is a mess of a game. A significant amount of playtime is taken up by literal story exposition. The story arc is pretty decent, but the writing is bad, the voice acting is criminal, and the game's systems are outdated, with character depth that is nonexistent.Story: Very standard story of political intrigue, betrayal and duplicity. Everyone's out for themselves in such a stereotypical way. Very little of what happens will ever come as a surprise. The game handles literal genocide in quite possibly the most boring way imaginable. You will be watching cut scenes that very blandly tell literally every miniscule detail of the story, lest you miss out on something between wiping the drool from your chin because you're not allowed to live alone or cut your own meat.Writing: Everything is the most prim, formal and rigid possible. There are exactly 3 personalities in the game and no variation between characters to speak of. Every character has the depth of a petri dish.Voice acting: When you can tell that the voice of a character is a very deliberate effort, it feels cheap. Hire real actors. None of the characters ever speak with urgency or with a tone that matches the situation. Game systems: Character progression comes in the form of class promotions, of which you get 2 (Veteran and then Elite). These are minor stat upgrades and offer no new functionality, other than gaining access to another ability or passive. Because there's no job system, you will end up trading out characters you like for characters who provide better combat functionality. The extent of equipment is having 2 trinket slots for items that offer minor stat improvements. Your weapons represent a very rough talent tree, and each talent is some basic stat or ability modifier. These upgrades become exponentially expensive very fast which necessitates grinding so that you can get your entire combat party upgraded. Once you're actually on the field though, this is as good as it gets until Tactics Ogre Reborn drops. I'd recommend it, but by the time I finished my first playthrough I was sick to death of the awful cut scenes and story exposition.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is GOOOOOOOOOOOD!!!!!  And that coming from someone who played Final Fantasy Tactics for 13 years. You see, when I started this game I wasn't that much impressed at first because I was expecting something closer to what FFT was, but damn I'm glad I kept going, the more you play, the more satisfaction you get, story seemed a bit clumsy at first but boy oh boy, the more you advance, more of the lore shows up and it is phenomenal, there is a few different paths you can take in the game that really show you how things could have been depending on your choice, not only that, but from different paths you can learn more and more about the story.  For those who are first going to play, I'm warning you that there is a golden route which is recommended after get most if not all characters if you play a few New Game+ runs, I thought it would be exhausting at first but you can just skip cutscenes you have already seen and watch the ones you haven't by taking a different path in the story, there is also the fact that the gameplay become more versatile the more you upgrade your characters, at first it will be a bit slow but once you are a bit ahead in the game it just becomes faster,.  I got to say for the Final Fantasy Tactics fans. this game doesn't have that Shakespearean kind of drama like FFT, but it is great in it's own ways. The combat feels similar but a bit different in it's own good ways.  Since many people have been commenting about the voice acting, I got to point out, the voice acting sound a bit clumsy at first, but I'm pretty sure it is the style they chose for the game... yeah, weird right...?  ...But if you check the ♥♥♥/ENG dub, you will see they do the same tone of voice acting, I feel like it is almost like they wanted to give you the feeling of people reading and narrating the story for you instead of voice acting. But hey, it's pretty decent still and once you get used to it you won't mind at all.  For those who are thinking about playing in Hard difficulty in their first, I don't recommend it at all, it kind takes out the fun of the game because it's more frustrating than interesting for a first playthrough, more likely because the instead of enemy AI being improved, I felt like it was just their stats that are always above your characters in a completely unfair way, which isn't interesting or fun in my opinion, and I'm stating that as a tactics genre veteran, Normal difficulty can be challenging enough without taking your fun away, but hey, you can try hard mode after your first playthrough to challenge yourself! There is also the possibility of changing difficulty any time you want ( except when mid battle), it is really up to you.I give this game a solid 8.7/10!I'm writing this comment on my 62.5 hours of gameplay, but I will keep playing because I want that 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic in its gameplay and presentation, however, I think the story is exceptionally weak and nearly made me leave a negative overall review of the game. The combat and characters are unique and create a lot of interesting decisions to make both in team building and on the field. The game's a bit on the difficult side, but I don't think there's anything wrong with that as it has two difficulties below normal. If you want an SRPG and don't care too much about the story, then this game will be fantastic for you.This is where the review will get a bit negative. A lot in the story works especially early on. However as you get later in the game, things start to fall apart. I won't get too much into spoilers, but I'll list all of my problems with the story.1. The conviction system and the persuasion system work in tandem to ensure some decisions are locked  behind NG+ which is immensely frustrating especially given that I may only play through the game once.2. Some story paths require an absolutely insane level of running around and interacting with whatever the developers decided you need to be successful.3. Inconsistent characterization. Certain characters make decisions that are both strategically foolish and make no sense for what they'd do from an emotional stand point.4. Confusing story reveals. (This is coming from someone who likes Metal Gear)This is a good game, but it is bogged down by its story. Which is strange because there are so many cutscenes, notes and lore that it seems like the game wants you to engage with its story. But the more you engage with it, the more cracks appear. But if the story doesn't matter to you, then absolutely get this game.

(Note that I originally played this on Switch, and so far it's identical except for now running at a locked 60fps & higher resolution. The roster is large (30 characters) with distinct movesets that are all useful in their own way+ Story is great - It's a slow burn about three neighbouring nations with different ideals competing for resources. These decisions come often and they change what battles you enter and where you go+ Hard mode is much more challenging than normal (the game's director says he couldn't beat the game himself on Hard). _childDocuments_.review: This is a squad-based fantasy tactics game. It might look like Final Fantasy Tactics or Disgaea, but it is more about strategy than about RPG elements. It looks and sounds amazing, the story is entertaining, it's decently challenging, and I have only minor complaints about it. It's the best game of this type, so I highly recommend it.Now to the specifics. This game is mostly about combat, and the combat is fun. There are stats and you improve them, but the roster of characters is very diverse and you mostly use characters because of their active and passive abilities, rather than stats. This is different from most tactics/RPG hybrids I've played except maybe earlier Fire Emblems: in FFT, Disgaea and even Fire Emblem Three Houses you pump up the stats and can mold characters a lot, while here character roles are set in stone. I've found myself using a lot of characters that would feel like a pointless gimmick in another game: in every battle I've deployed a weak character who has almost no abilities except to cast a decoy that lures enemies away. The game looks similar to Octopath Traveller and also uses similar ideas with the action economy, the system is very simple and easy to get but creates some interesting choices. There is a strong mage who can cast spells of every element but doesn't have any low-cost abilities and no easy way to restore power reserves, so he often has nothing useful to do. Meanwhile, you also have a weaker ice mage who has low-cost abilities (which means he can always do something productive) and eventually learns to replenish power reserves by standing on the ice that his spells create. The game design is elegant and not too complex. The difficulty is balanced well, with spikes coming at important story moments. I also like the idea of "mental battles": the game doesn't really have a side-content but as the story goes you unlock combat scenarios that somehow grant you resources and allow training characters. Those are not just throwaway generic battles, some of them have unique mechanics or maps not found in the main game.Apart from combat, there's also so-called exploration, which is very limited. It's just an opportunity to talk to NPCs and followers and find notes and items lying on the ground. Sometimes you also investigate something and look for information you can use later in the decision phase. Decisions are neat moments where you decide where to go on a branching story path. It's presented as not just a choice but as a dispute between your main cast followers. Theoretically, you can fail to convince people and be forced to follow a specific path, but you usually have to persuade just one person out of seven so I don't think it's likely. The choices feel significant and well thought-out, they're always interesting even if you feel like the right path is obvious, as through disputes you have an opportunity to present the information you found or appeal to the character's personality. The story branching is real, it affects both the narrative and the battles you face as well as your roster. Another thing is the morality system - everything you do, including your actions in combat, gives you points of Morality, Utility and Liberty, and those affect characters that join your crew.The story is fine. At first, I thought that R-rated Game of Thrones is missing the point. It has all the intrigue and backstabbing you expect from a story like that, but every single character is an idealist so it feels a little sugarcoated. The distances feel too small in this world and it interferes with the idea of a cohesive and complex setting: armies need just a day to march from one country's capital to another and this feels deeply wrong. Still the story captured me. It has an epic feel, it happens over a long time, and there are little Deus Ex Machinas that feel forced - it all feels like the result of character choices. It's also a relatively low fantasy world, so there are (almost) no supernatural things affecting the story. Sure, there are mages and healers, but it's more of a gameplay concession, the story is about dynastic struggles, resource control and ideology, there are no magical McGuffins. The story is also not as great as other parts of the game cause it doesn't feel as robust. Gameplay is elegantly put together, and there's nothing lacking or excessive in it, but in terms of story you have plenty of optional cutscenes to watch, and most of them are pointless, except the ones that shed light on very important events. You also find lore about the world and it's boring and there's little point in reading it. Almost all of the game cutscenes are presented with the same assets and camera that are used for combat, so cutscenes often lack expression. Music and voice acting are both excellent but aren't used effectively for those cutscenes. Plus there are character-focused side stories told through these optional cutscenes, and most of them are filler, but in the world of Persona and Fire Emblem we can't have a story without a girl trying to learn to cook to impress her husband.But enough complaints, this game looks, sounds and plays great. It's a rare occasion that I start New Game Plus immediately after finishing my first playthrough. NG+ mode exposes a lot of information that was previously hidden to make your decisions not feel "gamey", like how many personality stats you need to recruit different characters. I'm not sure I'll finish this second playthrough: while there are many endings (and a special golden ending requiring a specific path) the story feels complete. As I've mentioned, character progression is limited: by the end of your first playthrough you only get enough resources to fully develop just a few characters, and after that the progression doesn't go anywhere, so I'm not sure if the gameplay doesn't get too repetitive. _childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, but I don't. It's a typical tactics RPG, with many annoying features. The game tracks three invisible attributes which affect dialogue choices, it punishes you for not talking to every NPC, and it punishes you for not wandering around every single exploration phase to find all the precious few items, that there are really no other way to obtain. You better mash buttons and go to every single corner of every map, or else you miss out on the best gear.The game also features "voting" where you need to convince members of your party to make a decision a certain way, this is also affected by the choices made in previous dialogue due to the hidden attribute attached. The party seems to mostly default to the worse choice, i.e. give up party member to bad guys, or tattle on some smugglers. It turns every one of these moments into looking up a strategy guide to figure out which convoluted dialogue tree and convincing needed to guide each decision.Character customization is non-existent. Each character has a class and two upgrades gated by items you have to buy from a shop or acquire, every shop has severely limited quantities of items for some reason. You need a lot of those limited items to upgrade character weapons, which cannot be swapped, only upgraded twice. Aside from weapons each character has two accessory slots for mostly exciting items like ring of +1 attack or defense, but you'll have to visit the randomly placed exploration phase merchant if you want anything exotic, like an amulet lightning resitance.The story is boring and basic. The game is frustrating. The mechanics are annoying.
