_childDocuments_.review: An SRPG with multiple story paths to take, a large cast of characters to use in fairly simple but varied battles, and while it can be inconsistent in every area it's a frequent shift between average and excellent.The plot has you taking control of a young noble that is quickly betrothed to the half sister of the ruler of another nation and is given control of his house due to his father's illness. The continent holds three nations, Aesfrost in the north that focuses on ironwork and a system of freedom through meritocracy that has lead to a massive divide between the rich and poor, Holy State of Hyzante in the east that controls the one known source of salt on the continent where all the citizens seem to be cared for but all have to follow the teachings of and worship a goddess, and the kingdom of Glenbrook which boasts a fairer climate than the other two nations harsh snow and desert and whose rivers and location makes it a center of trade. After a long war ended 30 years ago a joint mining venture between the three nations brings many of the higher ranking members of each country together to celebrate their alliance, but shortly after the delegates return home Arsfrost attacks and takes over the capital of your kingdom. As the new lord of one of the kingdoms three most prominent houses you, your best friend and youngest prince, future wife that is descended from a persecuted people in Hyzante, and your father's long serving advisor have to decide the best way forward.The writing is often a more average JRPG quality with the normal ridiculous moments of characters things like "haven't we shed blood as well," "how can we hold on to our honor," "shouldn't peace and friendship be our goal." I've defended my party and people from bandits, a nation of imperialist cultists, imperialist betrayers, and bandits I don't think we need all the whining. But when the game hits the bigger moments, the character defining moments, the ends of narrative arcs, the clashes between some of the main enemies or ideologies the writing starts to get quite good, not Tactics Ogre Let Us Cling Together quality, but reaching a bar many games of the genre don't and in those moment the music often goes from a normal good but forgettable standard to also suddenly being excellent and working to further enhance the best moments of the game. It was nice to see that, despite the setup, I've again played one of the seeming few JRPGs where they did not take the narrative route of setting up a monarchy as a good system of government so long as it ends with a nice guy on the throne.A strong point of the game is that many chapters have two or three options laid out by different characters as a way to proceed and the main members of your house vote on which route to take, with you being able to attempt to persuade anyone to the side you want and with the deciding vote if there is a tie. You can more easily persuade people if your conviction in one of three areas is aligned with what and who you are talking to, combined with choose the right dialogue with some possibly locked behind information found through exploration. You build points in morality utility, and freedom by your choices when talking to people, vote choices and persuasions, and smaller amounts of points through more minor actions based on a variety of actions you can take in battle or exploration. While the routes are interesting and some of the choices are difficult to guess what will happen and how much it can change the story, the actual voting and conviction system I really could have done without as it isn't mechanically interesting and never had any real effect on anything.The conviction system thankfully stays out of the game enough where your past choices, potential for the true ending aside as that requires certain routes to be taken, won't lock you into any set options in the the future, which that just further highlights how meaningless it tends to be. You are really only using it to do two things, building up enough of one or two of the three types of conviction that side characters will come to join your house and higher values of a particular type make it easier to convince the seven main characters in your house to vote the way you want them to when making a decision that will alter the plot or change the next or next couple sections of the game. Unless you really focus on only one area, you can pretty much get the group to do whatever you want, and you should have so much of each conviction in a new game plus (which the game clearly wants you to run through multiple times to see that paths, get the true ending, unlock all characters, get all the character upgrades, etc) that you can definitely do whatever you want then. It is nice to see character's perspectives on different issues, but it might as well have just had them all talk it out and you pick the way the conversation gets steered instead of taking a vote where you may or may not have convinced particular characters of the choice and no one ever mentions any kind of disagreement again. I went into the game slightly blind and assumed that the voting system was you trying to convince other nobles of your kingdom or people from other nations to take up plans that change the games or that might give positive or negative effects to situations and battles, not that you would just be dealing with your seven friends that can typically be easily convinced of anything.The battle system typically has you deploying from 9-12 characters with two of the main mechanics being to manage each character's TP that allow them to access their skills and to maneuver your characters in such a way that you can attack enemies while having a character on each side of them (or firing off a ranged attack while an ally is on the opposite side of them). There are a few considerations to take into account such as archers having greater ranged if they are on higher terrain, attacks having a higher hit chance if you have the high ground or are directly behind an opponent, and terrain can either offer minor benefits or can have spells chain lightning over water or freeze tiles to slow movement, start fires in some areas, or melt ice to create puddles. Every character gets a move action and can use one of their abilities each turn, this can be done in any order and there are a few movement skills that allow you to move, use the skill for further movement, and then take another skill action. It's a fairly simple system as characters learn only a few active and passive skills as they level up and are promoted but it works well, is easy to get into, tends to play out fairly quickly, and some of the map designs combined with the varied types of characters you can use keep things interesting. Each character has a main attack that used no TP and abilities that use between 1-4, 0 (for some rare abilities you can acquire passives to reduce the cost of), or all the TP the character currently has. Depending on their current class promotion, each character can hold between 3-5 points, recovers one each turn, and starts a battle with three. Certain characters might have various ways to gain more such as killing an enemy, standing on a certain kind of surface, not moving, hitting multiple enemies at once, starting a battle with more TP, or being able to add or give TP to other characters or to remove it from enemy units.There is a large roster of characters that each have their own class and many with skills and passives completely unique to them. _childDocuments_.review: What a waste of time and waste of a game.  The hype over this game is seriously people with paid sponsorships or rose-colored glasses.I won’t say I am the biggest RTS RPG player.  I did play FF tactics years ago on a Gameboy, don’t remember it much though. Saying that I played Mercenaries Blaze and Rebirth within the past 12 months to remind and show me what makes a good RTS RPG.The good, it is voice acted, and has copied art from Octopath traveler.  It has an OK story as well.  It does have many job types to play, but that may also be a negative.Now for the negative:  The game feels like it was made by many spall teams then thrown together.  The jobs have variety but not really customizable.  And you can play a whole playthrough and not promote or lvl up all jobs.  The items needed wont drop.  Forcing you to play a second playthrough.  While this would be ok if it was a good game. It sucks.No treasure chest to get on maps beside two maps.  Even then it is only gold and healing items or elemental throwing weapons.You wont find any items to promote your toons in treasure chest.  Furthermore, the bosses have nothing unique to drop or steal for that matter.  Yes you can steal but nothing is worth while vs dps or heal instead.The mock battle system is also meh.  While ok, they are specific battles.  And they don’t have any unique items or treasure to find. Furthermore they are very repetitive and this is how you lvl up and spend most your gametime, outside of reading the story.If they made the mock battles where you could unlock jobs and units and maps along the way as you play the game then let you make your own team A vs B it been great.  But they didn’t.The fact there is no real unique treasure from bosses or shops means every job is just normal.  Compare this with Mercenaries Blaze.  You can get a saddle so your horse can go 1-2 extra spaces, or an accessory that allows your weapon to hit 2x or extend its range.  Things like this let you enjoy customizing your toons with items you find.  The bomb map, well 1 map uses bombs you must stop, but like treasures only giving gold and heal pots and on two maps only, the player can never use bombs himself. Hence when you have 30 toons its meh.  Even if you have only 20 at the time.  Poor toon management.Do your self a favor if you want a good RTS get Mercenaries Blaze or Rebirth. _childDocuments_.review: This is a great game if you're looking for a Realpolitik story in the vein of Yasumi Matsuno titles, with interesting branching paths in between. Yes the first 3-4 chapters of the game start slow but after that there's an exploration phase and battle in every chapter. Really though I think the gameplay is where the game shines the most, it's a great challenge on hard mode and New Game+ carries over pretty much everything, one of the best in any games I've played. You don't have job reclassing like FFT but you promote units similar to older Fire Emblem games, with the 30 playable characters you get there's plenty of room to experiment. Every unit plays differently and the game encourages you to try synergies between them, no one is OP enough to solo the game by themselves or completely useless that they should be never be used. I will say though that the English localization is pretty meh, it's like FF Tactics War of the Lions on the PSP, added sentences that weren't present in the original and using out of place archaisms. I switched to French text and it was a lot more enjoyable, and more faithful to the Japanese script too. I'd recommend this game to anyone looking for a SRPG with a good lengthy story and challenging battles.

_childDocuments_.review: Hidden Triangle Shaped GemResearching this game took me way longer than usual, on the surface it seems like a typical JRPG but the deeper you delve you realise its much more complicated than that. The poor marketing of this game therefore results in the consumer either easily writing off this game as just another one of those games, or being confused as to what they are getting and why it may be special enough to purchase and take the time to play it. It also doesnt help that it looks exactly like octopath traveller so when you see the game it makes one wonder is it just a spin off in the now collection of 3 games that look just like this. Overall the prior paragraph sets the groundwork for me to explain why it is a total tragedy that many folk will have reasonably missed out on this game and what a game it is. Many video games and especially in this genre are met with complaints that there are boring moments or poor pacing but Triangle Strategy does things differently. TS keeps your focus tight by making it so that everything in the game matters to the player via how it all culminates into your key plot point divergences, when the party has to vote for which direction to take the story in. As a regular skipper of dialogue etc I rarely skipped anything in this game and you will likely be the same. Its such an engaging feeling to know that your attention to details matter from what characters believe morally to how your act in the work via the 3 values system morality liberty and utility. The academic depth of this game is insanely impressive and one of the most ambitions attempts at a deep video game I have ever witnessed. How this developer firstly came up with this game and also had the guts to pursue something that is the total opposite of the common simplistic stories most games have blows my mind. I would love to meet the team behind this game because I promise you they are geniuses and I dont say that lightly. This game creation demands that they must of had a very good understanding of history politics religion and many others subjects. Much of the game parodies history from the european nations to russia and saudi arabia in a unique but believable way. The plot has game of thrones levels of twists and turns and I loved every minute of it.If all this wasnt enough the quality of the game is top notch with pro level voice acting better than anything hollywood has done top notch sound and great tactical gameplay in which you get to fill out a team to your unique fighting preference. Tons of quality of life options from speed ups to difficulty modes and the game runs like butter and would be a great steam deck title. The game also has strong replayability with all the characters and different plot points you will want to explore with 4 different endings and many ways to play. Sometimes certain films or games get passed by and it takes 10 years before a cult followings gets people to realise that actully this title was great. This is one of those game that I promise you in 10 years this game will be in the top 100 greatest games of all time. PS last 2 things firstly do not spoil the plot for yourself its very important u go in blind also to the haters of this game who mainly talked about slow pace and not enough combat, they are 100% wrong the pace can be fast as you want it via speed ups and you can do as much combat as you want via story and mental battles.If youre looking for a special game or your wondering whether to get this or the great octopath games get this first, its S tier game design through and through. Good luck and don't be afraid to to cause a splash for the greater good my fellow norezellians ;)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is truly fantastic, and one of the best SRPG's I've played in ages. Some of the features that are really good : -Story Choice. The game does a great job of making you feel your story choices. Some of the choice points are extremely brutal with no clear choice being better, and they have dramatic story implications. Additionally, a lot of your responses are based on your convictions which are built by you just trying to choose what is right for you instead of trying to max a stat.-Simplified Magic System. The TP system is intuitive and easy to use. I also like how you don't get bogged down in mp management or having to increase it as a stat. -Character Diversity. The Characters have tons of diversity in how they are created both in gameplay and in their  look/story arcs. You can create a team of 10 for most missions which is nice so you have a lot of characters to use instead of just a few.-Grind Solution. It's so much nicer to have the encampment instead of a map with nodes to move on. I love that you can just do all your work in one area. It helps with the pacing a lot. Generally, you only need to grind a map 2-3 times between story fights which is a nice change from some of the more oldschool approaches. Additionally, since each fight is clearly labeled as "You must be so tall to ride", it's easy to know when you are done grinding. Losing a fight lets you keep your levels so losing is in a sense also grinding, instead of wasted time. A++ here. -Kudos. The game rewards you with currency for playing right, using terrain, back attacking, team attacking etc. It's a great mechanic that helps new players onboard to the special tactics of the game while also being actually useful in your progression. -Story. Compelling and great. I played with Japanese voice actors and subtitles on my Steamdeck. Was a great experience. No spoilers, but wow. Also, has a NG+ mode that I'm excited to explore to see how it changes.Overall solid game experience, unexpectedly fun. Not too long (between 30 - 40 hours without NG+). Really great game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is from the same studio that brought Octopath Traveller to the world. However, it is not a JRPG but a tactical RPG - you will need to consider troop facing and terrain height differences in battle in addition to the usual damage mechanics (physical, magic, status effects, etc.). As the game progresses extra mechanics become active, such as skipping an action or move decreases the time unit the unit's next turn.Game play wise this is not a fast paced game. Each chapter generally contains 1 story battle, at least one map segment you can explore (these occasionally contain travelling merchants with access to the merchant limited to the exploration zone), and sometimes extra cut scenes. To train your units you'll need to visit the encampment bar keep. The more over-levelled your party is vs the recommended  level the less XP you'll get for all actions. You'll still want to do this for the loot though. You'll have mandatory story segments that you must navigate along with optional story segments. The two different types are colour coded to help you decide how much of the story you want to discover. I'd advise discovering as much as possible; as investigating an area and talking to NPC's can reveal information which can be useful later on. This is because the game's unique features are: 1) a hidden personality score with 3 elements (Liberty, Morality, Utility) which influences dialogue, the units you can recruit and your ending. 2) a voting system to decide which story path you take in certain chapters. The 7 guaranteed party members will vote and you are bound by the decision, even if it's the one you don't want. You are able to influence the decision through dialogue, but some options are locked out if you didn't speak to the right NPC earlier on. 3) Your actions have consequences, as the story branches during certain chapters. Who you choose to help or where you visit will dictate the at least half of the missions you'll play. What your choices won't do is shorten the length of the story. You have to select a specific series of events in order to activate the hidden game ending.The main downside to this game is that it is a port from the Switch, so some of the controls feel clunky on a PC - world map navigation conflict between mouse and cursor keys; camera angle controls [IJKL]; battle command selection (sometimes selects the simulation command by mistake).  The main game play gripe is how units gain upgrades as XP only gets you so far. You also have to acquire 1 or 2 types of material (stone, timber, iron, fibre) dependent on unit, to gain perks like +1 phys defence or a skill buff. An uncommon or rare material like a crystal to access the 2nd & 3rd perk tiers. All these upgrades also cost coin. Plus you must acquire 2 different medals to upgrade a units status (Recruit>Veteran>Elite) to improve the number of skills you can access to 7 and expand the skill energy gauge maximum to 5 points. However these cost a second currency, you earn through performing certain tactics like using the high ground.

_childDocuments_.review: This is Shining Force 4 if Shining Force 4 actually existed and was made by people with a severe case of graphomania. Gameplay-wise it's a decent tactical JRPG, again, reallly Shining Force-esque, can't stress that enough, as it was what kept me going, for I love Camelot's creation a lot. Story-wise though... I mean, it's okay on paper, like if you start blueprinting your story in a way like "character A goes to location B, there he meets character C and persuades him to march together to location D to save the queen E, but during that time character F conspires with characters G to M to <do something>", from this viewpoint it's an okay story, seen worse. If you zoom in on the story and actually read and listen the stuff the characters say, it's a boring uninspired neverending slop of blandness. Graphics... well, they exist. I'm almost certain that the game reuses at least half of the assets from Octopath Traveler. I mean, it's still a Square Enix game, so they have every right to do that, but damn, with a price tag of 60 euros you'd expect a little bit effort. Still, the game manages to look pretty enough, so there's that. Just nothing to write home about.Music is okayish, there is a couple of gems here and there, but overall not really memorable. Voiceacting is meh, seen worse, but not a lot.Now, the controls... the controls for this game hold a very special place in my heart, one that was previously held by From Software's games, because here they are even worse. I'm about 93% sure that this game was coded using gamepads only, as no sane creature that has ever seen a keyboard in their life can come up with such disastrously bad control scheme.And anyway, with all that, I'd still cautiously recommend buying this one. At a heavy discount, naturally, but it might be worth a shot. It's not really horrible, simply deeply flawed. There is actually a good game out there under all the negatives. Battle system is fine, storyline is heavily branched, which is never not a good thing, the encounters are well-balanced and always have some gimmick that makes them special, so, yeah, there. Put the story on autoplay or skip it entirely and you're looking at a decent title.

_childDocuments_.review: I really dislike giving a Not Recommended to any game, and I argued internally for a very long time whether I should mark this as such. Ultimately what made me choose it was that after 37 hours of gameplay, I sat back and thought 'Did I have fun playing this game?' That unfortunately came back as a resounding No.Triangle Strategy does a lot of things right; the story and worldbuilding is interesting, the characters are very compelling and fun, the art and music is gorgeous. The actual battle mechanics are fun and how I wanted it to play, as a fan of the FF Tactics series. But it does enough little-to-medium things to annoy me that make the game in general a drag to play.You have to grind SO MUCH in this game. Whether that be because the main battles leave you underlevelled, or because you need to grind for each characters' respective tree to get their stats up. I normally am completely fine with grinding SOMETIMES, but not after every main battle, and especially not after having so much narrative in between main battles. The most frustrating thing was that sometimes the materials I needed didn't even drop; I don't understand why this game did that. It's not a gatcha, nor is it competitive; it literally only serves the purpose of padding out the game time.I enjoyed the concept of the Scales of Conviction and choosing your own path, but I think Triangle Strategy made a mistake in choosing 'Morality' as one of it's paths. Some of the choices felt like 'hey do you want to do these two dubious choices or do you want to choose the only non-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ choice?' Almost every other faction besides House Wolffort is so comically evil and unsympathetic, which just doesn't work for at least my sense of narrative replay value. For me to play a game like this again and again and explore the full story, either all paths need to be sympathetic to a degree, or all need to be rat bastards. I just have zero desire to play any further runs, even the special ending run which I'm assuming will be the ultimate good run, because I hate any choice outside of the Roselle choices.I could probably add more things that made me frustrated at this game, but I have COVID and those two reasons were the main contributors of why I have to give a Not Recommended. Play this game if you're curious about it, I suppose, but at the very least make sure you grab it on sale. I commend Triangle Strategy for the things it tried to do, but it wasn't well executed enough to justify the full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I double-dipped on this game after beating the Switch version because I knew I was going to replay the game at least twice (and probably a third time with mods?) and wanted the best experience.  The PC version is an absolutely gargantuan improvement over the Switch version, which is shocking based on how the game looks, but the combination of tremendously improved load times, slightly more responsive UI, and better raw image quality smooth over a ton of the problems that the Switch version.The game itself is simply the best set of battles to appear in a Tactical RPG, paired with the best selection of units in a Tactical RPG.    Each of the 60 main battles in the game are well-designed with interesting scenarios and mechanics and layouts, in a game that is only around 20 battles in a single playthrough, giving the player a strong incentive to replay the game to see the various plot branches.  Fueling that replayability is the fact that the 30 playable characters are all wholly unique and designed, with no generic classes or generic characters or really notable repeat abilities aside from some of the basic elemental spells, and even those basic elemental spells are vastly more interesting than other TRPGs.  Fire can light grass tiles on fire to deal damage per turn and on passing through, or melt ice into puddles.  Ice can make difficult terrain or extinguish flames with puddles.  Lightning will damage units on all contiguous puddle tiles or metal flooring.   Bonuses like weaknesses, attacking from behind, or pincer attacks are more in the range of 30% bonuses to overall damage rather, than doubling as in many other TRPGs, which contributes to how often it feels like there are meaningful choices and tradeoffs. Things like rooting enemies, or knockbacks, or traps that fling enemies in desired directions ending their turn and dealing fall or collision damage, feel meaningful in a way that they just simply don't in most other TRPGs.There's a surplus of mechanics and design choices that leads to a longevity that easily spans 2, 3, or 4 playthroughs while being consistently engaging.  Characters being linked to progress in the three virtues, or the micro plot branches/convergences, means that you will have access to different units per playthrough as you play through all of those new and interesting scenarios.  On top of that, Hard mode is generally great and just the right amount of extra difficulty to make even the repeat battles interesting, and the NG+ is a full continuation of the difficulty curve and progress, with Chapter 1 starting at a level higher than the final boss.  Every aspect of the gameplay is remarkably well put-together.Even beyond the 60 core scenarios across the three or four main routes, there's a series of mock battles that are ostensibly used for grinding and materials, but also grow to be genuinely interesting as more unlock.  NG+, rather than just using higher level versions of the existing battles, goes on to increase the complexity with a series of new battles.  Even into NG++ there are new mock battles to unlock based on which main plot branches you've beaten.  Between the surplus of content and the genuinely interesting character concepts, the developers have done a great job constantly giving the players new and interesting experiences across multiple playthroughs.The plot and characters are generally engaging, let down by some bad voice acting and pacing issues (specifically the bridge from the first battle to the second, or before the thirteenth battle), but the latter is way less of a problem on the PC version that has load times that are a tiny fraction of the Switch version.I'm a way larger fan of the soundtrack than most.  This feels like some vintage 80s/90s anime bombastic orchestra soundtrack that gets edited out in the localization.  Sound effects and sound engineering are both way beyond what you'd expect out of a game that is so retro-inspired.This is a really great game that carves a totally distinct niche among Japanese TRPGs, and I'm looking forward to the inevitable sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: The game strikes a great balance between multiple aspects, which makes it a joy to play. After the slow-ish start, the game weaves exploration, combat, branching paths and enough plot happenings together in a way, that always makes you want to see what happens next. The level scaling ensures that you'll always have some amount of challenge, and normal difficulty feels really well balanced. The "HD 2D" style is visually great, although it'd be nice to see character portraits next to dialogue boxes with maybe a few different emotion faces. Music is good, but not necessarily something I'd jam to outside of the game. Overall, it's a very well designed package that works great as a whole. I hope they make this into a series.

_childDocuments_.review: They see me RolandThey Hughette'inPatreiatte is tryna catch me ridin' FerguieTryna catch me ridin' FerguieTryna catch me ridin' FerguieTryna catch me ridin' FerguieTryna catch me ridin' FerguieUh, actual review? Um, take Final Fantasy Tactics, add a couple decades or what have you and Square has a whole host of voice actors and dialogue writers and such so that it feels like FFX (or later FF's) had a baby with Final Fantasy Tactics and here we are.SPOILER ALERTAs far as the game itself there are some extremely dialogue heavy sequences which are actually somewhat laborious to even skip through, so that is a little tiresome.I did beat it on Hard difficulty with the true ending and was rewarded with a new title sequence. Only character I didn't get was Travis. Speaking of which the main barrier to getting through Hard mode is literally the first level because you can't choose your team. Protip: shielding stance and tight spaces alongside accessories (looking at you rejuvenation bracelet) are your friend. Other than that defeating Exhume in the third act in defense of House Wolffort without torching the town took literal hours using the rooftop house near the castle entrance to pile up rain and lighting for map-wide aoe while Milo did hit and run tactics from the other rooftops. I also surprisingly had to rely on Lionel, lol. I would use the clairvoyant boy to lure up soldiers, then displace them to the rooftop where the gang would take them out. After that the AI sort of gives up when it's only archers and mages and you can just fry them by targetting the ground from the rooftop (it shows it'll set off the fire traps, but it doesn't actually.)There are jobs and such but again it is dumbed down. The only thing that saves it is the fact there are so many characters that there is plenty of variety in team make-up. You do have to be selective about which skills you pick because otherwise the other ones cost more items (we're talking going from 1-5 superior materials to 10-20) and money items are somewhat hard to come by given the ginormous cast. The greed mental mock battle is good for farming, but doesn't seem to give the whole 9000 gold all the time despite that amount being literally labelled on the battle in the menu.The true ending is the only way it should be played with the other endings as sort of a "Ah, that's interesting, but nothing I expected to happen (like allying with Svarog) ... happened." The True ending fills all those gaps (at least it did for me.)Few more quick tidbits:-Aside from Cordelia's 3rd level skill, sped up, the game ran pretty much fine on my 8 year old Macbook Intel graphics. 100% playable. Keep in mind it's a Macbook, though, the Intel chips are pretty fast on them even only an i5. The only glitches I saw were in the Hierophant's palace, the skirt curtains would somewhat glitch out but wasn't bad.-Cordelia on the team opens up a lot of options as far as turtling up in a corner or on a cliff / valley and boosting your HP to massive amounts -- It's how I got through true ending except for the final battle which I instead used clairvoyant boy to displace Idore into the middle of my guys so they could kill him off as quick as possible.-Hard mode nerfs your physical damage and physical defense hard, magic and evasion characters are way better, Frederica and Ice boy are really good alongside the guy that gives his TP to other chars. Unless you go speed accessories on everyone you want to boost what they already have a lot of because all levels ,aside from mock battles, are capped at 50 -- assuming you try hard mode later on.) Speed does seem to be the overarching default "this is going to be good on this character regardless, simply because you'll get more turns and hence more TP.-The story is a bit like choose your own adventure until you get the final ending so that is a bit disappointing, but somewhat realistic.-There was a lot of thought and work put into this game, little niceities like auto battle speed going faster in new game +, not having to pickup loot in repeat playthroughs in exploration mode.-Story-wise my only complaint is that Thalas and Erika didn't have prominent roles. They're just annoying a**holes, but it would have been much better if they killed someone off and threw it in your face during a sequence or something. In FFT the story feels like there are real consequences and the dynamics of choosing what you will do next in the scales sequences might have prevented some juicier storytelling in TS.-Gustadolph can be dispatched in true ending mode by buying multiple ice amulets (the ones that give you ice resistance) stacking them on a couple of dudes and taking advantage of tight spaces and killing him, etc.Ah, one last thing: You can turn off the fog of war black blurry borders in graphics settings. It was the first thing I did because I found it unplayable with them on. (Why would I want to play a game looking through a keyhole??)Finally,DotDotDot

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, for me this would be a mixed review going towards a positive review.I enjoyed the story and how it was depicted. I enjoyed the options given, and that they are moral ambiguous, there are no right or wrong answers. I liked the troped characters, since somehow it gives the story a frame. I like the voiceovers, and the little stories here and there.Music and art are really gorgeous, and love political intrigue plots.I had never played an SRPG before, and I'm glad I played this one, since I found it really enjoyable.Buthere's the catch: You get so many characters that you need to improve, it actually ends up being as FF Type-0. Even if you wanted to play with less of them, the optional ones are few, materials are scarce (to upgrade weapons) and you have to replay battles over and over again to get so little. After the update in which you could replay previous chapters' battles I tried it again, because playing the same 15 battles over 300 times each gets boring, found that materials there were potions and that kind of stuff.And here's the catch: I'm overleveled, and still I'm not able to beat the main battles. Tried several types of strategies, upgraded everything I could as much as I could, and after levelimg up one more level, battle became astonishingly easy. So it is not well balanced, since my strategy there did not change much. And the same happened with the next battle.So what's the point? You have to grind mock battles endlessly to get some enjoyment out of the actual battles and story. And, in my humble opinion, it's just not worthy to do three times to get every achievement.Having said this, if this game didn't overstayed it's welcome, I would have fully recommended it. However, it is a mixed one for me, just for the time sink.

_childDocuments_.review: Important: The voice acting is abysmal. It's awful. It is so wooden and stiff. Very VERY lacklustre and unexciting. If they added character portraits for who was talking it'd be much more tolerableHowever, despite all of those issues this is a cool game so far. _childDocuments_.review: The clock amount is for my 3rd run midway. The game has 4 endings and I intend to discover all of them. Your first 2 playhroughs of the game will definitely feel like a 2 different storylines, but the rest only diverges on the end. So yeah, instead of saying it's a 30h game, it's a 50h game in my book (30h + 20h for second playthrough). Why do I still intend to grab the other 2? Because the endings are good, so far 1 have blown my mind out of the 2.Plot is good, it doesn't have the "protagonist syndrome", which basically shouts justice shall prevail and make you win against all odds. There's always something that ruins your plan, not save it. Twist and turns everywhere, makes you to always be skeptical about things.Voice acting is top notch (JP), while music is... not the best. My standard is very high (Nishiki, Okabe, Hisaishi, Uematsu, Mitsuda, Soken), so take it with a grain of salt. Though so far 2 music has really moved me.Now, combat and gameplay. Progression is good, exp curve is a very good mechanic (basically you won't outlevel your enemies by mistake and will be on par with them in just 1 battle), encouraging experimentation instead of sitting duck watching guide on which character is best. Combat is well.... FFT standard.My gripe is, this is a piss poor PC port. Nothing is basically changed to accomodate PC users, it's best to be played on controller, because your mouse pointer will behave erratically should you attempt to use it. Graphical wise it's not taxing, nor does it crash every so often. It's stable, but isometric camera for mouse and keyboard shall never lose to controller.

I did find the battle system somewhat enjoyable, but it also felt worse than some of its contemporaries, despite this, there is fun to be had if you’re patient and understanding of Triangle Strategy’s limitations. _childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic.The game does have a phasing problem, specially notorious at the start of the story, but as you continue through it, it gets more balanced between story/gameplay. So if you are not a fan of story driven games, I would recommend skipping this one.With that in mind, the game manages to balance out combat in a very positive way. _childDocuments_.review: RECOMMEND, especially on discountI go for true ending on 1st playthrough.HD-2D is really great for combining beautiful pixelart and lowpoly model.It let players fill some gap with imagination, and space better with 3d environment.Music is simply awesome. Fits the mood and theme.Final Fantasy Tactics, with some tweaks. Mostly go for easy approach.For RPG parts, there's no job/class, just purely level up and skill tree. Simplified a lot.The battle core is mostly the same.- Terrain has height difference- Units take actions based on speed- When action ends, Units have faced direction.- Backstab deal more damage.I think what changes most are1. Use TP instead of MP2. Unit can start a follow-up attack to adjacent surrounded foe.TP is pretty straight forward. It's basically action points. I think this is for balancing and avoid spamming.Follow-up attack is really good design. This make melee units have a upper hand in close quarters.Usually JRPG go "Lv1 help cat; Lv99 kill God" route. But Triangle Strategy is not one of them.The story is focus on Salt - basic need, and greed, betrayal, war caused by it.Our House is one within the flow. Trying to survive first then thrive if we're allow to.In short, a political drama.Problems, difficulties, and events are treated quite seriously, feeling they'll happen in the real world.Might be still Anime in some ways, but Triangle Strategy is really a good work.Triangle Strategy is a decent Tactics game with good believable storylineRECOMMEND.

_childDocuments_.review: Triangle Strategy is one of the best modern strategy JRPGs I have played. In a similar vein to Final Fantasy Tactics, but with a lot of modern UI and fully voiced dialog cut scenes. I have seen people complain about the story being long winded and there is a lot of story in between combat. That being said it is a well done story that I enjoyed. There are choices that impacted the story itself and various endings to check out. I think the best part of the game is the combat. You get plenty of characters and can build different strategies based on the units you want to use. I love how they handle leveling. Strategy RPGs often struggle with balancing a level system. Triangle Strategy has mock battles you can use to level which helps. If you use a character that is underleveled they will level up very quickly. This design encourages you to experiment with different team members and doesn't punish you for changing your team. There is no permadeath if a unit goes down. Some might dislike this, but I think it allows for players to accept their mistake and continue without undoing that mistake.Overall, I highly recommend this game. It has a well written story. It has fun and engaging combat. It has different routes for replayability. It has a new game + to keep all your stuff for a second playthrough. It's an impressive game for people with want to play a strategy JRPG.

_childDocuments_.review: While you may be spending a lot of time reading through long cutscenes (par for the course for RPG's) the story and characters are gripping enough to allow you some respite from the heat of battle. It takes place on the land of Narzalia where three nations break their 30 year peace to fight over precious salt. Yeah, I didn't know how scarce salt was in medieval times, or how important it was to the human diet, but this story really emphasizes its importance to our survival.Amidst all the political intrigue and military warfare are characters I grew to love rather quickly. They're all unique and have their own unique-ish personalities. Most characters are one note in terms of the supporting characters and villains, but the main MAIN characters have very interesting emotional drama and philosophical convictions.This is where I think the story shines: in its CHOICES it gives you in dialogue because each choice you make aligns your main character Serenoa to one of the convictions of the three important allies he has. Roland, Frederica, and Benedict all have differing convictions and suggestions on how you proceed in certain story spots, and the writers did a good job forcing you to weigh out the cost of your actions.I believe there's 7 endings including one bad one I got, so hey five more to go! This game can be beaten in 30-40 hours depending how much you retry battles, but imho the story is good enough that I'd want to experience it and its branching paths again at least once or twice a year to clear out as much as I can in the years to come.I was initially interested in this game because I loved Final Fantasy Tactics as a kid and having just beaten Octopath Traveler a couple weeks ago. So to have a tactics game with the same HD 2.5D graphics as OT I was intrigued.For the most part it's a decent strategy game. You have different characters that fill different roles and their unique abilities compliment each other. Each character class is locked to the character so there's no job switching. There's cool things you can do like pincer attacking enemies allows an ally to attack with you for extra damage when it's not even their turn yet.However, there are a few missteps that I didn't like in the combat and that's the TP system. You need TP to do certain abilities and it's tiresome for some characters like mages to not have any TP on a turn, thus not being able to cast a spell. While you can obviously attack and use items without TP, the fact that you only get one TP a turn means a lot of characters do a whole lot of nothing for a long time until they have enough to cast useful spells for your party. I found this pretty tedious and wish there was a better system. It only kind of helps when you have JUST A FEW characters that allow quicker replenishment of it, but otherwise very tedious.Also tedious is the upgrading system where you upgrade your party's weapons with a mixture of different crafting materials. Each character's set of materials needed for upgrades are somewhat different from each other and it's tedious trying to manage this. I found myself sprinting back and forth between two shops, one to buy materials from and the blacksmith to use those materials with. It felt unintuitive, but I got used to it eventually because I desparately wanted the meager upgrades they allowed.It's so weird that for most modern games, I hate how there's so many damn cutscenes all the time and I just wanna play the game. It was ALMOST opposite for this game where I just wanted to get through the battles so I can advance in the story lol. I still enjoyed battles for the most part, and while every battle is story locked, you can do optional mental mock battles on the side if you need to grind for EXP and upgrade materials.PHENOMENAL SOUNDTRACK!!! Wish there was a way to buy and download the full thing.New meets old, what else can I say? Sprites look cool, battle animations for special skills add a nice touch, and there are even some really cool sprite animations for cutscenes that keep them from being stagnant scenes with sprites just standing around doing nothing while text boxes fly around the screen.I loved the story and the decisions they force you to choose between, the way the party's kinship evolves throughout the story, and really loved the plot twists that come near the end and AT the end, at least the one I got.Gameplay is mostly nice but is held back by a system that forces you to waste turns and that's no good considering how long battles are due to the huge enemy count. But otherwise, it's almost as serviceable as FFT despite this.The music and the overall presentation is epic and beautiful and I cannot wait to try and get another ending now that I've unlocked New Game+ .

_childDocuments_.review: I love the concept but the default PC keyboard controls are terrible and of the 0.8 hours I spent in game, 90% of that was spent skipping through dialogue. If I had listened to all the dialogue it probably would've been around 2-3 hours. I had the opportunity to play one actual mission. If you buy this, you should expect a visual novel rather than a turn-based-tactics game. The authors clearly intended this as a visual novel with gameplay elements for flavor but that doesn't come across in the description.

_childDocuments_.review: As my first tactics game, I loved it. I played on Easy because I just wanted to enjoy the story. I love the quality of life feature of keeping all EXP you earn during a fight if you game over. The various ways that the different characters can interact with each map was really cool. Granted, some characters were more useful than others (at least it seemed that way to my TRPG non-experienced eyes), but all of the characters were interesting and lovable in their own ways. The Scales of Conviction mechanic was really cool, as well: trying to figure out how to game the game by choosing which dialog option you think the character would want to hear to convince them to take your side. But sometimes you can't convince enough party members to do what you want, and you have to choose what the majority of the party chooses. Really cool. Definitely recommend, especially on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Benedict, get the scales!So far I've come close to finishing the first path for Triangle Strategy and I have a pretty good understanding of the game. I purposely have played blind the first go through and it wasn't until the game told me I was in an "important no going back turning point" for myself that I decided to do some more research. This is a really great game for anyone looking for a story driven RPG, especially if you're interested in political conflict and hard hitting decisions. Most of the decisions you make are essentially (or how it feels) to be either choosing the bad or the worse. There are four routes that I am aware of that you can end. Three of which are considered "bad" ends while there is a Golden Route that you receive if you make all the right choices. (my people outright refused me in the beginning so I didn't even have a chance!) Which is a really interesting concept. While this is a tactile strategy, similar to Fire Emblem, it's strength lies in the unique decision making between you and the people surrounding you. You need to have the right conviction to persuade them to the route you want, otherwise they may not listen and choose something else entirely. It's interesting and I like it, until my group ignores me. I can't think of another game that does something like this. This is very, very story heavy and is more aligned with individuals willing to put in the time and effort to get these different outcomes. I enjoy it very much. The characters are interesting, though most are not THAT memorable. The biggest takeaway is the push and pull of information from the decisions you make. You think you're doing the right thing but then BAM the plot tells you otherwise. I like that in a story. So, if you're interested in a RPG with great storytelling prowess (not much romance) then play it! I'll finish up my first ending (backing Benedict) and I'll probably look into the Golden Route next.

_childDocuments_.review: I had been waiting for this game to release ever since I played the demo last year. TRPGs (Tactical Roleplaying Games) with a fantasy theme are my absolute favorite genres of video games. The first one I ever played was Ogre Battle 64, then I played Fire Emblem: The Blazing Sword for GBA (Gameboy Advance), Final Fantasy Tactics Advance and Valkyrie Profile II: Silmeria. I got this game on sale and I'm glad I did because . The replay-ability value of this game is too low. The plot-line is interesting and the lore is original, but the dialogue is poorly written. The game is also too short. If I compare this game to Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together, I would say that , in all areas. However, I have higher standards for JRPGs because I have played so many of them. This game is fun and the graphics are beautiful, but there is too much left to be desired. I want more character customization and better character design. I also want access to generic units, a better skill-tree system and a branching class-tree. Finally, I need more chapters. Again, this game is way too short for $80. I would charge $45 at the most.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game. Reminiscent of FFT, but clearly divergent in a few areas. You end up with a party of characters with their own unique aptitudes, synergies, and stories.It took me two play-throughs to get the ending I wanted, and I enjoyed every minute of it.

_childDocuments_.review: IMPORTANT: Make sure you set the voices to Japanese. The English voice acting is horrific and completely amateurish, while the Japanese cast are actual professionals from other games and anime. Trust me, it makes the game so much better to NOT hear the garbage English cast.Anyways. Phenomenal. 9/10. The writing is genuinely incredible, which was totally unexpected. I went in expecting fun FFT gameplay with a passable story, and what I got instead was an outstanding story with superlative gameplay. I really can't stress enough just how good the writing in this game is. The writer, Naoki Yamamoto, is truly talented. The man knows how to write interesting, complex characters and to thread them along an intricate plot with a soaring, operatic payoff.Yes, the gameplay is good too. It's Final Fantasy Tactics but with a better story. The fights are challenging and tuned well. Each character has their own unique set of abilities and upgrades. None of them feels redundant, and most of them are useful. I don't feel like writing anymore, because I'm tired. I'll just say, though, that this is a story all about how my life got flipped, turned upside down, and I'd like to take a minute, just sit right there, I'll tell you how I became the prince of a town called Bel-Air. In West Philadelphia, born and raised, on the playground is where I spent most of my days. Chillin' out, maxin', relaxin' all cool, and all shootin' some b-ball outside of the school. When a couple of guys who were up to no good, started making trouble in my neighborhood. I got in one little fight and my mom got scared, she said, "You're movin' with your auntie and uncle in Bel-Air." I whistled for a cab and when it came near, the license plate said "FRESH" and it had dice in the mirror. If anything, I could say that this cab was rare, but I thought, "Nah, forget it, yo, home to Bel-Air!" I pulled up to the house about seven or eight, and I yelled to the cabbie, "Yo homes, smell ya later!" Looked at my kingdom, I was finally there, to sit on my throne as the Prince of Bel-Air.

_childDocuments_.review: Not worth $60 unless you enjoy being talked at endlessly.This review is a rambling mess. But it's hard to feel bad about that when this game is also a rambling mess.The first problem with this game is its AAA price tag and sub 20-hour play time. You barely touch the unit upgrades and promotions before the game ends. And no, it's not fun enough to replay however many NG+ repetitions that would require. The game was also (apparently) shortened by being denied the "good" ending (more on that later).I can't remember the last time I was asked to pay $60US for a game with this little actual playing. Instead, what you get is MANY hours of very tedious dialogue, most of which is carefully calculated to take as long as possible. Long-winded dialogue, all of which are (for reasons I don't understand) fully voice acted, pad the game out to possibly much more, but I simply could not handle the writing after a certain point.My second big problem is the unit lineup. I've got about 20 now, and there are three actual soldiers that can fight toe-to-toe. With really, anything. You're forced to cobble together your army out of a huge array of goofy support units, which might be an interesting challenge except that so many of them are just objectively bad. The pattern I followed, at least on hard battles, was something like this:Play the stage with whoever needs experience, which is usually the crappy characters. Lose because, well, I'm playing with crappy characters. Rotate through the characters that are behind and repeat losing until those characters have leveled up. Now play with a team of my own choosing, and win, putting the winners ahead (by dint of going through the whole battle) so that I have to repeat the process the next stage.These support units vary from a merchant with no real attack and what feels like about a 5% chance to briefly charm an enemy to a healer whose only ability to actually heal is by using your consumables at double the usual speed. So you have to take your ONE dedicated healer every time, your ONE melee unit, and for most of the game, ONE ranged unit in order to win if you're playing a hard level. The mounted healer who can't heal herself, the glass-jawed lancer, and the pointless tactician unit are often benched except when you must level them. Finally, and this was what sealed my review as negative, I don't appreciate ending lockouts based on things I have no control over. In one battle, an enemy pushed one of my units into a statue, breaking it and starting a fire. This turns out to be the reason I was denied the "good" ending for the game. Furthermore, even if I had chosen to burn a house down to win the battle (as it happens all it did was burn a house down, nobody was even in the target area), I'm pretty pissed to have the game harp on using this feature, explain how to use this feature, the little in-game videos to help you see how it will work, the characters giving you advice on when to use it -- and then finally punishing you for... using it. As you are told MANY times you should. But it might make a baby cry, so no good ending for you. Sure, she'll be alive, but FEELINGS.And no, the game isn't good enough to replay for the other endings. Besides, even if I follow a guide the second time around, I don't trust it not to catch me on some other bit of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
_childDocuments_.name: TRIANGLE STRATEGY

_childDocuments_.review: Triangle Strategy, though lacking for a better name, is a very good attempt to catch the same lightning in a bottle as its spiritual predecessor Final Fantasy Tactics. The gameplay is very similar, the core cast of characters is relatively fleshed out, and I came back wanting to explore options that I had previously declined in favor of others. Though it's ambiguous what the "Triangle" in Triangle Strategy actually refers to (is it the nations? The 3 possible virtues to follow? The 3 "main" endings you get if you don't find the secret one?), it's aptly named, as there are plenty of triangles to speak of, and just as much if not more strategy. I will say I was surprised for a Square Enix game how low fantasy this game is, with little magic or gods to speak of outside a few recruitable mages, rideable falcons and an endgame boss, but what it lacks in magic it makes up for in political intrigue, and weighing the various options for storylines to follow depending on where you find yourself, carefully considering the welfare of your party just as much as the welfare of the continent. Altogether a pretty good game, would recommend for any tactical RPG fans.
_childDocuments_.name: TRIANGLE STRATEGY

_childDocuments_.review: The main question people will have is will this game fill the final fantasy tactic void. The only answer i can give you is absolutely! If you have played final fantasy tactics then you have basically already played this game. While it doesn't have  a job system like final fantasy tactics you still have a class system where over time you will promote your class to a higher rank unlocking more abilities to use. On top of that instead of your tradition weapons each character is equiped with a set one throughout the entire game. Eventually you will upgrade to unlock more stat or ability boosting skills. The world map exploration ... isn't great it's more of a streamlined point a to point b type thing you follow a set path that game has pre determined and thats it. You can't visit other towns or previous areas you've been to. You can venture off to side points every now and then and uncover more of the plot and there are also character stories to uncover. But it's not as indepth . So thats a bit of a let down. The sound track is fantastic it sets the mood of the plot really well. Speaking of the plot you are basically fighting for salt... It's interesting at times and the normal square enix stuff is here  character betrayels and  what the hell moments. Theres not much else i can say about it really.  As for the voice acting that seems to be the main talking point of this game. It really isn't all that bad. Some characters could use a little more enthusiasm as some seem like there simply reading the script. Other then that it's passable If you have been wanting a tactics game from square enix for awhile now then this will certainly fill that void.
_childDocuments_.name: TRIANGLE STRATEGY

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very good SRPG, just don't go in expecting FFT or TO: LUCT. The story never reaches the highs of those games but the gameplay is great. FFT and TO let you run wild with the customization, which, while fun, allows you to break the game into pieces. Triangle Strategy offers a more streamlined approach, where every character fills their own niche and party composition should vary dramatically by map (instead of say, deploying TG Cid/Agrias or Canopus & 10000 archers every chance you get).The worst part of the game is the pacing, especially in the beginning, but if you can push past it, it's worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: TRIANGLE STRATEGY

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but it just has too many flaws. First, the game is extremely linear; no subquests nor optional missions, which were a very fun component of others that defined the genre like Final Fantasy Tactics and Advance Wars. Second, the game has multiple endings, one of which has such specific requirements that the vast majority of players will never find it without a guide. Third, the class/job upgrades are locked behind story progression, which is frustrating. Fourth, each character has a linear class/job upgrade path with no real customization in your choices; to be fair, there are skill trees that allow for some customization, but it's not very in depth.The graphics are nice and voice actor is decent.

_childDocuments_.review: Every character has its own unique class and abilities. There is no job swapping but you do get to choose which units you want to spend resources on upgrading. The only equipment slots are 2 accessory slots and good accessories are extremely rare so there aren't many customization options here either. The game really wants you to spend time focusing on the initial toolkits of each character and how they interact with one another instead of on tinkering with your roster between battles.There are 4 different difficulty options to choose from and the AI can be fairly ruthless on Normal at exploiting your vulnerabilities if you over-extend yourself. In Newgame+, the enemies scale with you so every battle still remains a challenge.5/5 with 2D-HD.4/5 here with good variety.4/5. This would be 4.5/5 but Serenoa's voice actor slurs half of their battle lines as if they were drunk or something.4/5. They did a good job here with the story but you need to do 4 playthroughs if you want to obtain an ending that you can be happy with. This requires 100+ hours of play to accomplish so not every player is down for this undertaking. A guide is practically required as well because there is no way to modify your story choices after the fact and you'll have to wait until newgame+.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ll try to keep it bullet point for easy reading:1-50% of the game is passed watching cut scenes and dialogue and not playing the character you so desperately tried to level.2-You cannot ‘out-level’ the story by training (mock battle) because of the way the exp system works.3-Training in the mock battle system take a horrendous amount of time just for your ‘main’ party, so unless you are massively dedicated and love repetitive empty mock battle, then you will not be able to level up other character too.4-Upgrade resources are scarce, but there shouldn’t be any issue for your main party. However, same logic in (3) for level applies here for upgrade resources.5- While all character are unique, the characters are far from balance to one-another and there is clearly S-Tier rank character.6-Main story encounter are design to always overwhelmed you and unless you bring your main S-tier fully leveled/upgraded party to the encounter, you’ll most likely get crush (unless you play on Very Easy)7-All of the above mean, you will most likely not touched 2/3 of the characters, which is a shame given they put energy into creating them.All that being said, I feel like the game was hyped by paid Streamer and Youtuber. Comparing this to FFTA or Ogre Battle/Octopath Traveler game style, is in my opinion an insult to these games. Also selling this as a AAA game is mind boggling. I expected way more from the price range.

_childDocuments_.review: Editing for a more nuanced take: Yes, you can tell a lot of love and thought went into this "game". I still cannot recommend buying it if you are looking for an FF Tactics style GAME. It's more or less just an interactive "Choose Your Own Adventure" story/political debate class simulator.My first play through took about 25 hours, and - not exaggerating - less than half of that was actual game play; that 25 hour mark includes me getting bored and fast forwarding through most of the dialogue for the second half of the game because there is just a ridiculous amount. For comparison, my first New Game+ play through, skipping all cut scenes, took less than 10 hours.My total played time is for 4 routes, so I will give them credit for making me OCD about checking off all of the various characters and endings. Unfortunately, that's the only draw. The "tactical" battles are quite shallow and only require a little bit of strategy for a couple of very specific encounters on Hard mode, and the most interesting combat decisions you'll ever make only has to do with one very specific ending, where you split up your characters into 3 teams. Otherwise, only buy this if your enjoyment comes from the branching stories and having to persuade your party into going along with your decisions.
_childDocuments_.name: TRIANGLE STRATEGY

_childDocuments_.review: What I thought I was getting: Final Fantasy Tactics  / Tactics Ogre: LUCT successorWhat I got: An uninspired and frankly derivative graphic fantasy novel with some "tactical" fights interspersed.The game is too on-rails and there's too much exposition for my taste. I should have more seriously considered the reviews before I bought this. People can say what they want about character composition and strategy, it's there in form only,  not in function. You can win any fight in this game with literally any composition. There's no customization, there's no challenge and there's very little fighting to begin with. If you consider a spectrum of tactics games with something like Disgea being one extreme then this game is in the opposite extreme.

_childDocuments_.review: The game does everything in its power to slow the pace down to a crawl. The title cards fades after like 2 seconds, the "..." character speaks takes about 3 seconds. Characters talks infuriating slow. It gets really annoyed combining them with endless cut-scenes. I played for 5 hours and I had like 3 fights.It would be tolerable if the story is good, or funny, or bad in an interesting way. Instead this is one of the most bland story I've ever seen. Characters are boring and devoid of personality, I truly do not care about them. There are also no foreshadowing or  hooks that make you curious about the ending. Dialogues are also just not interesting. I don't know if I can come up with more variations or "boring" or "not interesting" so I am just going to stop talking about the story and characters.The combat is actually good, but anything outside of combat is bad. I usually plays the game for its story, but this is the first game I actively fast-forward every dialogue just so I don't fall asleep. Apparently there are more combats after chapter 4, so if you are willing to endure 4 to 5 hours of boredom maybe this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, I've had this Final Fantasy Tactics itch that has needed scratching since about 1998.  I figured, same company, same game play, what could go wrong?Well....  First, The story.  Not to say the story is BAD, it's just pointless and there's SO much of it.  Pretty early on, you get the idea that you're just clicking through an animated novel and not really playing a game.  But you do it anyway because you'd think that with such a ponderous story in place, each battle must feel super-justified and organic.  Like when the enemies finally DO show and they let you do stuff you have a very clear sense of why and the battle is that much more poignant.  Nope.  Had a friend act as a control and replayed the first 6 hours while skipping everything and he got just as much out of it.  If you are a human over the age  of 14 or have ever played a video game before, you glean enough of the story from the unskippable cutscenes to know what's going on without having it spoon fed to you.Second.  How are the graphics WORSE?!  Seriously, find a 1997 screengrab of FFT on PS1 and compare.  I understand this is supposed to be retro, but seriously, spend some money on the art department.Third.  No customization of your party.  Each recruitable character has their own archetype and can be upgraded only along those lines.  They get stronger of course, but they never really change their role.  You want two swordsmen on your front line backed by fire mages?  Well tough.  There's only one character each that does those things and you can't convert another character's class to do it for you.Fourth.  For a tactics game, it is seriously lacking in tactics.  It is LAUGHABLY easy on their "hard" mode, and they seem to have forgotten to program in the most basic tactic into the game of "place a bunch of your tanky units in a wall and put the weaker ones behind".  If you DO set up such a wall, the front-line enemies on their turn just walk right though your ranks as if to say "scuse' me imma just skooch by" and go his your healer (your ONLY healer) in the face.  So no body blocking or object permanence.  Therefore every fight is just the same "Advance and hit before they can" test.  You ALSO have to rely on their built in back-attack and combo attack system.  Without it, fights are impossible.  With it, fights barely last long enough to be considered fights.I'm going to finish the whole game out.  But only because it's too late to get a refund.  I'll drudge through it somehow and if I'm wrong I'll come back to change my review.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried, very hard, to like this game. 'Imagine its a parody!' I said to myself as I watched the confounding rubbish of a story unfold. But then it went on for so long that it became a parody of a parody, and I ended up skipping dialogues to not make my ears bleed. Mind you, the combat is fun. Simplistic, sure, in a very Square Enix kind of way where game design seem to be made by people who consider having backstab bonus damage be the height of complexity they can achieve, but at least its fun to play around with different units. I was especially happy seeing polearm units given their due, while they are literally *ahem* shafted in most games. But none of that saved the story. Maybe that's why they focus on Octopath games. Easier to write eight separate stories and have characters completely ignore each others' existence than to write a single multi-dependant plot where characters actually interact (gasp!) with each other.

_childDocuments_.review: Production quality is mostly top notch. Soundtrack slaps, and even if you're not into the pixel art style, it's still hard to deny the work that went into crafting the visuals. Only drawback is the voice acting, which is so bad that I had to mute the dialogue. I have literally never done that before with any type of media.The story and writing is mixed. The main character's motivations and relationships feel real and pretty relatable, but the actual world itself is flawed. There are some problematic tropes, eg. white Anglo people with high morals are persecuted by aggressive, militaristic Slavic people and dark-skinned, slave-keeping desert-dwellers. Doesn't make for super engaging worldbuilding.Despite this, I didn't find the long story cutscenes overbearing, they were mostly character-focused which helped, and you can always skip them if you don't care. It gave some respite after battles.These were challenging enough for me on the Normal difficulty setting. I've seen some complaints about grinding, but I found doing the repeatable 'practice battles' just once as they were unlocked gave me more than enough XP and resources. The core gameplay is fun - pretty much every character feels unique, and the larger battles give a huge amount of options with how you can approach the battle and the strengths and weaknesses you can exploit.The RPG mechanics are linear, however I found this refreshing. These games with huge rosters can get overwhelming with micromanagement of gear, skills, classes, etc. (Fire Emblem can get like this), but I feel like Triangle Strategy strikes a good balance having satisfying progression without overwhelming you with a mountain of micromanagement. Overall, fun gameplay loop that puts some genuinely interesting twists on an old formula. The story and writing have weaknesses, but that can be put to the side if you just want a fun and streamlined tactical RPG.

_childDocuments_.review: Triangle Strategy is one of the most interesting tactics games I've played over the past few decades. On one hand, it has one of the most dynamic and detailed branching story compositions I've ever seen put into a game. While there are, out of necessity, mandatory re-convergence points as the story goes on, the game nevertheless feels quite uncertain in your first go-round. With a rather mature storyline uncharacteristic of most games, there are many twists and turns which keep the story interesting from start to finish...and believe you me, this game is half narrative, half game. Given that the story manages to be interesting this generally doesn't hurt, but it definitely may put off those who shy away from heavy narrative.Unfortunately, the story in Triangle Strategy -- being far more core than in almost any other title I've played -- is not really all that good. It is interesting, sure, and it keeps your attention cleanly...but it's just a bit of an incoherent mess. The entire world built around this triadic "salt, food, and iron" tension between the nation states really makes no sense given that they'd all die if they did nothing but fight in such scenarios, and for a "low-fantasy" world that pushes a generally anti-religion narrative and is all about rationalism we somehow have magic floating around and weird other things that I will refrain from commenting on due to spoiling. Worse yet, the characters in the story seem composed entirely outside of the actual story. Despite your core set of characters being reasonable, most of your ensemble are the Clown Brigade (one quite literally an 8 year old clown...) with horrifically boring and meaningless backstory-things that don't make any sense. You have barkeeps, ultra-agile grandmas, physic toddlers, and assassin strippers all running around to aid your noble house in a Game of Thrones-esque bout of political intrigue. Even the main characters are all super tropey sans Serenoa who salvages the team by coming across as one of the strongest male leads I've seen in gaming. In a way it reminds me a lot of Fell Seal -- a generally interesting narrative flopped around by poorly-written characters and a bland and mediocre world.Fortunately the gameplay is such that, on your first run through on Hard, this title will given genre veterans a run for their money on difficulty. Before acquiring your full cast of characters and filling out your full toolkit, most missions on your first playthrough will be rough and tumble. The game does not have permadeath, and with good reason; some of the hardest missions will see you with 1 or 2 of your characters barely scraping out your victory. This balances the 50/50 split between gameplay and narrative well, as the gameplay itself is actually enjoyable. On subsequent playthroughs most of the dialogue and story can be skipped, and there is enough meat-and-potatoes variability with the branching story that New Game+ is enjoyable. The bad part is the game has many things which can be permanently missed in a run, and using a guide is almost mandatory if you want to avoid having to do extra playthroughs. Poor planning on my part resulted in the need for 6 runs to 100% the game where, if you do it "correctly" you will only need 4. That said, with powering through the story and knowing what to do, future runs can be trimmed substantially...and the 5th run I did to get some "oops" stuff for 100% achievements I was able to power through in about 3-4 hours.The game has several endings, one of which requires you to do a silly level of "optimal run." All are interesting, though the secret "true ending" was a bit of letdown as it's essentially just the other 3 endings combined into one with some plot shuffling to make it all coherent. The difficulty curve kept it interesting at first, but by the end of final run for 100% completion I was ready to be done. Each character has a lot of individual depth and uniqueness to their use, and yet running a circus is a bit offputting and ultimately individual character toolkits are rather one-dimensional with only a few rare exceptions.While I generally recommend Triangle Strategy, its generally bland narrative and somewhat simplistic tactical depth, even if well-balanced and challenging, do not make it overly memorable. The Ogre Battle style tactical variation of Symphony of War felt far more satisfying with a similar level of difficulty on the hardest settings, and the character building depth and enemy permutations of Fell Seal felt every bit as frustrating and challenging as Triangle Strategy with a lot more mechanics to toy with on the back end. Likewise, narratively the game is somewhere in the solid B range of performance, leaving many of the older titles like Ogre Battle 64 and Final Fantasy Tactics still reigning supreme as narrative giants with serious undertones. Certainly a solid title and an enjoyable pickup for genre vets, but definitely worth forgoing at full price and waiting until it has a reasonable sale. While the narrative composition of this game no doubt cost a fortune to make, it does not justify the large price tag when coupled with the simplistic gameplay loop.Still, it's nice to see a AAA title actually deliver for once. AAA has become such garbage that I generally steer well clear, especially with Square Enix and their volatile quality as a publisher.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved this. I'm making a major decision and even if I picked the right dialogue choices to "convince" the character to vote my way. If my stats in morality aren't high enough through the previous choices chosen, then they just vote for the unfavorable option. This vote system is a very bad game design, where choices are made for you and the consequences live as you continue the story. Character blames you for your decision that you had no control over.
