_childDocuments_.review: Solar Ash is a stylish, enjoyable experience. I came to it hoping for the smooth controls of a game like The Pathless, and while it does feel very smooth when you're getting things right, getting hit (especially during bosses) is harsh... but that's not a bad thing. I just needed to adjust my expectations, and realise that some sections are more like a time trial. Solar Ash is not a punishing game - with few exceptions it's very quick to restart when you die, and there are always shields around - so it wasn't too hard to change my approach to match it. There's plenty of incentive to explore every corner of the world, and it's a beautiful world as well, even (or especially) when it makes little physical sense. If you enjoy games with some active challenge to them but where you can also take your time and explore, Solar Ash is a good contender.If there is one thing I didn't enjoy about Solar Ash, it's the direction the story takes in the latter half, especially the main character. _childDocuments_.review: Heart Machine's first game, Hyper Light Drifter, was one of my favourite games of all time. Their second game, Solar Ash, therefore had some big shoes to fill.If you're going in expecting Solar Ash to be HLD 2 then you are going to be disappointed; while the visuals, music and narrative all feel the same (and are set within the same universe) they are completely different in their focus.If Hyper Light Drifter was a Hack and Slash Zelda-like with a focus on combat encounters then Solar Ash is more of a Momentum platformer with level design in the vein of Super Mario Galaxy and bosses reminiscent of Shadow of the Colossus. They both have that neon-psychedelic art style and hidden collectibles with a focus on isolation and exploring a dead world but that's about all they have in common.Solar Ash also reminds me of another game Annapurna Interactive published called 'The Pathless' which is probably the closest game I can compare it to from a gameplay perspective. You explore a zone, completing skill challenges to eventually awaken and confront the boss of that zone before going onto the next location. Unlike HLD and The Pathless, you start the game with all of your abilities from the very start, the only thing that adds to the learning curve are the platforming obstacles you encounter as you explore each zone. While platforming is this game's speciality, combat is not. You can make a three-hit combo on enemies and that is basically it, most enemies die relatively quickly anyway and are therefore not a real threat to your progress as the auto-save points are fairly common and consistent across the game world.Solar Ash has a more clearly defined plot in comparison to Drifter, from the beginning you are told what the stakes are, you learn quickly what the gameplay loop will consist of and you go on your merry way to explore and kill giants. There are notes and audio logs that flesh out this world and the few NPC side quests that there are were introduced in a fairly straightforward manner that made me compelled to complete them and see where their stories went and how it tied to the theme of the larger plot. In terms of gameplay length, it is relatively short as I completed my first play-through around 10 hours and 40 minutes (which included secret hunting for all collectibles and side-quests) while there is an achievement if you complete the game within 3 hours.Overall I'd recommend Solar Ash if you want an atmospheric platformer with tight controls and a surreal gravity defying world which really goes all out by the later levels. The plot was solid enough to support the gameplay but if you're not a fan of 3rd person platformers or want a more hack and slash style game in comparison to its predecessor I don't think I can recommend for you.If you accept Solar Ash on its own terms as an exploration based platformer then you'll most likely enjoy the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: If you are looking for a game like Hyper Light Drifter here, which I wouldn't blame you for considering it's made by the same dev team, then you'll probably come out of the experience dissapointed. The game is really great though, so I suggest you still give it a try even if it isn't normally your cup of teaWith that out of the way, this game is absolutely gorgeous. Its visuals feel like a natural evolution of Hyper Light's artstyle into 3D, with a vibrant saturated color palette and even more dreamy landscapes than everThe gameplay is a bit of a mix of things, but I see most people call it a combination of Shadow of the Colossus and a 3D sonic game. There's definitely an emphasis on speed, and it didn't take me long before I got into the game's rhythm with skating boosting and grindingCombat is minimal, as enemies are more like obstacles than full-on encounters. The main focus is definitely on platforming, with the main objectives being time trial challenges in each of the game's areas that, when all taken out, unlock the area's boss. Said bosses are definitely where the SotC comparisons stem from, but I won't spoil too much about them besides thatAll in all, while I don't think of this game as highly as HLD, it's still a great experience that I don't regret having, and seeing Heart Machine nail their first 3D game this well makes me really excited for how Hyper Light Breaker is going to turn out

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely beautiful and incredibly fun gameThe gameplay has a few issues, most being about the camera (Camera getting too close, or not rotating as you'd want it to) but, overall just really fun. The combat is kept simple which ties in well with the movement so it's really fast n smooth, bosses might sound a bit plain, you have to head towards a sequence of points, but I enjoyed them so much. it's really satisfying performing a sequence well.The overall difficulty is very good. There are 3 initial difficulties, which only affect the time to perform a sequence (which IMO is fine), and a hardcore difficulty which unlocks after beating the game once.The easiest difficulty doesn't really take away from the sequence experience, it's still a lot of fun, without it being challenging.The hardcore difficulty however, I found pretty hard. I can see how some people at that point would say its repetitive, as it took me quite a lot of tries for some sequences to beat but, that wasn't an issue with me. So, the hardcore difficulty can be quite a challenge and adds to that satisfaction when you finish a sequence.Overall exploration is just bliss. the map design is done wonderfully and the visuals are just amazing.I love the characters, with their cool personalities and the lore around them, you really start to care for them. Coming from a massive Hyper Light Drifter fan, I was unsure about the voice acting, but now actually experiencing it, it's amazing, the voice acting is just superb.The story is so great, it still keeps a bit of that Hyper Light Drifter "vibe" which I love, it had me interested, had me trying to figure things out, honestly, it had me at the edge of my seat and it just ties everything together so well.The sound design is lovely, the OST by the amazing Disasterpeace, Troupe Gammage, Joel Corelitz and Sky Lu/Azuria Sky is absolutely banging, the UI is lovely, the UX is lovely, the animations are lovely, the enemy designs are lovely, the character designs are lovelyIt's just a really lovely game, a game that shows that games are art.Definitely a 10/10 in my book

_childDocuments_.review: I saw this game previewed during a showcase a while back, but then after that, never heard anything about it. It seems like this game definitely flew under the radar a bit, but despite that I was able to track it down on Steam and try it for myself. On paper, this game is a lot of fun and does a lot of things that are comparable to other games. You have very fluid, high-momentum movement akin to Sonic Adventure 2 or Jet Set Radio. The vibrant, colorful landscapes evoke a similar feeling to Journey. The rotating gravity feels similar to Super Mario Galaxy. And scaling the bodies of gigantic bosses feels like a throwback to Shadow of the Colossus. All of these elements combine to make a high-speed adventure where you blast over beautiful landscapes and explore areas from top to bottom... when it's at its best. That said, the game does have a few hiccups that hold it back a bit. Combat vs. normal enemies is very basic and can be a bit repetitive as you only have a single basic attack string to fend off enemies. This becomes more noticeable later in the game when enemies become tankier, and some enemies can be a chore to fight where it's easier to simply try to run past them.... Although you better be good at juking because their tracking can be insane at times. The bosses suffer from a bit of repetition as well, because as you climb all over them you have to hit a series of spots in a specific order, or they shake you off and you have to start the sequence over again. While it is fun to figure out each boss's sequence and they flow beautifully when you get it right, they don't really have a ton of replay value as you fight pretty much every boss in the exact same way. While they have varied designs and different sequences... I can't say any of the boss fights felt particularly memorable because they didn't really stand out much from each other in execution. The overall narrative has some issues. The story is... not great. Without spoiling things, it felt like the game was trying to go for something more profound than it actually was in practice, so the ending felt like something of a flat note. And sadly, this game has the issue of a main character who is too talkative. Not in the sense of narrative dialogue, but in the sense of "telling you a hint or even an outright solution before you get a chance to figure it out for yourself". By the end of the game, I really didn't fell anything for any of the characters, which was unfortunate. It felt like the story and characters needed more time to be fleshed out.Overall though, this game was a fun experience, albeit a short one. Despite being a bit repetitive and having a weak narrative, at its best Solar Ash has got great high-momentum gameplay in a beautiful world, with plenty of optional content to discover which augments your ability. That said though, you can blow through the main story in 6-7 hours, and you can probably grab all the optional content within 3 more hours at most. Normally I'm not one to really be too harsh on a game's playtime... But for $40, I can't say I feel like I fully got my money's worth. So while I absolutely recommend the game... I'd also recommend waiting for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Solar Ash is an action-adventure platformer where you play as Rei, a Voidrunner set on a mission to save her home planet from collision with the Ultravoid, which holds many challenges set in her path to attune and activate the Starseed, a device that has the potential to correct everything.At first I was put off from buying this game, the pricing was a little too steep for my worth (60 AUD), and it caused me to leave it on the dust-collecting shelf of my wishlist for a few months. After it went on a -25% sale, I convinced myself to give it a chance, considering I had been listening to the soundtrack through recommendations and was already a huge fan of Hyper Light Drifter. I am happy to say it surpassed all expectations and did not disappoint at all.From high octane combat and platforming to uncovering the many hidden secrets sprinkled throughout immersing kaleidoscopic regions, Solar Ash takes you by awe with each reveal, with music progressively soaring in at the right moments, putting you in a zen-like state as you skate around. The movement is super responsive and satisfying to pull off, with grapple and railgrind combos at the touch of your fingertips. If you enjoy a good story, it is well worth getting invested into the handful of quests and the main storyline provides to experience, with an ending I guarantee will be worth. It never feels like a grind to complete the quests either, as in all cases I found myself glad to have a reason to return to sections of the world just to experience them a few more times. I recommend playing with a controller for the best experience.Overall, it's a huge 10/10 from me, I can't wait to see what the team cooks up for Hyper Light Breaker, but I'm sure it will be nothing short of amazing. Play Solar Ash, it's really fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Conditionally, I'd say I recommend normal, and don't quite recommend challenging. General Pros:-stunning visuals-fun world to explore with some great little bits of lore to find. -great controls in the over world exploration. Feels very flowing and exciting to skate around fluffy feeling landscape-light changes to the mechanics as you progress keeps it fresh for playtimeCons (Dark Zone and Boss Fights):-core premise is to hit a consecutive set of flags in order until you reach the weakspot. This repeats around 3 times in boss fights. These can be lovely visual treats to climb around.-Hitting each flag reveals the next one though sometimes a few will be revealed at once. Key note: you have sometimes under a second to hit the next flag. -in many situations (especially in the latter half) there's not enough clarity in where you're going to need to go. Sometimes you can see clear lines leading to the next spot-to-hit-in-1.5-seconds, sometimes the next point is obscured and it can be torment to find as your camera controls whip around an edge looking for it. if you fail to hit the next step in time, it will force a reset of the fight Each time I hit one of these (and more of them showed up as the game got deeper), they grind the fight to a halt and really sour the experience. -final boss fight is completely filled with these, and forces a very janky 5 second jump before you can restart the fight. -speaking of jank, your character auto grabs goo stuff, and can clip off tiny bits of scenery. When combined with the lack of clarity, it can feel like your mucking slowly through each flag until you've memorized the route and all the ways it could randomly failTLDR: I like it, but I'd love to have a clearer picture of the route to take, and a little bit of work on tightening up some of the routes could go a long way.

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10, must playFantastic experience, very enjoyable movement with some depth that makes mastering it pretty satisfying near the end. Then make a new save file and try to speedrun or play on a harder difficulty, then when you get to the end again, choose the other option, it really compliments the experience.After beating Hardcore difficulty and getting the VoidSprinter achievement in the same run, I can easily say this game is a masterpiece. 9/10Only complaints are that difficulty is a little bit all over the place in Hardcore, some bosses are relatively super easy while others took me a little while. And for the  boss on Hardcore difficulty, the third section has a spot that's very janky and difficult to control your camera in with all the gravity switch-ups and the camera leashing and the super tight timing makes it frustrating at worst to get past, but luckily it's  so it's not a huge deal.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very conflicted on this one.On the one hand, I really, really wish I could recommend this game, because it has some gorgeous visuals and a really nice soundtrack.On the other hand, holy CRAP the technical state of this game is awful.For reference, my rig has an RTX 3080, a pretty high-end card, even if it's not state of the art or anything. It'll effortlessly handle nearly any game on the market at max settings, at 2k resolution and a smooth 60 on even the most demanding games. For games that have less going on visually, getting 120+ at 2k resolution is very consistent. This game, MOST of the time, isn't too different; I can easily hit 120-144 FPS most of the time. However, sometimes, seemingly at random, the game will suffer insanely massive slowdown, dropping to as low as 40 FPS in some cases. In other words, even if I was willing to settle for consistent 60 instead of trying to go for higher framerates, I wouldn't be able to.And the video options are so insanely limited that the only one that does anything for my framerate is "overall quality" which also does nearly nothing until I go for the lowest possible setting, which makes the game look terrible but does at least give me a significant amount of additional frames. So thanks for not giving me options, devs. And in addition to the random framerate losses, the game is just kind of stuttery in general, it often hitches and stutters around which is really irritating and makes the game much less fun to play.And like, besides the technical state, the game is actually pretty good? It's legitimately difficult for me to give an objective assessment of the game since the technical issues piss me off so much, but if it weren't for those I'm pretty sure I'd recommend this game. The story's a bit meh, and the bosses are kind of underwhelming, but the soundtrack's nice, the visuals are great, and the movement is pretty fun, if kind of simplistic, when the game isn't eatING MY INPUTS ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ WHY IS THE FRAMERATE SO- Well. Yeah. I'd have a lot nicer things to say if the game ran well, but it doesn't, so I'm really struggling to be fair here. And the combat's really underwhelming, too. Barely anything going on there.In all, Solar Ash is what I think is probably a good game, buried under technical problems so pervasive and severe that I cannot in good conscience recommend this to anyone else. If it weren't for the framerate, my assessment would likely be "It isn't anywhere near as good as Hyper Light Drifter, but it's still pretty fun in my view, so as long as you temper your expectations and acknowledge that combat will be kind of a slog I think it's worth a shot." But I'm not reviewing some hypothetical idealized version of the game, I'm reviewing the game I have. So my assessment is instead "Don't waste your money or your time on this game. Go buy Hyper Light Drifter instead; It plays better, runs better, looks better, and is all around the superior product in nearly every way."And that really does suck, because I genuinely wish I could be here, gushing about how they've done it again, how they've managed to top the masterpiece that is Hyper Light Drifter, and how all of you need to go and buy this RIGHT NOW! But I cannot, in good conscience, do that. I can't even tell you that hey, it may not be as good as Hyper Light Drifter, but it's still good in its own right. All I can tell you is to skip this one, and hope that they manage to get it together next time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game...ahh, what do I even say?1. Heaven above, this game is gorgeous! Your character looks straight out a sci-fi novel, but the contrast between your character and the environment never feels out of place. The clouds are fluffy, the world around you both fantastical and yet familiar. 2. The concept design is inventive, and the structures are beautifully crafted. 3. The sound design makes and ties everything together. Music is awesome, sfx is awesome, 10/10!4. The story definitely has a captivating draw, with some real world parallels that can be drawn out of it if you wish. Leaving the past behind, protecting what you have, etc. But ignoring that, it holds up as a tale of both desperation and hope. Courage and cowardliness. Cause and effect. Holding on and letting go.Gameplay:1. Once you figure out timing, it becomes smooth. I was able to start doing things first try after a while, which felt amazing. 2. Beware of vertigo! (but it's oh so cool) The first time gravity become interesting my mind couldn't keep up. But you get used to it, and it creates such a cool experience racing around the pillars of clouds, watching the world spin below or above you.3. Boost is very helpful in combat, as long as you keep an eye on where the edge is4. While nothing felt "hard", the challenge was there. Respawn points are placed excellently, so even though you might die once or twice...thrice, you don't have to plod your way back through the whole map to get back where you were.5. The rails are a bit tricky, needing to hit some of them just right, but again, with the respawn, it wasn't too bad if you missed.6. Also, those crystals do have a purpose (you'll understand if you play it)I 100% recommend this game. It combines exploration with combat, puzzles, and rich world building, all things I love. It's not a fps, but there is a decent amount of fighting. Its not just exploration, though you will be rewarded for doing so. Puzzles are a key part of the story. Everything is well balanced, in addition to being beautiful. All in all, a great experience!

_childDocuments_.review: Solar Ash has a movement system that looks as fun as it is to play, and that's the reason I was drawn to the game (along with highly enjoying Hyper Light Drifter and being curious about what came next for Heart Machine). Its environment is beautiful and the environmental storytelling naturally draws you in to explore the corners of its world and discover what you can.Positives:- I enjoyed a lot of the puzzles in this game; most of it IS environmental puzzles, sometimes with the pressure of enemies to defeat first, which doesn't take much - some dodging, mostly just mashing X / attack until they go down, and once you unlock the suit that restores shield upon killing an enemy you should never Game Over again.- The movement, once again, feels great. You can cover pretty long distances by ramping off of slopes and holding your double jump while you have momentum. Be warned it's kind of a finger buster if you're using a controller, as "skate" is bound to the left trigger and you're holding that pretty much the entire time if you GOTTA GO FAST.- The setting is thoughtfully imagined and rendered beautifully, enhanced by another banger from Disasterpiece. The music helps carry a lot of the high and low moments, but so too does the scenery. The Mirrorsea is a particular favorite and a treat for the eyes.Negatives:- In boss fights, there's a lot of fighting the camera due to the way that it attempts to auto-rotate with the terrain. This can cause collision in moments where it's crucial to reach the next beacon on the boss and can cause (what feel like) unwarranted resets of bosses that feel otherwise pretty straightforward. I never really felt like I was fighting the bosses, mostly fighting to keep the camera in place while I was tackling each boss.- There are some terrain pieces that cause Rei to just...freeze? Lock into place? I'm not really sure how to describe this, maybe terrain clipping, but I definitely got stuck and was hit by enemies due to bad terrain collision trapping the protagonist in odd places. This generally wasn't as big a problem, but can be frustrating if you need to get back to the point you were previously at in order to scout collectibles like plasma crystals, particularly around Ames' ship.I'd still recommend this game to people who enjoyed Hyper Light Drifter and/or want a platforming game with less emphasis on combat but like going fast and solving environmental puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: 1) Story: 4/5. The game does a good job of providing an initial basis for what you're doing, but then it's on you to interpret what's really going on through finding logs and dialogue with very sparse NPCs/characters. If you don't speak to anyone and don't bother finding the logs then you'll get a pretty bare bones story, but the game would also be pretty short at that point. However, regardless of that the main story of the main character has a really good twist, one that can be inferred probably halfway through. Reading the logs will help explain the main story of the mission more and what the twist is there, simply playing the game will help explain the main character's story more and what the twist is there. Also, reading all the lore and getting all the dialogue helps lend a sense of connection and universe continuity with Hyper Light Drifter for those that have played the game. Only downside to the story is that progression is executed in a formulaic way. Each zone involves going to a certain number of spots to awaken the boss, beat the boss, and move on.2) Characters: 4/5. There aren't many characters in this game, of course since it takes place within a black hole not much can survive there. The characters have a fair amount of depth outside the main character and are very distinct with different personalities, motivations, and looks. But, there's not much character growth and development outside the main character. The connection between the main character and the enigmatic, presumably main "antagonist" is what brings the intrigue, depth, and drive to move the story forward.3) Setting: 4/5. Each zone has it's own theme, but all were built from the same baseline. If you take the details out, each zone is a plethora of brown cliffs linked by poofy, foggy blue clouds you can skate across to get to and from. But, each zone does a great job of building upon that baseline to differentiate from one another. The details make the difference in helping one place feel like a city, another a volcano, another a village, and so on. Also, considering the setting is inside a black hole it is explained well in the game that the zones are just amalgamations of consumed worlds and civilizations which gives rise to the differences.4) Music: 5/5. The music in this game is very subtle, slow, ominous, and sci-fi which really supports the immersion in the setting. It does a great job of setting the mood as you explore ruins of consumed civilizations, and contest void creatures at the same time. There is no difference between world music and combat music, all is ambiance. The music never gets energetic, which normally I like faster beats for combat but it worked well here. The music does change when fighting bosses but it keeps the same themes I described above but only upped to another level, which I appreciated in keeping the theme and immersion.  5) Gameplay: 5/5. For a game about skating you sure do get to shmove very fast sometimes if you can keep it up. The movement, besides the story, is the main draw that kept making me come back. It's not very complicated, but the movement is super smooth and skating around (not at the speed of sound) made me somewhat feel like a space hedgehog. For a game where your controls are limited to skating, attacking, boosting, and shotlock from Birth By Sleep, it does a good job of introducing progression through the zones. For instance, your first zone introduces rails and new enemies, the second zone adds mines and new enemies, the third adds colored switches and new enemies, and so on. Every zone up to the end adds something new to make the new environment feel like it adds its own challenges. Even later zones build upon the mechanics added by earlier zones to make the exploration feel more holistic building upon your exposure over the game. Further, the bosses get their own attacks since each is different, but bosses attacking isn't that significant. Boss fights are equivalent to Shadow of the Colossus, except since this game is about speed skating, you fight them by speed skating on their bodies, sticking to them with grav boots of course. It's made even better that you need speed to beat them. Unlike SoC there isn't just a few weak spots you hit repeatedly until a titan is dead, in this game each boss has a multitude of weak points you need to hit in a chain in quick succession. Bonus points that each weak point chain you have to finish is different, you don't have to repeat the same chain like 3 times over to finish off a boss. All in all, this game has given me a new appreciation of speed skating ;)Overall then I guess this amounts to an 88% B+. A solid indie game worth playing. A bit over priced, I'd wait for a sale, like $25 would be good.

_childDocuments_.review: Not great. I do not recommend.a lot of repetition, and the game doesn't seem to lean in to the fun parts. I would want to be able to skate around and move across the whole map at speed, exploring and platforming. Instead the game brings you to a halt regularly, and uses boring boring grind rails to get you up or onto places it wants you to go. So you never get to experience the fun of movement.Also the boss and "mini-boss" encounters are very repetitive and rely heavily on this lock-on mechanic and a timer that turns the floor into lava.The lock-on mechanic zips you to the trigger objects when you're in range, but also brings you to a stop once you get there, so there's incentive to try skating to it yourself to keep your speed up and avoid lock-on. However, some of them you cannot do that, you won't make it, and it isn't obvious so you do trial and error to find out.Even more confusing, some trigger objects cannot be locked-onto at all and you wont be able to tell until you get close and the lock-on doesn't appear. No clue why they did that, it's very frustrating expecting a lock-on and not getting it.I also found the skating was not reliable, would get caught on bits of geometry. That can be fun when the challenge is skating well, but the game so rarely gives you that kind of focused transparent challenge. It usually relies on rails and lock-on. _childDocuments_.review: Solar Ash follows in the footsteps of Praey For the Gods in being a sub optimal, lesser clone of Shadow of the Colossus. My primary issues with the game boil down to one very explicit issue separated into several distinct factors. Fundamentally, the skating/movement sucks. But why it sucks is extremely complex. At its core, the issue is that is nigh impossible to tell whether the character is touching the ground or not. This by itself isn't a huge issue, but when all of your movement capabilities are dependent on whether you are in the air or not, and they themselves lock you out of certain inputs regardless of whether you are grounded; fuddling through this process is a massive pain that doesn't go away for the game's entire 8 hour runtime. The Booster Dash requires the player to be physically touching the ground in order to be used. Maybe this is a balancing thing, or maybe not, its not clear. But timing the dash to an invisible timer *in addition* to the grounded state, makes actually being able to hit a platform and Booster Dash off of it (which is necessary to make the extremely narrow timings of several boss phases) a pain in the ass. Combining both of these factors make the game feel extraordinarily non responsive, ESPECIALLY when you cannot actually tell when you are touching the ground. In many cases Rei is only touching the ground for a fifth of a second before the physics or velocity push her back off again by a fraction of a centimetre (thus removing the grounded state); if the timer does not reset in that time, or it resets milliseconds after your character leaves the safety of the ground (through absolutely zero fault of your own), it just feels like yelling at a drunk toddler who doesnt speak your language. Meanwhile the Timeslip (grapplehook) only works while in the air! Or to be more precise, you can PRESS the button while on the ground, but it cannot TARGET and actually fire it unless you're in the air! And it is also, inexplicably and for zero reason, is locked to a timer. Thankfully, this timer is actually visible unlike the booster shot and the grounded state, but when you are trying to make 1/10th of a second hairpin grapples, and you get locked out of the system for 3 seconds everytime, and you accidentally used it while grounded, you just die. The game has extremely narrow timer windows for jumps and not performing them within a specific window is death every single time.I dont mind either the Grapple or the Dash being locked to air or ground, the real core issue is not being able to tell, let alone control, whether you are actually on the ground or not. A huge "thump" noise and a shockwave whenever Rei touches (or leaves) the ground would be immensely useful for telling when these tools could be activated, or perhaps just a specific glowing light on her legs while she is grounded would make waves on the usability of the control set.

I understand that it's better if the player figures out a mechanic on their own. But this game failed on both counts, it over communicated some ideas and failed to communicate others. So in a way it had the worse of both worlds, it had immersion breaking tutorials, self dialogue and beacon icons in tandem with a messy and inconsistent mechanics system that itself was immersion breaking.To be honest I hated finishing this game. I kept hoping the game was short because I just wanted to finish it and move on.Dev's if you are reading this. Sorry if it came off as harsh. Just remember that a lot of people did enjoy it and I hope my feedback helped at least a little.What do I mean by inconsistent?* What can you skate on? Well almost everything works, but not ooze. Okay that's great. But also not mushrooms? or the bones of oozes?* What about climbing ooze? Well normally ooze won't let you let go unless you specifically press jump, which is great I like that. But if the ooze gets to small then nope. It lets you go.Here are a list of things that aren't communicated:* Ability to dash on the ooze (whilst climbing).* Enemies drop plasma* The mushrooms that when you hit them let you activate the rails/doors* The needles for ooze/bosses split. They should (IMO) have a different icon.Here is a list of things that are poorly communicated* Suits* The rail shrooms* Rail flowersNote that all of these are primary mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay - 7Story - 8Graphics - 10Audio - 10More of a rant than a review. A good game. Felt a lot different than Hyper Light Drifter. When comparing the two. The only bit that felt similar was how the combat was dished out. And how the both games carries a somber tone. Hyper Light focused on quick action movements. If this game carries any quick action. It's associated with the platforming. While I would label Hyper Light Drifter as a action/adventure title. I would label Solar Ash an action/platforming/adventure title. Where Hyper Light Drifter shines on the strategy of it's action. It's lacks platforming. Solar Ash tries to combine the two. However I found the action to be in no way comparable to Hyper Light Drifter. The Platforming is pretty good. definitely could use more difficult scenarios with it. But I did like it overall. The combat however feels like a second thought. Only one encounter I recall near the end had some more thought behind it with enemy placement than any of encounters before hand. Even then, there was health everywhere. And if you used half your brain. You can cheese everyone pretty fast. Suffice it to say. I do see representation of how enemy placements in Solar Ash are directly inspired by how encounters were place in Hyper Light Drifter. Something of a chess board at time with what types of enemies they mix together. Solar Ash just doesn't do anything interesting with that. It's mixed up here and there. But nothing complex. There are Boss battles. There are nothing more than platforming challenges. Which is cool, but a little anticlimactic. Now the Story. It's a interesting story where you discover the downfall of several worlds. All the while saving your own. There is plenty of exposition added in the story compared to Hyper Light Drifter. And the main characters, as well characters you encounter on your travels. All have displayed personalities. While I enjoyed the story and some of the metaphysical complexities it hosts discussions on. At times I found the characters to be a bit cartoon/anime. While Hyper Light carries an aura of mysticism, and intrigue for the unknown around you. This game simply flaunts the idea of mysteries. Then simply gives you answers for them. Which is a massive difference between the two titles. While Hyper Light Drifter allows the player to develop their own story from intrigue. This game simply has a story to tell. And while it's a interesting story. I've come across it many times before. there is one bit about the story I really enjoyed. And I leave that to your for discovery. The music is really good I don't think it's as masterful as what Disaster Piece did with Hyper Light. But it's still good. Overall it's a okay game with some mature story themes. presented in a manner which is even appropriate for children to digest. While I appreciate that a bit. It feels like an attempt to reach a broader audience. And also undermines the intelligence of the players. Which isn't necessarily a bad thing. Just lacks a certain wisdom that was once there. A self respect if you will. I recommend this game for anyone that Enjoyed Hyper Light Drifter. Though I critique with the intent of being constructive. I still very much enjoy the work Heart Machine is doing. And I only hope that there is more of a return to form for them.

_childDocuments_.review: I can only best review this game by comparing it to Sonic Frontiers (which I also loved, but played on Switch and can't review). Sonic Frontiers is a game that went for something very similar to Solar Ash, but fell a bit flat mainly in focus and story. Frontiers was an action-first platformer; Solar Ash is a platformer with elements of combat. Personally, I think there's room for both, but if you had to pick one, easily it's Solar Ash. Less buggy, way nicer camera and, depending on how you define the term, more stylized than Frontiers. Plus the story is much more encapsulated and engaging. I think there is an element of mystery to Frontiers and that element I thoroughly enjoyed, but Solar Ash is able to solve its mystery within the confines of this game with a well-thought plot through and through.Like most all Annapurna published games, Solar Ash is another well-worth title.

_childDocuments_.review: Likely leaving this one unfinished, so I'll write my thoughts out here. I've got a fair amount of complaints and not enough care to go through everything so to be brief: I find the story uninteresting and the characters annoying. Highly subjective. I cannot stand when a protag narrates everything that happens, like I have eyes this is a visual medium, I can tell, thanks. Combat is too simplistic to be noteworthy. I suppose it suffices for the game's scale and the simplicity of the enemies, but it's often forgettable and doesn't feel like it adds anything, especially since the combat and the movement are completely separated, outside of the boss fights. The boss fights are annoying at best, being a test of quick reactions or memorization after you've been tossed off them enough. So far, 4 bosses in I've yet to ever actually die or feel any sense of urgency as there's always help lying around the boss's path. The flourish when you land the final blow is really cool though.Movement is largely disappointing. Unless there's a major shakeup in the mechanics past the 4th hour or so then you simply just don't have many options. hold or toggle RT to skate, grind on rails, climb specific walls, and that's about it. The movement LOOKS nice but it's not engaging and the level design doesn't lend itself to expressive play. There's usually only one method through any given area, and very little room to misinterpret how to do it. I often do speedruns of games, mostly 3D platformers and this had my interest to that end, but even aside from that my main interest was with the movement and it just lacks so severely compared to many other similar games. I'd highly suggest checking out the Arcane Kids unfinished project called Zenith. It's free to download and just accomplishes something similar to this project but much better.Finally the music and visuals are pretty good. The tracks aren't very memorable but they're serviceable. The aesthetic design of the game is pretty stellar, but held back a bit technically. Do some option tweaking if you do play, it can really help things stand out. I wish there were more flourishes and flashy bits like the final hits on bosses, or getting crushed in the big lady's hand, but oh well.Overall worth a play if it looks like the kind of thing you'd be into, just don't go in expecting complex platforming or movement options that allow you to be creative. This is more of a story game then anything, imo.

_childDocuments_.review: I've had this on my wishlist for a while now and had been looking forward to playing it given I'm a massive fan of Hyper Light Drifter. However I was really, really let down by the gameplay of Solar Ash. I generally like platformers, but the design choices in this left me shaking my head. To start with, the camera shifting is annoying when you're trying to move quickly to destroy a series of objects is really off putting and my main reason for saying "F this" and quitting. Let me control the camera, and don't shift it in a way where I can't see where I'm going on top of making my movement change direction because the camera shifted. Also, don't make my character stop moving for a second during the camera transition. Timed challenges should be smooth and seamless.My second main gripe is the combat. No real challenges from any standard enemy, and the boss fights are nothing more than "how quickly can you get from this point to the next." No skill challenge other than getting used to fast movement and timing. Just not my thing.Now, the visuals and audio/soundtrack are absolutely fantastic, but it's not enough to make me keep playing. Give me HLD any day of the week over this. It could be that this type of game (essentially speedrunning the whole time) just isn't my thing and not watching gameplay videos because I didn't want the game spoiled ended up kicking me in the ass. I can see why people like this a lot, but it is a very different game from HLD so if you're looking for something similar this isn't it.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game completely blind after looking forward to its Steam release. I am a big fan of Heart Machine's aesthetic sensibilities and this game is no slouch in that regard. There are some beautiful vistas here and the use of vertical landmarks helps the world feel cohesive while simultaneously making it easier to navigate the levels. Every area of the game has a distinct visual style and color palette with music that helps reinforce the tone. The music fell into the back of my mind for most of the game, unfortunately, but it was still enjoyable. The game itself is a sparse collectathon platformer of sorts with a focus on fluid movement instead of tight jumps and acrobatic maneuvers. The controls feel responsive and the physics for the movement are satisfying, although I kept wishing that I could just hold down a boost button to gain speed. There is a boost button in the game, but it only provides a quick nudge forward with a short cooldown period. You can use the boost to gain extra jump distance and airtime when zooming off of ramps. The levels you skate around are "open zones" where you are assigned a set number of things to find or destroy. As you might expect, there are a few basic enemies dotted around to fight you. Every area has a boss that you kill by skating around on its body, essentially acting as timed platforming challenges. There is a clear "Shadow of the Colossus" vibe with these fights as you mount the beasts and struggle to stay attached to them long enough to deal damage. There is a great sense of scale and spectacle, too, since every boss is wandering or flying around the level that you just completed to get to the fight. These must have been quite the challenge to create and they were the biggest highlight of the game for me even though they all felt samey by the end. The essential objectives have waypoints and everything else is up to you to find, which I liked quite a bit. The game isn’t “holding your hand” for the most part.  The levels aren't big enough for it to be annoying when you have to comb through it a few times to find the last part of a side quest, which is good because it keeps the pacing of the game brisk. Solar Ash isn't that long, but I think that ends up being a point in favor of it for reasons we'll get into…So far the game's construction is good on paper, but this is where I pull the rug out from under you and reveal my true thoughts on the game: it's not engaging. All of the content outside of the movement mechanics and the bosses that are closely tied to them feel malnourished. The combat is even more bare bones than Super Mario 64 while you're traversing the levels; you attack with one button and most enemies die in only a handful of strikes. None of the enemies pose much of a threat to you. Even if you do get hit or die by their simple attack patterns, there isn't any kind of punishment for it. You lose a couple of seconds of your life and move on. That's fine, of course, but it also means that there is never any tension when a group of enemies gets the jump on you or are floating around an objective you need to complete. Even when playing on the hardest difficulty the enemies never registered as a threat to me. There isn’t much to find when you go exploring; there are some pink goo collectables that you can use to upgrade your health, evil goop eyeballs that you need to kill to activate the boss, and audio logs scattered about that give you some insight into the plot. Sadly, the story is so dull that I can't even find much to say about it. Every level has audio logs from a specific character and they all have their own thoughts on their planet’s impending doom. The "Voidrunners" are trying to destroy the Ultravoid using some technology called the Starseed because it's threatening their planet, which is a serviceable premise for a game like this. Unfortunately, the dialogue is not very interesting stuff, nor does it tend to move the plot forward. I found it harder and harder to sit through 30-60 seconds of narration every time I discovered one of the audio logs. I'm disappointed that you have to sit and wait in a text modal for the voice lines to play in a game like this, they should have just let you move around while listening to every audio log. I can think of countless games that have taken the "audio log" approach to storytelling, but the biggest ones in my mind while playing this were System Shock and Bioshock. Both of those allow you to continue wandering around the environment or fight enemies while their audio logs run in the background.Every time you beat a level, you get a cryptic cutscene between a pastel goth dommy mommy named Echo and Rei, the main character, where they debate the futility of trying to activate the Starseed to save the world. The first one of these cutscenes was interesting and I thought it was setting up some mysteries for the plot to explore. Who is Echo and why is she so mad? Why is the Starseed needle thing stabbed right through her chest? There are answers to all these questions (and more!) but they are not revealed until the very end of the game. There are some hints about the true nature of the Ultravoid and your circumstances scattered around the game, but the plot fails to move itself forward in any of the cutscenes between Echo and Rei. They all end up being the EXACT same kind of bickering and vague dialogue with the same conclusion, even down to using the same animations of Echo and Rei to start and end them. The game sets up its plot in the first 5 minutes and then boosts across the finish line in the last 5 minutes. Everything else is just waxing poetic about the meaning of life, the Ultravoid's threat to Rei's world, and fungi. This is "fine" for a video game, I guess, but I was thoroughly uninterested in the story by the end. The big emotional climax fell flat for me and the plot twist made me roll my eyes because of how little it means for Rei and Echo as characters. The entire finale felt forced, but I suppose it was about what I expected by that point. I commend Heart Machine for trying something new and not just churning out a sequel to Hyper Light Drifter with higher production values, but the Sophomore slump hit this game hard. The game's strong art direction and boss fights are sadly not enough to save it from the Ultravoid of mediocrity. If you do want to play this thing, don’t buy it for full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful graphics and artstyle with creatively crafted zones each with their own gimmick to keep things fresh. The super fluid and satisfying movement along with the outstanding soundtrack makes this game super very relaxing to explore the environment. The combat in this game left me wanting as it pretty much just boils down to spamming the attack button, and some of the boss "fights" have sometimes frustratingly unforgiving timings. None of it really matters as you can't really fail a boss fight you just respawn where you left off and try again, making them feel really low stakes with zero risk. The gameplay loop does get a little stale after a while as youre basically just going point A to B doing timed platformer runs, a platformer boss fight, and onto the next zone. I wish there was more to do with the currency "plasma" you acquire from playing, as far as I know, its only used to buy back a health bar after beating a boss. I was playing the game with full health bars and an excess of plasma throughout most of my playthrough which left me wondering why its a mechanic in the first place.If youre looking for a relaxing 3d movement platformer with a great artstyle, atmosphere, environments, and music this is a good pickup for you, if youre here searching for exciting gameplay with satisfying combat and challenging puzzles, I would look elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: I got a 100% save file with no guides in 11 hours; for $40, that's bad. But even at half price, it's a 6/10 for reasons below. I'd recommend it under $20, if not just to preview Hyper Light Breaker's 3D world.Positives:- This is a textbook case of style over substance, but wow the style is perfect. The music, atmosphere, visuals, themes, NPC's, and voice acting are all top notch, and are very much what you could imagine a Hyper Light Drifter in 3D to feel like. - the title makes sense at the end- I found the exploration and combat to be simple, yet rewarding. Skating, boosting, and jumping is so good once you get into the flow. Past mechanics are used in more complicated ways, together, and the enemies add difficulty to the puzzles. Nothing was too hard, but figuring out where exactly a marker goes when it flies off-screen is frustrating. Negatives:- The plasma mechanic means nothing because health means nothing, by midgame you'll have 10,000 plasma and nowhere to put it. There's also a time-slow mechanic that adds range to your grapple, which doesn't make any sense. The extended grapple range changes with no indication; sometimes it seems infinite, but other times it'll completely ignore the target. Some of the suits make earlier suits useless. It almost feels like their QA team was asleep while testing, especially towards the end.- The bosses are the worst part of Solar Ash, and they're like half the game so that's not good. It's a slight remix on Shadow of the Colossus but really fumbles the appeal, You hit markers on each boss to eliminate phases and each marker has a limited amount of time to hit it, and they need to be hit in exact order to get the final weak spot to open up. This is an exact copy of SotC and it's a little odd. I won't even spoiler it because SotC has existed for 20 years already... ...-  This gets really old really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ quick. I'll never do the speedrun achievement because of this RNG-type gameplay.- The ending is pretty bad. Love the themes, but the ending scene is completely nonsensical , and the last boss has the same frustrations as every other boss.  - The last suit is kind of an insult if you've been following progression, even if narratively it makes sense.- This really needed more dev time. More testing. More focus. It's got some good ideas but the boss gameplay makes me not want to revisit it for a long, long while. Hoping Heart Machine can take the good parts of this over to Hyper Light Breaker.

_childDocuments_.review: So I just looked as saw that this has been out for over a year. Mostly on console and on the Microsoft Windows stores. Still doesn't change my thoughts on it, aslong as you don’t crank the graphics to 1 million it’ll still look amazing at medium. Graphic junkies aside, I think this is a really good game mechanic and gameplay-wise! I think this a great example of what is to come in the next game being currently developed, and I feel that once they work out the kinks in this game (with people complaining about the stuttering in frames when they crank it to a million) it’ll be amazing in every aspect. I’ll update later after I play it more.First Edit: So I can see more as to what some people were talking about that the game stutters some, but I haven't seen it drop below what I like it to. Other than that it's been smooth sailing leaving it on High quality. Though Low-end PC users might still struggle to play this game, so I can understand the deterrent there. That aside, I'm liking the story a lot. Being able to piece the story together myself and only discover as much as I am looking for it feels refreshing in a sense. Like I'm involved with the story, in a way. I wouldn't know as much of it if I didn't go looking for it. I feel that the environments are very fun to explore, and gives you an incentive to with how interesting everything looks and how rewarding to feels come across a good piece of lore. Though the only other gripe I have with this is the "bosses". They feel too same-y, and almost barely vary. I get to fight big boss, but there's no big twist so far as to what's different in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has so many baffling design decisions. I'm still deciding whether to refund because the artwork is so gorgeous especially at high framerates, it is simply beautiful in motion.Firstly, the character controller is unbelievably sloppy. The world is very large compared to your character, so you will end up boosting 24/7. Now this boost has a small cooldown, so you just have to get into the rhythm of boosting, waiting half a second, then boosting again. Over and over. It doesn't add anything to the game, it's like having to tap the button in GTA to get your character to run. And you will make approximately 0% of your jumps without a boost, so you better time your platforming around this too. So dumb. And there's all these goo piles everywhere that your player character clumsily climbs on, bringing the speed of the game to a halt. The game's flow is so inconsistent.Solar Ash is a master class in how now to teach the player mechanics. The grapple and time slow are both horrible mechanics that feel awful, and the weirdest thing is, when you time stop, the grapple range increases, how does that even work? It's not intuitive at all and by the time you need to use this, you will forget that that's even a thing. The very first area you have to complete a platforming challenge that is actually incredibly confusing because the pathfinding shows you're supposed to climb up some goo when really you're supposed to go around it via some other platforms and just jump to it that way. Well I sat there for like 10 minutes trying to climb the goo and wasn't sure if I missed a tutorial or what, because the jump was impossible. Why include climbable interfaces if you're NOT supposed to climb on it? It just confuses the player. Either the goo is purely aesthetic or it's for gameplay purposes, no BOTH. This game is ass.And then the health system. Again I don't know if I'm missing something but it hardly makes any difference if you die or just get hit because in both cases you just get sent back to the nearest checkpoint. So what does it matter? Just get rid of the health system altogether. The enemies aren't challenging so why even bother having them or health? Then there's pink goo scattered everywhere that you collect which I guess is like the currency but it doesn't seem to do anything so far, and it respawns so fast anyways that it seems like it's just there to give the illusion of something to do in the empty, boring world. Oh and whatever you do, do not play the game on Challenge mode. All it does is run down the timer faster on most of the challenges, making them borderline impossible.Overall the game looks amazing but every gameplay system reeks of someone who doesn't have a clue how to design a game. It's too bad when the artists go HAM only for the gameplay programmers to half-ass everything and make it unfun.

_childDocuments_.review: The art direction is amazingly stunning! I loved the design of all the environments, npcs, enemies, and bosses. It's a pretty short ride, especially on repeat playthroughs once you know where to go. I will say, the game does struggle from some performance issues. _childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: Movement and agility is the core concept here, and it really doesn't get old to zip around the environments. It feels a little clunky at times, either being stopped by a wall or never quite getting used to the momentum of the character. I love the visual style, the voice acting from side characters is surprisingly stellar. It's a good time at the end of the world.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this for the rail grinding and skating on water, ended up loving that, but also got invested in the story and the world. Amazing visuals and environments, top tier exploration, cool bosses. Mostly super smooth fluid gameplay, with only minor hiccups of getting stuck or clunkiness. I had a great time! Similar to Sonic Frontiers, The Pathless, Wavetale
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: The 3D art and colors in this game are gorgeous. Skating and traversing the landscape feels nice and fluid. The physics can get a little crazy but it seems that's kind of the point given the world you're playing in. The voice acting is super solid - I did skip some character dialogues (cuz I thought the writing and characterizations were a little lame) but you spend most of your time with Rei and Cyd and they're great.Some reviews have mentioned the barren environments, I didn't mind this so much cuz the game is still some great eye candy. Other reviews make comparisons to Shadow of the Colossus - one of my favorite games - and that's kind of apt but Solar Ash does put it's own twist on those kinds of boss puzzles. Even then tho, most of the boss designs are pretty great. There's also some pretty satisfying secrets and side quests to find if you want to just explore and discover.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: Damn what a great game. The platforming is fun and really satisfying to pull off, the visuals and music are great, and it even takes inspiration from Shadow of the Colossus. My biggest complaint is that once or twice the gravity will feel a little odd, and send you in a direction you didn't expect, but that's honestly ignorable compared to the quality of the rest of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a positive review, but I'm not sure if I would recommend this game to everyone. I'll start with the good. By far the most fun parts of the game are the timed boss fights and the similar eye-stabby sections to unlock the boss fights. Gameplay wise, the movement is buttery smooth and satisfying, the animations are fluid, and the level design is fun. Specifically, I like how seamlessly executed gravity changes are. The story is not bad either (albeit it being slightly pretentious and cliché), having an overarching more vague main story supplemented by smaller side stories found through the collectibles and character quests. The visuals and general art style are also really nice. Whether it's during the boss fights themselves or just exploring new areas, this game is always clean and pleasing to look at. Now the bad. I wish the combat was more than just one button. I would have preferred a little more skill expression than that. The enemies and combat in general always felt like a second thought or an annoyance, they rarely ever added any fun to exploring a new area. The interesting side stories need to be encouraged more. Although you are forced to encounter the NPC's a few times, you can completely ignore them every other time, missing out on their side stories, and they have no effect on how the story ends. The void caches give you tidbits of story throughout, but the only benefit of actually finding these caches besides the story is a new suit. The effects these suits give do not substantially change the feel of the gameplay at all and they definitely should as it would add more variety to the gameplay and further encourage the player to explore and discover the story. Also, there's basically zero player progression. The only thing you can do is buy an extra shield hit. There's no reason why there aren't more upgrades or maybe even special items you can buy from Cyd. Overall, I still enjoyed the game a lot, just enough cons where I can't 100% ensure someone will find it enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty fun. I do think that its gameplay is somewhat underbaked, with really good core elements left kind of underutilized. The fights with the giant creatures are fun but still fall into the same gameplay problem. Its fun to skate around a do some fun, all be it, basic tricks. Don't expect a whole lot more than that.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game from start to finish. The art style is gorgeous, the music is out of this world and even the SFX really sets this cosmic eerie tone of the game, especially at the end of the game. The music was on-point ! The game plays amazingly well. It feels smooth and responsive. It felt good surfing on clouds, rails, and even roots. The story is very deep in a way i wasnt expect how close to real life it would be (the "moral of the story" ofc). I liked how they make you collect stuff in order to know more about the story and the world around you. The boss fights were perfect! It felt like a combination between "shadow of colossus" and "Tony hawk pro skater". It was legit fun, and i really recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: This game just feels really good to move around in. The fast-paced movement that you execute while slashing the weak spots of giant monsters as you climb them is is just really fun, especially with the incredible visuals presented. You can unlock the hardcore difficulty after beating the game, which basically challenges you to execute every trial in the game once more while making no mistakes, resulting in a very satisfying new game+ experience. The visual aesthetics, music and the story's premise are also pretty good to boot.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: I'm glad I finally decided to play this game, as it was nothing but fantastic. The art direction and world alone are super interesting and well done. The locals you visit are so pretty, each with their own specific vibe and mechanics to go with them. The aforementioned mechanics are a lot of fun, reminded me at times of Jet Set Radio, what with the rail grinding and whatnot. Any game with an air dash is also a plus in my book. Nice soundtrack too. Quite a short game, as I was able to beat it in a day. Which isn't a bad thing, it's nice to have a little game to get through on a day off.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: Heart Machine has done it again. Solar Ash has plenty of amazing worldbuilding and artistic style. Great story oozing with desperation and desolation. There's a lot of optional exploring to find logs and piece together the lore. Skating movement feels smooth and satisfying (if you enjoyed Sayonara Wild Hearts you will likely also enjoy this game). I would say this game focuses on fast-paced puzzle platforming, with a little hack and slash combat added. Though, I kind of wish there was more mechanical complexity. Most character skills you use will be taught early on, instead the game keeps things interesting by introducing new environmental puzzle elements. You can use plasma you collect to upgrade your health bar, or equip suits you get from finding logs for different perks, but other than that there isn't much in the way of upgrades. Overall, very enjoyable game, highly recommend especially if you love games with movement that feels good.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: It took me nine hours to finish this game to 100% completion. Though it wasn't immensely detrimental to the experience, the areas, despite being visually diverse, do not have enough variation in environmental hazards to prevent gameplay from slouching into a boring sameness. The short nature of the game mostly mitigated that, but there were still times towards the end where gameplay felt mindless (for example, while dashing for minutes on and off of toxic water). And although the completionist in me wanted to collect all the voice logs, and while they were indeed relevant in some capacity, they lacked meaningfulness. It felt like a chore, not a reward, and I could have experienced the game almost identically had I not searched for them.But in those nine hours, I also received a narrative rich in an implicit journey towards existential absolution, filtered through captivating visuals and incredibly satisfying and fluid combat--both of which also feeling greatly unique. At its climax, its intensely visceral and grotesque personification of guilt made tears well in my eyes, for the first time, while being engrossed in combat. It was not as I watched a beautiful cutscene or listened to incredible music (both of which this game absolutely has), but as I focused on the tense dashing and slashing of a final battle. I felt the message of this game as if its quest towards an honest life was my own. I think there is also a viable transhumanist reading of this game that furthers the meaning of the variable perspectives of the other teammates, but no matter if you see this experience through that lens, or the religious or philosophical one, the lesson to be learned is all the same: To accept what's real, you must see past selfish desire in order to actualize morality as a praxis of the self. If you are unable to accept that, you will be trapped in a blinding cycle where you (and to a reasonable extent, many others) are incapable of growth, you will live a false life, and you will suffer. It is a meaningless frenzy in which you reach so hard for a goal that's no more than a blade, waiting for you to grab its edge so it can draw blood over and over. From star, to supernova, to nebula, to star again: Solar Ash, an incredible game.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: The devs from Hyper Light Drifter and Annapurna publishing, oh hell yeah.The world in this game is beautifully designed, it flows like the game Flower, sounds like Hyper Light Drifter, and plays like a fast-paced Shadow of the Colossus. Your objective is to wake and destroy these colossi that make up each of the zones, the destruction and removal of the creatures cleanses each area allowing you to progress. Fairly straightforward progression and objectives. There are some side quests but to me they were hard to track, to the extent that only one side-quest really gave any kind of direct interaction.The game has a fairly good story for being somewhat short, I clocked in around 9 hours and completed most of the objectives. I bought this on sale, and after finishing the game the price I got it for felt like a steal. Even $25 or $30 is well worth the price, but the base price feels to steep. Not to disrespect the game or the devs, it's just too short of a game for that price to me. The quality is absolutely there, the quantity not quite.My only gripes are that some of the boss fights are frustrating, I think there were two of them I just couldn't get right the first ten times. The other boss fights were fantastic, some just didn't work too well for me, others may not have the same problem depending on skill and strategy.

_childDocuments_.review: Worth a try? YES! But not worth full price. I really liked this game, but it does have some flaws you should be aware of before playing:- The first few areas of the game are very repetitive in feel, which is a shame since the later areas are awesomely unique.- Combat is nearly optional at first, but becomes way more fun and complex in later areas. Push through the beginning of the game and you'll be rewarded. - - - In all, it feels like I got to play 75% of an awesome game. The story is very cool and trippy. The movement is exhilarating. Bosses are formidable. It's just missing key elements.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was everything I was looking for and more. _childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: THIS GAME IS INCREDIBLE!!! I love this game so much. If I were to describe it'd be a mashup of Metroid With Loz Breath Of The Wild. It has a surprising amount of lore that hits really well. The controls are great and the sound track is fire. Visually this game is gorgeous! The main missions get repetitive as well but ended up being really fun as they got more creative each time. The maps are also fantastic!

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game, beautiful word, beautiful message.Heart Machine continues to nail "post apocalyptic space wizard" in a way that I find both original and comforting.Gameplay reminds me of the best parts of Prince of Persia, the Cell Shaded one, but a little simpler. My only complaint is that the "tangible" rewards for exploration are a little weak, but the story and character for doing it is well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: Solar Ash has a Shadow of the Colossus-style gameplay loop of fighting gigantic bosses, and it never gets old. That is mostly due to the great variaty in how the bosses are summoned and fought. My favorite boss was definently which is ironic because it's fought in my least favorite area. Along with the fun gameplay are the absolutley gorgeus visuals. The enviorments, the colors, the character designs are all amazing and make you feel like you are in a dream. I also really like the ending, which I obviously wont spoil.I don't really have any complaints outside of the afformentioned least favorite area. Otherwise this game awesome and I would highly recomend it to anybody who is a fan of action games, or platformers, or creative visuals.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: (kingdom?) is colorful title where you’ll be skating around on sci-fi rollerblades and also a completely different game from its predecessor.Artstyle, setting, and great sense of flow, while you could argue it’s often found in other games as individual elements this title has all three.It’s a very “deliberate” game, and by that I mean it’s light on the mechanics but great on the game-feel, movement feels great, it has its own momentum but still incredibly easy to maneuver, attacks don’t slow you down and reach incredibly far.Also sliding on colossal bosses to deliver a hit to their weakspot never gets old when it’s not just a climbing simulator.Explore the massive areas quickly with a combination of a skating run and a boost, platform your way through the discovered landmarks, do some light fighting with the enemies scattered about, solve some platforming puzzle to dispel a goo-like thing that prevents you from facing the boss.The bosses themselves are one of the highlights of the game, you can’t swordfight these colossi the way you’re slashing at other enemies, but you’ll have to run on them as if they were moving platforms. You find yourself beaten and in a strange world where gravity behaves weirdly, welcome inside Ultravoid, a black hole that pulls anything inside and you’re here to prevent your planet to be its next victim by activating a huge device called Starseed.Story is communicated through characters talking, and while environments are stunning, they do little to make a narrative out of how they are structured.Another way you’ll be fed information is through scattered audiologs of the crew.Combat feels very light on the rules, sometimes I’m able to combo enemies while they do nothing, some other times enemies just chain a slew of unavoidable attacks while I cannot do anything about it.Personal preference here, but I don’t much like voice acting, overly sarcastic tone all the time is not for me, and unfortunately is just a voice type and could’ve been forgiven if both the delivery and writing were better, to the point where I think it would benefit more from a silent storytelling approach.I feel like this game didn’t hit the level of success that Hyper Light Drifter had for a few simple reasons:HLD came out in a period where good indie titles scarce and far-between.HLD hit more of a nostalgia factor while being both fresh, beautiful, and challenging, prompting people to suggest it more.Solar Ash shares a lot of its aesthetics with HLD making people who wanted more of the same disappointed.The price difference is quite big too, HLD on launch was 20$ this is 40$ Still, Solar Ash is a great game about fluidity of motion that lets you slide around its picturesque locales, however, it’s a 6 hours game, 8 if you want to 100% it, wait for a substantial discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: The story is great. I didn't realize what it was about until the end and I think it is a beautifully done story. Play it for the story, which is good. The gameplay is uncomplicated and easy to get the hang of, but it is very repetitive in a way that does not serve the story well. Every area is essentially the same challenge with a slightly different environmental hazard each time. The difficulty progression is linear; there are no spikes except the boss fights and those could be thought of as having multiplicative difficulty as opposed to additive. My two major gripes are that the boss fights themselves are made needlessly difficult by poor perspective management, and the forced health damage at the end of each sequence is a bummer.It is a visually beautiful game. The cel-shading style works well here just like the 16-bit pixel format worked for Hyper Light Drifter. There were no major rendering errors. Some water(? clouds ?) clipped through the cliff environments from time to time, but it is by no means immersion breaking.The voice acting is phenomenal. Big props to the VA's.The sounds are mostly pleasant with a few exceptions for the misophonia-inclined among us:1. The mushroom vine grinding sound is a highly compressed, wet tearing sound and is repulsive.2. The boosters activation sound is a wet, wobbly rattle and is similarly irritating.3. The death sound is a heavily compressed crackling which is again irritating.These can be mitigated somewhat by turning the sound effects down, but the balance of sounds is not conducive to this.The music is fantastic.Overall it's a 6/10 game. Real good potential with some missed opportunities. I probably will not be getting 100% completion, but it's fun to play once.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: Solar Ash is a stunning game. The visuals never cease to amaze, especially for a game with what feels like a very simplistic art style. Every region has its own wonderful charm that made exploring feel so special.The art design isn't the only thing that stands out about this game for me. The sound also helped to give this game such a fun and alive feeling the whole way through.As far as gameplay goes, this game also manages to deliver on that incredibly well. It's not a very hard game, even playing on the hardest difficulty only proves mildly challenging (after playing on normal first), but wow is it fun. For such an easy game, it does a really good job of making you feel so badass the entire time. The movement is smooth and fast-paced, and the occasional bug with gravity does little to ruin my enjoyment of flying through the clouds similar to wavedashing in smash.The story isn't very complicated, and the big reveal at the end of the game felt obvious from the beginning, but it's not bad by any means. I definitely recommend picking this game up if you have a day off with nothing to do.
_childDocuments_.name: Solar Ash

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. The visuals are breathtaking, the sound and music are powerful and strong, the gameplay is smooth and fluid, and the writing is heart-achingly cathartic. And while it does express everything it wants to over its runtime, it is unfortunately painfully short. I managed to 100% it on my first playthrough, and it only took me a little over 7 hours.
