Customize your store, hire heroes to gather ingredients, befriend (or romance) fellow vendors to learn new haggling strategies, and go head-to-head with competitors in this narrative-driven, deck-building shop simulator.

_childDocuments_.review: First boss is weirdly hard given how relatively easy the game is up until that point, and if you lose to the boss it's just an immediate game over with no recovery or retry, so you'll have wasted 2-3 hours building up to the boss only to wash out and have to start completely over. Completely erased any interest I had in continuing to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: Very cute and quite gay. I love it to death! It's also moderately challenging management and making haggling into a card game was an interesting choice. The alchemy system isn't as in-depth as say Potioncraft, which is also a quite lovely game, but the character interaction and personality really put it over the top for me. I feel almost silly in having compared the two when deciding to purchase because they are quite different beasts despite the superficial similarity in being alchemy management sims. This game having a bit more focus on socialization and resource management compared to Potioncraft's strict emphasis on alchemy.
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: This game is probably the best potion-brewing game I have played so far. It has a good storyline, fun characters to interact with, and the actual mechanics of potion-brewing are also well designed. It took me about 38 hours to finish the game. Sadly, replayability of this game is very low, unless you want to go back and max out other character stories.The final 'week' was a bit of a slog to get through as I already amassed significant quantities of money and top-tier potions. Getting to know the various mechanics at the start of the game was certainly a lot of fun however. I highly recommend you try out this game. Uncharacteristically of the present trends in video game industry, this game is well-polished and seemingly did not feature any (significant) bugs. Prepare your strongest potions, potion seller!
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game thinking that this was just going to be making potions and I was already completely on board! Oh my god! I love the story, I love the friendships and being able to hire someone to get my ingredients! I love the whole selling my potions turned into a card strat game! This is amazing and if you are on the edge of getting this I'd def say to give in!
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: I really very much enjoyed this game. Let's start with the bad:-Performance issues weren't too common, but it was just as finicky as a source game; if you alt tab or minimize it, it WILL crash.-Some animations looped in really janky ways (Looking at you, Xid's guitar animation)-Luna's design is awful. Either go "girl, but with a few moth features" or "anthropomorphic moth", not this horrible in between. -Connected to Luna, her stupid smartphone, and a lot of her dialogue, but the occasional references to technology were really very jarring. It always took me out of it, compared to the very solid fantasy world. Speaking of . . .The good:-Some fantastic characters in this game, in particular my favorites were Mint, Saffron, and Muktuk. Muktuk has some genuinely really good advice for artists and any creative.-Art style is pleasant, and most animations are very smooth, which makes the ones that aren't more jarring because most are very good.-Fun gameplay, weird combo of time management and deck building, but you start to get it pretty quick.-Actually surprisingly interesting world. The island, the economic situation on it, its connection to the mainland, and how people deal with the effects of the island and its history are built into the story and characters very well.Other:-I was fine with it, but an easy/more chill mode that extended how many days you had before each competition would be nice for some people.-Special Orders should be able to be seen while at Quinn's shop. I had to start taking pictures of them with my phone to remember what ingredients with what traits I'd need.-Why do I need to travel to speak with the person who comes to live in Sylvia's shop? (Being vague for spoilers.)Overall, a very good game and I'm glad I got it.
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: ♥♥♥♥ man this game hits all the spots. For $30 I've gotten 8h out of the game so far and I'm expecting about 40h more. It's easy to get into without a low skill cap (as much skill as card games have). The math and planning when organising your brewing is well done and super fun. They give you a ton of ways to get ingredients, increase profits, and advertise your product. Even if you don't haggle there's a way to be commissioned, and eventually you can simply sell your potions at a fixed price. Bonus points for having some casual queer rep with Quinn too, and I'm sure there's no shortage of gays in the rest of the crew. The cast is diverse and fun to interact with (and all are romanceable as far as I've seen) and can lead to interesting conversations and friendships. Bonus Bonus points for the very well done art, the designs are super intriguing and unique.Tl;Dr It's a super fun diverse experience that turns haggling into a super fun and cute experience cute fun cute fun experience super cute experience the fujn cute gnrnrrrrr haglglingfn
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game. Played for 3 days straight.It's great! It's a linear game. Somewhat challenging but not over the top if you're familiar with this genre. It's also not a genre-breaking game. The gameplay is pretty standard -- which is great for people who enjoy this genre. Gameplay wise, it's neither frustrating nor mindblowing.What this game really excels, however, is in art and character development. Seriously, the character animation doesn't have to be this good for a game of this kind. The art style is lovely. The stories! It's pretty hard to have non-stereotypical characters in a fantasy setting nowadays. At least not in games that aren't elaborate RPGs. This game, though, the character stories are all so convincing! Sure, there are a lot of tropes in there, but they are carefully done with just the right mix of cliche and social commentary to be refreshing, intriguing, and enjoyable. Truly a lovely experience!
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: So, I don't do reviews much, but this game deserves one.When I bought this game, I did it purely on how much I loved how the characters looked!  Silvia is just adorable!  Each character is designed well and very fun.  A few bugs with animations or some facial expressions but nothing so jarring it was unplayable.The idea of the game is like most potion crafting games, get ingredients, mix ingredients, make more/better potions, sell potions.  What i was not expecting was the use your potions could have as well with adventuring  and the haggling game.  Every aspect of the game plays on each other so it feels good to build your relationships, make potions for adventures and not selling, only to make more and better potions because of it that sell for much more!All in all, if you are looking for a fun potion game with fun beautifully designed characters, fun mini games, and a small amount of time management, this is a great game to sink a few hours into.
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: Potionomics is an Indie that feels like a high production project.It's so good! Every note hits right. The facial expressions, the frantic gameplay, the music and ambiance, the writing, the lore.There's so much effort put in this game. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: It's a fun shopkeep/deck-builder game that I think is worth the money. And don't miss my Tips at the bottom.Deeper review:   At the start there are sorting issues, or a lack of sorting options. And it becomes more of a pain the longer you play. Hopefully they will address this soon.  That being Said, It is still a fun game. The most time-consuming part of the game is figuring out which ingredients will get you the perfect ration while maximizing your potions' value. However, it is easy to mindlessly get less than perfect and settle for stable or very stable, which will still give you a bonus. And unstable potions only run the risk of losing a star, which doesn't make the biggest impact. So if you don't want to take much time on the ingredients, you don't have to. Later in the game, you will get better ingredients that will make getting perfect rations easier.  There are several strategies you can go with in regards to building your card deck. You can embrace stress or avoid it. You can focus on buffs/debuffs or just hit hard and fast. Or you could be defensive and extend their level of patience.  In truth, I would like more customization and options on the shopkeep part of it. But it's fairly decent as is, especially since there aren't many good shopkeep titles.    The ability to autosell potions at a fixed price is probably the best part they put into the game imho. If you want, you can completely skip negotiating. But I use it mostly for passive income and getting rid of lower tier useless potions without wasting time. I can make a ton of potions in quick time with all the fuel I collect from quests and such. You also get custom order requests during the negotiation phase, which is just another avenue to either avoid using cards or get extra side income.     The artwork is cute, and the animation fun. The story is somewhat predictable, but still enjoyable. The music is pretty good, it won't blow you out of the water, but I still enjoy it.    There isn't much in the sense of replay value, apart from trying to do things even more efficiently. I feel the devs could fix this by adding more modes/newgame+ or, more preferably, adding more customization features to the shopkeep experience.    Dating and friendship meters seem to be separate, which is good. You can only date one person. There are about a dozen characters to choose from. Only two of those are straight options. And two of those are animals O.O   I wish we could do something about obsolete cauldron/shelves. Just be aware that if you spend money on upgraded equipment (which is a good investment) don't go too overboard, because after the next major event you'll want to upgrade them again, but all the money on those previous upgrades will go to waste. Some tips to get you started: - First, use more ingredients. The more ingredients you use, the more potions you'll get back; at a rate of one potion for every two ingredients. - Don't forget to upgrade your cauldrons. more and better potions means more money. - making a bunch of cheap potions is still a good option if you are tight on funds or resources, as you get a means later in the game to automatically sell a bunch of potions and make a lot of passive income. - It is worth leveling up friends. They will give you discounts and better cards - Friends like types of ingredients, rather than individual ingredients, and they most of the time correlate to their personalities, for instance, saffron likes plants. - It seems as though flirting with friends is unrelated to their friendship meters. 1 star and 2 stars are them liking something, and a heart seems to be a separate romance meter. I could be wrong, but I have no problem leveling up friends without choosing romance options. - Send friends out every day on missions. Not only is it a great deal on ingredients for the price, but they gain xp as well, which I think makes them better, but not by like a huge amount. You do get a lot of ingredients though, especially if you equip them with enhancing potions. - Buy discounted ingredients in bulk, and sell boosted potions in bulk. This may seem like a no brainer, but I've made 100,000 in one day just by selling my mega boosted potions. And you can make a lot more if you have spare ingredients lying around. - Use the cheapest fuel possible, as they have the best value money-wise. Later in the game, you should hopefully have enough money to not care to buy the more expensive fuel. - Avoid building up too much stress, as it can snowball real fast. I try to avoid at all costs going over 15% or 20%. You will automatically recover about 10-15% of stress after every night sleeping. - pick and choose custom orders as they are not all created equal. Sometimes you will get custom requests for lower tier potions that pay more than higher tier requests.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's the thing - this game is fantastic in terms of mechanics and gameplay loop. Get ingredients->make potions->sell potions->talk to NPCs to get more ingredients. It's fantastic and charming and a delight to play. But there's a problem. A Major Problem.Unlike most sim games like Stardew Valley, Holy Potatoes a Weapon Shop, or even roguelikes like Moonlighter, this game does not allow you to play at your own pace and locks you out of content due to an artificial time crunch they impose on you Day 1. Imagine if you started Stardew, you got the letter from your grandpa giving you his farm, you leave your desk job at Joja and find yourself on this new property that's brimming with possibilities, only to learn that "oops you don't only inherit the land but also the debt and this farm will foreclose in a week and the bank will take your life savings and also you will be sent to hell and live as a slave for life unless you make $1,000,000 right now."It would go from a relaxing, charming experience where you get to build and grow how you please into stressful rush experience where you're constantly worrying about wasting time and how you are going to raise that money so that you don't lose everything. Then they offer you a way out, through a competition where the prize money will pay off the debt's interest. Problem is, you go and do all the work for the competition, but there's no payoff. You win the prize money just for it to immediately get taken away.Potionomics takes positive experiences and turns them into negatives. It takes a relaxing premise and turns it stressful. It has all the makings for a fantastic game, but the developers didn't think about game design in terms of the player's emotional experience while playing. Every time they give you something, they take something of equal or greater value away from you, all while applying constant pressure.And this is a shame, because the game is fantastic. The deckbuilding card game for haggling is ingenious. Brewing potions is fun and interesting (though I'd like to see more 2-magamin ingredients and less 3-4 ingredients..), the character animations are cute and fluid, the character designs are fun and interesting, the time management aspect is fun too - or at least, it would be if it weren't for the constant crunch. The entire game is soured by that 1 decision.Other minor nitpicks would be the QoL regarding the shop where you buy ingredients not having sorting, so it's awful to use, lots of loading screens for things that don't seem like they would need loading screens - like opening menus in your shop, and the lack of voice acting draws your attention away from the beautiful animations to read the dialogue, so you either miss the animation or the context/dialogue. Fantastic beautiful game ruined by the decision to always put you under constant pressure. They made this otherwise relaxing and fun game into a stressful experience, and ruin rewards by immediately taking them away after you earn them.

_childDocuments_.review: I have yet to beat this game, so take my review with a grain of salt. It's been a wild ride so far, and i absolutely adore this game. clocked over 25 hours in the last few days and am not even close to slowing down. However, even though I find this game quite charming and fun, it has not always been so easy on me. The game itself is a unique take on several different genres and I think they balanced the aspects of each very well. There are so many things I can rave about from the character designs (each so unique and mostly likable) to the absolutely fantastic writing. I have never laughed at a game this much and I've been enjoying playing as the bold, expressive, and confident Sylvia. She is well written and well rounded, I have never enjoyed playing a crafted character this much. This game on design alone is already very impressive and well worth the money i paid for it.There are a few things however, that make it difficult to truly enjoy it to its full potential.  Many of them are small, easily fixable things. QOL updates and streamlining the menus a bit. Several things that would be useful would be things like being able to pin custom orders to the right of my screen while brewing so i wouldn't have to check the list several times, setting recipes for frequently crafted potions like health or mana potions, or being able to use escape to exit some menus so that i don't have to click return for all of them. Another I would love to see is when you click on a Magimin to search your ingredients, having an option to double click to exclude that specific magimin would be lovely. Small things that would make navigating the menus and potion crafting would be a big plus to this game because it is solely played on screen with the mouse. It gets repetitive to have to move through so many screens with just clicking your mouse, having a hotkey to escape menus would be a real time saver. Little changes like that would boost this game quite a bit. The few BIG glaring problems however, are a bit harder to fix. One would be the lack of post day 50 content, I was severely disappointed when i learned that all the progress i had made in my shop and with the people my character was developing will be halted just like that. Having a post game where you just continued your shop, business and relationships sounds awesome. That way people can naturally play themselves tired of the game and drop it when they feel like they're finished and not when an ending makes them. Most SIM games don't have endings and a lot of people love them for that express purpose. I like playing a game until I can't stand it any longer, that I am the one to decided when i'm done and not a cut scene. Another big problem with the game is the difficulty scaling. Some players thrived on the strict time restraints and the mounting pressure, but unfortunately not a lot of people thrive under pressure. I am not one of those people. I had such an awful time that I nearly dropped the game during Roxanne's fight. I was ill prepared and I got trapped and struggled for over an hour slowly losing my enjoyment of the game along with my patience and sanity. Having two different difficulty settings could completely negate this issue, leave the challenging route in for those who enjoy the challenge, but add a less intensive leisurely difficulty for those who want to enjoy the amazing world and characters these developers had made. Maybe add a few more time blocks to the day, lower the requirements for the competitions and ease up on the traits on the custom orders. Just those few things would make the game so much more enjoyable. Or at least have the Rank up for shops not require time but do not remove stress. That way you still need to spend time with an NPC to reduce stress, but you don't have to juggle your time so intensively when you are just trying to unlock cards for your deck. I absolutely love this game, and will probably continue playing it for several more hours. Even if they don't adjust anything, i'm still going to play it to its natural conclusion. It's just one of those things that I don't like staring over again after I've already banked a lot of time and energy into a play through. So after my first, i probably will not play it through all the way again. I hope that the developers will at least take into consideration some of the points that many of their players have brought forth. If they don't wish to change the game in any capacity, then that is fine. I just think it could be so much better with a few changes. Would i recommend this game? Hell yeah. It's fun, fast paced and once you learn what you are doing, very engaging. The world is absolutely lovely, the characters are fully fleshed out and feel like real people. The story is great and the writing is on point so much that i adore it. I just don't want other people going into thinking that it's perfect or completely flaw free. Because it does have its flaws, but if you can look past them I think anyone could enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, so, so close to being amazing but stumbles at the finish line.  It has some minor issues like a confusing and unresponsive UI, but the thing that stops this game from being one of those classics is the pacing and balancing.Let me just sing some praises for a while before I get to my problems with the game.  The writing is excellent, if not a little predictable. All the characters have really distinct personalities and their own goals and problems.  Relationships feel real and mostly natural which is important for a social sim like this; no voice acting though, which is a shame but I understand it's probably too expensive for a small studio to get the talent that would do these characters justice.  Visually this game is just amazing, everything has this storybook quality to it that just oozes charm.  Not much else to talk about here except that the quality in the trailer holds through the entire game.   Running your shop and making potions is enjoyable, the game settles into a nice rhythm between potion making and running out to get stuff done while they brew.  It's got a little bit of that "just one more day" energy too that can suck you in and make you lose track of time.  Potion making itself is fairly simple and satisfying.  The haggling card game also works surprisingly well, it's not Slay the Spire or anything, not even close, but it's flexible enough that you can build decks around multiple strategies and getting a perfect sale is difficult enough to be engaging, at least until you get some of the more broken cards.Okay, time for the problems.If you've read a few of the negative reviews already, you know that the game is split into timed weeks which puts pressure on the player to complete an objective.  My problem isn't with the timer though, I actually think the timer is an essential part of this game because the game systems themselves aren't really deep enough to hold up if you just had free reign to do whatever you wanted.  It's also a nice way to connect the player to Sylvia; she has a crippling debt and managing stress is a key game mechanic, so putting the player under time pressure is a nice way to do that through gameplay instead of just writing.  My issue has more to do with the pacing and difficulty of making potions, very minor gameplay spoilers, but the timed objective for each week is to make a set of high value potions.  This set of potions was hard to make the first week, and then essentially an afterthought the rest of the game.  You can just make the new sets on the first or second day no problem, the most pressure I felt was from trying to not accidentally sell them.  "Okay, so you're just good at the game, who cares?" The problem is that making these potions so easily ruins a lot of the games pacing, especially because there's no endgame whatsoever.  Once you finish the last timer, the game just ends.  All the extra resources you had saved up from the previous weeks of planning are useless, finishing your potions early and having the time to go around maxing everyone's social link and upgrading your shop is pointless, because you never need it for anything.  The game gives you all these cool ingredients that make you think there's some end game coming where you'll have to make crazy strong potions, but in reality you can pretty much max out everything with ease.  You also get cool capstone cards for maxing out relationships that are also worthless because, surprise!, making the high level potions too well for each week will just outright SKIP the card fight boss battles.  Your reward for playing well is... less content?  That's my main problem, they kind of half-assed the difficulty in this game and didn't really know how to pace the game out to keep it engaging without stonewalling the people who don't care much for planning.  What we got instead is something that annoys the people who just want to chill and make potions at their own pace, but also isn't balanced and engaging enough to satisfy the optimizers.  All made worse by the fact that there's no post-game or freeplay to mess around in, so the people who want to escape the timer are out of luck, and there's no fun in "breaking" the game and enjoying your spoils at the end for the people who successfully planned out all their moves.In the end though it's not that big of a deal for me, the overall game is still very good, probably like a 8.5/10.Also yes, there are potion seller memes.

_childDocuments_.review: What a charming, fun game. Took about 20 hours to finish the campaign. Wanted to address some of the negatives that have been showing up in reviews, that  originally kept me from buying this:The game definitely stressed me out at first, and you'll barely eek out the proper potions for  the first competition. Your options are limited when it comes to haggling, ingredient choice, and expanding your shop. It's rough and the  game's difficult at first. It eases up after the first week, and the end is pretty breezy.This is true, but I don't think this is necessarily a bad thing. I think the people upset about this like min-maxing and want the difficulty you have in the first week. I don't think this is an oversight by the devs, it seems intentional. I like that the better you get at the game / more options you have, you start really taking control of the loop and supassing the  challenges with ease. It's a really nice payoff, and gives you time to do the upgrades / chase relationships at the end of the game. You can also skip days if you don't want to do this, and just brew the competition potions in the first two or so  then skip to the next competition.I like the competition structure and think it gives you a nice goal to go after. A sandbox mode would be awesome, but I don't think the lack of one really  hurts the game. If you're looking for something cozy that's easy, the first week will be frustrating but after that it eases up a lot and gives you time to breathe (don't have to worry about maximizing your time as much, and you start raking in the dough)Overall, I love this game. 9/10 from me. One of my favorites of 2022

_childDocuments_.review: In , you will find a beautiful game designed to mesmerize your senses with gorgeous character animation, fun deck-building, a thoughtful resource/time management system and a stellar soundtrack.   have concocted the perfect blend of a visual novel with the strategy of a card-battler and a resource gathering sim.  You play as Sylvia, a young witch fresh out of potion college, who just inherited her uncle’s store ().  You learn the art of potion selling by forming relationships with an array of colorful characters, in order to unlock unique cards which are used to haggle with customers.  You make potions by mixing specific ingredients based on their particular color/letter designation.  These ingredients are gathered by adventurers whom you hire to go out into different biomes to harvest, or which you can purchase from other merchants.  This cyclical nature is both a reflection of the game’s mechanics as well as its overall structure.Sylvia’s story takes place on the island of Rafta, a vibrant storybook fantasy world full of magic, witches and anthropomorphic citizens, but also laced with familiar modernisms like social marketing, cellphones and bass rock’n bards.  Her goal is to get out of debt, not by selling potions, but by actually competing in a series of (5) potion brewing contests held every 10 days.  Each day is broken into 6 time segments, during which you have to prioritize what potions to make, what potions to sell, and which characters to “level up”, because every action takes time.  While this timing mechanism isn’t quite debilitating, as in a more dynamic game like , it nevertheless adds a strategic layer requiring you to literally plan your day.  What often dictates this are the daily events – special random effects that give a positive or negative buff to potions, customers and environments.The other strategy layer, and one of its core highlights, is haggling – selling your potions to customers. This is done through a very creative and impressive deck building system.  Every time Sylvia levels up her relationship with a character, she unlocks specific playing cards unique to their personality or mercantile strategy.  Even though every card is useful, and beautifully illustrated, there are certain builds and interactions that work better than others.  While this is arguably the most fun aspect of the game,  isn’t designed like a CCG.  There’s no endless mode where players can haggle with customers and test out various deck builds.  You simply have to play with cards as you unlock them, often saving your progress before a sale.Where  truly outperforms is in the character designs and animation.  Everyone has so much personality and expression you literally feel like you are interacting with an animated movie.  They even go so far as to animate characters speaking, even if no voice acting is involved.  This could have drastically altered the narrative presentation, but its absence works to enhance the visual novel style.  Instead we have an incredible soundtrack by film composer Greg Nicolett, whose score punctuates every story element and character in the game with movie-quality orchestration.  Adding to this is a romantic element where Sylvia eventually has to choose whom to form a deeper bond with.  While this doesn’t affect the gameplay in any way, it simply enriches the story and offers shipping fans an extra layer of fun in pairing Sylvia with...whomever the player desires...()Completing the circle is of course potion-crafting.  This part of the game requires a lot of mathematical balancing in matching the proper ratio of ingredients to brew the maximum number and potency of potions, depending on the quality of your cauldrons.  It can be very time consuming, especially from mid-to-late game when you’ve expanded your store to include 6 cauldrons and are preparing a batch before and after every daily action.  Your experience may start to slow down, but the rich economy this game has to offer fully blossoms to the point where Sylvia can make even more money than the debt she owes. is an odd mix of familiar game mechanics; not entirely defined by any one, but each system adding to the overall design of the game’s identity.  It’s a marvelous tale filled with beautiful characters, exquisite dialogue, heartfelt romance and a mystery that will have you enraptured until the very end.  An absolute treasure of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: Potionomics is a shop management game, and a deck builder game, and a potion crafting game, and a visual novel all in one. With so many different elements being put together, Potionomics lives and dies based on how well everything blends. Fortunately, all of these different elements manage to work together, far more than they clash.Every mechanic in Potionomics is so tied together that it is hard to talk about any of them in isolation. Nothing in the game is too complicated, and I dare say that on their own, each element of the game isn't all that impressive. The deck building is relatively simple, its not THAT hard to manage your shop, potion brewing requires experimentation but its hard to go far astray, and the characters in the game are interesting and likable, but not really that deep. However Potionomics is a game that is more than the sum of its parts. Every part of the game is fun, and you will constantly be whisked from one part of the game to another, keeping each aspect fresh and enjoyable. This is not a game where you can focus on one aspect and ignore the rest, Potionomics demands that you interact with everything it has to offer, and the game is much better for it.While the game does do a good job at combining everything together, there are some cracks where it doesn't work as well. For example, the main use for hero expeditions is to acquire upgrade materials for your equipment, however these upgrades are always very small, and will be outclassed by the next tier of equipment that unlocks after a set amount of time. The only time getting upgrade materials is ever worth it is when you unlock the last tier of equipment. Another example is the competitions. Competitions are the ultimate test of your potion brewing and deck building, however if you brew your potions well enough the deck building aspect can be completely skipped. It can be very anticlimactic to build up to a competition, and then just immediately win because your potions are superior. Fortunately times when I found different elements of the game not working well together were the exception during my time with Potionomics, overall everything blended together harmoniously.There are also some minor complaints I have. Potion brewing could get tedious at times, especially as I progressed through the game and expanded my shop to be able to brew more and more potions. I found myself forgetting the recipes to potions I had already made and having to rediscover them all over again. The game would be much improved if there was some sort of brewing history function where you could review everything that you had made and re-brew directly from there if you wanted another batch. There are also some other gripes: While the brewing menu has filtering options available, the shopping menu doesn't, which made it much harder to find a specific ingredient I was looking for than it needed to be. There are some other small UI issues. Sometimes the social interactions ended up feeling formulaic. But these issues were minor. They never stopped me from enjoying the game.There's one thing I haven't yet mentioned, and its very important. Potionomics is charming. It has wonderful graphics, great character designs with stellar animations that really bring life to the characters. There is a lot of music and its all wonderful. The writing was a surprise to me, but it made me smile and laugh several times over the course of the game. Yes I have some issues with parts of the game's design, but overall, I love what's here. I respect how bold this game is, combining a lot of different elements that I wasn't sure could even could be combined successfully. I will remember my time with this game fondly. If the game sounds interesting to you at all I highly encourage that you play it, I doubt that you will be disappointed.

In the first week, the game was pretty good at teaching you the systems and learning from failures, but after overcoming the first tournament, you're given wayyyyy too much ♥♥♥♥ to really figure out and never given any instructions on what these new systems are. _childDocuments_.review: I'm about at the half way point of progress and am really loving it so far! The characters are a breath of fresh air, and there's a wide array of romance options--the world design is pretty compelling and has clearly a lot more under the surface than you might think. Also I absolutely love the idea of potion making and spending time with your friends, it's just a really comfy idea for a game. My only real wish is that there was less time constraints around it--having to manage your store, gift friends/spend time with them, brewing potions, and all that is legitimately difficult work (who woulda thought). You're constrained by various competitions you have to take part in after about ten days each (so ten days pass then a new competition begins, ,across what I'm assuming is like  a month or so). You have a fairly limited amount of time to accomplish everything you want to do, and unfortunately not nearly enough to hang out with everyone AND progress through the main story And at that you have a pretty massive debt weighed around your neck, all the while. I get that that's the vibe this game is going for, but man, it kinda detracts from the whole experience. I'm still gonna see this through because I really do love this game, I just wish it was a bit less stressful terms of its general vibes.Game is definitely still pretty great, just wish there was consideration made towards it giving you more time to brew, socialize, etc--that's genuinely my only gripe with it!

_childDocuments_.review: This game has lots of positives for me. I will list mainly the negatives here, positives will be added when I get to second playthrough.This game has direction problem and it is unsure of its identity. Either it wants to be tight time management game with focus on running shop (I swear difficulty curve of this game is going down. Not because you are better. But because the game will give you things that would help you couple hours back. When you finally get them, they sort of lower the curve. To the point where you do not understand how the start could have been so hard) or it wants to be charming game with Pixar like characters and potion making on sidelines. Right now the game is stuck in a middle. The game is also (atleast for me) missing some very basic QOL stuff (list of ingredients for locations, saving presets for making potions, maybe loadouts for heroes for specific locations) and has fair share of bugs (first time I saw game breaking by using Esc to open menu or game not realising I have loaded save and letting me keep things I should not have).If you like mainly the hardcore aspect, this COULD be game for you (heard of other potion making games better balanced around this).If you want the game for the charming characters aspect, I would not recommend it. You could very well fail the first boss just because you decided to grind interesting character.Personally, I am somewhere in a middle. I will play the game to the end. But right now, I do not recommend this game for its price. 50% off would be good price to pay for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: At its core, a card battle game bolstered with social sim mechanics that excels at both. Vibrant, beautifully-evocative animation and wonderful dialogue smooths the transitions and unites it all with a delightfully humanist and empathetic charm and whimsy for every single character from friend to foe. What are at first confusing limitations eventually blossom to thrilling and responsive gameplay.However, all of this is pushed on by an anxiety-inducing turn-based time limit that conveys the stakes but doesn't fully allow the player to embrace every aspect of the game. As the days fly on and the side characters reveal more of their well-written personalities, the player has little choice but to press on completing task after task until the game just concludes. A hard stop with a clear main story resolution but, in my case, leaving unexplored threads with the numerous side characters as the game simply booted me out of its world never to return unless I started from the beginning.What keeps this game, for me, from a perfect score isn't the difficulty but the brutality of that ending. The sense of incompleteness and unnecessary gatekeeping comes across as kind of petty at worst, thoughtless at best of what a wonderful world they've created. A reluctant 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Absolutely incredible game, the story is good (), the animation and art work is stunning, and the gameplay is fun and engaging. Like other people, I think the game would benefit a great deal from an endless/free play mode for people that want to spend more time with the card game, potion shop and relationship aspects of the game without feeling crunched for time trying to preparing for competitions. There are a lot of QoL features that could be added, the minimum of which is a proper sorting and filter system for ingredients. Once you get to 10+ pages of ingredients it becomes a pain to find exactly which Megumins you need for the potion you're trying to make. Being able to see the card list/bio book while talking to vendors would help a lot too so you can see your current standing with them and other vendors while you're talking to them.I think that might be all of the criticisms I have for the game at the moment and all of them I imagine should be fairly simple to patch in later down the line, so I'm hopeful that the developers will see the echoes of comments telling them to add these things and they'll get it cooking ASAP.As far as the plus sides go, this game does shop sim REALLY well, there are a lot of aspects that go into brewing your potions that can increase/decrease their price, buffs and enchants you can buy to increase prices/remove negative effects from your potions and ingredients, and shop upgrades you can get to improve the value as well. As you go through the game you actually feel like you're getting better and better at running the shop as you get better equipment, better ingredients and better cards to haggle with. The relationships you can make in the game all feel fleshed out really well, each character has their own personality and backstory you reveal as you increase your rep with them which makes them feel like actual meaningful characters and not just NPCs you buy stuff and get perks from. This game also handles ingredient gathering really well compared to a game this one gets compared to a lot, Recettear. As you progress through the game you unlock heroes you can send out to gather ingredients for you, but they're limited by how well you equip them with potions before you send them off. If you don't properly support your heroes with good potions they're gonna bring back garbage, but if you do send them off with good potions they can bring back a huge haul that'll save you a ton of money over just purchasing ingredients from the shop. There are other methods of gaining ingredients down the line as well that are varied and feel rewarding, but they pop up a little ways into the game so I won't go into it too much, but they all feel like rewarding and viable options for obtaining ingredients. (Please remove the ability to get duplicate cosmetics though, it drives me nuts from a clutter perspective.)I mentioned it before but the time pressure takes away from the really fun and involved gameplay mechanics and while I don't think this is a bad thing at all for a story mode, it feels like it could be a game I'd play for a hundred hours or more if I had the incentive/ability to. Right now my only option after completing the game is to start another run on the exact same path and just.. do it better, or slightly differently. An endless/free play mode and possibly even a set of challenge modes would add a TON of replayability to the game. I'd love to take my time exploring all of the vendor dialogue options, but hanging out with them takes up huge chunks of time out of your day when you're already pressed for time. I feel like you could realistically only see a few characters' highest level (4 time points) dialogue without ruining your run by spending too much time on it, which is a shame because the dialogue options I've seen so far are great.Despite what it might sound like, the good FAR outweighs the bad in Potionomics and if the devs continue supporting/patching the game past release it's going to be one of the absolute best games in the genre. I'd recommend this game to anyone that likes shopkeep simulator games without a second thought. CAPITALISM HO!

_childDocuments_.review: A gorgeous game oozing with charm that'll give your brain a light workout. For 20 bucks, you could do a lot worse. Most video games employ some form of resource loop, especially those with a crafting system. Potionomics is a perfect example, with the game's resource loop being "convert ingredients into potions, convert potions into money, convert money into ingredients, and each conversion takes time, of which you have a finite amount". The game, therefore, is centered around optimizing and accelerating this loop to stay ahead of the curve. If the potion contest rolls around and you're not ready, you'll be running back to an earlier save with your tail between your legs- you have tons of prep time, but not unlimited time.The island of Rafta is bright and gorgeously realized, with a flavorful cast of NPCs who pull double duty as crucial vendors and buddies to hang out with. The character writing is constantly charming, frequently goofy, and sometimes genuinely insightful. None of the NPC plotlines are that subversive- they're pretty unilaterally a 10-rank "introduce the character->unexpected quirk->character has problem->character will solve problem on their own terms" affair, but it's cute enough that it doesn't stale- and the drip feed of new abilities they give you sweetens the pot dramatically.Potion crafting is probably where most players will spend the lion's share of their playtime, staring at a cauldron trying to figure out how best to balance the ratio between green and yellow magic. Generally, brewing is less a question of "I wonder what'll happen" and more of "how do I best get value out of what ingredients I have on hand"- the game makes outcomes quite clear in advance. Getting a fancy new ingredient added to the shop made my mind race, and the feeling of freedom at unlocking a newer, fancier cauldron was always a rush.Once your potions are ready, you can take part in a haggling minigame to pump the value of the potion further, and this is arguably the game's highlight. The card game battle system feels great to wrap your head around, and cards are varied enough to allow for a variety of (varyingly effective) unique playstyles. This haggling minigame comes back at the "boss fight" of each week, trying to convince the judges that you're the best potioner around. These contests are stylish, snappy, and almost over too soon.If the game has an issue, it's that the difficulty increases linearly while the player's ability increases quadratically- not only do you unlock new tools, moves, additional brewing slots, and what have you, but the average player, well, becomes better at the game as they play it. This compounds further when mechanics such as gardening and the vending machine let you start automating steps in the resource cycle, making time even less constraining. Factor in random events that let you leapfrog way out ahead of the curve, and ultimately the game starts out fairly challenging, but past the midpoint, most opposition is little more than a speed bump-  Overall, the game demands competence from an early stage, but never quite manages to test the player's mastery.Any further comments would devolve into splitting hairs- the game could really use a filter option to sort your potions, the music is wonderfully relaxing, value-boosting events prooobably shouldn't stack like that, Muktuk is the best- but honestly I think this game is overwhelmingly worth a try if you're into both cute witches and number puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun and entertaining single player game. It has a lot of content and a lot of small game mechanics that let you interact with the game in different ways. A lot of other reviews have mentioned this is good for min-maxing but it really just works if you want to play however you want to play. It doesn't force a specific play style to progress which lets you go at it in pretty much anyway you see fit. The difficulty curve does drop off pretty fast after the first 10 days because getting ingredients gets much easier so making a potion for the contests is just very easy. That said it provides enough of a challenge and has replayability in going down different date routes or your own challenge runs such as only interacting with certain characters or mechanics, etc. They also added a lot of quality of life changes to the UI which has helped tremendously. I do wish the Stress mechanic was a little more controlled and less just RNG but haggling can very easily become a 1 turn sale with over 100% potion price profits. Being able to pay off your debt with money you raised would be nice but they do have a story they need to tell.It's very refreshing to have a game that isn't hyper-hardcore that punishes for any mis-steps.

Also sorting by maginim qty/qty of a type would be amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I was NOT expecting this game to be as challenging as it was. I failed many, many times but I also really enjoyed playing the game until I finally made it to the end. I love all of the different characters, the art style, the story, and the music. Everything about this game is so charming. Honestly, my only gripe is that the game has an actual ending. I was expecting to be able to have more time at the end to romance and befriend all the characters, since every move in game is valuable and there's always a deadline for finishing potions. I still haven't managed to learn all the character's backstories despite playing the story a few times now because of how limited time is. I wish there was at least one more "level" that allowed us to focus on befriending the different characters, because they're all so wonderful. Other than the issues with managing time between potion making and making friends, I really loved this game and I would highly recommend it. _childDocuments_.review: Great game. Visually it's fantastic and the soundtrack is also top notch. The game starts hard but after a while it becomes pretty easy, to the point that the last 2 competitions were almost instant wins for me. The RNG involved in which ingredients you "discover" may be annoying, but it's not a big deal. I very much enjoyed all aspects of it, even if it has some rough edges, like loading times and too many constraints on a few things like the upgrades. The menus and UI in general could be improved too, like better indexing and being able to type how many of an ingredient you want to buy, instead of clicking "+" and "-" signals. Also sometimes it would be good to have information on some things that you can only get if you waste a time slot to do so(like if you are out of your shop, you can't see several things, like custom order requirements, time left to brew etc)However, I'm baffled to have finished this game and discover it has no post game/endless mode. How can a sim game like this not have it? I was really looking forward to finish all the character arcs and do the last dungeon, but the game just ends after the last competition! Reccetear, an older store management game had a really robust post game, with more story and characters to play with even after you pay the debt. I really hope endless mode gets added with a patch or dlc later on, because I really enjoyed this and would like more.

_childDocuments_.review: Potionomics is a great game with some extremely high visual polish, fun deck building, and fun potion-making. The game is not without minor issues (particulary UI related, such as not having the ability to sort ingredients by value).That being said, it's absolutely worth buying and a great game. I finished my first playthrough in about 35 hours.The game is definitely not a super relaxing experience - you need to use strategy on time management and you can't see everything in one playthrough. But the game is fun enough to warrant replays.A few comments seem to think the game is hard and I think that's not really the case. I had no trouble with any major contest or getting potions ready. However, if you go into this thinking it's Stardew Valley and you have unlimited time to do everything, you'll be disappointed. This is a deckbuilding, potion-making, time management game, and it excels on that front.Even if you're not big into card builders (I'm really not) this is well worth the asking price and really fun. Do yourself a favor and play it. You'll be glad you did.A hearty recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: For being my first dip into the "potion-brewing" archetype of game, i was thoroughly engaged and entertained throughout my playing of Potionomics. There are a lot of great aspects of the game, but a few frustrating ones, as well. I'll get into the highlights now:On a character writing level, I was consistently impressed by the conversations and scenes with each of the side characters's stories. I found each of the cast to be uniquely charming, gorgeously designed, and fully realized. Each storyline hits their emotional beats well and brings an interesting relatability to the oftentimes larger-than-life characters that inhabit Sylvia's story. The setting is also an interesting mix between modern-day and fantasy. Potionomics doesn't bog down too much of its writing with overzealous world building and sticks to its strengths, which is memorable and lovable characters. It's a lighthearted game, and it does its best when leaning into that. The art direction is also spot on and brings about the wonder and whimsy of the world well. Each character's animations reflect them well and give them even more personality. its obvious that all of the characters were lovingly crafted not just narratively, but artistically, as well. On a mechanical level, as well, the game is interesting enough for the length it is and keeps logically ramping up the complexity as the game continues. All around, the game is always engaging and built to keep you invested.However, there are some things about that game that get in the way of its strength. The biggest downside that I have with Potionomics is that the overall gameplay loop feels at odds with the strengths of the game. With the overarching threat of failure in the game being time-driven, it often took away my want to interact with the characters in the story, especially new ones who are introduced up through the mid-game. In the early game especially, I found myself frustrated and anxious with the time constraints and not being able to interface with the social sim aspects as much as I wanted. Mechanically, I think the game is just as complex as it needs to be, and I understood the urgency for the narrative to focus on the deck-building and potion-making, but the mechanical and social sides of the game are intrinsically at odds with one another. This wouldn't be a complaint if there was an endless mode or some kind of post-game, but that is sadly missing from the package. Going into it mostly blind, I expected to be able to finish each character's story after the final time limit, but the game just sort of ends.There are also a lot of little nit-picks about the game that I have. There's a lot of loading screens, some of the higher tier cards are worse than a particular ally's first ones they give you, I thought the game was incredibly easy by the end compared to the excitement of the earlier quotas, the over-arching narrative is a bit standard-fare (though I don't think this is actually that bad because it would distract from the other things a lot if it was overly complex).On the whole, though, none of those nit-picks or negative aspects should stop you from at least trying Potionomics. The core gameplay loop is wildly addictive, and I found myself deeply entrenched in Sylvia's story throughout. The whole game oozes with charm and it knows how fun it is every step of the way. Potionomics is by no means heavy, and it was something that I booted up whenever I wanted a cozy game to relax with. There's a lot more to love about Potionomics than to dislike, and I can easily see myself playing it again in the future. It is well worth the asking price and brought out a lot of joy in my playing of it.Overall, I give it a solid 8.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Literally just finished the game about ten minutes ago, and I enjoyed every aspect of it without reservation, except for one utterly baffling decision. I was completely caught off guard by the fact the game just ends after the last competition, instead of letting you continue playing without any time limits after you've completed your goals. The game has a wonderful gameplay loop and the way each elements affects the others is great, and I expected to be able to continue playing and developing my shop and the relationships with other characters after the main story concluded, so when I was just booted back to the main menu and realized that wasn't possible I was actually really annoyed. I had specifically left much of the content for later as I believed I could just do it after finishing the story, so the fact you're not even given a warning that there's a hard time limit to get everything done is unfortunate. I didn't get around half the cards, I had none of the relationships fully developed, my shop was still unfinished, and there were areas of the game I had never sent any of the adventurers to. I literally feel like I missed at least a third or even a half of the game because I wasn't aware there was a hard time limit on getting everything done. I still recommend the game overall, but it comes with a pretty significant caveat. Not being able to continue playing after the story genuinely soured my experience a bit, and was almost enough for me to not give an overall positive review. Potionomics is a great game, it just comes with one massive flaw.

_childDocuments_.review: Wild to think the size of team it takes and 6 years to make a game that takes about 20 hours to beat. Mind bending really. But that's how it goes!Short version, I recommend this game. I typically think a dollar for an hour of play time is a darn good rate and this game just about meets it. If it goes on sale at all beyond the initial 10% off it's even more worth it. And the fact that this game has been out for less than a week and has had minimal issues and I was able to play through it without any meaningful bugs or issues is a tremendous compliment to the team for actually taking the time to make a ready product. Below may contain spoilers to some extent, without specific details, but broadly. Some notes on the gameplay:*Haggling mini-game is a deck builder, similar to Slay the Spire. You earn cards from NPCS as you build relationship and can really customize your play style.*I found I spent more time in the potion crafting interface than anywhere else. It takes a lot of fiddling to get what you're going for.*The "boss battles" are fun but I think they overcorrected and made them too easy - except the final one - but that's more about the stress impact.*The artwork and graphics are really pleasant. I do wish there was some voice acting.Some feedback/comments for the devs:*Contracts need a rework. Especially with traits, it's not worth the effort. I didn't understand traits well enough to know if one good ingredient will override the others. So I just sold potions straight. Needs a lot of attention to make it a meaningful element later on, especially for the diminishing sense of reward.*Really wish I could upgrade furniture (or at least see what is needed to upgrade) with furniture that's in my shop*The treasure chests seem like a massive rip off*I wish you would add an infinite mode so I could do other achievements like relationship after "winning" as I can't fathom maxing relationship with 10 NPCS in one playthrough and actually completing the goals.*Marketing/Enchanting are overpriced for what they give you*Would love the magamins to be shown on the ingredient in small text*would love a filter system similar to brewing when feeding the slimes or shopping for ingredients by magamins

_childDocuments_.review: Potionomics will probably be my favorite game of the year. I played it almost every day for a month. It was the game I always looked forward to getting a chance to play at the end of the day above all the other games. It gets a strong recommendation from me, but I still have a few critiques.If you are interested in a shop-keeping simulator that falls into the deck builder genre while also building a fun world to work in, filled with cute characters to interact with then this game is for you.It’s important to note though that this game really requires micromanagement. Luckily, there is no real-time pressure so you can take as long as you need to strategize what you will do. That being said, there is a good amount of planning to make for a given day if you want to take the time to plan for it.[Minor game-mechanic spoilers past this point]This is actually what I find to be one of Potionomic’s larger weaknesses. It can sometimes feel like the game is the Swiss army-knife of things to do. Sure the Swiss army-knife has a lot of tools, but replace it with a few specific tools and they will usually be of higher quality. There are so many little tasks that you can plan to take care of in a day that I sometimes found myself wishing that there were less things to micromanage and that there was more depth to the tasks available. The characters are all unique and the game lets you learn about their story while building a relationship with them through various interactions. To me, the world building and characters are the most interesting part about Potionomics and makes it different from the rest! So I would much rather the developers put in little mini-games or some animations for the 4 time spending events you can use with each characters and remove some of the tedious tasks like custom orders and gardening.I personally felt that Potionomics would benefit from focusing on the world and character development that it has rather than the rigid rules of completing each contest. I was able to save up a large amount of money and basically not need to worry about the contests as they came. I would always be ready in the first 2 or 3 days, but then (especially late game) I found myself coming back to the gripe I had initially. People say the time limits are too restrictive, I think they are fine. That being said, I would rather spend my time selling potions day to day and trying to pay off my debt in 50 days with the contest as a nice boost rather than a strict requirement. I feel like this would actually add value to some of the tasks like custom orders. With the contests as a strict requirement, I found the game loop really boiled down to: upgrade cauldron, get ingredients from new worlds, brew contest potions. Then you’d spend the remaining days waiting around, getting coins for the next upgrades and spending some time with the other characters.These are really acute critiques though. As the game is, I really enjoyed playing through it. Calculating out the best potions for each contest, building out a deck to up-sell customers and interacting with the other characters was a lot of fun. If you like games that let you spend time making a lot of careful plans (I would often keep notes of what I planned to do for each day) and doing arithmetic to make the perfect “next move” for a deadline while also giving you a bit of story & character development, then you’ll like this game. I hope to see more from these developers and hopefully more from the brilliant world of Potionomics.
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a few patches short of being truly excellent.The animations are beautiful. The writing is witty. The individual gameplay elements are fun.Once you get past the highly structured first days, however, there is a serious time crunch on every action you do.I'll admit that time management is hard to do well, and I have very specific tastes about the genre. But as other reviews have shown, there is a lot of math working against you in terms of how you spend your time units.This game needs more granular difficulty options. Option to adjust the amount of time available each day would be a great start. The ability to change drop rates, base prices, and other numerical values in the player's favor would also be useful.Until a future patch includes these features, I am afraid I can't finish this game. The inability to play it at my own pace was disappointing. But I have hope the developers will continue to improve and adjust this game, to make it as excellent as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely killer of a game. High production quality all around. Fun story, stunning music, engaging gameplay, beautiful art and writing. _childDocuments_.review: This game is a little bit deceptive. The visuals and writing all suggest this will be a pretty chill run-a-shop/light dating sim type experience. It is not that at all. This is a time optimization puzzle game. You have" 10 days" (really around 54 time slots) to accomplish a set number of tasks. Then do it again but harder, repeat 5 times.Now, I really appreciate that this time pressure simulates what the main character is going through. I also think that the time could be doubled or even tripled and the game could still achieve that same effect. As it stands, the time limit feels too punishing even on the 3rd cycle.The unfortunate thing is that I really like this game's mechanics. I can see a LOT of care and effort has been put into the character animations, the writing, even the complexity of potion crafting is a really cool puzzle. I was really hoping that after the last contest, there would be an option to just continue running Sylvia's shop. I really like this world and these characters and these mechanics. But after learning that's not the case, I find my motivation to get through the game dying.  It's really unfortunate when a core mechanic makes a game a chore rather than the joy it so obviously could be.

_childDocuments_.review: As an avid optimizer when playing games, this game isn't quite built for that type of play. By making the best potions every day, and extracting the most value possible out of each day, I started maxing out potions when only 65% through the game. When there's nothing more to work towards, the game gets increasingly tedious. You can definitely find fun in this game, through the many different systems and personality of the characters, but the difficulty isn't crafted all that well.
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: The game may have a super colorful and friendly look with very animated and memorable characters, but once you actually start it, you get into a world of deck-building and strict time management where it is a balancing act of all the opportunities you have at your disposal.The premise is that you have inherited your uncle's potion shop, but unfortunately with that, his immense debt he incurred while putting together said shop. It might seem challenging to pay all the installments, but wait! There is a weekly contest where you can win big money and big prizes, just enough to pay off what you owe and free yourself from the shackles of your surprise debt. Seems pretty straight-forward, right? Just win the contests and you're done!To be honest, I was overwhelmed a bit at first with the first series of contests, and I always felt like I was up against the wall with trying to be ready before the big day. There are many options to make use of, and you only have a limited time to do them before the contest whereupon your failure means a game over (fortunately, they do have manual saving and auto-saves for each day so you have the opportunity to roll back to fix your mistakes should they happen). You can brew/improve potions, sell potions to customers, as well as visit/hangout with friends, but using your time wisely to both create what is asked and keep your income level high enough to afford upgrades to make and sell more potions involves a lot of plate spinning. This all includes seeing/improving relationships with the many characters you meet, which both gets you access to cheaper versions of their services and card to add to your deck. You even get to deal with daily modifiers that affect those options, you will have to be flexible and not expect one idea to work 100% of the time. So there are many systems/mechanics they introduce to you over time, which definitely can be advantageous to reach any goal you are currently aiming to accomplish.The potion brewing is generally straightforward, you can either use a recipe to help guide yourself, or improvise to balance out the right particular elements (in this case, A/B/C/D/E) to make the potion you intend to create. There are restrictions and such based on your equipment, but basically you want the levels to be on par so you have a chance for a boost upon completion as well as adding some positive characteristics to it so the potion is worth more (ex. add attributes like a good smell). They offer filters for all your ingredients and elements and that helps filter down the list. The only real issue I had with the brewing is that while you drag and drop (or double-click) your ingredients to add them to the brew, there doesn't seem to be an ideal way to check your trait balance to see what the result will be. You have to hover over each ingredient individually to see its traits, and sometimes even move it around (which sometimes can cause it to be accidentally removed from the cauldron and have to re-add). They seem almost there with the brewing process, but it's still a bit fiddly and frustrating in that regard. I did spend a fair amount of time using different ingredients to get just the right quality and output while not exceeding restrictions, especially in the late-game challenges, which was actually enjoyable and required some re-thinking at times.The deck-building aspect was fairly easy to work and understand (though I am no expert in the genre, but I do enjoy games like Slay the Spire / Monster Train), but I probably stuck close to my original options and used the new cards I received. I rarely ever had high stress levels outside of the late-game, but there's a lot of planning ahead based on the customer's buffs they use on themselves or the debuffs/stress they inflict upon you. As someone who definitely did not make a well balanced deck, I still made it through with little issue, and the character relationship upgrades earned me new cards that helped form it into something at least good enough to beat the game, so I'd call that a win.I really did enjoy the characters with all their particular looks and animations, as well as the dialogue for each one (especially the cats). There are many jokes where most of them hit and some heartfelt moments to see when you increase your relationship level enough. I somehow did feel extremely put-off in the early game though, since while I loved the characters, I felt I was barely able to spend any time hearing what they had to say because any extra time spent with them was time I wasn't getting to focus on my potion work. I eventually did find a sort of loop to both focus on upgrades/potion making and then I would have that finished early enough to catch up with all the characters. I was only see all of what one character had to offer (#TeamSaffron), but the rest I may look up online to see where the remaining interactions go. While the story itself was generally fairly predictable, I think the characters really liven things up and give you a good reason to see more and more of what they have to offer.I did enjoy this game overall, even with the stressful beginning, so I recommend it, but you have to be prepared for what you're getting. This is a game with a strict schedule of the goals you must overcome in a certain timeframe, and once it's over, there is no extra challenges or free-form "just make potions and sell them" mode. While it felt like a struggle with all the mechanics laid out in a fairly quick fashion in the beginning, I was able to turn the tides and be well prepared for the later challenges both flush with money and opportunities to spend time with the friends and worrying less about the potion requirements. If this sounds interesting, give it a look and see if it is a style of game that fits your interests.
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very fun, beautiful and worth buying- if you want something very fast-paced and stressful. There isn't a lot of time in a day, and often you have to forfeit romancing characters and leveling up relationships to try and get enough ingredients to make a couple potions to sell. You have a short window of time to prepare for the big competition, and if you lose, you have to start over from either a later save file or just restart the game. I do enjoy this game. I put ten hours into it the first day I got it. But it would be a lot better if there was any downtime. You don't even get to keep any of the money you win from the competitions. Your reward is that you get to keep playing the game. I constantly feel like I'm too far behind, that I have no way of winning, that I don't have time to do the fun things because I'm constantly stuck trying to get ahead of the competition or get some money. If you enjoy fast-paced resource management games or business tycoon games, you'll like this. If you wanted a chill, relaxing game with emphasis on dating and the other characters. this might not be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: After having played and beaten the first and second tournament, I came to the realisation that this was not the experience I was hoping for. Beating the tournaments was not particularly hard, however, it was very stressful as other reviews have pointed out. You will spend more time planning your day than enjoying the interaction with characters.The story is interesting and the characters are all very different and fun, but sadly you won't have time to interact with any of them properly because you are incredibly limited by time. Maybe an animal-crossing type of gameplay - where you pay off your store at your own pace - would have been more fitting, and that was honestly what I was expecting when I played the demo.This game also seriously needs a sorting option for all the different ingredients that you can acquire (you can sort by type of magimin, but for some reason it does not auto-sort not by amount, lowest to highest, as you might expect). The soundtracks are also fantastic, with each character having their own, and some of them are extremely wonderful, unfortunately, this game missing voiceover, which I think is acceptable. Potionomics is a game that combines various elements, such as Sims and card games, of course, you may raise the price of your potions by bargaining. Potionomics isn't a challenging game, but if you're excellent at making potions, you don't always have to negotiate to win. I absolutely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd give this game a 10/10 score but keep in mind that it's very subjective, it really depends on your sense of humor, how well you deal with switching between a few different tasks and how much you care about story mostly. Also it's just incredibly polished and with great art both visual and music.The card part of the game can be almost entirely skipped if you manage well your resources and make good enough potions, but it's still a pretty fun part with simple but interesting mechanics, not the best card game but it sure is good, the managing part is nice as well after you get used to it and accept that it takes time to make decisions but they're always limited by the time units you spend on them, a bit restrictive but it works to make the game hard enough to be interesting while still being easy enough to be fun.The story though isn't great, it's very simple with no incredible and unexpected twists, you can see every twist coming very early if you pay enough attention but it's still a nice story, very wholesome and just a chill time.TL;DR: It's a great game and I'd recommend it to anyone who gets interested enough by the trailers, especially considering how much it costs, even if you don't like it you'll still certainly have enjoyed at least enough to be worth the price

_childDocuments_.review: I loved every moment of this game. Its core mechanics are simple - as in, while visual novels, math-based crafting sims, and card games can be very complex, they can and do get by on much simpler presentation. Butevery part of Potionomics is eyecandy. The UI icons are cute! The character designs are fun and instantly recognizeable! The character animations are fantastic (probably my favorite part of the whole presentation - so much charm and polish on them)! Even things thar are more "budget", such as having 2D backgrounds, was done in a way that makes it look not cheap, but cute and exactly as the devs wanted it. I'm completely charmed by how much effort and detail went into this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Edited: Finished the game now, and overall it's a lot of fun. There are a lot of mechanics to juggle with the limited amount of time you have, and I think that time pressure adds a level of challenge that's a lot of fun if you're into management-type games. My main critique is just that the difficulty curve is a bit weird, and by the final week I was kind of coasting along no trouble. This did give me time to have fun trying out deck combos though.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to love this game, but I just can't. The style, the animation, the characters I love all of it so much it really reminds me of the game Wildstar (RIP) which I adored. but there is a reason game developers don't put fail states into their games any more. There's nothing fun about having to start all over for some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason. Weather or not you find the game easy or hard does not really matter. Fail states are an archaic and outdated system in gaming that was meant to take your quarters at an arcade or make a game last as long as possible. I got through the first ten days with little trouble but always having the looming threat of having to start all over from the beginning kills all enjoyment for me. So I see no reason for me to keep playing. I'm going to refund the game and go play something I can enjoy without feeling stressed out the whole time. TLDR 5/10 fail state ruins the hole game for me

_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: Well polished game, and yet with lots of flaws to prevent it from being a game I want to replay again and again. Which is evident with the lack of NG+ support or a more casual free play mode after beating the game.The game is heavily structured around the 10 day tournament arc and the quality of those 10 days can be significantly effected by randomness.The game lacks a proper way to organize your herbs so you are punished for keeping a wide variety of ingredients. A simple sort by Amount of selected Ingredient type would really help with finding where the heck I put the +A18 ingredients After 10-20 days the Capitilism portion of the game really seems irrelevant as all you are paying for is base upgrades and ingredients. Because of that  I spent the rest of the game leveling relationship which has the perk of giving you cards which would've been great for improving my capitalism if I felt my money had purpose. I do think the tournament arc was a compelling way to pull the story along but it came as a hindrance to core mechanics of the game.I also feel like the RNG of the game made it more difficult to balance the user experience, and as such, there will be wildly different complaints of difficulty and quality of experience playing this game.
