_childDocuments_.review: Read the description on the store page before buying so you know what you're getting into. A big improvement over Recettear and an easy recommend to anyone who enjoyed that game.A fantastic, charming shop management game with some light relationship and deckbuilding mechanics bolted on. The game follows the formula established by Recettear very closely, with a main game loop that consists of brewing new potions, selling them, and managing a cast of supporting characters to procure new ingredients so you can do it all again. Time is your most valuable resource, and it does a pretty great job of making you feel the pressure of barely staying afloat under the crushing weight of debt while also providing enough time and space to learn and experiment.Like Recettear, days are broken up into six segments with varying actions like brewing potions or traveling taking up a certain number of segments. But most of these options can be done simultaniously and learning how to balance them is critical to your success; potions will keep bubbling and adventurers exploring while you do other things, and you can visit multiple people while only paying the time to travel once, etc.At the end of each 10-day period is a competition, which will give you a set of potions with specific requirements that must be met in order to pass. Failing this is a game over, and it is the main source of time crunch. You will typically go into a new week with no real idea how to make the required potions or lacking the resources to brew them to the needed quality, but the game gives you more than enough time to experiment, upgrade your facilities, and keep expanding your inventory while still sneaking in social time to keep your stress levels low and build up your deck/access to discounts.Particularly good are the animations and the soundtrack written by Greg Nicolette and performed by the Budapest Scoring Orchestra. The game's presentation is polished in the extreme, and it looks, sounds and fees like it adheres to a cohesive theme despite mixing a few different art styles. Character dialogue is mostly charming and competently written, and the cast does a decent job of being inclusively diverse... but there is a complete absence of voice acting, if that bothers you. The dating options are also opt-in and generally obvious, and can be ignored if platonic business relationships are more your thing.Potionomics is a fantastic little potion shop simulator with a satisfying game loop, charming presentation, and a general look and polish that punches above its weight class. It can be challenging, and there are no difficulty settings at the time of writing, but it gives you the space to learn and the tools to succeed. If you're a fan of Recettear, this should be an instant buy. For anyone else, there's a lot here to love, but you should make sure to read the store description closely to make sure your expectations are in line with what it offers.First, a lot of people seem to be getting it assuming it's a dating simulator and then leaving disappointed because they can't breeze through or ignore the game's core mechanics so they can romance the cast. This is a shop management game first and foremost. People going into the game with these kinds of expectations are setting themselves up for disappointment. You might want to take a look at Boyfriend Dungeon or Kardboard Kings instead.Second, a lot of people seem to be getting slammed by "RNG" and the time mechanics. I'm less sure what to offer here, as I'd suggest a lot of these players may not be fully grasping how to properly manage their time in the game. Even allowing for entire days of experimentation and socializing with the cast, I found that I had no problems breezing through the first couple of competitions with potions graded an entire tier above what was being requested and about 40% of my time remaining.This is not a brag; I say this because, yes, while luck is a factor in what items you uncover, there are also a ton of options you can take advantage of to help mitigate it. Early adventures take little time and can be easily multitasked, you can brew potions to increase drop rates. Expeditions offer gaurenteed access to rare materials and some ability to target them specifically, even if you're having trouble with an area. And most importantly: expanding Quinn's shop ensures that so long as you've seen an ingredient , you can obtain more.Other things that might help would be making sure you  have something brewing, making use of fuel to speed up brewing, and prioritizing shop upgrades like new shelves and particularly new cauldrons so you can increase the size and quality of your potion output. Try to plan around getting all of your shopping and socializing done at the same time so you only pay the travel cost once. If you're aggressively pursuing all of your avenues for getting new materials, luck shouldn't be a run-killer. If you're still having trouble, focus on blowing past the requirements for two of the easier potions to win your competitions. You can actually win outright without even judging the third potion.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first played, I was (like many others) disappointed that I lost horribly on the first competition, and had to restart. It feels like the game doesn't indicate difficulty, because you initially set the stress level yourself. I was frustrated and ready to quit. To anyone struggling with that I implore you to ensure that you have at least  stars on your entered potions (I did not, and that was my mistake).After I got a handle on things it was a breeze. Making potions, making friends, and balancing time. It's a really fun deck building game, that I will recommend to everyone. The writing and the characters feel alive, so much so, that I want to max all of the relationships to learn the stories. However that's extremely difficult to do on a play through, and certainly your first play through, and that leads me into my few notes about the game: It took me about 40 hours to finish the game and I assumed that I could max my shop and relationships after the final boss, however that doesn't seem to be a possibility. I'm unsure if I will have the draw to play everything through again just to max all relationships, sadly. I feel that more play throughs would feel attainable if one play through didn't take 40 hours - but also I suppose you could go back into random auto saves to change relationship outcomes?Secondly, due to the 50 day limit, I was wasting a lot of time making potions and making money when it wasn't necessary for post-game. I could have been spending a  more time on relationships or even just choosing to not make as many potions, because it becomes repetitive after a while.Finally, I wish there were an auto-buy feature and a recipe saver because clicking through everything does get more tedious the further on you get in the game. I also wish you could save more than one deck so you could experiment more easily.Please know, these notes are minor and don't ruin the feel of the game. The conclusion and illustrations had me tearing up at the end, because I feel like there are so many more adventures to have in Rafta that I'm going to miss out on!P.S.: Say what you will, but if there's ever a DLC post-game I want to be able to date the bank-lady-witch. I'd play through the story again for some new relationship options, harder contests, and a new ability to combine potions.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 no real complaints.I need to put this at the top:  My first playthrough I kind floundered around and when i got to my first competition got completely stomped.  But I took that experience and started again, now knowing what I needed to prioritize and the game became TREMENDOUSLY easier. Get your ingredients, It is all about ingredients.  You get those by sending your heroes out. You get a good cauldron and you can put more stuff into it and make better potions, its that easy. Playthough the first 10 days just experiencing the game and then re-evaluate and try again, you will succeed.     Potionomics is exactly what I was looking for in a chill game.  I LOVE that there is no timer and that you can take your time advancing through the game at your own pace. The game puts goals to achieve within a certain number of days, but you can achieve and surpass those goals very quickly which leaves you time to go out in the world and hangout with the various characters and do errands and just enjoy the beautiful and bustling island of Rafta.     The potion brewing math is so fun to figure out.  I have paint and wordpad opened up with various equations trying to figure out how to min/max every potion. It is really exciting to unlock the next tier of ingredients which make brewing stronger potions (which seemed impossible at the start) a breeze.  It gives you such a great feeling of advancement and accomplishment that you can just produce a stronger potion with ease compared to the start of the game.     I really enjoy the card "battles" in this game.  You can build really cheap decks that can rack up the interest quickly... but you have to invest your time in building relationships with your friends so you can unlock some really deadly cards.  The haggling sessions get more difficult as the game goes on but its never anything that stresses me out too much.  At the end of the day, just going into a haggle session gives you more interest than just throwing it into an auto purchase thing so you don't have to feel too bad if you have to end the sale early because you are still getting a good markup on the potion without having to really commit to eating stress if you don't want to.  Each card has a fun art on it of your friends and it never feels like I'm rushed into anything bad.  Again, my favorite thing is that you can take your time planning your strategy because there is no timer counting you down and rushing you.  Everything can be calculated and planned just how you want it to go.  I thoroughly enjoy this part of the game its really fun and its really cool to have that one picky customer come in trying to stress you the **** out and you just say "I'm not letting this person stress me out, just take the damn potion and get outta my store" OR that feeling when you get just the right combination of cards to max out the sale and make a very pretty penny.     The characters and dialog and story are so charming and cute.  Every character has their own unique personality and it is all reflected through everything about them. From the music, to the dialog, to their aesthetic it really established a deeper connection with each character.  I really like that you have the opportunity to romance ANY of your friends. Sylvia is my favorite bi-sexual/pan-sexual protagonist.  She is everything that I want a witch to be.  She is relatable and awkward and surprisingly smooth when she needs to flirt. I LOVE that there is a non-binary character.  I love the bisexual energy. Big mowie-wowie mammers. Demon lady cleavage. Lots of people have big hats.  Everyone is just (I know I keep saying it) so unique.     The art style and animations are really well done.   Every character has their own unique emote that they do.  As you progress through the game you obtain cards from them and when Sylvia uses the cards in "battle" she actually does the emote from the character, which is a really nice touch. There is so much expression in everybody's movements, even the NPC customers that come in.  They have so much personality even though they just come in to buy a potion and maybe have 3 or 4 lines. I really feel the emotions from each character.  Sometimes they give you a specific look or sometimes they are animated with a specific quirk that makes each of them extremely unique.  I love the little chibi animations that pop up sometimes they are super cute!     The story of potionomics feel pretty special to me.  I really love the world building.  It is eased onto you as you progress through the game.  Sylvia is the newcomer to the island (as are you) so you get to learn with her about the lore and history of Rafta and its inhabitants.  Its a little predictable but the story doesn't hold your hand it just feels pretty organic as you advance through your 50 days.  The lore of each character is really cool and you have to unlock little bits as you flirt and build your relationship with each character it feels like a reward and draws you closer to that character. The climax of the story is lovely and it just builds so well on itself.     The music is really dynamic in this game.  Each character has their own unique theme that plays when you visit them.  The theme also changes depending on what time of day it is.  What a great work of art and what a great detail.  The theme is still there during every time of day but the music changes to be much more chill at night or a little brighter and peppier during the day.  It really sets the mood and gears you up for being excited like an adventure or prepares you to be more somber and ready to talk about real serious things with your friends.     The sound effects are really bombastic.  When you get hit with that debuff or stress you can REALLY feel it hitting you with the sound design.  The little bloops and plops and bleeps as you pick your ingredients and plop them into your caldron makes it feel like you are really doing these things.  Like I'm so invested that if i plunk ingredients in I can almost feel the splash of it hit me!  When you get that sale you can hear the number on the till going up as you rake in that cash, its very satisfying.     As I wrap up this review, I'm realizing just how much I like this game and how good it is.  Its like a graphic novel with Hearthstone gameplay and role playing flirtations AND MATH.  All the images are very cute and colorful.  The music is transportive. The sound design is very visceral. The characters unique and charming. The story is a delight. Thank you for making this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: After 11 hours into the game, I can say there's lots of fun things about this game. The characters are fun and quirky and the deck-building haggling system is unique, but all of that gets lost in the ridiculous, almost impossible execution of the game. Despite what you may think after checking out the cutesy animation style and cliched storyline, this is not a cozy resource management game. If you're not meticulously planning each and every move and resetting your day every time you accidentally forget to set a potion to brew or hang out with a friend for a little too long, you cannot pass this game. Oh, pardon me. Even if had the foresight and planning skills of Jeff Bezos, you still wouldn't be able to pass this game--unless you're equally as lucky. Grab your lucky rabbit's foot and scour your garden for a four leaf clover because whether you can get the items you need for potions or store upgrades is completely dependent on the RNG gods that be. Will Mint or Baptiste bring you back the missing ingredient to finally get that second cauldron? What about that blue-dominant ingredient you need for the competition potion? Only Lady Luck herself knows (and the odds are NOT in your favor). I was so excited about this game, but the points I love have been completely overshadowed by my frustration and disappointment with the difficulty level. Even if you do everything right (which is already extremely challenging) you still can't get anywhere if you don't get lucky with ingredients. If a normal mode difficulty with a less strict timeline and more balanced drops ever becomes available in the future, give me a ring.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is *shockingly* hard - it is quite possible for your save to end up in a no-win state. I'm considering restarting but I'm honestly so shellshocked by how tight the time and money management is I can't possibly bring myself to give it another go. _childDocuments_.review: I love this game to absolute pieces. I'm a strumpet for some good dating sim mechanics, and Potionomics definitely delivers. Not only are the romances heartwarming and wholesome, but the friendships are equally touching. All of the characters are so well fleshed out, it gives a depth to the relationships that really brings the game to life. The time management aspect is stressful, but it gets much easier as the game goes on, so as long as you can get past that first week you're basically in the clear. The deck building and potion-making mechanics are great, the plot is thicc- this game is a 10/10 and I'm so excited to play through it again.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: This is not a management heavy game. The best aspects of the game are in regards to characters, this is a narrative game, not a tycoon, though the tycoon is the core gameplay loop. I came into it expecting the shopkeeping and brewing to be the biggest draw to the game, but they are not what I at least found most compelling. A significant amount of time and effort is in the characters, you will get the most out of this game if you enjoy character narratives, and do not have much experience with strategy or management games.I enjoy the game, but I do have a lot of nitpicks against it.Firstly however, good stuff.-Game is incredibly charming with very good art, characters, sound design, and writing, even the flavor text is great-Core game play loop feels very connected-No completely useless mechanics, though some are inherently better than others-Free post game content-Free love lets me see more cute character scenes easily-Characters are distinct, fun to interact with, and have very good story-lines and developmentNegatives/feedback recommendations:-A little short in length, this is not a game you sink more than at most 80 hours into, but realistically you'll get 20-30 for a full playthrough. However, your mileage may vary. Especially since I personally don't see much replay-ability.-The difficultly doesn't feel to increase at the same pace as the player's strength and skill does on normal difficulty, especially in regards to shop prices when you can make tens of thousands before Finn if you play well-Some choices made by characters feel out of place, especially Sylvia in the Salt and Pepper story line, and also the conflicting nature of Maven's story presented by Saffron is never expanded upon, and seemingly is completely ignored later on-Due to the way bosses work in the game, you often end up not even facing their unique mechanics, skipping interesting interactions in the game, one way to fix this could be to make there be a setting to cap certain things you can do in competitions, such as a maximum on the price your potion can be, and a maximum number of cards you could draw-There is an infinite combo in the game, same problem as above, fighting the final boss especially should be challenging. The infinite can get about 700% extra value on medium, meaning you realistically would only need potions worth 600 gold to win, and you can do it pretty reliably before your competition can even get a turn in. Why is this in the game, why make it so the player just doesn't fight the boss, it's not fun to just win with no effort after a huge 10 day build up. -There's no indication anywhere of how people responded to previously given gifts, I have bad memory and mixed up plant and fungi a bunch, so this hurt-Severe lack of hotkeys, please just let me tab between my cauldrons when brewing, and use right click to quick move ingredients instead of double clicking -No ability to get rid of older items, I do not need 2 pages of cauldrons-Lack of numerical indicators in certain spots, knowing ho close I am to next friendship level up, or the ratio of my magimins in my current brew would help a lot-When crafting at either Muktuk or Saphron, you can't see how many of the ingredient you need you DO have, in other words you don't know if you're using your last of something, or how close you are to an upgrade-More achievements, more exploration areas, more potion varieties, and more craft-ables would be nice, having universally insanely powerful end game stuff that can't be contested with feels like a post game style to me, having to carefully brew your final competition potions instead of just "Shoving as many magimins in the pot as possible" would be nice, or a much longer exploration zone but with weaker monsters, and vice versa.-Having the minute details of potions matter in adventures, if you make them drink potions with negative traits they might charge you more, and vice versa. Also percentage based potions being more effective by stars as well as overall grade.-Custom orders need to pay more for the hassle of all the specific traits they want their potions to have, also could be interesting if they sometimes wanted negative traits instead-The farm slimes should have a standardized price in my opinion-Couple of annoying bugs, specifically having issues exiting the game sometimes with the menu not correctly loading, and adding/removing fuel not correctly registering, there are work arounds, but these bugs were pretty common for me-Tooltips on how much loot is estimated to come from certain drops, what exactly something like environmental disruption means, or what exactly increasing the price of potions on display shelves actually does would be very helpful-Some form of customer/potion encyclopedia on what customers tend to be interested in buying, what strategies customers use during haggling, what potions sell for at a base price, combined with a little flavor text, would go a long way for not an incredible amount of work-No voice acting for the hangout scenes, narrator text, and some haggling lines, I know it may be a lot of work, but the contrast that happens is distracting from the immersion-Heroes leveling should have at least slightly more impact, and be more frequent. More potion tolerance say every 8 levels, mana every 10, extra loot capacity every 5, higher chances of rare items and more items overall at some intervals, that sort of stuff would make the levels seem actually important.-Ability to upgrade the vending machine mimic. Also occasionally remind the player it even exists.-Please let me re-watch the final credits without doing the final battle again, the art is amazing

_childDocuments_.review: I wish the game did not get so many negative reviews as this is honestly one of the best games I have played in a long time. The animations are so cute and getting able to invest in every new character that comes by really helps the game feel fresh. A lot of systems get added over time that help a ton with making money and it feels like you actually upgrade as you go along. I understand why many people are having issues with the first part of the game and the bug that is there does not help. If you however just spam healing and mana early on you can win incredibly easily without any RNG. Just get those potions and send your hero out to the woods then just continue talking to people as the woods trip only takes 1 turn. So not only can you get cards from people and well get to meet and learn more about them. You get LOT of materials that can then be used to get quick sales for the cauldron upgrades (which you need to get higher quality potions). So yes I get that people are having issues but there are ways you can just play the game meet people and still have no problem with getting the first quest done. If you just meet people you can barter up your potions at the tourney like CRAZY because he has 30 patience. Like I was at least 150+ down from winning and just bartered it up.

_childDocuments_.review: The time crunch is one of the worst things I've ever encountered. Such a shame because the rest of the game is great. I love the characters, I love the potion brewing mechanics, but the looming, ticking clock of the competitions (and the fact that if you fail them, you have to restart TEN WHOLE DAYS OF PROGRESS) is this game's Achilles' Heel. You do not have freedom to explore the game's world, it's mechanics, to talk to the characters, to hang out with them, to try new potions, make mistakes, learn from them and keep going. There are so many different mechanics in this game that you simply do not have the time to tinker with, as if you make a single mistake it is very easy to get to the point where you cannot win the competition. It feels like the game wants you to save scum to figure out the best routes, which is unengaging gameplay in my opinion. I think this game suffered from a mismatch between the gameplay and it's aesthetic and vibe. I was expecting something more laid back, more chill, more akin to Stardew Valley: and compared to a game like Stardew Valley, where time pressures do exist (seasons prevent some crops for example), at the end of the day, you are free to explore the games multitude of mechanics at your own pace. That is what I want for this game, and if they removed the Time Crunch and allowed players to simply enter competitions whenever they felt ready/comfortable to, I would come back to play it and recommend this game to everyone in a heartbeat. But as is, I cannot. Also it's ridiculous that the game ends and there is no Free Play/Endless mode or a New Game Plus.

_childDocuments_.review: A crunchy management challenge dressed up with outstanding art and infectious enthusiasm, Potionomics is a superb and vibrant debut by Seattle-based Voracious Games, and one of the most enjoyable management games I’ve played in years. As many reviewers have noted, the game is more challenging than its bright colours and dating-sim elements might suggest. I, personally, loved it, finding the difficulty lent an urgency and gravity to decision-making lacking, for instance, from the similarly-themed Moonlighter. But be forewarned that a degree of min-maxing is needed not to tank the regular challenges Potionomics will throw your way. It would seem to cry out for a more open-ended, Stardew Valley-esque game mode to cater to all tastes, but currently its taxing and somewhat linear campaign is all that’s on offer.If you’re still on board after this caveat, you’ll find Potionomics to be a deep, satisfying management sim with an enticing array of interlocking systems. Taking over your uncle’s failed potion shop in a booming fantasy frontier town, you’ll set about acquiring ingredients, concocting them into potions, upgrading your emporium and haggling with customers. This involves juggling limited time and money, weighing short-term pain against long-term gain, engaging in a light card-battler haggling minigame, and cultivating relationships. Ah, relationships. Though you could skip all of the cutscenes and focus on the management, you’d miss out on Potionomics’ well-written and chuckle-worthy dialogue, as well as the gameplay benefits bestowed by buttered-up merchants and adventurers. Hailing from the Stardew School of Bestowing Daily Trinkets on the Target of Your Desires Until They Love You, there’s a dating sim tucked in here amongst the game’s fistful of systems, offering the opportunity to romance men, women, a neutrally-gendered person, a hunky walrus, a multi-armed moth-lady, and two cats, if that’s your thing. The character arcs mostly develop well, and can be quite moving. The game’s overall plot is more straightforward, with a couple of twists you can see coming a mile off, though well-served by smug villains it’s supremely satisfying to topple come challenge day.No discussion of Potionomics would be complete without considering its art. This is bold, charismatic stuff work by an obviously talented team. Quippy and arch without quite breaking the fourth wall, and with large-eyed characters vigorously emoting at one another, Potionomics was most reminiscent to me of superior latter-day Disney. Think Wreck-It Ralph and Moana, with perhaps just a nod to Studio Ghibli in the gorgeous hand-drawn backgrounds, a talking familiar and a cheery fire-sprite named Combustopher. The music is wonderful; catchy leitmotifs do a lot for the world’s characterisation, while urgent strings and guitar strokes add drama to haggling “battles.” Confident solos backed up by lush strings reminded me of Super Mario Galaxy’s soundtrack; high praise indeed. Potionomics’ composer and instrumentalists deserve major props. The game also succeeds wonderfully in depicting characters who are sexy but not sexualised. The sometimes-overwrought design and flamboyant animations are just a little too much for my tastes; restraint is not one of the Potionomics’ many virtues. Tolkien purists might also bridle at anachronistic digressions about ramen and ice-cream sandwiches, reminders about the importance of self-care and “letting your freak flag fly.” It’s certainly a distinctly American, millennial take on fantasy; a reflection on contemporary life, and a celebration of diversity with fantastical races as metaphor, not the solemn pseudo-mediaeval fair some people seem to prefer in their fictional worlds.Potionomics’ riotous and debonair fiction may be at odds with its demanding gameplay, then, brewing a concoction that may not be to everyone’s tastes. If not, Two Point Hospital offers similarly top-notch management challenge with a more restrained, British sense of humour, while Strange Horticulture and Potion Craft were Potionomics’ less libertine stable-mates in the 2022 boom in running fantastical shops. But I had an absolute blast with Potionomics. The world is a delight to explore, the visuals and music are outstanding, and the gameplay is varied and compelling. A generous and sumptuously-realised single-player delight, that this is the first-time work of a small team makes it all the more impressive. I can’t wait to see what Voracious Games do next. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Here’s a big yes. This game puts in the cauldron tons of good things to make a “superb brew”, providing a refreshing adventure. * The story, with a fun start, an enjoyable cast of characters highlighted by rather good writing and vivid animations.* Especially during the two first weeks, I was always figuring new strategical moves to make my business thrive (some of which I share in the tips at the end of the review).* Brewing potions like this really hit home with me, it’s rather fun and given the variety, you can beat the game with multiple strategies.* Haggling is easier in game than IRL… I felt like a top merchant, supplying customers with what they need at the best price (from the vendor’s perspective!), toping 2 million gold by the end of my playthrough.* First, there are too many loading screens! It really ruins the rhythm of an otherwise fluid game.* I felt like there were too many mechanics in the game. It’s not hard to adapt but it makes a “complete day” in game unnecessarily long… everyday. This is further aggravated by the lack of quality of life options for brewing your potions (saving recipes, filtering and organizing your potions) of preparing loadouts for the heroes that would help tremendously accelerate the pace of the game by ripping the boring parts. Special mention to the services provided by a “certain someone” that masks the natural potion traits characteristics of ingredients, making it a headache if you brew potion during the day.* Some mechanics aren’t explained and you’ll have to figure them for yourselves, just like how potion traits adds up or down depending on the number of ingredients with them.* Custom orders are a good idea with poor execution. They might be somewhat useful during the first two weeks but they get too troublesome for the reward they provide after that. At the end of the game, I could sell potions at more than 10k gold each, double the average value of painfully boring custom orders…* Hero expeditions really don’t feel rewarding, I'm not even sure they are worth the tons of potions you have to provide to get some measly ingredients…* Oh the hurt when the random daily events ruin your carefully thought out surefire plan brewing over several days in a hurtful twist of fate. Save for competitor’s moves that should stay unpredictable, the rest should be displayed on the calendar in advance to better organize and especially not feel down missing out a huge opportunity.* Since I made a lot of money, I really wanted it to be displayed with 7 digits, not 6! Not a major complaint, that’s just my ego writing for me…And last of them, my major grip is the end of the game. Since it’s story-driven, I understand that once you beat the challenge, though maybe “challenge” is an overstatement, you’ve proven you can be successful under pressure so there isn’t any meaning in going further down the line without an objective. I don’t have ideas how to, I would really like some other game modes, anything that would prolong the game. Because yes, even if I complain and put flaws on the front shelve besides the good points, I still found it enthralling enough to get all the successes in one playthrough and leave a review, wanting more of what this game can offer, maybe just not over a 50+ hours loop.I read that some people found the game difficult. Don’t know how they did but maybe I can help out.* Procuring rare ingredients is do or die in this game, so you have to make sure, especially at the beginning, to combo the services of the guild and of the ingredients vendor.* Some rare ingredients are best used when you have the necessary equipment to maximize the output and claim victory in the competitions with the best potions.* It’s simple but “make some cash, invest in better equipment and then make more cash”, rinse and repeat. Better potions, more potions, more shelves to sell potions provide the increase in income you need to beat the game. Be sure to befriend the merchants that provide the most useful services (and for which you want to get reductions the fastest) and be sure to have the most money to invest at the start of each week.* Separate the potions you want to sell and the options you want to use for hero expeditions. The latter only require “potion tier”, you don’t care about their quality or traits otherwise. This is even better when you plan for potion that will get a bonus star and rank up since it will take less time to brew and use cheaper ingredients for the same result as a 5 star potion full of good traits.* After week 2, you might want to slip out of your haggling deck the “closers”. The 5% price increase they provide isn’t worth the risk of getting them during the opening turns and lose precious time with useless cards.* Don't bother too much trying to get a "perfect brew" ratio, you'll just lose an immense amount of time after week 2.* I really underestimated the importance of some “enhancer” potions for the heroes, like speed or stamina, especially when you start making long expeditions. Don’t make that mistake, make the most out of those adventures!My final advice is a bit more concrete. It worked wonders for me throughout the game but, as I stated, you can play the game according to multiple strategies. Since you don’t usually know the daily events for the days to come, I usually used the first four time slots befriending characters, buying groceries, launching hero expeditions while letting brew over 4 time slots the potions that might benefit from said daily bonuses. Then, I sold those potions over the last two time slots while preparing a new batch of potions for adventuring needs.Now come potions makers, you have a debt to clear and your journey toward the top starts now!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really fun game that blends so many cool elements into something that actually works. The animation is really cute, the characters are great, and the mechanics of potion brewing are really cool and fun to work around with. The only really bad thing I can say is that I wish there was an endless/freeplay mode. I love Stardew Valley and part of why I do is that even if there were certain time based restrictions placed on you(for example getting a good enough item for the Luau or completing the Community Center quickly within a year or something), at the end of the day all of these restrictions can be bypassed by simply waiting for next year in game to try again when you're more prepared, and a lot of the focus on time restrictions is instead on the management of time within a day to make the most out of it, assuming that's something you want to do in the first place. Essentially I think a more casual mode could keep the same competition structure as the base campaign but instead of lighting a fire under your ass to complete everything in a short amount of time it instead makes the restriction more about needing to win the competition to progress in your potion craft(due to better potions and new adventuring areas being locked behind winning the competitions) but not needing to right away allowing you to spend more time enjoying the characters and world this game has to offer.I've just finished up the first competition and I'm both excited to see what else the game has to offer as well as what updates may be in its future given the dev team seem very passionate about it and making it the best game it can be.(Also just since I wanted to mention a very cool thing about the game after all that, one time Mint came to me to buy a potion and at one point she said "I just don't like having to choose between potions and food" or something to that effect and it just made me feel so bad since I was kind of fleecing her heavily so I just closed the deal as fast as I could right after that)

_childDocuments_.review: I waited until I was completely finished the game to write this review - I saw pretty much everything aside from the end of a couple of the social links.The early complaints about the difficulty were actually what got me to buy the game day 1 - I also went in taking the game fairly seriously so I didn't run into the issues others did in the first week (even pre-nerf patch). But it immediately grabbed me - I generally love time management games of this ilk, including Recettear way back when. I know some folks don't get it - but games like Dead Rising and Persona 3-5 really scratch a certain itch for me. It's not the time restriction per se, but the feeling of getting 'ahead' and snowballing in power beyond what the game expects of you. And oh boy does Potionomics ever deliver in that respect...too much for its own good, honestly.The first couple weeks are a decent challenge but all it really takes is one day where you end up with a double or even triple bonus on a potion type, and you're basically set forever. Past a certain point you don't need to engage with certain systems at all anymore - the 'custom orders' are utterly pointless when you can just bang out 200k gold in one selling session. I was still having fun of course, but it made me wish there was a hard mode of some kind. Like, if you had to pay off the debt without the prize money, and the custom orders gave far more reward, it could pose more of a challenge.My other main criticism is this game very, very badly needs a sort feature and better filtering options. You end up with a TON of ingredient types during the game and they are sorted by the time you acquired them. I eventually just memorized what every ingredient does but still found myself fumbling around in the inventory a lot.Maxing out all social links doesn't require you to play 100% efficiently but I did run out of time on them by the end. That was mainly my own fault because I kept selling potions when I didn't have to, because I found it fun (and I liked testing out new card decks). Might have been nice to get one more week as a 'victory lap' or even an endless mode after. As much as I enjoyed the character stories I don't think I've got the time or patience to play through the entire game again just to see the ending of 3 of them.Now, to be clear - I absolutely loved this game. I don't write Steam reviews often (this might be the first one). The music is phenomenal and pretty much all of the characters really grew on me over time. I just think the game could be even better with a few adjustments - the developers seem to be cranking out patches at a rapid pace so maybe it'll get there (and make this review obsolete). But I can still wholeheartedly recommend it as-is.

_childDocuments_.review: So I've recently discovered that optimisation games with mild RNG elements and relationship side arcs are my cocaine, so this game ticks a whole bunch of boxes for me straight away.It's basically three games rolled into one: A ratio puzzle game (potion brewing), a time/resource/relationship management sim (visiting the town) and TCG (haggling).I enjoyed all three, and each one provided the perfect change of pace to roll over to the next one such that I built up a daily rhythm: Brew potions in the morning for the day's raids while I do my opening sale, spend the daytime slots picking up resources and visiting friends while the evening's batch of potions to sell cook, run an evening sales while I brew potions for the next day. Once I got the slime farming from day 30, production went into overdrive because it's just a little bit broken.There's a great range of characters to meet, too. Not overly or overtly focus-tested to death like the Overwatch cast, but I found basically everyone I could be friends with appealing one way or another. I was also pleasantly surprised to find that at least one of them was much more than they seemed - I won't spoil, but credit to the writers for giving the setting more depth than just the typical fantasy frontier.I managed to overoptimise myself to the point where I actually had enough funds for my next loan payment WITHOUT winning the competition by day 30 and had my endgame winning potions ready 10 days in advance. That's both a boast but also a bit of a complaint about balancing, I guess.And there are a few things that bum me out, but this is really just nitpicking:- Unlike in Recettear, there's no knock-on effect of raw material price changes: When materials are cheap or potion prices are up, it's 100% good, when materials are expenses or potions prices are down, it only sucks. There's no silver lining or strategy to take advantage.- This is made worse by the over-reliance on RNG for daily events. I would frequently get events that conflicted, and debuffs always seem to cancel out buffs, so on the day when potions, cures AND tonics were both up AND down (Fighters Prefer Potions, Healers Covet Cures, Wizards Take Tonics), everything was actually just down.- When haggling, stress cards replace normal draws, which means even 10% stress can quickly cause you to death spiral. Having the odds just be a flat % chance means that even with 3% stress, I sometimes had 3 out of 4 cards be stress cards on turn 2 (0.000027% chance of happening but it feels like it happened a LOT more than that)- I didn't even know haggling was part of the competition until the final boss, as I effortlessly swept every contest leading up to that. Even then, while I know the point is to get your potion valued higher than your opponent's it would have been nice just to let the player run with it and see how high they could get.- It would have been nice for the end game letter to at least make mention of the other characters, especially if the player had spent the time building up a strong relationship with them.- Similarly, some kind of recognition for the OBSCENE amounts of wealth the obsessive optimizers can accrue would be nice - like the castles at the end of Wario Land for the Gameboy- Despite the dramatic reveal, the final contest felt like a bit of a let-down given the surprise antagonist's historyDespite the above, I really loved this game: The writing is fun, the music is catchy, the characters are unique and appealing and the gameplay loop is solid.I've clocked in about 325 hours of Hades and I could easily see myself doing the same for this if there was some kind of endless mode.Oh and please make some kind of DLC expansion where a certain transfigured witch returns to her full power and we need to have a proper face-off against her, possibly with an ending where a certain former hero can apologise for basically doing war crimes.That would be pretty cool.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is basically all the bad ideas Recettear devs scrapped while making their game.Deckbuilding? Becomes irrelevant very early in the game, and when you finally get some good cards after building relationships you are already head over heels in your money pile that you might as well shove everything into your vending machine, because a few points of stress is all it takes to ruin the deckbuilding entirely. Stress REPLACES your deck draws with unplayable cards. That's right, it doesn't ADD negative cards to your hand, it REPLACES them. And considering most haggling sessions would last 2-3 turns, card draw is of paramount importance.Crafting potions? It's just a spreadsheet game, you cannot discover any new recipes yourself, and the diversity is locked behind the story progression. On top of that, the spreadsheet parts are made inaccessible if you're not directly in the brewing menu, and the UI really doesn't want to help you succeed. No sorting inventory/shop wares, no quick references, and to even access the Recipe book you have to close most of the menus you're browsing. If you're out traveling there is no way to check your custom orders, or what you're brewing and how much longer it'll be brewing. You also have to take your cauldrons out if you want to upgrade them (even though it's never necessary, nor is it even a good idea to ever do so), even if you aren't brewing anything while visiting the forge.Gameplay loop is also a mess. Selling potions just never feels like the right thing to do unless there are stacking events for a specific one, in which case you had better abuse the hell out of it so you can actually use all the time units building relationships with the NPCs. Making sales is literally guaranteed, any potion will find a buyer the moment you open the shop and haggling never goes wrong unless you fail to pay attention to the customer's patience. Same goes with the vending machine, selling potions faster than you can make them.And that's without mentioning the bugs that persist through patches that supposedly fixed them. Gardening timers not resetting in the second playthrough making the strongest feature unusable is the main culprit, as it is really the one-trick wonder this game needs to motivate you past the second out of five ingame weeks. Competitions are virtually unfailable unless you have more fingers than braincells, exception made if you are playing your first time management game ever maybe; but if you're unwilling to explore and understand the game mechanics then you probably should look into games that don't require you to play them - aka visual novels.All in all... the game has potential, but at 25€ it feels like a ripoff. It's completed within a couple of hours and even those are just repetitive and flavorless beyond the scope of the relationship-based NPCs' side stories.AT LEAST GIVE US AN ENDLESS MODE AFTER BEATING THE STORY ???

_childDocuments_.review: e: They've released a QoL update with magimin filtering. There's more QoL they could do but this is the main pinch point that was driving me out of the game. Changed this to a positive, buy this game!previous:Great game, but I recommend waiting until V1.1 for Quality of Life improvements TLDR: This is a Good Game; the core gameplay loop is well designed and the timer loop is semi-stressful (as intended), but it's held back by not providing the right info in the right places, which interacts negatively with the aforementioned time pressure. I can immediately think of 4 QoL improvements which should be fairly simple to implement and would shift this to a recommend:I have to assume that a lot of these are intentional design choices to keep with the aesthetic of the game, but if this is the case I think the developers may have suffered from being so immersed in their game that they didn't realise how much they were loading onto the players.Some aspects like memorising what your timers are and what your plan is I can see as valid design choices, but the lack of menu sorting is hard to justify. It defaults to 'date added', which is the 2nd worst type of sorting they could have chosen behind alphabetical. I could see it working if there were fewer items so it was easier to become intimately aware of the items as sprites rather than stats, but I'm on 6 pages of the unsorted item shop and I'm only on day 25. i just want to know what item gives me 12 of magimin C, there's no value from scrolling through pages looking at items individually to do this.I wish I could give this a mixed rating rather than negative as it's not a bad game, I just can't grasp why menu features that have been present for decades in the genre have suddenly gone missing. I have no doubt they'll end up added in time, I'll be more than happy to change this to a recommend if they do.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. The characters are well thought out with unique storylines and great personalities, the story is good, and the lore is awesome. This is one of those few games that gets a 10/10 as far as the writing is concerned. As far as the game play goes, it's a massive improvement on the game's spiritual predecessor Recettear, but it is a pretty steep difficulty curve if you're expecting something like a farming sim. The first three weeks of the game were hard and somewhat stressful as it introduces a new mechanic about every two days all so that the characters you interact with have a meaningful purpose in being there. All of the characters you can form friendships with are vendors with different gimmicks who will give you coupons and haggling cards as a reward for increasing your relationship with them making them all important, and I'd highly recommend maxing out each one if you can. Back to the difficulty, the first three weeks are hard as you're learning all the mechanics, and the game is a bit math heavy and relies a lot on prior planning. Each day you're pretty much preparing for the next day and the end of week boss battle. For me, a note page to remind me of what I'd bought at the end of my play session and what I was planning to do the next day became invaluable and made the game much more enjoyable. That and a calculator are a must have for this game as getting the ingredient ratios right are critical for the majority of the game. But like I said, once I had a handle on everything and used all the mechanics I got super rich at the beginning of week four and breezed through the rest of the game focusing on relationships. You don't even need to know all the mechanics, I completely ignored custom orders and the good and bad traits mechanic and beat the game. My biggest advice is to have a refresher note whenever you're playing to help you plan out your days and so you can pick up easily when you come back, figure out how you want to structure each of the time blocks in a day (makes it less stressful knowing what you're doing everyday in a certain timeblock, for example, I did first three socializing and traveling, two to open shop, and the last buying ingredients and setting up for the next day), and don't worry too much. Oh, and keep your stress level down because those stress cards will wreck you fast. All in all, great game.

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance,  is a game revolving around financial struggles, gathering rare ingredients to make strong potions and marketing them for a high price to win competitions, but beneath that exterior,  concocts a deeper, more profound story about how, through perseverance, self-reflection, and the support from others, individuals can grow, transform, and rise above their obstacles. -And through that growth, you can help others and learn from their resolution.Through the protagonist's journey, please watch how success comes not from avoiding the challenges, but facing them head-on.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great!Potionomics is an absolutely charming mix of a card-game, shopkeeper simulator and a dating sim. Sure, the main mechanic is simple: you brew potions, you sell them. But the magic of this game is everything "extra" that comes on top: charming NPC's to spend your time with and get new haggle cards, heroes to send on adventures for rare ingredients, merchants whose wares might benefit your business, the story and speculation about historic events, even a sprinkle of mystery.It all stacks into a unique game loop where you juggle multiple tasks to stay on top of everything. You get up, throw some ingredients in the pots, haggle for a bit, and then go to visit your friends, resupply ingredients and fuel, set heroes on their adventures, etc.All that, and you get an amazing visuals and music on top, as well as good writing and expressive animations. This game is sweet and happy, and it makes me feel the same way!I've seen some reviews that say "It's bad for the game like this to have a ticking clock timer", but i found the timer and weekly challenges rather easy: you are NOT forced to min-max your time and efficiency (or even use all the provided tools) to meet set requirements, they act more like a "baseline" of what you should have by then. Truth be told, i'd drop this game sooner if it wasn't for an anticipation of finale. To reiterate, you CAN make the best potions that auto-win challenges and max out all relationships in a single play-through, even if you don't grind and try your best.

_childDocuments_.review: Having just beat my first play through I was pleasantly surprised at the challenge on the base difficulty. A word of advice, save half way through the week. If you miss manage your time you will have a lot of trouble catching up for the showdown. Once I figured out the balancing act of spending time building relationships for cards, brewing, selling and gathering ingredients I felt like it had a lot of unexpected depth. When I would lose a challenge I was able to rethink my approach and get it next time. Things like throwing a round early to avoid stress actually let me eek out a win when I didn't manage to brew a potion that was up to snuff. I like the problem solving it allowed in moments like that.I'm excited to mess about in endless mode to polish up my brewing skills so I don't need to rely to heavily on my deck-building experience to carry me.There are a lot of ways to enjoy this game. The characters are fun, the voice acting and animation are lively and I found myself alternating between sitting back in my chair chilling as I chatted up my favorite characters before having to engage try hard mode as I tried to throw together a halfway decent potion on the day prior to the contest with the collection of random ingredients I managed to scrounge up.My only gripe would be that time feels so tight and that clashes with the desire I had to explore the characters stories and get their cards for my deck. I felt like there wasn't enough time to build relationships with more than one or two characters. Whenever I tried I just ran out of time and money to brew the potions I needed. If you really want to get to know all the characters be ready to enjoy the endless or casual modes. If the developer is still adding content I think some friendly showdowns between the other characters every 20 days or so could add a lot of longevity after the main story is done.

_childDocuments_.review: Only one romance per play-through;No over saturated harem bull crap;Dating someone doesn't change anything game-wise besides flavor dialogue;Yes you can date the Walrus;Monogamy leaning devs are based.Oh yeah, the rest of the game is amazing too. Potion-making games on steam are a dime a dozen nowadays but this one shines above most shovelware simulators.Tips:- Make a different save at the beginning of each "week", 10th day has a challenge you need to prepare in advance, if you mess up, it's guaranteed game over- The potions your rival will bring are always the one pointed by the pamphlet. If you make equal ones, you can haggle with the judge. If you make even a SINGLE TIER ABOVE those, it's an instant win.- Prize money is 100% taken away by loan shark, don't count on it. Your profits are your only resource.- Don't stress over stress, stuff hits like a truck in the beginning, it's okay to suck at the beginning. You get a new mechanic every 5 days or so and making friends will yield better cards to give you an edge on your haggle.- Sleeping earlier will heal stress. Spending time with friends will heal stress.- The Moth girl deck works better when you have high stress- The Dryad girl deck heals your stress.- The Pirate Cat deck have two pickable effects, one will always work better when you're under stress.- The Rich guildmaster boy deck will swindle picky customers.- The Charming posh madam deck will charm customers to avoid stress.- Being productive as possible with your time is the best way to mix-max results. Don't sweat over it tho. Just like I said, make saves at the beginning of each week and remember to have fun. The game is way more than a capitalism simulator. There's a whole lore about the island you are in and everything.- The soundtrack is 10/10 and fitting to every situation you see on the screen.

_childDocuments_.review: Deadline:It's just stressful to have this deadline over my head the whole time I'm playing, especially when it's not super clear how I'm supposed to make progress towards making them. Does it make more sense to focus on earning money, or getting rare ingredients? Am I supposed to be sending adventurers to more dangerous locations than they can complete? Am I expected to be leaving the house more than once per day? Contest:The contest is set up a bit like a boss battle, and you get to haggle to raise the value of your potions, and my "barely good enough to qualify" potions allowed me to win easily, such that there wasn't even a round three of the contest! I don't know if they would have allowed me to enter potions below the threshold and just haggle my way up to a high enough score, but from how it's structured I get the feeling maybe it would, and if so this is information I would love to have before I stress myself out about making the minimum potion before the deadline.Upgrades:You can't upgrade something unless you bring it with you to the smithy. You can't bring it with you if it's in your shop. You can't even swap it out if it's currently in use. Finally, you can't even *see* what materials you will need to upgrade something if you don't have it with you. This results in needing to remember to swap out your cauldron *before* you start your brewing for the morning, just so that you can bring your better cauldron with you to see what you need to upgrade it, and then mark that down on a notepad somewhere so you can remember what it is for later when you might actually *have* that material.Brewing:I felt like I was constantly on the verge of running out of potions, because I make ~3 potions per 2 hours, and I sell ~3 potions in a two-hour block of having my shop open, plus all the potions I basically give away to the adventurer as part of hiring them to go gather more ingredients for me. I'm trying to upgrade my shop to have room for more cauldrons, but the materials have to be collected from multiple different places and it takes forever to gather them all.Technical:Don't alt-tab out of this game when in borderless windowed mode. Mine got stuck in a cropped size in the corner of my monitor, with no way to change it back because the drop-down box to set the resolution was on the right side of the screen that had been cropped off. My only option after trying to fix the resolution was to quit the game entirely without saving, because the button to *exit the settings menu* was at the very bottom, also cropped off, and there didn't seem to be any keyboard shortcut to get me out.Animations:The flailing around that every character does every time they say something is very well done! Looks like it came from a pixar movie! Very expressive. Unfortunately, I didn't get to look at them very often because the game is not voice acted, so I was forced to read the text at the very bottom of the screen while watching these expressive animations in my peripheral vision. Very distracting. The animation starts as the text starts with each new text box, so either I read the text and miss the animation, or I watch the animation out of context and then read the text. BUT that being said, I think it's for the best that there aren't voiceovers during the haggling battles, because the things they say are very repetitive and would be a lot more annoying if I had to listen to them. Maybe only during unique scenes?Overall:I wish this were a different game. I want to be able to freely just experiment with my potions, hang out with my various villager friends, sell potions when I need money for ingredients, without the stress of *you must make better potions by X date or you lose the game*. Like, imagine if Stardew Valley was like that. "You must have completed at least one box in the community center by the end of Spring or I'm taking your farm away!" Why can't this game be chill? Why do I have to have mysterious and impossible debt hanging over my head?This game needs to team up with Potion Craft and make something halfway between, because I loved the chill no-stress atmosphere and crafting of that game but I love the social events and friendship stuff of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely and very well made game.The graphics are really nice and the animations well done; I think nobody will contest this point.Discovering, talking with and getting to know every character in the game is really nice as well.The soundtracks are great. Every character as multiple unique themes, you have multiple "haggling session" themes as well as a bunch of ambient themes. They all fit nicely with the game.The deck builder mechanic works pretty nicely when you sell potions, but you will quickly notice that some cards you unlock are  good while others are here to "fill the gap".Some balancing are probably required. Yes, your starting cards are weaker than any equivalent card you may unlock and I think it is normal, but some unlocked cards are just better than other unlocked cards of the same tier. Some people already created "unbeatable"/"infinite" decks.You will find a lot of negative reviews saying that the game is "stressful" and/or "hard".From what I gather, those people either had a  bad luck (there is indeed some RNG; gathering new ingredients as an example, but I never got that much of bad luck in 2 playthroughs) or they thought they could just do the social stuff of the game and neglected the "upgrade shop" and "make good potions" parts.For my part, I had no issue with this and beat all opponents without a haggling session, some of them with the original difficulty.In the forum, you will find both people telling the game is too hard and others telling it is not.You have a time resource in this game, and it quickly becomes the most precious one with money.People saying that you don't have enough time to do everything are saying the truth, but you have the time to do all the  stuff.More details in the "game mechanic spoiler" below.Speaking of the devs, they worked dutyfully since the launch of the game, squashing bugs and reporting feedbacks.At the end of the game, I found on the contrary of most negative reviews that the game is . I never had to do haggling sessions during tournaments because you can just brew a potion that is so good that it beats the opponent with no contest. I would have much preferred to always have to fight and defend my potions for every tournament, meaning the best potion you can brew in the cycle is a .From the cycle 3 you quickly stop struggling with the money as well, , so you stop doing haggling sessions and just put every potions you get in the vending machine, which is a bit disappointing since you have more time for social interactions, you discover a big bunch of cards... that you will never have to use!In this regards, I do hope devs will implement a difficulty setting.That way people wanting a chill experience will have it, as well as people wanting a more challenging one.As a summary, I loved the game a lot and if the following listings are implemented, a lot of negative reviews will become obsoletes while making the game more enjoyable:For people interested in the Deluxe Edition, the artbook has a little more than 130 pages and there is 58 soundtracks; I think it is worth it and a nice way to support the devs.The artbook has one issue tough: if you read it, you will want a customize option for the characters! Some original ideas looked great. :)

_childDocuments_.review: Much like the potions Sylvia brews, Potionomics is a strange blend of weird ingredients. The magic is in the brew of everything together. It all just works. If you think you might like this, you will. For the developers, I have two minor complaints. 1. _childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Note, this review was originally posted in 9th January 2023. A whopping 21 months later - 22 October 2024 - they dropped an update (along with DLC) which ON PAPER fixes many of the problems noted here. I will have a look at it once they bugfix that update a bit.tl;dr; version:While not for everyone, it is a pretty good game with its own charm.Long version:++ While graphics are not the main thing in any game, I have to say that the sheer amount of effort they put into characters, their expressions and their smooth animations is extremely impressive.+ The card game is alright. You can break it pretty badly, though that might get balanced later.++ Characters are creative and their respective storylines are a delight. I think only one of them was lackluster in meaning, but it was still alright.-- Spending time with friends is a completely dead feature and should not be in the game as-is. A game which imposes a strict time limit on you, yet giving you the option to waste that valuable time? Just give them a Gift and you will gain the same thing without wasting time. Really, why is this literal trap in the game??- Poorly paced. The game dripfeeds new features to you to not overwhelm you, but despite this the first week requires a lot from you... even though some of the features you need don't unlock until weeks later! I doubt that this can be fixed as it is a pretty deep design flaw. The point is, if you can get through week1, you should get through all the weeks with relative ease as it just keeps getting easier.- As a result, in the last two weeks you can easily make enough money to pay off your debt. But you still get a game over if you lose (likely on purpose). So what was the point of the competition again...?- Every week of the game basically resets your progress. For example, you're expected to buy the new Cauldrons and upgrade them. Which wouldn't be that bad if it wasn't for...- Pretty random loot. Sometimes, you get the material you need to upgrade your Cauldrons on day1. Sometimes? You get them on the very last day of the week, which leave you on a mad scramble to get your ♥♥♥♥ done in time. In theory it is possible to never find the exact material you need (though it didn't happen to me)... this means that players can have VASTLY different game experiences. The vital ingredients should NOT be that random.- Sometimes the UI is great, like in its ability to sort stuff. But sometimes the UI is very lackluster. In particular what bothers me greatly is the lack of "how many you of this item you own" in tooltips. This would be particularly useful in Guild Expeditions, but oh well, I guess you had better remember how many of each ingredient you have! (stores and brewing UI show you much of an item you own - it's just a tooltip issue as they are static)- Certainly not a bug free game. I did not encounter anything game breaking, though I once had to restart the game to stop a looping sound effect as it wouldn't go away by reloading, or by going to the main menu, or by going back to where I got the sound effect.- In particular the card game interactions can be SUPER weird and buggy. This might get patched later, but based on previous patch notes it doesn't seem like they will.- No NG+. If you fail or if you want to replay the game, you need to start all over from scratch. This might get patched later.That's... a lot of negatives. Allow me to stress that I enjoyed my time with the game and can certainly recommend the game to anyone who finds the idea of "manage your time and resources to brew stuff, then sell said stuff to customers with a card game" appealing. Oh, and most importantly...+++++ Anubia is freaking ADORABLE. Sure she has basically no role in the game, but look at her! Just look at this cute little thing!

_childDocuments_.review: Potionomics is less about the act of brewing and selling potions than it is a game about budgeting time. You only have 6 notches of time per day. Brewing potions takes time, selling potions takes time, going out to buy stuff takes time, and spending time with people takes time. To top it all off, there’s a big competition every 10 days that you have to make specific potions for. When the game came out, a lot of people said the game was too hard and stressful because there wasn’t enough time. Thankfully, this isn’t an issue at all anymore. I WAS optimizing everything I did for competitions during the early-mid game (which is good, I think), but after that I caught a break and had a lot more freedom with my time. In fact, I think the game might be somewhat too easy now. It’s not so easy that it isn’t engaging, but I think it’s a shame that you can easily dominate competitions after a point; they have some good music and character moments in them!By the end, I found that the main draw of the game was actually the character interactions. I really liked most of the characters! A lot of them are fun, and all of them have a genuine, well-written internal struggle that you work through when ranking them up. My biggest regret with the game was not being able to see everyone’s stories by the end, so my advice is to prioritize ranking everyone up.The potion-brewing part of the game will determine how long this game takes for you. The more of a perfectionist you are, the longer you’ll be willing to spend to get those numbers balanced just right. Fortunately I don’t think you need to be perfect most of the time, so you can play at your own pace.As for selling the potions, it’s fun and satisfying! It seems like a lot at first, but you mostly only NEED to pay attention to one thing (Patience). Stress might not seem like a problem at first, but just you wait…As an aside, I know people are inherently opposed to games that use cards like this nowadays. In-universe, your cards are strategies that you learned from the characters (like keeping calm, pushing your advantage, or…channeling the ferocity of squirrels). While I think the context for this didn’t need to be cards, I think they still work for this fun idea.My only real qualm with the game is the need to save often. It’s not too hard to make a mistake that wastes time in the day, and I was paranoid about doing that fairly often. I don’t know if an undo feature is plausible in a game like this, but it’d be nice to have! I think the game is lenient enough that mistakes aren’t damning, but at the same time I DO recommend trying to optimize time to get all of the character interactions…When I saw it, I was excited to play Potionomics for the potion-making and animations. While both of those were definitely good, I ended up loving it for the characters. I can easily recommend this little gem; it has a lot of soul.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the concept and mechanics of this game. The characters are fun! The animation and music are amazing! You own a potion shop, but have some debt to pay off. Each 10 days, there is a potion-making competition that you need to win to pay down that debt. But you have to win it, or else game over. You can't keep any of the winnings to help you out either.The first couple of competitions are fun, if not a bit stressful. You need to maximize your time and money between brewing potions, selling them, visiting other characters, and obtaining new potion ingredients and equipment. If you're lucky, you'll get what you need a couple of days before the competition and can make the required potions. I (barely) beat the 3rd competition, and realized the game was not getting easier or opening up to play how you want, just more of the same trying desperately to get what you need to win the next competition. The game has everything it needs to be fun, but continues to impose a harsh deadline on what you want to do. I think it does need the competitions to push you forward and make you get better, but aren't implemented in a way that compliments the rest of the game. I would love to come back to Potionomics ifa) the time between competitions were longer or b) you had the option of losing them and trying again orc) there was another way to pay down your debt. I really liked the potion selling/haggling part of the game. If I could just slowly pay down my debt that way instead of entering the competitions that could be a choice.This game has many great ideas, but if you're looking for a chill time, this isn't what you want. If you want more stress in your life, maybe this is your jam.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best games I've ever played. I'm gonna point out some things I liked and some things I thought could've been improved:+ The potion crafting system is incredibly easy to understand but also very deep. There's lots of different mixtures of magimins you can make to craft the perfect potion, and the implementation of the positive/negative trait system later adds even more complexity.+ Every mechanic in the game, in some way, interacts with another. You craft potions not only to sell, but also to give to your heroes. Your heroes can help to collect ingredients for you. You use ingredients to duplicate, craft potions, and craft cauldrons/tables/upgrades. Your stress system is part of your card battling gameplay, and you can reduce your stress by interacting with your friends, which gives you discounts, stronger cards, and eventually also a partner that you kiiiiiiss.+ The time system flows naturally and lots of events easily interact with each other. Making your potions take 8 hours to brew so they finish the next day, or making them take 2 hours so you can have a new set ready after 2 hours of selling feels very clean. The game definitely rewards pre-thought in this way and many others.+ While the difficulty ramps up towards the end, it never gets too hard and does feel like a natural inclination. The final boss does feel needlessly difficult, though considering there are only 5 bosses in the game it's only fair that the last one really tests your mettle.- The stress system only ever really becomes an issue in the boss fights, and only really in the final 2-3. If you've completed Mint's friendship line , or really any of Saffron's cards, these fights can really be a cake walk. Even without them though you'll probably still do fine, until the final fight where  It really could've been more ingrained and not just artificially ramped up in the final 10 days.- Once you figure out the correct gameplay loop, and you will probably have it figured out by even before the third competition, the game becomes remarkably easy and stops rewarding interesting play as much. For those who haven't played, the gameplay loop is:  then 4. spend the rest of the 10 days doing pretty much whatever you want. Once I figured out this loop, money essentially became a non-issue. I had 197.000 gold before the final fight. Screw the competition, give me a few more weeks of that kind of profits and I'll pay off my debts on my own.- While the ingredient selection is awesome, it's fair to say that only 25% of them are ever really used. There are ingredients, especially later in the game, that have 4-5 different magimin types and they're essentially worthless. While they add to the game in fun world building ways, and if you weren't as focused on making "perfect" potions they would not necessarily be useless, they mostly just take up space. I wouldn't make this point if the ingredients that just give 1-2 magimins weren't plenty powerful enough to eventually create the final tier of potions.Regardless of it's flaws, I give this game a solid 8/10 for what it is. It's no masterpiece, and it's certainly not a triple A title. But I got about 50 hours out of it for it's price tag and I can see myself playing it again in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Potionomics is a game with charming characters you'll want to spend time with, a potion crafting system you'll want to delve deep into, and fun haggling with your customers.  Unfortunatly, Potionomics biggest enemy is it's own format.  You have so little time to spend doing these things and not in the haggard "wow I'm busy way" but in the "I am so screwed" way.  Following the game's hand holding tutorials puts you into an fail state, and the game's "game over" is a hard stop, you have to roll back up to an hour or more of saves to get enough time back to right your mistakes.  Mistakes you could only have known you were making after failing.This game could be wonderful, the animation is crisp, the world is well conceived, and the UI is clear and bright.  However, the game could either do to commit to a rogue like format and sacrifice the time it takes to fail or be more forgiving in it's failure or more varied with it's difficulty.THIS IS NOT A CHILL PIXAR-Y MEET CUTE AND BREW GAME.  Potionomics is a game about pushing your shop to it's absolute limit and reinvesting every dime into your store, maximizing your relationships, and brewing crazy potions as soon as possible. I loved this game for 4 hours, but I'm hesitant to re-love it for the same 1-2 to get "back on track" only to not see another hurdle I couldn't have predicted.  Not in this economy
