_childDocuments_.review: I loved Potionomics. However, I can recognize the game is not for everyone. I would describe Potionomics as a time management deck builder with some visual novel elements on the side. One thing to note is this game is not a dating sim. Potionomics has friendship and romantic aspects to the game, but that is not the core of the game.In Potionomics, you play as Sylvia, who inherited her uncle's shop and his debt after he passed. To pay off the debt, Sylvia must create and sell potions. However, the debt is so large that Sylvia must participate in contests to earn the prize money and pay off the debt. First, I will explain the haggling mechanics. When you create a potion, you have several things you can do with a potion. One of those options is to sell it. When you put a potion up for sale, you can haggle the price with cards. Each customer has a limited amount of patience. Each card you play uses a certain amount of patience. I, personally, find this haggling system to be a lot of fun and an excellent entry to deck-building mechanics if you are interested in trying out those types of games. To get new cards for your deck, you have to befriend the other NPCs in the game. You do this by hanging out with them or gifting them items. I found that gifting items was more efficient. This is where the friendship and dating aspect of the game comes into play. The characters you interact with run shops or do other things for the player. You'll discover that as you play. However, once you get their friendship level high enough you will enter a cutscene to learn more about that character and be presented with a card. This is also how you can enter a relationship. However, the relationship doesn't really affect anything. It is more or less just there which I understand is a letdown for some. It does change some of the lines the character says when you interact with them though and that is kind of cute.The core of the game is making potions for the tournament. You have a limited amount of time to make the required potions for the tournament. For some players, this can prove a bit stressful. You have to win the tournament to continue the game. If you don't it is game over.To this, you have to upgrade cauldrons to increase the quality of potions you can make, as well as upgrade your shop. You also need to get ingredients. The way you get ingredients is a bit random. You can send members of the adventurers guild to scout ingredients for you. You can also invest in the guild, which gives you a bit of ingredients when you return. You then deliver the ingredients to the shopkeeper, Quinn, who will start selling them the next day. If you have trouble securing the funds to upgrade items or acquiring the ingredients you need, this is where things get stressful. For some potions, I barely got the ingredients. It is very doable but can be a bit stressful. The other portion of this game is the potion requests that come in. Customers will come in and request potions. However, these potions require certain attributes. All ingredients have attributes attached to them. This means when you fulfill the request you have to make sure that your ingredients only have the attributes that the customer wants. I typically just accepted these requests but never filled them. There is no penalty for not fulfilling them. The art, animations, and music are wonderful. The team did an amazing job. You can clearly tell how much love and care went into them. I agree with the other reviews that an endless mode would be awesome. After I finished the game, I was bummed I couldn't continue increasing my friendships or running the shop. If not an endless mode then a new game + would be nice where you get to keep your friendship levels or something like that. Overall, I recommend the game. If you love time management and deck building, Potionomics is 100% worth checking out. Just keep in mind that after the last tournament, the game will end.

_childDocuments_.review: == There will be minor mechanical spoilers within this review ==I adore this game. Don't let the hours on this review fool you -- I've been playing this game offline and, at the time of writing, I've accumulated a total of a whole 24 hours on this game. I adore this game, but it's not without its faults. This game is a lot more stressful than the art style may lead you to think. Game is more along the line of Atelier or Recettear rather than something like Stardew Valley. Some flaws with UI design and no post-game hard and/or endless mode prevent me from recommending this game in its current state. However, if you're not scared of time limits or a little math, I'd definitely say to give it a shot.Presentation is probably the highlight of the game, as you can probably tell. There's not much to say that's already been said about the NPCs -- cute, awesome, and full of flair. Music is also quite stellar -- a must for how much time you can put into this game.  Devs have been quite attentive to bugs and complaints from the community, releasing (essentially) a day one patch to squash some of the more game-breaking ones. Of course, that doesn't excuse the fact that the UI is quite clunky. No way of sorting items in your shop or inventory leads to you having to scan through and hover over tons of items in the mid- to late-game. Also, there are some things that the game doesn't tell you outright that I do wish that you didn't have to wait to find out. I've also noticed a popular review talking about hanging out with NPCs taking up time and, as such, meaning you can't hang out with them and see their unique cutscenes. This is faulty info at its finest. While it's true that each activity is unique per character, there are no animations and only three or four lines, max, of fluff text. It's moreso used for the mechanical benefits -- stress relief and some affection points towards that NPC. Viewing the actual animations/cutscenes related to the NPC take up one time slot (out of six, per day) each. You definitely have time to max out your relationships with half, if not all, of your NPCs. There are also a few mechanics locked behind adventuring -- the activity is entirely passive, but the game doesn't make it explicit, if I recall. There are some players that may skip this mechanic entirely, only realizing until too late that it's one of the only two ways to unlock more items in the shop.There are also a few issues with difficulty scaling. A few people have been having trouble beating the first boss -- the dev team responded in that day one patch by making the boss easier to beat and making the RNG on the first week lean more in your favor to help beat the boss. While I'm glad the dev team is fairly responsive, I do wish that there was a difficulty slider so they could appeal to a wider demographic. On top of that, there's no colorblind mode, which gets in the way of a specific mechanic. I do hope that, once the wrinkles are ironed out, that more accessibility options are added soon.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good but it lacks a difficulty setting, and needs more Quality of life improvements like , bottleing all finished potions at once. The game isn't laid out to be hard fought, with a bit of time management and preperation you can easily defeat any opponent even the final boss which actually causes a minor script failure where my higher valued potion was labeled inferior when it was actually more valuable.Getting good relationships with characters was a chore also if you go for a completionist run, the characters themselfs are all interesting but loading times on scene transitions add up and if you want to befriend all or most of them you are in for a lot of them just to give the characters a gift for the day.Now that is kind of all sounding bad and I admit there are times where I just finished my potions for the contest and skipped the next 6-7 days to finish the game simply because the hassle was too much , but if you play this game casually it is fun. _childDocuments_.review: This is a good game overall. You run a potion shop, you have to pay off debt by winning potion competitions. The protagonist and side characters are all really fun and all have personalities that stand out. Potion making is a "Put in x amount of this magic vitamin" system. I thought potion making was polished, and for the most part, the ingredients you get all have some kind of use. The "potion combat" card system allows for a lot of deck combinations, and I've yet to see a card that wouldn't work in some kind of deck, even if you aren't running that archetype at the time.The bad parts: Animations take awhile, which isn't noticeable the fist time though, but on subsequent playthoughs, you're going to notice it. There are also a very small number of ingredients that are practically useless.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game about running a potion shop to get out of debt. It is part potion brewing trying to get the right mix of ingredients to balance for maximum effect, part card game when haggling to convince the customer the potion is move valuable, and part dating sim with some time management and interesting characters with well written story (the romance is all pretty kid friendly though and the actual romance is optional if that's not your thing, though you'll still need to talk to people to get better cards for haggling, or coupons for discounts).The whole game is exceptionally well made, and has an incredible amount of charm. The main criticism I have of it is that there isn't a way to continue playing past the ending to get all the cards and try out different decks.If it looks like something you might be interested in then I definitely recommend getting it.
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: Crafting potions is a ratio balancing system so be good at the multiplication table or struggle. The characters are all very likeable which is probably the biggest selling point for me, I even love the walrus anthro dude. 40% visual novel, 40% counting with your fingers and 20% inventory management and gear progression. I'm over half way done and enjoying it quite a bit.Followup after completion: The characters are very loveable and fun, the antagonists are interesting and the gameplay is stable until the second to last boss where if you're an intellectual player, you will spiral and become unstoppable. Day 2 of the last calendar and I was not only ready to take on the final challenge, but with 100% perfection such that I never was dealt a hand even though the game clearly expected me to.The plot is solid and the climax of the story is great. I'm going to be keeping tabs on this game studio from now on. I haven't been satisfied with a game ending in awhile now.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been enjoying Potionomics.  I bought it for my child, enjoyed the first session so I started my own campaign, and its been great.  The narrative impresed me, the timing of some conversations and things either being well guessed timing or very reactive.  There is a romance element to it, but culminates in a kiss and nothing PG-13.  Lots of math and planning.  As a veteran gamer, I was crushing it and didn't really realize by how much until the 4th of at least 6 bosses.  I expect a gradeschooler can keep playing and be allowed suboptimal plays without being crushed.  There's also a deckbuilding negotiation game inside it and it isn't really challanging, more just complex.  That might be too complex for her without guidance, and too simple for anyone who's played a deckbuilder.  There's a mechanic in the game fairly early that also makes it optional, which is nice. _childDocuments_.review: The game is really good.Presentation is amazingly on point, great music, simple and satisfying gameplay loop.Its a time management game so you do have to plan out your days but since its turn based you have all the time in the world to step back and consider your next move. _childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: Potionomics is a great game, ruined by   being too long.Where Potionomics absolutley succeeds, is it's character animations, they are simply excellent.The Visual Novel side of Potionomics (the dialogue/writing) is good, it's solid.The Romance part of Potionomics is a double-edged sword, it's great from start to end, but...After you have completed your romance arc, which happens in the middle of your playtrough, the game just... throws that in the trashcan.MOST games does atleast something afterwards, for example stardew valley has you getting married, and then that person lives in your farm.When game devs are too lazy or just do not have the funds, they ATLEAST DO A SHOWCASE IN THE CREDITS, telling you the "aftermath" of friendships and love interests, but Potionomics decides to have NOTHING, yet has the Dating/Romance aspect as a major selling point.The Nerve on these developers, i have never experienced a game with  such good romance, just to have it all thrown in the trashcan in the middle of the game.The Gameplay of Potionomics is suprisingley good, with a few issues.First of all, having a deck-builder in a shop sim is geniouse, it works really, really well, and is enhanced with the fantastic animations and visuals.A few balance issues here and there, and some useless cards, but stuff like that can be fixes with ease.BUT, the game is simply 3x too long.only 7.8% of players have completes the game, SEVEN POINT EIGHT.The game is divided in 5 chapters, when it should have been 3.The last 2 chapters adds nothing new, and just "ruins" the game.Overall, this IS a good game, but sadly not one i can recommend buying at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Potionomics while i was playing it! There's a charming cast of romanceable characters (which made it hard for me to choose!) and unique gameplay i don't usually see in dating sims. My biggest issue with the game is that i misunderstood the first main objective. If memory serves, you have to craft 3 potions for the big competition, and i thought i just needed 1 of 3. That's my bad, but to be fair, i was still starting out and getting a handle of the mechanics and figuring out how to best optimize potion brewing, opening shop, and visiting my friends. So by the time the competition came around, i lost because i only had one solid potion (though i put up a good fight!). Not to compare games, but in my head i thought it was going to be a bit like stardew valley where when you don't get first place at the festival, no worries, you just try again next year. Not so for Potionomics, this L was a hard Game Over. I could not progress, and even going back to my most recent save felt useless because it takes lots of time to prep for the potions that i needed for the competition. It makes me not want to return to the game because that's 12 hours of relationship building and shop enhancements down the drain because of a misunderstanding and because i was a new player i didn't have a grasp on the mechanics in the given time frame. I know there are mods I could install that adjust time and eliminate that approaching deadline, but I don't necessarily think new players should have to install mods to have a positive experience with a game.All in all, i enjoy the game, and i would like to return to it at some point. This was just a frustrating road block that i wanted to address.

_childDocuments_.review: We were on the verge of greatness, and that's exactly where we got..Potionomics is a game which immediately struck me as an excellent product with incredible charm that I could lose myself in. Almost everything that was the problem in my initial review has been, in time, blown away and now I can enjoy this amazing Alchemy game at my own leisure.+ Positives +The systems that you'd expect a good alchemy sim to have are all here. A very fun brewing and store management system which allows you to brew and pamper your potions at your own volition by using an incredibly large amount of available ingredients and reagents each containing varied amounts and types of elements, whilst customizing your own store to match the fantasy shop look you were always going for.The actual haggling is also approached in a rather unique way and that is through an enjoyable enough card game, which pits you against your own customers in a battle of wits with the goal of as much profit as you can acquire without depleting the customer's patience or becoming a nervous wreck.Speaking of stress a great way to unwind is to engage and build relationships with unique NPCs that the player can interact, become friends or even pursue a romantic relationship with. (Muktuk my beloved). The characters are all also introduced gradually as the story goes by and all of them are simply wonderful to interact with.The story is your classic tale of success through hard work and dedication in spite of great adversity and an overwhelming time pressure.In my initial review, I wallowed over the fact you couldn't continue after you finished the game, which is now completely possible with the introduction of Endless mode. As the name suggest, this mode allows you to continue the game after you finish the story and manage your shop, brew potions and hang out with the NPCs at your own leisure, any and all time pressure is gone (With the exception of special potion requests, which however you have more than enough time to complete)- Negatives -The one issue that I would say remains in this game is the varied and mostly RNG-based system of ingredient availability, once you get a hold of just one, you have the option to either give it to Quinn or grow it yourself, meaning that the worst part of obtaining ingredients is actually finding them in the first place. This can sometimes cause quite the limiting selection with which you cannot exactly craft the perfect potion you or the customer who ordered it were hoping for. Better stock up on potions and feed your adventurers like crazy to obtain as many ingredients as you can.All in all, I believe that this game deserves success, and I can wholeheartedly recommend it as much as I can. This is quite possibly the best Alchemy shop simulator out there with an incredibly charming atmosphere and wonderful gameplay. Looking forward to see what else the devs cook up as time goes by.TLDR; An incredibly fun, charming, although a little RNG at times Alchemy Sim. A game that made me change my review after a long time when it finally implemented the type of gameplay I had previously hoped for. Endless mode truly turned this game around for me and I hope it did the same for many others.

_childDocuments_.review: After the latest update:Thus far I love this game and the developers have acted quickly to release a patch to address certain areas of the game.+ great art-style+ unique gameplay+ great characters+ simple but fun brewing+ charming interactions- only one difficulty- easy-mode required for players not caring about a (while improved) contest- can't really interact with characters as much as one may want to, due to the contests- game over on losing a contestMy recommendation: include an easy-mode with either:- more days until the next contest (20+)- easier contest in general (almost story-mode like)#- contests than one can retry indefinitely after a couple of days (maybe while loosing X amount of money)All in all, a unique experience. But still, even after the update, I can't recommend it to players who want to enjoy the characters, the world and want to experiment with everything, because then they will loose the contests and it's game over. I am one of them.
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: Potionomics is a very fun, but stressful, little management game. Its art style and music and presentation gets a 10/10 from me, as its very cute and extremely charming. HOWEVER, this game suffers from a few major flaws. There isn't enough time in the game to do everything you'd like to. You're unable to get to know the characters you want to without dropping the ball on money, and potions. If the game had 2-4 more time spaces per day, this wouldnt be a problem, but if you're wanting to romance a character, good luck getting to max relationship level. I played this game, one play through, and had a blast in it. A little upset about the ability to not fully romance a character because of the time, but I enjoyed almost all of this game. *ALMOST*. The final "boss" of the game is a fight that I genuinley did not have fun with. It was unfair and unbalanced for the average player to beat, even on their third attempt. You need to have a god-tier deck, and have some ludicrously good RNG. The deck-building in the game is a little barren, but still is fun to theory craft, so theres no complaints with the systems in that regard. My only major complaints with this game, is that there simply isn't enough time in each day, or each cycle before the tournaments in the game. TL;DR If you dont like managment games and being stressed a little, don't play this game. If you like those things, this game is amazing and presents it in a cute manner too. I personally really enjoyed it, besides a few flaws it has. Worth the price point, as I got a good 10 hours from one playthrough, and I may do more. I wish Steam had more than a "yes or no" when reccomending a game, but because I feel it's good, I give it a thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: The dialogue between characters is amusing, but the gameplay itself is repetitive and frustrating. the game doesn't provide enough time in the course of each day, which makes you feel constantly rushed. Some basic quality of life improvements would make it less tedious, but frankly I don't think there is enough game here if the tedium were removed.

_childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous character animations and solid writing, combined with a pretty entertaining inventory management sim based around making cool things with math ratios.  The thing that sold me on this was restarting after about ten days.  I'd expected that the early path would be a fairly heavy tutorialization and there would only be one path forward for the first few days.  Almost immediately I started getting different ingredients and having to alter my strategy based on the randomized perks for each day.  The path you take is definitely not prescribed from day one and what you get and how you use it varies enough to make the game experience feel fresh and unpatronizing. This game cares about the decisions you make and it asks you to make a lot of them.  That means it's an appropriate level of challenging to match an appropriate level of charming.  And it is an extremely good level of charming!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful, has stellar graphics and music, fluid animations and lovable characters.Previously, I had given this game a negative review due to the difficulty of the time management clashing with how much the game made me want to relax. Ironically similar to the way the stress works in-game.However with the new difficulty options and even more so the joys of the free love mode (I get all the cute interactions my heart desires in one sitting), this game has clawed its way back into my life and shown just how great it can be.An artstyle that will stand strong in a crowd, adorable writing that evokes all the emotions it possibly can, with a catchy and earwormy soundtrack, all from the comfort of relaxing and making potions (or cranking that heat up if you so wish). _childDocuments_.review: Having just 100% completed the game, here are my thoughts. This review presumes you have read the base of what this game is about.The difficulty is front-loaded. All the stress about meeting deadlines and everything you feel you need to do with so little time was only present for the first competition to maybe halfway through the second (so basically the first 1/3 of the game). During the beginning, you have an uphill battle with little starting money, no good cards for haggling, no space to brew many potions, and limited ingredients. Everything you do will feel like it has only a little impact for a lot of time.If you succeed in pushing through this, however, you will be awarded with many quality of life upgrades that remove most of the stress from the game. Mild spoilers ahead discussing these upgrades. By the time you have beaten the second competition you will be able to garden and grow your own ingredients (essentially you will make copies of ingredients of your choosing). This takes off a financial burden of buying multiple expensive ingredients. You will also be able to sell potions passively through a vending machine. While you may not make as much as haggling yourself, this is done passively and frees up your time to hang out with the amazing cast. You will also get to upgrade your shop to have multiple cauldrons, meaning you can brew multiple types of potions at once. The three elements above combined into freeing up so much time and room to breathe. You may find yourself in my situation where you actually lack for things to do. Towards the end of the game, I was able to simply skip days waiting for the finale. It also allowed me to see what a delightful cast this game has. Everyone's story was enjoyable and they are all charming and fun to get to know. The mechanics of the game are enjoyable to engage with, but you may find some (like selling your own potions), become more time than they are worth.All this to say, try to not let the difficulty scare you. I would say give it a go and know that the game does give you multiple more mechanics that make it easier, you just need to get past a tough start. The only true gripes I have with this game are the lack of ingredient sorting, which makes buying and crafting potions take longer than necessary; and a lack of a fulfilling post story (which I can only hope will be addressed in a sequel).
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: (On a side-note, I wish I had given the game more time before criticizing the difficulty as much as I did. According to many others, after the first week the game becomes much more manageable; and having experienced it myself pre-patch, I can absolutely confirm that it did. Either way, the difficulty has now been toned down, so chill/casual playthroughs should be much more attainable from here on out.)The original, unedited review follows:This game  charm at every step and I really can't recommend it enough. It's also  difficult than I first envisioned it to be, which- while not necessarily a bad thing- does end up making it very stressful at times when I felt like it should have been easier. Multitasking is difficult with how few days you have between major events, and money is always just short enough to get me to skip out on buying upgrades that would potentially make life easier. I had  to get everything done before the first big event, and then was immediately thrust back into the fire.I would have a couple suggestions on how to make the game easier, either using both together as a new difficulty mode, or (preferably) choosing one or the other as a patch to the game going forward. • Adding more time slots to each day, even just 2 or 3 more. With the way the story is structured, adding more days before each event isn't something that could easily be done; I think this would be a really good compromise, extending out each day so there's more time to do more things like those rank-up events you get with the NPC's, without worrying about missing out on potion-selling time.• Increasing the value of potions- not by much, maybe just by 25% or so. Any more than that and suddenly you have every upgrade you could possibly want at all times, which defeats the purpose of being in debt in the first place. Having just a small bump in profit could make the time crunch more bearable, but in all honesty, I still prefer the first solution over this one, even though this would by far be the easier suggestion to implement.Still, I can't recommend this game enough. It's incredibly charming, it obviously has an insanely skilled team behind it, and it's very, very worth the price. I was just expecting a slightly less stressful game than what I ended up getting- but I'm looking forward to mastering the mechanics so that even that issue is erased as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed this game but it had its problems.Positives: Very interesting concept! The haggling sessions are fun and I've seen some people who've managed to get infinite combos so there's potential for some very fun decks I'd say. I loved hanging out with characters and ranking them up and getting to learn more about them. I personally never had much trouble with the boss battles. As long as you reach the suggested criteria it doesn't take much to win, though building decks that revolve around doing as much interest in one turn as possible worked best for me in boss battles as the stress applied per turn got really high. I loved the visuals for this game. I loved seeing the characters move around and how they all moved differently and unlocking cards and getting new card art was fun.Negatives: Making potions originally started out really cool but by the end I just really found it tedious. I wish there was something that automatically threw something together for a recipe and you can edit it from there. The final fight was really hard and the only reason I got through is cause I managed to pull the card that gives you infinite cards fairly early. I also kinda thought after I beat the final boss the game was just gonna let me play infinitely from there which I was looking forward to since playing without the time constraints seemed really fun. I don't really see myself playing through the entire game again just to romance another character or at least unlock their maxed rank.All in all I recommend this game. And only did 2 customer orders, since these could not compare to selling a single potion myself.Then there is the deckbuilding mechanic for haggling. A great idea that sort of works. _childDocuments_.review: Very nice little game, probably the closest we get to a modern Recettear atm. I really enjoy the haggle system in the game with cards. Though I will say that atm, there are some cards are broken based on the current challenge, so for example, every 10 days you have a match with the haggle system, and if you have Saffron's card where you gain interest based on patience, you get around 25-30 interest from the get-go, which basically makes the whole challenge kinda pointless when one card wins it for you like that.There is also the issue with a lot of loading screens, I haven't that issue as much because I have the game on a SSD, but I see many are having issue with it if installed on a HDD (though the HDD people have installed on might simply be bad HDDs, so take that as you will). I installed it on my own HDD just to test, and didn't find it too long, though I can understand people's frustration since there are so many loading screen points.Potion making in itself is fun to mix and match and work around lacks of certain ressources and try to make a perfect brew for extra points. Though, personally it seems some certain ressources are reduntant but this might change when I play more.There is also the mechanic of sending people to expeditions, which is a nice little thing, though personally would like to see more involvment of some kind except from just giving potions, just really liked Recettear did it, it broke up the standard pattern of just going to the store all the time, but even though it is lacking in that department a bit imho, it brings in better characters and systems around those characters.The characters are all, characters in every sense of the word (in that they can feel more like characters, and not like actual people that just happens to live in this universe if that makes sense), some seems to wear their stick as the one thing that they got going for them, and that is true to some extent, though after playing more and talking with the characters more, you pick up that they are more than just "Bad girl that likes the guitar and are kinda freaky (even accepts bugs as gifts)".This might change when I talk to them more, but seems alright overall.And that brings me to the animation of the characters and overall style, absolutely love it. The expressions and everything is over the top, but the good kind imho. It is so much fun to simply watch the characters throughout a dialogue, and see some quirks some characters have, like Luna with her eyes expanding and retracting all the time. And that makes some characters stand out of the rest, characters like Muktuk isn't bad, but I think it is mainly because you don't see his eyes that it makes him have less of an impact, atleast to me.All in all, great little game, especially to this price. _childDocuments_.review: After playing it for a little over 50 hours and finishing my first playthrough, I feel the need to write a review of this game, something that I usually never do. Words fail to describe the marvelous love and care put into this piece of art, which is why I have the urge to express my thoughts on it.I'll arrange these two into a single point since, to be honest, while the story is sufficient to drive the force of the game, it's merely a stage for what is the REAL selling point: THE CHARACTERS. Every, and I gotta emphasize this, EVERY SINGLE CHARACTER feels so unique and full of life and love and I can't stop thinking about them. Their personalities, designs, expressions, writing... every character is memorable to their last bit of dialogue. At first you may not think they're such a big deal, but once you start learning more about them, once you start hearing about their backstories and their beliefs, their aspirations, that's when the hook strikes, and oh boy was I HOOKED. After maxing every single relationships right by the end of my playthrough, I can guarantee, every minute I spent with these characters was absolutely worth my entire time in this game.This game is a mix of three genres at once: haggling-based cards, potion crafting and dating simulator. I was surprised at how all three core aspects of the game blended so well together. I won't go into too much detail about the dating aspect of the game, since I think it's the easier of the three to grasp; it falls into a common visual novel genre with some simple, yet hilarious, dialogues and reactions you have to choose from on every interaction. The potion making aspect is actually pretty fun and makes you use your brain more than I expected to; calculating how much of each ingredient you need to make each potion, while trying your best to keep a good ratio for bonus effects and a constrained stock, is very satisfactory and entertaining on it's own. However, my favorite game mechanic without a doubt ended being the card playing aspect of the game. The haggling is a mental battle with a customer that desperately wants to get each potion for the best price, while you also try to earn the most of out it. With a great range of cards and effects, building a deck and using those cards you've earned through your relationships creates a feeling of statisfaction that I feel is unique to this game. Playing with buffs and debuffs, as well as managing patience and stress while maxing the customer's interest is unreasonably addicting in its own right, specially after playing a perfect hand that closes the sale for over 80%, the gameplay loop will amke you wish for more every time.This game's artstyle and design is in a league of it's own, the characters and environments are perfect for the world-building of the game and its presentation. The 3D models look great and, while cartoonish and expressive, they never go into the uncanny, and I think it's something the game deserves a lot of credit for. The animations are hilarious and match each character perfectly, along with their unique expressions, you can tell the amount of passion put into the modeling, rigging and animation process behind the scenes. The 2D characters and items are charming, the environments are colorful and expressive, and the cards are not only pieces of beautiful artwork, but they're also an extension of each character that reminds you of their unique aspects and personalities. The music, on a final note, is charming and memorable, I love that each character gets their own theme, it really excells at setting a unique feeling once you step and switch between them on a single day. Be ready for that potion crafting BGM to live rent free in your head tho.As much as I love this game, it's important to note it's flaws and weaknesses, and I think the game has a severe difficulty unbalance, where the game is hard at the beginning, but too easy by the end. I personally didn't have any problems early, although I can recognize if you don't get good RNG, you may get stuck during the first week and hit a game over, which can leave a terrible first impression of a game that has so much good stuff locked behind that first threshold. However, once you get past those first blockades, once you get past the superb first weeks, you'll find that the game has a steady and constant raise in difficulty, which ends up not being enough once you arrive to the end-game, when you start sweeping through competitions without breaking a sweat. I believe this is due simply to how the shop upgrades and thresholds for the competitions are balanced, each week's required potions will scale at a constant rythm, while your shop scales exponentially, it'll inevitably rise above those requirements to the point you can have all potions for the next competition ready by the second day of an end-game week.The game features an upgrade system that, while fun and engaging, is ultimately worthless once you realize that every new week brings forth new items that absolutely powercreep every bench and pot bought before, even after upgrading them. This makes the upgrade system feel unnecessary and becomes only useful at the last week when you know there'll be no more powercrept items showing up. But then again, this ties to the problems in difficulty, since the game gets easier at the end and the pots available to buy at the beginning of each week are sufficient for that week's competition requirements, then there's really no point in upgrading a pot other than for feeling the satisfaction to do so. You can upgrade the benches to earn more money, but like I said in the previous section, there'll be no need to as you'll probably be swimming in money.During potion crafting, you'll realize that each potion can acquire traits, both good and bad, which can oversell or undersell a potion. These traits play a nice aspect of the game on paper and can create a new level of enjoyment and difficulty. The issue is that, once I hit that moment when orders with specific traits began bombarding my shop, that there was seemingly no explanation in-game of how this system actually worked, and that most of the time I simply didn't have the right ingredients to fulfill those orders. The biggest problem here I believe is that getting those ingredients with good traits is completely RNG. You need to do a good amount of hero expeditions to get good items, but a lot of times they won't be what you need. For this you can craft potions that can help boost the odds of your characters getting those ingredients, or you can try to use temporary enchantments to fulfill a specific order, but by the time you realize this the game has already tasked you with these orders, and you only have so much time and focus during the first weeks you'll probably feel too overwhelmed to worry about it.I love this game, so much that even after experiencing the dauntingly easy end-game, I still want more of it, and I realize I can't escape the charming impression it has left on me while I desperately scroll through steam's library trying to find anything that resembles it. I totally recommend experiencing this game for yourself, even if you fail during the first week, please give it a second try, as it has so much it wants to say and the gameplay gets so good, it'll totally be worth trying.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting shop sim with heavy time and resource management that make it a bit more of a challenge than one would expect. There is also a dating sim aspect with a range of charming characters to befriend in a professional manner or romantically, though not every character is available for romantic pursuit. The potion crafting mechanic as well as the haggling mini-game make it a bit more complex than other shop sims while the two mechanics are rather simple, giving various ways to get a bit more money for your wares though special displays, marketing campaigns, and the aforementioned haggling mini-game makes it easy to obtain more money on later playthroughs when you're more familiar with the system, though there is little incentive to replay game as most of it if not all of it can be experienced in a single run.I found the entire game to be a delight from the writing to the art and the music as well, I'd definitely recommend anyone who is interested in shop sims and management games to pick this one up.

_childDocuments_.review: A hidden gem! Underneath the cartoon artistry lies a very deep potion / brewing / foraging / economics game.  There's honestly so much to do that you feel like you can't do it all... and you shouldn't.  Managing materials with the necessity to bring in a profit against a looming huge debt to pay off.  This is not a light game if one thinks about the intricacies and depth in which this game has gone.  32 hours in and then this game still introduces new facets of potion making (aging your potions to make them more expensive!!) that I never even thought about!! This isn't just about brewing potions and such, it's about selling them.  The deck building aspect of this game really works.  The "battles" don't take a lot of time and are pretty fun and very strategic. Should you press your sales tactics or close them out and not take the stress and possibly get more negative cards that could tank your stress. My biggest beefs about this game are the lack of Quality of Life functions for this game.  For example, you spend a lot of time going in and out of different screens to do different things.  Moving ingredients  in and then clearing them from your cauldron is a chore if you're testing to see what to put into your latest concoction.  Alt tabbing to write this review screws up the resolution for my monitor.  Just all kinds of clunky screens to go through.  Potionomics is a refreshing revelation.  I truly can't wait for all of the Quality of life changes and possibly even more from this developer.  I wish I can put a highly recommend for this game with like 5 stars, and ring bells and bang drums because yes this game is that good!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game!  I initially had my doubts about both the character models and the touted NPC interactions.  I was looking for a nice crafting game, and those seemed unnecessary.  However, having finished the game, I do see why they both are so important.  The graphics are great, and the expressions and movement really help add depth to the characters, which in turn drives the story.Aside from that, the game play is fun.  The potion making is comprised of adding together ingredients to get the right ratios.  I found it more difficult to decide WHAT to make, rather than HOW to make it - which is fine for a shop running game.  I appreciate that it was a  pure shop game, and not a 'go out and fight monsters and then YOU sell the spoils' game.The haggling card game is fun.  I liked that you get to build your own deck from a stockpile of cards you accumulate.  Getting the cards from NPC relationships also ties the story and the mechanics together nicely.That said, I don't think there's much replay value.  The story is told.  The shop has more than enough money to max everything.  All the NPCs love me.  I'm glad I bought and played it, but a single play through is enough.

_childDocuments_.review: For a game that was featured in the Capitalism sale, the main mechanics of this game have very little to do with money. While the premise, art, and set up all point to this being more of shop-management type game, the actual game play and "success" criteria all focus on managing the almost overwhelming secondary mechanics. The best use of your time is not to be in the shop or selling your potions but acquiring ingredients for said potions - and making potions to give to your adventurers, to get more ingredients, to make more potions, to give to the adventurers... the time management piece of this was also frustrating, as it gives you six time increments to do things, but everything requires at least two time increments to complete any task. A misclick then wastes a time increment, which throws off the whole day if everything else is in sets of two. I really wanted to like this game but I found myself not having fun when it felt more like actual chores (going shopping, cooking, scheduling time for people) than a fantasy game.The art is beautiful, the game is well made and bugless, and the dialog is well written, I wish the mechanics of the game did not get in the way of the game itself.

_childDocuments_.review: I just want so much better for this game.  Pretend like I'm giving this a positive-ish review because I feel it does way more things right than wrong, but I would be remiss to not point out it's many shortfalls in the UI department, and I'm all for getting that extra attention with a thumbs down.But first, the Good:-Brewing potions is neat, and the fact there are many different ways to make the same potions, as well as an array of different options to dress them up.  The potions you brew to donate to your adventurers are functional and cheap, while the ones for customers can have positive quirks to up their value.  Do you strive for perfection, making sure your ratios are exact, or do you just kind of wing it with whatever you have?-Characters are narrativly rich.  I have not "finished" any of their stories yet, but the dialogue has a healthy dollop of nuance that means I'm always looking forward to the next level up in their relationship, and not just for the sake of discounts/card unlocks.-Bartering with Customers is rewarding.  There is wide selection of cards that can go into your haggle deck which I feel could lend themselves to a wide variety of strategies, and while it might be a bit of a chore to haggle tooth and nail to end up at +30% to your first couple of dodgy potions, later on it's much more rewarding, and more difficult as customers become more picky/stressed/arrogant.-There are a bunch of little systems that means that there is a healthy amount of random chance (say, what ingredients you get from adventurers/guild hall outcomes/day events) which gives you the spice, but the player also has some options to forge their own path (do you buy ingredients from Quinn, or take a random box from Salt and Pepper which would mean less money spent per ingredient? - Which ingredients do you grow in your slime farm? - What kind of haggle deck do you want to build? - when do you commit to an advertising campaign from Moth person whatever their name is I can't remember?) Now, the Annoying.-There needs to be way more work done to make the UI nicer, cause there are so many QoL features that could make things way easier, which I suppose is not surprising when there are so many systems in a game like this.  For example;Not being able to sort Quinn's stock by any method, only being able to view 10 ingredients at a time in Quinn's shop, having the double dialogue box come up showing what ingredients are going to be available after expanding their stock is unnecessary, if you want to by all 10 of a particular ingredient, you need to click all the way up from 1 to 10, there is no button to empty your cauldron of all the ingredients you have in it you need to double click each one, sometimes the ingredients stack on top of each other and so to remove the bottom one you need to remove the one above it you have to double click on each ingredient to add it to your cauldron, there is no way to sort ingredients in ascending/descending order of strength, the order of ingredients are in the order that you get them and you can't change said order, for some reason by default when going to the brew menu you are automatically looking at not only potential ingredients but also fire fuel and other potions you have making that menu even more cluttered, you can't see which positive/negative traits are of a potion you are about to/or are brewing you have to mouse over each ingredient and check, it can be way less clicks then it is now to swap to a different cauldron (just have an arrow at the side of the cauldron to go to the next one), there is nothing in game of a "shopping list" so you can remember what you need to go and buy from Quinn, you can't check what the monsters/obstacles are of an expedition in your shop and have to check with an actual adventurer, I want to be able to sort ingredients by type in the slime garden window, I want to change the order in which ingredients appear in, I want to be able to ignore particular ingredients, I want to be able to do like a "brew rehearsal" to see if a particular combination of ingredients is going to work before I go and buy/find/grow said ingredients, I want to be able to save a specific combination of ingredients to quick-put into a cauldron, there is an icon on an ingredient which shows which area that ingredient can be found - why not the reverse? (i.e. before I send an adventurer out I want to see what ingredients I might find or at the least what I've already found before), I would like an icon that shows if I have expanded Quinn's library so I don't accidentally use my last one of a rare herb, I would like to see a breakdown of the +% on what determines the current potion sale price, now that I think about it I'm not even sure if there /are/ any keyboard shortcuts //for anything at all//, or show prompts to indicate said shortcuts, I want a place to see where all the loading tips are cause there is some critical information in them and my computer is loading this game too fast for me to read half of them, why is when I sort by ingredient trait it shows both the positive and negative ones with no way to filter for either, while you can sort for ingredients that have for example A B and C (which shows you ingredients that have to have A, B and C)(which also still shows your fire material and potions at the end of that list why do I need to see that I don't want to have to keep clicking to turn off that filter), there isn't a way to filter for the /absence/ of say B and C (i.e. only show me ingredients that /don't/ have something), there isn't an option to show ingredients that you've previously had but how have none of (which is possibly only a problem cause of the poor search ability, i.e. there have been times when I've been trying to find an ingredient that I've run out of, but I didn't /know/ I had run out of it), there is no ability to have "favourite" ingredients (which I'm not even sure would fix anything, but it might help), when you have paid for a enchantment you are no longer able to check any potion or ingredient for that day as to what traits they /actually/ have, enchantments only show only one icon of what they enhance despite enhancing multiple traits, you can't mouse over said traits to know what they are (I know I have trouble remembering between the two ones that feature a head), it would be nice to see what the upgrade path of the various cauldrons are before I commit to buying one, potions you have made are not grouped in any meaningful way with no way to filter them.But this is what happens when you get older, you start to really focus on UI, and having a bad one just kind of hurts.While the development team are still working on patching the game as of 13-Nov-2022, little of the list I just rattled off are featured as it's mainly gameplay breaking bugs that they are focusing on, which I have encountered a few times already.If you wanted to play a more beefy version of Reccetear (sans combat sequences), with the character models from Sea of Thieves, deck building akin to Heathstone, a robust potion mixing system, with a dollop of visual novel/dating simulator, then this is an easy sell, and I think you should absolutely support the developer as I don't feel like this style of game comes around very often.If you are an old fuddy duddy that get's hung up on sub-optimal UI, come back in a couple of months.

_childDocuments_.review: Potionomics is a fantastic experience. Your gameplay is evenly split between two puzzles where you're trying to make the best of limited space: you brew potions with limited ingredients and limited space in your cauldron trying to make the best you can, then you haggle with customers' limited patience trying to get the highest price you can. The supporting characters are all wonderful and supportive as well, and it's from them that you learn additional haggling techniques to fit into your arsenal. There are a lot of improvements I want to see made in Potionomics 2, but the game as-is is well worth your time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to enjoy about Potionomics but it needs a handful of QoL adjustments to really make it enjoyable.I played the first half of the game unmodded and by the last half I had installed the Exploration Mode mod which allowed for Hangouts (relationship building/stress relief) to not cost any time. Without it, the game's time management felt stressful and daunting. Some people might want that added challenge but I'm playing games to relax; I have enough stress at work.I really enjoy all of the character designs, the dialogues are fun, and the characters feel fleshed out by the end of their story arcs. I love them each a lot and would love a polyamory mod.When travelling out on the town to socialise with these characters it would have been really helpful to have a page in the notebook akin to the deckbuilder (only accessible in the home base) which displays what your friendship rank is with them.Upgrading your equipment feels like a waste of time. Once you move onto the next chapter, Muktuk's newest items immediately outrank and outpace what you just had even if upgraded. It makes almost no sense to even bother. My preference would be to have a stronger upgrade based system rather than buying completely new each chapter; ie. allow your cauldron to be upgraded into the newest one with new materials like any other game.When Customising your shop to choose which equipment you want out on the floor it would be incredibly helpful to a) have a more organised system for sorting your cauldrons/shelves/aging-barrels and b) displaying what the stats are of the equipment you currently have on the floor, and/or c) allowing you to put away what equipment you currently have out without needing to replace it with something else in order to do so.While the haggling itself can be incredibly tedious after X number of customers I do like the gameplay of it a lot and would have preferred longer haggling sessions to see how my deck can really play. A larger deck would also be more fun in my opinion. Dialogues from NPCs and from Sylvia don't tend to match up. It's annoying but minor and you don't have to pay attention to it if you're focused on the cards instead.If you don't like the tedium of the haggling there's the option of a vending machine autoselling your potions for you.The Boss fights are severely underwhelming. Here's the chance to really sink your teeth into the haggling gameplay and test out your combos except --oh. It's over in three turns. That was boring. Artificially inflate the Bosses' values? Give them more buffs/debuffs? Maybe only one or two I felt Sylvia was actually going to get overstressed on me.Early game stresses are shadowed significantly by the later game once you have a rhythm and enough money, you really don't have to worry that much about the competition potions especially if you get them made in the first half of the week. This kind of progression feels good, it feels like a sense of accomplishment in learning new skills and Sylvia's growth.Overall, despite its flaws, I think Potionomics is worth playing but isn't a Must Play. 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly frustrating to me on 2 levels:1) It looks great and promises so much good stuff. I love brewing mechanics, adventures' guild commissions, social interactions and relationship developments. Hell, even card game system of haggling is neat. So I expected to love this game when I got it. And that's why it hurts so much worse when the second factor hit me.2) Time restrictions. This game has a time management system, and it's BRUTAL. You have 6 hours in a day. Pretty much any action (except maybe your shop organisation) costs time.Brewing costs time, working the counter costs time, talking to people and developing relationships costs time, and time is money. And money is resources, and resources are essential for brewing which is essential for making money, and so on. You can't brew better potions without better ingredients, and you can't just buy new ingredients - you must commission adventurers to go fetch them for you, and you don't always know ahead what you'll get. And commissions cost money too, as well as potions. And you need those new good ingredients, because you absolutely must win that competition that happens every 10 days (which requires you to make the absolute best things you can at your level), otherwise it's game over. And that is absolutely not enough time to do all the things that you need, let alone things you want. It really feels like this game was designed for people who want to optimize their every move with just the slightest margin of error. Sadly, that is not what I am looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my game of the year.Everything about this game is a triumph, really. The way the card-gameplay, potion-making, friend-finding, adventuring, and basically every element of the game tie together is immensely satisfying and IMPRESSIVE. (Especially the potion-making. Seriously satisfying to toss different ingredients around, numbers going up, maximizing the stars but also the balance... love it!) None of these systems are particularly complex, but with how often you do each of these things, I'd say it hits it right on the nose of being complex enough to engage you and simple enough to not leave you frustrated or perplexed. You'll be going through similar motions a lot, after all.Obviously, the art is gorgeous- the models and animations, definitely, but the little art on the cards are charming as well. Every character having their own little theme is cute, especially when I quite enjoyed each of them.I loved every single character in this game, and that basically never happens in the games I play, honestly. By the end, I was beating myself in the head for not unlocking every conversation with each one once I'd run out of time. Oh, and gay.If you have even a vague interest in any of this game's genres, I highly recommend you check it out. _childDocuments_.review: Potionomics is an item shop management game along with games like Recettear and Moonlighter. Recettear and Moonlighter divide the gameplay loops between managing your shop and an ARPG dungeon delver to get your items. Potionomics eschews combat in favor of relationship-building similar to the Persona games. Between Recettear and Moonlighter, Potionomics shares more in common with the former. In both games you will arrange your items to sell & haggle with each customer to get a better price. In Recettear, haggling involves a careful tweaking of the price based off the individual customer's preference without getting them upset. In Potionomics, the haggling mechanic is handled with a deck-building card battling mechanic. The plot and pacing are also similar: both games have you inheriting a shop - along with massive debt - that has to be paid off at regular intervals. The primary focus of Potionomics is gathering ingredients, brewing potions, and then haggling with customers to sell the potions. When you aren't selling potions, you are visiting the town in order to get more ingredients, buy upgrades to your shop, or increasing your relationship with NPCs.  The game is played out over the course of 50 days, which are divided into five 10-day weeks. The first 9 days of the week the player has full control on how to spend their time. Each day is split into 6 time units that the player has to decide if they will use it openings their shop to sell potions, or going into town to rank up with NPCs and buy ingredients. On the 10th day of each week is a potion competition which is a "best two out of three" boss battle where you present your best potions of a specific type. If you far exceed the recommended quality, you win outright - otherwise you go into the card battling/haggling game. Winning the competition at the end of each week is required to progress as it provides exactly the amount needed to pay that week's debt payment.  Haggling is handled by a card game battle using a 20-card deck that you build. The goal of this "battle" is to raise the customer's interest (and therefore value) in the potion before the customer's "patience" runs out. Each turn that passes and each card played lowers patience. If patience reaches 0, the customer leaves without buying the potion. During these haggling sessions, your character's stress level can increase. Higher stress leads to increased chances of drawing negative “stress cards.” If this ever reaches 100%, you fail. To be successful, the best decks balance efficiently raising customer interest while minimizing stress. In Potionomics there are 10 NPCs that you can rank up with, and possibly romance. The characters are colorful, beautifully animated, and fun/cute. Each NPC has 10 ranks that can be leveled. Upping your rank unlocks new cards of increasing power that you can use in your deck, as well as unlocking coupons that can provide passive price discounts for whatever service they provide to you. The cards given by each NPC all have a different playstyle resulting in 10 different deck archetypes to play with. As you rank up with NPCs, you will likely find the playstyle that works the best for you and can prioritize ranking up that NPC in order to get even better cards to build your optimal deck. For me, I found my deck consisting of 2-3 decks, with a few dips into other decks. Unfortunately, once I built my optimal deck about 60% of the way through the game, ranking up the other NPCs and getting their new cards became less rewarding as their playstyle didn't fit my deck's primary "win condition." There is a saying in the gaming world that "players will optimize the fun out of a game." Regrettably, I find myself proof of this claim as I often find myself spending more time than needed calculating, planning, and optimizing every little thing in order to play as efficiently as possible in this game. Because this game has a time management component, I found myself meticulously planning every day in order to avoid any "wasted" time slots.  Additionally, brewing potions requires careful balancing of ingredients which is abstracted numerically - meaning brewing the optimal potions turns into a math equation. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy the math, but it is definitely far less fun than running the shop & haggling with customers. By the end of the game I spent 20-25% of my time haggling, with the other rest of my time spent talking to NPCs, managing my time/planning my days, and staring a menus of ingredients to brew my potions. While carefully brewing a balance potion IS part of the challenge and gameplay of Potionomics, I wished there were a button that I could press to auto-brew the "best" version of a potion with the available ingredients I had after I have a made that potion manually at least once. The other main criticism I have about this game is that there are WAY too many menus you have to go through to do simple things. Even with an SSD, loading between these menus could be 3-5 seconds each time. This may not sound like a lot, but if you have to go in-and-out of multiple menus, this really adds up quickly and becomes noticeable. The issue is there are too many menus for a small range of specialized actions. For example: the main screen shows a visual of your shop - including the items & potions you have setup. However, you cannot change your furniture or arrange your potions from this menu. Setting up your furniture requires going into its own separate "customize" menu. Once you setup your furniture you then have to leave that menu back to the main one, then go into the "arrange potion" menu to place your potions on your shelves, then back out of that menu to the main one again before you can click "open shop" to begin selling the potions. In this simple cycle you had to go through a minimum of 4 loading screens. And this is in the best case scenario. Worst case scenario is you go to the "arrange potion" menu only to find out you didn't place your newly upgraded shelf, so you have to back out of that menu, go to the "customize" menu, go to try and change the shelf - only to realize you forgot to take off your potions (you cannot swap shelves if potions are on them). So then you have to back out of that menu, then enter the "arrange" menu again, clear off the shelves, back out again to just go back into the "customize" menu to swap shelves, back out again to re-enter the "arrange" menu to place your potions, back out again before you can finally "open" your shop. So forgetting this one little detail can lead to 10 different loading screens to fix something simple. It baffles me that in the "arrange potion" screen that I can't simply swap out my available shelves at the same time I am placing potions on them. Not to mention not having the option to "open shop" from that same screen. These two simple changes could cut down this 4-10+ loading screen interaction down to 1. Overall I enjoyed my time with Potionomics. The best parts of the game is the haggling/card battling when selling potions, the beautiful animations that give the characters their unique charm, and the lovely artstyle/designs. Despite my criticisms, I felt it was worthwhile time. It took me about 40 hours to beat the game with 100% completion (all achievements/maxing out all character relationships). As mentioned earlier, I spent too much time optimizing my time which did take the fun out of the game. By the beginning of week three, I felt I was far ahead of the game's "difficulty curve," so I was able to coast on through the rest of the game. I feel I would have enjoyed the game more if I were more lackadaisical with my time - focusing more on running the shop instead of planning my day and brews.

_childDocuments_.review: Adorable, Interesting, and there's NUMBERS TO CRUNCH! There are still ingredients I have yet to come across in some of the earlier regions, and I think having a balance of sending out heroes on quests in new and old territories melds really well with the amount of wealth I've amassed.There was a point where I was scared I wouldn't be able to pass one of the competitions, but I squeaked by the day before, making the potion I needed just in time!The deck building is very simple. _childDocuments_.review: Once again, Steam's lack of nuance makes rating this hard. I say "no", but with several caveats.First off, the style is immaculate. I love the visuals. There are a few graphical bugs but beyond that, it's a very pretty style and very colorful.Second, I love all the characters you get to interact with! They're so fun and seem to have promising stories. That brings me to my first 'negative'. There just isn't enough time to experience most of the characters' stories. The time management aspect made it almost impossible for me to explore more than maybe half the character story lines, which is a real shame. I don't intend to replay the whole game just to get story lines that could have easily been acquired with a post-game free play mode.My second negative is the resource and time management as a whole. It prevented me from experimenting with a lot of the different features the game had to offer. I didn't have time to brew custom orders, or play with the marketing, or even really bother with the haggling minigame towards the end. It was faster and cheaper to use the vending machine. Couple with my previous point, which meant that I didn't have the whole breadth of cards available, and I wasn't even able to experiment with my decks much.I really wish there were some sort of casual play mode or like I mentioned, some kind of post game so I could experiment with different things. I've seen a lot of bickering that "ACTUALLY the game is just FINISHED", and that's my point -- the developers finished it, and I think there were some simple options to expand gameplay just a little.The story was fun up until the final competition, at which point it seemed to be in a rush to wrap everything up. It presented a serious pacing issue.Overall I can't really recommend it as-is. There's some good mods out there to help ease some of these issues, so either try it with those, or proceed at your own risk. If you're patient, good at resource management, or just plain stubborn like me, you might enjoy some parts of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Potionomics is a wonderful new branch into the shop sim genre. If you are someone who enjoys challenging time management and deck building then this game is a great mix of the two. Potionomics first brings you into it's world with wonderful character design, a bright and vibrant world and delightful dialogue, but keeps you gripped with it's deep potion brewing system. With 5 ingredient types and 5 sense traits and 5 levels of potion tiers the combination of creations you can make seems endless. The initial difficulty curve might not be for everyone, but if you stick with it I promise that you'll be rewarded with a great sense of accomplishment along with the pride of defeating interesting rivals. There are a few quality of life improvements regarding UI and available information that XSeed could make that would make this game a perfect 10/10 for me, but nothing that would turn me off from playing. I'm more than excited to do another playthrough, and can't wait to see what a sequel can bring to this franchise!

_childDocuments_.review: I booted this up and found it really hard to put down. The gameplay is downright therapeutic. The writing is just so much delight.I honestly wasn't very sure about this game at first because I was put off by the 3D artstyle since it gave that stigma of being a mobile game. But now I realize the genius behind making it like that is to make the characters more expressive during the story-sections. It's always a treat to see their little animations.I've seen a bunch of reviews complaining about this game's difficulty but I've honestly had nothing but a blast even before the nerf and finished the game in one playthrough--technically.Here's a few things:--Quality of Life Suggestions--* A "Buy All" button so I don't get carpal tunnel from buying supplies* Include the trait outcome during the potion-making process* More sorting options for:** Total Magimin Count for both overall and per type** Separating Negative and Positive Ingredient Traits** Sorting in other places other than through brewing--Bugs & Glitches--* Sometimes the customer won't appear on-screen during the haggling sessions but the encounter would go on like they're actually there. This has only happened 3 times out of many that worked just fine.* Music would sometimes cut-off abruptly during the main shop screen.* The audio actually cut-off during the final competition. I had reset the game and that fixed it. It was just awkward to stop and reset during a dramatic part.* When I alt-tab too quickly as the game boots up the main menu, I get a "Fatal Error" message and it crashes the game.* This one already happened when I finished the game: I loaded the last autosave which was on the final day until I realized it wasn't NG+. I quit back to the menu really fast and the speech boxes were still appearing at the main menu. After letting the dialogue advance, I got the game over screen--which is the only reason why I got a game over but I thought it was funny.--Other Suggestions--* Endless Mode* New Game Plus* More content especially related to the other villainsOther than that, this is an extremely well-made game with a lot of love clearly put into it.I finished it today and I immediately went: "That was fun! Let's do all of that again."Games like this come far few in-between.Good job, devs. You made a banger.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: [Edit: The update added Cozy Mode, Endless Mode, GREAT voice acting and optional polyamory. Great stuff, strongly recommend this game!]I bought this game hoping for a chill shopkeeping game where I grind lots of low-tier potions and just vibe -- and Potionomics is definitely more demanding than that! Sylvia has a lot to do and very little time to do it, so using your time wisely is critical. The difficulty/RNG in the early game challenged me enough that I had to restart multiple times before I could beat the first boss, Roxanne. It's a game where you have to be prepared to give up and reload a save sometimes. I also had to take notes to help me remember everything I had on the go at one time (I'm chronically ill and my fuzzy brain forgets things in the time it takes to load a new screen). I often wanted to hang out with friend characters and do fun activities with them, but couldn't justify spending the time slots on non-potion-making activities. I'd love to have access to an Easy Mode story campaign, or a toggle-able option for extra days in between tournament rounds, or some sort of free play mode. But the game's difficulty does support the story premise: it's an experience of walking in Sylvia's easily-stressed newbie shoes. Despite being harder than I hoped, I like a lot of the stuff this game does! The music is wonderful. Some of my play hours are actually me wandering away from the computer while the music played. And the characters are a great cast of interesting friends (except for the few completely evil jerks in the mix). I haven't maxed out all the friendship meters yet, but the character arcs I've seen so far are great ways of engaging with a conventional magical fantasy setting. It's nice that everyone is allowed to touch on deep topics and systemic problems, while also doing fun lighthearted things like going shopping together, or using an enchanted cauldron to make ice cream. The characters will notice when you flirt with them a little but you end up dating someone else, so that's a nice touch that keeps replays fresh. Polyamory is unfortunately not an option in this otherwise queer-friendly story: starting a romantic relationship with one character blocks all other romance paths.I have some quibbles with the way the main story ends. But I think this game does a lot of good stuff and has a lot of heart. Give it a try if you want to make things in a cauldron, play card battles, and pick a cutie to date. Just make sure you save frequently in multiple slots!

_childDocuments_.review: Everything about this game is a delight to me. It's rare that a game is on point with so many things, especially as this seems to be the first game from an indie dev. The overall presentation and polish is so good that it eclipses the issues I have with it. That being said, I DO have issues, most pertaining to game balance. The opening week of the game is exceedingly punishing, with a single mistake having the potential to spiral out of control and end on a game over state once you hit the first boss. It's not too difficult to learn where you went wrong and correct it, but the way the game is designed it very much encourages save scumming with how important your early decisions are, which isn't the best way to introduce people to your game. After this hurdle, the game becomes acceptably challenging, with various new mechanics being introduced over time that allow you to have proper responses to the problems the game presents you and if you make a mistake. HOWEVER, After the 2nd boss the difficulty curve just falls over and gives up because you're presented with so many tools and and ways to handle the game that there's nothing stopping you from just making a batch of exceedingly powerful potions required for the competitions, sell the extras, then spend the rest of the week chilling out with your friends. Which is great as life goals, but in a management sim is a little problematic. For card game portion, there's a few easy to obtain deck strategies you can use to trivialize the shop encounters and competitions. If this required careful thought and execution to pull off, it'd be fine but nah, just speed run your relationship with the bard and win with an easy to execute infinite.Unrelated positive note: there's an neurodivergent-coded character who's entire card archetype revolves around stress that I hella appreciate and just wish she was more viable. Devs, pls buff Luna cards.TL;DRGame good. Will likely buy multiple copies.Unfortunate balance issues because card games are complicated and power creep is real.
_childDocuments_.name: Potionomics

_childDocuments_.review: Light recommendation.The game is very pretty and the characters are charming. It has a lot of clear mechanical inspirations (Stress snowballing reminiscent of Darkest Dungeon, Slay the Spire card combat, Recettear store management) and the gameplay loop is enjoyable (at the start) and very manageable if you plan anything ahead.Thing is, the game is very easy. This is not Recettear. All you need to get through a tournament stage is to send your heroes on the new adventures then get a new cauldron and upgrade it once. The time limit is very lax.I was victory lapping by day 20 (Had about 30k). By day 30 I no longer had to interact with the store portion of the game because I had so much money (80k). All it took was a publicity stunt and then 2 sessions of selling superior/masterwork curse cures. I was honestly just selling to kill the time and then I had 230k by day 40. More money than I could ever hope to spend.The more cauldrons you get the longer the days become and it gets really exhausting to play, especially if you're brewing 2 times a day. Feels like busywork. Minmaxing everything will burn you out of this game very quickly.Just take it casually and you'll have a good time.
