_childDocuments_.review: Having been a fan of Shin Megami Tensei and all its spin-offs for many years, I can say with absolute certainty that Shin Megami Tensei V Vengeance is the best to date in terms of gameplay. This version is a revision of the vanilla game originally released in 2021 on the Nintendo Switch, and all the highlights in this revision are positive.To begin with, you have the original route and the new route. "Canon of Creation" and "Canon of Vengeance" respectively. Both are accessible from the start, but it is still recommended to start with the original route to see the new areas that have been added to the maps and unlock the exclusive demons of that route, which are quite good (specifically Taira-no-Masakado, which can only be obtained at the end of the Canon of Creation). In terms of story, the original route wasn't particularly great, and no major changes have been made in this revision. However, the Canon of Vengeance route adds more context to the original story and significantly improves it.Now, in terms of gameplay, it must be said that this is where the game stands out as one of the most polished turn-based RPGs of all time. Considering that there are hundreds of demons available, balancing this type of game is an arduous task. The devs have done an outstanding job creating a much more balanced experience by taking all the feedback from the original game. This means that some abilities have been nerfed to avoid cheesing that ruined certain fights, but other aspects have also been significantly improved to make battles fairer. Now, for example, all demons have a fixed passive ability, which adds a lot of variety when forming your party and introduces many fun strategies to experiment with that weren't present in the original game.On the other hand, if you like RPGs with a very high difficulty curve, with very challenging encounters and a plethora of superbosses, you are probably facing an RPG that gives you all this and more. You have:3 Superbosses in the Canon of Creation route (Shiva, Masakado, Demi-fiend)Another superboss in the Canon of Vengeance route (Satan)A boss rush mode where you can repeat the fights with the bosses' original level.A boss rush mode where you can repeat the fights with the bosses' level modified to level 100.A boss rush mode where you can repeat the fights with the bosses modified as superbosses, at level 200.A new difficulty mode called Godborn where all encounters are basically bosses, and all bosses are superbosses.At least it’s safe to say that if you like tough challenges, you will have plenty of content in this game.Now, in terms of visuals and animations, as everyone says, this game looks spectacular. The maps are large and quite detailed, and it's impressive how well they look for the devs' first attempt at creating such large maps. It should be noted that before this game, SMT was not precisely known for having large maps with extensive exploration, but rather for being dungeon crawlers where you spent a lot of time in labyrinthine corridors. So for a first attempt at creating something different from the usual, they have done quite well.And the animations, they are simply put outstanding. Many demons and the protagonist have unique animations for different skills, all of them elaborated with lots of details and an insane amount of work put into them. All of them look beautiful. It certainly does feel good to style on the bosses delivering the finishing touch with flashy looking skills.And last but not least, the music. There are almost 90 new tracks in this revision, added to the 120 from the original. It's an impressive amount of +200 tracks. And of course, they are VERY GOOD, composed by Ryota Kozuka. Seriously, this game has one of the best OSTs with such a large repertoire and with bangers that you will never get tired of listening to. Special mention to tracks like: Dancing Crazy Murder, Battle Da'at, Seeker, Bounce and Roll, and Gliding among the many great tracks in this game.My only complaint is that the endgame farming is quite poorly designed due to the DLC practices they've been following for some time. Basically, the only consistent way to earn experience and money (especially the latter, which is a very necessary resource for the end-game and post-game) is with the Mitama DLC. Additionally, one of the best demons that you'll definitely need in your party for the end-game and post-game, Konohana Sakuya, is locked behind a paid DLC. So be prepared to shell out an extra $20 for all the DLC if you want to complete all the end-game and post-game content.In summary, buy this game if you are a fan of JRPGs with high difficulty, whether this is your first SMT or not, and especially if you love ultra-difficult challenges. You won't regret it. There's plenty of content.I give this game a 98/100, one point lost for the Mitama DLC and another point lost for the Konohana Sakuya DLC (buy it though, she is pretty.)

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Shut the ♥♥♥♥ up DazaiThis is an incredible game which I enjoyed very much, albeit with a major flaw that I'll address in a bit. For me it took ~78 hours to complete the main story plus almost all of the side quests so the price tag is definitely justified. Also this was the first game I've played in this series.Some pros: Fairly large open-world areas to explore and find hidden treasures in, fun turn-based combat system, a lot of different learnable skills/abilities, an INSANE amount of recruitable monsters, fusion system (like pokemon) that you can spend hours on, a bunch of "quality of life" features that makes menuing and farming fairly efficient and fast.Now the major flaw is, you guessed it - the story. It's generic and underwhelming to say the least, and the characters are all obnoxious and cringe-inducing - especially this cringe lord Dazai. Also the localization is not very good, can't really blame them for this but pronouncing Japanese names/terms with 4+ syllables in an American accent every 2nd sentence just sounds weird and unnatural.I do think, however, that the background setting and the lore are interesting, it's just the delivery of it all that fails.To summarize, get this game for an incredible turn-based JRPG experience - if you're willing to compromise on the story in favor of good gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: SMT V is a really, really cool game. I didn't buy the Switch version because of the way it ran (i.e., poorly) so I had no excuse this time.This game is awesome in many different ways. The combat system is welcoming, but allows you to be very technical by customizing pretty much everything about your party. Unique mechanics such as the Magatsuhi gauge and canceling your opponent's turns truly make this game shine. The amount of freedom the game gives you is really great!The soundtrack is easily one of the best I've heard! It's full of electro-industrial bops, sometimes with a post-punk twist. So if you like darkwave and stuff, you will enjoy it as much as I did.The story is... not exceptional. It's interesting enough to make you curious about how things will go on, but it's not a masterclass of writing skills. Who cares though? This game is pretty much the opposite of Persona, it's all about gameplay rather than an elaborated story. The game is not too hard, but it has its good moments, should you seek difficulty. There's no need to grind like crazy to keep going.I finished one of the two stories in 59 hours, and I still had a bunch of quests and half of the mimans left to find, which means that it will take a long time to complete it.

_childDocuments_.review: SMT:V was already really good.  Now you can play it without being restricted to 720p or 30fps.There are a ton of cool additions that weren't in the switch version.  The new story is actually surprisingly good if you can ignore how goofy some of the dialogue is.  The additional combat mechanics are fun and unlocking them feels organic.  Chillin' with your demons at the haunt, while largely inconsequential, is a fun occasional diversion with a few rewards sprinkled on top. I was skeptical of the Magatsuhi rails when I saw them in the trailers, but they are actually thoughtfully placed to make back-tracking and exploring much less tedious. If you haven't played an SMT game before, this is probably the best one to start with.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing vanilla 3 years ago on launch, looking forward to it since 2016, I was initially very disappointed going from how polished and original IV was. It was just missing the atmosphere and charm Nocturne and IV had. Vengeance fixes almost all of those small little gripes and then some with the new route. The new route is long enough to be it's own game. Just takes a bit to be it's own thing. If you've been curious about megaten it's a must play. Turn based combat can get incredibly repetitive by the end of most JRPGs, SMT's press turn system is unbelievably addictive. You'll be trying different combinations and trying to fight bosses with entirely different parties and figuring out what works. It's tough but fair. Plot is secondary though. Opposite of persona. Now let the 3ds and DDS games be ported to modern systems atlus.

_childDocuments_.review: tl:dr --- Gameplay and design is peak, so the paper-thin plot and one-dimensional characters are just forgivable enough to enjoy it. Firstly: On PC, everything runs buttery smooth. I've heard some horror stories about Nintendo Switch hardware limitations, but if you're playing on Steam, perish the notion. It feels great to Naruto-run around as we explore and slash things, and having a companion by your side to help find loose items is a nice touch. Music-wise, this thing is PACKED with bangers. Battles are fast and fun, and the boss fights are like epic anime showdowns.As always in SMT, the customization options are through the roof - even more so now with the addition of Essences. The character designs are unique and really pop. There is so much wonderful artistic flare. But cognitive dissonance comes in when their dialogue and voice acting feels so shallow and flat. My one complaint about this game, even with the re-vamped Canon of Vengeance: it feels like there's just....no plot this time around.  If we had the writing caliber of say, SMT4 or Strange Journey, then this would be a perfect 10/10. But it's just not. That knocks it down a few points. I've been a SMT fan-boy for 12+ years, and it pains me to say that it's a downgrade in that regard....but everything else redeems it. If you're a fan of the series, it's absolutely worth playing. But is it a "must-play"? I'm afraid not. Nor is it the one I would introduce someone to the series with.

_childDocuments_.review: Shin Megami Tensei V: Vengeance? A Divine Journey Through Chaos and Order!Shin Megami Tensei V: Vengeance thrusts players into a ravaged Tokyo where the lines between demonic chaos and celestial order blur in an epic narrative. This installment not only preserves the core mechanics fans adore but enhances them with substantial quality of life improvements and a visually stunning overhaul for modern consoles. However, does it manage to perfect the formula or does it falter under its ambitious weight? Let’s delve deeper.The game offers two distinct narrative arcs: the Canon of Vengeance and the Canon of Creation, each presenting unique storylines and moral dilemmas. These paths explore complex themes of revenge, betrayal, and the existential battles between mythic beings, providing a rich narrative canvas. However, while the game attempts to offer a deep story, it occasionally suffers from pacing issues and a reliance on conventional tropes that may not resonate with all players. Despite this, the dual-path approach allows for varied gameplay experiences, appealing to those who value replayability and depth in their RPG adventures.At its core, Shin Megami Tensei V: Vengeance excels in its turn-based combat system, which is both challenging and rewarding. With over 270 demons to recruit and command, players can craft a diverse team to navigate the numerous battles that dot the wasteland of Tokyo. The introduction of new quality-of-life features such as saving anywhere on the field and improved stat allocations for the protagonist enriches the tactical gameplay, making it more accessible to newcomers and satisfying for veterans.The post-apocalyptic Tokyo is vast, filled with desolation and decay, yet it beckons players to explore its every corner. The expanded map and the addition of new areas encourage thorough exploration, rewarding players with crucial items and opportunities to encounter and recruit new demons. However, while the increased scale adds to the game’s depth, some players might find the extensive open areas somewhat overwhelming and occasionally barren, which can detract from the overall pacing of the game.Visually, the game is a feast for the eyes. The dark, atmospheric settings combined with beautifully horrifying demon designs create a compelling world that is both enticing and menacing. The transition to modern consoles has allowed for an impressive graphical upgrade, though some of the reused demon models from previous entries somewhat mar the otherwise sleek aesthetic. The soundtrack, however, is a standout aspect, with its eclectic mix enhancing the eerie, mythic ambiance of the game.Shin Megami Tensei V: Vengeance is a robust entry in the franchise that largely succeeds in expanding upon its predecessors’ successes while also introducing meaningful innovations. The game offers an engrossing blend of strategy, narrative depth, and artistic flair, though it is not without its minor flaws in story execution and environmental variety. For those drawn to the darker side of RPGs or anyone looking for a deep, engaging gameplay experience, this title is highly recommended. Whether you are a longtime fan of the series or a newcomer intrigued by its rich mythological tapestry, Shin Megami Tensei V: Vengeance offers a journey worth taking.Interested in discovering great Steam games? _childDocuments_.review: This game surprised me, which is strange, as an avid Megaten fan, it shouldn't be that surprising that I very much loved this game. I've had an "issue" with this Shin Megami Tensei in particular compared to the likes of persona, which is that while I believe the game-play to be superior to Persona, the stories and characters they present just don't scratch that itch for me. What this ultimately led to was, while I enjoyed games like SMT4 a lot, I never loved them the same way I do in other ATLUS games and they didn't stick with me in the same way. The original SMT5 was maybe the embodiment of a game I  liked but did not love, however that changed for me with vengeance. The story is quite great in my opinion, it presented novel ideals that would make you think and come to your own conclusions for what is ultimately correct, as well is this, it  explored its characters in far more depth than the base game ever did. The largest point of satisfaction for myself was that it finally felt like the developers were able to fulfill their aims and ambitions for their game, riddled with a likely disastrous development schedule. I like to call it the Cyberpunk affect, revealing a game far before it was ever ready to come out never ends well, and it led to a game which had a 5 year wait still feeling rushed and unfinished.  The game play is fantastic, that was never a fault in the base game and it is nearly identical here. That is not to say there were not a lot of new things and changes but they feel like they added  to what already made the game play great instead of detracting from it with unnecessary additions, common to other ATLUS re releases. Every changed made does not feel like a cheap tack on, instead most if not all the additions feel like they do nothing but improve what already made the system great, in particular I very much loved building around demon innate skills, it gave another layer of depth to team building beyond having the right roles and coverage for what you are facing. Lastly, I don't feel it right to write a review without mentioning the music, there is an entire new games worth of new music here and all of the new tracks are an absolute treat to listen to, it's not even relegated to battle themes: area themes or even BGM for different story moments absolutely add to the experience. Shin Megami Tensei 5 Vengeance, is the best re release of a game ATLUS has done, bringing a game that lacked in several aspects into an entirely new level. If you like turn based combat, I cannot recommend this game enough, there's even a demo out now if you are unsure if it's worth the purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: 1st playthrough on Hard mode, Canon of Creation, Re-Creation ending.The good:- The core gameplay of collecting, fusing and battling with demons.- The essence mechanic really lets you customize your demons with much more freedom than ever before.- For the most part i liked the story. There were a few moments where it had it's "Meh.." moments but overall it was a good ride.- The soundtrack. There were a few bangers, a few "Hey this is pretty good", a lot of OK's and one absolute stinker that made me turn down the volume. The OST is still good but man do i miss Shoji Meguro. That feel when you enter the Hall of Chaos and you're reminded of SMT 3's godly music.. Let me repeat that, GODLY music. I'm not a musician so i'll explain this in MY words: Ryota has a (for the lack of better terms) weird, dirty and chaotic style when composing for SMT 4 and 5 at least, whereas Meguro always has a very clean, distinct sound. Now i'm not saying you can't experiment but way too often there were strange instrument choices, notes being played and/or songs just taking a different tone, kinda like two separate tracks glued together.The neutral:- Even if exploring is more fun with the added verticality and jumping, it hurts to have a scenery so bland. Sure it's a post-apocalyptic world but still, your options are basically destroyed city 1,2 and 3. Surprisingly i felt a bit disconnected from the world, probably because there was no world map, only teleportation from one area to another. I do appreciate the size of the areas and loot to be found though.- And while i'm talking about the world, i feel like there were way too many friendly demons inhabiting it. I can tolerate it but it still bothered me throughout the game. There's always someone around the corner who gives you a quest, thanks you when you complete it and showers you with rewards. Atlus please do NOT Persona-fy the mainline SMT games! Keep the happy, dating-sim, "love and friendship conquers all" stuff in the Persona universe and let us mainline SMT enjoyers have our dark, hopeless worlds to experience. I REALLY hope Canon of Vengeance has something good in store for me.The bad:- Nothing truly BAD about the game aside from some irritations here and there.A very solid turn-based JRPG as usual and i'm not close to being done with it. 8.5/10.Ps. Thanks to all the beta testers for funding Vengeance.

_childDocuments_.review: Major improvement over the original Switch version that released in 2021, from adding demon social links through the new Demon Haunt system to being able to save anywhere, qol with moving around, and of course an additional 60 hour campaign, but while still including the original 80 hour campaign.There's genuinely so much improved/added with this one that it feels like it should be a Shin Megami Tensei VI rather than just a re-release. Even if you've played this before on the Switch there's more than enough to justify getting it again on PC, it also runs buttery smooth with no frame dips/stuttering from my experience, and of course the ability to go over 60 FPS whereas the Switch version of the original was a stuttery 30 FPS mess.If you enjoy the Persona games, or just turn-based JRPGs in general then this is a must have, the only one with arguably better combat I believe would be Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth, at least in the beginning. But there's a lot going on in the combat in this game, especially if you play on higher difficulties that forces you to make use of all your items/skills/buffs/debuffs/status ailments that no other JRPG really makes you pay attention to lately... While Infinite Wealth might start off with stronger combat, eventually it becomes easy and you can spam any move, which doesn't happen in SMT V on Hard Mode, as the game just continuously gets harder even against random enemy spawns in the over world, and each boss is a calculated puzzle you need to manage perfectly to beat.TL;DR 10/10 must play for JRPG/RPG enjoyers, or even previous players of SMT V as nearly every fault with the game was fixed and there's so much more to do now.

_childDocuments_.review: Game wants to be philosophical, provocative, and groundbreaking. Instead, it feels like being locked in a room with a drunk theology professor and a horny middle schooler who both desperately want to tell you about Nietzsche, but keep getting sidetracked by memes and hentai references. While undeniably ambitious, the game, much like Icarus, flies too close to the sun and crashes in its attempt to soarAtlus continues to deliver a combat system that stands as one of the franchise's strongest pillars. The Press Turn system remains an exhilarating mental chess match, demanding you exploit enemy weaknesses while carefully managing your own vulnerabilities. The addition of human guest characters with unique abilities shakes up your options in battle, making team composition feel fresh, at least for a while. The occasional boss fight, like the Qadistu with their surreal animations, adds moments of awe amidst the chaos. If you're here for the combat, you’ll find pockets of satisfaction to cling to.If there’s one thing nails, it’s the music. The soundtrack masterfully blends foreboding ambience with pulse-pounding battle themes, creating a soundscape that pulls you deeper into the game’s apocalyptic world. The battle themes keep your adrenaline pumping.This game desperately tries to present itself as deep. The story throws around abstract questions about the nature of good, evil, humanity, and demons, but it all sounds like a disjointed monologue from a teenager who skimmed Nietzsche and missed the point entirely. Every character feels like they were ripped straight from some tired internet meme. There’s Yoko, the perpetually depressed nihilist who won’t stop telling you how awful the world is, and Tao, the annoyingly cheerful optimist who won’t shut up about how beautiful everything is. And that’s it. Character growth? Nah, why bother. Instead, you’re stuck in a philosophical pissing contest that drags on and leads nowhere.Dialogue veers between cringe-worthy and incomprehensible. Atlus attempts to inject levity but often lands somewhere between awkward fanfiction and a YouTube comment section. The game’s insistence on over-sexualizing female demons only adds to the tonal dissonance, undermining the mythological gravitas of figures like Lilith or Isis.The game's open world is bigger, yes, but not better. Instead of enticing exploration, you’re faced with barren stretches of lifeless terrain and tedious platforming sections that serve more as obstacles than adventures.  The areas feel devoid of meaningful secrets or landmarks, making traversal an exercise in monotony. Finding treasure or side quests often leads to disappointingly trivial rewards, leaving little incentive to stray off the beaten path. Fast travel points are scattered just far enough apart to make you groan, and demon encounters while exploring rarely feel worth the effort.  Despite its attempts to evoke a sense of scale and decay, world ends up being more of a chore than a playground. It's an open world for the sake of being open - a sandbox with all the toys buried deep under uninviting sand. Map are overloaded with pointless side quests, incoherent chunks of story, and design that is more likely to give you a headache than a desire to explore the world.

_childDocuments_.review: I originally played this game on my Switch back in 2021 and really enjoyed it despite its flaws. When this game was finally announced for PC, I was already interested in picking it up so I could play it at something higher than 25fps. So far I think this version of the game has done a lot to add and improve on the originals weaker aspects. The story additions have felt surprisingly natural, and I like the new demon haunts a lot since they also provide new story content as well as more gameplay elements to work toward.In addition, they've also tweaked the level balancing in this game to be more in line with prior entries. If you haven't played the original game, Vanilla SMTV had a system in place that determined damage based on how far apart yours and the enemy levels were. This meant that in order to even stand a chance against certain enemies, you had to grind experience in order to do appreciable damage. It also meant that players could grind above the level of enemies and bosses so that they could cheese their way through a fight, which removed a lot of the tactical elements and difficulty from the game, while adding an artificial layer of difficulty if you didn't grind. I'm not sure if they've removed or tweaked this system, but so far I haven't had to grind at all, which is a very welcome change.I don't have much more to say other than this. The game is much better with these aforementioned improvements, and there have been a ton of additions that make this worth returning to if you've played the original. If you're new to this game and even the series, this is also a great place to start. I'm very much looking forward to seeing what other additions they've made to the story, and I'm hoping Atlus can do a release like this to begin with rather than having to rush out an unfinished game and fix it with a new version next time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game for connoisseurs of fine games.  Its dry flavor may turn off the uneducated palate, but fans of this vineyard and most folks with a discerning palate for a classic JRPG will not be disappointed.The atmosphere is unmistakable.  As soon as that first note hits in the intro movie, you're sucked into dark netherworld.  You can feel its smell on the air like salvia.  It is not bubbly and clever like Persona.  It is dark and cold and very cerebral.  The lore is a clever take on western occult traditions, which if you're a fan of, will be a refreshing break form all the anime and games that misuse kabbalistic terms all over the place (looking at you, Final Fantasy).If you have played SMT games before, you know the sort of nightmare you're about to descend into.  There's enough new to keep it fresh while maintaining a definite loyalty to its own branding.  It presents a new chapter with nice updates, but doesn't try to outdo itself in the process. _childDocuments_.review: Perfection.Shin Megami Tensei V: Vengeance is the pinnacle of the classic SMT formula that was first introduced in Nocturne all those years ago on the PS2. Previous entries in the franchise, especially Nocturne, had a plethora of mechanics that some would call an inconvenience, while others may praise them for enhancing the atmosphere of their respective title. Vengeance does away with any sort of inconvenience in order to get straight to the best parts any SMT could offer. With quality of life improvements on such an advanced level, they brought back and combined everything previous entries did to make your life easier while keeping what makes SMT unique, especially in the fights. Be it exploration, saving, quests, fusing or the flow of battle. Every gameplay aspect of SMT has been refined to the highest degree and then some.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; I don't recommend this game due to its perplexing difficulty, unlikable roster of monsters and flat quest design. There are better titles with more consistent loops that are of equal or lesser price.If you're looking for a game with stunning character design, breathtakng storytelling, incredible turn based combat and a memorable soundtrack, look elsewhere. SMT V: Vengeance is a re-release of the title with the added "Vengeance" storyline. Most players will have no idea what that means but the game is kind enough to tell you when that point occurs. However, unless you've played and beaten the original title I would strongly recommend not picking up this game.SMT V suffers from a lot of the problems of turn-based combat: obtuse abilities with inconsistent and somewhat random results, a litany of symbology that takes far too long to feel inclined to learn, and a stream of quests whose storylines range from simplistic to vaguely threatening (in their longterm consequences. Again, no real indication of what any of these decisions will mean until it's far too late).I can stomach a lot for a 70$ title. I can deal with bugs. I can deal with glitches. I can deal with a game failing to handle edge cases well, or even just having a loop too simple to solve. SMT's problems are much deeper, however. Enemies are either made of tissue paper or titanium with no inbetween. Not using weaknesses means you're more likely to die instantly. Many of the demons you "befriend" are horrific in their personality and morals. They're cruel, ask you to speak bold faced lies to earn their time (not to mention bribes), and are frankly difficult to look at. Neko Shogun was a fantastic roster companion but the game's structure, even with its many opportunities to get free bonus score boots, demands a constant rotation. A frequent change from characters you may tolerate to ones that are skeezy but necessary. There are many random Cliffs in this game's combat difficulty. Bosses who can kill you in one hit, or stunlock your entire party with a variety of debuffs, charms, and other shenanigans that you don't really feel like you'll have access to until 20 levels or more in. Unfortunately you may never reach it.The Humans you meet are extremely unfinished, half baked character concepts that never had a chance to take away on the busier parts of their models, or so bland and lifeless you'll worry you missed some pivotal scene. Don't worry, there was nothing. The soundtrack is a questionable experience in dissonant tones. A cacophony of 10 second loops that seem unfitting for a game of this length.I really wish I could recommend SMT V but I'm stumped. I wanted to appreciate the work done here but I would insist that Persona, even with its own difficulties, manages to smooth over about 90% of the issues I had with categories in this one. Do not buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: SMT V: Vengeance is among one of the best purchases one could make on this platform when it comes to a challenging, expansive, and highly customizable JRPG, and it massively improves upon the original 2021 Switch release. Aside from obvious improvements like enhanced performance and resolution, Vengeance makes an immense number of changes to the original in terms of QoL and story. This review mostly covers improvements and Vengeance-specific content rather than general qualities about the game. Positives:- The level scaling from the original release has been mostly removed. Levels play a far less significant role in calculating damage which means that being underleveled is no longer as much of a detriment and conversely, being overleveled won't allow you to steamroll the game, so careful strategy and planning is required either way.- Regarding exploration: The addition of Magatsuhi Rails is not only a fun movement feature, but they've been meticulously placed to provide shortcuts throughout areas as well as shortcuts to side quests or bosses that you may have to later revisit due to their difficulty or recurring quests, so the run back is far less annoying now. You can also save anywhere now. You can now use a Sky View feature for a bird's eye view to find out how to get to a map icon, and Estoma (encounter avoiding skill) is now a standard feature that consumes Magatsuhi rather than a demon skill.- The ending you get for the Canon of Vengeance (new) storyline is now actually dictated by choices you make throughout the game rather than just one choice at the end.- The new CoV storyline makes far better use of the supporting cast and adds guest party members who fight alongside you with fixed skill lists. CoV also adds an entirely new open zone as the 3rd out of 4 major areas in the game which is a contender for one of the largest areas in the game. It also has a dungeon associated with it after completion to match that of the Canon of Creation story. You also revisit Tokyo a lot more frequently which allows you to be better invested in the city's fate, and they added side quests to give more life to the Tokyo segments. Even though the first two areas are the same between story routes, the story diverges quickly and the reasons for being in those areas and events that play out will differ. - The Virtual Battle Trainer lets you fight against previous story bosses and DLC bosses again, and at least in Canon of Vengeance, there are side quests that allow you to fight against Canon of Creation story bosses so that you can not only experience fighting them but can also unlock them for fusion without needing to play the other route. You can also fight stronger versions of the bosses increasing in level by increments of 100 up to LV 999. - I've only fought the new CoV superboss, but it is an amazing and challenging fight (especially on Hard difficulty), so those who were worried that Vengeance would go for a more casual friendly approach have nothing to worry about. The new story boss fights can also be challenging, replace generic demon fights, and are packed with unique mechanics.- For those who played the original Switch release, a common complaint was that beating a certain iconic superboss in the 4th area for the True Neutral Ending made the actual final boss too easy because the superboss was a higher level, but this seems to have been fixed. Before entering the final boss, I was given a choice between a powerful foe and an extremely powerful foe, and the latter option set the final boss at LV 99, so I think the game checks if you beat that superboss and ups the difficulty of the final boss accordingly. - The addition of many new demons in Vengeance ensures that you have a wide variety of choices at each level throughout your journey, and the demon haunts feature lets you talk to them in casual setting. They also added additional Aogami essence skills and passives to make magic builds more viable for the protagonist (although from my experience, STR is still much stronger). The Aogami essences are now more clearly highlighted on the map and are found on bright husks to make them easier to recollect after use, and players won't have to worry about wasting them as much. You can now also reset your added stat points with an item to swap builds.Negatives (more like nitpicks or things that were slightly lacking):- The common selling point that the game has 2 story routes or contains 2 games is a bit disingenuous. The original CoC story is pretty much just CoV with less content. Almost all of the bosses that got swapped out in CoV were generic demons in the original, and the 3rd area in CoC has far less story content in general, so it isn't as interesting. If you beat CoV, CoC is more or less just a sandbox to play around in. Even the demons that originally showed up in the 3rd area of CoC are present in CoV's 3rd area, and the loot is pretty much identical so they're going to feel samey when played back to back. There's an added superboss to CoC, but it requires an item from a CoV playthrough, so you're replaying the whole game with a worse story to fight one boss.- For as improved as CoV's story is, the 4th area is about equally as lacklustre as it was in the original. It's the same open sandbox type area with very few plot threads thrown around. Some bosses have been changed around but the bulk of the climax happens in the 3rd area and there's not much new to see in the 4th area compared to CoC. - The new STR skills associated with the new Nahobino form showed off in all the marketing all play into each other a bit too much. It's heavily evasion-focused with a skill scaling off agility and one only being usable after dodging an attack alongside a buff that guarantees a dodge. You pretty much have to replace most of your skill slots to accommodate this build rather than adding one or two cool skills from it, so it pigeonholes you a bit too hard for my taste, and I didn't use the new skills. - The new Periapt mechanic adding the tag-team skills are cool in theory, but I find them mostly unusable. They require really specific demon set-ups based purely on theme, not on their affinities or weaknesses, so you could end up wasting possible coverage by adding two demons to your squad that fill the same niche. For this reason, I don't think I ever really ended up using any of these. Omagatoki: Critical is still one of the best choices for your Magatsuhi Gauge at any point. - I'm not really enjoying the Godborn NG+ option as much as I thought I would. After beating the boss needed to unlock it, you can also raise the LV cap to 150, and stat growths improve massively past Lv 99 (3 SP per level, massive growth across the board), so I'm guessing you kind of NEED to hit that 150 cap since Godborn demons start at LV 150. I needed to make such a diverse and stacked team for the superboss to unlock this mode that I don't really need to change my demons for Godborn so the fun of puzzling out fusion combinations is gone. The fact that everyone is at level cap also feels like you don't really grow or improve (even though you can buy incenses and balms from Gustave now) over the entire run, so you're basically just dragging your feet to fight the superbosses and final bosses at the end again. Normal enemy encounters aren't that much harder because even with the inflated stats, your superboss-prepped team should Null all their weaknesses so they can't hit you, and you can't level up so why bother with anything BUT bosses? It is possible that the difficulty mode intends for you to work your way up to Lv 150 as you play and I went about it wrong, but I've heard conflicting opinions with some suggesting that you need to level up before you start that run because of how absurdly strong even starting demons can be.- You can't freely switch between the Nahobino forms on NG+ even though they're purely cosmetic and can use each other's skills.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the first game I've played non-stop for days on end. The gist of the game is that it's pokemon except it's demons with fusions. You'll be playing through the story getting your team together as your go and making/recruiting stronger demons.Be warned, this game has A LOT of grind ESPECIALLY early on. I think I spent most of the first 12-15  hours grinding on hard mode just to beat the hydra example before progressing passed the early game. It's pretty much a wall that you need to grind to beat. Get some of your favorite podcasts, youtubers, streamers, etc. to listen to/watch as you grind, you're gonna need it.The good news is, after you've defeated the hydra, grinding gets far, FAR easier especially as you unlock new areas. Example, 3-4 hours ago, I was around level 44ish. I'm currently at level 52, close to being level 53, with a free level up scroll so realistically, within the next hour I will be level 54. In other words, only grind what you need after you defeat the hydra and go back to beat the harder content later. Once you get stronger you won't have to wait as much either as you can develop strategies to dominate the bosses which all have weaknesses that you need to exploit. It was the same story for my grind from level 30ish to 40. If the grind looks bad at the start of the game, just try to get through it and you'll find that the game opens up more and is more willing to give you XP to level up.I do want to add as a tip, don't worry about keeping around your monsters. Even if the stats look like they "drop" when you fuse monsters in reality, you'll be getting a lot of levels once you unlock a couple miracles early on that give extra XP and stat bonuses when you fuse. The main points of fusing demons is to give them better skill sets/abilities. This is less important in the mid game as it's fairly easy to get what you want without needing to min/max. But for the early game it's very important to pay attention to what skills you unlock. There is a massive improvement in unlocking full party buffs/debuffs and unlocked 2nd tier magic, for example. Also keep in mind to make sure you READ skills so you know whether or not they do damage based off magic or strength. Just because something has an elemental affix doesn't mean it scales based off magic damage. Keep that in mind as you choose your skills later in the game. Your party size is also far larger than pokemon as well so you can keep demons on hand for different types of situations/strats. Just keep in mind these demons aren't your friends and fuse them away and treat them like tools! They'll tell you themselves that they don't mind it either.That being said, the sound track is great, the story doesn't feel like a total slog, and it's nice to be able to choose between the 3 endings making choices as you go (chaos, neutral, and lawful). Definitely recommend playing this if you like pokemon and demon/angel folklore.

_childDocuments_.review: I played and finished this game back in 2021 when it came out on the Switch. It feels like I'm playing it with new eyes again!People may say that the difficulty is quite high here, especially compared to the Persona franchise and whilst that is true to a point, it mostly comes down to your Demon party. Certain battles (usually Boss battles) just require you to shake things up and make sure you are opposing the strengths/weaknesses of your opponent with your current party (and by doing the traditional levelling up too). It's more trial and error than high difficulty per-se - go into the battle, realise you have the wrong line up for the job and either get lucky or die, rearrange your team and come back to success. But bare in mind that having the wrong line up for casual enemy battles does not mean you're screwed either, most normal battles can be beaten comfortably even if you have a party that isn't the best strategy for said casual enemy, so don't expect to be constantly changing your party - which is a good thing.Overall, a fantastic instalment to a hardcore franchise, in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: SMT V Vengeance is a great retelling of the original game. This version adds so much new content compared to other Atlus re-releases it is actually worth the money and time to purchase and replay it. The biggest issue with the previous game was its real lack of character development with the main cast and their overall lack of importance to the story. In Vengeance, it is clear the team has taken those criticisms to heart as you spend much longer interacting with and learning about the main cast. The Qadistu are a great addition to the story and act as a  motivating force to entice the player to proceed. In the OG version of the game the third area of Da'at was a real drag, but in vengeance it has been entirely swapped out with what may be the best area in the whole game. Overall exploration is even better in Vengeance thanks to the magatsuhi rails which lead to more secret areas with very useful items and they can even act as a way to quickly get around the map. The combat is just as good as it was in the previous version but quite a few meaningful changes have been made. The amount of useful Magatsuhi skills has increased drastically, compared to the previous game which had only a handful of useful skills. Also demon negotiation feels easier than ever? Maybe i was just lucky but i felt like I could recruit demons much more consistently than in other SMT games. Ah i know why its because of the new "Who's that Demon?!" mechanic and the gold card system. That make it so that the demon instantly joins up with you if you answer the question correctly, or in the case of the gold card its no questions asked they join your party. Overall the game is great would recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: SMTVV is pretty good.For the newcomers, it's an amazing JRPG experience with one of the best turn-based combat systems out there. For those who have played the original and remain skeptical about whether it's worth purchasing the latest Atlus re-release: . As someone who managed to sink 110 hours on the original Switch version, I managed to find reason enough to sink another 100+ on Vengeance. On my first run through the new Canon of Vengeance (CoV) route, I found plenty to keep me interested, engaged and amused at every part of the playthrough—even to things as minute as demon negotiation! Improvements to the story and the main cast (dear lord, there's an actual main cast) actually kept me tense and excited to see more—something that I rarely felt with the original story. The new additions to the OST add an immense amount of variety to an already massive (and absolutely goated) soundtrack—and Kozuka deeefinitely cooked, with many tracks rivalling (or even surpassing) the quality of SMT4/4A. There's plenty more depth added through the postgame Godborn mode and the new superbosses for those looking for more beyond the original superboss(es) and to explore (and exploit) the system—now even deeper with the addition of Innate abilities—to its maximum potential.With that said, I won’t say it’s a perfect game. I’m a firm believer that the original SMTV and the Canon of Creation (CoC) (which, BTW, barely got an update to its story content—even the unlocks feel a bit outdated with how much QOL CoV got) were just a few tweaks off of being an incredible game. SMTV was a game with immense potential to be one of the best; it just needed to tell a better story and flesh out its characters.:Ultimately, SMTVV is an amazing experience for SMT fans and newcomers alike. Its gameplay is truly the best of what the series has to offer and remains one of the most satisfying turn-based combat systems to learn and master; I’d even argue that SMTVV’s gameplay is among the best of the best in JRPGs. The music is PEAK. And while there’s plenty of improvement and depth to character and story that the original lacked, it still feels like they could have done more; yet again, there’s a lot of missed potential.And that’s a shame, because it’s not like they’ll re-release it again…right?Overall, I’d give it a biased opinion of . If I wasn’t such an SMT (and SMTV Vanilla) fan, this would have been more like an . Either way, this is a one-of-a-kind game that JRPG fans should definitely experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I love SMT5 so when I heard that there's an upgraded re-released version coming to PC I know I had to get it. This version surprised me with how much improvements it gives to a fantastic game that is SMT 5. There are new cutscenes and dialogues to further improve and make you feel closer to all the characters so that the key moments hit way harder. The game now has 2 routes that has vastly differences in the early and mid game so this is a big win for first timer. The progressing and leveling system feels much smoother and less grindy compare to the original. There are so many more QOL features that make the game feels much better but the "save almost anywhere, anytime" feature kinda took out the tension in the exploration gameplay. The og version doesn't have that so the exploration feels much more tense and scary because you can literally lose hours of progress if you die and haven't found any leyline. I kinda miss that feeling but the save feature is good nonetheless. The combat system is still as peak as ever. I'm hoping that Atlus will give P6 this kind of press turn combat system. It is infinitely better than the current persona combat system. It is calculated, strategic and engaging until the very last boss. The new music is great and it fits the og OST tone and vibe. SMT5 OST for me is definitely legendary, classic status. It is majestic, ancient, engaging, mysterious and exciting.The game is worth every single penny. It is quite pricey but trust me, after you finish this game you would find this an absolute steal. The Vengeance version is a massive improvement and expansion to the original game, I would say it did twice as much as P5 Royal or P4 Golden combined. A whole new story line, new side quests, new features, new demons, new "MASSIVE MAP". Definitely recommend at any prices, a must try game for any JRPG lovers.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid performance on the steam deck. Didn't have to mess with any settings and my deck wasn't running too hot at all. Yes it's a good game. I'd say it's great even. Amazing JRPG. Solid turn based gameplay. Music is bangin'. Demon negotiations and collections are always fun. And they put in even more unique interactions this time! Vengeance is the game V should had come out as. They added many great improvements in this game. Story-wise... Eh... I need to ramble. Skip to the last paragraph to bypass the venting. Story isn't exactly SMT's strong point. But V's really tapered off past the mid point. I played the original on Switch and got the True Neutral route after making the executive decision that... Everyone sucked. The character development for each alignment rep was lacking. Some were definitely under represented and the one particular alignment just irked me to such a degree that I'd rather nuke the world than go that route.  Vengeance DOES improve on that aspect much better this time, only to fall into the same pitfalls for some of the new characters they introduce. Sure Vengeance does add more characters and cutscenes to flesh out the story better. This is true, but it still suffers from the same problem as the original V/Canon of Creation: people got shafted hard. You expecting 3 new endings? It's 2. For all its new content there's still that one guy with an actual unique model and voice acting that's just there. You can remove him from the story and nothing of value would be lost.  The new antagonists? I like their motivation. If the mid point crap hadn't happened and they lose all their relevancy I'd like them even more. I understand Vengeance's setup is more focused on , but towards the late part of the game the gaps in the story become increasingly noticeable.   The main driving force that prompts the character development goes missing later on so character growth stalls. That's not to say the story is garbage. It is a flawed diamond. I am only lamenting that Vengeance could've done more with their writing. I don't think CoC received any updates to the story either...? What a shame. Outside of story though, this new update has many great quality of life improvements.You can save anywhere now! (A thing since 4 but not in og 5 for some reason) Auto battles in Vengeance is sped up and has auto skills too. Magatsu Rails are available in certain areas that allow you to speed up map exploration. (It was ass in the original to get around Shinagawa.) More Magatsuhi skills available! (SMT fans or mythology nerds geek out at the Cerberus brothers combo) More passive skills that aren't ♥♥♥♥! For those who enjoy a challenge Godborn mode is available in Vengeance after beating certain endings. Your level cap is bumped to 150 but the enemies are also harder. Shin Megami Tensei V Vengeance is a great JRPG that I would say is definitely worth playing. While I do admit the story is weaker compared to its cousin the Persona series, I would still consider Vengeance a must play and I don't regret buying it full price. (But this is also the fourth time I bought this game so my opinion is a weeeeeee bit skewed.) It's a... for lack of a better word, a real journey to reach the end. Had a few bumps but overall my horizon was expanded. I did enjoy how the game picked at my game because of the new characters. The new soundtrack really elevates the game as well. I have a favorite final boss now and the theme SLAPS. For all its faults and shortcomings, I find myself very invested in how Vengeance turned out and was mostly satisfied with it. Despite playing a few similar games in the past: Digital Devil Saga, Strange Journey, and Devil Survivor; I'm putting SMT V Vengeance as my favorite right now. (But SMT Devil Survivor is still really good in terms of story.) If you only have time to play one route, Vengeance is overall the better experience obviously. For complete story, Canon of Creation then Vengeance.

_childDocuments_.review: As a RPG, you are placed in the shoes of a Jouin student from Tokyo, who seemingly lives a ordinary life. One day, you, by sheer happenstance, are transported to the netherworld, a very hostile realm teeming with demons. Indeed, you almost die to them, but Aogami comes to rescue you, proposing a fusion into a Nahobino. From Aogami, you learn that not only is this world full of demons, but apparently there are angels as well, and a secret war between angels and demons has been waged behind the scenes for many years, unbeknownst to you. SMT has always suffered from a lackluster story for most of its titles, compared to its sister series Persona. Atlus, having chosen to rerelease SMT:V, opted to include a new storyline, Canon of Vengeance, in addition to the original, which is Canon of Creation. As someone who has played the original release of SMT:V, I can attest to how Canon of Creation's storyline was just... there. A lot of characters in the main cast felt underbaked and lacked proper development in the original storyline; however, Vengeance remedies that to an extent. Not only do they develop a lot of the main cast, there is several new character additions to the cast in Vengeance: the mysterious Yoko Hiromine as one of your allies and the Qadistu, the new antagonists in the specific storyline of Vengeance.Much of the story revolves heavily around the struggle between demons and angels, with you in particular on the side of the angels. However, the story heavily revolves around making choices that are aligned to be either towards the upholding of order (Law) or the creation of uncertainty (Chaos). However, some of these choices won't be fully apparent as to which they represent, so choose with caution...With everything said, I would heavily recommend those looking to pick up this game to play through Canon of Creation first. While I understand Atlus themselves have said that people can dive headfirst into Canon of Vengeance, at certain points of Vengeance's storyline, events occur that hinges on you having played Canon of Creation, and provides additional context.I have heard SMTV being called many things, but one particular description stuck in my mind: demonic Pokemon. It makes perfect sense, considering their similarities with gameplay. SMT is a turn-based RPG, and you control a party of demons. However, it differentiates from Pokemon in that you also are a combatant, and can also have up to three additional demons active in a front lineup, with the potential to have more demons as backup, to an extent. Teambuilding is immensely critical to progressing the storyline, but the developers have given you plenty of methods to aid with that. Recruiting demons in the overworld is one of many methods, along with the ability to fuse demons in your active party.As a turn-based RPG, SMT makes use of the Press Turn system, which provides actions to you and your party. You are incentivized to exploit weaknesses and critical hits in the process of defeating opponents, which will double the amount of turns you and your party are able to act. Be warned, however, the same goes for your enemies, for they too can exploit your weaknesses and can crit, which also double their own turns. However, SMTV's refinement of the Press Turn system adds one new thing. The Magatsuhi gauge is an addition that debuted with the original SMT:V, which allowed for a meter to accumulate before you can utilize one of many potential Magatsuhi skills, with Omagatoki: Critical being the default Magatsuhi skill you have at the very beginning (and also the most broken one still, even in Vengeance). However, as with the Press Turn system potentially giving your enemies an upper hand, demons and story enemies also have a Magatsuhi skill they will periodically use as well.As an open-world RPG, there is much for you to explore in the barren ruins of Tokyo. The developers made sure to incentivize prolific exploration off the beaten path, even if the storyline steers you through many of the areas so you can complete the story without too much difficulty.SMT:V is not particularly graphically stunning as opposed to quite a lot of recent triple A games, but what it lacks in graphical fidelity, it makes up for in world design and sound. Exploration is a joy, with vast different locales to explore at certain points in the game. There are urban jungles, mountains, deserts, small oases to wander around and stumble upon, and you will marvel at the inclusion of different set locations in this game. The presentation of these different settings is truly outstanding.The models in the Steam release now sport HD textures in the overworld as well as in combat, as opposed to the blurry mess they were on Switch. While the demon models designed by Kaneko may lack some of that shine compared to the newer models designed by Doi, I find they very much still hold up well to the newer demons, such as Idun or Abdiel, or yes, the protagonist's Nahobino form, in addition to the newly added Qadistu.I found both the ambient overworld music as well as the battle themes to be cohesive, and I know everyone who played the original agrees that there were definite certain battle themes that left them stunned. With the Vengeance storyline, Kozuka has managed to outdo what was already a great soundtrack in the original storyline, and you may perhaps find yourselves staying in some battles to keep listening to the music. With Vengeance, a lot of the graphical downsides are somewhat resolved. The Steam release provides support for up to 4K, the game now supports virtually unlimited framerates so you can theoretically run it at very high refresh rates provided that you have capable hardware to push said framerate and there is now Ambient Occlusion for better lighting.However, there is some little quirks that annoy me. Apparently, most in-game cutscenes are still rendered at 720p unless you play in 4K, which is especially apparent considering the amount of cutscenes in the game, so you will notice at some point. Additionally, the usage of FXAA in the game does not quite resolve nicely. For the above little quirks, I recommend everyone to download SMTVFix to fix all of those issues. I will mention that as a Unreal Engine 4 game, SMT:V Vengeance unfortunately suffers from Shader Compilation stutters, and there's not really much you can do about it. That said, performance is very top-notch, given how the original had to run on Switch, so I very much doubt you will have much issue with retaining a consistent 60 FPS.I very much enjoyed my time playing Vengeance even if I do have some nitpicks with certain quirks of the game and its storytelling. In my mind, I view SMTV: Vengeance as the pinnacle of what SMT currently can offer.Of course if you don't care for any of this: A few hours into the game, you will encounter Naamah, who flaunts her ass at you. Yeah.Also: Praise be to those who favor Agrat the most. Best Qadistu out of all of them.

_childDocuments_.review: This feels like such a massive improvement over the original Switch release, setting aside some limited graphics options, the lack of a camera distance slider, and the lack of ultrawide support, all of which have been improved or fixed by  anyways.There's a whole new story mode that's been added to the game to flesh the game out, and there's been a lot of non-technical quality of life improvements made to the game.For those wondering about performance, it runs smoothly on the Steam Deck (Can pretty much lock at 60FPS), and on my desktop (Currently a setup with an i5-13600K and 6900XT, 3440x1440 with 75% resolution scaling and TAAU), even with some extra graphical effects forced on (GTAO and SSGI), I can lock the game at 144FPS. I probably could go higher if I wanted to turn off the extra graphics options provided by the mod. For those wondering about Denuvo, I haven't noticed any stuttering caused by Denuvo, which makes me believe that the previous games that have stuttering issues was indeed from busted framerate limiters or other factors. Controllers sadly do not have any sort of rebinding options.Glad to see that waiting for the rumors of a multiplatform release to coalesce instead of dealing with the game on Switch (or an emulator that couldn't lock at 60FPS) was a good decision. Much like the Steam Deck and docked handheld gaming devices, thanks for beta testing, Switch users! May the double-dipping on subpar ports you already owned on other consoles and PC be in vain.

For an RPG it does feel as though there is a lack of any decent character writing beyond 'wowee demons sure are interesting' but I digress.So the gameplay is pretty alright, much more hardcore than the Persona side of the series but I liked it enough. My biggest issue however is that much like Persona (perhaps even worse) it devolves into nuke vs. nuke gameplay where there can be moments where you're just nuked because your party happened to be hard-countered by the next enemy without any indication that that would be the case.This is extremely apparent in boss design, which for some is probably very interesting to tweak your party to take on the boss. But by the end it starts wearing out my patience as you spam Murakamo over and over again because the bosses resist any elemental damage and more often than not render your attempts to plan ahead with your own nulls/resists by just saying 'no' and attacking through it for full damage.So if the story is nonexistent and the combat is not fun as the game goes on, why did I positive review it? Because I had fun at the end of the day, it was a foray into a more harsher JRPG and I can't deny that some may find charm with this game, which is basically Persona but without the story bogging it down and letting you get straight to the action.

_childDocuments_.review: (Trimmed version – see full review at  )When Devil Survivor 2 got a re-release via Record Breaker, the player was given the option to play the original campaign (with the new gameplay updates) or just head straight to the new content. I was pleasantly surprised that Atlus took this route with Shin Megami Tensei V: Vengeance as well, because it does allow one to choose the campaign of their preference from the get-go.Shin Megami Tensei V is a game with a lot of fascinating concepts but ultimately riddled with poor execution. There were quite a few cutscenes that genuinely felt like filler, just to pad the experience. The characters had no real personality to them; honestly, it was shocking that prior entries from the Super Famicom era had more compelling character arcs than a modern entry with decades of experience behind them. SMTV not only gets a much-needed overhaul narratively, but escaping the shackles of Nintendo Switch exclusivity allows it to finally look and run at higher fidelity.The marketing, despite its overwhelming nature, for this game was a bit misleading. While you do technically get a new game, I think the term "remix" is a better fit here because this is still Shin Megami Tensei V to the core, but with a few twists and changes. You will be roaming the same dunes, exploring the same ruins, looting dozens of vending machines, fighting for survival, and raising an army of demons, fairies, and deities hailing from different mythologies.However, certain aspects of the plot and character arcs will play out differently than what the returning player would expect. I was a bit sour at first upon booting up Vengeance, but by the end of Da'at Shinagawa, which serves as the second major region of the game, the plot will head in a different direction. You will be surprised. You will explore new landmarks, meet new characters, and witness major scenes in a different light than what you were expecting.The inclusion of Yoko Hiromine, a seemingly scrapped character from the original game and now exclusive to the Canon of Vengeance route, just adds so much depth to this world and its denizens. Her presence alone makes the other main characters crawl out of their comfort zones, which allows for some very tense conflict. I cannot understate how well she feels at home in this game. She fits like a glove, and prior remarks made by the developers during pre-release interviews confirm that she was always meant to be in the original game as well.The characters that were primarily alignment representatives with predetermined roles in the original SMTV—Law Hero, Chaos Hero, and Heroine—have changed significantly in order to break away from the norms and standards established by the earlier games. They were formerly high school students who had to abandon their old lives in order to defend Tokyo, but now you view them as valuable allies in the emerging conflict against the inevitable demonic pandemic. It genuinely does wonders when you aren't trying to copy your homework (Nocturne, in this case) without recognizing why the minimalist approach worked so well for that game.There are points in the game when they can join your party temporarily. This was a feature in the original game with Tao, but never to this extent. They can also participate in seemingly never-ending random encounters, with their fighting style somewhat mirroring their alignment. This does feel like a callback to some of the older games, but their inclusion in combat can seriously turn the tides in your favor. They can also use items during battles, providing both offensive and defensive support when their combat prowess wouldn't excel against a new threat. Your demonic allies can use combat items as well once you unlock the required Miracle, but being able to do so with human allies added an extra layer of strategy for these earlier encounters.Cutscenes that previously amounted to filler now offer actual exposition and character development. Yoko and Tao take up the mantle of this campaign's Chaos and Law representatives; both ladies offering their unique perspective on how the world should be reborn if one were to claim the throne.Like in the original Shin Megami Tensei, they accompany you for a large portion of the journey. During certain side quests that have multiple ways to conclude (finishing them contributes towards either Law or Chaos), their views clash, but in a polite, diplomatic way. As wildly different and extremist their perspectives may seem, never once does the game try to force them down the players' throats. This forces the player to give some thought to how they approach these side quests, because unlike the original SMTV, your choices do matter here, and you can't just effortlessly pick the preferred ending you want at the finale.For what it's worth, they really took player feedback to heart and made a lot of adjustments for the story and characters in Vengeance. We are far from the days of vanilla SMTV, and frankly, I am glad they have decided to try something fresh instead of regurgitating older concepts from the previous games. Whether one is satisfied with this approach is purely subjective; for me, this felt like Shin Megami Tensei IV: Apocalypse, but done much more professionally and interestingly.The gameplay loop of the original wasn't an aspect that needed an overhaul; outside of the previously mentioned problem with level scaling (which meant that you had a near zero chance against enemies that you were a few levels below), it has been fixed. I, personally, never had an issue with this, since I've done as many of the side quests as possible, and even by the end, I was still constantly getting gospels that allow one to level up the MC outside of combat. I can only think of maybe an encounter or two where I felt a bit underleveled, but with careful planning and party building, nothing is impossible, and this feeling is among some of the most rewarding things in any Megaten game, period.Your demonic companions now have natural passive abilities, which will likely drive the player to frequently change their party composition. On top of that, a slew of new Magatsuhi abilities have been introduced, including some that require a specific group of demons to be present in your party. Depending on the player's preference, this can feel a bit limited or underused, but it's still a nice addition because Omagatoki: Critical in the original game was just too good not to use all the time and gives other Magatsuhi skills the chance to shine and to be used more occasionally.The new additions in Vengeance are too many to detail separately, but every aspect of the game has been revitalized: exploration, combat, fusion, user interface, and so on. The Demon Haunt is a great addition, not only because it allows you to take photos of your demons but also because they can reward you with gifts for their frequent involvement in combat. These vary from simple consumables to major power-ups for the demons, such as stat and efficiency boosts or learning a brand new skill. In fact, Aogami basically grants the protagonist free level-ups after major events in the story. I really hope this feature will return in future titles, because it gives you a cool incentive to just chill for a bit and bond with your companions more.And my god, the music. It was already outstanding in vanilla SMTV, but Ryota Kozuka just went even more ballistic here. To think that the Mara boss fight is quite possibly one of the most memorable tracks in the franchise's history, and shockingly, it's only been used once. Funnily enough, Mara is not even a mandatory boss fight. The music track itself is surreal as hell—think of a mixture of 90's jungle and hard techno with industrial and noise.With that said, I'm glad Shin Megami Tensei V got a second chance and that the fans finally got a glimpse of the true nature of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember back when the original SMTV came out on Switch, being really excited for it because I got done with Persona 5 not long before it and was looking for that experience again. I found myself disappointed when the experience was something entirely different. When I let go of the idea that this was another Persona type game and recognized the game for what it was, it clicked for me and this game easily became one of my favorite RPGs. While Persona 5's main draw is the time management and social link system, the main draw of SMTV is its combat, how each encounter can be dangerous if you play recklessly, yet be rewarding for playing smart and adapting to what your fighting. The game gives you plenty of tools with essences, different demons, and items to turn what was a impossible looking fight into something you can win without grinding. You just need a change in strategy. Not once did I need to go grind for levels while playing, just needed to change things up a little or approach a fight differently. Early on in the game can be some of the hardest since your tools are limited and you may still be figuring the combat, but just stick with it and things will start to click. Guard to prevent weaknesses that would give your opponent press turns, change your affinities to immune or reduce major damage from bosses, and please do not be afraid to use items like the spyglass and dampeners. The games overworld gives you plenty of tools to find and utilize so use them to the fullest.Vengeance is a great SMT to start with and does improve on the original release of SMTV on switch. The story feels improved from the original and was more enjoyable for me. The quality of life changes are great. These include the Magatsu rails to make exploring easier, the map not being obscured abscesses, and, most importantly, being able to save anywhere. By the way, please save often and whenever you are told something dangerous is ahead just save again. If you are interested from what you have seen about the game, please give it a try. Don't be like me and come into this thinking it will be like Persona cause it is very much not. Enjoy it for being SMT and enjoy the combat this game has to offer. I have played through the original SMTV multiple times already and I can see myself doing that again with Vengeance.

_childDocuments_.review: The most important thing to be known is: is the game fun? And the answer is simply yes. It's not perfect by any means, but it feels like a good first step in modern SMT, as far as graphics and gameplay modernization go. There's a big difference between the two stories (called canons). The original canon of creation really, and I mean REALLY sucks story-wise. It really feels like it was just patched together as an afterthought just to give you some direction while you explore the really wonderful maps. Plus, in this canon, you can do whatever you want up until the ''final'' decision that locks you in any of the three alignment endings: why? SMT games are loved because one of the focuses is the consequences of your actions and choices.Subquests, side stories, demon interactions are abundant and some really interesting, but you can't have that many when the MAIN story is so bland and minimal.The canon of vengeance (the new part), on the other hand, really did a 180° and focused way more on the characters. The story is at least cohesive and the characters get fleshed out a lot more. Still not perfect, but at least you can feel some sort of attachment to them, or find (some of) them relatable. There's some minor things you would miss if you haven't played the original story first, but nothing that'll make you fry your brains thinking about. Also in here they brought back the ''ending you get is based on the choices you make throughout the game'' alignment system, even if it's kinda black or white as there's no neutral ending in CoV, and both choices imply some kind of extremist thinking, even for a SMT standard.Gameplay-wise, exploration is really good and rewarding, and it kinda feels like the main focus. The atmosphere and vibes are classic SMT and the OST, while not on a SMT IV level, is really well done and really helps with immersion. The new mechanic introduced with the magatsuhi skill is ok, you can tell they tried to spice things up, but it's not as good as, say, Persona 5 royal's baton pass, while still somewhat fun due to interesting exploits you can cook with it. Same with the demon navigators: if you want to explore every single bit of every map, or complete some subquests, you will need them, but the variety is just kinda there as it's really not needed unless you're focusing heavily (and uselessly) on some specific search. Trophy-wise, i really don't like gatekeeping platinum behind multiple cycles. They can be done realitevely fast, but still, you'll get bored fast and the main changes in cutscenes only happen in the second half of the game, so until then you'll just feel the need to rush and power through.All in all it is an enjoyable experience, but out of the mainline SMT titles, it's definitely the least memorable one. SMT III and IV, for example, had their problems, the first with secondary characters and the second with story/choices cohesion, but all fans can remember at least some portions because of how grand/immersive/relatable they were- this games lacks in that aspect as there's no apex or really intense story moment. Still, playing SMT on unreal engine and seeing everything in wonderful 3d sprites clearly make this a wonderful experience for any SMT and, in general, turn based fan. Here's hoping that now that Atlus has laid the ground for next-gen megaten, they'll get back to focusing on the story, and the canon of vengeance is already a really good indicator of them going in the right direction.Extra note is about DLC demons: they're good, especially konohana sakuya, and the mitamas really speed up the grind for godborn (in which you can level up to 150 thus requiring lots of exp and money). I really wouldn't recommend farming to 150 without the DLC sadly, it'd be a pain. Superbosses are as fanservice as they can get, but well implemented and requiring really good strategizing and optimization to beat, even on normal difficulty. They're the most classic SMT boss experience you'll find in the game (barring the 'true' final boss, you'll see).

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the original version of this game when it came out, despite it's flaws. It's great visuals and art style, amazing soundtrack (as expected of an SMT game), and cool premise about a highschool student who falls into another world and becomes a god to fight demons and recreate the world is such a powertrip and I loved it! I'm not even a fan of turn-based combat games and I have a tendency to get bored of long games and quit them part way through. Yet somehow, both the original and Vengeance kept me engaged for over 100 HOURS of gameplay. It was only held back by it's one-dimensional characters who didn't feel like actual people and more like cardboard cutouts.Vengeance fixed this issue and upgraded my opinion of the game from "really like" to "absolutely love"! It breathed life into the characters and made me care about them so much more. It also gave more depth to the story.My only real gripe with the Vengeance route is that the ending you get is determined by dialogue choices and certain decisions you make for quests throughout the whole game, rather than being a single decision you make near the end of the game like in the Creation route. This wouldn't be so big of an issue for me if I had known ahead of time that it would be like this. I got really lucky, I was making both law and chaos related decisions relatively evenly and I just so happened to get the ending I wanted. If I was off by even a little bit, I could've been forced into an ending I didn't want and have to restart the whole game again to get the right one, which would've killed my enthusiasm.All-in-all, amazing game. Just wish they wouldn't change how the endings are determined, or at the very least given me a warning that they changed it.
