_childDocuments_.review: I've also played and finished this game on PS4, I'm happy it got a steam release and hope it goes well.This game goes hard and I like it, it has a carefree arcade kind of nature. The level design is good, theres little to no backtracking, arenas and bosses are balanced (and the difficulty setting is a good addition), the story is interesting, the guns feel nice and the soundtrack is good. I also like the variety in the guns, although I do wish the selection had been wackier like a laser weapon, a canon ball or something like that.The addition of Co-Op is definitely welcome and I think will add a bit of value for quite a few people.For the price being asked I think this game is very fair. However, I do have some thoughts, and these are mostly small matters relating to the theme of the game and how some aspects break away from that theme, or are general design decisions.-In my opinion, pinata mode should be enabled by default, as I think a puff of confetti is more on-theme than a puddle of blood.-I can tell that considerable effort went into each area having two soundtracks, one for a general area theme and another metal variation of that theme for battles. I like the idea a lot but think the genre contrast between these two (as well as the loudness mixing of them) is quite jarring, and what would have worked a bit nicer is something like hollowknight where it's the same track but has additional layers like a drum track and some extra elements/instruments mixed in.-As of right now there's no vsync option so there is a bit of screen tearing.-A few more songs in the soundtrack for various conversation emotions would have been welcome, as sometimes the song doesn't really match the feeling of the conversation. In some cases I would have preferred hearing the area theme over the conversation song that switches in.-In general, loudness (not volume, but the average volume) mixing is pretty good, but at times the gunshots and metal boosts the general loudness of the game considerably.-The main ammo mechanic discourages players from using the same weapon, and that does keep things interesting as you end up cycling through all your weapons, but I personally feel that a more fun way to approach this would have been to reward players for switching weapons instead. Two possible approaches I can think of would be either a style system similar to spectacle fighters (where you get more currency for fighting well), or a boost in damage or particular effect from switching from one gun to the next (example, if you switch from flamethrower to shotgun, the first shot from the shotgun is wider and belches out flame or something like that)- On my first playthrough I struggled to find out where I needed to go, as the map objective was off the main screen and I didnt know  you could scroll the map. What would have helped if there was an indicator on the map pointing to the objective so I know where I have to scroll the map to, in order to progress.-I'm not a big fan of the final boss, I don't know what I'd do instead, probably some nonsensical primeval darkness monster, but this boss seems like its too serious for the general vibe of the game.Again, I still like the game a lot, I find its one of those ones where I'll play for about 10-15 minutes chipping away and then go back to doing some chores or other hobbies, which is great as you can save the game practically anywhere.Best of luck for future releases and I hope RainBite keeps at it. Special shoutout to my boy one of the developers.

_childDocuments_.review: The gunplay is good but it's one those "Where the hell do I go" of game. Gotta find the right key for the right door so there's lot of backtrack in a dungeon.The story is not interesting and I don't know why the developers chose this setting (Western teenage witches). The story isn't interesting at all, it just seems like the developers wanted to tell jokes about how funny it would be for witches to use guns and kill cute things.The music is good, but I wish the music transition between overworld and combat was less jarring.Probably won't finish it due to being stuck in the first dungeon (where do I go?) and not liking to backtrack so much, but it's still a well done good game that you probably will enjoy if you like 2D zelda games and twin stick shooters.(Before you comment "git good", no I don't particularely like metroidvanias. _childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, it's like a light Legend of Zelda game, mixed with a twin stick shooter, with some shmup sections. The story was pretty cool and kept me interested through the whole game. The default to kills is blood splatter and bit but you can change it to confetti, which I did, just because it seemed to fit the look better. I pretty much played this nonstop until I beat it and there's a new game + too, which I always enjoy having. Some light puzzles, not very difficult but not really easy either, I played on normal and it seemed pretty well balanced to me. Overall a unique, fun game that took me about 8 hours to beat, I wandered quite a bit but not everywhere so you could have less or more time depending on how you play. I really enjoyed this game and recommend it to anyone that thinks they'll like a game like I described.

Ever since I found EtG I've looked through dozens of games trying to find something similar and I've finally found it with 'Trigger Witch". Very much recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Trigger Witch

_childDocuments_.review: Magic and firearms make a deadly combo. Recalling the visual style and intuitive gameplay of 16-bit action-adventure classics, Trigger Witch puts an ultra-violent spin on cute and colorful pixel art. With a compelling and original narrative, puzzling environments to explore, a dynamic soundtrack, twin-stick shooter mechanics and a vast array of enemies to blast into smithereens, this is a tale that will grip you from start to bloody finish. From the creators of Reverie, Trigger Witch is a stylized 2D twin-stick action game set in an odd open world where magic is outdated and firearms are the new way of life. Players assume the role of Colette, a prospective graduate from the Stock, an academy for Witchcraft and Triggery. After a mysterious man invades her realm, events are set in motion that turn Colette’s life upside-down, casting her as the sole heroine with enough firepower to restore peace.

name: The Inquisitor
detailed_description: Digital Deluxe Edition The Deluxe Edition includes one copy of The Inquisitor game, the digital compendium, the original soundtrack, and the awe-inspiring Grandmaster's Attire. Get ready to fulfill your inquisitorial duties to the Holy Office in style and strike fear into the hearts of all sinners within Koenigstein’s borders. About the Game The Inquisitor is a story-driven, dark fantasy adventure game with action elements, that compels you to face difficult moral choices. The game is set in an alternative version of (religious) reality. Inspired by bestselling Inquisitor book series by Jacek Piekara. Once nailed to the cross and near death, Jesus becomes consumed by utter rage. He breaks free and unleashes violent vengeance on all the non-believers. Centuries pass and now an army of zealot Inquisitors brutally enforce the faith in this blood-soaked Church. You are Mordimer Madderdin, an Inquisitor in God's service, sent to the town of Koenigstein which is plagued by a series of mysteries and sin. Solve the various cases and crimes of those who have transgressed against the faith, all while uncovering the truth of a darker evil from another realm that is trying to enter the world of the living. Be the ultimate Holy Judge and Jury: Your role as an Inquisitor is to maintain order and enforce the faith in God. But the world is full of sinners who have lost their way. Decide the fates of those you judge in multiple story-driven cases and missions. This is a world where morality and what is right have long strayed from each other. So, will you show mercy or undying belief in The Holy Law? A morally tainted, non-linear tale: This is a dark and gritty story centered around a religion preaching revenge and violence. Multiple branching story choices will test your morality. Choose your path and decide what kind of Inquisitor you will be - one of pity or one of retribution - and ultimately what mark you will leave on this world. Enlightened sleuthing: Mordimer has unique skills and abilities that allow him to solve the various crimes and mysteries that have befallen Koenigstein. Track down and interrogate suspects. Discover the hidden truths of the city and its inhabitants. Piece together the evidence and make your final judgments. Delve into the Unworld: Unbeknownst to those around him, Mordimer has the ability to enter the mysterious Unworld. There he can discover the deeper secrets that suspects have tried to hide in their souls. But there is a grave risk when venturing into this world and the dark force which reigns supreme here will do everything it can to destroy you for stepping foot into its realm. Persuasive interrogations: The 1500’s remain a cruel era of justice. As an Inquisitor, you have free rein to use whatever methods and tools deemed necessary to persuade suspects to reveal ‘the truth’. These optional interrogations date back to the times of the real Inquisition and it’s up to you to decide if and how much force to apply to those under your investigation. Let your sword do the talking: Sometimes a tongue just needs to be cut right out in order to loosen it. A full sword-based combat system means various cases will let or even require you to use brute force. Master your blade, find your openings, and use your enemy’s weak points against them.

In this dark fantasy adventure you solve intricate cases and unveil abysmal secrets as Inquisitor Mordimer Madderdin.

_childDocuments_.review: It genuinely pains me to give this game a negative review. The concept? Fascinating. The plot so far? Intriguing.But everything else? Dear ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ God Unmerciful. The potato graphics, the unblinking NPCs staring into my soul while occasionally disappearing, the seizure-inducing flashing during the eavesdropping and awkward QTEs I can still forgive. But the combat? Absolutely unbearable. It's so janky you might as well smash your face against the keyboard cause it just doesn't matter what you press. But what truly hurts me is the fact that the game had managed to crash THREE times in the Unworld, and I've only gone there twice.It's sad because the game has so much potential, it's such an interesting take on religion with detective aspects but it's borderline unplayable in its current state, let alone worth the £35. I sincerely hope that the devs don't get discouraged by the reviews, but instead use this as a learning experience. It's too late to fix the faces, but please fix the crashes/bugs/etc and I will gladly change my review to positive.

_childDocuments_.review: The Inquisitor is a unlike any other game I have played insofar as it masterfully manages to blend brilliance with clinical retardation. The story is shockingly good once you get over the bizarre spectacle of 'Avenger Jesus'; it is dense, there is always a lot going on, and has depth that I've rarely seen. The occasional use of Latin I found tasteful, and (as far I can judge) grammatically correct. Some of the level-design (from a purely aesthetic viewpoint) is okay. That's it. Give the writers a raise and sack literally everyone else:- PERFORMANCE. I've seen a lot of reviews complaining about the graphics and the dead-eyed NPCs, but I disagree. Yes, the graphics are trash, and it would be easy to give dozens of examples of games from 2012 that look better. The textures are (even on the highest setting) so low-resolution it is impossible to make out what the NPCs munch on in the tavern. I could pretend I were playing Oblivion again and forgive this, but the performance is absolutely inexcusable. I run most games on high-settings at a stable rate of 60-80 FPS. I've barely ever got, in this 2010-tier graphics game, over 30 FPS.  I've never seen a game that could both LOOK and RUN this ♥♥♥♥. That's an achievement.- UNITY. I don't mind Unity games so long as they don't feel and play like Unity games, but this one does in every way. The lighting is terrible, the clothes and hair move unnaturally, and the way particles (smoke, sparks, etc.) are handled is tragic to the point of tears. Without the story, this would be little more than an interesting school-project.- GAMEPLAY. The Inquisitor manages, hands down, to supply the first 5 ranks of the worst ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gameplay segments in my life. I don't know what smooth-brained ♥♥♥♥♥♥ thought 'oh yeah, rocket-launching the player every 30 minutes onto a different planet to stealth-collect 5 orbs is fun', but it's not. It's really, really not. I actually physically groaned 'not again!' at one point. The combat is in a solid alpha-version state - the buttons more-or-less do what you want and there is a variation in tactics, but there is enormous room for abuse. The final bossfight gave me aneurysm and would single-handedly prevent me from replaying the game.Some closing quick points:- This game is at times really trying to be The Witcher. Stop it, you're not.- The game has a quick-time-event every 2 minutes at the beginning, but halfway through the devs forget about them, and you never see them again.- The story-progression at times feels rushed as if an hour or more had been condensed into a single dialogue-line. I guess they ran out of money.All in all, either buy for €15 or less, or if you're a story-driven fanatic that doesn't care about anything else. It's a real pity. A few 'eh, bro, let's not, this is stupid' among the devs could have prevented most issues, and this could have been a really good game. It's a shame. At the current I price, I cannot recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: At this writing I have 3.2 hours on record -- effectively 2.2 since I spent the first hour screwing up. You can miss some tutorial interactions by advancing the plot too soon, so when you get to a shrine that mentions it's a good place to visit some weirder place, back off unless you don't mind missing those side tasks. So, writing with a weighty 2 hours and 12 minutes under my belt, I can say: so far, I love this game.I have to warn you it's not for everyone though... the few professional reviews that are out there will testify to that, though they aren't entirely negative. You have to like a slow burn, and (so far at least) a lot more looking around than fighting, which is fine for me if the looking around is interesting, which it is. There will be QTEs and stealth segments, too, which I generally detest -- but here they're easy even for a chump like me (again, so far).Here, then, are some early impressions. First, unlike the Witcher series, the Polish dark fantasy books that inspired this game (guess there must be something good in the water over there) have unfortunately not yet been published in English -- but the setting is a hoot. The game takes place in 1533, exactly 1500 years by Church reckoning after Christ's resurrection in our timeline, or after His terrible vengeance in this game's.I know this setting offends some people -- it's a disrespectful, blasphemous mockery, they believe, and while I can understand their reaction, I really don't get the impression that this story is arguing the 16th century would have been so much better if Christianity didn't preach forgiveness and mercy and love and all. That said, the vengeful world this alternate Christ created still behaves by most of the same rules as ours nominally does; stealing, murder, and other offenses are still crimes. It's kind of like the Addams Family: they're creepy and they're kooky, mysterious and spooky, and yet aside from the sinister trappings they mostly behave the same as any other civilized people. Long story short, unless you're looking to take offense you probably won't be offended. Though, as I said, I'm only 2 hours in so I could be very wrong in the long run. (If so, may Christ forgive me, or may I at least endure my deserved punishment with dignity...)Performance-wise, I have no major complaints but I'm playing on a decent machine (i9-12900F/3080ti) and I'm using a 60 FPS cap. Even so, there are occasional hitches where the game has split-second freezes -- nothing game-breaking or frequent, but there will be a hiccup every few minutes. Graphically, I think it looks great; not quite as refined as Witcher 3, and the world is zone-based rather than seamlessly open, but still the art direction is pretty sweet (or convincingly crappy where it needs to be).I sprang for the deluxe edition mainly because I wanted to see the PDF world book that it includes, and while I haven't read it all because I wanted to actually play the game and avoid too many spoilers, it's fascinating and has some great back story for the 8 or so pages I've checked out. Considering that the deluxe edition is still cheaper than most mainstream games and also includes extra cosmetic gear and a downloadable soundtrack, it's worth considering (and I often skip deluxe editions).That's about all I can say so far. Short summary: if you're willing to drop 40 or 50 bucks on the twisted mutant baby of The Witcher 3 and L.A. Noire, here's your chance.UPDATES 2/13/2024:I inadvertently left out an important detail in my initial review: I am playing at 1080p. And it turns out that even at that resolution, the game sometimes dips to around 42 FPS. It's not frequent, but it happens.Leave the game paused too long and your character may (or may not) enter a mode where black smoke rises endlessly from the ground around him and you need to reboot the game.When the game says "stall for time", that's a hint that in the ensuing dialogue, you need to choose the options that stall for time.Overall, still enjoying the game, though the visits to the Unworld are a little too frequent for my tastes.
_childDocuments_.name: The Inquisitor

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Probably not, but it is still an interesting adventure that presents an alternative religious history. Jesus was crucified - and took revenge on his murderers with merciless brutality. In the world of The Inquisitor, Christianity is not a religion of mercy and forgiveness, but of revenge and retribution. God help me lest I commit the sin of mercy. If you have no problem with this fictional interpretation of the Christian religion, The Inquisitor (original name: I, The Inquisitor) is an adventure game in 3D set in a medieval fantasy world that puts you in the role of an inquisitor who mercilessly enforces the will of the almighty church and punishes unbelievers and sinners on behalf of the bishop. And by "punish" I'm thinking more of the dungeon or the stake than a few Hail Marys as penance. The Inquisitor is first and foremost an adventure game, you move around in a 3D world, but in addition to the puzzles you also have to regularly pass various action sequences in order to progress. Sword fights, chases, quick time events... working as an inquisitor is physically demanding and always life-threatening.We are Mordimer Madderdin, an Inquisitor, given almost unlimited powers by the Church, prosecutor and judge in one, and are tasked with maintaining order and strengthening faith in God. The most important task of an inquisitor is to track down anyone who commits a sin (especially against God Almighty). We were sent to Königstein by the bishop to investigate rumours of a vampire. But even without a vampire, the town is full of sinners who have lost their way - although it is up to us to decide whether someone has strayed from the faith and how to punish them. We decide the fate of people without having to deal with lengthy court proceedings or the taking of evidence. In this world, justice is efficient and swift - and we ARE justice. We are a fanatical inquisitor, but of course we can interpret the faith as we see fit. We regularly make decisions as to whether to mete out merciless punishments in the name of God or perhaps - if it seems favourable to us - to show mercy. This has little to do with morality and justice as we understand it today. The situations we regularly find ourselves in are a good illustration of what an uncontrolled abundance of power can lead to. Who is supposed to put us in our place? We are only enforcing the will of God, and nobody is allowed to oppose that!We move through the city, which is quite beautifully depicted graphically, while the 3D models of the characters are rather poorly represented, which is particularly noticeable in the dialogues. However, the possibilities for interaction during our explorations are limited, and the narrow streets sometimes feel a little deserted. Drunks stagger around from time to time, prostitutes wave at the roadside, traders stand behind their market stalls, jugglers dance around, but on the whole the city seems rather sparsely populated. Hardly anyone talks much, no-one shouts, no crowds of people are squeezing through the narrow streets. In some areas, it almost looks like during a lockdown, when only a few people leave their homes. The doors are locked and there are only a few hotspots where we can interact. Not even the market square is particularly busy. We can walk and run, but not punch, steal, jump or climb like Altair in Assassin's Creed. Most of the inhabitants have nothing to say to us and just stand around (with simple animations) without reacting to our presence. We always find altars where we can pray and thus top up our religiousness. When we pray in other places, we are shown hotspots as well as our next objective in order to advance the mission. This means that, despite the few interaction options, it doesn't become uninteresting so quickly because we always know where we need to go next. When we pray, our senses are generally extremely heightened and we can follow scent trails or various tracks on the ground. We have to track down suspects, conduct interviews, collect evidence, inspect crime scenes and make decisions and judgements. As a rule, the city guard then carries out our instructions. We explore a (in most neighbourhoods) filthy city full of sinners while searching for a supposed vampire. In the process, however, we are quickly drawn into something else - the vampire is probably not the only supernatural danger. We get to know the various inhabitants and the parties fighting for supremacy in the town. What game are the countess, the cardinal and the mayor playing?The multiple-choice dialogues are relevant and the story develops depending on the selected answer. It is not possible to simply click through all the possible answers. There are also always little puzzles to solve. The Inquisitor is basically a detective adventure and not an action adventure/souls-like game. You will spend a lot of time wandering through the various neighbourhoods of the city. After all, there are collectibles to find. Soon we are not only carrying out our investigations in the world of the living, but also falling into a trance through intense prayer and thus switching over to the Unworld. We are just as unpopular here as in the real world, only the inhabitants are less intimidated by us or even willing to help or talk to us. A flying monster is looking for us like the Eye of Sauron, its offspring chasing us on the ground. We have to avoid them and hide while we collect shards to finally receive a vision that shows us events from the real world and thus supports us in our investigations. Afterwards, we automatically return to the real world. We are a little weakened, but our vitality quickly returns after a few glasses of wine. The sword fights in the game (which occur from time to time) are ok - light and heavy attacks, dodging, blocking. Correct positioning is essential, it pays to play with a gamepad. Compared to a game focussed on combat (e.g. a Souls-like), however, the battles are very primitive. They are just one of several game mechanics in The Inquisitor. In the streets, we can often eavesdrop on other people's conversations. To do this, we sit down on a bench at certain points so that we can listen in on the conversations of some strangers and obtain clues. When we receive certain objects, we sometimes have visions that show us scenes from the past of these objects. We carry a small journal with us in which we automatically enter newly acquired information about people. We can also find our open and completed quests here, as well as any clues we find. Fast travel through the tunnels under the city is possible. However, we have no real inventory, no character values and no skill tree. The game saves automatically at certain checkpoints.The Inquisitor is a 3D adventure game dripping with blood and violence in a medieval fantasy world. Fulfilling our duties, we twist and turn religion as we see fit. In action sequences, we prove that we can also defend the faith (and our lives) with a weapon in our hands. If you have no problem with this alternative representation of religion and your own role as a fanatical inquisitor, The Inquisitor is a thriller adventure with a twist-filled story, although it is not always technically up to date.
_childDocuments_.name: The Inquisitor

_childDocuments_.review: “Christ who is vengeful, fill my heart with the desire for vengeance.”This is just one of the many inverted prayers people use to commune with Jesus Christ who had, as the Joker says in The Killing Joke, “...one bad day…”, on his crucifixion. Instead of dying for humanity’s sins, he flipped out, went into a vengeful, murderous rage, terminated Pontius Pilate with the wooden cross, led a rebellion against the non-believers, and conquered the Roman Empire. Almost 1500 years later, you serve as one of his Inquisitors, dispensing judgment in the name of your Lord, Christ Triumphant. That’s one hefty take on an alternative history of Christianity and the world, originally from the pen of Jacek Piekara, a Polish fantasy writer.Needless to say, if you’re easily insulted, have any qualms about reliving the Spanish Inquisition through your in-game choices, or feel your faith would be easily shaken by something like this, stay clear from this religious “What if…?”. Since this is Steam, and some crusader trolls have already started hoarding Steam awards, I can point you to a , and kindly ask you to read a comment on the last page, from 25th March, and perhaps glean a different kind of perspective.The Dust S.A. had quite a premise from the books, and I have to hand it to them for worldbuilding, crafting lore, prayers, Bible quotes, NPC conversations, and the entire vibe of the city of Koenigstein with its alternate morality wheel rather well. The almost super villain sounding name of the main character, Mordimer Madderdin, rounds off the entire bundle of joy. Upending the morals is also a great idea to subvert the player’s expectations, and maybe put a twist on obvious choices, but in practice it did not turn out that well in-game.Even with multiple endings, its linearity pushes you along the same path and the same solutions, regardless of your choices, and no matter if you blindly follow the vengeful teachings torturing people, or doubt your training and show mercy. After doing two playthroughs, one a speed run in less than 4 hours, it seems you only get judged differently at the end which depends on exactly one choice.On occasion it almost felt like a Telltale game with the amount of conversations, detective work, and some slight puzzling you get up to, which is not a bad thing. The town of Koenigstein is much larger than it needs to be, making it feel alive instead of just being your treadmill for objective hopping, and hiding lore collectibles, which will at least make all the backtracking slightly more interesting. You’ll quickly learn all its dirty, muddy streets, since the fast travel system leans into a more believable one through sewers, rather than an outright magic teleport.Mordimer’s faith also serves as a detective sight, highlighting every collectible and interactive point in quite a large radius in bright orange, like a beacon of hope. Considering it’s quite hard to tell what you can interact with, this is a welcome tool, but often starts feeling like a crutch since the other option is to blindly run around until you stumble onto something that pops up an interaction button.Every decisive moment in the plot pushes you into the Unworld, a dark, twisted realm Mordimer can enter by praying, and oh boy, does this become slightly tedious. Is the Unworld a manifestation of Christ’s vengeance? Is it a garbage dump for all of humanity’s fears, sins, and self-doubts? Why is it governed and guarded by a sentinel squid from The Matrix? You get answers to some of these questions, but they just open up more questions and pop up a giant confused smiley face over your head.You use the Unworld to get to the truth people won’t tell you, using a few mystical powers and activating light wells to heal, while looking for glowing orbs, and avoiding the guardian and its minions. When you collect enough orbs, the plot gets revealed and Mordimer returns to the real world. This is repeated a few times too many, with increasing difficulty and length, and supposed emphasis on stealth. Turns out, legging it like the legendary Greek messenger due to dramatically poor AI makes for a slightly less tedious Unworld. This also kinda begs the question why would you even mince words with anyone beforehand if you can just do this every time.There are occasional bouts of combat where Mordimer’s fancy swordplay and menacing demeanor should come into play, but all you get is some awkward shuffling, moonwalking, awfully delayed swings like the characters are struggling against glue, wonky hitboxes, and too many buttons for something as janky as this. Oh, there are also QTEs shoved in there on occasion, which are not limited just to combat, some even instant death ones. A few boss fights particularly reveal all the issues with these sporadic brawls, the ending one baring all the faults, like Jesus exposing the Pharisees.Visually, the game is quite a discrepancy. There are areas of Koenigstein where you momentarily forget this is a eurojank nominee, but the town itself takes the crown for most of that. You’ll be shocked out of your reverie by the next NPC with eyes bulging out like he’s been squeezed too hard by the Inquisition, or by having a head too large for her shoulders, and bent to the left, maybe from turning the other cheek too much. Let’s just say the game is artistically inconsistent, further emphasized by occasional drunken marionettes with entangled strings animations, and the odd overeager voice acting.   A large patch has been published since the game came out, fixing lots of technical issues. It still drops a few frames here and there, but it’s not that noticeable anymore. More importantly, some quality of life toggles have been added, like easy combat, automatic QTEs, and the ability to skip puzzles, which are all welcome additions considering those are some of the game’s weak spots.The Inquisitor is slightly too expensive for what it offers and the way it offers it, with a somewhat short running time, but the industry needs things like this, and it delivers on many points, particularly with the story. By this I mean good eurojank, with all its faults and tropes, not necessarily another berserker Christ, crusader attracting alternate history tale. The spineless, out of touch, sheltered, and living under a glass bell 3A industry will never produce something like this, and this is why, in spite of this review perhaps sounding negative, games like this should be cherished. Yes, cherished on a sale, but still cherished. Don’t let the QTEs chase you away from Mordimer’s gravelly voice and awkward innuendos to a lady whose hair dances around like Medusa’s snakes. It’s properly lovely, is what it is.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to be honest. This game is janky, the combat sucks, the optimisation is ♥♥♥♥ and some of the character models look like they were made 10 years ago.The story however is very interesting and dark. In this world Christ did not die on the cross. He broke free and unleashed bloody vengeance on all. Ages pass and now a new fate has taken hold in Europe.You play as an Inquisitor: Mordimer Madderdin. You are dispatched to the town of Konigstein where you will be tasked with dealing with the various crimes and transgressions of townsfolk.Meanwhile you are uncovering a bigger conspiracy that you will have to stop.As an inquisitor you pray to merciless Mary and you are supposed to cast the first stone as a follower of this new religion of revenge and violence.As said before the character models look dated. However the city of Konigstein has a certain charm and can look very nice at times.The atmosphere of this game really reminded me of The Witcher 1.Sadly the studio seems to be on the verge of bankruptcy. I would really like to see what they can do with a potential sequel with a bigger budget. The game has alot of shortcomings that most likely won't be patched. However i still recommend this game if you can get it on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I pondered long on what to say about The Inquisitor - there are aspects of the game that are done extremely well, and others that are of notably poor quality. Ultimately, I decided to give it a bad rating, and what prevailed is how, without any hints, following the story in the manner the game world constantly tells you is right, I reached the "bad" ending of the game. This is extremely poor storytelling, and up to this point, the story was the main strength of the game.Good things:The story. The world of The Inquisitor is intriguing, a twisted version of real medieval times. I was interested in learning more and more about it.Graphics. For a game made with minimal resources, the graphics are okay.Sound design. Indie games rarely have full voice acting, and when they do, it's often at a very low level. Here, with some exceptions, they've made an effort.Bad things:Game play as a quest/mystery. The things the game advertises - investigations, crime scene examinations, interrogations... they're few, rare, and have zero effect on the game - just filler.Game play as action. The battles are laughable; I killed all bosses by spamming the "heavy" attack. Bad controls don't help much.Game play as stealth. These, for me, are the hardest parts of the game. Especially if you really try to stay hidden. I just slaughtered the enemies - it's much easier that way.Interactivity - despite the numerous dialogues, clues you gather, decisions, everything is just filler. Whether you reach a good or bad ending depends solely on ONE choice in the last 20 minutes.Bugs - the game crashed few times on me. Few times i was stuck into different solid objects on the scenery. Few times the resolution dropped from best quality to something from the PS1 eraVerdict: 4/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Inquisitor

_childDocuments_.review: It's an interesting game. I first thought I'd be playing something like The Witcher 3 but with the background of an inquisitor. That wasn't really what I got. I'd say it's more of a visual novel with quick time events and some third person melee fighting. If you can live with an RPG that offers no map, no skills, no health bar and no inventory but that relies on telling an interesting story, then I'd say this game can be of interest to you. I'm not sure if 40 € are really an appropriate price tag for this, but then again I'm not a cheapo. The game runs - for me - very stable and smoothly. The voice acting is very good, the graphics a bit dated and overall the questing feels a bit railroaded. There are some interesting approaches to the whole "detective" setting. I'm a little shy of 3 hours in and while there are some things that I would have liked to done differently from a game design perspective, I'd overall say that I find the game enjoyable and intriguing. Therefor a "thumbs up" from me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Inquisitor

_childDocuments_.review: The alternative history and dark medieval fantasy drew me to this game. The Inquisitor is an action-adventure game in which you play as Mordimer Madderdin, an inquisitor sent by the Holy Office to Koenigstin after hearing about a vampire lurking around. This task will soon be forgotten as a murder occurs; the first of many, he will start investigating and learning the dark mystery behind it. Your actions and responses effects significantly on the game's outcome; you'll either be a friendly or ruthless inquisitor, some of the character's fates are in your hand, and at some part of the game, your actions will lead him to side with either of the groups or none at all. So, choose carefully. I enjoyed the details of the artwork, the city, and the environment. The character's style and animations are lacking; the NPCs are identical. I even suspected the wine merchant to be essential in the game since he kept showing up, but it turned out he is a random NPC design. I liked the cutscene artwork; however, they did a fantastic job with those, and the loading screens are nicely made as well. The voice-overs are good, and the writing is excellent. There is nothing special about the soundtracks, but they are not bad; they fit the game's atmosphere. The combat system is the only bad thing about this game; it is very clunky and not smooth. I appreciate all the fighting styles they introduced, especially in the unworld but it felt frustrating. Speaking of the unworld, there are seven stages you have to clear to uncover some clues from your visions. Those were nice at first, but they became challenging with the clunky battle system. Puzzles were easy to solve, and the journal is handy with all the information you collect during your journey. However, there is no map or an interactive one until later in the game; you get five key areas to travel between as a shortcut, which sometimes affects getting some of the missable achievements.Pros:+Interesting, dark well-written story.+Great detailed artwork.+Choices have real consequences.+Fitting soundtracks.+Very well-done voice overs (Game is fully voiced)+Medieval fantasy+Good puzzles.+Useful journal with characters' profiles and collected information.+Multiple endings.+Manual save (Three slots, and there are autosaves)+Skipable cutscenes (This is needed especially if you fail a fight and keep trying)+Steam achievements.Cons:-Some backtracking is required. (There is a fast-traveling map to unlock later in the game for only 4 areas)-Clunky battle system. -Characters, animations, and design are lacking.-No variety of NPCs faces.The game has a dark theme and is gory. It is not for everyone, as it has an alternative religion, Christianity, which is not a religion of mercy and forgiveness but of revenge. The adventure was interesting, It took me around 13 hours to beat it, but I couldn't find all the collectibles. I recommend it to people who enjoy this type of games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Inquisitor

_childDocuments_.review: I played the game all the way through and I can definitely recommend it. It has a rather clunky combat system, and the graphics and animations look like something out of a 2000s game. But at the same time, it has an interesting detective plot, memorable characters, a well-developed city that can delight you with atmospheric landscapes.I really hope to see someday a continuation, a sequel, where the developers will take into account their weaknesses and delight us with a full-fledged open world and a more polished combat system. Yes, and I would like the plot to be longer, I completed the game in just 14 hours, and this, by modern standards, is very little.But I was still satisfied overall, and I can recommend it to those who love some mystical and detective stories; the game has its own atmosphere and a charismatic main character.
_childDocuments_.name: The Inquisitor

_childDocuments_.review: The purest and most delicious of Eurojank. Grimdark, unintentionally funny sometimes, intentionally funny other times, with a no-nonsense protagonist with just enough real personality to make you believe his motivations, which include visiting an "Unworld" to find clues for some baffling reason, then chasing down crazy people wearing masks to torture and/or politely ask them questions. Is it an RPG? No. It's a point and click that thinks it's The Witcher, except when someone makes your character angry enough and then he IS a witcher, swords knocking daggers out of the air and all. By turns horrifyingly grim and satisfyingly nasty, with a slew of European accents that don't match and the occasional American ones, this alternate universe Evil Militant Catholic Church Takes Over Earth thing is a pretty fun experience. But it goes without saying that as surely as you should fear a rhyming jester who tortures people and forces you into an Arkham boss fight, you must be a purveyor of the finest of Eurojank to appreciate this.

_childDocuments_.review: Reminds me of original Witcher game: rough around the edges, but a really interesting world, lore, and dark atmosphere. BUT, if your priority is story and the atmosphere of an original and intriguing dark world - then I would definitely recommend this! I really hope 'the Inquisitor' gets a sequel! It would be great to see what the team can do with a bigger budget.

_childDocuments_.review: The idea behind this game seems pretty awesome. The setting and the overall vibe is pretty awesome, even if the gameplay feels a bit dated. You definitely play this game for the atmosphere.However, the performance is absolutely terrible. You have to make quite a few compromises and use ultra-performance scaling to get even close to 60fps, and even then the game stutters quite often. The DLSS scaling doesn't always work, either, so you're stuck with FSR2.I've been waiting to see if any performance patches come but there really doesn't seem to be much at all on the horizon. It's a shame, but it seems like the game is made by a team that probably doesn't have the publisher support to continue developing for it. The game has a lot of potential for B-level hidden gems, but you have to pick between 30fps okay graphics or 60fps blurry mess (with stutters in either case). I recommend it only if you're willing to overlook some of these major drawbacks.

_childDocuments_.review: Positives: story, atmosphere, voice acting for most NPCs, environmentNegatives: everything else...The combat system is terrible, QTE are an absolute relic, the puzzles are more annoying than fun, the character animations and especially the facial expressions are terrible.But the worst are the Unworld passages. There's literally not a single thing fun about them, quite the opposite, with each successive Unworld it gets more annoying. I immediately thought of Vaas' line from Far Cry 3 - one time it's funny, two times it's f****** annoying.I didn't finish the game in the end, according to youtube I had about the last half hour left, but I can only take so much.I really wanted to like this game, but unfortunately there isn't a single fun thing about the gameplay.And I haven't even mentioned optimization - I have a 4090 and an i9-13900K and I have to use DLSS to even get a stable 60 FPS and even then there were dips below that. _childDocuments_.review: I first heared about this game from an indie YouTube channel. I thought it was interesting and added it to wishlist. Then my favourite streamer played and said it was trash, but I realized - I got to play it. Got bad endings and I'm not ready to replay the whole game right now. Don't get me wrong, it is a low-budget game, designed in a very old-fashioned way yet not in a good one.The story and narrative design are great and I would very much want this game to be the beginning of the next Witcher franchise because it has the potential.Yet there are a lot of problems:- The game should have had a manual save system in order for players to experience different choices without the necessity to spend time in a long corridor sequences.- The optimization became better, but there are still problems. If you put the croud density to balanced, most of the levels work good, but the Library still experiences serious FPS falls. Perhaps it  has something to do with NPCs and the amount of their detalization and shadering.- Game crashes often, either due to Kalypso laincher or other reasons.- The battle system is really old and it wouldn't be much of a problem if battles were 1 on 1, but it gets ugly when there are more than 2 enemies. It would be better to unite the block and heavy attack making Mordimer use the heavy attack automatically during parrying thus rewarding player for the skill. Also because too many buttons in battle was mostly left out after Batman Arkham series, making battles more dynamic.- The Unworld is the classic example of old-school design, which is too long, too clunky and has the unnecessary stealth. Firstly, because many players nowadays absolutely forgot about non-linear stealth. Secondly, because in the game it is still very primitive and ene,ies are short-sighted. However, when they agro they will stay that way a half map away from you until you fight them.What can I recommend? If you want to make it a battle game, then re-think battle system and make non-battle stealth or other mechanic elements more dynamic and modern. If it is an adventure you want, then follow the Quantic Dream path: dialogues, puzzles and dynamic QTEs with some simple exploration, leave battle away.I really wish to see the next part, but with the homework on the gameplay, graphics, and optimization done. Thank you for your game.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommended playing this game, but I wouldn't buy it for 39.99 USD. For all its flaws, I'd like to see a more fleshed out sequel with AAA funding. _childDocuments_.review: The Inquisitor invites players into a dark realm, weaving a narrative that promises intrigue and mystery. Set amidst the backdrop of a medieval town plagued by enigmatic murders and the looming presence of a vampire, the premise holds promise for an immersive experience. Players navigate through the game, engaging in the meticulous search for clues and navigating complex conversations and interrogations, all while piecing together the intricate web of the storyline.However, despite its ambitious premise, The Inquisitor falls short in several key areas. Most notably, its graphical presentation leaves much to be desired, especially considering the standards of 2024. The visuals lack the polish and detail expected in modern gaming, failing to truly immerse players in the atmospheric world it seeks to create. Additionally, while the audio aspects are serviceable, they fail to leave a lasting impression, hovering in the realm between mediocre and forgettable.Further detracting from the experience are the stiff and wooden animations, which detract from the overall immersion and fail to convey the depth of emotion or urgency required in critical moments. Action sequences lack the necessary challenge to truly engage players, and the choices presented throughout the game often feel opaque, leading to a sense of frustration rather than empowerment. One of the most glaring issues is the game's tendency to overly guide players, robbing them of the agency that is integral to the detective genre. Rather than allowing players to truly engage in the process of deduction and discovery, The Inquisitor often spoon-feeds clues and destinations, resulting in a gameplay experience that feels overly scripted and lacking in true detective work.In conclusion, while The Inquisitor presents an intriguing premise and sets the stage for a captivating narrative experience, its shortcomings in graphical fidelity, audio design, and gameplay execution ultimately prevent it from reaching its full potential. Players seeking a deeply immersive and challenging detective adventure may find themselves disappointed by The Inquisitor's inability to deliver on its promises.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a lot of shortcomings, such as boring and repetitive Otherworld, poor combat mechanics, rough modeling, non-interactive world and almost no side quests, but I can't help but give it a good review, because the story of this game wonderful degree once let me think of when playing The Witcher 3 feeling.

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to not be able to recommend this game.The story, the setting, the character development, the atmosphere, they're all amazing.Yet this game lacks the most important feature for a game: Gameplay.The movement is clunky and non responsive, might as well use a hammer against the controller and it'll still do whatever mordimer feels like doing. The combat is beyond terrible, unresponsive and slow, dodging works only half the time (mordimer will just step into the attack or not move during the other half) and the deflection timing is very, very inconsistent. The boss design is genuinely pathetic: Out of the three boss fights in the game, only one was passable.Despite the Witcher 1 comparable graphics, the perfomance is laughably bad and unstable. It stutters at almost every turn of the camera and feels non responsive and I don't think my setup is the one who should take the blame (I'm running on a 1080 ti with a ryzen 5 3600x and 16gb of ram).To sum everything up: This game has an amazing story and catches the atmosphere perfectly, but story alone is not enough to make up for such terrible gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: The story, interactive, and investigative features are fantastic, and you can easily miss key elements of the stories or cases you're looking into along the way and the story will go on without warning you you've missed something, unlike for example the Judgement or Sherlock series games. The sudden shifts and turns in the plot are genuinely unsettling, for example early on suddenly being thrown into the Merry Executioner storyline while in the middle of a case.Not everything necessarily works well. Graphics obviously aren't the best, but you really only notice with faces and speech; costume and environment design is pretty detailed and movements are smooth. Nothing is going to be a punch in the gut like Cyberpunk, but that's not what this game is trying to be. QTEs are awkward, and combat is more than a little clunky. Parrying in particular has an odd timing to it, with a perfect parry having a massive window to it, and a simple parry sometimes not even registering. Hitboxes are enormous going both ways, and combat mostly breaking down to button mashing, followed by an easy perfect parry, followed by button mashing. Chases can be awkward but forgiving for the most part.The Unworld is probably the most divisive section thus far. Some have apparently taken it to be a stealth section and hate it. I've run through the Unworld levels as fast as possible, pathfinding away from obstacles and enemies and looking to get through the areas as quickly as possible, and actually found the areas a jolt of adrenaline when compared to the more cerebral areas of the game. If anything then I'd say the Unworld portions present a separate challenge and separate playstyle from the rest of the game, something that some players have struggled with, but personally I've quite enjoyed.To sum up, if you like Frogwares mystery games, or the alternate world and conspiracy plotlines to the early AC games, or ludonarrative style gameplay, you'll love this game. If you're coming at this thinking this is going to be like Witcher, or expecting some AAA action gem, you've sorely misread what this game is trying to provide.

_childDocuments_.review: Title: The InquisitorDeveloper: The Dust S.A.Genre: Action-Adventure, RPGPlatforms: PC, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/Series X/SRelease Date: 2023"The Inquisitor" is an immersive action-adventure game that plunges you into an alternate history where the medieval Inquisition never ended. Based on the popular book series by Jacek Piekara, the game takes you on a dark, morally complex journey through a world ruled by religious fervor.Set in the late Middle Ages, in an alternate world where Jesus of Nazareth did not die on the cross but instead took revenge on his enemies and established a strict regime, you step into the shoes of Mordimer Madderdin, an experienced Inquisitor on a quest to hunt down heretics and criminals in a city full of secrets and betrayal. The storyline is rich with moral dilemmas, constantly forcing you to weigh justice against mercy."The Inquisitor" offers a blend of action, adventure, and RPG elements. Combat is challenging and requires strategic thinking, while investigations and dialogues engage your intellect. You'll need to gather evidence, interrogate witnesses, and carefully weigh your decisions. Every choice you make has consequences, providing a high level of replayability.The graphical presentation of "The Inquisitor" is impressive, with detailed environments that beautifully capture the darkness and oppression of the medieval setting. Character models and animations are realistic, enhancing the immersion. The sound design is atmospheric, heightening the tension, with a soundtrack that perfectly complements the game's ominous and sometimes eerie ambiance.    Unique Storyline: The alternate history and moral dilemmas make the narrative compelling and distinct from other games in the genre.    Depth in Gameplay: The mix of combat, investigation, and decision-making provides a varied gaming experience that challenges both your reflexes and intellect.    Immersive World: The detailed graphics and immersive sound effects draw you deep into the world of the Inquisition.    High Replayability: With numerous choices and consequences, you can play the game multiple times and have a different experience each time."The Inquisitor" is an excellent game for fans of action-adventure and RPGs who are not afraid to explore moral boundaries. It offers a deep narrative, challenging gameplay, and a beautifully crafted world that will stay with you long after you've finished playing. If you enjoy games with a dark atmosphere and complex storylines, "The Inquisitor" is definitely worth playing.

The main flow of the game is that you watch a cutscene, then you either run to the next glowing object and click it, or you perform a QTE, and then you watch another cutscene. The occasional combat scenes (and there aren't many) are simplistic, the engine is clunky at best, but most importantly, nothing you do has any real effect on the world. The plot was set before you opened the game, and the choices you are offered either do nothing at all, or decide whether you kill a character when their part in the story is complete.

_childDocuments_.review: is a unique and enjoyable adventure with a very cool concept, that also comes with some amazingly cheesy moments and B movie type quality. Those moments help the game stand out among many others and have a certain charm to them.✅ A unique and fun story concept✅ Cheesy voice acting and dialogue that fit the game✅ A rich city to explore with different collectibles⛔️ The combat segments are wonky⛔️ At certain parts, the art style can feel lifeless and dry⛔️ Minor stuttering and some graphics issues⛔️ Some pointless quick time eventsMainly focusing on themes of religion, the game is set in an alternate reality where Jesus broke free from the cross and hunted down the ones who wronged him. Now, centuries later, you play as a member of his church tasked with hunting a vampire in the city of Koenigstein. With excellent story concepts but some diversions along the way, it feels like the game isn't sure what it is, sometimes feeling like a smaller detective story, and at times trying to evolve into a dark fantasy epic.A major element in the game that many players might find unappealing but I actually believe makes it stand out, is some of the cheesy dialogue, the older graphics style and some of the voice-acting. Being more of an AA game than a triple-A one, it kind of makes sense, but with the medieval style the game goes for, the crazy concept and some of the wacky plotlines and characters, I feel it all gives the game a truly B movie type feel, like some kind of low-budget fantasy film you'd find playing in the middle of the night on your old television. A major thing that is pretty jarring however, is some of the environment differences. At parts, the game is pretty colorful and nice to look at. At others, it's so dry and lifeless that it might even stop you from progressing. Overall, everything here feels very different from other games, you might like it, or you might hate it.Switching between a detective game, an action adventure and an exploration game, it feels like the game doesn't exactly fit a certain genre but instead tries to go all in. This all might feel overwhelming at times, with some side activities that are so nonsensical, they might deter and take away from the seriousness of the main plot. The combat segments are very weak and could have been avoided entirely, which would have helped put more focus on the investigative and exploration elements.🔹 This review was completed on a Desktop PC. The specs for this unit are as followed.🔹 CPU: Intel I5-12600KF🔹 RAM: 32GB DDR4🔹 Graphics Card: GigaByte GeForce RTX 3070tiThe game had some rendering issues and a few minor stutters, but nothing game-breaking. is a niche game that a lot of players might find strange, offensive, or overall not very enjoyable, but if it's your type of genre and you'll give it a try, you really might find something to love here.

_childDocuments_.review: "The Inquisitor" on Steam plunges players into the dark and enigmatic world of medieval intrigue, where morality is as grey as the stone walls of its ancient cities, Placing players into the heavy boots of Mordimer Madderdin, a Holy Inquisitor tasked with unearthing heresy in a world where divinity chooses violence over martyrdom..:Pros:Compelling Narrative: The game's story is its strongest suit, offering a rich, dark fantasy world filled with intrigue and moral ambiguity.Character Interactions: Moments of genuine connection and well-executed voice acting provide depth to the world's inhabitants, making each conversation a piece of the larger puzzle.Atmospheric Setting: The medieval dystopia coupled with the otherworldly Unworld, provides a backdrop that is both visually and thematically engaging.Cons:Gameplay Pacing: Combat and puzzles often feel underdeveloped or overly simplistic, lacking the challenge or depth that might engage more seasoned players.Technical Troubles: A plague of technical bugs and performance issues frequently undermines the immersion and can frustrate efforts to progress.Narrative Dissonance: Despite its strong start, many moments in this game can feel a bit underwhelming at times."The Inquisitor" has a lot going for it and is worth a playthough, but also feels like it misses the mark in comparison to similar medieval fantasy adventures. With that in mind, I bestow upon "The Inquisitor" a penitent rating of 3 out of 5 satanic rituals stopped.

_childDocuments_.review: This really depends on what you want from it.Good:- Story is solid- Worldbuilding is interesting- There seem to be different paths you can take through the game (though i am unsure what they depend on)- ArtstyleBad:- Combat would feel right at home in a mobile game.- Graphics look like 2008 wants them back. Didn't bother me, but certainly not looking modern by any stretch.- Length. Got through it (I think) in a bit over 7 hours.- Unworld is an interesting concept, but quickly becomes a chore.- End fight is just so annoying I eventually uninstalled. It's a boss who you need to make attackable by destroying 4 boxes at the corners of the arena, while slowwalking intimidatingly and being pelted with floor effects, adds, and the occasional strafing run. And then you have to fight which consists of just the same as before, but with the enemy taking damage if you get a hit in. Might work in a combat system that is 99% less clunky and awkward, but here it is just painful, and I dislike this kind of fights to begin with.Verdict:If you get it on sale for 10-15 bucks, don't mind dated graphics and like boss fights that are simply not fun (or don't get bothered by the fact you will not see the end). "I, the Inquisitor'' is a story-driven, dark fantasy adventure game with action elements and difficult moral choices. Based on the bestselling Inquisitor book series by Jacek Piekara, the game takes place in an alternative religious timeline. Once nailed to the cross and near death, Jesus becomes consumed by utter rage. He breaks free and unleashes violent vengeance on all the non-believers. Centuries pass and now an army of zealot Inquisitors brutally enforce the faith in this bloodsoaked Church.

You are Mordimer Madderdin, an Inquisitor in God's service - sent to the town of Konigstein which is plagued by a series of mysteries and sin. Solve the various cases and crimes of those who have transgressed against the faith, all while uncovering the truth of a darker evil from another realm that is trying to enter the world of the living.

name: Cryptmaster
detailed_description: Feature List • Say Anything You Want : Interact with the world and conquer quests by typing or speaking any word you can think of - each encounter has multiple solutions to discover! • A Weird, Wild World : Travel through mysterious underground kingdoms and meet talking doors, flirtatious toads, sarcastic ghouls, and more. • Use Your Words : Dungeon battles are fueled by words - decipher forgotten spells, then type their names in battle to unleash the might of your undead heroes. • Endlessly Evolving Gameplay : You'll constantly encounter new gameplay mechanics - from creature collecting, to card combat, to bard rap-battles & more. About the Game SAY ANYTHING in Cryptmaster - the bizarre dungeon-crawling adventure where words control everything. In the ancient past, four brave heroes banded together to destroy a terrible evil, giving their lives to save countless others. But now their eternal rest has been disturbed by the Cryptmaster, a capricious necromancer in whose thrall they must ascend through the buried strata of the city above them - the gloomy Bonehouses, mysterious Sunken Sea and freakish Downwood. With the enigmatic Soulstone in hand, the four adventurers must recover their memories, solve whimsical puzzles and defeat outlandish enemies. From fishing and card games to bardic rap battles, finding the right word is the key to success. Who knows, maybe you'll even remember a little more than you bargained for...
about_the_game: SAY ANYTHING in Cryptmaster - the bizarre dungeon-crawling adventure where words control everything. In the ancient past, four brave heroes banded together to destroy a terrible evil, giving their lives to save countless others. But now their eternal rest has been disturbed by the Cryptmaster, a capricious necromancer in whose thrall they must ascend through the buried strata of the city above them - the gloomy Bonehouses, mysterious Sunken Sea and freakish Downwood. With the enigmatic Soulstone in hand, the four adventurers must recover their memories, solve whimsical puzzles and defeat outlandish enemies. From fishing and card games to bardic rap battles, finding the right word is the key to success. Who knows, maybe you'll even remember a little more than you bargained for...
short_description: SAY ANYTHING in this bizarre dungeon adventure where words control everything. Fill in the blanks with text or voice to uncover lost abilities, embark on strange quests, and solve mindbending riddles. Can you conquer the crypt and uncover the mystery at the heart of CRYPTMASTER?

_childDocuments_.review: My philosophy on both drumming and weightlifting is: do whatever you're bad at a lot.I'm dyslexic. To me, spelling is a incomprehensible void that I stare into when I don't have a spellchecker. Thankfully, Cryptmaster offers a "turn-based" mode. I can actively see how regular spellers would see this as an easy mode, but for my brittle brain, it's the only way I could engage with this game. Thank you devs for not falling back on, "git gud."The game itself is extremely endearing. This crypt is cozy af. The NPCs have the right amount of silliness, and the Cryptmaster himself is perfectly written.Gameplay wise, this is for word-game lovers. Any of them. Additionally, you'll need to tease out fun riddles, and light environmental puzzles to progress. If I had to give a criticism would be that the way you navigate the world, (via grid-based movement). IRL, I'm VERY good with directions, in this game however, I just pull up the stitched-together map on the Steam Guides. I've probably spent double my game-time backtracking looking for specific riddles or NPCs. [edit: dev is adding a map to the game, disregard!] Overall, a great puzzler with amazing writing. If you like games like Inscryption, you'll probably dig this.

_childDocuments_.review: SUMMARY:  A typing/word puzzle RPG that leans HARD into it's core conceit, delivers a unique visual/sound experience, and is also fun and funny.  Not for everyone, but it's a brilliant and innovative game that is DEFINITELY for some people.Cryptmaster at it's basic is an dungeon-crawling RPG where typing and word games are how you fight enemies and solve puzzles.  This is both true, but hardly explains the game.  Cryptmaster is A THING.So you awaken in a tomb to the voice of a slightly wacky necromancer.  Seems you're four heroes who are dead and not that great at remembering that past heroing.  Fortunately your new best friend helps you shamble out of your tomb - as long as you help him get to the surface world where he was "unfairly" banished from.And how do you do this?  Words, my friend.Every character always has "a word" they're working on - and if you can guess it, you unlock something.  It may be a new move, it may be a memory - but it'll always come with a bit of lore and maybe some extras.  How do you even get a hint?  Well find treasures, answering the riddles of lost dead, fishing, and defeating enemies may give you a letter or more that might give you ideas of what's next.  Or you can keep repeatedly typing every word of a given size, good luck with that.You'll want to unlock more memories and abilities as you will face enemies that get increasingly tough and have special abilities.  In combat, if you choose real-time, a counter clicks down so you want to type fast to have your team use assorted skills and spells - and they have to recover each time.  It's a classic active/countdown battle system but with typing - and fast typing only goes so far when you trigger a bunch of skills.But new abilities offer new options.  You might even get more hit points - in this case represented as letters in a character's name!  Yes, your names get longer to show more hitpoints.But it's not just combat!  You can fish as noted, and you have to type the name of waht you catch.  You can grab bugs by typing their name.  Both are useful because being undead is hard, and you need a bunch of souls to keep powering your actions!  Also they act as money in this mysterious underworld.And why fight?  Sometimes you can play cards with the denziens of this underworld.  Or you can do alchemy.  Or solve word puzzles.  Every part of the game uses wordplay, letter games, or SOMETHING related to typing.  Some games have a bit, some games commit to the bit, Cryptmaster IS the bit.All of this is delivers in an atmospheric, black-and-white world with great voice acting and memorable characters.  The game has its own aesthetic.Finally, the game is humorous and it is authentically funny.  I actually laughed out loud a number of times.Now is it perfect?  No.  Sometimes it's not clear what to do, but hey it's got that old-school wander-a-dungeon feel.  You'll probably find yourself doing runs to refresh your souls to meet other challenges.  Certain puzzles just seem frustrating.  The last level is very challenging unless you unlocked a lot of abilities, so you're gonna have to wordgrind.  It has it's flaws.But the flaws are pretty much part of the genre and the mechanics.It is NOT for everyone.  You have to like riddles, typing games, and dungeon crawling - including some grinding.  If you don't like those things, you'll lose interest.  If you do, enjoy, this game is for you.I consider Cryptmaster an actual evolutionary moment in games.  It really shows how you can combine genres and mechanics not often associated with each other. Also, simply, it's FUN.

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance, I think it’s easy to see Cryptmaster as a sort of hodgepodge of confused, incoherent ideas and gameplay systems unceremoniously smashed together: dungeon crawling full of riddles? Semi-turn-based typing bouts? Bardic rap battles? It all sounds like the kind of nonsense that loses sight of its identity almost instantly. But not so in Cryptmaster: underpinning every aspect of this experience, tying together all this absurdity, is the oh-so-simple ability to type and say what you want, when you want.Suddenly, anything and everything is an inspired, varied and delightful word game, suddenly, there’s a cohesion in the chaos, and suddenly, coupled with fantastic writing and voice work that deftly matches the silliness of every twist and turn, the unpredictability is instead just utterly and wildly entertaining every single step of the way.Many hundreds of years ago, four intrepid heroes gave their lives ending a calamitous threat to the continued existence of man. Now, an infamous necromancer known only as the Cryptmaster, emboldened by the growing power of his mystical soulstone, reanimates these once great men and women, for who better to escort his incorporeal presence upwards to the unsuspecting realm of 'delicious life'?Honestly, that's about all the plot you'll ever get, even as the adventure comes to a close. There’s a smattering of lore and other backstory here and there, but Cryptmaster's overall narrative structure is much more akin to a selection of short stories, usually involving some eccentric, often whimsical request in exchange for further passage to the surface. Your first stop, for instance, sees you courting a giant frog king after discovering your ticket topside entertains nothing less than royalty; it's all rather light-hearted and silly.However, it's leveraged exceptionally, and I couldn't imagine a more appropriate method of storytelling; in lieu of involved character arcs and dramatic plot twists (save a couple), there's a veritable revolving door of some of the most overwhelmingly charming, brilliantly written, and exceptionally voiced characters in genuinely all of the medium. Everything from the casting to the performances to the vocabulary used all fit each face flawlessly, and although some see barely a few minutes of screen time, the impressions they leave far outlast them, resulting in a wonderfully memorable, diverse, and altogether mesmerising cast created and cycled with astounding efficiency.There's plenty hiding under the surface, too. At any time, whether in conversation or just wandering around the striking, dilapidated lower floors of the city, you're able to type in and say any one word at a time and, surprisingly frequently, you'll not only receive a response, but one specifically suited to the phrase inputted. The script is ridiculously adaptive and accommodating, equipped for all manner of player antics: you might well expect some form of acknowledgement after proudly proclaiming some expletive and, yes, the Cryptmaster will emerge facetiously appalled by your vulgarity, but type in something obscure like the name of a dance and he'll tell you he 'doesn't take requests', type the name of a bird and he'll inquire about your interest in ornithology, type what feels like almost anything else and he'll more than likely have multiple, bespoke responses for each subject.Granted, Cryptmaster isn't the latest iteration of ChatGPT, and there'll still be a fair few instances in which a particularly creative retort goes over a character's head; however, this isn't a game that only understands yes or no, nor is it one that nonchalantly fills out words for you regardless of the keys pressed, and I can't even begin to overstate how that contributes to the feeling of player agency, that what I choose to type matters, and how much more alive the world and characters ultimately feel as a result.Simple conversation is just the tip of the wordplay iceberg in the crypts and beyond; from crafting to combat to player progression, every aspect of the experience has a unique and similarly excellent word game governing it. The most common of which, you'll find offered by talkative skulls and inside curious chests lining the walls of your journey—either a classic riddle, needing no introduction, or this sort of 'guess the object' style game in which the Cryptmaster takes a peek at an object, gives you five questions of your choice (look, use, smell, etc) before finally offering a single chance to name whatever it is he's describing. These are generally very well put together, with a superb range of styles and approaches; it was not at all uncommon for me to figure one out long before the question had finished being posed, just to turn a corner and find another that had me stumped for the better part of fifteen minutes.The reward for solving one of these puzzles is the answer itself, the individual letters of the solution drifting to the bottom of the screen, filling in blank spaces just above the portraits of the four heroes, almost Wordle-esque. Upon acquiring enough letters to complete a full word, or skilfully guessing it prematurely, the respective hero will receive a memory, small written snippets and insights into their past lives or, better yet, a new skill to be used in combat, both of the same name as the word that unlocked them. The overall catalogue is gargantuan and even more varied, with far more in total than you’d ever manage to unlock organically, even over the course of the fifteen or so-hour playthrough.Unfortunately, it’s a range that doesn’t see a whole lot of practical use in combat. The idea of battle is great: frantically typing out the names of your newly acquired skills whittles down enemy health, heals the party, or activates one of all manner of other effects, and various craftable consumables can see occasional use as you wait for cooldowns to refresh. However, vanquishing foes generally lacks challenge, lacks any need for strategy, lacks any real consequence for failure, and coupled with how overwhelming the ever-expanding grimoire of spells and skills for each hero can be, it's a little too easy to slip into autopilot, falling back on the same tried and true combos of words to dispatch most opponents. Although some adversaries come equipped with shields blocking the use of a handful of specific letters, and others can grow stronger upon a certain trigger letter typed, both reasonably encouraging one to delve a little deeper into the party's bag of tricks, enemies provide only a single letter towards skills and memories on defeat, and in tandem with how easy it is to simply slip past most encounters undetected, I often found myself doing just that.Yet, combat is just a single, largely insignificant stumble in a pantheon of otherwise truly superb word games and puzzles. Cryptmaster’s bold creative vision is unlike anything else I’ve ever experienced, one I won’t soon forget, and one I can confidently and strongly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw Spoony playing this and was intrigued right away. English is not my first language and I'm having trouble with obcure words and puns in all those riddles. I started using external help, but I hate to alt-tab out of the game to do it. Makes me feel dumb. This game is pretty demanding on a cognitive level. When you play with real-time combat you need to think fast and memorize many commands and that list gets longer and longer. Also I'm bad at typing even though I wrote a lot in my time. Nevertheless playing something like this is a nice change of pace. I really like the atmosphere and attitude of the writing. It's tongue-in-cheek but retains its gloomy and mysterious mood. It isn't short either. By now I wasted a lot of time collecting bugs and fish and because I got lost in the swamps but mainly because I like the card game so much. Didn't expect to find something like that in there. Navigation is a little slow but there many QOL features so I can't complain too much. Actually from what I have experienced so far Cryptmaster is all good. I find it astounding how much of what you write is acknowledged and spoken out loud. Must've been a real hassle to record and implement half the dictionary. Since you can only give one-word responses and inquiries, the repertoire of all iterations from yes to no could be a little richer. Some NPCs didn't understand my extravagant answers like 'naturally'.I have the feeling you could spoil your own experience when you watch someone else do it or a video compiling all easter eggs. Or worse consult a guide. Not knowing what you should type to discover things is the whole point. You should experiment on your own, figure stuff out. You might find some treasure you never expected. And when that happens, it's hilarious. Although it might be fun to have an audience while you play. Share some of the burden. Unlocking outlandish memories and solving riddles on your own could make your head smoke.It's kinda daunting but also amazing seeing how each character has dozens of skills but also non-skill memories that serve as a hurdle. I believe the progession of your skills is deterministic. Also what artifacts are in the chests. Should that be the case it harms the replayability. If I could make a suggestion, it should be randomized to some degree.I tried out voice control with gamepad controls. It works but isn't too helpul because your operating system handles the voice recognition and it has problems with homophones and all those fantasy terms. There is an on-screen keyboard to fall back to but it's pretty slow. I would only recommend playing it this way if you're really having troubling typing in the first place.I still have ways to go. Maybe I'll update this review later but as of right now Cryptmaster is just pure awesomeness.Edit:I've seen one ending. It was pretty underwhelming to be honest. While the presentation and writing stay good all throughout, I'm afraid the game gets worse the longer it takes. It is only half as long as I thought, doesn't have many quests and still there are three times as many skills as needed. When you really want to complete it, you need to do a buttload of grinding. And the crypticisms are just ridiculously obscure and misleading. Gladly they addressed some difficulty spikes on the main path since release and increased the playability. Didn't get to benefit from that much, though. Still nice to see a developer care, if you couldn't tell from their attendance in the forum.
