_childDocuments_.review: The game is pretty fun. There is some jankiness around ranged combat, such that I stopped engaging with it entirely in favor of strong combos of combat words in melee. _childDocuments_.name: Cryptmaster

_childDocuments_.review: This game is less an action packed dungeon crawl where you scour for loot, and that isn't a bad thing. This is very much a riddle based game, and so far everything I have done has been trying to determine answers to riddles. The only real typing element is combat in which you spam words, but even that can be simplified as there are obvious combos you can do that are sometimes disrupted by enemy traits.I very much love this game as its something I have never done before. I sit there and think to myself a lot and I quite enjoy the challenge this game gives your brain. It's fun to explore a dungeon, and on top of that every character is fun to interact with. Riddles to doors, riddles to chests, and even riddles for your own abilities.For a price of $25 this is well worth it, and recommend for anyone who can handle a slower paced dungeon crawler as this will give you a unique twist on what you have probably played tons of times already.
_childDocuments_.name: Cryptmaster

_childDocuments_.review: Cryptmaster is a unique dungeon crawling RPG where your greatest weapon might just be the dictionary. But this game is more than just a simple dungeon crawler - it’s an adventure that cleverly uses language as a through-line, and it’s filled with riddles, jokes, and clever puzzles that players of all ages can enjoy. Every familiar RPG trope is brilliantly distilled into a wordgame here - leveling up, combat, exploration, loot, experience points, ALL of it is filtered through the lens of wordplay, which makes this game a perfect introduction for first-time dungeon crawlers. And at each turn, the game puts new surprises in front of the player. A rap battle? A fishing minigame? A collectible deckbuilder? Crafting mechanics? There's a lot to unpack here, and it's a constant joy to do so due to Cryptmaster's polished presentation, excellent voice acting, and humor. We highly recommend that you delve into these dungeons yourself. Just… be sure to keep a dictionary close at hand.
_childDocuments_.name: Cryptmaster

_childDocuments_.review: As a man in my late 30's everything Cryptmaster aims to show as inspiration hits me in just the right place for nostalgia.It's Knightmare with an art style that reminds me of Fighting Fantasy Choose-Your-Own Adventure books and very old White Dwarf magazines.Cryptmaster manages to bring the enjoyment of old VHS board games such as Atmosfear (coincidentally called Nightmare in some regions) into the 2020's with more varied dialogue, choices and all the modern QoL features you would expect.Every character is brilliantly voice-acted, the game is actually funny something I hate to say most, which try, fail at.The Cryptmaster themselves is always a joy and the thousands of voice lines recorded seemingly having a response for any word said has yet to be impressive.Some my find the combat slow paced, but it's still more kinetic than rolling some dice (and I love tabletop games) and the mechanics it slowly builds adds great texture, plus avoiding combat itself is never a poor tactic.An easy recommend for me. Fell in love with this game during whichever NextFest or the like I tried it and even amongst a great slew of indie releases it stayed atop of my must-play pile and hasn't disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Cryptmaster

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a triumph of storytelling.  Its turned scrabble into a dungeon crawl.  Extremely unique letter guessing game and typing mechanics.  If you like riddles, word games, wheel of fortune, scrabble, boggle, anything of that nature you will really like this game.  That said this is an early review will the game hold my attention for 10? 20? hours... i don't know but this developer deserves a purchase just for how unique this game is.  There is nothing like it that i have ever seen.Don't spend your money on roguelike deckbuilder #873, give Cryptmaster a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Cryptmaster

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a cool experience so far! I've kind of fell out of traditional gaming in the last year and have just been doing little idle games and the wordle to pass the time, but this sucked me back in. A great puzzle / wordplay RPG that rewards anyone who likes word puzzles. It's like if Wheel of Fortune was a dungeon crawler. The writing, art style, and combat are all great as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Cryptmaster

_childDocuments_.review:
SAY ANYTHING in Cryptmaster - the bizarre dungeon-crawling adventure where words control everything.

Gather your crew of undead heroes, then fill in the blanks to uncover their lost abilities and defeat eerie enemies. Along the way, choose your words carefully to conquer strange quests, charm weird characters, and play a variety of unexpected mini-games - from fishing, to bard rap battles, and so much more.

Flex your imagination to conquer the crypt and unleash a whole new kind of "spell casting!"

name: Betrayal At Club Low
detailed_description: Tonight you’re on a surprise mission at the inimitable Club Low. This former coffin factory-turned-nightclub has, for years, been a beacon of nocturnal energy, a haven for wild-limbed dancing, mind-altering music and shady characters aplenty. It's also a place to prove your skills as an undercover agent. An old colleague is trapped in the club, caught up in an intel-gathering mission with a notorious business captain. Your mission is to sneak into the club incognito and get him out before he blows his cover. Can you do it? Betrayal At Club Low offers up a surreal setting rooted in Cosmo D's previous games, tactile dice-driven gameplay, and tense decisions at every turn. There are multiple ways to approach your mission, and eleven possible endings based on the choices you make along the way. • A Bespoke tabletop Session Come to Life Inspired by short, punchy, independent zine RPGs, this game evokes the feel of a one-off tabletop session, with Cosmo D as your guide. • Character Skills As Customizable Dice You Physically Roll You show up to the club with seven skills: Athletics, Cooking, Deception, Music, Observation, Wisdom and Wit. These skills manifest as dice you'll be rolling throughout your mission. In Club Low, you upgrade your skills by upgrading individual faces of your dice, then roll 'em live with real-time dice physics. • A Reactive Narrative Club Low is a deceptively dangerous place that rewards the curious, the bold and the whimsical. You can approach your mission in a myriad of ways, and depending on the choices you make, the outcomes of your mission are numerous. Care to discover all eleven endings? • A Scoped Experience Sure, Betrayal At Club Low 's mission can be played in an evening, but it can also be replayed with new challenges and difficulty modes to uncover new layers of risk and reward. • Pizza... As Dice It wouldn't be a Cosmo D game without pizza, and in Betrayal At Club Low , pizzas take the form of dice, too! Roll your Pizza Dice to get paid, get healed, and gain an edge in the club. • The Off-Peak Saga Continues The story of Club Low folds into the wider narrative tapestry of Off-Peak City.
about_the_game: Tonight you’re on a surprise mission at the inimitable Club Low. This former coffin factory-turned-nightclub has, for years, been a beacon of nocturnal energy, a haven for wild-limbed dancing, mind-altering music and shady characters aplenty. It's also a place to prove your skills as an undercover agent. An old colleague is trapped in the club, caught up in an intel-gathering mission with a notorious business captain. Your mission is to sneak into the club incognito and get him out before he blows his cover. Can you do it? Betrayal At Club Low offers up a surreal setting rooted in Cosmo D's previous games, tactile dice-driven gameplay, and tense decisions at every turn. There are multiple ways to approach your mission, and eleven possible endings based on the choices you make along the way. • A Bespoke tabletop Session Come to Life Inspired by short, punchy, independent zine RPGs, this game evokes the feel of a one-off tabletop session, with Cosmo D as your guide. • Character Skills As Customizable Dice You Physically Roll You show up to the club with seven skills: Athletics, Cooking, Deception, Music, Observation, Wisdom and Wit. These skills manifest as dice you'll be rolling throughout your mission. In Club Low, you upgrade your skills by upgrading individual faces of your dice, then roll 'em live with real-time dice physics. • A Reactive Narrative Club Low is a deceptively dangerous place that rewards the curious, the bold and the whimsical. You can approach your mission in a myriad of ways, and depending on the choices you make, the outcomes of your mission are numerous. Care to discover all eleven endings? • A Scoped Experience Sure, Betrayal At Club Low 's mission can be played in an evening, but it can also be replayed with new challenges and difficulty modes to uncover new layers of risk and reward. • Pizza... As Dice It wouldn't be a Cosmo D game without pizza, and in Betrayal At Club Low , pizzas take the form of dice, too! Roll your Pizza Dice to get paid, get healed, and gain an edge in the club. • The Off-Peak Saga Continues The story of Club Low folds into the wider narrative tapestry of Off-Peak City.
short_description: Tonight you're on a rescue mission, infiltrating a nightclub that was once a coffin factory. Will you succeed? Will you fail? Or will your night take an unexpected detour? Roll the Pizza Dice and find out!

_childDocuments_.review: Betrayal at Club Low surprised me: I've played most of Cosmo D's games (all, maybe?) and loved every one of them. There's a   that all of Cosmo's games present, and Betrayal is no different. This is no mistaking this as anything other than a Cosmo D game: from the wild and diverse characters to the jank aesthetic to the strong focus on music, this is Cosmo D alright.Where Betrayal surprised me is in how robust the game mechanics are. This game is immensely replayable, with a large handful of endings and a variety of modifiers to change the game up. The dice-rolling action checks are surprisingly fun, and are never so punishing that I feel like I need to save scum my way through the game just to progress. Your first successful run of the game will probably take somewhere between 1 and 3 hours, and only get shorter thereafter. What this means is that hopping into a new save with some wacky modifiers isn't a huge time commitment: the game jumps right to the action, and there is a well-thought out web of characters and scenarios that all play off of one another in interesting ways. All of this combined means that the game continues to shine after the first playthroughs. I've said it a few times now, but I'm really surprised at the mechanical depth of this game, and how well it gels with the funky atmosphere of Cosmo D's work. I do think that the Off Peak games and Norwood Suite have a bit more character in terms of the  environment and music, likely due to the fact that they're played in first person and take place in larger areas, with more to see. Make no mistake though, this is a Cosmo D game through and through. Just looking at the trailer should assuage any fears of this. I think this was absolutely the right direction for this game to take -- it's fresh, while still presenting a well-defined athmosphere and funk.For the price of a movie ticket, you really can't go wrong with this game. It'll give you a couple hours of fun at minimum, and if you connect with the mechanics, potentially a lot more.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: I have enjoyed all of Cosmo D's games.  I love the surreal artwork, the outstanding sound tracks, and the quirky characters and dialog. So, I was delighted to discover Betrayal at Club Low.It is a very different game from the prior adventures. Disguised as a pizza delivery guy, your job is to infiltrate Club Low and extract an undercover agent. Although the club is not terribly large, there are a plethora of tasks to take on and a number of characters to engage with. The difference is that the outcome of almost every action is determined by rolling a set of dice. Since I never played Dungeons and Dragons, the whole dice concept was new to me.You gain dice by acquiring 3 pizza recipes and the sides of each are populated by the pizza ingredients you find and the way that you arrange them. You have cash values on the dice as well as multipliers, health, nerve, and special actions. You earn cash from each roll of the dice and then use cash to build your skills (which are also reflected on the dice). All in all, it seemed very complicated but, with the help of a 'Tips for Players' guide posted on the Steam Forum, I began to make sense of it. Although the game is fairly short (under 2 hours), it took me about 4 times through to successfully complete my mission. Along the way, there are 10 other endings to experience. Circling back through the game is not tedious because the chance factor keeps things interesting. Although the game does have an autosave to a single slot, wise use of the manual save/load to multiple slots will eliminate much of the replay required for different endings.You can vary the difficulty level of the game. I played on an easier setting which gave me an extra re-roll of the dice, per action.  Although you can lose your health and nerve, this was never an issue for me. Club Low has additional modes of play which are less predictable but not required unless you are looking for 100% of the achievements.While it took me some time to warm to the mechanics of Club Low, I was charmed enough by the art and music to stick with it. After my second time through, I began to really enjoy the interactions, the strategy, and figuring out how to accomplish my mission. I recommend this to fans of Cosmo D and to those looking for an enjoyable adventure with interesting game play.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Betrayal at Club Low is an RPG about infiltrating a dance club to rescue a hostage but in a surreal dream-like world. Like Disco Elysium, you build a character and try to progress by doing die rolls. The game is about 1-3 hours long, but the focus is on replaying it multiple times to find out all the paths, secrets and endings.The systems are all very confusing at first, but after a few minutes, you will get the hang of it and start to play ways to min-max your dice rolls, get the best bonuses from your pizza, cook a great stew and be the best DJ in town. Maybe also rescuing the hostage in the process.Highly recommended, one of the hidden gems of 2022.

_childDocuments_.review: I am not impressed. _childDocuments_.review: : Club low is the first Cosmo D game that feels like it experiments with gameplay as much as with visuals, and the result is a wonderfully absurdist adventure that I think could be further expanded upon in Cosmo's future work. I learned of Cosmo D’s works through one of the countless Jacob Geller essays I have playing in the background as I perform the various menial tasks my life demands of me. Drawn in by the eclectic, unforgettable style the way one is drawn into a hoarder’s pawn shop by the cluttered window display, I decided to give Off-peak - C. D.’s first game - a go (it also helps that it was free on steam). Five minutes after booting the game up I was struck with the scope of C. D.’s visuals. The game feels like a crazy display of music and street art, a walk-through, interactive exhibit, with its pieces so oddly arranged that they somehow fit together, leaving me feeling like I'd had a hefty dose of fungus with my dinner. Most of C. D.’s library shares this formula: wacky quasi-psychedelic visuals, funky electrojazz tunes that force their way into the foreground, and very light, simple gameplay. The latter was indeed something I wished C. D. would elaborate on: although I was enjoying the atmosphere, I always felt like the games had space to experiment with wacky gameplay concepts, and that Mr. D hadn’t quite hit his stride yet. I hoped that Club Low would be the first to expand on this. Boy did it deliver. ImageThe concept of the game is simple: You’re a pizza delivery guy who has to infiltrate a nightclub. You do this by rolling a whole load of dice, a whole load of times. The whole gameplay system is heavily inspired by Disco Elysium and TTRPGS, the latter of which C. D. has shown his fondness for in the past. The random dice-infused system meshes perfectly with the mish-mash mess of colours, music and designs that make up every Cosmo D. game. The amount of ridiculous things you’ll feel compelled to do while playing through is magical and I really wish my poor vocabulary could describe the feeling of playing this game blind. The game is polished too - contrasting with C. D.’s older games which wouldn’t always feel that way. That said, I still feel like Cosmo D has yet to hit his stride. This game feels like a giant leap forward for a developer still testing the waters. The mechanics could have been expanded upon, the systems could encourage you to go for more specialized builds, instead of generalist ones, and the story could allow better for multiple playthroughs. That said, this game is still a masterpiece, and I highly recommend it to anyone happy to toss themselves into the unknown for a couple hours, just don’t forget your pizza dice!
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Another excellent entry from Cosmo D! Betrayal at Club Low takes many of the memorable and interesting mechanics from previous titles and puts them in a new, strategical light with the tabletop RPG setting. The setting, level design, and narrative are all thoughtfully developed and promise players another exciting entry into the Off-Peak universe.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: I feel bad saying this, but I wish there was  gameplay in this game. I'm a massive fan of the prior Off-Peak games in part because of their surreal characters and locations, but we get less of both here - we only really get to see the inside of the titular club and most characters are limited to a few lines of dialogue. In exchange, we do get a quirky dice-based RPG system, but I can't help feeling like the trade wasn't worth it.First, the positive: this RPG system very much suits the Off-Peak world, featuring 'sensible' skills like Deception and Wits alongside Cooking and Music. The challenges you deploy these skills against are equally unpredictable, and the approaches and outcomes are often joyfully silly. These challenges all take the form of a simple dice game, but re-rolls, modifiers and extra dice get involved to give it some excitement and complexity. You earn and spend money on upgrading your skills to improve the corresponding skill dice and hence improve your odds, and this ends up defining your character in much the same way that levelling up would in a more conventional RPG.Unfortunately, there are some issues with the system: the freedom in character development encourages repeat playthroughs - particularly because there are some Deus Ex-style alternative paths - but ultimately the gameplay fights the role-playing in this respect. Passing skill challenges is the best way to earn money and hence increase your skills, so it makes sense to complete as many easy challenges as possible in order to maximise your chances of success later. As a result, I found myself doing almost all of the early challenges on every playthrough despite having very different skills each time, meaning a lot of repetition before I could get my skills high enough to see new outcomes. Equally, the higher you level a skill the more expensive it becomes, so most of the time it's better to be a generalist with one or two higher skills rather than a master of a single skill.Punishment for failures, particularly on tough challenges, can be steep, too - typically removing health, removing sanity, and/or bestowing a debuff that harms your result for a subsequent challenge attempt. These punishments generally just make everything harder, so again it incentivizes levelling up as much as possible early on to avoid them. With the random nature of the dice-based checks, you can sometimes fail even with high skills and on top of this is a permadeath system where losing all of your health or sanity results in a game over, making the compounding effect of a failure even more frustrating.Although this is my least favourite of Cosmo D's games, it is still an enjoyable experience once you've adapted to the quirks of the system (personally, I resorted to save-scumming fairly often). We do learn some more background lore and interact with some returning characters, and it's always nice to be back in the Off-Peak world. Still, I can't help thinking that some of the magic was lost by putting more gameplay in the mix.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: What a totally original game! It's like playing a tabletop RPG run by a wildly imaginative and eccentric person. In this wacky, surreal, espionage story, you  have to infiltrate a nightclub to rescue a fellow agent. The game's small setting is dense with things to interact with and alternate paths to victory.The RPG mechanics involve using customizable dice that you can pay upgrade the various faces on as you earn money. It's very intuitive but amazingly original. Each dice roll is a battle as you reroll your dice (and sometimes your opponent's) in order to get ahead.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly fun disco elyisum style of game that encourages a mix of roleplaying and tactical character building to overcome what is honestly a pretty tricky gameplay situation. Short, but amazing story, great atmosphere, hilarious writing, funny characters and really intresting gameplay systems that blend the forbidden fun of gambling with the forbidden fun of minmaxing. Also has many multiple endings, but due to the way the gameplay systems work you will get the best chance to win by seeing most of the game's content on the first playthrough, so unless you fail really badly in the ending theres no strong incentive to replay, beyond tackling the game another way.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been aware of the Cosmo D series of games due to their occasional featuring on Rock Paper Shotgun and Eurogamer, but while I could dig the 3D-zine-style visuals, there was never really anything in the features to draw me into the games. However, a while ago, I started the , and for Christmas I was sent Betrayal At Club Low. I was surprised, delighted - a new Fixed Multicam game! (And one that recently picked up three nominations at the IGF (plus one for the Seumas McNally Grand Prize!))Loaded it up, played it for ten minutes, quit out, had enough.I'm used to playing dice games and tabletop RPGs, but I couldn't really see the point of their implementation in what appeared to me to be a fairly straightforward (deliberately janky) adventure game. Add to that, the control seemed to be mouse-only, with a giant cursor waving around, and the character walking to player-designated points on the ground. Additionally, the camera angles continually smoothly interpolated from angle to angle instead of presenting clear, deliberate cuts. Mmh....Nah. No thanks. We'll go our separate ways....And then, almost immediately afterwards making that decision, I actually happened to have a fortuitous conversation with Cosmo D, the creator. They pointed out that there were, in fact, pad/stick controls, and explained their use of interpolating cameras as being inspired by Michel Gondry's excellent video for Massive Attack's  (although I'd equally reference the Bride's entry to the House of Blue Leaves in Kill Bill 1).So I went back. And I spent some more time looking at the dice-rolling mechanics, and walking around with the (somewhat wobbly) direct control inputs and......do you know what?It's flippin' brilliant.It's actually f**king great.The secret sauce of this particular pizza is in the reroll and customisation mechanics. These turn the game away from completely random chance and into to a game of continually scrabbling for an edge, finding some application or conversation you can target your best skills at, failing, readjusting your roll slightly and then sailing through the eye of the needle, giving the finger to fate and immediately converting your winnings into another chance to reconfigure your pizza-delivery-spy-guy into exactly the kind of agent you need to overcome your next challenge.Whew.The dice / gambling elements are enhanced by a broad variety of approaches to your mission goals and sub-goals, with success at one node propagating into opening new possibilities at a collection of new mission nodes in your near future. The effect is quite intoxicating, as you desperately try to ride a wave of luck that overcomes a small obstacle, and then turn it into a tsunami that drowns out a previously unassailable fortification (or bartender).It's funny. It's witty. It is CAREFULLY daft - Cosmo has chosen to give opponents deliberately silly and cheap exits from the environments on their defeat, and yet has spent time and craft on making environmental loudspeakers throb in time to the background music, in adding helpful popups to guide the player as they learn to exploit his systems and cope with every new and bizarre challenge, etc. This is someone who has spent their limited time and resources on exactly the elements that enhance the game.The music is dope. The animations are janky, but silly and functional. Characterisation is broad, but effective... and there might even be a twist in the tale!It's a shortish package (though I got 3+ hours of fun from it), with quite a lot of replay value. Does the playtime entirely cover the €8.19 entrance fee? Perhaps... not entirely... but when you consider the sheer novelty of the mechanics, the goofy, joyous nature of the play, it's definitely worth the asking price.This is a night out on the town that you won't forget.

_childDocuments_.review: didnt even look at gameplay footage prior to playing this so this threw me thru a total loop. my preferences are more for the tactility of the first person perspective but part of what makes cosmo one of the best devs out there is unwillingness to take even comfortable things for granted. a minor flavor of disco elysium-esque view of dice rolls, failure, and even the expectation of save scumming as less something mechanical and more a possibility space to explore and prod at. perhaps the least disorienting of cosmo's games once u understand the mechanics, not the least of which because your mission is in such clear always-accessible words rather then a vague menacing thing that everyone around u seems to understand more then you. probably the friendliest and funniest cosmo game so far in spite of the fact that its the only one with a fail state. as with all their games im sure it will only benefit from further playthrus!

_childDocuments_.review: Betrayal At Club Low is a refreshing example of a game that's both remarkably well-thought-out and irreverent--even joyously stupid at times. Alongside the visual and written gags that flesh out the distinctive sense of style, there's an extremely engaging dice-based resolution system that ties in excellently with the resource management that underpins the entire playthrough. Like many RPGs, you'll frequently choose whether your character overcomes obstacles via their wits, charm, & might (plus less usual skills like music & cooking), but within that familiar framework come a number tactical decisions about how to execute your approach and the optimal order for your long-term success. Never before has a game prompted me to so thoroughly consider the myriad consequences of punching a laser gate with my bare fists to bypass security, let alone while listening to such a bumping soundtrack. I also have to respect the scope of this game, which manages to cram hours of hijinks into less than a city block of navigable space. It's both impressively dense and taut in construction & pace, ensuring nothing wears thin by the end.The one main criticism I have of the game is fairly inside-baseball: No longer being able to see Success/Tie/Failure outcomes for a roll after you select your action is a frustrating bit of interface obfuscation. There are occasionally cases where breaking even on a roll or even failing & retrying is actually better than getting a full success, and with how many variables there are to consider for each roll, it's very easy to forget those now-hidden elements. If this were changed, I would consider BACL an unequivocal success, and the game's still great in spite of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: I just want to preface this by saying I do recommend every other Cosmo D game to those who love getting lost in surreal environments.  This game is not quite that, though I do recommend it for anyone who likes this new trend in table-top simulations, as in card or dice rollers.  This game is set up like a point and click but rather than having a lot of puzzle solving or interaction, each person or object you encounter is more of a barrier that you must cross by rolling higher than they do while utilising, being affected by, or incurring various bonuses or penalties.  You also get money for each interaction that can be used to improve your dice.   If you like that aspect of Dungeons and Dragons that's all about the math and element of chance, then knock yourself out.  To me one of the great advances in computer roll playing was that the computer handles all of that behind the scenes so you can focus on the immersion.   I'm one of those guys where if I see a rouge in a tavern who asks me to play a card game he made up, I'll be clicking the option "another time friend...I'm off to loot some rare artefacts."   I'm only bringing this up because there's a good chance that we'll be playing some variation of Yatzee or Boggle as a requirement for interactions in the next instalment of Off-Peak which would be a shame if it takes away from the relaxing exploration element.  I do not need or want excitement or instant death (start over) in this type of game because they generally are not so much games as experiences.  I'd rather forget that it's just a game but instead a world I'd like to live in for a while.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Cosmo D generally made their name with broadly music-themed, surrealist walking sims, always strong on environmental- and sound design, but burdened with weak writing and a let's say "unique" approach to character design, so I don't think anyone expected their next venture to take them into the burgeoning genre of Disco Elysium-clones, nor that they'd do such a good job at it. But while DE offered up a seemingly endless torrent of dialogue to the point of occasionally feeling more like an interactive novel than just a very wordy videogame, BoCL is much more tight-lipped and just kind of small in general. A single playthrough is unlikely to take more than 2 hours and a lot of that will consist of running through the same few areas anyway. Said playthroughs can be quite varied and there's a quite a few different endings, but even so, it's difficult not to feel a bit disappointed once you've fully explored the handful of available locations and realize that that's yer lot. And speaking of the locations, environment design on the whole has definitely taken a few steps back compared to the dev's previous endeavours, generally being a lot more realistic and grounded, which, along with the lack of content easily serves as the game's achilles heel. Sound design is expectedly top-notch however, from the ominous droning in the main menu to the energetic rhythms bouncing around the club's interior to little things like the clattering of dice during the skill checks or the choppy string sequences that serve as impromptu voice acting, it's all good, full marks on that front.The writing is surprisingly solid, which runs in tandem with the skill-check based gameplay. Unlike in other heavily text-based RPGs, dialogues tend to be extremely short, frequently involving singular sentences, interspersed with ubiquitous dice-based skill checks. It lends the writing a sharp, concise quality which was sorely missing in some of the devs earlier games, and works wonderfully with the humor, which manages to be silly and quirky without feeling forced or becoming too random. The difficulty is higher than one might think, since unsuccessfull dice rolls often cause negative status effects that can negatively affect successive rolls. As a result, reckless play can easily lead you into a seemingly inescapable doomspiral, repeatedly falling over your words until you faint from sheer embarrassment and have to start over. Success ultimately comes down to careful risk- and resource-management, plus a little bit of luck, or failing that, considered use of the quickload function. It's an occasionally frustrating, but very absorbing system and satisfying like you wouldn't believe when you've been playing your cards (or dice rather) right and the positive status effects start stacking as your character develops into a towering monument to the art of charisma, opening hearts and minds left and right with their bottomless knowledge of house music and flamingo thigh stew. Fun stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Initially I was slightly disappointed because the game seemed harder to get into than Cosmo D's earlier style of games. I restarted it on easy with 'laid back' mode on and quickly started to enjoy it. I recommend anyone looking for a chill play-through where they can easily soak in the great environment to do the same. I'm looking forward to playing it another time or two now.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Another game from the amazing Cosmo D in his "Off-Peak City -verse", though this time the walking simulator gameplay is replaced by a point & click adventure with Tabletop RPG elements including the dice-rolls. For people who suffer with videogames RNGs, know that this game has options to tone down the difficulty (or make it harder if you are a masochist).
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know how to exactly describe this game, but I like it a lot. It feels like playing a Call of Cthulhu scenario, except the keeper running the game is super hungry for pizza and obsessed with music. I want to say this game is insane, but everything is strangely grounded. I really like the dice mechanic - definitely my favourite Cosmo D game.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Sticking with the usual air of cool and weird and the usual musical flair, the latest Cosmo D entry changes up the FPS gameplay for a dice rolling RPG with quirky characters and little surprises to be found (and making pizza, of course). Can be beaten in a couple of hours but rewards multiple playthroughs for different gameplay paths and endings that can be mixed up with difficulty modifiers and challenges.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Previous Cosmo D games were really more like an FPS galleries to walk by and admire, but this time we get more focus on mechanics. Now its more like point & click adventure and rpg, with fancy dice mechanics, stats and dialogue system.Usually in a game like this story would be the main drive but because Betrayal is relatively short, it has to rely more on its humor (it works). Overall the game is fun and doesn't overstay its welcome, much like in Disco Elysium, your previous actions or stuff you are wearing can affect the outcome of conversation, but the system here is not that strict and usually gives you plenty of chances to repeat actions.Cosmo D style is here and pizza is involved, however I do find the overall visuals rather weak compared to previous games (its all kind of too... normal? Maybe its because of new perspective that makes it harder to show off cool stuff or maybe I'm just too used to it by now).If you are new to this, starting from Norwood Suite or Tales from Off-Peak City might be a better idea, unless you really, REALLY like throwing the dice (it feels great!). But no matter what you pick, you will probably end up wanting more.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Creative, eclectic, surreal, funny, musical, and gripping. All of CosmoD's games could be described this way but Betrayal at Club Low is his best, and most realized work so far. I was apprehensive about all the dice rolls as I'm not big on board games but he pulls this off with style and wit, and I thoroughly the gameplay. The writing is delightfully understated and humorous. Love this game and can't wait to put more time into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Another brilliant game by Cosmo D. This guy is COOKING. This time, however, we have switched to 3rd person, from 1st person, that his first few games were. This along with the fact that there isn't really a straight forward story really makes the game a hit or miss, depending on who you ask. In my opinion, this was a great format, and because of how there is multiple different ways to play game, and therefore different endings, this game has high replayability. The music is absolutely wonderful, and I love the dialogue. Great work Cosmo D, and I can't wait for your new game.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: The best pizza-espionage dice RPG that money can buy. A game that satisfies a very specific craving, like a secret menu item that can only be ordered at the side window of a food cart located at the corner of Choose-Your-Own-Adventure Ave and Dice-RPG Drive. That first ending only lasts as long as that first mozzarella stick, but if this is the kind of flavor that you savor, you’ll be compelled to chomp your way through the rest of the batch. A single playthrough lasts around 1-2 hours, and with 11 endings to unlock this game is WELL worth the price of admission. The offbeat presentation, quirky writing, and mitigated dicebuilding in Club Low makes for a strange recipe, and therefore an acquired taste, but give it a try - you might like it!
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Expect nothing straight or simple with this game .This game feels like taking every gas station pill at a art museum. Imagine going to your 9 - 5 pizza job & getting kidnapped by some ♥♥♥♥♥ to rescue your buddy from a mobster. Most of all it's surreal art style & characters will pull you. the dice game mechanic make this trip fun & risky. Like a night out in a city should feel like. you'll like it im sure.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a short one, but is really fun. I don't think I understand it at all, but that's the joy right? _childDocuments_.review: very unique and engaging game. the game gets your attention with its eccentric spy thriller premise and further pulls you in with its brilliant dice based dialogue and skill check system. there are multiple endings that encourage replay (although you can get a lot of them by reloading a save near the end) and many paths to get to the endings. somehow the atmosphere, the gameplay, the music, and the dialogue all come together to create this brilliant little gem. _childDocuments_.review: This is not a big, fat, open-world, complex 20 hour CRPG. It's a small, concentrated, rules-light, 2 hour one. It's an RPG for people who don't have time to play RPGs. It sounds a bit awkward when you put it like that, but it actually works.The overarching story and writing won't blow your mind, and I think it's a bit *too* short to really leave an impact. But on the other hand, you've got thick atmosphere, nonsensical humor, a quick pace, and multiple ways to solve each problem. I think it's worth it just to support these sort of projects. Just make sure to pray to RNGesus.

_childDocuments_.review: Betrayal at Club Low is the latest game from auteur game developer Cosmo D. This title breaks through the walking simulator mould, going in a whole new direction as an isometric, board game inspired, story driven RPG with dice roll conversation checks, taking a leaf out of Disco Elysium's book. I was apprehensive about the point and click/dice rolling gameplay as I always enjoyed exploring Cosmo D's games in first person, but I was pleasantly surprised at how intuitive and enjoyable I found it. Right off the bat its a lot of information to tutorialise, but It's skilfully done. The dice game where you create 'pizza dice' with different toppings that modify your score or allow you to make more money is actually oddly enthralling, I found myself invested in particular skill checks and making decisions based on what my character is most strong with or which conditions I have active. It's fun, perhaps as you'd expect, considering its gambling. The dice rolling game can get addicting and I found myself virtually blowing on the dice and crossing my fingers on the harder throws. I would want to win at every interaction, both for the monetary gain and opportunity to get stronger and to progress the story further, explore more of this world which I've been with since Off Peak. There's much to be gained by being a fan of Cosmo D's previous work, though this one has very accessible gameplay to bring in newcomers.His trademark slightly odd, psychedelic designs and way of writing dialogue continues to interest me and may others. There's just something about this world that encourages exploration and although this map isn't particularly big, I did enjoy unlocking new areas and seeing behind those doors.Theres around 3 hours of content here and the price is very reasonable. Give it a go, this world of Cosmo D's is truly something to experience.Video review incoming, In the mean time check out Tales from Off Peak city

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first and likely last Cosmo D game that I've ever purchased. I bought it because of the high rating and because I historically like games that let you take several different approaches to scenarios. However this game was extremely disappointing to me. It looks like a bunch of store-bought assets thrown together with janky animations, and the gameplay is purely dice rolls based on your stats. The main character and several others don't even have skin textures; they're just blue. You can write it off as a stylistic choice if you want, but I feel like it's just laziness.  There's different endings you can get, but after getting two of them, I honestly don't care about the others. If I had to guess, I'd say the other endings are based purely off of what stats you decide to invest in and luck with the dice rolls. Some paths are very obviously only meant to be taken if you heavily invested into specific stats because their skill checks are insanely high, so your only option to see each ending is to just play the same exact map again over and over with different skill investments. Not a lot changes, and it's definitely not something that you can have fun with by creating your own solutions, as there are very clear solutions intended for you to take dependent solely on your chosen stat specialty. That may be fun if the new paths were interesting, but this isn't exactly Disco Elysium or Baldur's Gate. If you pay more than $1 for this game, you've been scammed.

_childDocuments_.review: Betrayal at Club Low is fun and goofy while having a pretty tight and interesting system. You're tasked with getting into a club and rescuing your inside man who is pinned down by the guy he has secret info on. The game plays a lot like an rpg, however your stats are kinda silly. Some of them are pretty standard, like "physique," but you also have skills for "cooking" and "music." I love how they make those seemingly random skills still be viable in a lot of situations. How you level up is interesting too. You get money which functions just like xp to spend, but each of your skills is represented by a 6-sided die and you spend money upgrading each face of those dice. So you can kind of play around with it. You might have one die be balanced and another have five faces showing 1 and one face showing 6. There are also a bunch of modifiers that go into rolls, affected by things like how you're feeling, what your opponent thinks of you, or what pizza you're carrying. My only minor complaint is that I think the game makes you level up spread fairly even if you want to do well. I played the demo and did a very balanced build, but when I went into this one I thought, "Okay, I'm gonna be a dumb as bricks, jacked, pizza guy, and just spec into physique and cooking!" But I was pretty quickly spreading out my xp to all stats because you kind of need to. Betrayal at Club Low was a ton of fun though. I love the creative dice system.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommended. The latest visionary release from CosmoD incorporates a roleplaying and chance system, but set within the strange world of Off Peak City. Perhaps influenced by Disco Elysium, in its use of D&D style skill checks but against stats such as "Tolerance for physical comedy", and with a strong focus on pizza and music. The simulated dice are very satisfying, especially in 4AM mode, in which it is not unusual to be rolling ten at once.To continue comparison with Disco Elysium, it would be interesting to see greater exploration of failure in Club Low, with new options opening up on a failed check, as an alternative to repeating the roll with increased challenge. The debuffs, such as "Terrible dancer", are great. The music, as always, is perfectly incorporated and well worth buying in its own right (Raze is such a good song, see the DLC here or Bandcamp). It's also nice to see the club used as a setting, despite perhaps not occupying the central cultural role it once did. Club Low both parodies and celebrates the ramshackle dives where many spent their youth, from the interminable queue to the disparaging remarks from regulars on the loading screen. All four games in the loose series are highly recommended, and I eagerly await the next one.

_childDocuments_.review: A bite-sized nonlinear espionage RPG with a surreal, whimsical tone. It absolutely oozes charm. The action resolution mechanic does a great job at supporting the tone of espionage, where most encounters are social. When you make a stat check it works like this: you roll the die for your stat (which has upgradable faces as you "level up"), and your pizza dice (yes, you read that right - it's too much to explain here but it makes sense in the game, essentially they are another layer of character build options). This is contested by a roll from your opponent.The twist is the rich buff/debuff system that also influences the rolls, so often to prepare for a challenging stat check you need to scrounge around for buffs that can help (which are also locked behind stat checks). Fail a roll and you'll usually land with a debuff. This system makes each encounter feel like an open-ended puzzle of how to get the right combination of dice and buffs (or circumvent it entirely with an alternate route). Although the game does fully explore its mechanics, it is quite short and ends in a way that left me wanting desperately to see what happens next. Recommended for fans of RPGs looking for a compact experience as a break from 100 hour epic "save the world" CRPGs.Review library:

_childDocuments_.review: Cosmo D does it again!I've been in love with this series for a few years now, and every new entry never fails to blow my expectations out of the water! I love this strange and mysterious world Cosmo D has created, and it's always a treat being able to dive back in and experience more.Betrayal at Club Low marks a distinct turning point in the series' design philosophy, foregoing the first-person adventure model of previous games in favor of a fast and punchy RPG system, drawing apparent influence from Disco Elysium specifically. While I do miss the first-person perspective of prior entries, this new approach to gameplay works wonderfully, and makes navigating the variety of strange social encounters feel fun and involved.The experience is short, but offers a good amount of replay value, allowing players to experiment with new character builds, endings, and modes. The roleplaying elements are played fast and loose, but add a much-needed depth to the character interactions compared to previous games, but I'd be lying if I said I didn't miss the first-person perspective and exploration/adventure elements and sense of scale found in Cosmo D's previous work.In the future, I think it would be interesting to see a synthesis of the two, combining Club Low's roleplaying and character building with prior entries' first-person exploration and level design.Otherwise, though, just about everything there is to love about previous games is here in spades, from the quirky sound design, to the surreal and uncanny visuals, to the deeply atmospheric soundtrack. If you're new to the series, definitely check out Off-Peak first, since it's free, and if the rest are your vibe, then check this one out as well!I had a great time with this little adventure, and I'm very excited to see where this series takes us next :)

_childDocuments_.review: A well-made and fun game by Cosmo D, if you enjoy the general weirdness of their games I would also recommend this one.  The game follows a detective-like storyline where you play as disguised pizza-delivery person and go around trying to solve the case that you were given by your superiors, every interaction requires you to do a skill-check (this is done by both you and the opponent throwing dice for a max. of 3 rounds) and  you can either win the interaction and earn nice bonuses that will later help you on, or lose and gain bonuses that difficult your chances, however the "losing" part isn't too frustrating, you can always go and do something else to gain better stats or change around the mechanics to your advantage.   The 6 different difficulty settings definitely help to adjust to your play style and to make the game replayable - it's one of the few games where you really see the game trying to adjust and think about the small things that a player might need (I think all Cosmo D games have this kind of charm).  Overall, great experience that was worth the price, I only played around 4 hours but you could play less or more, I also feel like the humor and story can generally be enjoyed by anyone even if they don't like the aesthetics.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard game to dislike- low stakes, pleasingly weird, doesn't outstay it's welcome. _childDocuments_.review: Cosmo D excels at making games that just ooze confident creativity and Betrayal at Club Low serves as proof that the studio is equally capable when it comes to mixing gameplay and narrative.BaCL tasks you with infiltrating a night club to rescue a missing colleague of yours. You'll achieve that by interacting with various NPCs that either get you closer to that goal or introduce new objectives for you to turn your attention to. The game has several endings and you'll need to play your cards right to see some of the better ones.I say cards, but this game is all about dice. Everything important that happens in BaCL takes place through dice battles that start out simple but get increasingly more complex as new factors are added. You could rely on luck to get a higher roll than your opponent, sure, but how is that fun ? There are many ways to influence both your and your opponents' dice rolls, and finding out what they are is half the fun of the game. The other half comes from experiencing the game's world at your own pace. The play area might not be huge, but it is positively packed with things to do, characters to meet  and self contained stories to unravel. It would be criminal to talk about a cosmo D game and not praise the writing. The prose on display is full of personality but never feels verbose or pretentious: it's relatable yet strange, down-to-earth yet whimsical. That's to say nothing of the soundtrack: it is a wonderful assortment of electronic tracks that feature traditional instruments that never feel out of place. It's groovy and creative, as is the game as a whole.Fair word of warning however: this game is less about role-playing as your protagonist and more about exploiting its systems to make positives outcomes more likely. If that doesn't sound like something you'd like, the game's difficulty can easily be tweaked to suit a more laid-back, story focused style playthrough. Lastly, this game is not a roguelite, contrary to what its user tags say. Its campaign is always the same,  only your actions will change how it plays out.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a really unique take on TRPG and video games. Every dice roll feels risky and thrilling, and every win feels great. It's difficult to makes a balanced RNG-based game, and to let players feel like they've won because of skill. So props to Cosmo D for making this a fair and fun game. I've also learned to love the conditions especially in 4AM mode. One dice and make or break your run.Music, characters, dialogue, and environment are top-notch as always. The way your character solve problems are very creative and quirky as well. For example,. The NPCs are clearly inspired by real life people and have pretty realistic motivations. Every time I play a Cosmo D game, I wish I can visit these places and meet the characters. Decent replayability because you can choose the difficulty and paths. Fun to play with friends and see how they'd do things differently.Highly recommend this game for a chill night with friends or for a challenge. Try going into this game blind for the best experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun albeit short addition to the Offpeak series. The game consists of a dice rolling mini-game where every encounter goes through a check. You can get buffs and debuffs for passing and failing checks. There are also a couple of permanent upgrades. The other main aspect of the dice rolling is finding "pizza" die that you edit with "toppings", each giving you a different bonus to your final dice roll. I highly recommend the game, but I would maybe wait for a sale if it doesn't look like something you would be super into. It's worth the price if you're already a fan of the developer's work and know what you're getting into with one of their games.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: This very much reminds me of the Elder Sign/Arkham Horror board game, but instead of defeating ancient Lovecraftian elder gods with spell and artifact modifier dice, you're trying to convince the chef at a fever dream night club to let you cook the flamingo thigh stew using your deception and pizza dice - all with customizable faces. Complete with run timers, stats, and several difficulties. $10 is a steal, great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Its hard to describe why this game rules so hard. The aesthetic is absurdist, akin to the  ideas laid out in Bennet Foddy's getting over it, but with a layer of gloss over everything so it all fits together. The combat system of dice is sick. You get a good sense of your ability to test your culinary abilities against the finer points of puddle water. The biggest issue for me was that it is too short, but I'm intending to go back and play through again. Its some how unrefined in all the right ways.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: I love Cosmo D's games, and expected to have a good time with this one. What I wasn't expecting was a total overhaul of the mechanics of the previous games, which were mainly exploration-based puzzle/adventure games. In this game, there is a very cool dice roll mechanic, that does remind me quite a bit of Disco Elysium's; dialogue based skill checks that are determined both by the roll of the dice and how many points you've specced into certain skills, which are mainly different kinds of social skills instead of traditional RPG skills. This made the game for me challenging and rewarding and I liked Cosmo D's new spin on the atmosphere and world he has been creating since The Norwood Suite. When I completed my first playthrough, I saw that it was only one ending of many and immediately was compelled to start a new playthrough to try and get a different one. The switch to third person I'm not a huge fan of however. But that is a preference thing. I much more enjoy controlling my character's movements than clicking on the ground where I want them to go (you CAN use the WASD keys to move around but the moving perspective of the camera makes this a little difficult so I stuck to point and click.) Also, first person allows you to get up close and personal with all the interesting and bizarre objects and characters. That being said, the player character animations are great and we just wouldn't get that with third person. This is a preference thing and I'm just a First Person kind of guy.I again applaud Cosmo D for another really interesting and intriguing plunge into his world, his music and art, and hope he keeps coming out with these. I'll pick them up every time. Final thought though: still no Cosmo D game has topped The Norwood Suite for me. If you haven't go play that ♥♥♥♥ ASAP.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: found this game via secret sleepover society - brought it in the steam winter sale. I love it so much! nearly 5 hours into playing different routes and I love all of the options it gives me - I can choose different play styles, and that allows me to try and get different endings. _childDocuments_.review: Betrayal At Club Low is somehow enthralling, very punchy, and deserving of substantially more attention than it has right now. _childDocuments_.review: Always happy to open up a new Cosmo D game, he's one of the most soulful indie devs around. If you're looking for a short review, this is somewhat like a roleplaying tabletop one-shot, with Cosmo's signature groovy beats, trippy aesthetic, and mysterious plot. While it is fairly short, Betrayal has a lot of replay value due to build variety and quite a few endings. If you've enjoyed his previous games (Off-Peak, The Norwood Suite, Tales from Off-Peak City), I'm sure you'll have fun with Betrayal too.I love that Cosmo is innovating with each game, and the progression in design from Off-Peak to Betrayal is really impressive. In almost every way, this game is a step forward, or at least a step in a new direction. If you don't believe me, take a look at the rest of the reviews. That said, I want to provide a bit of feedback in the hopes that the next game in the series can be even better.Betrayal is definitely a different experience from the previous games, and the most obvious reason is the camera. The skill points and RPG options are also new, but they feel like a natural step to capitalize on the great dialogue in the other games. The 3rd person perspective is fun, and clearly an experiment, but for me, it made me feel less immersed than previous games, and getting to examine every oddity in the environment up close is part of what I loved about the series. I would really love to see the next game take some of the systems and structure of Betrayal (this is a ton of work, maybe consolidate the number of skills?), expand the physical location and world to a size more like Tales from Off-Peak City, and bring us back to first person. Obviously some people will like the 3rd person perspective more, but as someone who's played all of Cosmo's games, I think it's an opinion many players will end up sharing.Anyway, buy this game, it's great. Best of luck on the next one, Cosmo!EDIT: Wow, thanks for reading my review! Can't wait to see what you're cooking up next, I'm sure it'll be awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Another excellent game by Cosmo D! It took a while for me to really get into this one, since the gameplay was so different from his previous work and not something I'm very used to, but I ended up really enjoying this game. I still prefer the games before this, but I'd be lying if I said this one wasn't also great.I totally recommend this game to anyone who likes Cosmo D's previous games and those who just like strange, surreal experiences.

_childDocuments_.review: Cosmo D. is back again serving up Pizza with strange toppings, chill vibes with some fantastic music that gives a wonderful atmosphere, strange visuals in a style only they can pull off, and a rather interesting Dice game that has some randomized and customize-able elements allowing you to change a fair few aspects at the beginning of each play-through. The game is a bit short in terms of length, but in that aspect it is also very compact and dense with what you can see and do, giving you a bunch of endings and interactions you can discover over the course of a few play-throughs.In some ways it is the best game Cosmo D has released so far. _childDocuments_.review: This game lets you explore Club Low and interact with its many characters. The world feels a little small, but the number of things you can do and characters you can meaningfully interact with is large enough that it really isn't an issue. Every interaction you have with an NPC (or group of NPCs, or thing, or concept) has you rolling dice to advance the plot. Your success or failure on an interaction affects your character in the form of traits, dice that contain positive or negative effects on their faces for the next interaction. I would compare it to something like a tabletop RPG, but in the form of a point-and-click adventure. The art style of this game reminds me of Xavier: Renegade Angel but with more detail. It feels like something I'd be watching on Adult Swim. The soundtrack is the music of the DJs playing at Club Low, which is very pleasant to listen to. It's mellow but still driving. Each track blends seamlessly with the next and there are very few, if any, silent moments. Characters are given voices in the form of discordant and abrasive string instruments, among other things, which is endearing. It very much fits in with the game's sense of humor. I had a great time playing it. It clocks in at a chill 3 to 4 hours to my first "good" ending, and there are many possible endings. Each run through once you know what you're doing will probably take a couple of hours max. I tried to explore as much of the content as I could on my first play through and feel like there are still several threads I left untouched that would make a replay feel fresh. If you're looking for a short, relaxing, funny game to spend a night on this is a great choice.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: I have no clue how Cosmo D games manage to be -this- good every single time. And "Betrayal at Club Low" is no exception. Played it to (one of) the endings in one sitting because I couldn't put it down - and I immediately want to play it again. It's that addictive. How can it not be, with such an insanely polished game mechanic, the hilarious setting and as always a fantastic ~vibe~ Get it. Get it now. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Cosmo D is one of the only developers for whom ill buy a game just because I know they worked on it. I did this with Betrayal At Club Low and it did not disappoint! _childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Kinda meh. Doesn't live up to Disco Elysium but that's kinda an unreasonable bar. It's a Cosmo D RPG regardless and that's something I at least thought I wanted. Those who would approach it with less perfectionism may have a better experience.The top negative review seems to say that this is too game-like and I'd say I agree with that. The surreal story (which requires informal rules) doesn't mesh well with the challenging gameplay (which requires formal rules). I ended up ignoring the surreal in favour of trying to play optimally. This system, or even concept, isn't well suited to trying to play optimally. If it were just dice rolls without the levelling system or strategy then I may have liked the game more. I appreciated the structure that the pizza delivery's brought to the previous game, but this dice mechanic overshadows everything else in this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a real trip. It was very easy to get lost in the world of Club Low. _childDocuments_.review: More of the same Cosmo D while adding a new inventive game system to an already intriguing world. I was excited for the release and my expectations have been met! The dice mechanics further adds a new challenge and interesting perspective to an already interesting world. _childDocuments_.review: This game continues the Cosmo D trend of "weird" aesthetics and low-brow/deadpan humor found in Norwood Suite and Tales from Off-Peak City, which I absolutely love. Gameplay-wise, it's a dice-roller, where you roll your skills vs an opponent to pass or fail a skill check; the numbers on your skill dice can be increased with money you earn for rolling, granting you better odds. In addition, there are temporary and permanent bonus dice to help(or hurt!) your chances.In spite of me getting VERY unlucky with my rolls, barely scraping through it, I'd still reccomend the game. I was just unlucky, but that's how these games are. Additionally, there are options to make the game much easier if you're just interested in exploring/story and don't want to deal with RNG as much(likewise, options to make it much harder, or crazier.)There are many different endings, and I've only got 3 so far, as well as many different ways to play through this deceptively simple game. Definitely one of the more creative indie devs out there!

_childDocuments_.review: There is nothing that feels like how Cosmo D's games feel, and this game is no exception. I waited with bated breath for this game and I was not disappointed. _childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: I've always been curious about tabletop RPG's but never got a chance to dip my toes. However, as a fan of previous CosmoD games I picked this up and it's been a really nice experience despite being a departure from the first person adventure games of their past publications. _childDocuments_.review: A great game, as were Tales from Off Peak City and the Norwood Suite. My one and only "complaint" about Betrayal at Club Low is there seemed to be fewer areas to explore. _childDocuments_.review: this game is just really funit's kinda like a compact disco elysium mechanically where you pretty much just talk to characters and roll dice, but instead of being just dialogue choices, there's strategy around rerolling dice, improving your dice, and weighing verious temporary status effects that you get from both good and bad encounters. also this game has pizza dice, pizza dice are great (custom effect dice). you also have the 2 types of health thing. you can also pretty much pick and choose who to talk to and when, so there's some more strategy with that. whole game takes place in a pretty compact area, but is pretty event dense.one run took me like 2 and a half hours, but the game seems like it definitely wants you to replay it and I want to as well. if you wanted to speed through it might only be like 30 minutes - an hour though.

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes, change is good. Change can bring about new experiences and situations you never thought you would see. This is very true of Cosmo D's latest addition to the "Off-Peak" universe - Betrayal at Club Low. Instead of a surreal, intricate first-person adventure where you're discovering the world through direct action, we're presented with a surreal, somehow-more-intricate, third-person dice-rolling strategy adventure where your choices matter more and the conditions you're presented with affect how your decisions are made. While I'm more of a fan of the first-person immersive experience, I did not dislike Betrayal in the slightest. Cosmo kept that surreal, trippy, unique air of experience that's presented in all of his games while also adding new mechanics that encourage replayability and introduce challenges that haven't been quite as prevalent before. It even introduces new game modes, difficulties, and 11 different endings that can inspire laughs and more one-of-kind experiences. My only "complaints" are that I wish the map was larger so you could do and see more. While I prefer the original style of Cosmo D's game layout, I welcome the changes to the format that Betrayal brought and wouldn't mind seeing these used or referenced in future games. Stellar gaming experience, I highly recommend. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure I would like the different gameplay from Cosmo D's previous games, but Betrayal at Club Low hooked me completely. Very addictive mechanics, great soundtrack, heaps of weirdness and dream logic, multiple endings... A true bite-sized RPG with excellent replay value. Can't wait for Cosmo's next game.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not familiar with the Cosmo D franchise like many other people in the reviews seem to be, but I can honestly say I enjoyed the game. Reminds of Disco Elysium a bit but much easier to play through. Has a lot of charming humor and dialogue and there are definitely a lot of options. I've only gotten one ending so far at 2.5 hours, though I will probably just save scum to get some of the others.I imagine after you know what you're doing you can probably finish a playthrough in about an hour if you have a specific goal. I would definitely say if you like tabletop rpgs or if it seems interesting to you, at least pick it up and give it a spin
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of Cosmo D's weird, lovely games and this is easily one of my favorites. It has a good amount of replay value since there's a new RPG-ish system which determines how/if you access certain areas/items/characters/etc as well as multiple endings. You don't need to play the other games to play BACL but I would suggest it. All of Cosmo's games add to the overall story of Off Peak City; not playing the other games would cause you to lose out on the significance of what you're doing. I really love this kooky world Cosmo's coming up with and am pleasantly surprised by how the gameplay keeps improving from game to game while maintaining and building on Cosmo's tone. Hope y'all enjoy this game as much as I did. I'll be over here with my pizzas, contentedly waiting for a new trip to Off Peak.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Another amazing game by Cosmo D.This time the gameplay is different from the walking simulator style gameplay of the other games, but in a nice and interesting way.As someone who likes tabletop games I really enjoyed the dice throwing, tabletop RPG style gameplay.The game is a bit short if you just want to get one ending, but the new gameplay adds multiple endings and replay value to it. Depending on how completionist you are, you will probably get about 2 to 6 hours of playtime out of this. Also the price is pretty low.So overall I can really recommend getting this game, if you are into experimental surreal type of themes and also enjoy tabletop style gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Another interesting addition to the Cosmo D universe.  Club Low is... interesting.  I can't decide whether I hate or love it honestly.  As always, the music in the game is a massive highlight.  But the gameplay can be very very unforgiving at times.  Mind you, that is not a bad thing just something I feel is worth mentioning.  Unlike previous entries, this game operates almost as an odd roguelite game where conversation results are dictated by dice rolls, and whether you pass, fail or tie will decide which kind of status effect you are afflicted with.These effects can be good or bad.  Sometimes you'll have an amazing suite of statuses that will make a roll amazingly easy, or other times you'll have a bad setup where one diceroll can completely knock you out of the game.Gone are the walking simulator mechanics of previous entries.  The game feeling like it was designed for multiple playthroughs with quite a few different endings.  The game offers a bit more insight into the wonderfully diverse and odd world Cosmo D has crafted.Overall though, I plan on revisiting this game many, many times as I have Offpeak and Norwood Suite.  It's a wonderful jaunt into a new genre of game and plays competently.  Bringing the same surreal flavor and further deepening the lore of the universe that leaves me hungry for more.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of all of the Cosmo D games - the music, the surreal environments, and obviously the pizza. _childDocuments_.review: I usually don't buy games at launch but I made an exception for Betrayal at Club Low since I'm a fan of CosmoD's previous work.I must admit I was disappointed with this one. Sure, it's still a decent game and the dice system is fun but... that's it. It's missing the soul of the previous games, there are almost no traces of surrealism and the lore has almost no progress or explanation and there isn't enough content...On the bright side, CosmoD's game development skills are really improving, I guess Tales From Off Peak City Vol 2 is next... I still trust him to make a great game.But Cosmo my man please start explaining the world already ;-; it's been 4 games! I can't take any more "small hints" I need a whole documentary!

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10Update: After the glow of a new game, I have reduced BACL's rating to 9/10.Back in 2015, I spent over a thousand hours playing on an RP server for the multiplayer mod of a different game. Eventually, people realized that dice could be used for outcomes, and for a while, we all engaged in increasingly complex scenarios such as bank robberies, murder mysteries, and chemo-terrorist plots. The server died a while ago, though, and I've missed those absurd runs.This game brings it back.If that obscure reference didn't make sense: It's a bit like Kingdom of Loathing except with literal dice rolls.+More content from the Off-Peak universe!Great soundtrackVibey aestheticAccessible but challengingAbsurdPizza-Camera clips onceA bug here or there, but the dev responds very quickly.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy this, it is fun. A smaller environment that previous games but same type of surreal atmosphere. The game-play is a departure from the standard first person exploration stuff, but the dice-rolling thing is fun and there is some strategy to it. I liked it. This is really unique. Well worth a try and lots of replay value, as there are many different possible endings.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: Cosmo D has done it again. If you liked any of his previous games, you will like this one. The vibes and atmosphere continue right where Norwood Suite and Tales from Off-Peak City Vol. 1 left off - but instead here you find yourself controlling a strange pizza delivery man made of silver from a third-person POV, pointing and clicking to navigate the environment and interact with objects. Not only that, it's got full-fledged table-top RPG elements which play out as you interact with things and people. This means you have a couple many different styles and methods for getting through the game, and of course figuring out the different endings. It's extremely enjoyable to get into dice battles with the characters throughout the club, and to come up with unique ways of overcoming them and besting their abilities (even if they are experts in their craft). And like always, the narrative and soundtrack are stellar and highly addicting. It feels amazing once you finally make it to the dance floor and work your way into the crowd. Overall, this is a really special and unique game - and it's been highly influential in game developer circles that follow Cosmo D's work. Don't miss out!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review: A departure from Cosmo D's previous games, this complements the typical absurdist, music-infused, pizza-obsessed narrative with an intriguing dice-rolling mini-game governing success or failure for your choices. A few rough edges -some of the dice mechanics have an almost first-draft feel about them- but an engrossing experience nonetheless.
_childDocuments_.name: Betrayal At Club Low

_childDocuments_.review:
Tonight you're on a surprise mission at the inimitable Club Low. name: Another Crab's Treasure
detailed_description: Another Crab’s Treasure is a soulslike adventure set in a crumbling underwater world. As Kril the hermit crab, you’ll need to wear the trash around you as shells to withstand attacks from enemies many times your size. Embark on an epic treasure hunt to buy back your repossessed shell, and discover the dark secrets behind the polluted ocean. TRASH OR TREASURE? In this undersea society, trash is not only a way of life, but a valuable resource, used for everything from fashion to firearms. But with the presence of trash comes a mysterious infection known as the Gunk, which could spell doom for the entire ocean. LEARN FROM NATURE As Kril explores the ocean, he'll gain a variety of Umami Techniques—powerful attacks learned from the denizens of the seas. Punch your enemies with the overwhelming might of a Mantis Shrimp, ensnare them with the horrifying Bobbit Worm, and much more. UNEXPLORED DEPTHS The ocean goes deeper than one can imagine. Fight your way through kelp forests, coral reefs, sand castle cities, and even the unfathomable darkness of the deep-sea trenches, all in the name of getting back your prized shell. PLAY AT YOUR OWN PACE Designed to be an approachable experience for newer soulslike players as well as provide a challenge for hardcore fans, Another Crab's Treasure offers something for any level of skill or time commitment. Assist options are provided for those seeking a less frustrating experience, but gluttons for punishment are sure to find the default game a challenge. Challenging soulslike-inspired combat A grand undersea world to explore Over 50 shells to try on and fend off attackers A variety of powerful Umami Abilities to smite your enemies Way Too Many Crabs
