_childDocuments_.review: Unique puzzle game with a generous hint so that everyone can play and follow the story.You follow Paige, a young girl who lives with her parents in a small house and whose ultimate dream is to be accepted to university. However, when she finally receives an invitation, her parents refuse to let her leave. So, one night, she decides to sneak out and go to university on her own.The tale takes you to nine distinct locations. Each place is made up of multiple panels that you can explore and solve puzzles. A single panel or page is gorgeously created, with incredible details and small animations that bring the landscape to life, such as trees swaying in the wind or frogs jumping out of a pond. On your adventure, you'll meet several unusual folks. They will speak with you, either offering clues or simply sharing their story. People speak gibberish with subtitles, but Paige has a voice during tale segments.Because this is a puzzle game, you'll need to get acquainted with a fantastic and clever mechanic. Each page can be grasped by the side or corner and folded like a piece of paper. The only limitation is that you cannot fold it over a place where Paige is standing. Because you can only walk on a predetermined path, a puzzle usually includes some sort of obstacle blocking your way.Folding is how you address such challenges. This is because the back side of the paper square contains a different image with its own details. The majority are similar to the front of the image, but some have distinctive characteristics that help you solve problems. You may see the other side by clicking the right mouse button. However, folding is more of a tool because each level introduces new mechanics. There are rocks to push and pull, switches to press, moving platforms, and so on. If you get stuck on a puzzle, there's a useful tip system providing step-by-step solutions. If you simply want to play the game and follow the plot at your own pace, you have complete freedom to use it as much as you want. Although hints will prevent you from grabbing a unique achievement, you can easily earn it by starting a new game. You are encouraged to replay any finished stage to obtain some of the missable achievements. They can be difficult to uncover because you must perform a specific action, but it is possible to earn a surprise here and there simply by experimenting.If you're looking for an extra challenge, each stage includes a number of collectible origamis. They are normally found on the other side, and usually require some tricky use of objects and environment.

_childDocuments_.name: Paper Trail

_childDocuments_.review: Feeling super torn over this one. While the folding mechanics and art themselves are occasionally wondrous the narrative and puzzles that weaves it all together borders on boredom. This is a game very much carried by the way that it feels. The art and soundtrack are stellar, with the paper folding system feeling amazing on a Steamdeck. Using the haptic touch pads or the touch screen results in an extremely novel control scheme. Folding back the edges to create origami shapes is immediately captivating.However as you dive further into the game many of the puzzle solutions are not necessarily intuitive. Even when I knew what I had to do, it took a lot of folding back and forth to eventually settle into the solution. Not a deal breaker but it didn't have that same satisfying 'aha moment of other great puzzlers.Unfortunately the story just continues to meander around, with the characters of each area being introduced without any real thought. What feels like a tale that has something to say quickly squanders its potential by having lots of smaller plots that amount to nothing. This was so frustrating because I can tell so much love went into this game. Hopefully the story just went over my head, but I fear that it will for most other player as well.If you love puzzlers and want something fresh and pretty but don't crave something deeper mechanically or thematically look no further than Paper Trail.
_childDocuments_.name: Paper Trail

_childDocuments_.review: This game is about folding space and time to solve the puzzles. A very simple idea on paper but when you get in to the game the more you realise how in depth and difficult it can get. Very fun and not too hard that you feel that you can't do it but also not too easy that you find yourself flying through the levels. Balanced just right for a moderately difficult puzzle game.It has some collectables that are attached to achievements, where you have to do extra puzzling to acquire them so that is a nice touch from the devs! I like the background story it's simple but that's all you need with a puzzle game. The sound effects are decent with some nice background music.The art works is in a basic cartoon looking style however for how the game is put together it works, really well thought through; the animation flows in to itself even when you're folding different bits of art in to another section of art.I like that you can also go back to certain levels/cut scenes to redo for achievements that you missed without any consequences and with 3 save game slots you have plenty of opportunity to mess around with different saves.Overall I love the game 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Paper Trail

_childDocuments_.review: Paper Trail is, all in all, a delightful puzzle game. It's "origami" concept elevates it to a higher standard of quality while simultaneously grounding it on a framework that we're all intimately familiar with (unless you never messed around with a sheet of paper in your life). It's also not only perfectly complemented by the game's art style and sound, but also improves the puzzle solving gameplay in general: you'll rarely truly solve a puzzle in this game by "brute forcing it", and must instead think out of the box. If I had to give one criticism, it would be that the mysteries in the game's plot seem to be left purposefully vague, perhaps to tease the possibility of a sequel, yet nevertheless leaving the narrative feeling more confused and disappointing at the end. However, in practice, this did not hamper my enjoyment of the game, as a challenging, beautiful, yet relaxing puzzle game experience, one I would certainly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This would definitely need to be a conditional recommendation. I'd say If you're a fan of puzzlers-- The Witness in particular often came to mind-- this is worth a look. The quality is undeniably high, the core game mechanic is clever, and there are more than enough scenarios to satisfy that that desire for frontal lobe action.My main complaint is that it feels like they stopped short of doing something truly interesting with the mechanic. The entire game is essentially the same thing over and over, with each "location" having its own gimmicks. (I got my hopes up when they briefly introduced fire.)The other thing is that they really could've stood to break up the gameplay some more. Your "reward" for most puzzles is another puzzle, with no indication of progress, and your only accompaniment being the "atmospheric" music. Not exactly "engaging."For the right audience, this could certainly be worthwhile.
_childDocuments_.name: Paper Trail

_childDocuments_.review: Paper Trail isn't a game I would typically buy but I got it for free through Playtracker and I am a big fan of puzzle games. It kind of reminds me of Carto, even though I haven't played it, in it's main puzzle feature of folding paper to change the world around you. The game is pretty short for it's price, taking me around 3 hours on my first playthrough, so i'd recommend picking it up on a sale.Each world in the game is split into puzzle levels that you must solve by folding the environment to be able to reach the next puzzle, at the end of each world you are presented with a series of small interconnected puzzles that lead you to the next world, usually a culmination of all the puzzle mechanics you learned throughout that world.There is a lot of hidden stuff throughout the game, little interactables here and there, each world has a level where you must fold a level to reveal a hidden symbol and of course there are collectibles in every world that require an alternate puzzle solution to be able to reach, sometimes involving going to the next level in order to be able to backtrack and reach it.There's also a story here and characters you can talk to as you journey through the worlds but it's secondary to the gameplay with a short interactable story after each world.You can probably get all achievements in a single playthrough but if you wanted to experience the game for yourself without a guide then I'd recommend 2 playthrough's so you don't have to rush beating the game under 4 hours.The music across the game is very calm and relaxing with ambient sounds that suite each world you visit and the song that plays during the game's epilogue is great.Game has hints that show you exactly how to complete each level. Everything in the game is possible with mouse-only so you can play with 1 hand. A few visual accessibility settings. Mouse and keyboard supported with rebindable controls, gamepad also supported. 12 languages supported for text, English and Japanese are VA supported.Short but unique puzzle game with story elements. New mechanics per world. Collectibles to find. Very accessible. Excellent music. Fairly straightforward achievements.

_childDocuments_.review: Paper Trail is charming Puzzle adventure game with a cute art style and unique gameplay mechanic. The story is touching and the credits are well worth playing this incredible game. If you love beautiful games and brain triggering puzzles it's made for you.

_childDocuments_.review: A unique experience in the puzzle gaming genre. You play as Paige, a curious and intelligent young girl. She is ready to leave home for the first time in order to pursue higher education at the university. Along the way she discovers that she can alter the fabric of her world by folding and joining paths together in an origami type twist. You’ll have to solve various puzzles, as they progressively grow more challenging, in order to successfully get Paige to the university. I thoroughly enjoyed the concept of this game. It felt incredibly unique to other puzzle games I’ve played and I have such an appreciation for that. However, some of the puzzles were just way too challenging and it no longer became a cozy game for me. As you progress through the game, a new component is added to each world…..and they stack. There will be moving paths, light beams, statues, etc. So once you finally make it to the city, all of these things come together to create one difficult final path to the university. A hint/solution button is provided, which was definitely a plus. I felt like the overall game could have been a little shorter, by maybe two maps. Once I reached the city, I was ready to be done and finish the game. I also didn’t understand why some of the characters were so mean and trying to trap Paige so she couldn’t move on! I mean - I get that it’s why she would need to find and create new paths, but they didn’t have to be so harsh. I did think the overall story involving Paige was beautifully written, and a little heartbreaking. When I completed a world, I was looking forward to learning more about Paige during those little cut scenes. If you enjoy puzzle games, this one's for you. It provides a decent challenge and excellent storytelling. Just know, you might get a little frustrated and spam the hint/solution button - and that’s okay!

_childDocuments_.review: One of the coolest ideas for a puzzle game I've seen recently. At first it felt like I was just guessing my way through it, but after getting used to the folding mechanic and the way it moves things, it became as satisfying to play as it is to look at. _childDocuments_.review: There aren't many games that use the paper-folding strategy to navigate around a level, but Paper Trail is one of the better ones. Its graphics have a nice hand-drawn feel that fits with the paper aesthetic, and there's a novel mechanism for puzzle-solving: a handful of movable platforms that can move in and out of folded locations to help you access places you may not get to otherwise. Add in the always-appreciated bonus areas where you can pick up optional collectibles, and you have a fine and entertaining game.
_childDocuments_.name: Paper Trail

_childDocuments_.review: What a creative game! Paper Trail is a simple yet unique game that challenges the mind. As the levels progressed, I found myself consistently impressed by the ingenuity of the developers. The puzzles were not only challenging but also beautifully designed, making each solution a satisfying accomplishment.The origami-style gameplay is a breath of fresh air. Each level introduces something new and unique, such as folding pages to connect lights or reveal hidden pathways. This mechanic keeps the gameplay fresh and engaging throughout.While the story is simple, it is heartfelt and touching. The narrative, which follows Paige on her journey, is enough to resonate emotionally with players. The art style, reminiscent of an illustrated book, fits the theme perfectly and adds to the game’s charm.I won’t spoil the ending, but it was a wonderful conclusion to the game’s journey and my favorite part. The soundtrack is soothing and relaxing, complementing the gameplay beautifully. Additionally, the humor in the dialogue adds a delightful touch.I thoroughly enjoyed 'Paper Trail' and look forward to seeing more from Newfangled Games in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Paper Trail

_childDocuments_.review: I was lucky enough to be gifted an advance key for this game, and I really enjoyed it! The art is beautiful, the story is sweet, and the puzzles can be mind-breaking at times - which means they're good puzzles! The voice acting is also hilariously adorable at times. My one biggest piece of advice is that if you're after the collectibles (origami), do your best to pick them up as you play - you essentially have to replay the game in a lot of spots if you want to go get them later, which was admittedly frustrating. BUT! I still really enjoyed the game, and now I know to pick up the collectibles on a future replay!

_childDocuments_.review: This was a great game to play through, the puzzles gradually got harder the further you got into the game and I loved how the story slowly progressed as you went Even the way they did the start of the credits was very well done.I received an early access code to this game to stream on Twitch and completed this game over 3 shorter (for me) streams. Although I have not yet gotten all the achievements for this game I do intend to go back at some point and finishing collecting them allThe only slight negative thing I would say is I would of liked to see more accessibility options for example an option to make the font larger and also I would love to see a save option so you don't have to finish the full level before finishing your play session (especially if one of the puzzles is bothering you and you need to take a break to look at it later with fresh eyes).Apart from those couple of things I would give this game a solid 7/10 , the art style was gorgeous, the puzzles were the perfect level of difficulty and the story was good. _childDocuments_.review: Wow! A totally unique puzzler, I can't say I've played a game with even a similar mechanic. I love the hidden collectibles, the beautifully interwoven story, and the unique approach to a top down adventure. I'll admit, I was totally struggling in the beginning, but the more you play, the easier it is to see the breadcrumbs the game offers you to solving the map without using hints. Though no shame if you need a hint - the step by step fold guide gives you only what you need as the next step, if you want it. I also appreciate the fact that you can reload each world individually, if there was something you missed grabbing your first run. My one complaint is the music. Its too soothing! Its actually very lovely and well done, but with the relaxed game play, soft artistry, and nondescript nature sounds and humming, it makes me sleepy every time D: If you want to try a new type of puzzle game with a relaxed aesthetic, this ones for you! Highly recommend, even just as something novel!

_childDocuments_.review: Paper Trail is a top-down puzzle adventure about leaving home for the first time, set in a foldable paper world. As Paige makes her way to University, she must find creative ways to traverse the new world around her all while bending -  - reality to her will.Along the way, Paige shares snapshots of her life before the journey. The cutscenes feel more like flipping through a watercolor photo diary. As we fold & unfold each photo, we learn more about Paige, her family, and the wider world of Paper Trail.But the endearing atmosphere makes it oh-so easy to underestimate the puzzles ahead. What feels simple at first, will have you questioning the ways you think about folding paper.Some puzzles will take longer to crack than others, but the game is entirely self-paced. You never feel rushed through the mind bendy environment. In fact, the sense of serenity in each landscape encourages the player to be in the moment with each obstacle. Each page poses a unique challenge so the gameplay never felt repetitive. Even when the solution seemed impossible, frustration feels like the wrong word. It felt more like all the impatience & anticipation of a big change. Each step felt intentional and almost meditative. I never wanted to quit or rage. I just wanted to move forward. Making the time it took figuring out each obstacle feel like an eternity. But the dopamine boost from thinking your way through each area hit every single time.My ADHD brain quickly found that there were two ways I liked to play Paper Trail. Binging it in sessions -- or leaving it open in the background to mull over throughout the day between tasks. No matter the approach, be warned, the puzzles are frustratingly addictive. So much that it's easy to lose yourself in the game. Paige happens across many supportive and helpful villagers throughout her journey. But a few don’t hesitate to critique and full-on doubt Paige's choices. It's clear that they can't quite see the world in the same way she does. Where many of the villagers only see the limits of the world around them, Paige sees the opportunities and is the creator of her own reality.Paper Trail is a sweet coming-of-age adventure about how perspective can shape reality. If your wind down --or wine down-- time includes mildly challenging puzzles, Paper Trail is…easier than real origami -- trust me.

Cunning warriors and bold magic users are desperately needed to reclaim Baldur's Gate from a dark sorcery that threatens all in its path. • Five new heroes with new class feats and abilities • Hack your way or cast powerful spells through over 80 perilous levels • Hidden areas, secret characters, and hundreds of items to discover, customize, and use • Forge unique magical weapons and armor to maximize the damage you inflict in battle • Conquer hordes of beasts and armies of Hobgoblins, Ghouls, Golems and dreaded Dragons • Compelling single or two-player cooperative modes of play

_childDocuments_.review: Please port Champions of Norrath and Champions: Return to Arms!One of the best ARPG genre ever! I highly recommend this game if you have played the original PS2/Xbox version! And yes, the game does support Xinput controller which I had no problem with my Xbox Series Elite 2 Controller. Sadly, the game forces to run at extremely high framerate in 60Hz which you will need to cap at 60fps while you leave V-Sync On/Fast-Sync (if you own NVIDIA Graphics Card). Other than that, it feel classic and fun, inspired by Dungeons & Dragons. Lastly, I also love gem system which adds more playstyle and replayability. And of course, there's Extreme mode to unlock after you beat the game. P.S. You can also hold down Alt and Enter on your keyboard to run in Windowed mode. Then run with Borderless Gaming Software to force the game to run in Windowed (Borderless) Fullscreen mode, and also use either NVIDIA Control Panel or RTSS to cap your framerate at 60fps since framerate is tied to game physics, otherwise it'll play the game at extremely fast speed!  Running with V-Sync On is also optional to force the game run at 60fps/60Hz.By the way, in order to unlock Drizzt, beat the game on any difficulty. Additionally, in order to unlock Artemis the Human, complete the game on Extreme Difficulty and start a new game. Move the cursor to Alessia Faithhammer (Human Cleric) and then press DOWN once for Drizzt and DOWN, DOWN for Artemis.

Prior to that it has other smaller bugs that were tolerable: randomly choosing a monitor on startup,  (Fixed), slowdown/delay when using menus, dropped inputs, etc. Other than the bugs the port itself is pretty much a lift-and-shift to the platform. _childDocuments_.review: There are a few release day game-breaking multiplayer bugs.  Once you actually hit the town of Baldur's Gate (~2 hours in), twice, we've hit a crash-to-desktop bug every time player 2 scrolls through spells.  We've had to create a new character for player 2, defeat Bloodmire manor, return to Baldur's gate, and then - player 2 scrolling through spells causes crash-to-desktop again.  That's very repeatable, and disappointing that something like that in a game that came out 18 years ago that apparently had very little modernization done.  Can't recommend until progress-halting bugs like this get corrected.Edit: Day 2 patch stated addressing this issue.  Fixed for one character; the other still crashes to desktop when browsing spells with quick browse.Edit: after playing through Act IV over the last few months, the game has stabilized.  It's still a little...imbalanced, perhaps, and outside of some widescreen support, it doesn't seem like much was done, but it's the game you remember.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are considering buying this game here are my opinions on it, after two full playthroughs and getting all Steam-achievements:Is this game fun? Definitely it is!Is it worth 29,99€? Maybe...As you probably know this isn't a new game, but rather a PS2/XBox Port, it's not actually a remaster or remake.Here are the differences to the Old PS2 Version: - higher in-Game resolution- in 2-Player-mode both players have there own Gold, it is not shared as on the PS2-Version- Texts are more clearly presented- Steam Achievements!! :-D- Keyboard+Mouse Support, although I didn't test it but rather played it with PS2-Controllers via an USB-adaptor- Unlockable characters can't use ranged weaponsWhy wouldn't I call it a Remake oder Remaster,Besides the higher game resolution, I would wish for higher resolutions on textures, icons and menus, made from the same source images, for PS2 and Xbox there certainly were limitiations on how big these could be due to restricted memory and maybe even more deciding space on the gamedisk-DVD (the download size for this game is around 4.1GB, which would fit on a regular 4.7GB DVD)Also the audio clips suffer the same compression artifacts as on PS2. I would assume that those original image and audio files, which could have been used for a remaster, were just lost in time, since the PS2-Release there was a lot happening around the publisher Interplay.But still, it would have been possible to "remake" those images an audios. If there is no possibility to get the original files back and put them in higher quality into a remaster, I would prefer, especially on voice-lines, which are almost impossible to get exactly right, to have settings in the options menu for the player to decide for which parts the game should use the newly recreated high quality files or the older lower quality files which are exactly the same as back then in the olden PS2 times I'd say this Port to modern platforms is a bit late...By now you can run the PS2 version of this game just fine on a PS2-Emulator, also with resolution. If this Port came out when the PS4 was new 29.99€ would've kind of a good deal, back then this game only rendered half the screen in emulators or would be deadslow due it needing to be software/CPU rendered.But still this port runs better than a PS2Emulator, although my PC can handle both at 1440p, compared to running it in an emulator it didn't break a sweat running this PC-Port.Should you get this game if you played it back then on console?Absolutly! But maybe wait for it to be on Sale, or consider the Nintendo Switch Version, I can imagine it'd be a really chilled way to chop down some goblins while laying down with your Switch or SteamDeck or to play it on a longer train ride or sth like that. This Game is for sure better than some p2w ad-filled mobile game (and you don't have to be online)Should you get this game if you haven't played it before?Do you like simple controls and like a game you can pick up any time again and don't mind the graphics being a bit dated?Do you want some story but rather than that want to runthrough dungeons and kill everything that moves?Do you want a rewarding leveling, equipment and crafting system, but don't want to learn complicated mechanisms before you can even compete? (Yes you can get nerdy on skills and equipment, but you don't have to.If you answered 3x Yes then get the game whent it's either on sale or for your handheld device before your next longer train/bus/whatever-ride.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game, but your enjoyment of it will be based largely on how much you enjoy games from this era and/or enjoy Dungeons and Dragons and hack and slash type games. You don't really have to be a fan of the original Baldur's Gate series since Dark Alliance plays totally differently. It seems like this game shouldn't exist since the original Dark Alliance came out on the Gamecube and this one still plays like a Gamecube game, despite the fact that it was originally released on PS2 and Xbox.Now, the port is not perfect, since some of the key bindings do not match what it shows on screen and it's still designed to be played with a controller. You can use the hotkeys to pull things up but when selecting different skills you still need to painstakingly scroll through a wheel and the spells seemed to be ordered randomly. If you've played games like this, you already know what to expect. Much like Diablo and other games you kill enemies, level up, complete quests all with the goal of progressing through each chapter and defeating the final boss. With that said, there really isn't that much of a story. Baldur's Gate is just the name of the town, and I believe every game has its own story that centers around the town. This one is kind of boring since it just involves vampires taking over, and each quest is just a collectathon of finding a specific item in a dungeon and returning to the quest giver. With that said, it is nice that this is somewhat of an open world game. You progress in a linear fashion, but the game doesn't really feel linear since there are sidequests and other things to do.You start by picking from one of five characters, and this is where the game turns out to be either great or terrible depending on how you decide to play it. The biggest flaw with this game, and what keeps it from true greatness, is the fact that it seems to be optimized for a multiplayer experience, even though 90% of people who play this will probably only be doing the solo play. With that said, it is kind of ambitious that the game gives five characters to select from and also has two hidden unlockable characters (Though they don't really add much so you can skip them altogether). Now, you might think that having five different playable characters is great, and to an extent it is, since you can easily get 100+ hours of gameplay if you decide to max level each character. But the game is ridiculously unforgiving, and by that I mean that the character you pick must be played a certain way, and levelling up will not correct any deficiencies with the original character's base stats. Basically three characters are great for single player mode, and two are just about useless. Dorn Redbear is your generic warrior type, but he's actually the best character for beating the game since the game is optimized for characters who use melee and spam the use of potions. Now Vhaidra, the monk, would seem to be a great character, after all, she's all over the artwork for the game. But she, like most monk classes in video games, is just weak in general as she is supposed to rely on her fists instead of weapons. Granted, she is very fast, so that almost makes up for it, but she has a lot of different types of skills and excels at few of them. Now the Moon Elf Ysuran is also a great character, since he's the closest thing to a mage type, the main reason he works is that he gets a summon that allows him to kite enemies and distract them while he casts spells at a distance. He is the most varied and interesting character, and he can also drain health from enemies and transmute different potion types, making him the best for stocking up on gold as well since you don't need to buy a lot of potions. The Dwarven rogue Borador is your typical archer / rogue class, but he's probably the most fun to play as. Mostly because he has a lot of different ways to kill enemies, whether by sniping them with a bow or dropping down remote detonated bombs. It seems like they put a lot of effort into making this character fun to use, even though he's not really the best character to beat the game with since he doesn't deal a ton of damage to the bosses. And last there is the human cleric Allessia, who should be a great character but ends up being really weak in single player. She basically has two modes of attack: casting a ton of stat buffs and running in for melee or using a heavenly fire attack to deal area of effect damage to groups. While this should've been the best character in the game, she is not optimized for single player, so she always ends up dealing less damage and taking more damage by default. I tried to beat the game with her on the extreme difficulty and it was too irritating to proceed, largely because even at level 40 she still has terrible defense. I suppose the developers designed it this way since she has the ability to heal without potions, but that doesn't make much of a difference when she dies in 2-3 hits even when playing on easy mode.Now, speaking of the difficulty, this is your standard hack and slash. You kill enemies, collect gold and level up. But the game is so oddly designed in this regard since unlike a game like Diablo, if you just play this however you want you will probably just end up getting frustrated and dying a lot. Some abilities are extremely useful, and some are totally useless. The boss fights are relentlessly difficult, even on the easier settings it is still possible to die in a couple hits if you are 10-20 levels over the boss you're fighting. With that said, the simple act of clearing different dungeons, collecting loot and leveling is as fun as it is in any other game of this nature. Each time you level up you get to pick new skills or upgrade skills. About halfway through the game each character has a unique quest that, one completed, unlocks a second set of skills. You really will probably want to play through this game with each character twice since that's how you max out all of the different skills. With that said, some of the skills do repeat among characters. The monk, for example, unlocks a second set of skills that are basically for stealth kills and these are basically useless since by that point you're going to want to run past most of the enemies.This is actually probably the weirdest thing about this game: about halfway through, killing enemies is pointless. If you want to sit there and hack through each enemy for a little bit of gold, by all means, but the game stops giving decent experience at this point. The quests and bosses, on the other hand, still give legitimate experience that will help you level quickly. Even odder is the fact that the game gives every character access to the "sprint" command. When you sprint you can speed through the dungeons and dash past the enemies with no resistance whatsoever. The only way you can die is if you accidentally spring into a pit, which is rare. So basically the game is encouraging the player to stop killing enemies and just run straight through to the bosses. It's kind of funny, and strange, since on subsequent playthroughs instead of thinking about methodically clearing out each dungeon I instead just did the estimate of how many health potions I would need to defeat the remaining bosses. Then, simply dash past everything, ignore the gold and treasure, and kill the bosses. So unlike a game like Diablo where you have a limited number of potions on your belt, this one just gives you up to 99 that you can use with a hotkey. The bosses are tough as nails, but if you carefully save up your potions for the harder fights, it's impossible to die. It's a weird way to design a game for sure, since it can be very easy or very difficult depending on the choices you made earlier in the game.  The music is the best part of the game, since it was composed by the guy who worked on Morrowind, it sounds more epic than what the game deserves. And the graphics are dated. Still, worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is exactly what i remember as a kid just better tbh. the load times are instant and the game runs perfectly smooth so far. this is definitely no remaster, the graphics seem slightly sharper (except on the character select screen,, hoo boy that was like 5 pixels xD) but they're just about the same as they were on PS2. it's just a port of my favorite childhood game and i have no squabbles with that. i really dont see why people are so angry about the price though. this is a full game that i know i'll spend hundreds of hours in and greatly enjoy playing. i've spent $60 on newer games that i finish in 40 hours and likely wont ever pick up again.also i loooove that there's achievements now. im big on achievement hunting and i can't wait to add this to my 100% list !the only issues i have run into so far are that there is no option to rekeybind the "delete save" button. i remapped select to be E and now both select and delete are the same button which just means ill need to remap select again. i would also love to see something implemented to allow LMB to be held down to repeatedly fire arrows so i do not have to spam click. minor issues but things i'd like to see changed regardless.Edit: Multiplayer was a bit confusing to get running, bit it does work. KBM only works for single player. to play 2 player, both users need to be using controllers. it also does work with steam remote play and the second player plugging a controller into their PC. both controllers do not need to be in player 1's PC.Edit 2: 1 major bug has been noticed in multiplayer. After arriving to baulder's gate, the character chosen by player 2 will be corrupted and they will not be able to change abilities without the game crashing. the current workaround for this is for the host of the game to create a new single player game as the preferred character for player 2. play the game up until you reach baulder's gate and save. you can then load into your 2 player save > go to start > change players > hover over player 2 > import > select the save file you just created. player 2's character will no longer be corrupted and you can continue as normal. make sure player 2 drops all loot and it is picked up by player 1 before doing this or it will be lost.as i get further in the game and try out multiplayer i'll update this with any more info i find is important !

_childDocuments_.review: + controls very well+ story full of intrigue and drama+ lots of variety in level design+ lots to unlock with subsequent playthroughs- can feel repetitiveThe Dark Alliance series was the cornerstone of couch co-op console RPGs way back when they first came out nearly two decades ago. They might not really match up to more modern RPGs in terms of story or stakes, the Dark Alliance titles are more smaller scale and local. Nevertheless, they're fun little stories that exemplify the now stereotypical D&D tale.The story is full of tropes but has charm. It does meander a touch, especially with the addition of side content, and at a certain point seems to overstay a little. It's not a very memorable story and is more a vehicle to bring you from location to location. The game is a lot more open ended, with optional areas and quests, and there seems to be a much larger variety in locations, too.It is also accompanied by some really fantastic music and general sound design. Plus, the voice acting is pretty good. Cheesy at times, but it suits the game very well. There are some issues with sound mixing, as there's no way to control voice volume, and by default it is drowned out by music and effects.Dark Alliance, and other games using its engine, have always controlled super well and in this port is no different. Console ARPG gameplay of this era really stood out to me, even today. The combination of perfect controls and the gameplay loop of combat, loot, explore is a joy to experience again in 2022.The game took me 16 hours to complete as a cleric on normal mode. There's five classes initially to choose from, and multiple difficulty modes. Additional classes and difficulty modes can be unlocked on game completion, so there's a lot of opportunity and incentive for replays.Dark Alliance 2 translates great to PC. There is M+KB support (although a controller is highly advised), and support for both higher resolutions and widescreen (including ultrawide). Unlike the first Dark Alliance port to Steam, this one includes achievements. Unfortunately, the game is locked to 60fps, and going above will impact physics.While the game does look generally sharper than when it originally released due to higher resolution support, that is about as far as the graphics have improved. Textures and models don't appear to have been improved much, and this is especially so for UI elements including menus, where it looks particularly poor. Notably, cutscenes look downright awful as they are stretched 480p. That said, it was a pretty good looking game eighteen years ago, and while the transition to 2022 might not be super graceful, it still looks good for its age. Dark Alliance 2 always had great artistic direction, really evoking the D&D aesthetic of the 90s and 00s, and this is not lost in this port.But, have realistic expectations going into the game, especially if you compare to other remasters of recent memory. Dark Alliance 2's remaster work feels a little flaccid, but the game underneath hasn't changed, for better or worse.Just like the first Dark Alliance port, the price can be difficult to reconcile. CAD$34 for a nearly twenty year old port is admittedly a lot, but for many of us who grew up on this game and others like it, it might be worth the price of admission to experience these titles on PC. It's clear nostalgia factors into the price, but this may not bother everyone.At maximum resolution, the game maintains 60fps with or without edge smoothing. Because it runs so well, you can drop the maximum wattage down to as low as  and it will still keep 60fps without dips. Really stellar performance, and at 3W, the Deck's internal battery measure alleges it can last for over five hours. Impressive, but I haven't verified.The Deck's 16:10 aspect is supported without letterboxing. While Dark Alliance 2 added a zoom feature, something the first title did not have, it's not particularly close enough to see great detail on your character. The game seems a little too far zoomed out sometimes; this goes for text, too, which is sometimes difficult to read but not completely illegible.Suspending play seems to mute the game on wake-up. I've been able to reproduce this consistently, it happens every time the game is suspended. The only solution is to quit back to Steam and launch it again. Other than this, I did not experience any other bugs specific to the Deck.Overall, Deck performance is excellent, but also the experience of playing on the Deck is really quite nice, too. Everything controls super well and it's a joy to pick up and play. Highly recommend.Ultrawide is supported out of the gate and works well. UI elements do not stretch for 21:9 and many menus pillarbox to 16:9. I don't think ultrawide necessarily improves the experience, however, because while it lets you look ahead to a degree, most of the time what ultrawide reveals is of little significance, typically you see outside the level bounds.It's not a demanding game, plus it's only a slightly updated port of a twenty year old game. It goes without saying my 5600X and RTX3080 can max the game out, especially with the 60fps cap. Chances are any PC within the last decade could play it well.

_childDocuments_.review: Like Baldurs Gate: Dark Alliance, the game has perhaps aged a little poorly. Difficulty very much depends on which of the characters you chose to play, with the necromancer having the roughest time both due to the frequency you face undead and having the lowest hit points. Naturally. Some areas are so oppressively dark that it's hard to see where you're going or what you're doing. But despite all it's flaws, it's still a very solid game and earns it's reputation.The story is predictable and simple. And each character has a character specific side quest that boils down to "give a few tons of gold to this specific NPC over the course of chapters 1 and 2 in order to unlock a new dungeon in chapter 3". None of the character specific side stories are particularly deep either. Then again story isn't really the main reason to play an isometric brawler type game like this.  For as basic as the combat system is, it's rather fun. And character builds can be customized, to an extent. Eventually you'll have all tiers of every feat, but that'll take multiple times through the entire campaign with the same character. And the item crafting system means that you need never worry about getting the exact drops you need for your build. It's expensive, but you can make your own gear to precisely tailor your character to the desired play style.Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance 2 may not be for everyone. If you're not a fan of punishing difficulty or top down brawler style dungeon crawlers then you may not enjoy the game. But I would highly recommend the game to others.

_childDocuments_.review: Well ♥♥♥♥ this is a nostalgic blast from the past. I used to absolutely play the hell out of this game, so some advice for new players who may not be used to it, I'm currently going through the game again as the Necromancer:1: Murder EVERYTHING. Explore the map and kill ANYTHING hostile to you, you'll want the XP2: The game isn't shy with potions, especially not in the beginning. Dont be afraid to make use of them.3: Enemies in this game know how to block, you should figure it out yourself. The first two bosses both have very readable attack patterns and telegraph when they're going to attack you quite well.4: If you're REALLY having a ♥♥♥♥♥ of a time, play the Elf Necromancer. It might seem counterintuitive, but in this game the mage is probably the best solo character. Get his Animate Dead spell, put at least one level into armor, and then start maxing Animate Dead and your two starting spells Drain Life and Shield. Your mana comes back fast, and at its max level Shield negates a solid 50% of incoming damage while its up, combined with the Life Drain and your skeleton to tank hits for you, and you can be VERY hard to kill.Also, this game was designed for use with a gamepad, and it REALLY shows. Especially on ranged characters. If you're really struggling, consider switching to a controller rather than  mouse and keyboard.

You don't have to play the first game to start this one. This game brought quite a few quality of life changes and improvements over the original Dark Alliance. It also has more playable characters and a longer story. $30 is a bit steep, but definitely worth more than paying full price for the first game, imo. I'll still gladly pay it if it means we can get a Champions of Norrath release next!I did try remote play for about an hour and it works great for co-op! We did not make it into the city yet, so I don't know if the bugs other people are reporting will pop up. Hoping for Norrath next, and maybe, just maybe, development can start over on a new Dark Alliance III to finish the story!

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR An improvement over BGDA in all waysWot I liked- WASD+mouse control scheme. It befuddles me that it is not the staple control option for all ARPGs;- There're 5 classes which are quite fleshed out, especially in comparison to BGDA1;- Arrows stick out of enemies' bodies;- Very extensive crafting: there're dozens of modifiers enhancing the gear;- Extreme difficulty has a point now: it allows you to upgrade gear to +15 (Hard's cap is +5);- Extreme difficulty is basically NG+: tougher enemies, old character, more loot;- The story is not so braindead and ends in a cliffhanger;- You can actually fall to death;- Combat is simple but fun and improved since BGDA1: block and strike, dodge range and magic.- There is more than one build for each class - they are not much but the gameplay is quite varied. Jousting from BGDA1 was fixed, which is a plus in my book;- There's some item customization (no description of what magic modifiers do though);- There're actual feats that'd slightly change the way you play your "class";- Monster variety has been greatly improved: there are different races, monstrous and otherwise, elemental, abberations and undead - it really looks like a D&D licence game.Wot I disliked- It did not look great in 2001, it does not look good in 2022;- It is expensive. Charging a basically full price for a 20 y.o. game, which wasn’t hat good in the first place is madness;- WOTC has no right to sell this game: it's been made by Obsidian 20 years ago. You'd rather buy some title that Obsidian owns to support the real developers not licence holders;- Bladed weapons' (bastard swords, greatswords, etc.) textures are 2d and you can see how 2d it is most of the times. As a matter of fact all weapons are 2d but it's most obvious in bladed weapons;- Sloppy gamedesign: subtitles cutoff, no item descriptions;- Combat and pathfinding for AI is weird: you're going to see some weird dances;- On harder difficulties there is a lot of downtime as you have to regen health: health pots are too expensive to heal in between battles and there is no rest mechanic. Besides the enemies have too much hp and dmg thus aggravating the problem.To sum it all up, BGDAII is an example of how WOTC ran the franchise into the ground. BGDA is hands down worse than Dungeons & Dragons: Chronicles of Mystara. It has nothing on ARPGS from other franchises. Its gameplay is better than Dark Alliance 2021, which only further proves my point.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a special place in my heart for this game, but first about the port / game. I am having a good time playing it on my Steam Deck. The port seems decent and serviceable enough (as of writing this, I am almost to Act 2). Controls are tight, no crashes, and only a couple of bugs that have all been solved by restarting the game. I have some issues with the audio where it sounds "scratchy" even with the latest update (07/27/2022). Hopefully they can clean up the audio.OK, now it's story time about why this game holds its special place. Many moons ago, when I was in the seventh grade, I got appendicitis. My appendix ruptured and I was in the hospital for a little over two weeks due to complications. It took me several months to recover, but that's long in the past. I'm fine now. :) When I was recovering in the hospital, the hospital had an OG XBOX available for me to play with to distract me from my pain. They had a couple of games, but I wasn't really enjoying most of them. The day after my surgery, my dad had gone to a video game rental store and picked up this game for me to play. I was really hooked and I almost beat it during my stay in the hospital. However, just like every rental, eventually he had to take the game back.Since he took the game back to the store, I haven't played it until now. While I do have some rose tinted glasses towards the design and the "simpler days" it's still a treat to have this relic of my past in my steam library. It's super easy to pick up and play on Deck, and I'm looking forward to playing many more hours of it as I have time in my busy life. Thanks to all who have helped make this game happen (and to its most recent port).

_childDocuments_.review: The original Dark Alliance is one of my all time favorite games mainly because I have so many good memories playing it when I was young.  I never got around to playing much of this one (II) because only my friend owned it.  I decided to try it out.  It's basically a more polished version of the 1st game with additional textures and more interesting creatures.  Otherwise, it feels the exact same.  Compared to today's game (even similar ones like Gauntlet or Children of Morta) it's quite simple and the combat is super repetitive.  I would recommend it to people who don't like super complex games or maybe if you want something pretty easy to play while also watching YT videos or something.  It's also one of the few local co-op games on PC.  Otherwise I think younger players will get bored easily, especially since we have things like Baldur's Gate 3 out now.  My main complaint is probably the price. The original game was like $20 on PS2 and I realize that ports take effort and inflation exists but $30 still seems a bit steep IMO.

Maybe they have other problems with their computers.This game is very different from the other Baldur's Gate games for PC, but I feel it is much more accessible to  players.  You don't have to know a lot about playing action rpg's to get into this game and it is not a game that will make you rage with anger over its difficulty.  You also don't have to have played the first Dark Alliance game to get into this one.  The story is a continuation, but not so much that you will be lost following along, there is also an NPC in the beginning tavern that will recap the first game for you with the story. _childDocuments_.review: Solid game. Not without a healthy dose of jank but if you played the original you knew that already. Makes a lot of sorely needed QOL changes, such as being able to hotkey spells (so you don't have to awkwardly shuffle through them one at a time anymore), better mobility with the Sprint ability that every character now has access to, and some unique quests/interactions based on the character you are playing as. For those hesitating due to the $30 price tag: This game is about twice as long as BGDA1, give or take. Besides having way more content, there are now 5 playable classes instead of 3 (the original classes are gone but have all been replaced with better versions IMO). Crafting exists so you can now customize your character much more than you could before, removing the reliance on random drops. There are also optional side quests in addition to the main quest, a nice change from the entirely linear first game.The main downside of this game is the difficulty. It is substantially easier than the first game, meaning it is much more of a button masher and tactics only matter in a small number of fights. I would recommend playing on Hard, it's pretty close to Normal in the first game but IMO still a bit easier. Haven't played Extreme mode yet but it wasn't that bad in the original if you knew what you were doing and I suspect the same here.Overall just a better game than the first, and that's not a dig at the first game but rather a commendation of this one. The original is undoubtedly a classic, but the developers really put in a lot of effort for the sequel and it shows.

_childDocuments_.review: In a world where games like this exist and can still be played with friends via Remote Play Together (that's how I played through the campaign with my bro) there is no good reason to play live-service trash like  etc.As with the first game, it is a fully 3d, top-down game which just works when you turn it on. (It's sad that the game running as intended without tinkering is something I have to note but that's the state of gaming in current year 2024.)As with the earlier game in this series (my review for that is ) this game is basically the same as  in most respects, having been made at about the same time by the same company. To be honest, I was disappointed when I found out that  was a sequel to the old CRPGs rather than to this game. I understand why people like those games but I think that a straightforward hack and slash like this is just plain fun and the story, gear, customization etc. still has enough RPG to give me that  feeling.This game was actually so good that I even toyed with the idea of buying the new  game (despite the reviews) simply because I want more like this one. On a related note, I really hope that this company can bring  to Steam in the same way that they brought this.  My introduction to hack and slash games was via a controller so I always default to that when I play games of this type. Fortunately this game works very well if played this way. One of the features I did NOT like about the earlier game in this series is that you use up arrows as ammunition which means that if you have a bow, you will find yourself relaying on melee instead to save money/conserve arrows for the boss. Even if you use the item duplication exploit (see the section below for that) it would be tedious.Fortunately, in this game as with many other fantasy games, you have infinite arrows so the economic element in choosing arrows vs. melee is no longer a factor. Now its just a question of tactics. This has a decent RPG character upgrade system. It also has a good loot system... though I can't really say for sure how well the economy is balanced due to the item duplication exploit described below.  One feature of these games which is carried over from the PS2 era originals is that you can save the game, then drop your loot and have a friend pick it up (or do it yourself with two controllers and an alt character) then reload your character with all of the loot you just dropped. (If you don't have two controllers or a friend to play with, just dropping and then reloading your character does work but sometimes things disappear so it's more reliable to have a friend pick it up and then return it to you.)Using this method, you can essentially duplicate anything you find as if you had a  replicator... though this doesn't break the game as you might expect since enemies don't usually drop loot that is too high level and even if you did, you have to be the right level yourself in order to equip high-level items. Rather than breaking the game, this exploit just basically removes item scarcity and gives you a  style economy. If you want an enjoyable top-down hack and slash game set in the  world and don't mind PS2 era graphics, you can't do much better than this game.Here's hoping that  gets the same treatment.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my third session with the game and I laughed so hard my face hurts.  I never had this game as a kid so I'm playing without nostalgia.  The jank is incredible, delicious, and never ends.  Best played with a friend over remote.  Joystick is mandatory.  Haven't had any serious bugs. If one of you can't buy or sell at the merchant, just reload the save.  Do not take this game seriously and you will have a good time.  There are bosses that can't fit through hallways, early monsters that are best killed at range a screen and a half away and absolutely no design in the level design.  This game has a bizarre feature I've never seen in any other game. You can import characters from other saves into the current one.  So you can cheese the entire game by doing the following:1. Save the game before a quest turn in.  Note the time and date of the save so you know which one it is. This is save A.2. Turn in the quest, and make another save (Save B).3. GO BACK IN TIME by loading save A, then importing your characters from save B by the in game menu.  Now turn in the quest again, and save. Load back Save A and do it again, and again.The developers had to know that this game's fun was mostly in jank, I salute them.  Sometimes a game is just fun and this is one of those.

_childDocuments_.review: It's as advertised: a faithful port of Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance 2. A classic experience.While this means that the quirks of the original are in this game as well, it's still something I would consider an enjoyable experience despite how old it is now. Looking up a guide or two on the crafting will be worth the while for anyone looking to seriously approach the Workshop of the game as it can be a little bit of a hurdle. Be sure to avoid or block damage and stock up on potions. Don't feel ashamed to spam heal yourself with potions if need be.The game has had only a few problems at launch, but that already looks to be getting resolved if not already by the time of this review. I had a few crashes at launch but now didn't have any issues on extended play sessions. For anyone who has ever attempted to emulate these games in the past, I'm sure we can agree that just getting these games to run without issue is a huge feat in itself. Big props to the team that managed to make it run so smoothly!There is no online co-op, unfortunately, but Steam at least offers their Remote Play Together feature for anyone looking to couch co-op with a friend. I haven't had a friend to test this with, but I'll be sure to give an update on the sort should I ever do.If you're looking for a glimpse back into the era of gaming where companies cared more about making fun games over exploitative cash grabs, then this is a solid pick. I would say that the price tag was well worth the price, but anyone new to the Dark Alliance games can wait and see if it's something right for them be it on sale or from seeing others play it.And if you're reading this, Black Isles devs, please do consider finding a way to obtain the ability to port over Champions of Norrath! It's basically the evolution of Dark Alliance but with actual, online multiplayer! I would love to see that game come out and flourish with an active online community again^Until then, I'll happily keep playing BG:DA2 and grab some more achievements along the way.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game as a kid and had a lot of fun. It is and was fun to play with a friend for a few hours. With that being said, this game does not hold up very well in my eyes. First off, this game is not worth $30.00. At most, it is is worth about $10, which thankfully it goes on sale quite often and if you are a huge fan of the Baldur's Gate series, is probably worth playing through at least once. There are also some Easter egg characters in the game that a fan of D&D will be aware of. The reason for me not recommending this game is mostly due to the length of the game itself and the core gameplay loop becoming very stale. Combat: Combat is about 98% of the game and is fun for about the first 7-8 levels. After this, you tend to just hold the A button (or B button if using magic) until the enemy dies. You rinse and repeat for the entire game with 0 thought process involved. Very few bosses have any mechanics you need to consider and basically all of them are just target dummies. I found myself being super bored of every combat encounter and towards the end of my first playthrough and skipped the majority of the enemies to get to the boss. It felt like the game was wasting my time. To my surprise there is a decent amount of enemy variety throughout the game, but because the core gameplay loop is pretty boring, these unique creatures do not get the chance to shine very often. Every enemy feels the same with different health, armor, and damage volumes. If each unique creature behaved a little differently, I think the combat would be more enjoyable. For example, Trolls require Fire to actually kill them. This is great! Another example is the rust monsters only attacking you if you have metal equipped (seemingly only applies to the weapon of choice, but still) is another great idea for monsters. There is just not enough of those little unique features to enemies which make killing them, fun. Story:The game has a pretty cookie cutter D&D plot, which is not bad for a game this old, but it gives you the illusion of choice without any real payoff. I am unsure why they decided to give me a dialogue selector where 99% of the game gives me one choice option. It does not feel meaningful to zoom in on an NPC talking to me, only for my only option to be "Okay." At this point, why give me the option at all? It would have been wiser to have a silent protag so that you could at least self insert or perhaps have prerendered cut scenes instead of the in game dialogue options. There are also some aspects of the game which clearly are a relic of its time, for example, every "important" female NPC having massive breasts, most of them in revealing outfits. Coming from a perspective in 2023, it feels very off. If I feel like the males got the same treatment, I would be more on board with the sexualization of characters, but it is not the case. Act 2 is needlessly long and tedious. Almost nothing in act 2 is memorable and the idea of going on 4 separate fetch quests back to back to back to back without any break between them, felt really bad. I think if you ended up cutting all of act 2 and maybe giving me one fetch quest towards the end of act 1 instead, this game would improve dramatically. With that being said, It was a nice touch having your previous characters from Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance 1 be involved in the opening cut scene + later on in the game, so I give them props for that. Overall, if someone is a big fan of D&D and or Baldur's Gate series, would I recommend them this title? I really wouldn't. I would point them in the direction of Baldur's Gate 1 or 2, or even more so with the upcoming BG3 from Larian. I think it is possible to make a Hack & Slash game that is great with the setting of Baldur's Gate or D&D in general, but I think this game just isn't it.

name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden
detailed_description: Voice of Cards Trilogy + DLC set A set containing the Voice of Cards Trilogy that brings together all 3 titles from the Voice of Cards series and all the DLC items for each title. Voice of Cards Trilogy The Voice of Cards Trilogy bundles together all three titles from the series; Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars, Voice of Cards: The Forsaken Maiden and Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden. Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden ＋DLC set This product is a set containing the game: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden, as well as multiple DLC releases. About the Game Outline This is the tale of a girl who swears revenge on monsters. After losing her home, she joins hands with a mysterious boy and sets out into the unknown. But will it be the light of hope, or the darkness of despair that awaits them at journey's end..? The Voice of Cards series are RPGs, told entirely through the medium of cards. In this episode 'The Beasts of Burden', you can trap the monsters you defeat in cards and use them as skills in battle. Enjoy a truly unique gaming experience from the minds of YOKO TARO, Keiichi Okabe and Kimihiko Fujisaka. Unique Features The story in this game progresses under the guidance of a game master (the person who controls the action in a tabletop RPG). The world this story takes place in, including all the towns, dungeons and fields, is represented entirely by cards, as the player moves avatars to go on their adventure. The outcome of the battles and encounters at the many different places you visit, and even destiny itself, will sometimes be resolved with the roll of a die… You can also play a new and unique card game at the Game Parlour in town. Would you like to accompany the Game Master on a journey into the world of Voice of Cards, brought to life through beautiful art and music? *This game is not a direct sequel to Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars or Voice of Cards: The Forsaken Maiden and can be enjoyed as a standalone adventure. *You may find that the gamemaster occasionally stumbles, corrects themselves or needs to clear their throat, in order to give you the most immersive and true to life Tabletop RPG experience. *Product bundles that include this game are also available. Please take care to avoid making duplicate purchases. *Please be aware that services which require an internet connection to use may be discontinued after a time has passed from the game’s release.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy this game so far, but DO NOT buy it if you're looking for a "Card Game" or "Deck Builder" . I really think the card gimmick for this game was to save on art budget; It's a standard JRPG in gameplay and aside from all characters, monsters and items being cards, it's just menu based combat with a light "mana" system. It's like Octopath Traveller with OG FFVII's materia system of skills. Loosely. I really hope this review helps people as I would be sorely disappointed if I bought this looking for a deck builder.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden

_childDocuments_.review: I've become a huge fan of this series as a kind of under-appreciated hidden gem.First thing to say, it looks like a card game/TTRPG but could be redone as a pixel RPG with almost identical game mechanics. Think of the cards medium as more there to facilitate the style of storytelling-- this is basically Yoko Taro and Alim creating their own RPG Maker engine.If you're into the Drakenierlore iceberg kind of stuff, the series is a must play. (Spoiler from first couple hours) Not positive yet, but I'm pretty sure there are two paths that branch *very* early on. There are darker-color cards during dialogue that seem to be path-specific.The difficulty seems like its in between Isle Dragon and Forsaken Maiden, not as tough as Maiden but definitely more substantial than Isle Dragon.The card-game-in-a-game had its mechanics improved! There are better set collection effects now that can really swing a match.Not too far through yet, will update when I finish the story.Completion update: Unfortunately, I think this is my least favorite of the three so far. [story reception spoilers]  Overall I still recommend the game, but my order of preference is definitely Forsaken Maiden > Isle Dragon > Beeps of Bourbon

_childDocuments_.review: Love this version of Voice of Cards and it's an easy recommendation to those interested in this series. Each version of VoC has a gimmick that sets it apart from each other and this game has a monster catching mechanic to it. It honestly adds a fun and new layer to building a team that the other versions did not have. The narration and world building through story telling continues to prove effective and enjoyable at a casual level with characters to love and hate. My biggest gripe so far would be the RNG aspect of monster catching. This is an opinion coming from a VoC completionist: Each monster card has a rarity from 1-5 (some exceptions) and you have to encounter them in the world, kind of like pokemon. It wasn't a problem for me until I came across an NPC requesting specific rarity monsters that it's becoming a problem. Even with a cheap-to-acquire item to increase card chances, it has not been enough. an example of this, I just spent more than an hour looking to get a 2* monster card and was unable to achieve that since you need RNG on top of RNG on top of RNG (spawn the monster, spawn the 2 or 3 treasures at the end of battle, 33%-50% to pick the right chest). Now this mechanic might not bother most, but for those that intend to maximize what the game has to offer, this might be the thing that has you pulling hair. Other than that, I still love this game and all the previous VoC.

_childDocuments_.review: I hadn't heard of this series, so this was my first experience with the franchise. I finished the game (once) and walked away vaguely unsatisfied with the whole deal.For the good, the weird mashup of card battler and Dungeons and Dragons makes for some really neat aesthetics. As you explore fields and dungeons, cards are flipped over as you walk across them, square by square. The card art is fantastic, and I sort of loved the story's presentation of being told via cards through a "Dungeon Master" narrator of sorts. And the music! Fantastic stuff from the NieR team again. The whole package is sleek and shiny in appearance.........but then you hit the bad. The battles are incredibly repetitive, and those sleek, sharp-looking card art aesthetic transitions and moves suddenly make each battle take longer than they should. Your overworld random battles are also incredibly frequent, often just two or three squares away from the battle you just finished. The cards you use in battle can be "leveled up" by finding higher star rated cards from the same line or replaced with newer cards you find later, but I used basically the same loadout from beginning up until the final boss fight without issue making the whole card diversity thing meaningless. I also thought the difficulty was paced strangely as well. I mentioned frequently to the friends I was streaming the game for that I never felt challenged at all by any of the fights. I approached all of them the same way with the same moves in the same order and basically emerged victorious each time. The final boss fights though were a weird ramp up in difficulty I wasn't prepared for, but after a wipe I was able to cheese it rather easily with just swapping in a single new card. The boss fights at the end aren't particularly nuanced or engaging, just big HP sponges you need to outlast.The story also wasn't very engaging. I won't speak on the ending so as not to spoil (though I have strong feelings on that as well), but the story told throughout the rest of the game was....kind of boring. The characters also weren't all that memorable, except Tralis who I think deserves her own game and carried my entire experience.So, I guess, with music I really really really liked and story/gameplay I really really really didn't, I give it a lukewarm 3 stars out of 5 for my overall experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly speaking, It's an okay game. If you're expecting anything similar to "VoC: The Isle Dragon Roars" prepare to be disappointed. The plot was okay, the characters were cute looking but also okay, the combat has a lot of stuff added in that made it worse in my opinion.I don't regret the 13 hours I spent playing and finishing the game, but I would discourage anyone who would consider getting it.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a fan of this series and am having a blast. If you're a fan, pick it up; if you're undecided, wait till it's 20-30% off. The story in this entry is fun and charming so far. The art is stellar, as always. I wish there was more new art and monster/NPCs. The environments feel slightly better than Dragon Isle. The random encounters are far less annoying than Dragon Isle, but I'm also taking my time; I advise that you take breaks when playing any of the games. They've added passive skills from leveling up; I love it. I do wish they were a bit more impactful and plentiful. The new beasts are a fun addition, replacing old skills. Collecting and acquiring the beasts feels poor because it has a mixture of RNG that includes regular items and pointless duplicates - if the beasts are equal or lesser in value to your current ones. There are also multiples of the same beasts in the selection. There is no way to combine duplicates or level up already-owned beasts. Lower-level bests feel unimpactful because of beasts' general cost, especially abilities with dice rolls higher than 4. Items feel pointless; I haven't used many of them. It's frustrating because they are in the potential beast pools. Armor isn't interesting, mainly just stats; I wish there were more unique abilities tied to them.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden

_childDocuments_.review: Considering the horrible experience I had with the second game I am really glad to give a positive review to this one. The characters are interesting and the story of a long voyage over a desolate and (who could have guessed?) hopeless wasteland is extremely rewarding.As the second game there is no challenge at all, I've never used an item or a revive, you just steamroll over everything but at this point I consider those games a non-static VN. I don't have a problem with that, and I still hate the game parlor.This time get the platinum trophy will require insane levels of grinding. To get some specific skills you have a 1\10 and after that a 1\3 or 2\3 possibility to get the loot you need. This is completely random and can't be helped in any way. It took me two straight hours to obtain the last skill i needed. Just saying.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden

_childDocuments_.review: I only tentatively give this a recommendation. Gameplay is fine and the new monster skill mechanic works fairly well, even if the way to obtain them could have been worked out better.The story feels like a much more personal one than a grand one like in the other voice of card games and it cuts off right as the story seems to really pick up speed. It feels like the first episode of a bigger story than a complete one on it's own.The cast is varied, but due to the skill system they don't differ much mechanically. There is some, but the story doesn't really have room for any major character development.I'd put this one a little below forsaken maiden, but not by much. It misses a lot of opportunities and backloads all the story twists and explanations and the story left me feeling more like a visitor in a grander world that I wouldn't get to fully explore. Also the mythical place of legend sure is easy to get to after you party has arrived there ;PI really wish the next game (if there is one) tackles the biggest issue of these games: the status effects. There is just too many of them and they are either too crippling or too inconsequential, the same goes for the item system, vast majority of the items are useless save for very niche situations and only serve to take up your limited item slots.Hey...maybe we could even stay in this same universe and play as a group of monsters next time and add random events to dungeons other than just monster battles, getting one on the overworld was always a breath of fresh air and broke up the tedium.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden

_childDocuments_.review: I saw a comment in another review highlighting that this game isn't about building your deck, and I want to emphasize that too. The world of this game appears card-themed, giving it a unique style, but in reality, it's a jRPG with an engaging story and a fairly easy difficulty level, which I absolutely loved! Surprisingly, moving a token around to flip cards and unveil the world was incredibly captivating. The narrator's voice is soft and soothing, a real treat for the ears. This is the third game in the series, but each one stands alone with its own story, so you can start with any of them. If you enjoy one, you're likely to enjoy the others. I've completed the first two games (and the demo version, which is a prequel to the first part). Absolutely delightful! I'm thrilled that there's a third installment and I hope there will be more :)
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the previous two Voice of Cards games, but The Beast of Burden has proven to be infuriating due to its design. Initially, the changes to skills seemed exciting - blue magic in a Voice of Cards game! - but the randomness involved in acquiring skill cards is incredibly frustrating.To obtain a specific skill card, you must first encounter the right enemy, and some of these, like Dryads, are notably rare (Dryads hold the only early multi-attack skill cards available). Then, there's the hope that a chest reward spawns from these encounters, which is entirely based on chance. While there are items designed to aid this process, they are costly and only provide a 70% success rate of a chest spawning.Even when a treasure chest is awarded at the end of a battle, you're faced with choosing from three options. This means you have only a 33.3% chance of obtaining the reward you want, assuming it's even among the choices, as this is also randomized. The other rewards are typically inconsequential items, available for purchase in the item shop, rendering them pointless and they just clutter your very limited item inventory space.And if you get a duplicate card? Well, it just gets discarded and you don't actually get a reward at all!The implementation of this system is beyond frustrating. It's perplexing why the game's creators didn't opt for a capture ability similar to a Pokeball instead, rather than relying on a random treasure chest mechanism. This heavy dependence on RNG significantly diminishes the game experience. After spending three hours trying to secure Galestorm from a Dryad—encountering it in the chests about seven times—I consistently failed the one-in-three chance, regardless of which chest I chose.This direction is profoundly stupid. It's regrettable that Yako Taro has turned a series that was previously grind-free into a tiresome grindfest. I'm done with this game. I like the other aspects of it, but the rng of skills completely ruins the game.
