_childDocuments_.review: There's still a vast amount of clicking to go through the dialogue and the game over explains everything.While this game lets you equip all your party member it badly botched the skill system. After each battle there's a chance you'll get on the enemy's skills. This might sound good but the problem is you have to select from 3 chests, which can contain skills or items. If you get an item you don't get a skill. This quickly makes combat dull as you have to keep using the same skills while hoping for something better.Even when all 3 chests have a skill the problem is that if you select a skill you already have at this level or a lower level then you get nothing. Thus through bad luck it's possible to only have low level attacks because you can't randomly get something better.This badly made system also makes the merchant's quest to find certain level monsters exceptionally onerous due to the random nature of the whole system. This is why more people have completed the game than found the third level 2 monster he wants.Senators decide they want the heroine's power, so they send monsters into her underground village to kill everyone. Since they don't expect a level 2 girl to escape alone they send a level 2 emo boy with basic equipment to help her.Next these Senators decide they need a powerful monster (primal) to conquer a neighbouring village, so they send the level 5 heroine and emo boy to defeat it with basic equipment because the entire fighting force of both villages seems to be less capable that two children.These two then capture the primal, defeat the Senators, and flee; ending chapter 1. After this the plot lacks any clear direction. This type of story only works as the plot of a game, not the first arc, as everyone looks stupid for not being able to accomplish what low level characters can do.Then you help some orphans for no reason and defeat another primal at level 11. Given how easily you beat these primals at low levels they don't come across as capable monsters.Afterwards you have to climb an ice wall, and fight 2 enemies that can freeze a character while 2 party members are missing because the developers don't understand how to balance their game. Next you fight and defeat the frost primal at level 16. So all 3 primals weren't much threat to anyone and it would be idiotic if the game pretended they were powerful.On top of the icewall you find a destroyed human village and a monster village that keeps humans as pets. After beating the monsters you free the humans.In the underground area you learn that humans were attacked by abberations that randomly appear, so they sent the weakest away and transformed into monsters to become stronger than the abberations. Then the weakest of the humans somehow managed to defeat and enslave the monsters; even though the strongest of them struggled against abberations. Then Mother tells you her evil plan because the writers forgot to give the characters a motive, so you have to stop herFinally you have to fight a very drawn out battle. First it's monsters, more monsters, Mother, yet more monsters, even more monsters, the 3 primals, Mother and the 3 primals, and the population of Steel town. Then everyone just wanders off since the writers forgot to give the cast a goal they could achieve.The plot says we should feel sorry for the monsters because they used to be human who saved the world but are now being oppressed by the remaining humans, even though the humans were too weak to save the world. The problem is the gameplay shows the opposite.For the majority of human towns you visit the inhabitants are dead, dying or trying to kill themselves. Only Steel town, the circus, and the roving market have any humans who are likely to remain alive. By contrast everywhere else is filled with monsters who seem to have no interest in creating any infrastructure and even have wiped out several human towns.If anything it's the monsters who are about to wipe out the humans.

_childDocuments_.review: Unbelievably annoying. I understand what the intent was, which was to make a tabletop-like role-playing experience. This didn't do it.I hate being told what I'm thinking, especially when I'm given a choice that I make. Don't tell me that I didn't really mean it because I didn't make the choice you wanted me to. Don't give me a choice at all if it doesn't matter what I choose and you're just going to tell me what I think. That's not role-playing, that's you telling me a story about me for some reason, and it's not fun. It's annoying and patronizing.The sound design is nice and it's pretty creative. The character designs are mostly interesting, though some really don't work. Gameplay is usually fine, unless it's an encounter where you're not allowed to do anything because the GM decided to tell you, again, what you think and feel despite not doing their job very well if they have to force you to make decisions their way to make their story work.DLC is all style over substance. While the Reincarnation extras are nice, they don't really have much of an effect on the story, so you might as well not have them. The Mama token is rather nice though, since the default one is pretty unexceptional. The Reincarnation soundtrack, I will give it, does improve the experience significantly as the default soundtrack sounded a little too stock and unexceptional to me, aside from the parts where it was just not pleasing my ears to listen to.But that also touches upon the real problem with this game. It's style over substance, because Yoko Taro couldn't write his way out of a wet paper sack, and as usual he has to lean heavily on exceptional sound production and a quirky presentation to get anyone to play along. The weaknesses of the game system are unfortunately very obvious, and dictating the player's feelings so that the weak storytelling can happen is just lazy. That's not what happens in a tabletop setting. Real Game Masters learn quickly that either you think fast and adjust to your players, or you stop trying to pretend you can run a game.Nobody wants to have a story forced upon them. Especially when it's a poorly-told story as this is. It's supposed to be a game, and games are supposed to be fun. If it's not fun, it's not worth anything.If the aesthetic choices and the stripped-down production also came with dynamic adaptive storytelling, or choices that actually mattered (but they can't include even one choice that makes the slightest difference in the game), it would be a very different thing. Basically, if they bothered to put forth the slightest effort to balance out the limitations on the production that were taken on by choice of the production, it might be something special instead of just a lazy cash-in RPG done in a half-baked system.This is not an exceptionally presented game, and the card mechanic is just a motif. It's aesthetic. This isn't a card game.It also has a really detrimental effect on the game, because the maps all seem artificially congested and slow to navigate. Even with the ability to jump from one point to another, it raises the question of why you need such large, empty, homogenous areas, consisting of dozens of the exact same card copied over and over again, that take a significant amount of time just to move between. I should mention that there is an option to speed the game up, but it also comes with a disclaimer that it may actually mess up the game's ability to function.When you take away the artificial motifs and look past its attempt to define aesthetics, you have basically nothing. It is nothing but decoration for a poorly-told story that doesn't really need the player's participation. It gives the impression that the storyteller would just tell the story, no matter who if anyone was around.It's impossible to recommend this. The storyteller comes off as sadistic and manipulative, and that really doesn't work for a role-playing experience that's supposed to draw you in. It asks you to accept all these things it wants of you, including playing a character who is almost as nuanced and unique as any average anime OC on Popular Art Site of the Moment.This was probably a noble experiment, somewhere along the way, but it did not succeed at what it set out to do. This is a mediocre-at-best RPG trying to rely on a different presentation and some familiar elements, though wholly superficial, through DLC to cash in with minimum possible effort. They could have made this in RPG Maker, but it would have probably required them to put real effort into it. Once again, Square-Enix and Yoko Taro team up to create a regrettable experience that's phenomenally overpriced, overproduced, and not worth the waste of time it is to play.Play literally any of Kemco's output and you'll have a better quality and surely more interesting game, with greater longevity and more to keep you interested. Or better yet, play a Kairosoft game and drop the RPG genre until supposed icons like Square-Enix can remember how to make one that isn't crap.

_childDocuments_.review: The Beasts of Burden is the third chapter in the recently released JRPG series Voice of Cards created by Yoko Taro (, ) in which everything is represented by cards. If you haven’t played the previous ones,  and , then don’t worry ‘cause each title has a different setting and narrative, despite sharing the same structure. The game follows the story of the Guard, an unnamed girl (we can choose her name later on) living in an underground village that is suddenly threatened by monsters appearing from nowhere. After losing her family and being rescued by a stranger, the Guard leaves the underground in search of revenge, exploring a world that is new to her and in which she discovers the power of controlling monsters. As per Yoko Taro’s tradition, the plot is deeply existential as it investigates the intricate nature of humans and beasts. Storytelling is great thanks to an always present female narrator, who describes characters and events in a very immersive way. There are still few stereotypical parts that are common in most JRPGs (hero losing something, being rescued, meeting new allies and trying to reach a distant place), but the twists and quality of the dialogues are guaranteed by Taro’s unique art direction.While the world and characters are artistically represented by cards, this is not a deck and cards game. It’s a standard JRPG experience with turn-based combat, stats, skills, items and more. You move a pawn on a board that represents the world, uncovering new cards as you move and revealing towns, dungeons, characters, treasures, battles and random events. The newest addiction that probably differentiates this title from its predecessors is the possibility of collecting monsters and using them in combat. After each battle, there might be a chance to get these monsters as a reward by picking a random card. You can also purchase them at some shops, but the rarest and most powerful ones need to be found in battle or bought from a random and pretty unique merchant. During combat, you fight with your party of four members performing one action per turn, which grants you a gem. Standard moves and attacks don’t require any gem, while performing monster skills requires a cost in gems that depends on their power. Some abilities also require a dice roll to determine if the attack is successful or not and the amount of damage dealt. There are 54 collectible monsters and each one can have 5 levels of power, with some good variety that allows you to try different strategies and playstyles. For example, I gave to one character only monsters that could heal or deal status effects, making him a sort of healer/magician. Another character was equipped with only monsters who increased his standard attack damage and dealt status penalties (attack down, defense down). Trying different combinations is fun and of course you can also change your characters’ equipment (weapon, armor, accessory) that can slightly change your stats.Now the only bad thing I can say about combat is that it’s probably too easy, especially after you have leveled your characters up enough and found some pretty good level two or three monster cards that you will likely use for most of your playtime. Some real challenge wouldn’t have hurt this type of combat, and that’s why I appreciated the few boss fights, which feature stronger enemies overall and random events afflicting stats bonuses or penalties. Another thing that I recommend to change immediately is the game speed, as the standard one is way too slow, unless you feel pleasure in watching cards being slowly turned. That said, the game also features a fun mini-game that is more like a poker variant with the addition of skill effects, event cards and dices, which is accessible from the main menu but can also be played against NPCs when visiting certain towns. As a reward for winning you can get bonus items and customization options for your cards and table, which can be seen in the main menu.Voice of Cards: The Beast of the Burden probably isn’t Yoko Taro’s most memorable game (or series), but it’s an enjoyable journey for fans of his works and this third chapter brings enough variation to the table. The game aesthetic is absolutely unique and the music composed by Keiichi Okabe (who also scored  and ) is incredible as always, perfectly fitting the voice of the female narrator. For a low budget game, it has a decent length too, but no replayability outside of the cards mini-game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. I played through the first two when they came out on the Switch and finally had some time to come back and play through this one. I think these games are genius ways of making a great RPG experience that feels like you're playing with a Dungeon Master and going on an adventure. If you like classic RPGs like Final Fantasy 1-6 and you like more visual novel kinds of games then this meets that nice intersection and is a blast to play. You also don't need to play the first two games.Highlights:- You might notice that some of the art looks reused from the prior games. They pretty much are but tweaked. I don't mind this as the pieces are used to tell a story. Its not intended to provide you with 100% fresh assets each game when its doing the job. I think of these as like small fantasy novels you could get at grocery or book store. They're paperback, has some cool art on the front and then get you into the world and wrap up leaving you to want to pick up another book. The framework used for VoC is really where I think the game shines from possibility standpoint and I wish Square would continue to pump these out event if they needed to get different writers. This game SHOULD be really cost effective to make and is one of the few times I had no problem shelling out 30 bucks once every couple of months to get a new story.- The art and the music is great. I love listening to the score and it never gets old, which is good because this game requires some grinding.Mid:- The story serves its purpose but I think this one is particular has nothing amazing to write home about. I don't think there was anything bad about it nor does it need to be improved, its just what it is and its fine. Now I want another one, please and thank you.- The grind is manageable. Its very RNG dependent especially with the additions of the monsters and how you get skills from them. It was only when I was going for some very specific things, like a frosty turtle, where it was a little much. Main thing is when playing games with grind, you've got to give accessibility options to turn off animations to reduce wasted time. They give you a speed up option but its not fast enough.Low:- The parlor games can go fly a kite and burn in fires of a volcano. I normally like to 100% complete games I really enjoy but I'm not going to for this one because of a card game inside a game of cards where you can't win without growing a lucky rabbits foot out your bum. I played over 20 rounds of the last rule set to finish it up and each time I would be robbed of victor in the last rounds or shut out completely. Whats worse is it takes forever for it to get back to your turn and if you're loosing you can't quit in between your turn. The AI also will gun for you regardless if you are in first or last it doesn't matter. The Joker is a joke, it keeps stealing my best cards and but doesn't steal the best cards from opponents just whatever cards will screw me over the most and force a loss. I've gone through many different strategies on this and still not a single win. It would be fine is the parlor games were remotely fun but its uninspired and always the low points of this game. Save some dev time in the future and scrap this POS feature from the game unless you're going to make something better and worth playing with NO bs JOKER mechanic. Seriously, it almost made me want to not recommend this game. Don't waist your time on it and if you do, hopefully you're lucky and it takes you one attempt.To the Devs:Thank you for making this game and the ones before it. I've really enjoyed playing them. Hopefully, you'll be able to have more come out soon. If you do just one note... no parlor please.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly I think this might be my favorite of the 'trilogy'. More of a return of the style of the first game, but with a new added mechanic, being the monster catching for skills, to keep things fresh. (Parts of this review have been copy-pasted from my reviews for the other two games)I feel like this deserves it's own section to be talked about in the review as I would say it falls into all categories. Basically, after every battle, there's a chance where you can get treasure. Except in this game, either one or two (when there's three) or both (when there's two) will be monster cards of a monster that you fought in that battle. These monster cards entirely replace the skills from the first two games, and also have their own tiered versions, with the quality getting better whether it's through the gem cost, damage modifier, or base damage. The positives of this system is that since every character can use every monster, no character is locked to a specific archetype. You can't entirely escape the class system though as it's visible what each of them is meant to be played as through their exclusive gear and stat growth. The negatives of this is that essentially all of your non basic attacks are tied to RNG, because you not only have to get the chance for a chest to be rewarded, but you also have to pick the correct one. Overall I would say the monster catching aspect of this game doesn't exactly fit into place into a card-viewed RPG, but it certainly is built well enough to not feel awkward. - : This kind of falls into the monster-catching part, as beyond the regular RPG aspects, that's the thing that most stands out. I will say though, almost the entire later half of the game is just a stat check in every fight. - : While there's still reused designs for the general NPCs, the art on the more major characters is just incredible, leaps and bounds better than the characters from Forgotten Maiden.- : ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, the lore on this version is just great. Not only is there almost a plot twist every chapter, the pacing and progression is just perfect, and there's incredible lore bombs dropped every so often. It really gives you insight into the whole Voice of Cards world. - : Honestly, wasn't too bad. You may think it would suck because of having to get all the RNG monster drops, but a majority of them you can just straight up purchase with Gold, and another bunch you'll get from just naturally playing through. I think I only had to grind for about 4 of them. Unlike Forsaken Maiden, the post-game boss in this game was actually good. Had interesting mechanics, wasn't too bad especially considering how boosted the stats of everyone are. I personally also never found money to be an issue, and even had maxed out my wallet before heading off to the post-game boss. - : In terms of difficulty, it's essentially on par with Isle Dragon Roars, except every stat is multiplied by 2. For reference, It was lucky to have someone near 40 max HP in Isle Dragon Roars, but in this game, all 4 of my party members hovered around 70 max HP. Honestly, if you get some of the better healing skills (ex. First-Rate Healing, Vigor Spore), and a half-decent attack spell (Anything that's low cost and "Deal ATK + X"), you'll be pretty set for a while. So if you liked the difficulty in Isle Dragon Roars, you'll probably like it here, and vice versa. - : The $30 price tag is a little steep for the amount of time you get out of the game, I'd recommend either waiting for a sale or buying the Trilogy (which effectively cuts the price of each game in half), or both if you want.- : There's a side activity in every town called the Game Parlor, and beyond the first game mode (Simple), all the other ones are entirely RNG-dependent, and the NPCs don't even try to hide that they're hardcoded to target you except for if another NPC is winning by a large margin. And wouldn't you guess, there's an achievement for winning a game in each of these modes.- : There is in fact a NG+ mode unlocked when you beat the story, but there's really no reason to play it besides unlocking the exclusive NG+ ring for starting it, as besides seeing the outcomes of a few different stories, which usually have no larger impact, nothing is really changed.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: 8/10 (an ambitious attempt of a sandbox RPG with good story marred by its lackluster implementation)Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden is the third entry of the trilogy and chronologically last in the group (it goes 2-1-3). The story like its predecessors remains dark and still deserves a PG 13+ rating with the first game having the least display of horrible and hard to explain topics for children aged 6. The worst offender is part 2. This game tows the line between both with motives of suicide, genocide and ostracism, as well as brutal murders, the survival at all costs and the general human condition.Yes, even the convoluted and slow UI of the first two games still lingers in this game, even though a lot of criticisms of the former rushed game were addressed and the general engine was sped up.Story: 9/10 (Dark and grand coming of age story with little pitfalls and a bit of humanity to look into the future)This story is not an epic tale like the first game that slowly loses its glamour to the harsh truth of the world. It also is not a cruel battle against fate and a tale of sacrifice like part two. This game is a coming of age story, where a girl born underground has to leave her home after a calamity to find her place in the world, grapple with her origin and find a way to conquer the hatred her traumatic events have placed in her. Overall it is a tale of friendship and people pulling you back from the bring and you pulling them back. As you venture forth all of you will grow together and face a harsh and radicalized world that seems unforgiving to either side. Faced with religious motifs, specism and pure exploitation and war, you will find your place in the world and live for the little things. Join "the guard", the young boy, the scholar and the interspecies circus girl on a grand journey.The entire narrative has a goal, few things feel setup and you are not the savior of every place you visit. You are just one group of people in a post-apocalyptic world that survive by relying on each other. Enjoy the ride, it may be dark, but it holds true to humanity and while not the most fantastic of the three stories it is one of the most relateable.Gameplay: 6/10 (A great RPG attempt marred by bad balance, execution and easy fights!)Supporting this further grim dark entry into the parrallel world in the Drakengard multiverse is a new system of capturing monsters to gain new abilities, which can be equipped to any character and thus for the first time allows a true fully adjustable RPG party. Unlike part 2 which had next to no r in its RPG, this game writes RPG with a bold R. This sandbox, however, has several weakpoints. Cards and effects can be upgraded and are mostly only useful when of a high rank. This can not be achieved until 85% of the game is done. Before that nearly all cards are locked to rank 3. This means most skills are worthless and a few skills will dominate the game, like the Dryads Galestorm AoE.Further cards can only be obtained from the normal 3 chest drops or rare new 2 chest drops (with a guaranteed monster card, but only about 10 per playthrough), These cards can not be combined and duplicates below your star level vanish with no treasure or money to replace them. The extra items added to guarantee a chest drop at 70% and later 100% thus feel worthless, when most of these drops end with nothing to show for it as double monster card ruin the loot drop. The poor balance of the sandbox RPG card system and the waste of the player's effort and time is thus also the main reason for its gameplay to face punishment. Aside of that many bosses are uninspired in their mechanic and the final special boss is a pure all resist, potential bad RNG 80 AoE dmg spam fest, that only asks how much items the player can chuck and how much DPS they have to rush it down. Meanwhile the bosses prior to this secret boss are all easy and no challenge.This game thus ranks in difficulty below the first game and far below the second game short of the hidden boss. Which combined with its bad skill balance is likely a consequence of said overpriced and bad skill system. Healing skills are nearly always worthless, as items do the same and still generate gems instead of consuming them. Overall the battle system is one of the least entertaining. Most battles become Gaelstorm AoE spam with the fastest high ATK character.The sandbox true RPG aspect gives the game a bit of new life, but its horrid implementation through the ancient loot system is lazy at best and punishing the player at worst. Combined with some ultra rare skills of monsters only in ONE area (Yeti in Subterran Ruins B2) makes this quite insulting at times.Unlike game 2 where money was hard to come by and grinding was often needed, having over 80k extra at the end of the game is normal. A bit of exp grinding may be needed, but the skill grind for completionist will take longer than the exp regardless. Unless someone is very lucky. The game is not hard to complete, but not really worth it either.For fans of the mini-game in the game parlor, the AI finally plays it fast and loose, allowing for games to only take minutes and not half an hour. Thus people can finally enjoy "grinding" the achievements. Although the game is still as easy as always and offers little incentive to play it after all is won.Art & Sound: 9/10 (New music and strategic application of it combined with new and interesting card designs and art)Unlike part 2 which didn't stop to consider if the "Costa del Sol" type chill music was appropiate at every point in the game, part 3 decided to add several new soundtracks like game 1 and delivers them in good moments. Overall the audio design supports the narrative whenever possible, even if it is a bit too melodramatic in some instances. With limited reuse of old assets, this is one of the game's strong points.Most fitting, the new female main character comes with a female narrator. Both of which do an adequate job, but the Japense one excels again. This extra element is appreciated, even though I missed the friendly Japanese narrator from the first two games.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the Voice of Cards trilogy but take in mind that those games are EXTREMELY  niche. Expecially this one seemed like a bunch of random ideas from Yoko Taro's head put into a game.All the games are standalone, but if i have to sort them for the story TBoB > TIDR > TFM. But for the gameplay TIDR > TFM > TBoB.I really didn't liked the monster catching system, I don't despise some RNG but this is too much. But the story made up for me.But if you have to choose a chapter I would suggest the first one more.

_childDocuments_.review: Prefacing with the fact that this is a wonderful experience. It is refreshingly whimsical, with a smear of darkness and really intense emotional moments. This game is a great reminder that role-playing is all about the story, the world-building, character synergy and interesting mechanics; some of my best role-playing experiences have been text based or old pixel games (aka. low graphics quality or minimal graphical representation at all.) This is a reminder that those core creative aspects are what really drive a good RPG, not graphics, not budget, etc. Also, since it's the Nier: Automata team, it also has a very beautiful, heavy and emotional soundtrack that lends so much more to imagining an environment otherwise just shown with description and pictures on cards. There IS a lot to really love about this game, BUT........ As a long-time JRPG veteran, I have to say (and I wish there was a sideways like yellow thumb for good, but one part is just so absolutely bad, I wouldn't recommend:) The bad, that has almost made me not recommend this game: Got to the last boss. It's 6 phases, no saves. Took over an hour twice to eventually die to ramping fatigue and difficulty. Don't even care. Uninstalled and threw my hands up in the air. Whatever. Worst boss fight ever. I usually don't give up; maybe I'll try again down the line some time, but good lord, it's not a fun thing to try over and over again. It's exhausting, frustrating and tedious (though I must say the presence and artistic quality of the phases themselves are pretty epic and engrossing.) Whoever came up with the final boss should be brought up on criminal charges. I might just watch the end somewhere. C'est la vie.EDIT: Went back with beer and beat the last boss. It was terrible and long, but I did it. Sweet, simple and open ending. A great experience, nonetheless, and I'd still recommend the game. Just stock up on lots of healing and ailment healing items and grind levels a bit and make sure you have the best gear possible. That's pretty JRPG 101 going into a final boss, but ahh. Still an immersive experience that felt like a sweet and terrifying dream. Sorry for being mean, Yoko Taro.

_childDocuments_.review: I LOVE this game. The story is amazing and has your heart hurting so good in the opening minutes. Each of the characters are endearing. The game is very similar to the other voice of cards games, but the combat is improved on by having each of the characters be a bit more customizable with their skills this time around. Here's to hoping we can get more installments for this fantastic series!Also has the best narrator yet!
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden

_childDocuments_.review: The Beasts of Burden is easily the best of the 3 Voice of Cards games we've gotten so far. All of them are nice simplistic JRPGS, but Beasts of Burden's mechanical adjustments and better difficulty curve make it stand out from the bunch. The monster capturing mechanic adds a lot of attack variety and gives you the ability to really customize what roles your party members take. The main drawbacks are the same as the other Voice of Cards games, the "pick which item you get after battle but you can't actually see what any of your options are" mechanic feels bad, if I can't see what I'm getting anyway just don't give me the option. The randomness of the drops can be a huge pain when trying to get better versions of monsters.The last boss kind of sucked because there are 6 fights you need to do in order to get to it which weren't hard, but they made doing a retry a slog and having lost with the boss down to 25 HP just left me a bit sour on it.  I see there is some post-game content, and the rest of the game has been solid enough that I'll look into it.It doesn't really fit anywhere in the main review, but it does irk me a bit that none of the customization items work between games, especially the DLC items. It's the same engine and system, it would be nice if there was a way to use the other tables and dice sets across the games.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden

_childDocuments_.review: The final boss is unbeatable once he goes into rage mode and hits for 50 base DMG. Monster Catching is reliant on RNG which caused my party to not even have the mushroom that heals your whole party by the end of the game, buying a level 1 shroom at the final shop isn't good enough to withstand the damage the boss does when he boosts himself. The entire final battle has 6 phases and is a giant stat-check which is a bummer...or maybe I just suck. Either way I enjoyed the game until the ending.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: New interesting way of acquiring skills for your characters and customizing them.Story isn't half bad, though the game itself is not very long.Cons: Skill acquisition is heavily RNG dependent, which can make the game drag out for longer than it needs to be.If you were expecting something different, this game is more of the same of the previous 2 installments. Not necessarily a bad thing, but be aware if you wanted something new.Overall, I rate it a 7/10. A nice and relaxing game that you should probably wait to go on sale before purchasing.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely great game. A lot of connections to the hole Nier and Dragongard Loar. It is really creative and a must play in my opinion. The polish of the English voice over is very good, but not as polished as it should be (microphone or settings seem to change every few minutes of audio dialog). I still like the English voice-over from the first game more, but great work regardless. The JP voice overs is as before absolutely great.  It's the 3rd game in the series and a great continuation. But this should be the final one because this kind of game can only do so much before all the games in the series become samey. I am thrilled to see what the team behind the Dragongard, Nier and Voice of Card  games do next!

_childDocuments_.review:
This is the tale of a girl who swears revenge on monsters.
After losing her home, she joins hands with a mysterious boy and sets out into the unknown. But will it be the light of hope, or the darkness of despair that awaits them at journey's end...? The Voice of Cards series are RPGs, told entirely through the medium of cards.
In "The Beasts of Burden", you can trap the monsters you defeat in cards and use them as skills in battle.

Enjoy a truly unique gaming experience from the minds of YOKO TARO, Keiichi Okabe and Kimihiko Fujisaka.

*This game is not a direct sequel to Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars or Voice of Cards: The Forsaken Maiden and can be enjoyed as a standalone adventure.
*Product bundles that include this game are also available. Please take care to avoid making duplicate purchases.
*Please be aware that services which require an internet connection to use may be discontinued after a time has passed from the game’s release.

name: Solium Infernum
detailed_description: Prepare yourself for Solium Infernum, the grand strategy game of politics, intrigue and betrayal, set in the ultimate arena of Hell. Satan's mysteriously vanished and Hell is in an uproar. Play as one of eight all-powerful and menacing Archfiends and indulge your Machiavellian dark side. Command legions, enlist champions, cast sinister rituals, and trick, rob, and insult your rivals to be crowned Hell’s new Dark Majesty. Experience Solium Infernum's legendary devilish political machinations. Requiring nerves of steel and a true heart of darkness, every order you give will have lasting consequences. Get into the minds of your rivals, second-guessing their every move both on the map and on the floor of Hell’s parliament as you sling insults and demands in the only truly political strategy game. Eight playable Archfiends Eight single-player Chronicles Single-player Skirmish mode Revelations Tutorial Scenario Sessional and Asynchronous 2-6 player Multiplayer Dozens of Infernal Legions, including unique enormous Titans. Champion Praetors and dark Artifacts fit for any Archfiend! Play 2-6 player multiplayer games with your soon-to-be ex-friends in a single session of deceit and politics, or put your friendships to the test in quick daily bursts with Solium Infernum’s infamous asynchronous multiplayer for a truly harrowing scheme-in-your-sleep experience. If you love dark art, you’re in the right place. Brimming with striking visions of Hell unlike anything you’ve seen before, Solium Infernum is an infernal feast for the eyes with multitudes of individual dark paintings to enjoy. Every item of the game is accompanied by mind-blasting artwork, a feat declaring Solium Infernum a winner of the 2022 Game Makers Sketchbook. Originally inspired by Milton’s epic poem, Paradise Lost, League of Geeks’ (known for seminal digital board game Armello) sophomore title is a re-imagining and modernisation of Vic Davis’ critically acclaimed cult-classic of the same name, hailed as a masterpiece of strategy game design. Once again, prepare to lose yourself within ‘the cold glory of a difficult decision’ as we resurrect Solium Infernum from the depths of Hell. Note: The following quotes refer to the original Solium Infernum (2009) by Vic Davis. “Solium Infernum is a political wargame set in hell… The game is now finished, and none of the friends survived. By which I mean, we all hate each other now.” - Rock Paper Shotgun “It’s a game about playing other people, in both senses of the word…. This is game design based on psychology as much as rules.” - Quarter to Three “More than any game I've played in years, Solium Infernum nails the sensation of staring at a screen and losing yourself in the cold glory of a difficult decision.” - Game Developer (formerly Gamasutra) “Solium Infernum kicked my knees out from under me ... this game took my past experience with strategy games and threw it, like a pro basketball player, into a bin eighty feet away.” - Eurogamer “One of the best games of the year.” — Three Moves Ahead

short_description: Take the Infernal Throne in this hellish turn-based grand strategy game. The Prince of Darkness has vanished, leaving Archfiends to conspire: muster your legions while intoning dark sorceries, devilish schemes, and machiavellian plots. Who will be the new ruler of Hell and ascend the Throne?

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the most interesting strategy game I've ever played. You aren't competing for land, as such. You're competing for Prestige: Fame, respect, fear. It's one of those rare games that's ACTUALLY able to provide the player with a dozen ways to scheme and win. Treachery isn't just: "ha ha, i invade you now while you are weak." No, treachery in Solium Infernum looks more like: I'm going to demand tribute from you because I know you desperately need those resources. I know you'll refuse my demand, because you have to. This will give me justification to challenge you to a duel, which you MUST accept or suffer a severe loss of prestige. Your champion is stronger than mine, but that doesn't matter, because I've bribed the Arbiter. I win the duel automatically, and rob you of a mighty champion. I will then use my next turn to harass all of your neighbors, and frame YOU for it. They despise you now, and bully you relentlessly for the foreseeable future. With just those three actions, I've set you back immensely. There's only one way for you to win now: You'll have to become my vassal, and one day betray me. It's a huge risk, I'll gain all of your current prestige and be that much closer to winning. But it also puts you in striking distance of every critical location in my realm. The risk is worth it. I take the deal. But you never betray me. The opportunity never shows up, because I never let you get that opportunity. The game ends, and I win. But I DON'T win. YOU win. I watch in horror as the scoreboard shows very clearly that I came in 2nd place, and that you came in 1st. How? Why? It was because, at the start of the game, you chose the crown of the 'Power Behind The Throne' as your Archfiend bonus, and quite literally stolen my victory from under me by swearing to be my vassal.You were never crippled. You were never in danger of losing. It was all an act, a ruse to get me to lower my guard and get cocky. I played the game, but you were playing me.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wanted to know what it's like to be a Baron of Hell vying for supremacy in the infernal pits of damnation? How about being a general manager at a retail store? What does the latter have to do with the former? Why, they're practically identical.It's 5:45 in the morning. Your shift begins in fifteen minutes. Getting there on time will require you to take a wet-wipe bath, down half a bottle of Niacin, slam a Monster Ultra and speed the entire way to work in your 2005 Ford Fusion while blasting Papa Roach's seminal hit from 2000, "Last Resort". That ♥♥♥♥♥ Carla has been stirring up drama and went over your head to complain to the regional without observing the chain of command — looks like someone just acquired open availability on their weekends. There's a promotion available in the Twin Cities that you really want, but you're pretty sure that the brown-noser who hand-makes posters for store fundraisers is going to get it. Thankfully, you've got the ace-in-the-hole in knowing that she's been sleeping with her subordinates — and more importantly — the texts to back it up. Promotion secured. The day will run smoothly as long as the homeless people don't ♥♥♥♥ in the public bathroom's sink again. You don't get paid enough for this. You still have to find a babysitter for Friday so you can go to court and press charges against the crack head that was trying to steal condoms at 2:42 in the morning and assaulted you at the register. Thank God for CCTV. One day it will all be worth it. All the blood, sweat and late nights binge drinking alone in your car while doom scrolling Tiktok and daring to dream of a better life beyond the 9-to-5. One day you'll break the cycle and avail yourself of the chains of post-industrial indentured servitude. You can dream beyond the borders of your squalid Dollar Tree for the pristine, Swedish, Elysium fields of an IKEA. My brother in Christ; you know whether you're going to buy this game or not. You see the hexagons. You see a polished UI. You see animated, lovingly crafted avatars for the principle personalities of Hell. You've been promised subterfuge, politicking and conquest. You already know. If you need the last little push, then fine; here it is:Buy the game.It's good.Your objective is simple: entertain the bag-of-cats known as the Conclave of Hell enough to win their support to become the new Dark Lord. The Conclave is responsible for the myriad of byzantine rules, regulations and forms that make up the bureaucratic viscera of Hell. Getting anything done is similar to trying to get Comcast to give you an extension on your bill only with slightly less threats to your family. Wars are short affairs known as Vendetttas with clear objectives - kill that army, seize that place of power. It's essentially the same as having a brother or sister. It's your turn to play Playstation but your weasel sibling woke up earlier than you believing that, that entitles them to the game. Show them how incorrect they are by faking a medical emergency and making it look like they intentionally poisoned you. You now not only get a controller, but a couple days off from school while your beloved kinfolk face criminal charges until the cops untangle your web of lies. Hug it out a couple days later because ultimately you share the same house until you're legally responsible for yourself and let's be honest; in this economy, the likelihood of sharing the house after your parents are dead isn't 0%. Build an army and conquer the ash-blasted vistas of Perdition. Or use that army in Theodore Roosevelts wet-dream of gunboat diplomacy by constantly demanding things from your adversaries fully-well knowing that they're going to cave or face the wrath of your legions. Erode the foundations of your opponents economy with rituals and intrigues. Constantly make fun of Beelzebub's stupid hat and force his hand into declaring a Vendetta against you so you can humiliate him further on the fields of battle. Go full war criminal and do something so heinous that even the politicians in Hell find you repulsive enough to kick you out of the Cool Kids Club, stripping you of your protections and more importantly, your need for their superfluous rules and regulations. With the same determination and knowledge of impending self-destruction as a man planting lawn ornaments onto his yard in front of the HOA President, you sally forth into a new world and shape it in your image - no Gods, no masters. Become the Morningstar. The game is deceptively simple, but without sacrificing depth or choice. The order economy makes each decision feel meaningful and keeps you wondering whether you made the best use of your actions. I hired a deadly Praetorian and constantly challenged my rivals to duels, with nearly all of them declining to participate for fear of losing their precious Praetorians to the killing machine I selected as my champion. Sure, it could use a little work. Some additions to the Encyclipaedia Infernum to clear up some of the finer mechanics like dueling. Some people don't like the models for the Archfiends - I'm fine with them. Sure, if they had gone with a less stylized and more realistic approach it would have better fit the gorgeous artwork - but it's completely serviceable. The AI doesn't appear to be able to play the game very well at this point in time. Having to combine currency is a small bit of tedium that they added to basically make unlocking certain things take two turns and is easily the most mystifying part of the gameplay. But there's a lot of charm, heart and love here - as you often find nestled within the most forgotten of places. I am sure with time, further development and content it will iron out some of these wrinkles and go from a 'good' game to a 'great' game. Oh, hey - and the game actually works the day it came out. Isn't that something?You really only have to ask yourself the following: Wouldst thou like the taste of butter? A pretty dress? Wouldst thou like to live deliciously?I guess it doesn't really matter if you buy the game or not. Given the trajectory of world events we'll be able to play this in real life in a couple months as we're all sloughed off the edge of oblivion and into a lake of fire of our own making while the monoliths of our shattered world topple and crumble to dust, heralding the arrival of The Great Dragon in the twilight of our species. Have fun!EDIT: Regrettably, the studio didn't recoup their finances and have basically gone into "contract for work" mode. I have never personally see a studio recover from this moment, having seen at least four do this and never pull back out. RIP. It was a good game and a fine studio.

_childDocuments_.review: There's just no other game like itFirst a bit of history - forgive me if I do not get all the details right.Back in the good 'ole days, a talented chap by the name of Vic Davies worked as the one-man shop Cryptic Comet Games.By his lonesome, he devised some of the best strategy games on the PC I have ever played: Armageddon Empire (which you can still find on Steam), Occult Chronicles, Six Gun Saga and, his magnum opus, Solium Infernum.As a one man band, he built his games with Adobe Director (no longer exists, I believe?) and yes they did not look super sexy but they played just fine. Most important, they were all pretty unique and very engrossing.Sadly, Vic retired from making games, and I can tell you that we lost one of the greatest game design talent that day.Fast forward to today: we are incredibly lucky that LoG picked up the game and gave it an unbelievably attractive face lift for a modern audience.The core experience is still there, with QoL improvements and a stunning UI and art style.Asynchronous multiplayer is where the game truly shines. You have plenty of time to carefully weigh your two actions per turn, and believe me every action matters. The game encourages diplomacy, and not just in a mechanical way: playing with friends, you WILL want to send each other (via in  game messaging!) little notes to look for alliances, play the mind game, or just add some colourful narration to what is going on in hell.There truly is no game like SI... anywhere. There are many games that mimic one aspect or another, sure, but no other game has that full package combined into one fiendishly engrossing experience.Do yourself a favour: get your friends together, and play. You will have stories to tell. If you want a taste of what kind of stories are created, I highly recommend looking up an old game diary on the game review website Rock Paper Shotgun. Gold.Thanks LoG for giving the game justice... now please reboot other Vic Davies games? ^^

_childDocuments_.review: I played my first game as Mammon with three friends & two AI. I was dead last for half the game, bumbling around unsure of how to maneuver the disparate parts into a longer strategy until I finally got a prestige engine churning with max rank Charisma and rank 4 Prophecy. Methodically, I maneuvered the Gilded of Mammon to bully Beelzebub and earn small prestige victories, as I continuously levied demands against the stupid AI -- as we all did -- and I prepared my ritual table.Belial and Andromalius were making political maneuvers all game; so I popped a midgame Elocution earning me 6-30 prestige a round as my rival archfiends desperately tried to crush each other, then I popped Burnt Offerings, the max level Charisma ritual, to milk my subjects for 9-11 prestige every turn. Over the following half of the game I swung from last place with an overwhelming prestige in the 300s as Mammon's economy engine finally earned me massive notoriety in hell.The Archangel himself then descended from heaven up high and systemically erased all of my legions, including my Gilded of Mammon, who had made themselves tremendously powerful over a long series of small victories. Any attempts of war neutered, I sat on my economy and farmed prestige.Belial, previously vying as the conclave favorite, realized favor was slipping from him and plotted against the crown. He summoned massive super legions and swarmed Pandemonium, Hell's capitol, eliminating all prestige victories and excommunication himself, but if he retained control of Pandemonium for 5 turns, he'd win the game.At the same time, in a bizarre stroke of fate, the stupid AIs triggered events sealing the gates of hell and preventing us from collecting tribute, stifling our economy, and soon followed by another event which closed our ritual tables; Belial weaponized this with his max rank deceit to loot our stores while tribute was shut down, stifling his opponents' economies even further to maintain the upkeep on his massive infernal hordes, and took advantage of the disabled rituals to make himself virtually untouchable.I anchored down and maxed out my Prophecy so I could wait for the moment to unseat Belial the Usurper and waited for my quaking opponents to band together and slay him. Andromolius recruited a moving Fortress and forged a dimensional cube to warp the Fortress right next door to Belial's stronghold one turn before his Usurper victory, and, in the penultimate turn, I used Demonic Interference -- the max rank prophecy ritual -- to exile his artifacts, terminate his rituals, and destroy his ritual table. With his ritual table destroyed, he had no means to protect himself from Astaroth, who levied powerful Destruction rituals at Belial's stronghold, nor Andromolius, who had a fortress ready to blow him into oblivion.In his final breath, Belial teleported his massive hellish beasts across hell, destroying Andromalius' and Astaroth's strongholds in the very same turn his stronghold was conquered; all three of them were crushed in one pivotal turn, leaving me the only surviving Archfiend -- excluding the idiot AIs.Belial weighed destroying me by conquering my stronghold the turn after usurping Pandemonium, but instead decided to warp his legions to protect his bases, leaving him too far away to get to me in that one turn my other rivals were systemically murdered. Three turns before his impending victory, I activated an event restricting all legion movements to 1 canton per turn, creating the conditions where Belial now felt unstoppable and teleported his beasts within striking distance of Andromalius and Astaroth, then yet unaware Andromalius had that dimensional cube.With Belial, Andromalius, and Astaroth all ended in one fell swoop, my Gilded of Mammon returned reborn. I, the infernal Mammom, swat aside the meaningless Murmur and Beelzebub -- the idiots -- and was legally elected by the Conclave the rightful ruler of hell, standing atop the corpses of my opponents and a veritable horde of wealth.With countless moving parts and a few strokes of luck wherein if one thing had happened a turn sooner or later it might have been a dramatically different conclusion, it was maybe the most satisfied I ever felt winning a multiplayer game.all 3 of my opponents eliminating themselves in one turn was godly. 10/10 experience

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to say this isn't a recommendation, but the AI is really so poor in this game that if you have any interest in playing singleplayer you should reconsider.Individually, I've seen the AI grasp the correct thing to do in some battle situations, but other than that, it fails at the core idea of the game: Gathering prestige, or at least gathering forces and attacking Pandaemonium. The AI physically seems incapable of either of these actions, even when they absolutely have the strength in legions to try. They will waste most of their turns floundering around insulting each other for no real gain, expending prestige to rank up a system that only improves your economy on the last few turns of the game when they should be hoarding prestige.I've played and completed two games, having never touched the original before, and even without understanding what I was even doing very well on the first run I was several hundred prestige points ahead of the AI at the end, and at max rank. In the second game, I was enormously ahead. At the end of the game I was casually slapping the AI about for fun and had about 600 prestige when the the next runner up had just over 100.It's so bad, that I have to say it's not fit for function the way it is. They are a complete joke. This game is fine if you're only going to be playing it multiplayer, but the AI needs a serious and complete overhaul if you want to play the game in any other way than that.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool/unique strategy game, based on a cult favorite 2009 game of the same name. Mostly-faithful recreation; differences are mostly favorable. Success is measured by how unapologetically ruthless and aggressive one can be every single turn. Ruins relationships better than Monopoly.Unfortunately the game (in fairness, like most games anymore) was released in an advanced-beta state. It rec'd one PI of hypercare with the playerbase as the QA team, and is now +/- abandonware as the developer LoG has gone into "hibernation".While most code bugs have been squashed at this point, the game is still very unbalanced in a number of ways that make it easy for experienced players to abuse. Worth noting perhaps that LoG has said that they "never intended to create a balanced game", and the mentioned opportunities for abuse do fit the thematic overtone of the game, however the overall nuance and depth superficially offered by the sheer number of mechanics and possible interactions becomes in reality quite limited as there are only a small number of viable strategic options and counter-options available in the meta when experienced players face off. LoG has stated that they have enough funding to keep the multiplayer servers operational "for the foreseeable future" - which, critically, is decidedly vague while still being clearly far short of a commitment to permanence.One-player mode, in my opinion, doesn't offer much of an entertainment experience. It is essentially a training ground, providing a vehicle for exploration/education of the various archfiends and artifacts.$40 is steep for what you are getting, and a lot of my willingness to pay that price was based on the promise of game balancing and a stable of additional archfiend DLCs. The developer went down due to poor sales on the game, and while I'm not sad I own it I do understand why.This could have ended up capital-A Amazing, but with the "finished product" label on it and the uncertain state of multiplayer availability, it can't be recommended. A shame.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic re-implementation of a turn based strategy game created by indie designer Vic Davis, who has given his blessing for this remake. I have a lot of hours in the original, so I am a bit biased, but for someone who is curious, here is a brief summary of things about the game:1. This is a very slow paced game, takes many turns of development and movement to get anything done. Takes quite a bit of planning and scheming to dominate the board.2. Graphics on the game are most excellent and are a huge improvement from the original. The UI has seen much needed changes as well, everything is easy to find and use.3. There is an Encyclopedia filled with useful information if you are hazy about something in the game.4. AI appears to be competent so far, however I have only played a bit of the new one so far. If you are interested in the theme and enjoy involved thematic turn-based games you will enjoy this game. I give the game 10/10 stars as I have been waiting forever for this new version and plan on playing a lot of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Solium Infernum is a game that lets you unleash your inner devil and compete with other archfiends for the throne of hell. It's a turn-based strategy game with a lot of depth, complexity, and replayability. If you like games like Civilization or Crusader Kings, but wish they had more fire, brimstone, and backstabbing, then you'll love Solium Infernum.The game is set in a Milton-inspired version of hell, where Satan has mysteriously disappeared and left a power vacuum. You play as one of eight archfiends, each with their own unique abilities, attributes, and personalities. You can customize your archfiend to suit your playstyle, whether you prefer diplomacy, warfare, sorcery, or treachery. You can also recruit legions of infernal creatures, champions, and artifacts to aid you in your quest for domination.The game is not easy, though. You'll have to contend with the harsh terrain of hell, the whims of the infernal conclave, and the schemes of your rivals. You'll have to balance your resources, your prestige, your demands, and your vendettas. You'll have to make alliances, break alliances, and betray alliances. You'll have to be cunning, ruthless, and adaptable. You'll have to be the best devil you can be.Solium Infernum is a game that rewards careful planning, strategic thinking, and creative problem-solving. It's also a game that rewards being a jerk. You can insult your enemies, steal their stuff, curse them, frame them, and even challenge them to a duel. You can also play dirty tricks on them, like sending them a gift of a cursed artifact, or sabotaging their rituals. You can even try to corrupt their champions and turn them against them. The game is full of devilish humor and dark comedy, and you'll find yourself laughing at the misfortunes of your foes and the absurdity of the situations you'll encounter.The game is best played with friends, though. Solium Infernum supports both synchronous and asynchronous multiplayer modes, where you can play with up to six players in a single session. Playing with friends adds a whole new layer of fun and challenge to the game, as you can communicate, negotiate, bluff, and deceive each other. You can also form pacts, trade favors, and share secrets. You can also stab each other in the back, of course. The game is a great way to test your friendships and see who among you is the most diabolical.Solium Infernum is a game that deserves more attention and praise. It's a game that offers a unique and immersive experience of ruling hell. It's a game that combines strategy, politics, and betrayal in a compelling and satisfying way. It's a game that will make you feel like a true archfiend. It's a game that will make you say, "Hell yeah!"
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool concept, so much love went into this(!!), and so much respect for the core design. I love what is going on here across the board. Art, gameplay, theming, are all hitting the mark. The card arts are freaking awesome! Even the UI art is beautiful.As someone who grew up with Master of Magic (choosing starting perks and specializing in schools of magic, etc) this is exactly my type of game.That being said, some major issues make this difficult to recommend. I truly hope to flip my score here but we might be several months away from that, due to the first point below:- The AI is severely lacking. Ended the game with 1/10th my score. This AI has truly no idea wtf is going on and cannot figure out how to perform the basic function of scoring victory points. It seems to understand the concepts of moving its troops and completing goals, but severely lacks sufficient aggression, capacity to set up enough scoring windows for itself, or even ability to understand whether it can afford to maintain troop upkeep costs. We are talking tutorial level difficulty. So be aware that you'll have fun once and then the game is trivialized. So I would say to think of this as a multiplayer game with an AI warm-up mode on the side. I expect a decent competition when spending $30+ dollars on a strategy game. Suffice to say a lot more work should be done here.- Some elements appear on the surface imbalanced to me. One starting relic lets you steal victory from the highest scorer at the end (they have to choose who in the first 10 turns but still, a goldfish could get lucky on this and end up stealing your win). Finding out that your opponent has this item and has used it on you to steal your victory seems incredibly difficult. You need a maximum ability score in the Prophecy school and then to scry ALL your opponents to ensure they haven't done this to you, and THEN win three vendettas against them and THEN initiate a blood feud and wipe out their capital. I love the IDEA -- but this is DEEPLY UNFAIR for the targeted player. Simple solution: The two players share the victory.- Personally I found the tribute combining mechanic irritating. It is a clever idea but unfortunately was not fun (IMO). I'm trying to buy troops and am stuck spending my time merging coins together. In the late game i was forced to do this constantly and I rolled my eyes every time I was stuck wasting my time choosing which coins to merge together for next turn. Suggestion: An "auto-combine" button so I can skip manual selection.- My little demon avatar says the same ONE voice like 500+ times while taking my turn. Order units? OFZARAYA. Click for Tribute? OFZARAYA. Over and over, for hundreds and hundreds of actions. Seriously annoying. Needs to be removed or have significantly more variety to not feel grating.- The game clearly states the conclave will meet decide the winner on turn X (default turn 50). When you reach turn X the winner is NOT decided for MANY more turns (+12). That's about 25% of the entire game length happening after it was implied it would end. The conclave simply "begins to decide" on turn 50, which means absolutely nothing regarding gameplay as far as I can tell? This is entirely misleading. It should be made 100% transparent to new players when the game will actually end, it should not be something they need to google for the "true answer" because the tooltips are obfuscating it to add a sense of one-time mystery.- The in-game UX design needs a bit of work - specifically, the placement of back buttons is a bit all over the place and can even be difficult to find, so I ended up using ESC frequently to back out of menus. This should be given a second pass for better consistency. Moving the X button to the same corner of every menu etc.If you plan to play against friends or just want a good one or two sessions, then I can recommend this. If you are expecting a long-term solo experience to sink your teeth into (a la civ, humankind, etc) which I imagine MOST strategy gamers do, then I suggest you let this game bake in the oven a bit longer. Good AI in a strategy game is my expectation in 2024.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for this ever since I read Rock Paper Shotgun's excellent game diary series over 10 years ago. It was always too difficult to convince my friends to play such a strange outdated looking game. Now that LOG has given Vic Davis' original design a new coat of paint it really is spectacular. I will say despite appearances this game has very little similarity beyond surface level to 4X games like civilization or age of wonders. Solium Infernum rather takes on the pace of a boardgame; it's not difficult to imagine deliberating over this for hours on a kitchen table. If you've ever enjoyed the Game of Thrones Boardgame, Diplomacy, or Dune (the 1979 game recently re-issued by Gale Force Nine) this should be right up your alley.I would not buy this game if you are only interested in single player. The AI is frankly barely serviceable at best. Singleplayer mode is there for you to learn the UI and mechanics and push you into multiplayer. You will want a dedicated group of at least 4 players, if you do not have interested friends I would find a game on the Discord. The multiplayer absolutely sings however. This is a game that plays out as much in Discord DMs as in the game client. Turns are carefully constructed and your plans hinge on the slightest ordering of actions or a single hex. I have played largely live games thus far but am quite excited to get some long running asynchronous games going.The variety of powers you are presented with to invest in and use is endlessly entertaining. As one example the Deceit tree allows you to forge orders to move someone else's army. Yes, you can use this in your wars to force weaker enemies into your powerful legions or hold powerful enemy units at bay. But what if you step them into a pool of lava? What if you offer your manipulative services to someone else? What if you casually order an otherwise neutral legion to suicidally charge a fortress?  The theme is also phenomenal. The flavor text has just the correct amount of flair without bogging you down in tedious "lore". It's a game about being a backstabbing power hungry bastard and as such it is only proper that you should be able to play as the Prince of Lies. The art is in my opinion phenomenal, but the screen shots are just above.For all this effusive praise I will point out two large (but not game breaking) issues that stand out to me:1. The UI, while aesthetically immaculate, can be occasionally obtuse and buggy. Most visual bugs I have encountered have been sorted out by exiting to the main menu and rejoining the game. Some interactions are slightly bewildering until you figure it out (attempting to teach a move to a Praetor without a matching move appears to freak out the UI currently). The "mask ritual" option is a button that triggers an animation you have to watch every turn as far as I can tell, despite masking an action being the obvious default choice once you have the ability to do so.2. At some point you will want to dig into the in game encyclopedia and get into the nitty gritty of mechanics and there are a few things it just... doesn't explain. The resolution of rituals in particular is hand waved in a way that is frustrating for a crucial part of gameplay. The encyclopedia in general reads as a great primer to the topics of the game but is sorely lacking an in depth explanation of mechanics. This is a game that asks you to carefully consider your turn for a day at a time, please give me the exact information I need to do so.This are slight flies in an otherwise luxurious ointment that I can't wait to rub all over my body for a long time to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: If you like turn-based strategy, Solium Infernum is a must buy even if you didn't like/never heard of the original version. Shines in asynch multiplayer, but treat single player matches as (excellent) expanded tutorials until the bot AI is fixed.I own every Vic Davis game ever (I think), but I never actually played the original SI. I bounced off the manual, which I was already primed to do for a multiplayer-only game. But I buy any Vic game that comes out on Steam immediately, including Armageddon Empires for the third time, and I also like League of Geeks. I was just hoping that a modern update might make it more appealing this time around.And, holy crap, did it ever. Say what you want about the Tutorial, it made it so much easier to get many of the basics down. It’s far from comprehensive, and even the encyclopedia has its holes, but it put me on much more solid footing. And, yes, the AI needs some work. I just finished my first single player match with an election victory of 250 more prestige than my nearest rival. But there are many systems to learn, and a few matches with dummies to get that down is both useful and entertaining. Plus, LoG have already committed to continuing to strengthen the single player bots.And I swear I haven’t felt such a strong “one more turn” feeling in many years. I’m sure it doesn’t go this far back, but the comparisons that first came to mind in terms of its addictive qualities were Civ IV and HoMM III. “Must…resist…checking message log…must sleep…WHAT DO YOU MEAN MY PRAETOR LOST THE DUEL???”Highly recommended. Please buy it so they'll do Armageddon Empires next!

_childDocuments_.review: Is the game fun? YesIs the game ready to be played? NoPrimary issue here is that the UI/UX is atrocious. -Menus glitch constantly. -The 'back' buttons on the incredibly cluttered screen is always in a different, un-intuitive place for nearly every popup window.-Escape button only works to close about 1/3 of menus while the other 2/3 it opens the settings menu. -There are approximately zero useful settings options.-No way to jump to your units in any reasonable method.-The only two game/animation speeds are "Slow enough that you need to shave between turns" and "For added challenge, everything happens instantly and you don't get to see any of it."-They added screen panning when you touch your mouse to the screen edge, but didn't enable any way to lock the mouse inside the game window.-They added an (unsearchable) encyclopedia that spends more time making bad puns than actually explaining how anything works.-Tooltips are unhelpful and unreliable. There's a huge emphasis on making your 'Orders' in the correct order and allowing you to rearrange them, but there's no way to actually see what the order you made was. -Clicks (MouseDown vs MouseUp vs MouseClick) are unreliable and different depending on which button you're trying to press.There's plenty more, but I think my point has been made.Fun game, but I'd wait for a sale or just let it cook a little longer.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw a YouTube comment about the game that said, "The game is boring and looks like ass." That makes me feel like I need to make a bunch of excuses for the game, but no, I won't do that.  For some players, it will be a boring game that looks like ass.  You need to be aware of that if you intend to try the game.  It's a slow game.  The graphics are limited in their appeal unless you really really like painted card art.  I really really like the painted card art.  And I don't mind the slow gameplay.  But then again, I am an old man.  And a card game nerd.  That's just the sort of thing I like.Sometimes good games are divisive.  But I think that's a sign of integrity of the design.  Solium Infernum does not apologize for itself.  It's either your cup of tea or it ain't.I've enjoyed it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm having a blast playing this game daily. The other games I enjoy playing daily include Through the Ages and Lords of Waterdeep.  There's a lot to love for someone like me, who thoroughly enjoys turn-based multiplayer strategy.   Getting your skills up vs the AI is lot of fun, and once you are able to crush 5 other archfiends at the highest possible difficulty you are ready to get online!  The playerbase is small, so live games are rare, but jumping on discord has helped me find players to duke it out with.Is the game balanced?  maybe not.  Lilith and Belial are clearly the strongest archfiends, but an expert can win with any of them.  There are certainly a lot of "tricks" that the AI won't teach you... you'll have to get beat in multiplayer to learn them.  Once you know them all, the playing field evens up a bit.  Yes, there is a clear "meta" which can prevent creative and unique strategies from succeeding.  But there is room for variance within the meta, often by leaning into the particular archfiend's strengths and shying away from their weaknesses.  Sadly, no new updates in the foreseeable future, as the developers have gone into "hibernation." The game is not fully polished, so a few bugfixes and balance updates would be greatly appreciated.  However, I still firmly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys multiplayer turn-based strategy.   Both victory and defeat are satisfying, as each game is a learning experience.  Live games get very exciting and chaotic, with a heart-pounding crescendo come late game.  And async gaming allows for added role-playing with cleverly timed messages, agreements, under-the-table deals, and betrayals.  Just an absolute blast in multiplayer, through and through.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna start by saying, I really love this game. The theme is perfectly executed, the artwork is INCREDIBLE, the archfiends have tons of personality. There is a lot of depth in decision making, and I think the political red tape and Hell's bureaucracy are fun to navigate, which is hard to achieve for mechanics that are supposed to be limiting for the players. it's a very compelling game. The asynchronous games are also a genius idea.I'm not gonna discuss about any balancing issues in terms of legions, artifacts etc, the game is new, I'm sure there will be tweaks etc. Thats all very minor stuff. But for me, I think there are two major issues that drag this game down.1) The AI is not good. I dunno how realistic it is to improve it but, it needs improving. Obviously a game like this is balanced around weaker players working together to stop stronger players from getting too far ahead and the AI can't do that. But it should at least be able to understand not to suicide its legions or walk back and forth aimlessly.  I really enjoy single player mode in strategy games, I think it's a nice way to wind down and relax but it's not fun when the AI is this dumb.2) The way excommunication works is straight up game breaking. First of all, the state of excommunication is so punishing that, unless you are so far ahead you already won with military might, being excommunicated is the equivalent of getting kicked out of the lobby. Now, that would still be alright, if not for the fact that there is a random event where players VOTE to excommunicate other players, and apparently, there is a mechanic with masked ritual where you can frame people for attacking Pandaemonium and have them excommunicated. I cannot tell you how bad this feels unless you experience it yourself. The above problems are a non-factor if you have a friend group to play this game with. It's like playing a board game with your friends and if you are fans of the genre, I promise you, you will have a blast with this game. I hope these issues are adressed soon, I will change my critique into positive if they do, because I really love it. If they are not addressed however, I cannot see it seeing much play outside friend groups. Which is fine but, still kinda disapointing.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Seems amazing in concept, has a whole lot of moving pieces that make a good first impression, but is hampered by extremely polarizing balance. The absolute strongest strategy is ignoring almost everything in the early game to build a strong economy since resources also buy more actions per turn; trying to take out the early game leader without focusing on your own economy will just guarantee you fall further behind, and trying to take out the late game leader is often an exercise in futility since they snowball so quickly that they cant be stopped before winning a military victory. The game seems to require everyone be on roughly the same level of skill to maintain a balanced board state. Even a single AI will guarantee coordination is impossible since they are extremely ineffective at any sort of offensive strategy and will often just repeatedly feed the same player prestige and unit experience, so this game barely even functions below 4 human players.Novel concept, but I cant ever see this game being worth the $160 risk to get yourself and 3 other people playing a game that has inherently unstable balance.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite a simple political turn-based strategy game with great eye-catching art direction.It is not a "4X strategy," and I wouldn't call it a "grand strategy."Systems are versatile but shallow. Even a "long" game session is relatively short and condensed, but I think those are advantages of Solium Infernum—think of it as one-evening skirmishes, not as lengthy campaigns.
