_childDocuments_.review: SI takes inspiration from John Milton’s epic poem , set in a version of Hell in which Satan has suddenly vanished and thus created a power vacuum for the various Archfiends to now scramble to fill. As with most games of the 4X—Grand Strategy—genre, there isn’t really a lot of storytelling involved; no overarching narrative as to how and why this development occurred, nor is there an aftermath as to how any chosen Archfiend ends up ruling Hell. Instead, it merely serves to flesh out the setting and provide a framework for SI to massage in the stunning presentation through its amazing Event artworks and flavor text.As a turn and hex-based Grand Strategy game, players take control of any of the Archfiends vying for control over Hell. They each have a unique ability that can have drastic effects on the game if played properly, such as Astaroth having the ability to begin a single-turn war without any prior politics needing to be involved or Mammon being able to tie another Archfiend into a mutually beneficial contract that increases their resource gain each turn. Additionally, Archfiends come with multiple pseudo-skill-trees. These are the same between all the Fiends, and merely the original point distribution is different. They are the most important definition of what tools, spells, and actions players have available to them throughout the game.Skills can be bought with the basic resources—money tokens—that can be sought out every turn. Naturally, these can also be used to buy items and armies, but also to cast rituals and invoke potentially game-changing events. Which rituals are available depends on the category of the skill, but Events are drawn each time the turn order cycles once through each player. For example, such an event may be the invasion of an Angelic super-unit, which goes after each player in order of their amount of units on the board.Parallel to these multiple skill trees, there is one more aspect of static progression—your actual political rank in Hell. These are raised via Prestige, which is a passive resource generating every turn dependent on the number and quality of the points of interest the player possesses, or via diplomatic actions. This is one of the most appealing aspects of SI and makes up the heartbeat of every decision, as the basic win condition of the game consists of having the most Prestige by the end of a turn count specified at the start—a "vote" then follows as the players have a few turns of a grace period to try and wring out the last couple points to secure their victory.There are still further win conditions. For example, by eliminating every other player, by besieging the capitol of Hell, or by manipulating other players through items, like a trinket that allows you to win the game instead, if you have otherwise been vassalized by the end of the game.This last point deserves some more explanation; in stark contrast to other Grand Strategy games, wherein resource management and endless army and colony number crunching are the lifelines of the game, in Solium Infernum it is the Diplomacy screen. In fact, there are only five resource tokens to even keep track of. Likewise, the number of armies a player can control is severely limited, as is the amount of actions per turn.By default, players have two action slots, and virtually everything you can do requires a slot. These can be expanded by the aforementioned skill trees, but this tightens the decision-making significantly. As such, aside from the fairly mundane actions of resource gathering, buying items, or moving your units, diplomatic actions are a lot more weighted, so much so that entire characters like Belial are solely built around the ability to manipulate other players into taking (un)favorable actions.This is through SI's Vendetta system, which introduces conflict as a consequence for every political action available. Among the multiple options, a player might, for example, extort an opponent for resources. A turn later, the other player receives this demand and can either decide to accept and surrender their resources or reject it. This will then give the player who made the demand an opportunity to declare a Vendetta and opens up a war. Depending on how the Vendetta is started, any of the two players sets a condition for the aggressor, for example, taking a certain number of hexes on the board, and once again wagering Prestige. Prestige permeates every design decision of the game, and it works fantastically well with this loop of manipulation and trying solely to one-up another by abusing all these systems that hook into the subterfuge of how all these actions, spells, items, and rituals can shake up the game board—however, it also opens the door for some nasty balancing issues.For example, it is exceedingly easy to bully single players out of the game very quickly. This is due to the inherently low amount of actions allowed, the low income in the early game, and the low number of units available. While the comeback potential is pretty high as even in the very late game defeating an enemy’s main base will immediately eliminate them, it is nevertheless difficult for a single player to meaningfully defend themselves against colluding opponents. Trinkets, of which each Archfiend can choose between one and three to start the game with, are also massively unbalanced, with some choices like a Crown that allows for an additional action slot right from the beginning being just universally incredibly strong. Graphically, SI is a mixed bag. The Event screens are hauntingly gorgeous, and while the Fiends are heavily stylized, they still fit the overall tone of the game very well.The game board, however, is less detailed, and with only three maps to choose from at the beginning, offers neither pretty visuals nor much variety. Even now, after multiple games, I doubt I could tell them apart from just a glance.SI does not have a particularly extensive OST, but it is a reasonably strong one. Featuring some somber, fittingly melancholic ambient tracks such as , but also grander tracks like —frankly, a song so good it has no right to be in a game of this genre.I have no complaints about Solium Infernum. It ran perfectly well throughout my various games. Multiplayer functioned with no issues either during active sessions, or the fantastic feature of asynchronous multiplayer, which allows for players to take their turns without needing to be in the game simultaneously.Going into Solium Infernum was a fresh experience. I despise Grand Strategy games, and I have tried again and again to find a single one that was for me—and I have found it. The fast pace, flexibility with its multiplayer options, and exchanging mind-numbing resource management for such a deep diplomacy system, which has the potential to completely flip the game on its head while also allowing players the freedom to truly plan schemes for tens of turns prior, is utterly fantastic.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely phenomenal multiplayer experience. The asynchronous nature alone is a godsend for friend-groups with busy schedule, allowing everyone to participate. As someone in my thirties whose friends are all getting married and having children, it turns meetups into something that happens a couple times a year to a couple times a week.It has its problems, for sure. It's not very well optimised, there are definitely balancing issues between the archfiends. But it's never so skewed that it's insurmountable. The fundamental nature of the game is one of limited information and a severely restrictive action economy, and there are methods in play to make it difficult (but not impossible) to truly pull ahead of the pack.Ultimately, my friend group have been playing game after game in a continuous stream since we discovered this. We keep coming back, we keep having a blast, we keep being *able* to come back even with vastly different, busy schedules. That's really all the praise it needs.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent "social strategy" game, convoluted in all the right ways, and a perfect way to spend time scheming with and against friends. Avoid single-player except for practicing - the real deal is trying to figure out what everyone else is thinking, tyring to pre-empt movements by a few turns, ruining plans and getting your own plans ruined in turn. Gather your pals and bring light back to the throne of flame.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Solium Infernum is a game of patience, both in and out of game. This isn't a fast-paced, get in, get out sort of affair; you will embark upon 50+ turns (by default settings) of political machinations, strategic maneuvering, and diabolical schemes, and only at the end will you know if you've managed to bring your plots to fruition. You must take your time.Games can be played live - with turn timers at 5-6 minutes per turn - though this will typically take you 2-3 hours to finish, with no breaks in between. There is no pause button. You can also play asynchronously, which is how the original was played, with turn timers ranging from 24 hours to 1 week, allowing for a lot more flexibility. Async games will typically take quite a bit longer than live sessions, naturally, but if players submit their turns early, it will progress faster.NSI - new Solium Infernum - does a fantastic job of sticking true to OSI - old Solium Infernum. League of Geeks has updated the graphics and brought this stellar experience into the modern age, both graphically and in gameplay. All in all, a faithful adaptation.SI isn't for the faint of heart. You will need dedication and stamina to see your games through to completion, but when you do, and when you see your name at the top of the pack, that feeling of accomplishment can't be replicated. Truly, you will earn your place in Hell.I was chosen to participate in the closed beta process as well as the "Hellraisers" testing run just prior to launch, and while I am predisposed to speak well of this game - I absolutely adored the original - the team has done an absolutely fantastic job and I look forward to the game finding new fans.See you in Hell?
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Like Civilization, but set in Hell. Solium Infernum was originally released in 2009, but failed to garner popularity. This remake from League of Geeks stays fairly faithful to the original.Satan has vanished, leaving the throne of Hell empty. The most powerful archfiends rise up to stake their claim, gathering armies and collecting tribute to fuel their efforts. Whoever has the most prestige by the final vote of the Conclave is elected the new ruler of Hell. This is accomplished through Schemes, army clashes, gladiator duels, capturing Places of Power, and hurling insults and demands at your rivals. Alternatively, you can eliminate your rivals in open warfare, or you can capture the heavily-guarded citadel of Pandaemonium, though both of those victories require more work.Though I compared it to Civilization, this game has only superficial similarities. You move legions on a hex map, perform diplomatic actions, and manage your empire's resources. The difference is in complexity, both more and less of it. Solium Infernum's big resource is money: four different types of coin that fuel Rituals, pay for stat increases, and are used at auction in the Bazaar to procure legions, praetors, and artifacts. You never create new settlements, but capture existing places of power to generate more prestige. All units are created through rituals or purchased through the Bazaar; you never build units at your stronghold. The diplomacy is where this game shines. The epitome of devilish contracts, crooked deals, and red tape, everything passes through diplomatic channels in an orderly fashion that can make you a superpower or deadlock you into a prestige loss spiral. If you outrank your opponent in Hell's hierarchy, your proposals and demands take precedence over theirs. You cannot cross into a rival's territory without a cassus belli, a Vendetta, unless you have been excommunicated, which officially removes you from the race for the throne. If you win enough Vendettas, you can declare a Blood Feud and openly attack your rival until they (or you) are eliminated, unless someone plays an event card to nullify it or they become vassal to another archfiend.Overall, if you want a game that looks like Civ but makes you feel like a chess-playing devil, this can scratch that itch. Sadly, League of Geeks have currently paused development due to issues in the studio, so keep that in mind.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Thus far,  appears to be a great game. If you come in with the right expectations. For some reason, the game is often marketed as a 4X or even a grand strategy. And it really doesn't belong to any of these genres. Nor does it offer significant singleplayer content to justify the purchase. What it does offer, however, is a deliciously devilry-flavoured multiplayer board game. Hell is other people, after all.Basically, think a more complex , but virtually every game interaction and system is some form of a subtle intrigue, betrayal or maniacal powerplay. That makes  perfect for a group of friends with flexible and sophisticated understanding of the whole 'friendship' concept. You can't really spell "friend" without "fiend", let's be frank. But it's plenty fun with random people, too.  It's a highly customizable experience. Ranging from 2 hour-long sessional games to asynchronous affairs potentially lasting weeks if players only have spare time for a couple of turns per day. But the learning curve is slightly steep, and the tutorial doesn't cover the peculiarities of rules in their entirety. In-game rules encyclopedia comes to rescue. Aesthetically and thematically the game is top-notch for my taste. I mean, endless wasteland of dust and char? More of that, please. Characters are distinct in their unique brands of vile, wicked and warped. UI could use a bit more tuning, though. Particularly, adding the option to close any windows with a click anywhere on the map and adding a camera scroll speed slider would be neat. Overall, really hoping  does well and stays healthy for years. If it doesn’t, I’ll have to go into real politics to satisfy my dark manipulative urges. And real politics is yucky. See you in hell.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: A fresh take on 4X strategy formula!You don't play as a civilization. You are a power hungry fiend here.You develop your skills, rise in hellish ranks, learn rituals, hire legions to fight for you and politic your way to the top of underworld's foodchain.Basically, diplomacy is a biggest part of the game. And it's a Hell's kind of diplomacy built around demands, extortions, insults, humiliation, bribes and blood feuds.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: The art direction is good, but there is far too little playable content to justify the price. It needs a campaign, not just a few scenarios which must be completed in a specific way, greatly reducing player freedom and fun. You are paying a lot for what you are getting. There were a lot of missed opportunities.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I've got hundreds of games in my library, and Solium Infernum is the first one I've ever felt moved to write a review of.  The problem with pretty much every strategy game I own is that the AI is bad, and multiplayer games take too long to be viable.  Solium Infernum solves this by being designed from the ground up for asynchronous multiplayer, which means you can in involved in up to ten matches simultaneously, and play them out over a period of weeks.  Each turn all players submit a series of orders, and once everyone has made their submissions the whole turn plays out at once.  A limited number of orders and lots of interesting things to do with them makes each turn feel significant, as there are always more things you would like to do than you can actually get done.  Also, the community is awesome, I keep getting in-character messages from demon princes, which so far have included signatures in Latin, and one message in actual poetry.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Might be a great tabletop game, and might be really fun against other players, but as a solo experience where every AI ennemy votes against you at every occasion, that really limits the enjoyment you can get from the finer aspects of diplomacy,  intrigue and betrayal that the game pretends to be offering.The art direction is great, but i'm not sure that the core gameplay loop is really good with how limited you are by the limit of orders per round. And it takes a while for everything to resolve, so it takes you a while to understand how to properly use them.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I have played enough to tell you that at it's peak, it was perfect, everything. Down to the last minute detail. However unless you have a designated group to play the game with. You will have a hard time even finding a game. With this in mind, I will go over the pros and cons of the game as I see it.Pros:It is very strategic. You can plan things 10-40 turns ahead of time, and there is a high skill ceiling for the game. It has a great theme, I am a big fan of the Divine Comedy. So the flavor is on point. And I would say the visuals and sounds are some of the best I have encountered in a strategy game. Furthermore, the designs on the fiends themselves are great.It is one of the best games I have played when it comes to politics, the array of political actions, and how you can talk to other players is great. Truly makes you feel like you are in a race for power with other cut throat people with the goals of winning the throne of hell. Cons:A good game of SI is long. For instance if you are losing, which will happen when learning the game. The game will drag on for hours if in a sessional. If you are in a async, it is even worse. Furthermore, while the game has a casual crowd, unless you really learn the game truly, you will not be able to compete with the rest of the players if they have been playing for as long as I have.Meta is a word that describes a general strategy, and one I would use to describe the gameplay. It very much is a slow and methodical game through and through. With this in mind, the first 20 turns of a game with a good player, they will do nothing but accrue resources. Sure other strategy games have this. But not at this level. If someone has 4-5 order slots by turn 20-30. And you are at 2. You have lost the entire game. Thus all of the great politics and diplomacy means nothing when it cannot be used from turns 1-20/30My last con, is that of personal bias. I do not like luck based things that are beyond a realm of understanding. For example, you can spend 4 turns building resources to buy an end game troop, just to lose it to a random event card. That had a 1/16 chance of hitting that one unit. That just makes anyone mad, or upset. So a lot of the random chance things should just be a target, or like a less random event. Even if it is better (A target), I would be less mad than losing the entire game to a d12 dice roll. More so since I spent hours in contemplation on what I should do. And months on the async game. This has been my own personal review. If you can find active players that are not too skilled, then I will 100% endorse this game. If you cannot, then I am afraid you missed the window on this wonderful game. I would rate it 9/10 as I very much think it is one of the best strategy games I have played.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I absorb these kinds of games. I love turn based strategy games and I have an extra special place for asynch multiplayer like dominions. This game crushes it. The art is gorgeous, the setting is awesome, and the biggest thing that makes this game stand out is every decision matters. You can only make a few moves per turn but the control you have and the impact of those decisions is massive. Like chess, I've already felt that one move can just ruin me and sometimes I play it right and crush because I made the right call. I'm only two games in but I am obsessed with this game.If you are into turn based strategy games there's nothing better out right now.Edit: I'm already in heated games and figuring out how nuanced the vendetta/diplomacy systems are. This game rocks. And when people role-play as their demonic avatars even better. I hope this explodes because it's my favorite game in years. Easily the best strategy game since Old World or Distant Worlds: Universe only this one has PERFECT asynch multiplayer for a guy like me. Runs great on the deck too other than the small text, which is always a concern with these kinds of games.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I have hundreds of hours spent in the original Solium Infernum over the years. My loftiest hopes for this remake was that League of Geeks could capture the unique vibe and flavour of the original and add some quality of life features. The original game was very complicated and a little obtuse. And, really, there's nothing that quite plays like Solium Infernum. It's a game about conquering hell as much as it's a game about navigating the complicated bureaucracy that governs its higher echelons. You can't just pull up to your enemy's border, declare war, and march into their cantons. We may be the damned, but that's no excuse for rudeness.Instead, you need to show up to the weekly demon nobles meeting, point across the table, and demand that an archfiend give you their lunch money. If they say no, you can declare a wager and seek to claim territory. If you manage to do so when the vendetta has completed, you receive prestige (which will let you raise your rank within the demonic nobility).Or maybe you challenge them to a duel, so you pick your best fighter that isn't currently serving as a general for your hellish legions, and your opponent picks their best duellist, and they duke it out.Or maybe you do none of that stuff and keep to yourself, quietly amassing wealth and eldritch manuscript pages to further your magical power and standing within the depths. Or maybe you never bother with direct legion-to-legion combat and spend your time in your study casting horrific spells and generally being a miserable nightmare holed up in their tower.The AI seems generally improved over the original Cryptic Comet release. I'd need to spend more time digging into that. I like the different single-player scenarios, as well. The star of this release (for me) has been a direct integration to Steam notifications for asynchronous multiplayer. Not everyone has time for a multi-hour strategy marathon, so being able to play out a match at the rate of a turn per day is really neat.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Note: This game was received as a gift from a "friend".I'd like to first preface this for prospective buyers: This version of Solium Infernum is not a 1:1 of the classic game. While it follows it spiritually, a good number of mechanics are altered, leaving this as more of a re-imagining. I would generally describe it as less complex, less varied, and more accessible. Different enough to be considered its own game.It's overall "fine" for what it is, but while I do appreciate some of the visuals, many of the implementations are nonsensical in the extreme and the game is hardly balanced.Starting with that first bit, and this is the piece that tipped the scale towards this review: Blood Vassals should not be able to vote against their Blood Lord in events. If they are forced to adopt the same diplomatic stances as their Lord, why are they suddenly free to vote for themselves to the extent that they can screw the Lord? There needs to be consistency here, the entire vassalage system at the moment functions more as an armistice. Accepting is more of a detriment to the Lord than anything else, because they then become responsible for that vassal with near-no return.Apart from this, Prophecy should not be required to view Vendettas you are involved in. Vendettas between others yes, but if it is issued against you, you have no knowledge of the competition unless your strategy that game has mandated you invest in this attribute. It is, frankly, stupid.As part of the re-imagining, the character creation has been replaced with preset characters and a far more limited "Reliquary" system that allows you to select 1-3 artifacts (using a managed inventory) that give varying buffs to the character. This is indisputably a serious step down from the original game's system and its large number of choices, but as I mentioned this game is not intending to follow the original, and in the end is a more accessible option. The issue is that each character follows a specific archetype, and thus everyone knows the starting abilities and general strategy everyone is aiming for. Credit to the developers, there is room for misdirection here, you could instead go with an entirely different strategy to mislead people, but that starts you off at a serious disadvantage because you're left without access to any of those tools. Players should not be left at a disadvantage because the developers chose a system that does not  in a strategy game based around deception and instead provide so much information as to nullify much of the opening game,  in an adaptation of an older game that had a better system.There are other things I could talk about, but the point I'm making is that so very many of the game's elements have not been thought through or are underdeveloped.In terms of balance, the game has so many outliers that even just a single event can grind the game to a halt.Every turn, a rotating "Regent' is designated. This is the player who will move first on the turn order, and they also draw a special event card that they can hold and play as they wish. Some of these cards are . There exists one to turn off rituals for several turns, when 3 of the 8 characters are intended to focus on rituals. One which just closes the item shop. One disables the ability to receive income. One which calls down an angel to smite armies. That last one is also misleading, as the event text specifically states that it aims to kill "one legion from each Great House of Hell", in reality, it will simply continue massacring until it has killed  one legion from each player. Yes, this means if it descends near you, it will just kill all of yours then move on to the next player. In effect, most if not all of the legions in the game will die. It is possible to kill this angel, but honestly? That thing is beefy. Players need to band together against it to have a chance before it does irreparable damage.The point I'm making this time, in relation to these events cards, is that the event cards should be  the game, not just turning things off. Instead of disabling rituals, increase their cost by 1.5x.  Instead of closing the shop, change prices or items. Many of these events need to be altered because at this point they're not temporary strategy changers, they are severe enough to introduce permanent repercussions for the whole game.Going even further, the preset characters themselves are unbalanced.Belial is good, his unique ability is to frame others for insults. The only other framing available is at high rank Deceive, so effectively, his ability is to start conflicts between others for free from the beginning in the vein of an endgame ability.Murmur absolutely blows.- His unique ability summons a weak unit that decays rapidly (lasting effectively 3-4 turns). They're weak enough that they aren't able to do any fighting, and we've theorized at best a single use case for them.- His primary stat is "Destruction" for direct damage spells. The issue is that these spells cannot be used against players unless you are in an open conflict with them, and while one or two of the spells are powerful, it takes most of the game to get them online due to the costs of increasing Destruction further, as well as...- If you want to be able to use your main gimmick without being in open conflict, you need Deceive 3 for the Masking Ritual, which will "hide" who performed the spell. Of course, everyone knows it was Murmur, because he's  Destruction guy, so you just make an enemy doing this. The only solution to this is Ritual Framing, which is Deceive 5. The best case would be then to enter open conflict with someone, but you can't do that because...- His starting legion is also almost entirely Infernal damage, which is performed last in combat, so they're likely to just die before ever getting to their useful stat. You're effectively left relying on RNG that an "Infernal First" modifying Praetor (hero unit) shows up in the shop to attach to that legion, and that the RNG income system has provided you the currency types (there are 4 different currency categories) to purchase them before another has.All-in-all, Murmur has nothing going for him. You're better off playing Lilith so you at least have a second ritual slot in the beginning, as well as a Ranged-damage legion (Ranged goes first in combat), or maybe even Belial and everyone just fights each other while you steal their money. You can also cut out the middle man, play Mammon, and just make a ton of money yourself, power-leveling your attributes, and becoming an unstoppable force of Charisma.He clearly needs a change, and the best solution I have come up with is a simple one: Give his summons the "Infernal First" attribute. This is exceptionally well-balanced. They become suicide squads, running in and dying to the subsequent Ranged and Melee sections, but delivering the Infernal damage of a , which should be your higher stat one. This damage would be low, as supporting legions only contribute half their stats, but allows him to actually utilize them while not needing heavy investment in purchasing additional legions. This frees up resources to be spent on attribute leveling, which he desperately needs for many reasons. It'd be a fantastic alteration and if the developers take anything from this review, I want it to be that, though I hope they improve Destruction itself as well. The returns are overall low for pretty high investment, though rituals suck generallyl.So this game. I think it needs some pretty strong revisions. Many of the events are game-enders rather than game-changers. Much of the design for different playstyles is unbalanced, Andromalius and Mammon striking me as the best. Events fire off rapidly, sometimes multiple per turn, rendering you unable to respond. Game info given can be misleading.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Basically the best strategy game on the market right now. Perfectly simplifies the genre and gets to the good bits, huge impactful decisions made each turn. It's like a boardgame mixed with a 4x. Just complicated enough to not be a board game and just simple enough to not be a full on 4x where you're managing tons of resources in tons of different areas of control. In this game, everything is small enough to where you KNOW what's important and WHY it's important, pretty much the first time you play the game. Good job guys.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really high quality game a little marred by its own theme.My first impressions on this game were wonderful, some really unique game mechanics and a ton of possible strategies and tactics for winning, making it very replayable and versatile in its gameplay. Sounds and visuals are wonderful, with the ambience really adding to the immersion. My biggest gripe with this game, and also the same reason most of my online games fade into nothing, is the system in which in handles the turn based flow. You have two options, a live game that runs for a few hours, or a Asynchronous game in which you take a turn or two a day, lasting a month or two. This Asynchronous mode was praised by the community, but its a failure. Most if not all games in this style pretty much die out with a whimper, as players drop out and quit, one by one, for whatever reason. And its the type of game, where if you miss a turn, you might as well quit since each turn is so very important. That wouldnt be such an issue if the live games were more frequent, but they are not, the live rooms are always empty, but in my opinion, live play should be the ONLY option for play, since the existence of Asynchronous mode makes everyone choose that mode instead, i wish there was only one mode, live, to force people to play the game properly.Anyways, devs have just basically announced that the game was a failure, and they are stopping development. Which to be honest is quite sad.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played solo so I can't speak to the MP, but this is one of the most unique and freshest takes on the 4X genre I've seen. It may not be for everyone and it ultimately wasn't my cup of tea, but I have to recommend it, as it's incredibly well made and well worth checking out if you have any interest in the strategy genre. It could easily become one of your favorite games.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most satisfying multiplayer competitive strategy games I have ever played.The possibility of logging in 10 minutes a day to do a couple of turns with meaningful and satisfying decisions is great and every time you open a game, that moment of anticipation as the map loads and you just hope so much that your clever move paid off is amazing.Another thing I really love is the possibilities the game organically opens for soft-role-playing your terrible terrible demon doing terrible terrible things to your fellow demons. If you are extorting someone, accompanying the request with a nice message is the least you can do...One thing that could turn off people is that there is a certain degree of randomness and a lot of unknowns, so it is not uncommon for a move that you planned very carefully to fail terribly for some small thing that you had missed or could not have any kind of control over. It is important to keep in mind that this is part of the game and happens to all players. This is not a fair game and it really lends into the theme.Very very recommended even if just for the boundary it is pushing in adapting boardgame mechanics as a videogame with incredible talent, innovation and charm.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I have become completely obsessed with this game in recent times and i wish to put forward my words as to why as it truly is a hidden gem in the strategy industry. Though it has it's ups and downs and roughing around the edges i see such amazing potential for this game if support continues.Solium Infernum is best thought of as a mix between Civilization and Armello but much more underhanded in it's diplomacy. No alliance is permanent and none but one can win the crown. You must meticulously plan your way to victory, keep track of everything going on in the game and generally be forward-thinking.Speaking of which, i should probably illuminate the core ”Shiny thing” you are fighting for. Pandaemonium! This place is the core of your victory, whether it be by diplomacy, conquest, sly underhanded tactics or a myriad of other options. Your goal is to control Pandaemonium.You can play as one of the titular ”Archfiends” Who might i add, have absolutely stellar designs and each represent their respective sins quite well. Beelzebub is my personal favourite.I should also mention one of the main draws towards this game, Asynchronous Multiplayer. Long ago when a house was affordable we had this feature in many games and i am entirely unsure as to why developers dropped it entirely. The charm of async is the ability to play whenever you can. Instead of sitting down for a long session of the game over several hours you can instead just submit your turn within a timer (these usually range between 24 hours to 3 days though this is decided by the host)Solium Infernum additionally has a welcoming community on discord. The devs even listen to people's thoughts and opinions along with providing explanations behind design and balance choices! Wish we had this sort of stuff still in the gaming industry.I could go on and on about how much i adore this game and it's potential but it would be misleading to not point out some of the current flaws. The main one at the moment being the extreme economic build-up in the early game and a lack of options, if you don't seek tribute every turn until turns 15-20 you are likely out of the game. It is also extremely difficult to play aggressively early on. The system is definitely geared towards more political intrigue and meticulous planning (Which is the highlight of the game) thus it may be quite difficult for the devs to solve these issues. They made some sweeping changes in a recent patch along with a new DLC archfiend, these changes were good but haven't done much to resolve the overarching issues in pacing.Overall Solium Infernum is a promising game with an absolutely stellar artstyle and i do truly hope that they continue to support the game with more updates and DLC. The potential is sickening.Better to rule in Hell than serve in Heaven.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, first let me say this re-imagining of Solium Infernum is really really good, I played the original version alot and this is just as good but with Jaw dropping art and graphics....The Devs also listened to my and others feedback from the multiplayer trial, that version used 100% of GPU usage and overheated my pc like crazy, now with the release version, its way better optimised and my GPU is alot cooler....If you like strategy games that make you think and liked the old SI, get this, its Awsome...
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: As an emotional & intuitive role-player -- who does not care about rationalistic calculus, mechanics, and optimised pathways to Victory -- I find this game extremely fascinating, with its Demon/Gothic, dark & flame-red visuals, its eerie & sinister atmosphere + soundtrack. If you are a role-player, you will find this game very attractive : no need to stress with the pressure to win; if you don't feel like it. I personally ignore the prestige-point victory condition, so I set very long 70-point custom games against A.I. players, and then enjoy the dark ride, delighting in sinful role-play -- without any care for my prestige-point status.The game seems very complicated at first, but this can appeal as a mysterious trip -- navigating inside an evil Unknown. You can enjoy the game without understanding all of its rules and tactical technicalities -- unless you are a rationalistic competitor who always plays to win by masterfully manipulating a game's logic. As an irrational role-player, I really do not care about rule-books, strategy guides, and optimal pathways to Victory. My psyche is submerged inside an imaginary Hell : not the time & place to think like a nerd accountant or obsessive chess-player.Program has never crashed, had no game-stopping bug. It looks awesome -- even with AA turned off -- on my "old" Windows 10 w/ a Radeon RTX 3050 card and "merely" 8 GB of RAM. Playing inside a 1600 x 900 window, it is fast & easy to switch to a web browser or check emails : no stalling, no stuttering, no crash.A YouTube reviewer mentioned that some of the visual representations of "Archfiends" were too cartoonish, specifically targeting Lilith. In this specific case, I agree : her head looks grotesque -- in a non-demonic sense. Recommend that the devs rework Lilith's face -- to make it more analogous to vampish Erzsebet's awesome head & facial expressions.On Steam, a reviewer deplored the game's price. Considering the extensive & deep work the devs have invested in this awesome game, I consider the release price totally fair. (Paid CAN $ 60 w/ tax : totally worth it, no regrets.) The high Quality of this game merits such a price. Game was very recently released : if you are waiting for the price to come down in a sale, you are "stealing" from the devs and from yourselves -- in terms of all the devilish fun you could sinfully enjoy now.Update Edit >  This is NOT a "wargame" : generating "doom stacks" with the intent of bulldozing the map as you (sadistically) please does NOT work at all in this game. You are located in an orderly Hell, where "rules of engagement" are rigorously in effect : 1) You may not attack rivals unless you have an official "casus belli" against them (called a "Vendetta") ; 2) You may not attack on the same turn the war was declared ; 3) Your armies may not pass through the territories of other players to reach your target -- which represents a fatal problem when your target is located far away ; 4) When the "Vendetta" (= temporary war) comes into effect (one turn after being diplomatically initiated), you are contractually bound to win within strict parameters, in merely a few turns -- you may not repeatedly attack as long as you want ; 5) even if you are militarily much stronger, if you do not fulfil the Vendetta's contract within the prescribed time (rather short), you lose !! In conclusion : This is NOT a wargame, and building-up huge armies is not a recipe for assured victory.For example > In a current game, I have the most armies of all players ... but they are stuck inside my home territory, with nowhere to go -- since I am surrounded by owned territories that I am not allowed to move into + since I have no legitimate "casus belli" (Vendetta) that allows me to attack them !! A situation arose where I did acquire a legal Vendetta, but since my adversary was located too far away, I had to choose a hero-v-hero arena fight instead of an army-v-army map battle. I am very happy with that, since I am a mystical role-player, not a military brawler, but brute-force warfighters will be very frustrated.Update (example) > In the recent game where I had the most powerful military, my neighbor foolishly decided to declare war (Vendetta) when I had 3 armies stationed near his border. First turn, 2 of my armies invaded his territory and smashed one of his 2 home armies. On the next turn, I planned to crush his remaining army ... but somebody played the "paperwork restructure" event-card that imposed a universal cancellation of all diplomatic relationships, including Vendettas. Consequently, my 2 armies were ejected from my neighbor's territory -- since the Vendetta had been cancelled and you are not allowed to remain inside an owned territory when there is no active Vendetta !! This example illustrates that even if you have more military might and are winning a war, somebody can pull off a trick and prevent you from continuing your winning fight, As I said above, this is NOT a wargame where you can bulldoze a map with huge armies : there are sorcerous spells and diplomatic tricks than can curb military might to useless impotence. Since I am not a brawler, I find this unexpectedly entertaining. Am tired, in other 4X games, of creating "doom stacks" and then running around a map bulldozing the A.I. players ;)Addendum Edit > You sometimes can avoid an army-v-army clash on the map by asking for a hero-v-hero Duel. But -- as it is now -- duels can be too dicey : I have had 2 strong Praetors permanently killed by the same weak Praetor ("Mulciber") who used a duelling Technique that prevented my 2 heroes to escape permanent death (by deploying the Veil of Smoke duelling technique) because its own Technique trumped the Veil by nullifying it -- so I lost 2 precious Praetors to a basically weak opponent. And then, you cannot reload a previous save to modify your Technique, because the nullifying Technique would beat anything you could put up -- unless you possessed your own nullifying Technique, which is not easy to get hold of. That's too bad : the concept of Duels is great, but the risk of permanently losing a powerful army Leader is too great. It is consequently wiser to "forfeit" a Duel (by not sending any hero inside the arena) and lose a few points of Prestige, than permanently losing a Praetor who boosts an army's military power. I believe the mechanics of Duels should be re-evaluated by the developers to make them more appealing as a viable gameplay option.Update > This is an AWESOME game : it is full of trickster surprises, so you cannot manipulate the A.I.  by rational calculus. For example : My strongest army was blasted (= loss of hit-points) by an A.I. spell, and other spells could have totally wiped it off the map ;) Control-freaks will freak-out, but as an emotional role-player, I find the unexpected chaos AWESOME. I do hope this game financially succeeds, in order to warrant DLCs : paid $ CAN 60 (w/ tax) for this game, and I sincerely believe that it is worth more, so purchasing DLCs would not represent an issue. Gamers sometimes forget that the sale price includes Steam's cut + that the developer team needs to acquire revenues and must pay income tax : if we love a game, we must finance it. Hot-seat mode is not yet included. In the abstract, it would seem easy to include it, but developers have limited programming time, so I prefer that they invest that time (+ salaries) in creating new stuff (in a revenue-generating DLC) than wasting it on a marginal feature. Reading Steam reviews, I am tired of people complaining about DLC pricing : they do not seem to understand that game developers have families to feed + taxes to pay. Developing new content requires to be financed ;)

_childDocuments_.review: It says I have played for 3 hours, but I also played a lot during the multiplayer beta.  I also owned the original Solium Infernum and played multiplayer back in the day.  Believe it or not we had to send each other our games files via dropbox, move them into a different folder, then load the game up and constantly repeat this process every turn.  It took forever.  I always wished someone would just make a utility to make the process easier.    Well, this is even better!  All new graphics and sounds and a much better interface to boot!    Solium Infernum is like chess in hell.  There is a lot of room for player expression because there are so many items, relics, artifacts, armies, praetors (commanders/hero units), manuscripts, rituals, etc!  Starting off the bat you have a wide choice of relics to choose from to customize your play style.  You could get a crown that gives you +1 orders per turn, which gives you much more power because normally you start with 2 orders per turn.  You could choose to get even more orders by raising your rank and raising your archfiend's stats to level 4, up to 6 orders per turn.  Let me tell you when you have that many orders you feel very powerful because you can demand a lot of tribute very fast and pay for anything you want.    Instead, you could pick a relic that promotes your starting legion to get a military advantage right off the bat.  You could get a relic that gives you the win if the person you choose at the start of the game actually wins by vote.  There are so many combinations to start with and that is before the game even starts!  Once you're playing there's lots of paths you can choose.  You can try buffing your stats in different areas like wrath/deceipt/charisma etc.  Some rituals you gain from this will allow you to do things like damage enemy units, steal enemy units, steal enemy money, trick other players into fighting each other, etc.  There are a vast variety of possible strategies and playstyles you could use.    The game does take a while to get going.  Often you'll find yourself blowing a whole turn just trying to get more tribute (money).  But the game gets more and more interesting as it goes on and the power curve ramps up.    Speaking of playstyles, you could try to win by prestige, or you could just go all out and attack Pandemonium which immediately excommunicates you and makes you the #1 target of all other players.  But if you've got the army to handle it it's a valid strategy.    The game had poor optimization during the beta, but is much better now.  I put settings on medium and it runs fine.  The game is very atmospheric with random hell based sounds and atmospheric sound effects.  Just don't play this game if you have religious parents, LOL!  All in all I highly recommend this game if a chess like game that takes place in hell and requires cunning and subterfuge and plotting and scheming sounds appealing to you.    Last but not least:  The fact that you can play this asynchronously and just take 1 turn a day makes it great for playing with friends who are spread over the world.  An actual game would take quite a lot of time if you're only doing 1 turn a day but would definitely feel epic! tldr:  Atmospheric hell based chess, improves on the original, asynchronous multiplayer is convenient, endless possibilities for playstyle and strategy

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT:After playing some more, I need to update my review.It's a great remake of a great game.The original Solium Infernum is a really tight design with boardagme-like mechanics. The remake tries to rebalance some things, and that's a mixed bag with some decent and much needed changes (like decoupling income from Charisma), but also with some unnecessary simplifications (like changes to Praetor duels); but overall it still retains the core of what makes the game great.The clash of the gorgeous 2D art and the 3D cartoony characters with their animations more suited to Disney villains is quite jarring, but other than that this release is a really nice package.In short, if you haven't played the original - If you enjoy highly interactive strategy games, marrying behind-the-curtain negotiations with outright warfare you should definitely give this one a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Solium Infernum is the perfect game for me.I want chaos. I want agony from my opponents. I want to insult them to their faces and they just have to admit I'm correct. I want to give them choices that are either terrible or awful. I want to screw someone over and frame someone else for my deeds. I want to be the new ruler of hell by any means necessary.Mechanically, this game is unique! It may look like another civ-ish game, but no. It's not. This game is a diplomatic game. You have few armies and war can't be waged freely, most of the time. Honestly the map and the happenings on it are all fuel for the social core that this game runs on. It is a mechanically relevant social game. Talk is cheap if you can't back it up and this game provides an almost overwhelming amount of avenues to do so.I believe the heart of this game is played async (24+ hour turn timer and will start a new turn once everyone puts their simultaneous action in). When this game has time to breathe, its at its best. It's all about being irrational. Plotting schemes to set up entirely fabricated reasons to claim rightful vengeance because you wanted their land is a 1:1 thing that is mechanically tied into the game. I believe that playing a match over a longer period of time (5 min a day?) lets these moments really sink in because you're itching. Itching to find out how your plots you've toiled and planned for days turn out and there is no pressure to hurry. Scheme as long as you'd like. Ai.....aint great. thats fine for me, if you are a offline gamer and will never try online, I'd say....eh, maybe? It's not the same.This is a game in hell and all of us are a*holes. Thats how it goes down here. If you want one of the most interesting social dynamics you will ever find in a multiplayer strategy game, this is 100% worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the original game with some friends back in 2011 and this remake more or less brought in all the improvements I wanted without making any major changes. I also have to emphasise the Async play, since we've all got families now, allowing us to play without needing to try and get everyone free at the same time. I still recommend trying to do that for the first ten turns or so since those can be done fairly quickly and it helps move things along to the scheming stage faster.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, the best diplomacy system i've ever played in a strategy.Every mechanic of this game is mired in bureaucracy and it's hilarious and extremely fun.You are in hell, and nothing happens without bureaucracy. Getting paid, Marching and even talking takes paperwork that needs to be submitted to the infernal court. You need permission to go through claimed land, and you claim land by marking it with red tape. And because everything is painfully inefficient you have to deal with four different valid currencies. And because of politics many people demand multiple currencies at once, and any transaction involving more than 8 coins is too complicated to track so you need to do accounting in your off time for the big purchases.I needed to take the mines of Gehenna before the conclave assembled  for the vote to win the game, but I reached it because a couple fallen angels blocked the way with their territory. I wanted to declare war on them, but I needed to fabricate a grievance to be able to submit a vendetta. I made an absurd demand of tribute to the strongest faction in the game. They declined, and I took the opportunity to declare a vendetta against them. This isn't America, Wars must outline what their purpose, must have a clear reason, and a time of expiry.  After stamping and submitting to the infernal court my vendetta, the declaration of war was ratified by the opposing party. Now we can fight.War is almost never the end for you. The Infernal Court will not let you wipe out another arch fiend without a Blood Feud or something. So I didn't have much to risk, I just needed to paint a line through their territory. But before I could get through their barrier they vassalized under a weaker archfiend far away. This invalidated my Vendetta, because you can't have one against a vassal. My War was no longer justified so I was stuck in a strip of awkward gerrymandered territory. Eventually I found a loophole in the library to get across and take the mine just before the assembly. I had the majority of the support in the court so I was sure to win. Then the  Vassal attacked Pandemonium while the court was gathering. They lost that army, Pandemonium will almost always destroy anything you attack them with, but they also became excommunicated. When you are excommunicated you are not bound or protected by the laws of hell. You are pretty much considered a neutral, and you do not even get a ballot. The former vassal still had a powerful military and immediately destroyed his lord's capital. (Normally this would be impossible without the Infernal Courts approval) then was on their way to take my mine. I wasn't powerful enough to fight their titanic Sons of Typhon, and it was reinforced by the indestructible Adamantine Guard. I just had an out of place Legion with a battering ram. I went back to the library to find some manuscripts to teach my forces to march without rest to race to their capital first to destroy it just in time to save my mine. When you are winning you should always protect the bureaucrats who keep you in power.This is the best strategy game I've played in recent memory.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a volunteer Play-tester "Hellraiser" in the month prior to the game's release, a testament to the developers aim to tackle and quash bugs prior to the launch, I received the game for free, but have also on launch purchased two copies for friends. My experience as a volunteer was positive with frequent game updates and good communication with the community management team. I think the game is in a good state at launch and look forward to seeing the community grow.The designers have meticulously crafted a dark, immersive atmosphere that pulls you into the heart of Machiavellian demonic politics and warfare. The attention to detail and vibe created in the character designs, lenticular/2.5D unit cards, and animations is commendable. I think like Armello there's enough variability and challenge in the design to find the single player enjoyable and worthwhile with a series of chronicle missions with interesting and different play-styles.But the multiplayer is where the game shines. Engaging in demonic diplomacy with other players adds an unpredictable element to the game. Timing is key, knowing when to demand tribute from your friends and awareness of the tempo to the game enforced by the rules of the devilish conclave, can set you ahead or back, creating a dynamic and ever-changing landscape where alliances, counter-play, and betrayal is always lurking. Never though do you fear a run away score, as there's always the nuclear but difficult option, full blown war for control of hell. Setting yourself as the archenemy.I think Solium Infernum is simply good game design, offering an engaging blend of turn-based strategy, atmosphere, and politicking. It's an infernal journey that leaves you craving more. Whether you're a seasoned strategist or a newcomer to the genre, I think it's a must-play that will undoubtedly stand the test of time under the good curation of League of Geeks and is a worthy successor to the original game of the same name.tldr: It's a triumph of strategy and infernal machinations. Play it with your friends!

_childDocuments_.review: I rly like this game.I have played a lot of Civ5, Civ6 and Endless Legend previously and that experience is what made me turn my eyes to Solium Infernum initially, me see hexes me click. This is not like them, Solium Infernum has a lot of very big twists compared to those 4X turn-based games, and to be fair, the main resemblance is a hex board, with some important hexes and the game is divided in turns, and I cant go further than that but I like it nonetheless very much and it was a good suprise to not match my initial expectations,The experience so far is very captivating due to a lot of player interaction throughout the whole game and an action limit tied to order slots is a new "resource" to be managed each turn.  The various actions are all very interesting and full of flavour although some might seem to be weaker than others in the current game state.I very much appreciate the constant updates and new content (free and DLC) being added and consider the devs to be very engaged with the playerbase. So far, some small tweaks have already provided an improved gameplay experience and I consider that still some work is required. For the record, I agree with all changes made so far and think they are directed to the same goals as mine.My position so far is that some QoL features, more control over game turn timers for async and for live games are crucial. I am currently playing with mostly friends on async and it would be a great to pause the game if anyone is in a busy week and wont manage to submit their turn. Furthermore, I think some gameplay balance/changes can better improve the experience. A topic that has fueled a lot of discussions is how to unlock extra order slots during a game to viabilize new strategic "paths" viable and make gameplay less streamlined.To summarize, I recommend this game. I am really unsure what type of player would enjoy it as has a very distinct gameplay and mechanics to all that I have played before so I guess the reader could allow themselves to a good surprise. I still think it needs some work to make each new game more interesting and to allow different play paths.

_childDocuments_.review: Hello.I've invested something around 50 hours in this game (demo+multiplayer test). I have no experince with original game from 2007 (?). First thing i would like to tell you - it is not 4X game, closest game i can think about is Armello. I even call it Armello 2.0 when i advertise it among my friends. You can misjudge what this game actually is based on trailers, check demo first is my advice.It is a really deep pseudo board game (you cant built this game IRL, to much stuff to calculate behind the scene). Replayability is insane, there is a lot of ways to get a victory. Matches can keep your attencion until the last turn because of multiple ways to counter play showball and achive a victory. You will question every step your enemy takes and even more if he do nothing on the map. After 50 hours i can say i got a grasp on a early\mid game strategy for a single archfiend, but i keep loosing late game. And there are 8 of them, each customisable with relics. As i said replayability is insane.Game have really deep mechanics, which you cant tell from a first view. Even combat which looks like a basic mechanic, actually is really deep, every unit is unique. Throw in preators, rule changing artefacts, terrain, support, events and combat alone will be a hard to master. Not gonna tell you about each mechanic this way, beleave me there is alot to learn and master.On other side of things beside gameplay game itself is pretty simple. There is no progression, matchmaking or anything else to add up to intertainment modern game usually have. Creat a lobby, play a game. That's it. But looking at Armelllo im sure game will develop and become another digital board game gem like Armello.

_childDocuments_.review: (I was privileged enough to be a playtester but will be gifting a copy or two to friends)Solium Infernum from 2009 is one of my all-time favourites and while I was thrilled to hear it was being remade with the blessing of original creator Vic Davis, I was also apprehensive given how close it is to my dark heart. Well I shouldn't have been! League of Geeks have done such a brilliant job of not only bringing everything up-to-date, but they've made some really smart changes to help streamline the experience without diluting what made the original game so remarkable.Solium Infernum is a deliciously thoughtful and devious strategy game where every decision has weight. While it does have single-player, the multiplayer is where the real magic is, especially with friends, and it's the best way of losing them. It has live play but the slow burn of asynchronous is so dramatic and intoxicating.The presentation across the board is top notch too, from the music and sound effects to the 2D artwork, user interface and, of course, the archfiends themselves. I've spent a lot of time just ogling at it all! But to think that such a niche and beloved game would get such a full-blooded remake is still unbelievable to me, but here we are and I couldn't be happier with the results. What a treat.This may very well dethrone the original, which is quite something, and basically means that it'll probably be my game of the year!

_childDocuments_.review: Solium Infernum is a Hell-themed, glacially-paced, 4X strategy game, with a very strong retro PBeM style.  Normally this would be a good thing, and I have moved many PBeM games over the years.  Unfortunately, I can't recommend Solium Infernum.The primary issues for me are the pace and the generally fussy, tedious nature of the gameplay.  At it's core, you're restricted to just 2 actions (later expandable to 3).  To say this slows the pace of the game would be an understatement.  And there is a lot to do!  Literally everything takes one of those precious actions.  Move a legion?  Yup.  Cast a spell?  Yup.  Spend your prestige to increase your rank?  Yup.  Buy an artifact for your legion?  Yes.  Send that artifact to the actual legion to use?  Yeah.  Send a diplomatic request?  Need to merge your coins into larger sized coins so you don't run out of space in your treasury?  Oh yeah.  It goes and on.  You get the idea.And on that fussy gameplay, the coin/treasury "mini-game" is a great example.  You earn coins in small denominations (think 1 or 2), but you only have so many slots both to store and also to spend, so you will need to keep merging your coins into higher denominations (and mix them together for space), which is both annoying and makes losing them to enemy spells all the harder.  Note all of this work takes at least one of your 2 orders for that turn.There are hints of grand strategy games with the idea of only fighting a way with "cause", which I typically find tedious, but in this case it is trivially easy to start a vendetta so it didn't seem to slow anything down.Visually, the overworld map looks good, if a bit plain due to the drab features of Hell (like the Moon with some lava rivers.Overall, though, the game just doesn't seem that fun.  Obviously the design is to make you prioritize the most important action that turn, but really, it just slows things down and doesn't seem to add much.  Perhaps it made sense in a PBeM game where you'd want your players to only spend a few minutes per daily turn, but that doesn't work in a game you'd want to sit down and really dig into like the Civilization series.

_childDocuments_.review: A true indie gem! This game finally managed to 'scratch the itch' I had for about 20 years! A bit of context. I got my first PC really late, so, naturally, as a kid, I used to hang out at my friends' house who already had PCs. That's where I first discovered Disciples II and fell in love with it's art, gameplay, and the genre in general. I've always been on a lookout for similar experiences, but kind of given up seeing what happened to the Disciples franchise as well as industry's overall shift to more accessible games. While Solium Infernum looks and plays nothing like Disciples, personally for me, spiritually, it feels very close. This game delivers on all important aspects that make up a unique strategy game -- great systems depth, unorthodox approach to strategic play, absolutely amazing art and the asynchronous multiplier ties is all together into an even better package. I would love for more people to discover this game and support the developer by owning it so that we could send a message that players appreciate these kinds of games and experiences. No weird battle passes, skins, requirement for online connection, no gotchas or lootboxes. It's a pure game worth supporting. With that said, if you are even remotely interested in this type of game or even the strategy genre as a whole, I strongly urge you to consider buying Solium Infernum.

_childDocuments_.review: This game requires deep strategy and careful planning. Some other 4X titles give you hundreds of options and involve intense micromanagement. Solium Infernum further rewards scheming and acting like you are the arch demon you're playing as. Enacting rituals to drain another players treasury, releasing a titan while a war is going on to further sow chaos, and vying for the favor of an enclave that can be usurped is just a magical combination. Highly recommend trying this game out!

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT (Apr/24/24): Patch notes listed, and its a case of throwing a lot of minor changes that in many cases contradict each other (wanting to reward interaction by reducing default unit count, wanting to reduce Crown of Bureaucracy's impact by making it even more important for  more expensive Lv4 Powers, meaning a longer period of time behind ahead both on the initial order and on turns with Lv4 Power orders, etc) and in other cases are narrow adjustments specific to the Discord house ruled meta, which don't impact the experience of most MP or SP players.To sum it up - if economy was too essential prior to this patch, you don't "nerf" it by making it even more relevant than it already was! The meta will be the same this patch - heavy turtling followed by diplo/ritual wars in similarly skilled private rooms, while public room meta will be the usual Pandaemonium/Stronghold rush by Turn 12-20 if there's a good player in the room.On a positive note, looks like there's AI handicap levels now. Many AI bugs/logic issues remain unstated or unfixed (the patch notes are intentionally vague in many areas), so I'm not sold enough to check it out, but maybe there's hope that the AI won't intentionally sac units on striders or infinitely attack places of power for 1 damage anymore?---EDIT (Apr/9/24): Now with DLC, holding the next patch hostage behind its release on April 23rd!I've since been personally called out by a developer for being blunt about some of the many issues SI has in its current state, source: Note that we're 8+ weeks removed from the delayed "full release" launch window and that I can name 20+ bugs and blatant AI logic issues that exist in the current build, not to mention the various major balance issues that have been reduced to a specific pocket meta by this dev team, that of Discord private lobbies that ban ritual excommunication, and so I have no hope that the upcoming singular balance patch will address nearly enough of the issues SI multiplayer has.I'm done with SI, and this is likely to be the last update to this review unless the developers continue to double down on bad policy. Perhaps the best game I'd never recommend to anyone, in the sense that I got a lot of hours out of it in spite of its many issues, but do keep in mind that a majority of my playtime was spent labbing various interactions and openings in singleplayer in hopes SI would be viable in MP longterm, which is a big part of why I know about all the outstanding bugs and balance issues that persist.---This used to be a Positive review.I'm now convinced, post-launch window, that this was a rushed out MVP (Minimum Viable Product) which is just functioning enough for them to sell.Hotseat support? Never coming, "because it wouldn't increase sales enough to justify". Direct quote: LAN support? Hah, you think they want for a family not to have to buy one copy for every player?AI support? Technically exists, in the sense that its set up to self-sabotage through a lot of faulty priorities. But hey, look at our roadmap, we totally know it sucks, and will remind you constantly that online multiplayer is the "real" way to play and that our AI "will never reach human levels", which is a strawman that nobody is actually asking for. This, while being surprised that the majority of their playerbase plays single player in a game that "supports" it.But hey, don't forget to join their Discord! Otherwise, all sorts of undocumented aspects of our game will remain a mystery, because we can't be bothered to have a functioning tutorial/AI/in-game reference/manual/etc for our MVP.There's also plenty of bugs. Lots of broken tooltips, lots of log flooding capable of eating up a GB or more of storage space in mere weeks, crashes on open/crashes on close, timer stalled multiplayer lobbies, the list goes on...which would be fine if this were an Early Access game like their currently shuttered Jumplight Odyssey, but its not.I'll probably continue to play since its a sunk cost, but any amount of good will granted these devs thanks to Armello is gone. Not that they'll care, since they have my money through multiple copies already...

_childDocuments_.review: This is a unique idea, though sometimes creativity comes at the price of quality. This is one such scenario. I've tried developing my own RPG systems before, and it is truly tempting to make all sorts of complex hidden action mechanics in order to make pvp 'fair'. The problem is, that unless carefully constructed, it bogs down the gameplay significantly. In this case, for diplomacy, the time it takes to get anything done is staggering. One turn to make a demand. One turn for them to accept or reject demand. If they reject demand, you have one turn to declare vendetta. That's 1-3(!) turns for a diplomatic action, and you can make no other diplomatic actions with that player in the meantime - even if they're the ones enacting the diplomacy! That means, in effect, you can actually DDOS your enemies by sending a pointless emissary for up to 3 turns, preventing them from doing anything diplomatically against you. That's bonkers.The very narrow number of orders is also quite annoying. You do get to expand your order pool quite a bit, but that does mean that the early-game feels incredibly tedious and grindy as you simply work up resources to get the first order boost. Like, nothing much is happening in that time for anyone, really.The resources in this game is also atrocious. The theming is arbitrary. Every currency is stored as an object, and you can at max pay with 8 of these objects; which means to pay for expensive things, you and your hellish accountants has to put all your devilish scheming on pause for the price of an order (which are limited per turn) in order to... Merge objects into a more valuable object so that you can then next turn buy that thing you wanted. That's... Annoying and obtuse. Add to this that there are 4 types of currency stored in this object, of which you have **almost no way to get a stable income with any of them**, rolling randomly between resources every turn in an otherwise strategy-heavy, hidden-action, mind-against-mind game, it's just... It feels like someone introduced dice mechanics into a game of chess, it makes no sense.I don't know. I'm disappointed. This game is on the surface something I'd love, but it's just so rough around the surface. So many of the design decisions just make absolutely no sense to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Solium Infernum is a remake of the acclaimed turn-based strategy game originally released on PC in 2009 and now remade by League of Geeks, the team who previously developed Armello. I haven’t played the original, so I can’t really make a comparison, but what I found in Solium Infernum is a very interesting 4X strategy game with some pretty unique mechanics. At first glance, the game seems like the perfect marriage between Civilization and Game of Thrones with a dark setting and a great focus on diplomacy. The story takes place in Hell immediately after Satan (the Prince of Darkness) mysteriously disappears. In this infernal land multiple factions fight against each other for the control of the throne; these factions are guided by 8 Archfiends, each one with different stats and playstyles, but also customizable with relics that provide different bonuses and must be equipped before the start of the game. The tutorial is quite lengthy and explains everything in great detail, yet due to the complexity of the game it takes some time to learn mechanics, understand Archfiends pros & cons and how to build an effective strategy, so you will inevitably fail a lot. I’m saying this because if you are not a lover of strategy games, this certainly isn’t an easy game to start with the genre.You start by picking one of the Archfiends and the goal is to take control of the throne, but there are many ways to achieve it. The standard route, also suggested by the game, would be winning through democratic election. After a certain number of turns, the Conclave declares the player with the highest Prestige (a sort of reputation that can be increased in many ways) as the winner. You can also manipulate the Conclave by lying and cheating, but in this case, you must equip a specific relic which changes the objectives of your entire campaign, essentially pushing you to befriend another Archfiend and betray him at the end, stealing the victory. There are of course less diplomatic options for winning. You can try to take the throne by force and conquer Pandaemonium, the capital of Hell. This isn’t an easy task, because the city is heavily guarded and you only have a chance after becoming strong enough, so probably very late in the campaign. The other brutal way of winning is by eliminating all Archfiends by taking down their strongholds, which is a really difficult job, especially when playing online against real players.Regardless of your course of action, the gameplay is all about manipulating and gaining an advantage over your enemies. You only have one stronghold during the game and you can capture tiles by ending a turn with a legion standing there. Capturing tiles is a basic but recurrent mechanic because it can block enemies’ access to important places. You can’t really enter into battle against enemies without any reason, but you can easily fake one, for example by insulting your rival or demanding a tribute and then declaring a “vendetta” (essentially a declaration of war), which allows you to obtain prestige by conquering the enemies’ tiles and destroying their legions. Capturing Points of Power on the map (before other enemies) is another effective way of quickly obtaining prestige. At the beginning of the game, you only have two slots available for orders, which for example you can use for moving your legions, performing magic rituals, voting an edict and having diplomatic talks with your rivals. With time, you can unlock more slots (up to 6) and upgrade your Archfiend abilities, expanding the possibilities of your strategy.Single player offers a skirmish mode where you play against the AI and the Chronicles mode, which is a series of 8 specific scenarios where you play as each of the Archfiend and must face continuously growing challenges. A classic online PvP mode is also available, but one of the best features is the impressive asynchronous multiplayer mode, which allows you to play a game that can potentially last for weeks or even months, but you can close the game and when you open it the next time you can see the consequences of your orders and those from other players. It’s a really a fun alternative to standard multiplayer mode, well suited for those who don’t have enough time to play long sessions but are willing to dedicate some time to play against other players. The game also sends notifications from Steam (client and mobile app) to remind you about your turn, which is really a useful feature.Graphically speaking, the game looks quite good, even though the Archfiends look a bit cartoonish. The artwork for your units, item and event cards is also very beautiful, better than the actual 3D design. The PC version seems to be greatly polished and fortunately I didn’t encounter any noticeable bugs. Solium Infernum is one of those strategic games that is better experienced with online players, because the Archfiends’ basic stats and playstyle can be subverted by the individual choices of each player who can keep your stress and paranoia high all the time. The AI isn’t that impressive unfortunately, so single player mode can be less fun, especially after more playthroughs, but still, this is a very particular strategy game that stands out for its charming setting and its complex system.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've ever played Armello and enjoyed it I think you'll find Solium Infernum well worth its price and your time.
