_childDocuments_.review: Solium Infernum is a hell of a game - literally. You play as one of eight Archfiends vying for the throne of Hell after Satan's mysterious disappearance. You must use your cunning, diplomacy, and military might to outwit and outfight your rivals in this turn-based grand strategy game.The game is based on John Milton's epic poem Paradise Lost, which depicts Hell as a fiery lake of darkness, where the fallen angels suffer eternal torment. Milton also portrays Hell as a state of mind, where the demons are haunted by their own pride, envy, and hatred. Solium Infernum captures both aspects of Milton's vision, creating a rich and immersive world that is both fascinating and terrifying.The game is full of strategic depth and replay value. You can customize your Archfiend with various attributes, perks, and artifacts, and recruit different types of infernal legions, including massive titans. You can also cast rituals, perform events, and manipulate the infernal conclave, where you can make demands, insults, and accusations against your opponents. The game supports both single-player and multiplayer modes, with sessional and asynchronous options.Solium Infernum is a complex and challenging game that requires careful planning, patience, and ruthlessness. It is also a game that rewards creativity, experimentation, and deception. You will need to adapt to the changing circumstances, exploit the weaknesses of your enemies, and forge alliances that may or may not last. You will also need to deal with the consequences of your actions, as every move you make will have lasting effects on the balance of power and the fate of your soul.Solium Infernum is a masterpiece of strategy gaming, and a must-play for fans of Milton, Hell, and devilish fun. It is a game that will make you laugh, cry, and scream, as you experience the joys and sorrows of ruling in Hell. It is a game that will make you question your morals, your sanity, and your humanity. It is a game that will make you say: "Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven."

_childDocuments_.review: Not very impressed with the mechanics.You have lots of decisions to make, but can potentially have your hand forced in to using orders just to respond depending on whether you are targeted by others or not. They may have contributed nothing to the game, ignored all prestige gain, but as long as they have been able to spend all their orders and tribute on ranking their powers up they can essentially Uno reverse card the game because of how powerful they will be.The rest of the players need to have identified this some 15+ turns ago somehow to stand a chance to gang up on them.  And most of us are playing with randoms, not a friend group.  So getting all the other randoms to respond correctly while they all have their own agenda and designs on winning is going to be a long shot.As there are random, and by it's nature imbalanced maps, the player who gets to sit under the radar is largely going to be luck.Like a lot of these 'diplomacy' games, playing with randoms is a crap shoot, you will get people leave the game and the very sub par AI will skew the game. I can't recommend it in it's current imbalanced state.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing SI since it's first release by the original developer a decade ago. This is a great game, although I would say that the new devs didn't always improve on the original. This will be half review, half a comparison between SI1 and SI2.Graphics: The most obvious difference bewteen SI1/SI2 is the complete graphical overhaul. SI1 had very stark (and initially off-putting) greyscale graphics for the main map screen, although the unit/card art was phenomenal. SI2 continues to have good card art, but has implemented 3D map graphics and animations for units moving and fighting each other. There are... okay. They make the map harder to read and aren't particularly remarkable. But I suppose the devs felt like they would not be able to sell a 2D version of game. Ultimately though, the switch to 3D is more of a sidegrade than an upgrade. There is one net negative though: if you're playing a live game, it can take 30-60 seconds to watch all of the animations play out, which is a substantial chunk of your 5 minute turn time!Writing: The writing is noticeably worse than in the original. Card descriptions and other types of flavour text in particular are not as well written as in SI1. This was disappointing, since the new devs could have simply carried over the crisp and yet somehow Biblical tone of the original descriptions and flavour text.Sound: The music and sound effects are okay, but didn't stand out to me either.Gameplay: There are so many changes that I'll only touch on some of the most important.1. Your archfiend is now chosen from a list of pre-defined archetypes (the deceit archfiend, the praetor archfiend, the economy archfiend, etc). This is a reasonably interesting choice, but it can be annoying if you felt like player a particular character, only to join a multiplayer game and find that your top choice is already taken.2. Some customization options are retained through choosing rings/amulets/crowns. I'm very glad they kept customization, and I like generally like the options that are on offer.3. The powers have been rebalanced, and crucially Charisma is no longer overpowered, since tribute quality now depends on rank rather than Charisma itself. Simialrly, wrath has been rebalanced by removing the overpowered tier 5 spell that would supercharge legions and make them unstoppable killing machines. These are all welcome changes.4. Rank is now improved during the game, rather than being determined as part of character creation. Higher rank gives better tribute (its most important effect), as well as unlocking better diplomacy options. Another welcome an improvement.5. Praetor combat has been completely reworked. Rather than queuing up a series of moves over several rounds ,you now choose a single move, which belongs to one of three types. The three types counter each other in a rock-paper-scissors fashion. This is generally an improvement, since SI1 praetors tended to be a fairly homogenous bunch. And SI2 praetors seem to be less vulnerable to a single praetor getting a runaway lead over all potential challengers.6. They took out the census mechanic that awarded prestige based on number of cantons controlled every ten turns. I think this was a bad idea. The census added pressure to expand your domain, made vendettas over cantons more worthwhile, and added yet another early-game priority competing for your limited turns per round. It also provided an alternative way to score prestige for someone who did not have access to capturable places of power in the early game.7. There are now occasional votes in the Conclave about events. They are okay, but feel like event cards with an extra step. They aren't bad, but I would not miss them either.8. There are many new rituals, a handful of new items, and a great many legions/items were removed. The quantity of trash legions in particular was greatly reduced, which is another positive change.9. Players get some free tribute drip-fed to them every 5 turns. This is a nice way of smoothing out balance between players and another good way reduce the importance of charisma builds.10. In SI1 combat, the two side made a level check and based on the results, the winner got +1 or +2 to a random stat. This made it risky to launch close battles, since the roll might go against you. That has been eliminated.UI/UX: This is one area of the game where were nothing but missteps.- Archfiends are sometimes identified by name, sometimes by portrait, sometimes by a really annoying symbol that is hard to distinguish from other symbols. It's never consistent and requires you to memorize all of the portraits and symbols, when it should have just standardized to using the name everywhere, I found myself constantly clicking back to check which archfiend was represented by which symbol/colour/portrait. Not good UI/UX design.- In the ritual room you drag cards into slots and cannot click them into slots, unlike all other screens in the game. Only the vault/payment screen uses dragging, and even there you can right-click to move items. Ritual screen breaks this rule.- The bazaar will tell you that you cannot afford an item, or that you need to consolidate tribute to make the payment, then dump you back to the item page for the thing it just told you that you cannot buy, obscuring the consolidate tribute button between an extra menu screen that now needs to be clicked away.- Hitting escape sometimes closes windows, but not always.- Many UI elements are quite small and discrete, even though they are ones players will use regularly. Sometimes this occurs because the UI is being cluttered with useless buttons (why is there a "turn off visible borders" button at all, since players will always want to see this information? Any why is it given equal size and prominence to the main menu button!).- The icons for the four main screens (sanctum, diplomacy, bazaar, and ritual) disappear once you click on one of them, which means that changing screens takes longer to correct than necessary, since you have to quit back to the main screen and cannot simply switch one from screen of interest to a new one, you have to go back to the main menu first. It surely looks prettier this way, but player convenience is compromised.- Prestige totals for other archfiends are not displayed on the main screen, even though this is information that a player will want to consult on a regular basis if they are playing multiple online games at once.- Text telling you that you bid on an item obscures its price, which is information you might want to consult when trying to figure out if cancelling that bid will allow you to buy something else.... I could go on. Virtually every screen of this game has a UI/UX flaw that adds unnecessary friction to the user experience. If there was one thing the devs should do, it's put a lot of work into the UI.- If you're into SI2 multiplayer, you'll be logging on several times a day to process turns. For some reason, the game does not want to show you your list of active games by default, and instead makes you click an icon to open it. Why would the default state be to hide information that a player will be constantly checking?Other- SI1 has pretty bad AI, although it was frankly astonishing that AI could play a game this complex at all, once you learned that the AI in question was programmed on an archaic Adobe product never designed for making games in the first place. The new AI is much better, although in a game this complex, it still struggles compared to a human player.- The original SI had a fairly harsh ruleset, particularly around excommunication. The devs here have chosen to smooth over a lot of that harshness. It definitely makes the game more welcoming for newbies, at the cost of some ruthless strategies being denied to veteran players. Your mileage on this change will vary depending on which group you fall into.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals are top tier with fantastic art and atmosphere. Character designs are especially awesome and channel the spirit of some of my favorite dark and hellish artists like Mike Mignola and Kaneko Kazuma. Lore and writing seem great. And the theme! I've been really looking forward to it. ... But after the tutorial and a scenario later, I quit and refunded. Why? Because it just wasn't fun to me. Very limited actions per turn combined with "3 turns to complete X" objectives, and shallow number vs. number combat were not great, but the thing that broke my enjoyment in particular: the Currency/Tokens/Resource system. Its a big part of the game and one of my least favorite in a strategy game, ever. I get that this is a board game style game, not a 4X, but it just put me right off. Again, you get limited actions per turn (until you invest tokens in unlocking more), and an action includes doing everything from moving a single unit, undertaking a single diplomatic action, upgrading, rituals, etc. You also have to have the right resource tokens on hand to undertake actions that have costs... and you have to spend an action to generate a random spread of tokens. Passive resource granting events happen, but they're also random. And then there are 8 slots that you can put resource tokens into to pay for literally everything in this game: rituals, leaders, units, artifacts... Tokens have values of 1-3 with 4 types. Rarer/more powerful purchases cost more tokens, so you have to combine multiple tokens into higher value single tokens. This act to combine tokens, yes, you guessed it, *takes an action.* And takes a turn to complete. These tokens can also be stolen from your inventory. The resulting waste of turns generating random tokens and combining those tokens to just do basic things like buy units and upgrades for them felt needlessly tedious, and even more annoying when thinking about how to plan out bigger purchases. Amusingly, I can't help feel the devs know this at some level, because the tutorial narration by Belial calls the economics of hell as dull and the "Rule of 8" as arbitrary and annoying... I think he got it right. The economy side of this game sunk it for me. I'll keep my eye on it to see if they adjust anything but for now... Just didn't feel as epic as i hoped at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: A passable implementation of the original classic, but in this day and age, with an AI this sadly inept, the lack of single-player is conspicuously felt. I'm also not sold on the interface. Sure, it's an improvement on the original, but so is a sharp stick in the eye. This should have been better than it was.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: An archfiend swore to be my vassal then it started to steal from my vault.Demand tributes from an archfiend, I killed their army for refusing.Bid for a nice artifact in the Bazaar, but was outbid by another cunning Archfiend.Archfiend was going to be elected by Hell Conclave, But I intervened for having more prestige at the last turn.It's just like democracy, but with corrupted voting and also the chance to f**k democracy up if things don't go your way.That's pretty fair in Hell.Better to rule in Hell than to serve in Heaven.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I played and loved the 2009 indie-darling version of this game and have always described it as "like Diplomacy except you're all literal demons (as opposed to figurative demons, yes I too am aware of anarchist critiques)". That part has absolutely not changed, and the changes that HAVE been made are largely for the better. League of Geeks have remade an already excellent and underrated game in an actual game engine rather than Adobe Flash, made a ton of visual and audio upgrades that ooze theme, built in really helpful documentation and SP tutorials, and clarified a few of the mechanics (like Archfiend customisation) in really intuitive ways - and all on top of the underlying well-designed and creatively mechanical board game experience.It really is best played in MP (both live and asynchronous game modes are avaiable!), so if you can't convince your friends to pick this up then definitely look into one of the forum or Discord communities playing this game to find opponents. But I definitely don't regret picking this up and I hope you won't either. You'll cultivate a demonic laugh, you'll ponder the wine in front of you and your opponent, you'll feel like a genius sometimes when you pull some cunning trick out of the bag, you'll be knocked into the dirt sometimes when one of your opponents pulls one out instead, but find a way to claw your way out and pull the bastard down with you. You'll learn to hate your friends in the way only the best games teach. It launched at a high price point for indie but if this is your vibe it's worth every penny.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Deceit is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ op, stealing an fully upgraded army for minimal cost and defence spells against it dont work. Only counter is to also tech deceit and steal it back. Lost 3 games in a row to deceit spells even when i try to counter with prophecy or attacking them directly but they can only be attacked voluntarily and even if they say yes they just steal the army.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: This is an easy recommend. For those familiar with the original diamond in the rough this is an updated version. Some QoL changes, better graphics, a few minor changes, but the overall gameplay is the same. If you liked the original this is a must buy. If you didn't play the original this is a very slow and methodical strategy game that is both remarkably simple and dense at the same time. Its simple in that you aren't really building cities, looking for the best spots for new cities, and managing upkeep and economics of a civilization. So on the surface it would seem like a lot of turn based strategy game tropes and features are missing. What its replaced with is theft, magic, backstabbing, false flag operations, and various other tools for people who prefer victory through means other than direct force. It plays more like a board game then a standard strategy game.The artwork is great, performance is excellent I play on a 3 year old laptop that was mediocre in specs when i bought it let alone now and it plays flawlessly, and the gameplay loop is satisfying.There are some flaws in it though. Tribute is still overwhelming powerful which makes Mammon the best Archfiend by a wide margin. Played him my first game was able to max rank him, almost max out all his stats, raise massive amounts of armies, relics, and praetors, and still win with more than 800 prestige with my nearest competitor at only just north of 100. No other Archfiend that I have played has been able to win by such a staggering margin.Maps are too small even the large one, due to this game length isn't always satisfying but there is something to be said about a strategy game that can be won in a couple hour sitting rather than ten or more hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: A solid remake of the 2009 classic.  The art and UI design is excellent, much improving the onboarding experience from the Cryptic Comet version.   About a dozen turns into first Asynch game and the Turn notifications in Steam is a handy/clever function.   At $52 CDN it was a bit pricey to buy a copy for friends but at $32 it's WELL worth it if you have a few friends interested in asynchronous turn based strategy.*EDIT*Got about 24 hours worth of games into this now, 4 Asynch games played between "Friends" (After this game using that term loosely).   Still HIGHLY recommend as long as you have "FRIENDS" to torment with!
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: The best Asynchronous multiplayer game I've played to date. Respectful of the player's time in a way few games can manage, and devilishly intricate in all the right ways. Don't be fooled by the low hours of reviewers; You can sneak your daily turn in fifteen minutes before bed, as well as all evening sessions with friends.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is very fun just from a game design perspective. Every action you take feels like one of your opponents can exploit it or use it to their advantage. It feels like everything you do could just fall into one of your opponents traps. I also really enjoy how the game feels like it encourages bravado or showing your hand even though that makes it easier for your opponents to try to counter you.    In short this re imagining is really fun I recommend it if you want a turn based strategy game that can throw a wrench in all the players plans randomly. From experience my first multiplayer game with friends the early game had us surviving with no ability to collect tribute for 5 turns and then a Angel coming down and destroying all the players units.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great however I do have to say, do NOT buy this if you're looking for something akin to Civ or any other grand strategy out there tbh. Many people have described this as "Civ in Hell" but it really isnt it. If you're familliar with Armello, a previous game of these devs, think of this as that but instead of having one character, each player controls their empire. Its essentially more of a political intrigue game with grand strategy elements.The goal is to basically become the ruler of Hell and you've got a TON of ways to do that. Build up prestige and get elected, kill everyone else with armies, manipulate stuff with rituals (spells) and diplomacy, backstab etc. The combat in the game isnt anything crazy, its literally a maths game where the higher numbers wins, however due to every army having 3 seperate phases (ranged, melee, infernal) and different slots that can interfere with the values of those numbers plus the rituals, the combat can be surprisingly deep. Imo where the real meat of the game is at is the intrigue and the way you interact with other players. Hoping into a multiplayer game and figuring out what everyones plan is while also trying to build one up yourself, constantly changing your tactics while trying to hide the true win con you're going towards is VERY fun. When you get a basic grasp at all of the systems and try to incorporate them all to your playstyle, you have a really, really deep game with a lot of flexible options as to how you wanna tackle problems.The art is also beautiful but I'm also a sucker for gloomy, dark colours so people that like vibrant colours might be a bit turned off by it. Then again, its inspired by a very specific version of Hell so it makes sense why they chose to make it the way it is.The only real issue I see with the game is, unfortunately, the player numbers. I understand that these games are quite niche, especially one that seems to be not really grand strategy, not really 4x, not really armello but more of something in-between but even so the numbers are low. Its peak was 1,1K players and its currently sitting on 660 active players and the 24hour peak at 770. Yes it is not a game where you need a lot of people to have fun but its still disheartening to see, especially considering how a lot of people in the community expect the game to be supported, which probably wont happen if the numbers of the game are deemed to be too low. Its a really good game and it deserves more attention.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: This is an INCREDIBLE game. 14 hours and 3 games in, and every "archfiend" offers a completely different playstyle, and with 8 separate leaders to choose from, that variety will keep paying off. The game seems to be at a sweet point somewhere around 40-50 turns without being too hard for newer players (especially ones who are newer to grand strat games) also without being too easy. My first game past the tutorial was a 70 turn game with maxed out opponents and maxed out "places of power" (buildings you can take over for bonuses) and it got rather boring the last 15 turns or so. The game gets easier as you go longer, at least against AI's, so for people with small friends lists or those who are less socially inclined, id suggest aiming for shorter games. The game does seem to edge towards players over AI as it doesn't seem like the basic game mode is super challenging. The AI also makes odd moves from time to time, but part of that is almost certainly linked to the "order slots" mechanic where you can only make a limited number of moves and gain more throughout the game. A sister mechanics to the base game is the "reliquary" which is a selection of treasures you can start the game with that act as bonuses. I'm unsure if the ai opponents get these items, but as a player, there are definitely stronger items for certain archfiends but some stand out so much like "why wouldn't i take that?"Regarding other game modes, there is a set of challenge scenarios aimed at learning the game beyond the tutorial where you pick from each of the different archfiends' stories and some of them do seem quite challenging at a glance.In regards to actual cons:The game feels like it needs a certain layer of polish. One of the neat things about the game is this huge roster of armies and "praetors" (generals for your armies). Every one of them has a different piece of lore behind them, but the "models" shown in game are all basically identical within each archfiend's faction. Also, a secondary mechanic of "praetor duels" is present, but they present merely a text-based "win or fail" notification rather than having individual models fight each other within pandemonium's grand arena. Rituals could be done differently as well; a small cutscene of your archfiend walking up to an altar with a pile of sacrifices and eldritch energies bursting from within your stronghold. Instead we get a colored swirl around your stronghold and some "dark whispers" and its done. Overall: solid 8/10 game. Some key visual upgrades and some re balancing on the AI for longer, grander games would go a long way for gameplay longevity. Oh, btw, got sent here for the game thanks to  PravusGaming. Praise Pravus!
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I'm having fun!This isn't a typical 4x, and it's definitely not Civ in Hell like a lot of YouTubers are saying, so if you come expecting that you might be disappointed.But if you enjoy deduction type board games, this will sit well with you. If you like RNG shenanigans, be prepared, there are many. There are reviews here that criticise the RNG, but these are part of the game and part of the fun. You aren't supposed to be able to control everything, most of this game is about trying to tip the RNG in your favour rather than negating it.So if you don't like games where you can be exploited, misled and fooled by your opponent in ways you can't see coming, then don't play this game.But if you feel a little devilish and mischievous inside, come join the fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: A remake of a 15 year old game, Solium Infernum is an extremely complex board game made extremely simple by letting the computer handle all the backend math.A strategy/politics game, you move pawns around the board, collect resources, bid on auctions, make alliances, and try to hide your power level until the end of the game, winning out of nowhere. It's simple to learn, with a depth to master, and a LOT of potential for multiplayer.The quality of the remake is very high, so I recommend you try it out solo or with a group of devious friends. Give it a go! It's so rare to see a good remake of an underappreciated gem like this. Support good efforts like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: This game is going to be great one day but the devs need to fix a lot in order for that to happen. This is a tentative positive review.The UI and tooltips are really bad. You have to learn what things do by making mistakes because the tutorial and tooltips leave out critical pieces of info about what different items and abilities do/where they go.$10 for a single character is also pretty egregious. Could be the first ever successful implementation of 4x online multiplayer but it needs some work at the moment.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I'm greatly enjoying my time with this game. I like the initial simplicity of the kind of Rock Paper Scissors systems that is easy to pick up, and the variations that make them complicated to master. It's great to learn how to manage all the different aspects to keep your little region of hell functional and thwart the machinations of your competitors.That said there are some aspects I don't enjoy as much. Currency management is a bear, as is getting key information like turn order and action resolution. I can see how on the tabletop you could manage your currency and see your current statuses between turns, but in this game you're locked out while the actions resolve, So you end up constantly jumping around through UI panels to assess your game state before you decide your actions next turn. It would be nice to see clearly when your potential actions would fire off, so you don't waste actions. It would also be fantastic if you could pay for multiple turns of a ritual with overflow currency, instead of just losing it to the nether because the game doesn't give you small increment coins once you rank up.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: This is a PVP strategy game unlike any other you'll ever play, and I cannot recommend it enough. It's a faithful remake of an original cult classic that applies modern game design principles to considerably improve upon the original experience.Hands-down, the best format imo is to grab a group of people and play via asynchronous turns. It's an ideal format for adults who don't have as much time to binge games all at once, and need to play when they have the time. You pop in, take in the board, play a turn that takes 20 minutes or even less, if that's all the time you have for it, and then wait for the other players to submit their turns.The kind of excitement you get from a notification of a new turn becoming ready is a thrill that's really unique to this type of game. Give it a shot, you won't get this kind of excitement from anywhere else.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Solium Infernum is unlike anything I've played before.  The game is primarily an asynchronous multiplayer game based around diplomacy.  The theme is a perfect fit for the gameplay and the game itself is very polished.  While the multiplayer lobby is typically empty, it doesn't mean the game isn't active, and it's fairly easy to get a multiplayer game started if you create your own lobby.  Because it's asynchronous, you can create a game and then log out while you wait for players to join.  Once the lobby is full, the game will start and your async timer will start (notification via steam).  You'll need to play a few single player games  to get the hang of the gameplay, but async multiplayer is the best way to play the game.While the game is great, and I recommend it, there are a few quality of life and game design issues that need to be worked out.  The biggest issue is the lack of incentive to play games to the finish.  You aren't penalized for leaving games early if you are losing.  It's really anticlimactic to be winning a game only to find every starts leaving and you are left with bots to finish the match with.  Another issue is there seems to be no incentive to be vassalized other than stealing the victory from your blood lord or 'Crown of the Kingmaker' where you select who you think will win and steal the victory if they do.  This makes players suspicious of any player who offers to be vassalized because coming in second place really isn't any different from losing so there is no other reason to do so unless you are planning for either of these victories which you have to decide on before the game even starts.While the UI is clean, its difficult to keep track of what has happened or will happen without leaving yourself notes (there is an in game notepad) or cross referencing a bunch of different menus.  Examples:* No countdown for upcoming votes* Your currency isn't visible from multiple menus making it difficult to determine if you have enough left over to pay for other things* Resistance isn't explained very wellTurn timers leave a bit to be desired.  Games can last anywhere from 45 to 65 turns depending on game length.  You hard set turn timers (1,2,3, or 7 days) and have no way to adjust them mid game.  I have other hobbies/obligations that occasionally require me to be away from an internet connection periodically and its really difficult to fit this game around that, as a game can potentially take months to complete depending on the turn timer.  It would be great if there was a limited system to temporarily pause or extend turn timers to account for this.  Right now the best you can do is find other like-minded players, set a week-long turn timer with the understanding that players should be taking their turns in a shorter time frame as much as possible.Also, the end of turn resolution only has two speeds: slow and instantaneous.  I'd like a speed setting so I can still see what is happening but at a much faster rate.The developers seem active at addressing QoL issues, so I'm sure this stuff will improve over time.  None of these issues are a dealbreaker though, the game is great and you shouldn't wait to play it.  A unique game like this takes time to fully iron out as there aren't standard/best practices that already established for the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: The theme alone was a sell for me but I actually ended up enjoying this a lot more than even Civ games. The mechanics are fun and it does capture that real tabletop board game feeling. I can see what other reviews mean when complaining about AI, as I am not very good at these games typically and I have won both matches I have played so far. However this game obviously seems meant more for playing with people rather than AI as much of the strategy is social and I don't see the point or fun of things like manipulation or the deceit skill tree if playing against robots.I think the game could do with a demo to play the (excellent) tutorial as I think many people would like this game if given a chance.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic reboot of the original. A solid, digital 4x board game with plenty of meaty decisions to bite into. All the destruction and backstabbing expected from a good ol' game of "dudes/ladies on a map", plus all the fun of demonic red tape pinning you down  to keep things ever so slightly civil. Sprinkle in some random events that can wreck havoc on everyone playing, and it's a guaranteed hoot. Asynchronous, turn-based play is a much appreciated option for those of us with a varied schedule or for playing with friends across time zones.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Rough around some edges but oh so good in so many ways, not least the fact that Solium Infernum is easily playable now, thanks to Steam integration (no more play-by-email, Dropbox, loading turn files, etc). There's a Feedback button within the game, and from my interactions with some of the League of Geeks people they are receptive to considerate feedback.I'll see you in hell.20240508 edit to add:This is to me now what Battle Chess was to me in the early 90s; chess (which I enjoy, then and now), with extra and thematic complexity. I've completed the first two Chronicles, one multiplayer game (not counting the ones where everyone bailed because either something didn't go their way or for some other reason- this is why I set my games to a week-long duration; to give players some leeway), and my dance card is full of half-way to almost-done games that are all so much fun, even the ones I'm definitely losing.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: In its current state do not consider this a single player game.  The AI is a pushover and all the real fun is in multiplayer.It might look a bit like it's a 4x or a tactical/strategic army movement game, but it's not at all.  It's a multi layered paper-scissors-rock, diplomacy, scheming bluffing and backstabbing game.I have some early on concerns around balance of a few things, but overall the game is excellent, dripping with theme and very well made
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Bought it because I played and replayed their previous game, Armello, which also happened to be an online boardgame.This one? Quite different. Instead of a single character, you control several troops. You have to handle borders and board colors too now. The result? It's both quite different and improves on what they did before with Armello. There's once again several ways to win the game, and at every turn you wonder if going for a different build wouldn't be better. The builds are a lot more differenciated now, and there's more ways to be vicious (hidden plots for the win), making the final victory somewhat more of a tossup than in Armello (as long as one doesn't very clearly dominate the game... but with shifting alliances the first place is not necessarily where you want to be for most of the game).The assymetric online game seems tailored to solve the issue Armello had in online play, where the turns took a loooooong time to be resolved. Here, you can just play your turn, then wait a day doing your stuff instead of having to wait before the screen. And from what little I've seen, it does work quite well.So all in all? Unless you're allergic to board games, this one's an excellent choice.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: A great game with amazing art style and unique mechanics.You play as an Archfiend - only below Satan in the contest for being "Objectively the worst person to have ever existed", and now that he's gone that number 1 spot could be yours. The game revolves around this Trial for the Throne, where you and other equally awful people have to prove who's truly the most awful to be around. Because this is almost a court trial, hence the name, the diplomacy is a VERY prominent aspect of the game, which sets it apart from other turn based strategy games. To get ahead you'll have to demand and extort others in the discovery phase, insult their credibility, and just steal stuff from them, because what's not nailed down is literally free like in real life. Should people decline your reasonable demands, the judges grant you an opportunity to deploy lethal force for their amusement and to redeem yourself in their eyes, as any disregard of your will is ultimately an insult to your own claim as the next Moderately Dim Majesty. To this end you can use infernal legions, infernal crackheads with a variety of combat experience and your own ability to conjure surface-to-surface missile strikes.In the end, Heck can be ruled only by 1 individual and should you master the art of being a scumbag it could certainly be you, or the dude who's been manipulating you from the start, or the dude that's been manipulating him from the start, or...
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: This game is probably the best 4X game for multiplayer I have played so far for the following reasons:-turns are always simultaneous since the game has a turn order among other things to determine which things happen first-it has a GREAT asynch game mode. you can play up to 10 games at the same time with turn timers ranging from 1 day to weeks or even a month. steam notifies you comfortably when you can make a move again-due to the limited amount of actions per turn it never becomes work (no 50 units to move in one turn and 30 cities to build in)-a live session takes about 2-3h depending on game length, shorter ones work just as well as longer ones-despite limited actions per turn, your options appear endless and figuring the best moves out is super rewarding-you can bet on an opponent to win and if he does, you win instead :D-nothing beats teleporting to the guy who is about to win and devour his capital so he dies a painful death shortly before the game ends-this game has often left me surprised by some moves enemies pulled out of their hatsFor singleplayer you're probably better off with other games, even though it is great to learn and practice the mechanics. The challenge missions are very well done and make you use all kinds of mechanics so you're well equipped for the real deal.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Getting back-stabbed and betrayed has never felt this good before. The theme of this game is fantastic! The way diplomacy is handled is the most engaging I have seen in similar games. Super fun with randoms on the internet, friends, or people from the game discord.More akin to playing Twilight Imperium (or similar) than a proper 4X game, but that's a plus as far as I'm concerned. You can play a game in a single sitting of 3-4 hours, or play over multiple days with the turn timer being 24h or more. Throughout the game you have a very limited amount of things you can do during a turn, almost everything costs you one of your "order" slots, of which you start with 2(generally) and can get up to 6. This means every decision is important, and it really feels that way.The production values are quite good, nothing too extraordinary, but the sound design is on point, and the visuals fit in very well with the setting.There are some balance issues once you try most things and figure out what is good, but the game is still very enjoyable, and the devs are actively listening to the community and working on the biggest issues.Now I just need to brainwash more of my friends into picking this up so we can have enough to fill a lobby.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I can't believe I didn't hear that they were making a remake of this game! I really wanted to play the original version but could never get my friends on board. So glad this has online multiplayer. I really love the new artwork, that's one thing that really got me interested in the original game. So far, the game has worked perfectly! I really like the way they implemented the asynchronous multiplayer, it makes it easy to play 3 or 4 games at once.Only improvements I'd suggest are: Making it easier to play on the SteamDeck. This game seems perfect for it. I've been playing mainly on it and it works fine, it just needs some control/UI updates to make it feel better. Other thing is the AI, it's a little too easy, which isn't the worst thing given that this game is much better with human opponents, but they could have them be a little smarter.Overall though I'd very much recommend this game. See you in hell!
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like classic political board games like Avalon Hills Dune or Diplomacy? How about political thrillers like game of thrones?  Well have I got a game for you! Solium Infernum fit's the mold of those half social deduction/half war games to a tee. League of Geeks remake stays true to the original Vic Davis game from 2009 while doing a lot to streamline the arcane systems in that edition to the game... and they also made it absolutely gorgeous while they were at it.The card and event art is all absolutely lovely, if occasionally in a grisly demonic fashion. Pretty much all of the mechanics and systems play into it's themes of a demonic war for the throne of hell. Streamlined as it has been, it's not a hard game to pick up and learn, the new tutorial is actually quite good at explaining the basics now, but mechanically it's extremely deep and intricate enough to keep you wanting to come back for another match, or just one more turn. I will say that the Ai is quite weak, and anyone with a basic understanding of the mechanics can beat them 9 falls out of ten. This is not a game for people only interested in offline play, but thankfully the Asynchronous turn system means that even busy people can play a grand strategy game, a few turns at a time over weeks... so unless you're totally terrified of human interaction, give it a go. Hell is other people after all.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing game that benefits from asynchronous multiplayer with the same impact that a fighting game benefits from rollback netcode.Also... I've never seen a strategy game with so many devilishly clever ways to mitigate snowball effects WHILE staying thematically correct.This game is a crimson jewel of value & fun.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most entertaining games I've played this year. Solium Infernum is one of those games where the underlying mechanics are straightforward. Diplomacy, magic, war, and everything else are all pretty easy-to-learn, yet they do not play quite like other, similar games. Wars are generally short, sharp affairs designed to attain a specific objective and end as soon as that objective is met (and unusually, you determine the objective as well as the time required for it). Politics between the arch-fiends consists of equally brief events....insults, demands, and short-lived alliances. This is Hell, after all. Territory is not as important as Prestige. Your legions can be all-conquering, but you're not trying to conquer land. You're trying to impress demonkind enough that they see you as a suitable candidate to sit upon the throne. There are many ways to earn Prestige, but at the end of the day becoming Dark Majesty revolves around accumulating as much Prestige as possible while using war, magic, diplomacy, and skullduggery to ensure that your fellow archfiends are but pale imitations of your masterful evil. There are several ways to win....there's even an option for pretending to be someone else's servant, letting THEM win, and then usurping their victory right out from under them. It's a very fun game. Five out of five stars, even with the occasional bug.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: A devilishly good digital board game. It's definitely got more board game in its DNA than 4X or turn-based strategy, which you'll see a tight action economy, the fact that it expects negotiation a deal making (and deal-breaking) among the players, and some of the random event draws. The single player is good for learning the mechanics (and there's a fair chunk to learn here), but the meat of the game is multiplayer, ideally with a group of friends who can really get into the back-stabbing spirit of things. There are a number of viable paths to victory, and the victory points can swing wildly in a couple of turns - part of the art of the game is not pulling too far ahead so every is tempted to focus on taking you down. If you enjoy tabletop games like Scythe or Twilight Imperium, and want a similar experience in a digital form, give this a whirl.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Loving this game so far! The maps are small but I feel like this is a good thing for an asynchronous game because you don't need to spend turns marching towards a guy before the stuff you do to each other becomes relevant.  The maps are also a "tiny globe" so if you go north you end up in the south etc.  The game feels surprisingly intense from turn one onwards.

_childDocuments_.review: If you love turn-based strategy game and want something new, then get this game. _childDocuments_.review: Solium Infernum excels at all levels of strategy.It's best to treat this game as a strategy board game, as action economy very much shapes the course of play. Many diplomatic actions can be denied by being first to interact, as this cancels opponent's diplomatic action. Same with combat, as each legion can only move once per turn, the one who acts first can escape or engage at will.Every approach and game plan is viable and strong on its own, but there always exists a way to decisively counter it - strong legions can be destroyed through rituals, so raise wards and seek ways to increase destruction resistance. Powerful praetors win every arena fight? Steal or banish them with rituals, or use diplomacy to gain them through extortion. Even a losing position can be skillfully maneuvered to win, as Prestige (victory points) can be gained not only through diplomacy and warfare, but through locations, rituals, plots or artifacts. Starting loadouts which give alternative win conditions, solo campaign, well made encyclopedia of all things found in-game and phenomenal art direction, all show the love put into this game.TL;DR Fresh, replayable,  well made, go buy it!
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: I'm writing this review on 22nd of March. I loved both Armello and Old Solium Infernum, so I'm a fanboy and want the game to succeed. It's a very cool and unique concept and I was happy LoG decided to carry the torch.As of today though the game needs quite a bit of work. I would not say it's buggy as hell, but there are a few bugs and questions I experienced personally:- Even in single player the game sometimes lock up due to unexpected game state. You will have to re-load the game and do something different on your turn to avoid this- There are a lot of unclear messages and opaque mechanincs: Sometimes you get a cryptic "diplomatic action was cancelled" without explaining why or what. Some people on discord reported that also had it in a multiplayer game, when a vendetta was cancelled and they were not able to find a logical explanation as to why- Sometimes you get "This is not currently possible" again with no explanation as to why- The Encyclopaedia lists costs but for some items this cost displayed as what ever cost you saw on the previous item you looked at Additionally, it is known in the community that additional certain things are not explained in the game very well, and there are certain frustrating strategies, that work but make for very unfun gameplay. Tribute spamming, framed excommunication and Dark Interference to name a few.I know that the studio has undergone a massive lay off recently, so I'm also worried that might not be able to fix this game, especially if the sales are not what they were expecting.May be if you considering buying it wait and see...

_childDocuments_.review: I have played two games of Solium Infernum as of writing this, both in multiplayer with some bots added in. I would like to start by saying that I do not think this game is worth the forty dollar price point: this is a very, very steep price for what you're getting, and unless you're a big fan of the aesthetic and mood (I am), you won't feel like you've gotten your value out of it. The fact is that the game more or less requires you to get at least two friends to play it with to have any sort of challenge and sense of intrigue (which is the primary purpose of the game). The game gets better with more human players, but to achieve a full lobby of friends who are communicating and getting the most out of the experience costs, effectively, 240$ (that is, 40 bucks per player, up to six). Without friends to play with, you might try the (allegedly) inferior random lobbies, which has always been a negative experience for me, or you could play against the AI. I've seen the AI work in our multiplayer games: it is resoundingly stupid. Provided with complex tools of subterfuge, it is a simple matter to get the AI to repeat the same pointless orders and mostly work to its own detriment. I've seen them position their armies on lava for no reason, repeatedly. Mostly they will repeat the same actions over and over again, even if they aren't working.I have spoken so far about the bad. I will now speak about why I do think this game is worth your time, at least, if not the money they're asking for it. The game does have a level of depth and complexity to it not available even in big ticket opponents in the 4x/strategy scene- the diplomatic weaving of Solium Infernum is not matched by Stellaris or Civilization or Total War. You will find a litany of actions of various flavors you can use to harm your enemies, and a number of hidden schemes that allow you to boost your own political standing. Solium Infernum captures the infernal bureaucracy better than any other game ever released. It is also a competent enough war game, although I would call this secondary to the diplomacy (even though I personally find greater joy in watching my armies beat each other up). If this is of interest to you, Solium Infernum will be a game you enjoy- maybe even without friends and against an AI that can only feign intelligence in a good light. It's a good game. Good luck convincing your friends to get it. If they do, it's a great time. Cheers.

_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent grand strategy with a very boardgame-y feel (in a good way). Playing it feels very reminiscent of games like Twilight Imperium, Dune (the old one), and Eclipse - flexible political free for all, brutally punishing and decisive combat, with just the right amount of randomness and uncertainty. Every decision feels critical and impactful - there's never enough times or actions to do everything and be in a perfect position, which makes the game incredibly tense.The art and sound design are top notch, beautiful and evocative. It's also one of the few games to offer asynchronous multiplayer - which is IMO the main game mode. So far the only drawback the game has is that the AI isn't competent, but that's still a vast improvement on the essentially non-functional AI the old game had. Still, definitely a multiplayer focused title - hell is other people, and all that.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: on playing some more, the AI has some bugs that make it play quite poorly. For example, it'll purchase Rank while in the final phase of the game when it should be accumulating Prestige, essentially flushing its chances of victory down the toilet. It also recruits too many legions without the Orders to be able to effectively use them. I think the AI could be fun for a single player game, because it does actually play thematically and makes an effort to work together to take down the game's leader. But there are some serious issues with it. I've not played the original for years and years but I've won every single match I've played so far, with different playstyles, because it's just way too easy.I think if you're buying this to play against the AI, I'd wait until the developers address this. For MP, go ahead and get it.-------------------I like it! Not a bad remake (and I usually hate remakes) and suitable streamlines the original to make it a bit easier to play for newcomers. There's some fine detail lost, and the inability to create custom Archfiends is a big miss, but I don't most casual players, who're gonna pick this up and play for a couple dozen hours and drop it again, are gonna care. For the multiplayer community though, this might be a big problem.What's important here is the accessibility of the game mechanics and the AI for single player: the first is pretty good with a fairly decent UI. There's some odd decisions in there and finding what you need is a lot more difficult than in the original game, where all your actions were laid out in one place, but once you've got your head around it, it looks quite nice and is fun to use.The game AI for a diplomacy-based game that was mostly intended for multiplayer is not bad. It makes some duff moves occasionally but the different Archfiends play to their role and will come out with some surprising moves. They'll also work together to take you down if you get too strong too early. My only real complaint about the remake is the aesthetic choice: some of the Archfiends look like really bad, poor quality cartoon characters and are mismatched with the rest of the graphics which are otherwise quite suitable. It's a real shame that the developers didn't have a stronger art direction, and I feel this is going to cost them players. It's quite immersion breaking to be trying to take over Hell as a character that wouldn't look out of place in a Aardman Animations film. All in all this is a solid remake of a really good game. I still think I prefer the original, mostly because of the UI and the awful design on the Archfiends, but I think this is a good effort and I've enjoyed playing thus far!
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: (Note: I received my copy of the game as part of the developers' volunteer playtesting program.  I am otherwise unconnected to the developers, but it's worth disclosing.)There is nothing quite like Solium Infernum.  The original Solium Infernum was a unique gem from a now bygone era, a brilliant and evocative political game impeded by the technical limitations of being a one-man project.  This new version removes almost all the friction from the experience, particularly regarding the logistics of asynchronous play, and adds some stellar artistic presentation to boot.  I'd even say that the tweaks made to gameplay are significant improvements, though the bones of the game are all recognizable from the original.For anyone with an interest in political multiplayer games, board or digital, I must recommend Solium Infernum for being so unique - and so focused on what makes it unique!  It takes a fraction of the time that it's closest comparison in asynchronous political multiplayer games, Dominions, takes to play - and Solium does far more to encourage political interaction and shenanigans than Dominions' war-centric format can.  Given how quickly turns flow, and how little commitment per sitting is required for asynchronous play, the barrier to entry is low compared to most multiplayer strategy games.  It's very much worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Excommunication mechanic ruins this game, and I would not have purchased if I understood how it interacted with the systems. For a game that sells itself on the idea that there are multiple ways to win, not just conquering your enemies by force, this mechanic absolutely breaks that by making you have to achieve victory by elimination of players, or by taking the capital city. The art work is gorgeous and some of the diplomacy options are very good ideas. The problem is, excommunication literally renders these features useless, and against the AI is basically an auto loss after a 4 hour run.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start by saying this is one of the most unique strategy games I've ever seen or played, and is honestly one of the first 4X type games I've picked up and played in a long time.This review is a little longer than I thought it would be so TLDR: Interesting and unique strategy game, with unbalanced gameplay aspects that may get annoying.The gameplay is unique, the artwork is all absolutely beautiful. At first it might seem simple, with 4 resources, and your legions having 3 attack numbers, and a health bar, It all quickly becomes more in depth, (whiles't still being fairly easy to grasp) as you learn about all of the other factors that come into play throughout a game of solium infernum, from "diplomacy", to rituals, to artifacts, places of power, edicts, praetors, the list goes on. The major feature you will notice however, is the limited number of orders you can give out per turn. With it starting at 2 orders or 3, if you have a certain relic equipped on your archfiend. This can take a little getting used to, but it does result in every turn feeling meaningful, plus you get more order slots as you progress through a game. (up to 6 I believe)However, It certainly isn't without issues. First off, this game is definitely NOT for everyone, some people may find the order slots too limiting, or certain gameplay aspects too frustrating. (You CAN be badly screwed over by RNG for example) another issue is the AI is too stupid for my liking, it doesn't seem to grasp the concept of prestige, or conquering pandemonium, among other things.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I rarely write reviews but, as though an Archfiend of Hell was controlling and manipulating my mortal whims and desires, I feel compelled to leave a review for this absolute gem of a game. I have been looking for a game like this for ages. I've played crusader kings, Europa Universalis IV, Old World, Star Dynasties, Realpolitiks 2, Endless Space and Legend series, Age of Wonders series and none of them quite left me with the feeling I was after. I wanted to scheme, and plot, and wield diplomacy like a finely honed surgical blade, and ponder and strategise over difficult decisions... None of the other games ever quite had the right feel. Some came close, but they never felt quite right. I felt often, such as with CK3, that I was constantly fighting against the mechanics to do what I wanted to do. All those games had that feeling; they all seemed to be constantly telling you "oh no, you can't do that yet" or "no, no, you have to jump through seven hoops and balance this fork on your nose first" I even tried more obscure games like secret brotherhood or star dynasties and shadows of forbidden gods to try and get the hit I was after. No such luck. The mechanics always seem to be suggesting you can do cool stuff, but in reality it always feels like it falls short or makes it far too difficult to be worthwhile.This game though... Oh man. It's a smorgasbord of delights. Whereas other games feel like you have to work to get to the fun stuff, Solium Infernum is more than content to throw open all the doors, lift up all the lids on all the treasure chests and says "help yourself, it's all yours"And everything you unlock just makes things better. You can scheme and be a cunning, evil mastermind from turn one. The game is just complex enough to entice you to learn more and immerse yourself in it's systems without being so obscure and shrouded as to be off-putting or require 40 YouTube video tutorials to figure out. The genius of only having a handful of orders actually has me, on multiple occasions, sat staring at the screen, my fingers steepled, contemplating and deliberating over the state of the hellscape, the riches in my vault and the many actions available to me, all equally enticing. I have thoroughly enjoyed *not* playing this game as I've sat for 20 minutes, narrow eyed, planning and observing and going "hmm" whilst stroking my mephistopheles-like beard, barely even touching the mouse and keyboard.  I love this game. I've been a warlord, hell bent on destroying my peers and burning hell down to ash. I've been a corrupt treasurer, controlling the economy of the game with careful pacts and devious ruinations. I've been a master manipulator, orchestrating the other Archfiends like pawns on a board. I've gleefully conducted feuds and betrayals between my foes without them ever knowing it was me and then, after careful political plays, had one of my adversaries crowned whilst secretly stealing the victory for myself as the Wormtongue-esque snake in the background. And it's not difficult to do any of this. The tools are all there for you. Go play, says Solium Infernum, go play and have a wickedly fun time!I sincerely would love to see the developers expand this game. I'd love to see new Archfiends to play, new Praetors and Legions and Artifacts, new maps, hell, even a new mechanic or two to spice things up. And if they don't produce any of that, I won't care. I just keep finishing a game and playing it again and again. I'm content playing against the AI even if it's not always the best, and the asynch multiplayer is a riot, especially with a few friends. Congratulations developers on a fiendishly fabulous game. Now go to hell. I'll see you there.
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: This (still) is the greatest board game never made.  I love the game, I try to play it every day.Lately, I've been getting very frustrated with the game.  The current system doesn't reward aggressive play, and that's something this game has had a problem with since launch.  Before the big deal was getting the Crown of Command (+1 order) turtling, and spamming Find Tribute (gather resources).The devs took some steps, and I think they balanced it pretty well, but the meta has shifted to "Find Manuscripts", turtle, and just dominate the game with a super unit no one can possibly hurt.  I really don't like this, it just hurts everyone because it makes the game break at around turn 30.  The fun of the game is when you have multiple people using every dirty trick they can to win!  The backstabbing politics are amazing, it's quick, it's fun, and you can go off and actually have a life and play this game.  Now, ugh, now there is a very clear path to victory and you can't counter it. I would still recommend this game, but I'm dropping my rating from 9.5/10 to 7.5.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of diplomatic wargames, as well as a prior player of LoG's Armello, I'd been following the development of SOLIUM Infernum's remake for quite a while. I'm normally hesitant to recommend games right on release, however for Solium Infernum it mechanically is something I can stand behind. The game itself is diplomacy incarnate, similar to Illwinter's Dominions series in its asynchronous design. However, while Dominions is primarily a wargame, SI is a game about betrayal, manipulation, and coercion. Each player has only a few meaningful actions they can perform each turn, with the total number of them slowly increasing as the game goes on by the empowerment of your stats or the acquisition of artifacts. Each action advances your game state, either by providing you with access to Hell's currencies, increasing your influence, or manipulating the board itself. However, where the game truly shines brightest is in the diplomacy between other human players in the space between turns, as realpolitik takes grasp and devils plot betrayals days in advance.Other reviews may go further into depth, but my feelings can be summed up as a wholehearted recommendation; hop in and slaughter your rivals online, and let the devil find the details!
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a little jewel.The 2D arts are gorgeous, the 3D ones are goods too, but maybe a little bit cartoonish, which create some weird contrast. Not a fan a first glance but finally it is ok, and it undoubtly gives the game some kind of 'artistic signature'.The mechanics are very innovatives in the strategy games landscape of today. The asynchronous system is great, it allows some real depth in multiplayer. The game is indeed slow, made for patient player. And this is this slow pace that allows the diplomacy to shines and salt things up.The guys from LoG have put a lot of passion in this game, it is very palpable! The overall production value is quite good, which is clearly a great achievement considering the relative small size of the studio. With love and passion you can move moutains they say, surely LoG devs have outdone themselves once again with Solium Infernum!

_childDocuments_.review: Y'know, I'll give it a thumbs up, but I'm really torn.Pros (or maybe cons):Tabletop game with a grim depiction of the Underworld, and suitably evil looking minions.Players can summon very tough angels or leviathans via occasional events that will rampage against everyone for quite a few turns.You can send minions on occasional wars/skirmishes against heaven.Cons (or maybe pros):Players can be cancelled, similar to RL cancelling, via excommunication. This can happen randomly.You can frame each other for taking forbidden actions.You can loot, steal, and destroy just about everything other players have.This game allows max level trolling - there are artifacts you can choose at the beginning of the game that mean if someone else wins under certain conditions, you win instead.No succubi in this place, minimal nudity.Ultimately, I'm certainly confused. My opinion is clearly unclear and I'm sure I don't know if it's going to change sooner or later.

_childDocuments_.review: Solium inferno is a game not quite like many other available right now. On the surface it is closest to a 4X strategy game, but whereas most emphasise combat and expansion, with player ignoring each other for the early part of the game, SI puts you straight in the drivers seat in your political grudge match to claim Hell for yourself. The focus on political machinations set its apart from other, and a tight restriction on actions means every choice you make will have consequences. Its probably not for everyone, it is certainly a slow burner, were plans are made heavily in advance, and the restrictions on actions may frustrate people who are use to more freedom. Lean into it though and you have an experience not like many other things you can play these days. Coupled with an evocative atmosphere and some gorgeous art works and you have a fantastic game on your hands for those with the patience to make the most of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Damn, this is such a great game! Been a while since I saw such a nice breath of fresh air in this genre.  In short, it's a civ-like game which is nothing like civ.Turns are simultaneous. You can give multiple orders per turn and they resolve in order of players. Each turn a different player starts.The map is infinitely finite. It's hell, so if you walk to the left end of the map, you return to the same place from right. Works the same for top-bottom.You cannot directly declare war on someone. You first need to be insulted, then you can declare war. Or you can demand tribute from someone and if they don't give in, you can declare war against them. The war has rules - you need to declare your objective first (e.g. kill units or conquer buildings or tiles). If you fail the objective, war ends. This makes all the decisions be very dynamic.This is game about insulting your opponents, not letting them get away when they make an insult against you, it's all based around "prestige". A lot of politics and bickering.Every turn something happens. You never have to wait a few idle turns like in Civ. The lore and atmosphere of the game is top-notch (but that's highly subjective).The only issue I need to highlight is the AI. There is a single player mode in this game but the AI is so weak that you really should consider this game multiplayer-only. It's as weak as in Civilization but in Civ you at least have an option to let them cheat on higher difficulties. It's just one difficulty here. I hope they are working on improving this. I also haven't seen many games in the multiplayer lobby, so buy if you have a friend to play with, you won't regret :)
_childDocuments_.name: Solium Infernum

_childDocuments_.review: In isolation each game mechanic is pretty simple, but they interlock to create a good level of tactical and strategic depth. That, plus the semi-humorous tone of the game combine to give it that magnetic 'just one more turn' effect.Another plus is that, generally, you're never going to be managing more than a handful of units. It doesn't have the Civ issue where later turns take an order of magnitude longer to play out as the factions amass huge territories and dozens of different units.In fact, perhaps my only complaint is that the game makes it a little *too* hard to expand your units and tactical options. In a typical end game I found that each faction was managing about the same number of units, with the same number of actions available to them, as they had in the mid-game. I kinda wish there was *more* of a feeling of growing more powerful over the course of play, instead of slow, incremental improvements that can still disappear suddenly if you have one bad turn.

_childDocuments_.review: The Premise:Solium infernum is a grand strategy game like no other. It's a game where 4-6 players use politics, deceit, schemes, manipulation, and warfare to win the game. The premise of the game is that the prince of darkness has vanished and now one of the many Archfiends in hell plots to take his place. In the center of it all is Pandaemonium, hell's parliament of power which dictates the laws of hell from warfare, to the rules of claiming canton (hexes), and to actual laws. As one of the Archfiends, you have to use everything in your power to come out on top. The Pregame:When you launch the game you have a few options. You can do a single player which has a tutorial (highly recommend it but i'll talk about it later), chronicles which are like single player missions, and you have skirmish mode all against the AI. In terms of multiplayer you have two options. Live and Asynchronous play. Live gameplay is a single session ranging from 2-4 hours (depending on your map settings, player count, etc). Asynchronous play is slower paced with games lasting days, weeks, months, or even in some cases years. It is great for people that are busy and Steam gives you a notification when it's your turn in any of your games.It also great for people that want to finish a game in one day, but not have a short turn timerOnce you pick which mode you want to play you then pick your archfiend and your relic loadout. Archfiends have different playing styles with their dark arts. Relic loadouts are additional tools to cater your gameplay to a certain playing style. After you do all that you jump in-game. The Gameplay: There are a lot of moving parts to Solium infernum and it is going to be complex to a newcomer. While many strategy games in general open you up to new mechanics as you progress through the game or limit your choices based on predefined actions, Solium Infernum hits you with everything at the start. While this might make the learning curve steep here, it actually is a great thing because there are a lot of different strategic opportunities from the start of the game. The core of the gameplay is your are sending on your minions to collect resources, using said resources to get more power though a variety of ways, and outmaneuver and out play your enemies with events, diplomatic plays, deception, and many more ways. You can even be a king maker and win the game when someone else wins the game, just have to hide that info from the other archfiends. There are a lot of moving parts in this game and it's going to take a lot of you guys a while to understand it all. So don’t feel too bad when you make a mistake, we all do that.   Now you most likely won’t like this game if you want something super fast paced like a RTS, if you dislike turn based strategy games, or if you have a strong moral compass and don’t like PvP. I would say this game is not for you then. It's all about being evil! And trust me when I say it is a great game for that! Just look at my hours.Audio, Art, etc:The audio is great. Music is amazing for the theme, the voice acting for the archfiends are on point, everything for sound design is great. The art looks super nice in-game, but that is to be expected since it is LoG who normally does great art like they did in Armello. I also really do like the general art style in-game for everything. Pretty happy with all this.Improvement Needed:The tutorial is great, but it is missing some important information and even the in-game encyclopedia is missing info. But hopefully LoG fixes this soon.The only other area that needs massive improvement is AI. The AI makes some very strange choices at times, starts wars/duels they can not win, and makes some very strange moves. I get this game's primary appeal will be multiplayer, but a lot of my friends like single player content and the AI could use a lot of work. So if having a good AI is your thing and you are a very experienced strategy game player, I don’t think you will find it here. Multiplayer is where the game shines, but hopefully LoG can get to looking at the AI some more. Though the AI can never replace multiplayer in my opinion.Even with all that said I still feel strongly this is a great game and highly recommend you try it out, if you like strategy games and want to try something really different from what is usually on the market.Note: Don’t listen to the people who insist that LoG does not support their products because of what happened with their other title Jumplight Odyssey. It was not a choice they wanted to make and if this game does well enough they will go back to that game to support it. And no they do not leave games to die, because if that was the case why did Armello (another early access game from LoG) which had 5 years of patches and DLCs after its EA release? Answer that question to those who think LoG is a bad company when I have seen bad companies. Trust me we are not in a short supply for those.
