_childDocuments_.review: AVOID | LACKING | MAYBE | WORTHWHILE |  | UNMISSABLEWorldless is an action-adventure exploration game with RPG, platforming, and metroidvania elements, and a heavily stylized design. In terms of what I liked, I'll start by saying that the game is outright beautiful in its design. It's like if Gris and Onde had a baby and named it Worldless. The atmosphere is incredible and the music only adds to it. During exploration moments, you feel a sense of serenity and during fight scenes, the game feels extremely intense. The combat is unique and relies heavily on parrying and learning your foe's patterns to effectively block their attacks and create combos to beat them. There is an 'absorption' mechanism that added to the fight's complexity and led to many moments of (fun) frustration when I failed and delight when I was successful.  Comboing is usually fun and satisfying (see below). The platforming elements were generally enjoyable - there were a few areas that require some thought and ability, but overall, there's nothing too crazy on this front. I also enjoyed the metroidvania elements. While not a huge focus of the game, it's almost always something I enjoy seeing (you only obtain a handful of new traversal abilities throughout the game, but they allow you to explore the world's depths). I loved that the story doesn't hold your hand - many things are implied about the world the characters find themselves in, but it's not explicit and yet also not too abstract. I'm sure there are many valid interpretations of what's happening in this world.In terms of what's neutral, the game in general doesn't hold your hand. You get thrust into a world and you're mostly left to your own devices to figure out what a particular door leads to, what certain things mean, how to successfully beat enemies, etc. It took me probably ~4 hours to really get into the game because of how the map and combat works because of this, but the style/atmosphere kept me going. Once things finally clicked, everything opened up and the world became mine for the taking.In terms of what I dislike, I found the complexity of the combat to sometimes be overwhelming, and the skill tree and lack of feedback from fights to be a bit confusing. You will need to learn combos to beat enemies, and sometimes there is just...a lot...to have to combo. And it's often not like one particular combo will work again and again. Instead, you have to learn different combos for different parts of the fight, and you have split seconds to implement them. Luckily, the bosses have patterns to mostly help with this, but certain enemy attacks/enemy blocks are random, and so you better git gud lol. The descriptions in the skill tree were sometimes a bit impenetrable. I still don't know what a "technique" is, for example, but it's referenced in several skills. In terms of lack of feedback from fights, by this I mean that, for example, there is one enemy that can only be beaten by using one particular skill. That particular skill is literally just perfect timing of two buttons over the course of nine attacks. Ok, sounds simple enough. But, once you fail at it, you'll likely think to yourself, "What do I need to do differently?" and you simply won't have an answer. Did you hold the first button too long? Not long enough? Hit the second button too fast? Too slow? Wait too long in between the nine attacks? Not long enough? You don't get the answer to these questions via anything in game (at least as far as I'm aware). Fortunately, with practice, you'll likely be able to brute force it, but it was kind of frustrating to fail several times and literally not understand why or how to do better.The game says my playthrough lasted exactly 15 hours, but I have 17 hours on record, though I left it on twice by accident, so that makes sense, and I ended with 18/24 achievements. I did not complete the boss rush (no shot of me completing it lol. I have no idea how long this would take, but it's almost certainly in the ballpark of several hours, given how hard some of the bosses are and the need to do them back to back), the Path of Determination (would probably take ~an hour of practice), or the boss at the end of that path (probably another hour or so). These are all optional and do not require completing to finish the game. The remaining 6 achievements are tied to doing these. If you were mostly focused on just completing the game, you could probably reasonably expect to finish it in 7-10 hours. In summary, if you enjoy combat that focuses on combos/pattern-learning/parrying + exploration games with metroidvania and platforming elements + games that are beautiful to look at, this is an easy sell.

_childDocuments_.review: Worldless is one of the most unique games i've ever played, both in terms of its visuals and its mechanics. It's a blend of genres that don't seem to work at first glance, those being a metroidvania sidescroller and a turn based parry focused action RPG, but somehow it does. While the game as a whole is very cryptic in both the story and the mechanics you do get a hold of it after a while and it becomes exceptionally satisfying at that point. Unfortunately the difficulty just keeps ramping up and by the end defeating enemies requires several minutes of near frame perfect inputs. I only got about 40% of the achievements, but i feel like i did explore about 90% of what the game had to offer. So if you're not dead set on completing the game i would recommend it, however if you do want to go for 100% be warry of the exponential difficulty!This difficulty is not found in the platforming, which is rather doable for anyone with moderate platformer skills, but in the combat. Your first few fights serve as your tutorial where each aspect is gradually added to ease you into it. Once you've seen the aspects you're left to figure out things on your own. Unfortunately not every aspect is explained well enough, for example there's these status effects on enemies that require specfic attacks to trigger for a bonus. But this aspect is only mentioned in one line during one of the last tutorial segments despite it being one of the most important facets of combat. Most enemies are beat the same way but some require these status effects to be procced. So when i was unable to do any damage at all on a certain enemy i had to resort to youtube for guiddance. Understanding these mechanics made the later fights much more manageable so i wish they'd done a better job at explaining them.In fact the game doesn't explain many things. Like i said some enemies are more of a rythm puzzle than an actual fight so i had to resort to said guiddance more often than not. Even by the end when i had figured out most of the intricacies of combat the actual skill required to pull it off become excesive. Out of around 60 encounters found throughout the game there were 5 that were just impossible to me. They were 'too tanky' being able to take hits for about 3 to 4 minutes before going down, while themselves dishing out enough damage to kill you in 3 combo's. The thing is, everything in this game is timing based so if you wanna make the most out of your turn then you have to be very deliberate and fast on your inputs. While weaving intricate combo's is immensly satisfying, in no small part due to the outstanding animationwork, having to do it for minutes on end is pretty tiring.And it's not like you get a break during your opponents' turn, for their attacks need to be parried. This parry window is absurdly tight, and if you mess up your progress on the absorption bar from your last turn can be completely negated. This gets kinda frustrating when enemies get very tanky near the end. Sweating like a tryhard for many turns only to lose a lot of momentum due to one mistake. Later enemies also do ridiculous combo attacks that can and will one or two shot you. The thing is just beating them isn't desired, what you want to do is absorb them so you can get a skillpoint for the skilltree. Sometimes it's hard to be able to absorb an enemy without killing them outright, although finally getting them down is very rewarding. This is because the skilltree is very well implemented in this game.Each node gives you either a very powerful passive or a completly new attack to weave into your arsenal. Each character has more than 10 attacks and when you unlock switching between them mid combo the potential is limitless. The skilltree is the real star of the show here, it's brilliant not only in the gameplay but also in its UI. The skilltree spreads out from your character in this immensly cool and intuitive way. Most of the game's HUD fits in very well with the game, although not all of them are equally clear. The 'map' for example is very very simplified, consisting of several points and lines between them like a constelation. I have pretty good navigation skills and memory but people with these skills less pronounced can have a hard time finding their way. Luckily the main objectives are marked so you have a vague idea of direction at the very least in this expansive world.Speaking of the game world, worldless has some pretty cool level design all things considered. Each zone has a main colour, setting and mechanics. Exploring them is a joy and is pretty rewarding as there are also some skillpoints up for grabs in the 'overworld'. There's some metroidvania elements as well, things like an air dash, grapple and double jump that are required to progress to new places. These are sprinkled throughout all the zones so backtracking almost always lets you discover something new. In fact the later encounters are so hard that this is sorta necessary. Other than playing great the areas also just look phenomenal. The minimalist art style reminds me of GRIS more than anything, but rather than watercolours that fade into eachother the shapes are more well defined. The designs are just all around phenomenal not only for the environments but the characters as well.Just like the world the characters and enemies are very abstract. With cool and well thought out designs that are brought to life with some of the best animations i've ever seen. The characters in movement look amazing, and it gives the gameplay extra smoothness on top of the responsive controls. The sound design also syncs up perfectly to accentuate the impact of combat. The soundtrack lulls you into the gameworld and when you're idly exploring outside of combat the game is rather tranquil. It's worth picking this OST up with the game as i can see myself listening to it later when i'm doing some writing or art. The whole audiovisual aspect of this game combined with the unique blend of genres make this game truly unique and stand out from the crowd. The game is extremely polished in terms of performance and is also bug free. It's worth picking up if you don't wanna 100% or if you're up for a uniquely challenging game

_childDocuments_.review: Worldless is a very solid combination of a Metroidvania platformer and an active combat turn-based RPG that incorporates more interactive attack and defence than usual.Player turns give the player a limited time window to combo different attacks and skills together, while enemy turns are spent defending against the various attacks of the current opponent.Combining this with an unusually abstract, surreal art style and you have something quite distinctive.There are plenty of rough edges that could do with smoothing out, especially in the back half of the game, but for what looks like a first outing from this studio it's a very strong first outing.To preface, the long version is largely going to involve diving deep into the negatives that I glossed over in the short version, but I do want to highlight first that I did genuinely enjoy Worldless.I liked how a lot of the enemies had a puzzle-like aspect. Deciphering what strategy to use to successfully absorb a given opponent and refining that strategy was rather satisfying, and having the option to simply defeat opponents you didn't have the means to absorb was, more often than not, a positive.I found the atmosphere, abstract art style, music and light-touch story to be refreshingly distinct.There were quite a few elements that displayed a nice integration between gameplay and story, which I tend to appreciate.In general, I found the game effectively delivered on the ideas showcased in the Demo.With all that said, there's quite a lot of feedback I'd like to offer. A lot of the negatives I'm going to cover really only become prevalent in the late stages of the game, and it's possible to reach the end of the game without touching most of the content that causes the flaws to become noticeable.If I'd known I was going to write a review, I probably would've made notes as I went, but alas, it's primarily from memory.I'm gonna go into a lot of fine detail with my feedback, that's what makes this the long version.Long enough that it doesn't actually fit in the character limit of a Steam review, so I'll post it in the Feedback Forum.

_childDocuments_.review: I stumbled upon Worldless purely by chance, browsing the list of upcoming games to be released on Steam, and I got hung up watching the trailer while my eyes widened. The visual aesthetic instantly bought me in, and the turn-based combat with active player interaction finished winning me over. It really didn't take much to get my hopes up, and I must say that the game lived up to the arbitrary expectations I built up in my head, not only because of the aforementioned points but also because of an intriguing story that lends itself to interpretation, and a soundtrack that melancholically accompanies the entire journey.Wordless is charming, so I have to start with the visuals. It's what caught my attention the most in the first instance, and I certainly admire how they approached it. It's a very stylized art, and at first it looks very simplistic, with respect to the characters, but with each special movement, like running or attacking, it adds a fleeting glimpse of the true "form" of the creatures, and I feel it's something very creative and particular. It reminds me a bit of those games of old, of "stick fights" as some of us call them, but elevated to the maximum and most epic exponential. Through these visuals we are presented with a somewhat enigmatic and curious story. While we are given the narrative in some texts by emblematic characters, most of the story is left to the player's interpretation, and this makes the atmosphere feel more mysterious and mystical. In the beginning, we are shown a kind of astral war, between sides of "stars" whose clashes conflagrate the firmament; and we will take the role of one of those entities, embarking on a journey of self-discovery and understanding.As we progress we’ll see very beautiful and somewhat abstract environments, but what stood out most for me were the little details that can be perceived in the distance, such as the clashing lights of far battles that filled me with a hostile feeling, of a war field. There are other kinds of touches later on, each map has its own theme so to speak, and its particular musical accompaniment. The music is crafted to generate different emotions depending on the situations and locations, and was a key aspect of the experience. From desolation to hope, a very neat arrangement.The world of Worldless is interconnected, and navigation through the maps feels fluid. On our way we'll find varied platform sections, and we'll use abilities like the classic dash, and some others that we'll find around. But not only will we discover moves for exploration, but also health upgrades, among other things; but the most notorious will be the enemies that will get in our way.This leads us to talk about combat, which at first glance seems like classic turn-based and little else, but in reality it also offers active actions to make it more dynamic and entertaining. By pressing buttons at precise moments, we'll be able to perform perfect guards to negate damage, or hits that deal more damage to enemies, having a certain amount of time per turn (which can be extended via upgrades, but I'm getting to that). But wait, there's more! Each enemy has a "deposit", visually represented by a sphere that fills up as we hit them, and when it's full we can absorb them to add a point to our skill tree. Thanks to this system we will be able to acquire new attack moves, combos, more turn time and so on. It should be noted that the opponents have their own strengths and weaknesses, either to blows or elements, and hitting them in their weak point, so to speak, fills the tank faster; in addition, the game promotes the variety of actions, because repeating the same type of attack over and over again lowers its effectiveness.One more detail of the combat is that the enemies show us what attack they are going to do to be able to block it correctly, with visual light indications, and this turns the confrontation into something more rhythmic. Leaving aside normal enemies, there are some more hidden and secondary enemies, which the developers call "more demanding" and that border on perfecting the combat. They really aren't a piece of cake, so getting used to pressing those buttons at the right time is almost mandatory in case you want to face these creatures; I, for one, received such a frustrating beating on one of them that it made me drop the towel, I won't say more than that.On the bright side, there is no game over, and each fight can be attempted as many times as you want. It's a good addition, as it lets the player choose between hitting a wall until it breaks, or going for a walk and coming back stronger and more resentful. I'm not speaking from personal experience. I will add that Worldless doesn't hold your hand either, some things you have to figure out on your own, like some movement combos for exploration. It might seem strange, but these are pretty intuitive, and I was very excited to discover each interaction.Now, I saved the best for last, and that is that past a certain point we will get a new character with its own repertoire of skills. This part left me totally surprised and hyped. It gives a little more depth to both the platforming parts and the combat, as we can switch between both characters to take advantage of their different moves. I don't want to delve too much into this aspect, because I loved seeing it myself, and I hope others can get that same feeling without spoiling too much.To conclude, Worldless was a wonderful and very unique experience for me. I felt a great amount of creativity and passion from the developers, embodied in a game that made me feel both frustrated and excited. I feel it has an undeniable charisma, between the successful audiovisual elements and its mechanics, and a very curious interpretative narrative, it is a game that will be among my favorites of 2023.

_childDocuments_.review: This game...I was looking for something to tide me since I was bored. I found SO MUCH MORE in this game. Now, quality of life wise, the game is lacking in a few areas, No fast travel or detailed map to help with maneuvering through the different areas, you can't just return to the main hub...and a few other things I can't think of now, but it's minuscule compared to the Pros this game has. The actual game-play itself is phenomenal. It's one of those games (ie Undertale/SMT/Mother/Persona/Insert other awesome turnbased RPG's I can't think of) that takes all you knew about standard turn-based combat, and flips it on its head. You're given a period of time to do WHATEVER you want to the enemy in your allotted time. You're a bit limited in the beginning, but as you level up your skills and combat abilities, you do some CRAZY (SMOKIN' SEXY STYLE) type ♥♥♥♥ later on. It AIN'T just you though. Enemies get tougher and gain shields, limiting what attacks you can use, so you have to play tactically and utilize all your tools. They have complex attacks that can become HELL for you to block and PARRY because....uh...if you don't parry you're pretty much ♥♥♥♥♥♥. So, get guud. The skill tree gives you the choice to pick whatever upgrades you want as you unlock them. (I remembered a qual of life issue...) You can't refund the skills you invest in...so choose wisely. However, some GREAT upgrades are sometimes hidden behind meh ones, (I say meh, but it's more-so useful if you aren't good at parrying. i.e. Defense boosts.) so swallow the bullet and get those to get to the GOOD stuff. Don't feel obligated to purchase all you have just because you have the blue/orange orbs to spare. Save them, wait for GOOD ♥♥♥♥, get that. (Up to you though.) :)The Metroid-vania style game play comes from the other half of the game: Exploration. You journey through landscapes that look really cool and are funny to platform around in, though they're only memorable in the sense of: "Hey, I've been here before when I got 'X' thing, I need to go this way instead." DON'T GET ME WRONG, I love the simple, yet beautifully-cool style of it all, but you'll find yourself getting lost fast if you wander aimlessly. (I still had fun just wandering and platforming, but you DO want to progress.) Your "map" is a small grid that can stay open with your character as you go about your business, though it's very generalized. "You are HERE, You either HAVE or HAVE NOT collected 'X' thing HERE, other 'X' things are shown in a general direction which somewhat gives you an idea of where to go. I like that this isn't hand-holdey like most games are, but at the same time, you DO want to progress. (Can also just give it your all, and if all else fails, use a guide :) Like I said earlier, main issues are quality of life stuff, so it doesn't bother me too much.) To touch on the combat, the GOAL is to build up your meter and "absorb" your enemy to gain points that go toward unlocking new abilities (Passive and Active) However, I LOVE just beating the ♥♥♥♥ out of the enemy and learning to completely decimate them. You CAN "kill" the enemy, but you don't get any upgrade points if you do that. You need to strategize what moves you use because using the same ones will stale and not fill up your meter as much, BUT WILL DEAL THE SAME DAMAGE. THIS IS B A D because remember: Your goal is to absorb the enemy. You can't do that unless your meter gets filled to a certain point. Some enemies will have a "displayed weakness" you take advantage of that and use said attack to target their weakness and gain extra meter fillage. In some cases, your enemy will have J U S T enough health to get the meter filled, so that you can attempt to absorb. If you guess all the button combinations right, GREAT! If not, you both go back to your starting positions and the enemies health is healed, allowing you to build up meter and try again. (Just gotta say...THIS IS A REALLY COOL COMBAT SYSTEM for a T U R N BASED GAME. :O) I want this game to do well, It's VERY MUCH worth your time to at least try the demo. I don't see many people not liking this with all it has to offer. I think if you're REALLY bad at games, the parry timing m a y be rough for you. Aside from that though, this game is something you should try and if I had the money, I'd buy it for EVERY SINGLE PERSON THAT USES STEAM. I'm not kidding. Not to mention it's only 20 bucks? Sign me the ♥♥♥♥ u p. TLDR?    P L A Y  T H I S  F U C K I N G  G A M E ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! :OOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO NOW Plz and thank you :D

_childDocuments_.review: The combat in this game is seriously amazing. It feels like turn-based sekiro but with even more depth to it. Every fight is so engaging and fun, it's one of the few games I've been motivated to get 100% in. Exploration is so rewarding because the reward for exploration is *more combat*.I came into this game expecting a mostly-combat focused metroidvania with okayish platforming in between. However, I was very pleasantly surprised that the platforming also gains a ton of depth after the halfway mark of the game. Somehow this game manages to have amazing combat AND amazing metroidvania platforming, which isn't something a lot of games can do.The offensive-turns in this game are also super engaging. Compared to sekiro, where you just mash R1 to attack, this game's offensive turns are really deep and require a ton of thought. The fights swap between challenging sekiro-like deflection and combat puzzles where you need to figure out the best way to deal damage given an enemy's current statuses.My only real complaint is that sometimes the 'slowdown fx' that occur when you perfect-parry can throw off my timing. There are a few early-game fights where this is really egregious, but it gets better as the game goes on.The music, art, and atmosphere are also all superb. All-around an excellent game.Highly recommend giving this game a try if you like difficult parry-focused action games.

_childDocuments_.review: Worldless is the debut title of Noname studios, a small hidden gem of an indie title which manages to reach the same heights as the most legendary metroidvania games out there. Offering a visually stunning and distinct style with a unique and refreshing new take on turn based combat. A fair warning however, the game is quite difficult and relies a decent amount on parrying, so if those are things you struggle with then I would recommend skipping this one.The gorgeous minimalistic visual style combined with the fantastic special effects design and beautiful environments are continuously pleasant to look at, even to a point where you could screenshot pretty much any frame and hang it up on a wall. There's a good variance in different kinds of biomes to explore, but as my only criticism I wish they had more variance so that each section wouldn't blend in together as much. Exploration wise you'll have a decent amount to find, from armour parts which increase your HP to secret green petals (which you should totally find all of) and your obligatory abilities to unlock more paths because this is a metroidvania.The combat is what surprised me the most, as someone who doesn't really enjoy turn based combat I was unsure of the choice but after playing further in my doubts were completely nullified. The combat system is outright ingeniously thought out and executed resulting in a very smooth and satisfying outcome especially when combined with the excellent sound design and special effects. Instead of going for the standard choose attack and then receive attack system, they mixed in a light fighting game combo system and blocking/dodging/parrying. On your turn you'll be using a wide array of moves to deal damage and build absorption meter and on the enemy's turn you'll be trying to block, parry or dodge accordingly to the enemy's attacks. This way you'll always be an active participant in combat one way or another.I mentioned "absorption meter" a moment ago, but what's that? It's a system in which the game allows you to defeat the enemy by absorbing them to receive a perk point, which you can then use to unlock even more moves. You increase the absorption meter by damaging the enemy, but the game encourages you to use as varied moves as you can by giving you a significantly higher absorption percentage when doing so. You do have a choice of defeating most enemies by just depleting their health bar with damage alone, but that doesn't award you with perk points and only allows you to remove a temporary roadblock if you are struggling. However, you can always return to that enemy later on and reattempt the fight so that you can get that perk point. Speaking of enemies, there's also a very good variety in different types and you'll have only a few instances of reused enemies, keeping the combat fresh and interesting.I'm also happy to see Berlinist as the composer for the soundtrack, previously he did such a great job on GRIS and that track record does indeed continue. Chill vibes, but really hits you when it needs to.This is a game I've personally kept track of since their first initial post on Twitter in May 10 of 2018 showing their combat animations and 5 years later I'm extremely happy to see the game finished, published and not disappoint.PS. Funk you for Path of Pain 2: Electric Boogaloo lmao

_childDocuments_.review: At first it was a good game. But after a while the platforming / puzzles got stale. Combat became much less about reflexes / good combat and became more like a pokemon game where your trying to find out what to use and when. Once you are aware of the patterns it was all about the timing which is fine in other games but this is very robotic. Enemies would literally use the same patterns in the same order unless prevented. The game could VERY much use a fast travel system or at the very least place more portals to help get around. The map is just too cryptic. Other 2d side scrollers have moved away from this mapping system because all it does is frustrate players. There is no good reason for this as it only slows the player down a bit with backtracking.

_childDocuments_.review: This game deserves a thousand times more recognition than what it's getting right now. The combat is immensely satisfying, being a mix of the defensive gameplay in Furi and the turn-based action seen in Valkyrie Profile and Indivisible. It's almost a boss rush game where most enemies have an insane amount of variety to their moves and don't go down easily. There's a lot in your moveset to play around with, and the game makes achieving mastery a complete delight by making it tangible. Not only will you be naturally getting better at the combat as you play, there's also an extra mechanic to consider where, rather than simply beating down an enemy's life bar, you can focus on breaking down their guard so that you can absorb them and get a skill point to unlock more moves with. There are entire new enemy phases and behaviors locked behind going down this route in combat, and it's a joy to discover each one. Once you've gotten used to the combat, there's a fantastic flow to it where you're effortlessly fending off enemy attacks and unleashing your own barrage. And if you're struggling with the combat, the game does well to not make the learning process frustrating by not having a "game over" screen. You're simply beaten back by the enemy and are welcome to challenge them again by approaching them once more, or perhaps come back later. Not that the game requires absolute perfection to beat either, as there are many alternate defensive options and tools to tip the fight in your favor, and even outright cheese things if you feel like playing dirty. The system is very refined with visual and audio indicators so that you always know what's coming and to signpost the extra combat mechanics, and had lots of care put into giving it variety. If you think an action game where you only attack on distinct turns sounds a bit boring, then this game knows how to keep things interesting on that front too. My only complaint is one minor visual clarity thing where The combat was definitely the highlight for me, but the visuals are no slouch either. The artstyle might not seem like much at first, but it's quite mesmerizing in motion. Seeing yourself and enemies flash into your full forms to punctuate the delivery of your strongest attacks gives the combat lots of flair. The animation itself is also top-notch and I never get tired of seeing my character strike an end-of-battle pose. There are also a handful of standout environments that had me pausing to take in the view. The exploration is very rewarding because of the aforementioned absorption mechanic because every single enemy you find is another milestone for your character. There are also other things to find that extend your skill tree or improve your abilities outright. Some places definitely need some more shortcuts to each other though, to minimize backtracking. The story is very open-ended and interpretive, but not in an obtuse way. It's a simple and abstract tale about duality that gives the game lots of room to give you memorable encounters.I've played a lot of new indie games this year and this one managed to stand head and shoulders above all of them. I highly recommend giving the demo a try if you're the least bit interested, as it's how I found this game in the first place. There's a lot I didn't cover in this review that you need to see yourself and, frankly, I feel like the things I mentioned in my review is already too much of a spoiler. Worldless is a ton of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is breathtakingly gorgeous with a striking visual identity, utilizing bold colors and shapes to differentiate the different zones, characters, and even the skill points/trees themselves. Platforming is tight and fun, and combat, in contrast to most all other metroidvanias, is reduced down to intense, 1-on-1 confrontations. Battles act almost more like an action RPG than a typical metroidvania, but it's slick, satisfying, and rewarding.Thematic through-lines about being cognizant of when conflict between factions is real, or when it might potentially be manipulated and orchestrated by higher powers is not only weaved seamlessly into both the story, gameplay, and presentation, but is also sadly still a very relevant lesson to be learned today as much as it ever has been throughout history.This has been my most anticipated game of the year, and I am not disappointed in the slightest. We stan a sexy, energy-based warrior queen today, tomorrow, and beyond.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is such a mix of genuinely amazing combat, decent platforming, and bad metroidvania mechanics that I'm not even sure how to express that on a ranking scale, much less within steam's yes/no system; I suppose I'll go for a negative since that's the feeling I am left with; that said, it's a still solid pick on sale for its positive qualities.While starting out fairly simple, combat gets much more complex before long and holds up until the end. While technically it is turn-based, player's turn functions as a time slice to perform whatever attacks you see fit, rather than being strictly limited to N actions; attacks themselves are fairly varied and, depending on if you're going for just defeating the enemy or absorbing them - the latter of which is usually harder, but gives you the equivalent of skill points - you adjust your strategy accordingly. Sometimes, you'll even want to heal the enemy, so that they'll last long enough to be absorbed. There are shields, elemental damage, parries - it truly does work well. Despite all of the problems I have with this game and am about to talk about, combat mechanics are easily 10/10.Platforming is passable overall - you'll have to keep switching between two movesets rapidly for certain challenges, which is a bit of a questionable decision, especially given that both movesets only have two special functions at most and could have been easily mapped to a standard controller all at once. Just as odd is game's decision to map basically all of platforming abilities to controller's shoulder buttons - do yourself a favor, rebind at least some to face ones. A somewhat minor but very annoying issue I've faced when doing platforming is that if you fail, you sometimes will fall outside of the challenge, with checkpoint being reset. All in all, this aspect is not super fluid or polished, but it's not awful either. Most of the time.Now, I got to the metroidvania aspects, and, sadly, those range from bad to outright non-existent; game tries to excuse such decisions as minimalism, but that does not mean they have no negative impact on gameplay in practice. Take the graph-like map as an example: while you can reveal locations of upgrades by using a certain never mentioned and easily missable mechanism, these remain only accurate to within a single graph node/room, which in a game with a pretty open world and no doors often seem arbitrary; this is especially evident if you look at fan maps and notice that nodes are rather irregular and thus it may be hard to tell to which node a specific place belongs. This minimalism extends into game's visuals - while they're undeniably pretty, everything within the same area tends to looks same-y, which certainly made navigating around the world harder for me - and lack of a real map certainly does not help here. There are certain weapons/weapon upgrades to collect, which can make some encounters much easier - a problem is that you're never told that these even exist, or how many of them are there; as a result, good luck wondering if you're missing some weapon or should get better at combat and avoid getting into a certain situation entirely/are missing a solution with tools already at your disposal. Finally, there are special collectibles, one per area, that unlock a secret place. There are no hints to locations of these at all, so yet again, good luck combing the map over and over for some of these - others are hidden behind powerful enemies, so you're in luck at least for some.Still, even with everything I've said so far, I've originally been thinking of giving a thumbs up. Unfortunately, after getting into the secret area, this is no longer the case. Gameplay and story spoilers ahead:Which brings me to the game's story, unfortunately suffering from minimalism as much as gameplay does. By itself, having little story is not bad, nor is vague story inherently bad either. Sadly, Given everything above, I can only sum up my experience as "an incredible combat system in serious need of a better game". That said, given just how damn good the combat system is, everything else just might be worth tolerating - although it's somewhat hard to justify at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Worldless is a somewhat metroidvaniaish tour through abstractly beautiful landscapes, sometimes punctuated by a kind of turn taking rhythm combat. Overall it's been an amazing, if not quite fully polished experience.The progression feels slightly off; early on I was getting new abilities with little time to master the last one; the game is set up in such a way that you get one ability per fight, and sometimes you get free points as well. You don't really get any practice time before something new comes along. After getting drowned in new abilities, you eventually start running into much tougher enemies, and you have to go back to review your abilities, try things out and figure a way to deal with them.Some mechanics also use extremely precise timing; expect to spend several hours on some encounters figuring out the right moves, working on timing, and training your fingers to press the right buttons under time pressure. One thing it's systems do seem to capture is room for skill expression - while there are many helpful abilities and some numerical upgrades, even the toughest fights feel doable if you were just a little bit better at timing or picking the correct response to the situation.The game has some tutorial screens that come up when a mechanic first appears, but otherwise mostly leaves it up to you to discover the mechanics. In several cases features of movement abilities are not explained - the game simple creates situations where the most obvious thing to do sets you up to discover the feature.Landscapes can be hauntingly beautiful, although in a few cases it was hard to tell foreground from background. Myself I did a lot of back tracking and exploring; some of the areas aren't the most exciting to move though repeatedly.Overall though, it captured my attention with unique art and novel mechanics, and delivered on it's promises, plus a few little secrets and puzzles to work out.

_childDocuments_.review: Worldless is a game with beautiful atmospheric environments. In it's best moments, it is like a very, very well written fairy tale. The sound effects are powerful and make using the abilities you unlock feel rewarding.Worldless is dragged down by a hyper-restrictive combat system in which guessing is one of the main mechanics. In order to get the reward for a fight you must build up a meter by attacking the enemy, but it is also incredibly easy to kill the enemy and have to start the fight over again. There's some sort of timing mechanic the game tries to add, but the visual cues get buried in the experience.Worldless is also dragged down by a mostly-wordless story that could be taken in some interesting directions, but just... isn't.Worldless is also also dragged down by the single worst ending fight/scene that I have ever encountered in my entire life.  The ending retroactively ruined all the goodwill I had for Worldless.Worldless has a beautiful aesthetic, but the rest of the game is slightly enjoyable at times and utterly aggrivating at others. It's not worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty mid.Combat mechanics are there to facilitate more restrictive scenarios during combat rather than increase player expression. High level combat either becomes part rhythm game for parries and part puzzle game for optimizing your absorption damage and keeping the enemy alive long enough to absorb for a skill point, OR with bosses, they set the absorption meter's minimum to a full meter, meaning you're now filling a bar to kill the boss/enter next phase like an old school spectacle fighter.Game simultaneously punishes repetitive moves by reducing their damage while encouraging specific damage types through a weakness system. Feels really odd, like the game would've benefited from just the latter.The presentation is delightful, though not extremely memorable to me. The story is... even less existent. When they say interpretive, they mean you're going to get exposition from a single NPC for the whole game instead of exploring the world and discovering environmental storytelling or piecing things together over time. When you ARE shown something on screen, it's never explained.5/10, I guess. I've never felt more "meh" on reviewing something, but I'll give it a positive. Someone might like this.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 I love this game so muchWhole game feels like a lovely dance between you and the environment. The battles are wonderfully paced and so satisfying to complete. Once you find your rhythm is a beautiful thing. I cannot recommend this game enough.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------                                                            Some note on aspects of the game--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------The combat is a action turn-based hybrid. You'll cycle between attack phase and guard phase. Your attack phase has a timer and your free to do whatever offensive action you want. Certain things will give you extra time. You have plenty of combos to work with and 2 types of damage you'll need to deal. Your guard phase has a different pace too it, as you'll be playing too the enemies rhythm. You swap between physical and magical guard, (later getting some other options) good timing rewards you with a counter to interrupt the enemy combo. Some encounters require a more creative way of fighting such as healing the enemy. I also never felt bottle necked by any encounter, every really tough fight is optional, everything else is open enough that if you struggle you can just leave and get more skill then come back.Moving thru the world is safe in the sense that you wont be randomly encountering enemies, every encounter is in a set spot that you choose to engage (only if you lose the first attempt; that one starts auto once you walk into the spot). The platforming is very responsive, skills are well utilized in the jumping puzzles. I never felt like I was getting screwed by the game, every mistake was just a skill issue. There is a parkour section that makes you think this game could have just been a really good parkour puzzle game separate from the combat. All in all this game is outstanding. I highly recommend it too anyone. Even if your not big on turn based combat or metroidvanias, this game is a fantastic buy, its not intense on the metroidvania, and the combat has plenty of action where is really doesn't feel turn based

_childDocuments_.review: If Stephen Hawking, Picasso and Hans Zimmer made a game together this would probably be it.But seriously...This game sports some of the most unique visual art and turn-based combat I have ever seen. The music is phenomenal and really set the tone for each area and encounter.The story is very abstract and vague, and even now I'm not really sure what the premise is - that being said, the arc of the 2 characters (Edda and Aven apparently) was very touching, climaxing in an emotional final battle that left me in awe.There are some aspects I think are in need of improvement though. For one, the input registry is a bit whack - I found it to be very limited, as often when I input while the character is mid animation, the game would simply ignore it. Very frustrating at times. Also, the REAL final boss of the game feels very broken, especially during your first encounter with him. Took me a few days to actually beat him.All in all, this game is a shamefully underplayed hidden gem worthy of your time and worth every penny!9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Worldless is beautiful.The combat is great, with fun combos and moves, as well as challenging (maybe not that challenging, I would love to have combat difficulty options) and fun to master, includes parries, which are fun and used all the time unlike a certain game *cough* Hollow Knight *cough* (just kidding team cherry, Hollow Knight is great (Silksong when?)), and has statistics that are interesting even for a casual.The movement is great, with the interesting "switch" mechanic I won't expand on (spoilers) that I find very fun to chain, especially in the endgame green section I won't name, and is very fluid, especially with the sprint and double jump.As I'm writing this, I almost 100%'d the game, there are a few neutral shards I'm missing, and I do wonder if something happens when you 100% the game, maybe a stack of korok seeds would be nice.There's one bug and that's that when using controller there's a glitch that causes the game not to detect when I stop holding a direction (including d-pad) when in menus, so I hope they patch that.There's only one actual issue with the game and it's that I feel it takes away there's only one ending, and it's a "bad" ending, I feel.However, in short, I love this game.

This videogame is criminally underrated, and you'd be doing it a disservice not to tell literally anybody you think might enjoy it about it. Now, onto the review. I'll keep it short because people have bad attention spans and you probably didn't want to read a massive wall of text anyway.First off, my one and only complaint: I want more. I want more of the characters. I want more worlds. If ever there is a game that could use DLC, or a secret ending, or anything like that, this would be that game. Of course, there's plenty of secret stuff you can do (see edit below) but I just want more.Now, the positives, and there are plenty:- The movement is fluid!- The soundtrack is immaculately composed!- The navigation is (really) not that hard to navigate at all! - The combat is CRISP and makes you feel like a real badass for pulling off something cool! It feels intuitive, and it's not very punishing if you 'die'.- The sound design, often not talked about, is also one of the best I've heard in a game!- The story and ending, while divisive, tell a complete and interesting story that... well, I'll be honest, left me just a little bit existential.The best word I would use to describe this game on the whole is . It all culminates into what I would consider to be a work of art. 20 dollars well spent.TL;DR: Buy it, Beat it, Cry for hours, Tell your friends about it, Go 100% it, cry again but this time in pain.EDIT: I beat him. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incredible game, stellar ideas, but also absolutely incredible is the sheer lack of engine functionality on Linux and Steam Deck. Fights are timing based, which is cool, except for the fact that the game has horrendous framerate issues during combat and during combat only. This is fixed by playing the game in true windowed mode (likely not a solution for deck users, due to the nature of a tiny screen made smaller), I want, so so badly, to be able to enjoy this game... but the game engine said no, not today,  It would be so, so easy for the devs to have made a linux version of the game; unity has easy, accessible build methods for all platforms... but they just chose not to.EDIT: Three months later (or perhaps less recently idk for sure) THEY FIXED THE CRASH on launch in windowed mode. Hooray? It still has all the other issues I've mentioned, and as I've been replaying the game I'm realizing even with a better framerate it's still really hard to tell exactly when I'm supposed to time most attacks. Not pressing buttons as much sometimes means I just don't attack, and unfortunately I also haven't memorized exactly what links to other moves cleanly and what forces me to wait for a second before I can do it... so I just mash anyways, even though the express purpose of this combat system is to discourage mashing. Deeefinitely needed more time in the oven.

_childDocuments_.review: Worldless is such a beautiful masterpiece of a difficult and surrounding environment. Put into a magical place with compelling platforming and complex story building Worldless is one of the best games I have ever played. I find myself determined to complete challenging foes because of the amazing combat system along with the large skill tree. While there are some navigational issues I find myself in it doesn't stop the enjoyment of this game.             First the beauty of wordless. I love everything this game shows to me. The broken and magical environments you explore in this game is unbelievable. The combat abilities and elements are explosive, enlightening, and complex. The connection of you and this game is incredible and is such an incredible aspect of this masterpiece.            The exploration of this game is amazing. With combat enemies hidden behind simple and difficult puzzles. With collectives posted in interesting spots. With difficult time trails that give a challenge to long explorations. The exploration is truly amazing to experience.            The combat and skill system is spectacular. With a unique combat type of perfection this game rewards you with parries and untouchable turns. The absorption system is one of a kind and is challenging to complete. The enemies are complex with different skills and abilities along with unique weaknesses and types. The reward of a challenging battle is a resource used in a skill tree system. Unlocking new abilities and combos for the player to strategize with. The combat is truly difficult but personally I love this aspect of this game. The practice of the fight and no real consequence of losing a fight allows the player to continue with the incredible foes in this game.            However there are some downsides. The map system is very simple without a lot of detail for specific navigation. The simplicity of the map is amazing because of the more enlightening experience but I must have spent ten percent of my time backtracking through everything. I also wish for a more fast travel experience because of my perfectionist needs going through an incredible but large setting. Some of the movement is difficult to get used to but is a small downside in this incredible game.            I truly recommend this game to anyone that wishes for a beautiful but challenging experience. In around ten hours you would fulfill the incredible story of Worldless but still has double the amount of playtime when completing all achievements. Please play this magical and beautiful game, it really is one of the best games I have ever played.

_childDocuments_.review: Such a nice take on game design. I was looking for turn-based games when I came across this one. It's turn-based and has swordplay? And looks like a metroidvania? I had to give it a shot.The difficulty was well balanced - neither frustrating nor easy. I would love to see a little more refined (see feedback for details below) combat system in a future game. There are are a couple of abilities shown off on the store page that I didn't find. I'm not sure if there is an LB-like skill for the red guy.Oh and it has a meaningful skill tree! No silly stuff like +3% health, +5% damage when the boss is on fire after 3 consecutive launch attacks.If none of the above turned you off, just get the game and give it a shot.(Potential spoilers ahead.) For feedback, here are my 2 cents:- Parry windows could be a little more lenient. For example, some big enemies have "beam" attacks that are not telegraphed well, so it's hard to time the parry.- Red's dodge didn't feel great. i-frames window wasn't clear and it felt like I couldn't dodge in succession. I ended up sticking to blue for defense.- I got the grapple ability too late in the game and I couldn't explore a bunch of areas. Not sure if this was intended but I was basically in the endgame by then. Maybe it could have been made part of main progression before the unstable foes.- On that note, I didn't feel like backtracking partly because there is no marker system. I LOVE the minimal map on R3 but maybe if I could mark things on the dedicated map menu.- The ending was very cryptic. Maybe I didn't figure it out properly but was anti-climatic for me.

_childDocuments_.review: A 10 out of 10 hidden gem.This game has one of the most beautiful and unique art styles. The world, the character design and animations are gorgeous to look at. It's a platformer with ability gated regions, that are full of hidden collectables which increase you stats and combat skills and even unlock a secret level that will test all you learned platfoming and combat skills. The combat is quite different to what you would expect from a platformer. If you encounter an enemy, the game switches into a turn based mode with offense and defense phase, where in each you have a certain time to perform real time actions, that require precise timing esp. in the defense phase. Enemies can either be "killed" by reducing their HP (after which you can choose to fight them again) or absorbed by performing special attacks to fill the absorption meter (after which they grad you a skill point to unlock or upgrade your combat abilities). The main game will take you about 6-8 hours on your first try, finding all collectable will take you a couple more hours and the final challenges of the mentioned secret level can take even longer, depending on how well you mastered the game mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: After 100% completing the game I can say that the visuals and combat stay amazing throughout the game and continue to improve as you go. Even going back through levels to collect items didnt feel bad just because of how good the music and maps are.The enemies are interesting and unique, each having separate methods to attack, counter, and memorise the moveset of. The combat can be really difficult whilst also being fair enough that if you are good enough you could first try encounters, just like how some you can spend hours on.The final bosses of the game tie the story together and match the general aesthetic of the game really well, altogether there isn't too much wrong with the game. I just wish it was a bit longer because it is a really fun game

_childDocuments_.review: Yes and No. + is absolutely gorgeous, a true feast for the eyes and ears. +You've got to give credit to the original execution of the combat, even though it can feel painfully awkward for some players and preferred play styles. +The pacing is exceptionally good, the game hits you with hard ♥♥♥♥ constantly but also showers you with progression.  +The enemy fight restarts are borderline instant. Such good design. Take note, souls-like devs!-Many of the platforming sections can feel like total ass  -No mouse support??? HELLO??? (<-- Note this if it's a deal breaker for you) -The combat is a double-edged sword. At times it feels super clean and that you've got the hang of it, but the literal next enemy wipes the floor with you 20 times in a row. -You really have to stick with the game to figure the combat out, it's not as simple as it sounds on the store page, and if someone goes into this game thinking that the "turn based" combat is something akin to your Darkest Dungeon or Deck builders, you're in for a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nasty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ride. May god be with you.  -Some of the combat encounters are just pure guesswork- while the pacing of the game is really good, IMO it suffers from it as well. You get bombarded with new skills and combos every 5 minutes, and you just randomly start applying ♥♥♥♥; while some specific enemies can only be defeated with some convoluted combo, which you've no idea that you've even unlocked such. Also the absorption mechanic is pure guesswork as well, and can draw out the already long fight even more while you fight against intentional input delay from the game and your own keyboard LOL. Could've been done way better. -Even Sekiro has more forgiving parry timing than your random indie metroidvania here and that's saying something :D you have to be frame perfect if you want to decently parry, which will be a major turnoff to some. -The last boss is just a literal exhibition art piece that you just sit & watch through and wait for the credits to roll.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Just absolutely incredible. This has to win game of the year award in style/art direction. I've never seen something so incredible! The animations are flawless. And this absolutely unique artstyle of "formless yet with form". I have no idea at which point of completion I am in the game right now. It is so mysterious! A true metroidvania with all its mystery! I've encountered at least two things that seem to span the whole game and I have no idea how to unlock or how to find them!The combat is absolutely incredible. Turn based but still real time in the sense that you have to time everything! The game is also not punishing like the dead souls gerne which I despise. If you lose a fight you are stepped out, one second before you can start the fight again. There is no death and no having to walk 5 minutes to reach the fight again. What an incredible idea that improves game experience a thousand fold!A gripe I have is that there appears to be no teleport system. And there seems to be very minimal map which shows only 1 of the 3 major collectibles in the game... That is unfortunate and unecessary. If I can write the information on a piece of paper it should also be in the game itself. It only makes things more clunky not more mysterious!EDIT: Oh yeah, forgot to mention that this game is super cheap for what it offers. Incredible!!!

_childDocuments_.review: I have fallen in love with this game. The platforming is serviceable/interesting, but the unique combat is downright addicting. Mixing attack/defense phases with perfect timing and combos seamlessly is a splendid idea. The exhilarating ambiance and combat themes, gorgeous level design and unique fragmented artstyle really help shape this shattered world. I cannot recommend this game enough. I really only have a couple of complaints about the game: the game's map is just not that useful(and quite confusing), outside of helping you track the upgrade points you've acquired. It could've at least been used to tell the player the names of the enemies, constellation branches, player characters(and not through an achievement lmao) and the movement abilities they acquire.And, I'm not sure if this counts as a negative, but there is only 1 Ending. The final boss doesn't reward you with a different one. Noname Studios, PLEASE update Worldless so that the game doesn't end on a sorrowful note after the last cutscene! Conclusion: Worldless is a peak metroidvania game that can easily entertain you for 10~25 hours, depending on what you want to achieve. I highly recommend it if you like games based around skillful combat with large skill ceilings and varied combos, awe-filled tracks and magnificent landscapes to be explored that do not hold your hand at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game, great scenery and art, perfectly flowing animations and by far the most confusing but most engaging combat system I've ever seen. Your thoughts would start along the lines of "Where did all of my health go? How do I deal damage to this thing. IF VERTICAL IS MAGIC AND HORIZONTAL IS PHYSICAL THEN WHAT DO I DO IF IT HAS BOTH?" but once you have properly learned the mechanics, they will change to something closer to "Ah yes, another godlike entity to mercilessly pummel into the floor. I wonder how many brick walls I could throw it through before my turn timer ends." 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: What a brilliantly crafted game. Not a lot is explained so you will have to make your own discoveries (or use guides if that's how you like to play), some simple yet subtle puzzles to solve.No two enemies are the same and all will require different approach.Weird (the good kind) but interesting backing story. Visually stunning and the combat animations are quite epic. Props to the soundtrack too, which compliments the game's atmosphere extremely well.Overall an absolute blast!Thanks for the game <3 - definitely something to be proud of.---A little nitpick tho, not being able to teleport directly back to hub/home was little annoying/frustrating at times. _childDocuments_.review: This game is really interesting and I advise you to try out the demo. To me it felt very reminscent of Gris and Grime, aesthetically for former, more thematically for the latter as well as in the way the platforming gameplay works, with a lot of small action you constantly slip in-between your dashes and jumps. Reminding me of those games is both good and bad, because I love them, and I'm always happy to see more of that. But at the same time, you can't escape the comparison, and it's hard to compete with them. Especially so because I experienced them first. But it doesn't matter, because Worldless ABSOLUTELY finds its identity in its combat system. I've never seen anything quite like it. It may be sold as turn-based, but don't you expect something chill, I have never felt so panicked and pressed for time as in this game's combat. And I loved every second of it. Many timing challenges, many things to understand and discover, many concepts to juggle and consider at once. Each enemy needs to be known and figured out. If you like to discover and understand things, if you like a challenge, if you like to try things over and over and feel yourself gradually improving until you eventually overcome, and do that in something unusual that you most likely haven't seen before, I highly recommend this game.The controller is a bit stiff, but taking it the vibes and trying to coordinate all your fingers uses enough of your mind that you don't notice too much. Some mechanics aren't explained very clearly, and the game's conclusion can be a bit frustrating as it is only narrative and not mechanical (although you can find culminations of the gameplay in other places if you so wish). But I would consider those to be its only flaws, and I think they are greatly compensated by its qualities.
_childDocuments_.name: Worldless

_childDocuments_.review: It is a great game. The combat is really unique and badass as ♥♥♥♥ and it has an archetype you don't really expect to see in a metroidvania but it works AMAZINGLY. It has a fighting game type combat system where you can use a variety of different skills and abilities to deal damage which is enhanced by precisely timing your strikes so it feels really rewarding to actually play well. The movement of the character feels really smooth and the puzzles are pretty interesting although not TOO hard. Frankly i had an overwhelmingly positive experience with this game, and quite frankly, the only down side i can find is that it was way too short of a game, seeing as i finished it in just 10 hours of gameplay, having no prior experience with the game. 9.5/10 (if it was a tad bigger it would have been a 10/10)

_childDocuments_.review: Although I'm apparently at least halfway through the game, maybe three quarters at best, this game is one hell of a hidden gem. TL;DR at the end for anyone who doesn't want to read this college-level essay.On the gameplay side of things, imagine the deceptively simple artstyle of Geometry Dash, combined with the fluid platforming of Hollow Knight, alongside a combat system not unlike Bug Fables with the difficulty turned up to 11. Don't worry about dying, though - if you lose a fight, you're sent back to... right outside of that fight, within a second at most, having lost nothing. Fights are also few and far between, and once you win one, it WILL reward you. Literally every fight gives you one of few currencies which can be spent on the game's skill tree, and each point in the skill tree is a whole new ability for you to exploit in future combat. Which currency you'll get is obvious - blue fights give orbs, red fights give diamonds. If you accidentally reduce the enemy's health to 0 without absorbing them, you don't get the currency, but you can respawn them immediately after until you do. However... *PLEASE* use a controller. I don't have one and at this point, I need to resort to button mashing for stuff that's new, and trial and error for stuff that isn't.When it comes to environments, I... don't think I've seen a prettier game. There's some good competition, such as Hollow Knight, Baldur's Gate 3, maybe OneShot if pixelart is your thing... but this game just barely jumps over all of them. Every location is a stark contrast from every other location, and all of them are gorgeous. They are never given names, so you can call them whatever you like - I personally call them by whatever color and shape is most present, such as Blue Circle, Orange Square, or Pink Triangle. The music complements each area WONDERFULLY - Blue Circle's music is tranquil and feels about as "home" as you can get. Meanwhile, Orange Square's music is almost industrial by comparison, and Pink Triangle's music feels enchanting and mystical. Despite no words being spoken about ANY of it, the ambiance in this game is second to none.And now for the lore. I haven't found too much of it - yet - so take my words with a grain of salt. All I know is that the summary for this game on Steam includes the words "In a newly born[...] universe." I can imagine the characters in this game, then, being some kind of fundamental, or at least subatomic, particle. The blue things are matter, the red things are antimatter, and from a hint given by the only speaking character in the game, I can extrapolate the stony fellas are somehow related to dark matter. Or maybe the blue things are electrons, and the red things are protons, and they fight each other because of their innate electrical charge? Maybe this is also a hint at how each area represents their own fundamental particle, themselves - I just kinda found myself relating Orange Square to Gluons a lot of the time, simply because of its inorganic and mechanical feel. All I know is that this game doesn't just leave you in the dark - it turns out every single light and caused the heat death of the universe. I dunno, though, that might be your jam.Although this game could use some amount of difficulty settings, I think the difficulty it currently has is incredible for how quick the player can get back into the fight. When I tell you defeat doesn't really matter... I mean it. You can restart a fight INSTANTLY. I genuinely don't know if it takes longer than a second or two. The only game I've seen with faster respawning is ULTRAKILL, which gives you a death screen on the same frame your HP reaches 0 - no fanfare whatsoever - and a single press of a button during or after that frame gets you back on your feet. If you weren't expecting to die, you probably won't even know you did until you saw that you were back at the last checkpoint. Somehow, this game gives even ULTRAKILL a run for its money in that regard. This lets you die, over and over again, and shrug it off dozens of times in a row. Although... the game doesn't expect you to actually die dozens of times in a row - If you find yourself doing that, either try finding an easier fight, or switch up your strategy a bit. Some of the enemies flee if you don't do a certain thing, so they're more like puzzles or QTEs than actual combat. The only thing that might be problematic is the game's replayability. So far, it seems like a one-and-done scenario, where once you 100% it, there's no more enjoyment to be had. However, it is pretty damn cheap and extensive even for one of those types of games - and trust me, every other point I made will give you one hell of an experience.If you're personally not sure, I recommend the demo. It includes a lot of the first area, with a few changes, and ends after you beat that first tidbit of game. I'd say it takes 30-40 minutes, maybe an hour if you take your time. If it's not on sale - PLEASE try the demo to make sure it's your kind of game. However, if it is on sale, or if it's your kind of game, or even if you're just looking for something to do that's new to you, I'd say, go for it! TL;DR - Platforming is very smooth, combat is very difficult but losses do NOT affect you, lore is quiet but not exactly a selling point, and the ambient energy is literally second to none. Trust me, I've played some games with ambiance. This game is somehow able to dwarf the likes of Hollow Knight, Baldur's Gate, the entire Crysis series, hell - even some feature films such as A Quiet Place and Hunger Games. Best impulse buy of my entire life. PLEASE FOR THE LOVE OF GOD PLAY THIS WITH A CONTROLLER.

_childDocuments_.review: An aesthetically pleasing game that tasks you with exploring a lite metroidvania to engage in intense "turn-based" battles where you play Marvel vs Capcom on a short timer and then pause to juggle high-stakes QTEs.It took me some time to learn, but when I got my brain around how combat really works, I couldn't get enough of it, which is good since Worldless can be rather challenging at times. The extreme poses and arcs of the animations for combat are all so tactile and make both attacking and defending a spectacle. Failure isn’t as disheartening when you simply want to be a part of the show. And the way the game kicks you out of combat (instead of killing you) when you run out of health makes you want to run right back in there and properly parry those new flashy swooshes the boss keeps throwing your way.Absorbing vs killing enemies is a well-executed mechanic, yet it's an idea that needs a little balance. It's engaging to have two objectives to consider while fighting and absorption can often prove you've not only defeated but mastered your opponent, and you're duly rewarded for taking that time. The other mechanics based around absorption also provide direction for your turns that prevents the game from becoming a mash-fest or linear optimization problem. However, it’s occasionally too easy to chop through an enemy’s health before you’re anywhere near absorbing them. This leads to several awkward attempts where you sorta just take it easy on them in order to get the more valuable outcome, which is counterintuitive. Additionally, having to guess buttons when you're attempting to absorb an enemy at the threshold (instead of at 100% charge) is playing with randomness in a way that doesn't feel right.As for the metroidvania overworld, it's nice to look at, offers a serene atmosphere, and the platforming is fine (a breeze compared to combat), but its structure is a little all over the place. Moment-to-moment traversal with your limited overworld powers is perfectly passable, general navigation is less so. Areas are wide and take time to backtrack through. Side routes come and go within the same small regions and the intended path isn't often clear amidst all the similar objects and limited pallets. The constellation map has a cool thematically appropriate dietetic design, but it's terribly impractical when it comes to, say, finding the singular elemental power that's required for later gameplay is uniquely tossed, without any marking, somewhere in the world. As an aside, the ending is one of those endings that  Sure it fits the vague, celestial artistic themes of the game, but .Outside of a few overarching inconsistencies, Worldless is a fantastic meshing of surprisingly cooperative ideas wrapped in energetic geometric visuals with an ambiguous, silent narrative. The quick-witted and tactile combat kept me playing even when things got tough or the game wasn’t acing its cartography. Not really a full-on metroidvania, not conventionally “turn-based”, and not exactly a fighting game, but something else delightfully unique.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best metroidvanias, along with the Ori games. The combat is very unique and fun. It's divided in two phases - attack, where you try to do as much damage as possible - and defense, where you have to be very precise in parrying the enemies moves. Some bosses took many tries, but there's no real penalty for losing a fight, you can always start again or keep exploring, and the game is very non-linear so you can return to a tough boss when you get stronger. Unlike e.g. Hollow Knight, this game doesn't try to make its difficulty frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. The visuals, music, and sound design are all fantastic, and the platforming is responsive and no harder than it needed to be. Even the hardest platforming challenge, the Path of Determination, is significantly shorter than its (likely) inspiration, the Path of Pain from Hollow Knight.The combat is where this game shines brightest. Quite literally, every single enemy is unique, with unique designs and moves. This on its own is a huge accomplishment, but the best part is all of that variety is enhanced by some of the best turn based / active combat of any game I've ever played. When it's the player's turn, you have a time limit, and during that time you can freely use any attacks you want, in real time, not just selecting actions from a menu. Across two characters, the player has access to basic attacks, charge attacks that launch opponents, 4 different spells which each have 3 levels that all work differently, 2 extra weapons for each character that also have unique charged attacks, aerial attacks, and 10 special attacks. And all of that is just on YOUR turn. When it's the enemy's turn, the player has access to parries, dodges, blocking, and counters, all of which are dependent upon timing and reacting to what attack type the enemy is using. Through 3 playthroughs, one of which fought the hardest boss of the game, Summum, I still haven't gotten bored of the combat even a little bit. There are so many ways to play, and to improve, enemies that made me struggle for dozens of minutes are now just a test of how few turns I can use to win, even on new playthroughs without most of the upgrades.My only issue with this game is that there isn't more of it. What is here is already fantastic, and while it is a little short, it doesn't feel like anything in particular is missing, aside from maybe a secret ending of some sort. Summum and the Ultimate Trial provide just enough postgame content to satisfy, but some extra story or something for 100% completionists would have been great. I'm very excited for whatever is next for this studio, but honestly I would love to see a Worldless 2 or expansion to this game or something. If this game looks even a little bit interesting to you, do try the demo. It gives a pretty good idea of what the game is like, although it only lets you play as one character (in most of the game you play as two characters simultaneously, so if the combat feels too limited at first, know that it does open up after a short while.)

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun and pretty game. The soundtrack is stunning and the art is beautiful without being overstimulating during fights. The turn based combat system is something new and easy to pick up because you can focus on offense and defense separately, yet hard to master as certain enemies have gimmicks you need to figure out and work around to defeat them. The story isn't rich (The only actual pieces of text you get are rather cryptic) but you'll get the basic idea of what's happening from the environment and backgrounds without needing to dive in too deep. You can also theorize a lot, especially with the ending, which I'll admit feels a bit underwhelming and confusing, without going into spoiler territory. Overall a great game that's still fun for people who aren't the biggest metroidvania fans, or want to tip their toes into the genre. Once you collect everything and beat every enemy, you'll get access to really challenging post-game content as well, for those who want to get the most out of a game. As for bugs, I've hardly noticed any that are worth bringing up.

_childDocuments_.review: A very unique experience, definitely not your average metroidvania. While the game is very ambiguous, it is pretty easy to understand the basics of whats going on in the story, and i wont say too much to not spoil it but for the most part its pretty good. The combat is separate from the world exploration, as in you be able to run around the environments while fighting enemies because engaging in combat locks you into a special state. Combat is very unique, you and the enemies you fight each get a turns at attacking and defending. During this time, if you are attacking you are aiming to lower the enemies 'health' or absorption meter. Lowering and enemies health to 0 finishes combat and you can move past them, however you get no rewards. Absorbing an enemy is the proper way to defeat them, permanently killing them and giving you the rewards. There are also different mechanics for both combat and exploration which you learn throughout the game by  unlocking new abilities. Weakness types are a thing with different attacks affecting different weakness meters. once weakness meters are broken the enemy takes significantly increased absorption damage. That's pretty much the core aspects of the game. While there isn't much dialogue and the lore is pretty much up to you interpretation, the music and environments you explore and incredibly evocative and remind me of hollow knights areas, while being unique and not too similar. I've never really cared much for space themes but this game blends fantasy in with it very nicely. game is a little short and i would love if a dlc or second game could be made, but overall a very good and unique experience in my opinion. PS. I played this on keyboard, definitely doable and not too bad but controller is probably better. Just make sure to change your keybinds to whatever is comfortable, and take note of the separate combat and navigation tabs, between the two overlapping keys is fine and make sure to keep keys like switch as the same or it can get annoying and confusing.
