There's all these little hints in the background, the UI, little touches that just really sing and make you go "was that there the whole time?" I never thought a game with virtually no dialogue would have such compelling characters that I want to know more about. I want to see more from the Worldless world (I'm not sure if thats an oxymoron or not) and from the beings that inhabit it.If I had a complaint, it'd probably be trying to find half of the things you don't have yet, or at least a hint that it exists. Most upgrades that aren't tied to absorbing are very hole-in-the-wall like, and I'm sure those who like exploring every nook and cranny of the map will love that sort of thing. For me, though, I think that's a bit far for just a little bit more health or combat time. Similarly, it'd be nice if certain encounters gave a heads up about "yo, this enemy is like REALLY difficult. maybe come back later with a few more skills?" but maybe I'm just having a major skill issue and my stubbornness is convincing me I'm him.Either way Worldless is bloody beautiful, and I HIGHLY recommend it. I wish there was more to say without spoiling, but everything about it is beautifully crafted.[EDIT:]Okay so one of my only complaints have been thrown out the window. _childDocuments_.review: With a name like that, you wouldn’t ever expect the sheer world of pain that this game can put you through. And I loved every second of it. That being said, It isn’t perfect. I’ll go over my positives and negatives in this review while avoiding any story or significant gameplay spoilers.I won’t lie, when I first saw that it was turn-based, I was definitely skeptical. Those generally aren't my genre of game, I've almost never enjoyed them. The combat in this game is FANTASTIC. It’s fluid, fast, fun, incredibly stylish, and difficult. Each move is generally unique enough to warrant using it at some point, and none of the keybinds and combinations are too difficult to perform. I do love how doing well on the defensive turn not only rewards you with minimal damage taken but also can empower you on the next attack in a variety of ways. It honestly doesn’t even feel like a traditional turn-based game, more like a general fight, where you have to defend when the enemy decides to attack. It’s incredibly fun.Though it is worth noting, this game is VERY parry-heavy. Get ready to learn some timings! It’s honestly not that hard, the window is relatively generous in this game.The movement, while not super in-depth, is very nice and smooth. Each movement upgrade has totally unique uses, and while combat and movement are almost entirely separate, I honestly didn’t mind it much. There isn’t much else to say here, feels solid.It’s definitely stylized, and I LOVE it. I’ve always been a fan of more stylistic games over ones trying to emulate real life, and this is a great example. The clean lines and unique shading style, along with the visual motifs that link different characters together are incredibly nice. In particular, I love the way that characters briefly flash into a full body while attacking or moving quickly. It’s such a unique stylistic choice, and it fits incredibly well. Whenever a character deviates from that style, it’s for a very good reason.The music is very nice in my opinion and fits the environment well. Although vague, I like the story. The game does have some pretty difficult endgame content, which is fun for the masochist in me. Most importantly though, the game doesn’t outstay its welcome. It’s brief, though this could be considered a downside. I blitzed through this game relatively quickly, so my 20-hour playtime is probably on the lower end of a 100% run. And yes, I did 100% of the game.Honestly, these negatives are what I’ve seen commonly complained about. I don’t personally agree with these, but they are worth noting.Don’t worry, I’m not one to spoil games. I know first-hand how much it sucks. However, this is going to have to be vague due to the nature of the complaint. Many people seem to dislike the ending and final boss of this game, and I do understand why. It’s kind of anticlimactic, to say the least, and definitely leaves more questions than answers. However, with my understanding of the lore, I honestly understand why it ends that way. It makes sense from that perspective. For those curious, the spoilered text below is a brief version of how I understand it.And even if you dislike it, the hardest and final enemy in the game more than makes up for it in difficulty.The map seems to have a lot of people confused, and it confused me at the beginning too. But a bit of critical thinking and I managed to figure it out. The best way that I can think of to describe it, is that the entire map is cyclical. Going off of one end pac-man style teleports you to the other side. This is represented by the dashed lines. With the hub area, think of yourself walking along the INSIDE of the circle. The structures coming from the ground each represent a part of the map, just from the perspective of that part on the circle. It’s a cool design honestly, but maybe making the hub circular in the other direction would help people.The combat, movement, and art style are incredibly good and unique. While it is turn-based, it truly doesn’t feel like most other turn-based games. It’s incredibly stylish and fast. The OST is pretty good. Most importantly though, it’s fun and doesn’t outstay its welcome.The negatives are very minor, and I don’t even agree with them. The story might feel a little anticlimactic, but I think it’s almost supposed to be that way.For a $20 indie game, I highly recommend it. If you're questioning the combat, try out the demo. It’s free, after all.Edit: For those looking to get more from this game, please check my comment on this review.

_childDocuments_.review: Wordless is an expanding world game that takes place in a newly created universe where blue beings and their counterparts orange fight in a never ending cycle of fight, defeat, repeat. The player plays the role of a nameless blue being whose goal is to fight and defeat their counterpart while exploring the universe on why this universe was created. The game play is split between platforming exploration and turn based combat. Platforming is simple starting with single jumps and expanding with new abilities such as a dash. In the platforming exploration the player’s goal is to obtain key items and abilities to progress through the world. Combat turns are split between defense and offense. When the player is attacking the enemy is defending, while the player is defending the enemy is attacking. When defending the player has a physical guard and a magic guard that will degrade with enemy attacks unless a perfect guard is performed. Perfect guard gives more offensive time to the player and prevents guard degradation. During offense the player has access to physical attacks and magic attacks. Physical damage primarily does health damage while magic damage primarily fills the absorption meter. The enemy can protect their absorption meter by blocking with magical or physical barriers that can be broken with the appropriate skill type. If the opponents health falls to zero the enemy goes into a hibernated state where they can be refought, if the opponents absorption gauge is at a certain percentage then the player can end the battle with an absorption quick-time event and gain a skill point. In combat the goal is to fill the opponents absorption meter to absorb the enemy and gain skill points to unlock new abilities or improve current ones. Skill points and other upgrades can be found while exploring such as health upgrades. The game’s first impressions were visually stunning with an simplistic abstract art style and colors. It took awhile for the combat to sink in, with my parry timings being off by a few frames. After learning the timing for the guards it was an extremely immersive experience having to constantly be engaged within the systems to be victorious, especially against special enemies and bosses. One of my favorite parts were the unique solutions to some of the enemies such as one enemy needing perfectly timed attacks to defeat them. Overall, I do recommend the game for its short length, interesting turn based combat and abstract art style. If you liked this game and want to play some similar games I would recommend GrimeGrimm’s hollowMomodora SeriesThanks for reading!

I want to start off with why I liked the game, then take a moment to just talk about some small mishaps that definitely could've made this a much better (though already great) game.I heavily enjoyed the combat system. As you progress through the game, if you're a perfectionist from the get go you'll find your combat options evolve more quickly than you can learn them. Normally this is bad, but the game doesn't really punish you for not perfecting some things, and you can evolve the skills you want as you adventure. The challenging fights in this game are all very rewarding to complete. Fights quickly go from you not knowing what is going on to mastering enemy movesets and getting into a rhythm of fighting.Generally, if you like the description of this game, I wouldn't let the negative reviews get in the way. Yes, the ending is meh, but I don't think it takes away much from the enjoyment of playing, especially if you're going for a more completionist playthrough.Onto the small negatives- Lack of quick travel options combined with a non-descriptive map can make it tedious to collect everything. In my opinion, the game would've benefitted greatly with at least one of these things being there- Ending is pretty meh because SPOILER: - Platforming could be a little bit more smooth/responsive, especially for . _childDocuments_.review: Evocative and atmospheric, Worldless is interesting and vibrant even if its design issues ultimately result in a marred experience. The movement abilities are rote and having to change forms to use your entire kit is needless busywork without the depth of Ikaruga or Outland. Combat is fascinating as the turn-based real time attack strings offer a lot of interesting opportunities for finding combos and cool synergies, but the problem is every fight is on flat ground against a puzzle boss who must be attacked in specific ways and defended in specific ways. There's no marriage of your movement and the combat, there's a constant stiffness in the platforming that prevents exploration from feeling truly great, and the result is a game that's too fascinating to simply reject outright but too flawed to really recommend.Worthwhile experiment, interesting game to play, not particularly good.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a good time and worth a buy if you click with the combat system, which I find rather unique and enjoyable.PROS:- interesting combat system, allows quite a bit of player expression- looks good- sounds good- an option to re-fight any foe you encountered before as many times as you wantCONS:- map is confusing- no way to fast travel to hub area (leads to annoying backtracking if you're like me and get lost sometimes)- moving under water or rain is cancer (there's no dash/run abilities available)PS In summum fight there's a phase when they take over one of your characters temporarily. It might be a me issue, but I found it rather frustrating to defend against their attacks if you don't kill them off in one turn. _childDocuments_.review: Just achieved 100% completion in the game, and I must say, this is one of the most unique Metroidvania games I've played, Gotta admit, I didn't really like it when I first started the game, you basically wandered around and only see a few enemies in between, the game feels pretty slow to me, but after you get the run ability, fuiyoh, everything started to look interesting, there's a bunch of cool stuff you have to figure out on your own, like how to get the hidden items, how to absorb the enemy, etc.The combat and the animation are smooth, like playing Sekiro but in 2D. You've got to be on point with parrying and timing, which adds a satisfying layer of strategy.The map design is unique, but I did get lost a few times trying to find the "main hall." A teleport button to instantly get there would be handy, but the map does suit the game's style.The music vibes well with the game, setting a great atmosphere. Now, the story is a bit meh – I couldn't quite figure out what it was trying to tell, and the ending left me a bit disappointed.Overall Score: 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: The Good;Stunning visuals, a simple-yet-atmospheric soundtrack, enough of a challenge to be fun, easy enough to not require a guide. Exploration is rarely frustrating. A simple, but intriguing story (so far). Unlocking new abilities usually gives you a button to push to make it happen and nothing more, resulting in a fair number of puzzles that revolve around discovering for yourself certain interactions those abilities have with the world beyond the basics. The thrill of that discovery I very much grew to love over the course of the game. Similarly, combat is fun and very puzzle-like. A theme between the two kinds of foes you will be facing is established very early on, giving you a strong idea of what direction the battle will go towards "solving" them. Abilities and upgrades have short demonstration clips to effectively help players learn the required timing and effects.The Bad;Honestly, it's hard to tell whether the problems I have are because I'm not understanding something or if the game's not functioning properly, so take these on a case-by-case basis, k? While the map is stylistically cool, the lack of details beyond the foe you face in each area makes repeat visits more difficult and progression more annoying than it needed to be. Certain combat abilities are either laughably ineffective or, in the case of one particular ability, straight-up fail to function. Verdict;I found this game by accident looking for games that released around the 21st. After watching the trailer, this game became the first I ever installed the demo of, and it was an excellent experience. For all my complaints, I must say that my experiences with the full game have been rather positive overall. The issues never turned me off the game beyond mild frustration and even made the eventual success feel all the more rewarding. There's room for improvement, of course, but overall I can comfortably recommend this game to all. I wasn't expecting to find a new game that would pique my interest this late into 2023. It's certainly taken the top spot for the most interesting game released this year, and I wish nothing but it's success.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game with familiar platforming game play mixed with turn-based combat. Very minimalist which I enjoy.As other reviews have pointed out, you do really need to love parrying mechanics as the combat becomes increasingly reliant on them. There are some skills that ease this a bit, but overall it's a primary mechanic that needs to be mastered.The map layout is interesting, and does follow the aesthetic of the game well, but leaves something to be desired. Areas are too decently sized just to be represented by a single line. My one "issue" (personal, not necessarily an actual issue) is the amount of input combinations that become available over time for combat. With how battles work and your turn being on a timer, remembering everything available to you in the moment is a bit much. _childDocuments_.review: Worldless is one of the most beautiful and atmospheric titles I've ever played. It's gorgeous, animations are superb, the score is haunting and contributes greatly to the game's mood. Controls are very smooth and responsive, whether you are traversing the environment or fighting enemies, something that is fortunate to have in a game heavy on platforming. The combat is a curious mix of real-time and turn-based, which is part-puzzle solving, part-execution in terms of skills required. Your goal is to fill out the absorb bar and consume the enemy, earning a skill point. The latter encounters are pretty challenging and will have you reviewing the tools at your disposal and thinking of the best ways to approach the challenge. One of the key features is swapping between two characters that have different movement and combat abilities on the fly, which works fairly well.  If there's something to complain about, it's that there is a significant overlap between the move sets you possess, with a large amount of skills being equivalent except for the elemental damage type, but at the very least they have unique sounds and animations. Some of the combat encounters are frustrating, in particular those featuring fire enemies. Fire enemies have a health bar in addition to an absorb bar, and it's a race between the two, many a time you will accidentally kill the foe before having a chance to absorb them, which, for all intents and purposes, is as if you haven't beaten them at all. Luckily, it's more of an exception than the rule, and most encounters are well-designed. The game can be a bit obtuse at times, and is on the shorter side, you can probably beat it in 10-12 hours, but I'd still strongly recommend it. It is very unique, and its ambience and visuals are unparalleled.

_childDocuments_.review:
Worldless is set at a time where the rules of existence remain undefined. Players will explore a shapeless world of two realms, one filled with entities forming their growth and understanding, the other is the place they aspire to. This inevitably thrusts them into a war against polarities in a battle for transcendence.

In this 2D Action Adventure Platformer, players will jump, glide and dash through an indeterminate setting, uncovering its secrets and finding their place within a mind-bending reality.

Along the way are encounters with beings who believe their superiority has automatically earned them a place in the next existence. Using turn-based rules along with a unique defend and combination system that requires patience, timing, and the desire for development, your strength and capabilities will truly be put to the test.

name: Ib
detailed_description: A young girl named Ib visits an art gallery with her parents. While perusing the various works of art, Ib suddenly realizes that she is alone. As she searches for someone – anyone – else, the museum begins to change... ◆◆◆◆◆ A 2D exploration adventure game set in a creepy, mysterious art gallery. Inspect the area around you, discovering items and disarming traps to find your way out of the strange gallery. Game Features A mysterious adventure set it an art gallery full of puzzles to solve. Pieces of artwork beautifully crafted in pixel art. Basic controls consist of movement and an interact (speak) button, enjoyable by players of all levels. Seven different endings to unlock based on player actions and choices. Upon completion you will be rewarded with the True Guertena exhibit where you can collect the artwork found throughout the game and be able to visit an extra dungeon that you couldn’t access in your first playthrough. New Features This game is a remake of the 2D exploration-adventure title Ib, set in a creepy, mysterious art gallery and originally released in February 2012. Virtually all of the graphics have been updated, with many upgraded and additional effects as well. Significantly improved screen resolution and graphics allow players to experience a classic in a whole new light. Brand new graphics for maps, characters, and stills. Addition of all-new and redesigned pieces of artwork. Further improvements upon the original concept of making the game enjoyable for Players of all level through optimizations to the many puzzles in-game. Brand new puzzles, effects, and tricks that were not present in the original. Addition of “Zoom Mode” for improved visibility, allowing players to spot small items more easily and view the many pieces of artwork in greater detail. New “conversation system” allows companions to offer hints and engage in conversation. Brand new BGM composed specifically for the remake.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the original, and this updated version is just as good.The additions along the way are very nice, and the improved graphics are noticeable. Since those were the more difficult parts of the original game, I assume this was done for a more streamlined experience. Instead of your flower wilting to represent your life, it is now replaced by more accurate "points". Although this makes it easier to tell exactly how many hits you can take, I miss the more original old design.An iconic music track was also changed, likely due to licensing issues... Can't completely replace the original for me, but it's still a very worthwhile experience! Still wishing for a sequel a decade later.

_childDocuments_.review: Words honestly can't describe how much I just genuinely love this game. I remember when I first heard about it by watching PewDiePie play it back in 2012, and ever since then it's been my all time favorite RPG Maker game. I spent probably 200+ hours just replaying it over and over again, I have no idea what it was about Ib, but the kid me was just so in love with this game. I had the soundtrack on my PSP which I carried everywhere and listened to often, I replayed the game what had to have been at least over 100 times, and I was there for Every update. I remember when the Extra Dungeon update dropped and I was so excited, I had thought the game wasn't gonna be getting anything new, and there the Extra Dungeon update came in. I kept doing the steps to unlock the Dungeon wrong, and I ended up replaying the entire game 4 times in one day, Just to get to that Dungeon, because I wanted to play through it so bad. I had known about other RPG Maker games before, but Ib was the one that Really stood out to me, and got me into the rest. Ib is one of my biggest inspirations for wanting to make my own unique and bizarre games, and stories. There's just so much I could say about what this game has done for me, but I'm sure I'd run out of space to type, honestly. When I read that there was a Remake coming to Steam, I was beyond excited. If not for an excuse to replay the game once again, then for the fact that I'd get to hopefully see the game with some new ideas and changes that Kouri would have wanted to make to the game. It was all just so exciting to me. I bought it as soon as I could, and even though it's not in English yet, I still played through the game as best I could. When I couldn't use my memory to complete stuff, I would try my best to translate the dialogue into English. It was so much fun revisiting this game, the new artwork, new puzzles, new ideas, and just generally, everything about this remake warms my little heart, and brings such a big smile to my face. I imagine now that I've gotten back into this game, I'm gonna be replaying it over and over again, just like I did back in 2012-2015. What else can I say? This game holds the most special place in my heart, and it will always mean the world to me. I'm really grateful that this came to steam, and I'm honestly really grateful this remake happened at all! What a pleasant surprise. I'm just so uncontrollably happy, Thank you so much Kouri for making one of my most Favorite games of all time, I really hope to see more from you in the future, and I am extremely glad, and happy to see you still around. You're my hero! ^w^ ♥

_childDocuments_.review: This review was initially framed for veterans of IB who have played the original and want to know if the Steam version is worth the price over the original, as well as if this version is the definitive version of IB. I will also remark on if new players should buy this version at the end of the review over the free version. This review is a bullet-point list of things better, mixed, or worse compared to the free version. If you are a new player, you can skip just to the conclusion to avoid spoilers.-You can talk with Garry at any moment in almost every room (and with different dialogues depending on different location within the room, so a huge chunk of new dialogue). This is - by far - exceptional fan-service since one of the biggest draws for fans to buy an expanded version of games they've completed is to spend more time with characters they love, and you have that in spades with this version. Alongside Garry, Mary also has this expanded dialogue as well when she's in your party. -IB's dream (nightmare) sequence right after the end of the Grey Area is executed more artfully and a better and richer dream sequence overall.-So much level streamlining, rooms that did not need to be rooms are deleted and some puzzles are streamlined on unnecessary aspects (6 tile pieces instead of 12). Not all of this is better, but quite a bit are an improvement.-Characters have better portraits, especially Mary who has a cute fang now when she's angry at you.-The top-down pixel art is better overall, but there is some minor inferiorities here and there -True Exhibit picture tracking is streamlined across save files, so the game remembers which picture you've already seen not just from inside one single save-file line, but across all save files (as long as you saved).-The puzzles overall. Quite a few puzzles have been replaced for completely new puzzles and many original puzzles that were kept were streamlined in some ways. On the whole, I personally felt the new puzzles are easier than the old puzzles, either more obvious or just less steps, and I don't like this. The new puzzles are not as interesting as the old ones, but they are more streamlined and less prone to getting new players stuck on a step, but I don't mind if the player gets stuck on a good puzzle because it's ultimately worth it.  Some players might prefer these slightly easier and more streamlined puzzles, but I don't.--Excessive puzzle hints. In certain areas, not all, there are too many hints to be gained from just talking to your companion character, whether it's Gary or Mary. You will have hints all the way through to the finish line, Kouri doesn't want any player to be left behind which is noble in some regard, but I see great value in letting players get stuck and having to push themselves to figure it out. By getting stuck, the puzzles become a bigger achievement since the players had to work harder for the solution, so hints that guide through the entire puzzle undermine the satisfaction in a real way. This doesn't always happen, but it does happen. -Music. Kouri switched around which tracks are played during which scenes (some not all), and also replaced some tracks with completely new songs. This was never done in a way that improved upon the original free version, there was not a single switch or new song that was better than the track and scene matching of the original, so it's just overall worse.-Rpgmaker Engine version. MV is a lot buggier than Rpgmaker 2000, so there will be a longer period of bug-crunching to make it as bug-free as the free version. I encountered a bug that forced me to restart the game once during my playthrough. There have been several patches now, so it should in theory be better.-Sound effects. I am so sad that the very aggressive "HWAA!!" that the red headless statue shouts at you when it comes alive is removed and replaced with silence. Really Kouri? Why? That sound effect alone establishes the danger and urgency for running away from the monster so strongly for the game, and you removed or changed this central aspect of tension not just from the first red statue, but also for the black hands coming out of the walls and the red lady as well. This dilutes the horror so much, it was central for establishing tension inside the initial monster encounters and how could you possibly remove this sound effect? I am baffled that Kouri who created the original IB is the same person who made this remake that doesn't see the value of these sound effects. Overall, if you are a big fan of IB and have played the free version many times before, just the fact that you have so many new lines of optional dialogue with Gary should alone be enough to make you purchase the Steam version so I can recommend it to veterans who love and are passionate about the original game. But is this the Definitive version of IB? I would say No it is not because the puzzles, while more streamlined, are less rewarding and imaginative than the original and more importantly, the horror is inferior to the free version because of some decisions of redesigning events as well as removing certain sound effects that set the tension. The Definitive version is still the freeware version 1.07.So for new players that have never played IB, the better experience is within the original free version so I recommend playing that over buying this. For veteran players, the game is worth it for the expanded time and dialogue with Gary and a nice trip down memory lane inside this beloved game. I would like to give a mixed review rather than a binary thumb up or down, but for the sake of new players I will thumb it down.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has fond memories of playing the accessible version of Ib about ten years ago, I was over the moon once I heard it was released on Steam. This horror visual novel about Ib, a little girl caught in the illusion of a museum alongside Garry, surprised me with its engaging storyline and appealing characters.The game conjures an exciting world that one would very much like to explore, to unlock the said world's mysteries, and also to understand its history. Ib, Garry, and Mary themselves bring layers to the story, making each interaction meaningful and every session of solving the different puzzles satisfying. Even though the puzzles might prove somewhat problematic, they continue to balance not being too challenging to complete and allowing a good gameplay experience."Ib" is a game that is going subtle on horror: no sudden scares, no overpowering gore. Instead, it builds up that feeling of unease and fear as the story progresses. Creepy encounters with disturbing artwork and the strangeness of the museum keep players on edge without giving away cheap thrills.The Steam version of "Ib" is updated with several enhancements that make the overall gameplay experience better. With better graphics and dialogue screens, up to the ability to talk to the game's companions whenever you like, these editions help make the game more immersive and further aid one in building a stronger bond with the characters in the game. Sometimes, the puzzles change; generally, the changes favor better game mechanics, yet some classics may upset die-hard enthusiasts.This is a vital aspect of the game that raises feelings while it raises introspection. I had an episode of depression at that time, which brought many thoughts to the fore concerning love, loneliness, and time. The moving soundtrack, which I still listen to for inspiration, further added the depth of emotional experience while playing the game.In the end, "Ib" is more an artwork than a horror game; it resonates profoundly and stays beautifully created for the ones who get to partake in its enigma. Be you picking it back up again after years or new to the experience, this is a journey well worth taking, one that will stay with you long after you finish playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Ib manages to do for me what so few horror games manage to accomplish, and that is to actually give a sense of unease and dread. Without going into spoilers, it's only a few minutes into the game that things start to tread the path of uncomfortable surrealism, with the art growing considerably more disturbing in how Ib interacts with it, and how the art interacts with her.With all due respect to more conventional horror titles, say, Dead Space or The Evil Within, Ib maintains a feeling of dread and discomfort. Enemies can be evaded, yes, but there's a feeling of being stalked while trapped in a world you can't possibly fully understand. Contrast Dead Space remake, where soon enough the horror gives way to cutting off an abomination's arm, then using telekinesis to impale it or another horror with said arm, then simply setting fire to the more mobile enemies.This is not, I repeat, not to disrespect games in which reducing enemies to a smoldering heap of charred body parts is an acceptable tactic- there is a time and a place for the cathartic destruction of the nightmares that haunted our closets and lurked under our beds. Ib, however, leans firmly towards the horror and self-preservation of being in a hostile and unknown environment, where the only feasible option is to run, hide, and hope whatever nameless horror eventually loses track of you.And let's face it- some modern art galleries are creepy enough already, even in the daylight.

_childDocuments_.review: How do I even go about reviewing this? Of all the rpgmaker titles in my library, from  to  to ,  or even , none have hit that level of being an absolute icon in the rpgmaker/indie horror fandom. Well, all those other ones are actually franchises more or less now, so I guess that claim is debatable. But  itself become the posterchild up there with  (which we have surprisingly yet to see a return to Steam for, as of writing this, despite every other game I mentioned making the move) for the big rpgmaker horror boom that took over gaming-YouTube circa 2012. And for good reason!The music, the characters, the aesthetics, the endings, all absolute classics looking back, which I was more than happy to relive 10 years later. It absolutely held up.Like other Steam versions of these games, these are remakes you pay for as opposed to the freeware we downloaded years ago. It has all the most recent content (including extra dungeons and endings that people who played before 1.04 may not have seen!) with updated graphics and UI, and quite honestly I am more than happy to pay this creator regardless.Exploring everything  can be a little headscratching at times. You'll want a guide handy to explore all the endings, or even just to get the best ending because the requirements for forming emotional bonds (or doom) with your party members can be pretty strict. And as a personal note, it's my opinion that the health meter is a little harder to read than in the original.That being said, save smartly, and you can see everything in 2-3 playthroughs and roughly 8 hours of playtime, going by my stats, roughly 2 hours per route. A short, sweet horror that people love to death as the little darling of the genre, and I am counted among them. I can't see myself not naming this as one of my favorite games at any point in the future, distant or not. Just... look at them beautiful pixels!

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot praise Ib enough. I consider this to be a triumph of art and creativity, the very definition of breathing life and love into your work. To me, this is more than just a game with beautiful artwork, fun characters, and a spooky adventure through a mysterious wonderland. It wasn't created just to be observed and admired, but to take root and blossom inside the player. This is a living work of art that happily paints upon you while you play. It colors your soul, it draws on your heart, it doodles on your wishes and dreams. It is very playful, and it is always thrilled to be seen and enjoyed.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing the free game 10 years ago and simply being sucked into the game. I'm so so happy that I get to re-play it again on Steam.Ib is a horror VN about a girl (Ib) who gets trapped in a fantastical world inside a museum of a famous artist. She and another poor soul who gets trapped in this world (Garry) now must navigate through this world and find a way back to their reality. This game gives us a very fascinating world that makes you want to explore it as much as you can, as well as know why it even exists, it has also a great set of characters such as Ib, Garry, and Mary who also are this game is great, and the puzzles itself are rather nice to solve, a bit of a challenge but nothing too difficult. It also has 7 endings in total.Horror-wise, Ib is pretty light in that department, no jump scares or gore, it does have a couple of chase scenes but overall nothing too terrifying. This paid steam version, adds a lot of improvements like, bigger resolution, clearer artwork, the ability to zoom in the screen, better dialogue screens, and my most favorite feature, the ability to talk to your companion anytime in the game. The characters are part of what makes Ib great and being able to talk to Garry at any time was an added bonus. It definitely enhanced the game.Some puzzles were modified, which for some I did not mind (it was an improvement) and for others, I felt disappointed but it's not a deal-breaker.Overall, I definitely recommend anyone to buy Ib, it's a great game that will suck you in.

_childDocuments_.review: A really good remake compared to the original, it feels much more full of stuff without it feeling like its strayed too far from its identity. I had a lot of fun trying to inspect every art and dialogue piece garry had to say, the new higher res art allows for more detail while keeping its charm. The character portraits are awesome, except for the dad who looks very odd? but everything else is amazing. Its a short but sweet game, im pretty sure theres some replay value to be seen but i havent checked that out yet.Overall the game is great, ive watched youtubers play it a long time ago when i was really young and even played the original for myself a year back before i knew a remake was being made. It was nice to see it remade and would recommend this over the original.

_childDocuments_.review: Never was I fond of pixelated graphics but Ib made me look past that. What stood out for me was the soundtrack which is surprisingly very pleasant to listen to. Kudos to that.For maximum effect, I recommend playing this in the middle of a dark, silent night.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the free version a long time ago and bought this on short notice after the announcement of an EN translation. I expected it to be the same old game with "higher res" sprites, but it had more to it than I thought.For one, the revamped puzzles are less number-heavy and more dynamic; certain puzzles are never the same from one playthrough after another. Being able to talk to the party members is also a big highlight considering the game's characters; if you're all about that character interaction, this version has you covered while you backtrack. Qualities of Life are also welcome, such as the game not spamming "You don't know this word" after the first time you see it, easier ways to get back to the title screen and/or reload, the accurately pointing out how many artworks are available. These are all a refreshing take especially if you're trying to get all artworks and endings.A notable change is the Sadly some nuances from the original were lost along the way; certain sound effects were completely changed in favor of being "less scary" such as the wall hands, the wooden fish puzzle, and even damage effects. The revamped layout also pushed certain events out of the way . Minor details, but in a game like this, details matter.While I like the simplified puzzles, we ended up losing steps along the way, notably in the bonus dungeon on your second run.  A shame, because the puzzles are a big highlight for a creative game. I simply wish there was more in it, minus the numbers.Overall, the remake is worth picking up, whether you're a freeware veteran or a newcomer just for the sheer amount of creativity put into it. How often do you see art museum-themed games with clever solutions and endearing characters?P.S. Fix the grammar on the only achievement this game has.

_childDocuments_.review: Ib is a remake of kouri's 2012 RPG Maker horror game of the same name, though odds are you're already aware of that if you're here. Regardless, whether or not you've played Ib before, you've likely heard of it if you have any interest in RPG Maker games. It's an RPG Maker classic, and for good reason. Everything about this game is masterfully done. The spritework is charming, the soundtrack is ambient and eerie, and the story is engaging and bittersweet. Being an RPG without any battles, there's not much to talk about in terms of gameplay, though there are a healthy handful of puzzles scattered about the museum you'll be traversing, and the atmosphere is so cohesive and captivating that the simplistic gameplay won't bother you much anyways. This version of the game has been entirely remade in RPG Maker MV, with all new sprites for absolutely everything, uncompressed music tracks, and even a few new puzzles and areas here and there. However, the changes aren't drastic... certainly nothing that necessitates playing this remake, I would say. It's about 95% the same game. It's definitely a fun new way to play through Ib if you've played the original before, and if you're a new fan, you won't be missing out on much by playing this over the RPG Maker 2003 version. I cannot stress how much I don't want to dissuade anyone from buying this remake, as Ib is still a fantastic game either way and kouri deserves all the support he can get, but I would only do so if you've tried the freeware version first and enjoyed it. They are so similar that there's no real reason not to, unless you just really want to burn through 12 bucks. If you DO end up liking Ib, however, definitely consider buying this remake. It's a great and easy way to throw a few dollars kouri's way and show him some appreciation for putting out one of the most iconic and memorable RPG Maker titles ever.

It's a short game, but you really bond with the characters (And I mean Garry. I freaking cried TWICE?) and the whole atmosphere makes you jumpy af. It's creative and great, and it will make me look forward to find more horror RPGmaker gems like this (I am, however, passing up Corpse party for now because I don't have an stomach for gore)

_childDocuments_.review: One day back in ye ol' 2014, when I was hanging out with a friend, she decided to pull this exact game up while I watched her play through it. I was so intrigued, that I ended up downloading and playing through the game myself so many times that I was able to beat it in my sleep (My obsession with it was so bad I even ended up emulating it on my phone so I could play it on the go). _childDocuments_.review: Been playing Ib ever since the old version came out, it's safe to say I've replayed this game for over 100 times, so comparing the two made me notice some things that I wish they would have added in this version as well. (Don't focus on the time spent on this game from Steam, I only found out about it being available here today)First of all, I'm really pleased with the graphics improvement, and the ability to zoom so we can see paintings even closer. Being able to chat with Garry and Mary throughout the rooms is another bonus that I really enjoyed, it made the game more immersive and gave us more depth to the character's relationships with each other. However, with the improved graphics also came some negative aspects, where some of the paintings do not seem as eerie as they used to in the previous version. Take the lady who smiles after Ib takes her first key for example. She is no longer creepy, but rather...just cute. Another thing that bugged me was the fact that the hands from the green and yellow room now no longer produced a sound that I found in the old version scary at first, it really added to the horror aspect of the game. Speaking of sounds, again as you're chased by the statues and ladies in the paintings, the sound effect no longer has an impact that had you feeling like you were actually running away from something. Mary's theme also changed, but maybe that's just my nostalgia that's speaking that prefers it over the new tune, but I don't mind that change that much since the melody is also nice. The thing that I did really like was the addition of another Lady in the painting with white hair and hollow eyes, which made perhaps the toughest (tough is a hard word, but compared to other rooms it is tougher to complete) level even better, and I really liked other new artworks, such as Porcupuss and Guardian of Time, although I wish some of the things from the older version still remained in the game, such as the maze which helped you raise your points with Gary.All and all, I still adore this game, and it has been my obsession for the longest time ever so the remake was, in my opinion, much needed to bring people back to this masterpiece.Will absolutely be playing again. 11/10
_childDocuments_.name: Ib

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible re-imagining of one of my favourite games. The new option to chat with Garry or Mary adds so much, and easily my favourite change to the game. The new visual style is great, along with the map layout changes, the updated puzzles are much better, none of them are too tricky, but they're all much better than the ones they replaced.The only change I didn't like was the change to Mary's theme, even if it was overused in RPG Maker games, I think this is the game that defined it, and her new theme just doesn't fit sadly. It's not like this change ruins anything, though, as it's still the beautiful and charming game I remember playing, but enhanced to be better than before <3

_childDocuments_.review: Ib is one of the bigger reasons I fell in love with art as a kid. I adore painting, I love creating things with my hands- creating! With all of the beautiful pixel art, music, and lovely characters you can't help but adore! All with this wondrous fairy tale feeling of dread- I really can not recommend playing this beautifully done remake enough. I could absolutely go on, but to avoid any spoilers-It is my promise that you'll have a wonderful visit to this museum! I do hope you'll give it a try <3

_childDocuments_.review: The 2022 remake of Ib is a solid remake of an amazing game.This game's story, characters, and beautiful art have been an inspiration to me for years. The atmosphere is fantastic and the distinctive visual style is a lot of fun. Just looking at all the bizarre paintings is a motivation to continue in itself. As someone who grew up with this game, I obviously have a lot of investment in the original game.The rest of this review is less about the game itself and more about its' quality as a remake.I can say without doubt that this version is definitively the best. There is now a button to press for dialogue with characters in your party at any time, and it's a nice treat to get new dialogue for them. The graphical quality has received a nice little boost, and it's easier to tell what some of the paintings are supposed to depict now.Some of the puzzles are slightly less obtuse, meaning this version might be more accessible.I'm not fully convinced that all of the improvements truly justify replacing the original version, though. Ib (2012) is still available online, completely for free. There are no major flaws that needed to be addressed by a remake, and the experience really isn't that different. The only change that I'm truly not fond of is the health bar. Ib (2012) had a picture of your character's rose in the corner, with the visual state of the rose showing your character's state. If the rose wilts, so too will you rot away. However, in Ib (2022) that visual has been replaced with a symbolic rose icon, where your health is instead represented by thorns. This change weakens the impact of the rose in the story; Visually seeing the rose lose its' petals gave you more of a connection to the characters' situation.Other than a few paintings missing, that is the biggest problem I have with Ib (2022). Rather small compared to the good changes, but as a long-time fan, I feel that the iconography of the rose is important to the game. All of that being said, Ib (2022) is most certainly best version of Ib, and personally I'm happy that the game is getting more attention. In any form, this game will be a good time, and if you want to pay 10 dollars for the small improvements then I see no reason not to, because this game is good.(I have currently only completed the main route of the game; If there is more to be said about subsequent playthroughs and post-game content then I will be sure to come back and re-make this review.)
_childDocuments_.name: Ib

_childDocuments_.review: You know, I have a soft spot for indie horror adventure games, and when it comes to classics, Ib holds a special place in my heart. I mean, it's been over a decade since its original freeware release, and it's still as captivating as ever. Now, with this remake on RPG Maker MV, I was a bit skeptical, wondering if it would retain the whimsy and charm of the original or fall prey to the dreaded soulless remake curse. But boy, was I pleasantly surprised.From the get-go, Ib sets the stage with a strange and unsettling art exhibit that pulls you right into the madness of artist Weiss Guertena. The atmosphere is eerie, the puzzles are creative yet challenging, and the characters, though brief in appearance, are endearing and fully fleshed out. While it may not have traditional RPG elements like combat or character progression, its meaningful story and multiple endings make it a standout in the adventure game genre.As you guide Ib through this bizarre world, you can't help but feel the influence of Alice in Wonderland. But believe me, Guertena's world is darker, claustrophobic, and far deadlier. Yet, it's so wonderfully appealing with its weird and whimsical art style. The way the bizarre creations come to life is both captivating and unsettling, and the use of crayons in certain scenes adds to its childlike charm.One of the things I love about Ib is that it knows how to build tension without relying on combat. Running from foes, solving puzzles, and avoiding danger keeps you on your toes. The difficulty is forgiving, and the generous autosave ensures that failure is a learning experience rather than a punishment.The haunting music and spot-on sound effects make the whole experience even more immersive. The eerie soundtrack perfectly complements the creepy ambiance and adds feelings of loneliness and helplessness. It's easily one of the game's strongest points.Sure, Ib's gameplay may be simple, but that's what makes it so compelling. The interactions with the characters may be limited, but they quickly become memorable. And despite the short playtime, the game packs a punch with its multiple endings, which can be a bit tricky to figure out without some help.As a fan of indie RPG Maker horror games, Ib was a delightful journey into the past—a golden era of creativity within a limited toolset. It's a testament to what independent developers can achieve when they let their imagination run wild.So, in conclusion, Ib is a special little gem that still holds its charm over a decade later. With its haunting aesthetic, unique world design, and clever puzzles, it's a must-play for horror fans and adventure game enthusiasts alike. Sure, it may have its quirks like the unexplained bond mechanic for certain endings, and the controls might feel a bit stiff, but those are minor bumps in an otherwise fantastic experience.If you're looking for a short and sweet adventure that leaves a lasting impression, Ib is the way to go. It's well worth your time and money, and I highly recommend diving into this eerie and captivating world.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game 10 years ago and it's still a fantastic experience.One of the coolest additions in this remake is the insane amount of new dialogue with Garry/Mary. Not only is there new dialogue for each room, where you can speak to them by hitting E, there are also an insane amount of variations based on location in the room, events that you've just triggered, etc.At one point, Garry and Ib have to cross a small rainbow bridge, and I was shocked to see that he had optional dialogue before, during AND after crossing it. Entire sections of the game that easily could have been blocked off from before you meet him also have unique dialogue the entire way back to the beginning, which was incredibly fun and encouraged me to return and reread the painting titles for the 100% achievement.If you're in too poor of a financial circumstance to purchase this game, I'd heavily recommend the original 2012 release in lieu of it, though this remaster definitely trumps the original in most/all regards.

_childDocuments_.review: The beloved 2012 RPG Maker classic Ib is back. I highly recommend it for old-time players seeking to relive the nostalgia and new players alike.Some of the key differences in this remake are some of the level layouts and puzzles being changed, removed and even brand new additions to make the Art Gallery make more sense and be less difficult and more streamlined. The graphics have also been improved and a zoom mode was added which I didn't use much, but it's cool that it exists. Plenty of UI changes/art improvements too.However the best feature of this remake in my opinion is the talk to your partner feature. It's really interesting hearing Garry's thoughts and opinions on various areas, events and puzzles and learning a bit more about him (Mary too!) and seeing their relationship with Ib. A TON of dialogue has been added via this feature alone, I recommend using it alot. It primarily feels like fanservice for old-time Ib players and might be a bit tedious to new players though but it adds alot of life to the game. I just kept talking to Garry after doing literally anything lol.Oh and a useful piece of advice to keep in mind is that there's an achievement for seeing all 150 of Guertena's artworks, so be sure to interact with everything (and with Garry present if possible since they don't count if Ib's 9 year-old brain can't understand the words).There's a few minor downsides(?) in my opinion, though I don't even know if I'd actually complain about them, but I thought I'd list them anyway. The UI is different and while I'm all for it, I do miss the old health system of seeing the rose decay and wilt with missing petals the more damage you've taken instead of the color just fading like it does now. Mary's theme also seems to have changed due to copyright, but I ended up warming up to her new theme in the end. There's also a chase sequence which was alot more intense on the old version (loads more enemies), but it's super dumbed down and easy on the remake.Basically Ib modernized but a bit more easy with some additional features and some new content. Interesting for old and new players. The original is still free, so you could always just play that too. If you're brand new to Ib, you could go with either version honestly but it's nice to support the creator after such a great game being free all this time.

_childDocuments_.review: Ib, an evergreen. I remember watching videos on YouTube and playing this many, many years ago. It was huge, everyone talked about it and it led to a series of successes to similar games such as Misao, Mad Father, The Crooked Man, To The Moon etc. If you were around during the gaming landscape in the early 2010s, you knew about Ib. It was really creative then, and to many degrees it still is now.Preview of Ib below, if you want to support my channel. I upload videos to support my reviews!When I saw that Ib was coming to Steam, I just had to wishlist it. It's been at least 10 years since I played this.I felt I've never really forgot about this game, since everything felt so familiar when I began playing. And that's because your first playthrough will be exactly as you remember it to be. The only real differences are of course some mild added mechanics such as a simple zoom in to further look at the various paintings or characters.The gameplay is exactly the same: a linear adventure with various puzzle elements, easy but satisfying to solve. You  can talk with your "allies" while walking around various areas, and there's quite a lot of dialogue. Speaking of which, dialogues are not particularly complex and for the most part they fall flat and feel sometimes too "anime-ish". Ib's strength is not found in how dialogues are written, rather than the experience and the atmosphere it manages to put you in, which for me makes up for everything else. On the other hand, though, art description is well made and interesting to read all the way through.The premise is rather simple. You're with your parents and you're going to visit an exhibition of various art pieces made by the fictional artist Guertena. While exploring around the area, strange things begin to happen and suddenly you'll be introduced to an otherworldly section where you'll have to find an exit in order to survive. This, of course, isn't Ib's main focus. The whole core concept is based upon art, and it's safe to say that it delivers in such sense through the interestingly vivid yet minimalistic Guertena works. The subtle animations give depth to the things you see and manage to describe the artist very well. Even though many years have passed, I have to say that Ib doesn't lose itself while going forward, meaning that art will always be the main concern with the plot. So much so that the plot revolves around that in every sense, but I won't tell you why since I don't want to spoil everything. :)To sum it up, the art direction on this game is clear and manages to be coherent all the way through, with various interesting ideas scattered here and there, and an atmosphere which will always be remembered. I haven't said anything about the score, I know. I'll just say that the melodies of Ib are echoing in my mind since I've first booted it up. I think that speaks for itself. Moody, warm, deep and "Rule of Rose"-sque. It captures well the whole "rose" deal they came up with.I'll admit that having the possibility to get other endings is exciting and I'm willing to go through the story one more time to discover additional areas. The fact that after so many years we've gotten new content in Ib is really cool, and I can't wait to play more. I'll eventually update this review after I've done a second playthrough.With that said, I can't recommend this enough. It's an interesting game, and it's basically history. It's a must have for people who liked games such as Yume Nikki, Misao, The Witch House or To The Moon. If you're into those kind of games, you won't be disappointed, trust me on this! If you've played this in the past, I still recommend buying it to support the developer as well as enjoy the new content which has been added.::

_childDocuments_.review: One of the game's main strengths is its ability to create a pervasive sense of unease and tension, achieved through expert design of the environment, music, and sound effects. The game offers an immersive experience, with intricate and detailed environments that convey a sense of familiarity and discomfort at the same time.IB features puzzles that are both challenging and thoughtfully crafted, requiring a combination of observation, exploration, and logic to solve. The game offers multiple endings, each dependent on the player's choices, adding an extra layer of replay ability and encouraging players to fully immerse themselves in the game's intricacies.The game's story is another standout feature, as it offers a complex and twisted narrative that keeps players guessing until the end. Characters are intriguing, with backstories and motivations that are gradually revealed through carefully placed clues and interactions.Overall, IB is a well-crafted and effective horror game that stands out in the genre. Its attention to detail, immersive atmosphere, and intricate storytelling make it an unforgettable experience for players who enjoy psychological horror games. If you're looking for a game that will keep you on edge and fully immersed in its world, IB is definitely worth checking out on Steam.

This version didn't disappoint. Polished graphics, expanded dialogue, fixed puzzles, and extra content! It changed quite a bit but still had the same charm. It was like playing it for the first time again. The bonus dungeon and the True Exhibit gallery were awesome additions to this game, I spent two days making sure I completed everything for the steam achievement. If you've never played Ib, YOU NEED TO! Especially if you're a fan of other RPG horror games like The Witch's House, Mad Father, etc. It's a bit on the shorter side, but the characters are so well-written and unforgettable. The music and the atmosphere is one of a kind and will have you fully immersed into it's strange world, but I won't say too much so you can experience it for yourself. I can tell the creator put so much love and passion into the game's story, characters, art, and mechanics. You might feel pretty emotional by the time you've completed all the endings of the game, so bring tissues. And again, PLAY IB!! You won't regret it! <3

_childDocuments_.review: I've loved this game for so long and have always wished for a way to financially support the creator somehow, and I'm so happy people finally can. This game genuinely changed my life and was the first horror game I've played and completed by myself. As for the remake, it retains most of the core game while improving and adding new character interactions and puzzles (no more math!) that are very welcome. I will say that I felt some of the scares had more impact in the original, but otherwise is a significant improvement to an already incredible game. This game is just very atmospheric in a way that sticks with you for years and its scares don't rely on blood and gore. Proper care is put into each painting and extra info about the museum to make it really feel like you're wandering through the gallery of an actual famous artist (even though he's completely fictional). Something I really appreciate about Ib is how accessible it makes horror to people who might otherwise be scared of it. As someone who loves horror games but usually can't play them myself, Ib gave me plenty of scares but it wasn't so terrifying that I couldn't progress. It's also about 2-3 hours long but it genuinely feels longer than that. If you want to see everything the game has to offer, it WILL be much longer than that. There is a story that helps make everything cohesive, but it doesn't get in the way of anything. Many RPG maker games tend to focus heavily on story with gameplay as an afterthought, but Ib's puzzles and atmosphere are well thought out and memorable. If you really like good puzzles and heavily atmospheric games, I'd definitely recommend this. Now I just want more accessible merch LOL
_childDocuments_.name: Ib

_childDocuments_.review: I first heard of Ib when I was a young teen, and at the time I thought it was one of the greatest stories I'd ever seen. Now as a young adult having 100% completed the remake, I can say with certainty that Ib remains an excellent story-centric horror adventure that could both warm my hardened heart and keep me up at night with worry (thanks, Final Stage.) While the decision to switch from dark, messy sketches to brighter pixel art may be questionable as an aesthetic change, I enjoyed many of the other changes and new features like zooming in and the ability to talk to Garry on command.Talking to Garry itself is especially praiseworthy as there are multiple location/event sensitive lines in a majority of rooms in the game. For example, if you find the hider in the room of curtains on your first try, you can get a unique reaction from Garry for every other curtain if you backtrack there. That's a ton of optional dialogue that is incredibly easy to miss since not every player would be tempted to backtrack after finding Garry, and those who would backtrack would've also probably checked every curtain before moving on. While talking to Garry in this way is now tied to getting the game's good ending, it is only necessary to see 20 of the 200 or more new Garry lines to get the highest possible bond from doing so, leaving you free to not talk to him for long stretches without getting a less happy ending.The sheer attention to detail in Ib is commendable, and feels increasingly special as the AAA games industry slides further towards rushed releases, homogenized gameplay, superficial choices, live services and maximum monetization - with few exceptions.

_childDocuments_.review: The original RPG Maker horror classic, redone in a higher screen resolution and new engine for it's tenth anniversary. If you're new here: Ib's brand of horror comes with a focus on puzzles, characterisation, and atmosphere. It's popularity partially comes from the fact that it was designed with genre newcomers in mind, so if you don't usually like horror this is a good place to start. There's no shock imagery, the scares are pretty restrained, the puzzles are fairer compared to other games of the era , and while some horrible things can happen to the cast if you're not careful they can usually be undone in another ending. ...Y'know. Usually.If you're familiar with the original: keep in mind that this version focuses on art/quality of life improvements, and doesn't contain much you haven't already seen. Some of the more obscure puzzles have been tweaked or outright replaced, chase sequences have been rebalanced to be more forgiving, and as far as I can tell there are no new areas or endings. It also adds the ability to talk to your companions at any time, which either gives you puzzle hints or fun dialog depending on what you're looking at.Bottom line: If you can't afford it, you can give this version a miss and play the original without missing any story beats or endings. If you can afford it, then this is a very solid remake that refines the clunkier parts of the original without messing with the parts people actually like.Either way, Ib is one of my favourite games of all time and worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: Ib, a game that defies expectations and captivates players with its unique blend of art and horror, has secured its place as my all-time favorite game. Despite its short duration of only 2 hours, with an additional 3 hours for alternate endings, the game manages to deliver an experience that lingers long after the credits roll. While the lack of substantial new content may deter some, the game's innovative approach and unforgettable elements make it a recommendation that I wholeheartedly stand by.One of the standout features of Ib is its distinctive art style. Released in 2012, the game introduced a visually arresting world where slender and ethereal characters wander through an art gallery. The meticulous attention to detail is apparent in the slight thickness and plumpness of the art, setting it apart from the human characters. Unrealistic designs add to the allure, offering a glimpse into the boundless creativity of the artist behind them. The inclusion of a few 16-bit full artworks further enhances the game's visual appeal, creating an enchanting atmosphere rarely seen in other titles. Ib's art style is a breath of fresh air, and its impact is magnified by the absence of the typical pixelated representations found in similar games.Beyond its visuals, Ib's concept is a stroke of brilliance. While many games incorporate art in various ways, Ib takes it to another level. The entire game unfolds within the confines of an art gallery, where each painting and statue poses a potential threat. The fear of the unknown permeates every step as players navigate this treacherous world, never knowing when a harmless piece of art might transform into a nightmarish adversary. This integration of art as a tool for horror is truly groundbreaking and elevates Ib above its genre peers. Furthermore, the abstract nature of the artwork invites individual interpretation, adding depth and intrigue to the game's multiple endings. The lingering question of whether Ib's journey was a descent into madness or a twisted reality enhances the game's replayability and fosters a dedicated fanbase.The characters in Ib also contribute to its enduring appeal. While the trope of a young, defenseless girl accompanied by a fatherly figure has been explored in various games, Ib adds its own unique twist. Ib herself embodies the curiosity and vulnerability of a child thrust into a bewildering world. Her interactions with the environment, from touching and taking objects to her limited inventory capacity, evoke a genuine sense of exploration and innocence. In contrast, Garry, the unlikely protector, becomes emotionally invested in Ib's safety, exhibiting an instinctual caretaking role despite not being a natural father figure. Their relationship, shaped by their shared experiences, is both heartwarming and believable.Notably, Ib introduces a character named Mary, whose manipulative and malevolent nature initially elicits disdain. However, as the story unfolds, a surprising understanding and even a desire for an ending with Mary emerge. This complex portrayal adds depth and moral ambiguity to the game, challenging players' perceptions and leaving a lasting impression.In conclusion, Ib is a remarkable game that pushes the boundaries of what can be achieved within the horror genre. Its fusion of art and gameplay creates a captivating experience that defies expectations. While the lack of substantial new content may limit its value for some, the game's unique art style, innovative concept, and emotionally engaging characters make it an unforgettable journey. Ib is an experience worth undertaking, though potential buyers may want to consider the game's price point before diving into its haunting world.

_childDocuments_.review: Ib is a psychological horror masterpiece set in an art museum that tells so much within its short 2 hour runtime. Despite being a short game, Ib poses many complex themes and ideas that it gives most major games a run for their money at showing them how to create immersive worlds and levels without getting dragged out. The setting of exploring an alternative world of the museum where all of the artworks and statues are the main enemies is such a amazing unique concept that is incredibly engaging to play through. The music is fantastic and sets the eerie atmosphere, and loud well timed sound effects shatter the silence when exploring the map. Ib plays with themes of psychosis and alternating perspectives, combining these two things delivers a one of a kind horror experience that is perfectly brought to life in this remaster, one of the better remasters ever released. The characters are memorable, the setting is stylish and the whole experience is unforgettable. 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I am a writer, words are disappointing with how they could never truly convey the immense, unyielding love I feel for this game and what a perfection the game truly is. I have been with this game since it was initially released in 2012. For some reason, February seems to be the month I revisit Ib, replay it, write about it, and listen to it's music, and February 2022 seemed to share my nostalgia with the announcement for the release of this remake. I was ecstatic, to say the least. How do you make a piece of truly beautiful, artistic perfection even surpass itself? The concept of this type of attempt is rarely ever successful, but Kouri found a way.  I didn't think I could love this game anymore than I did before the remake's release, but I was proven wrong. I adore this game. This game has worked its way into my everyday life, it is painted into my skin (literally, I have a tattoo of a blue rose and a red rose), and it has taken permanent residence in my heart. The creator is a genius who speaks uncensored to the essence of my soul. This game is criminally underrated, but my hope is that a Steam release will enlightened many more to the true value of this game. My warmest gratitude to Kouri. Please know how loved your masterpiece truly is.

_childDocuments_.review: Ib is a fantastic game. There's slight differences to some of the puzzles, but not an overwhelming difference, and they can be quite fun to solve. The sprites are also different, and look much more clearer than before, along with the dialogue for the characters being fantastically written and not too unrealistic. The English translation is very good and coherent! The zoom in tool, although I didn't find much real use for it, was also a very nice addition, especially for looking at the paintings closer.It's a shame the rose in the top left (representing Ib's health) in the original wasn't kept, now using a different picture, and I preferred some of the art for sprites in the original. I was also hoping that there would be at least another new ending or more backstory explored here, but I'd still recommend trying this one out alongside the original.All in all, a brilliant game that anyone can get into, and worth checking out, even if you've played the original before.

_childDocuments_.review: The moment I saw Ib appear on Steam, I paid the $12 and played through everything in 1 session till I 100% the entire game. Perhaps this is because I'm biased, but Ib and The Witch's House were my 2 favorites back in 2013-2015. I had no idea Ib had a remake until the day I wrote this review.That being said, I can tell you with absolute certainty that this version of Ib is the better version. They changed the art style significantly, and Ib looks a lot more fleshed out as well as all the other characters. The dialogue is mostly the same, with some extra things thrown in here and there for touch-ups.They also changed some of the puzzles for the betterment of game design which is a MASSIVE plus. They did away with a lot of the "number" related puzzles (One example is the green room that once involved figuring out 3 numbers to multiple and add together to get the code to a door, now has been completely reworked so that you don't have to do that). Also, the new options of being able to talk to side characters at any point, as well as the new Zoom In/Zoom Out feature is absolutely incredible. They really outdid themselves this time by going above and beyond with the rework.As for criticism, I think this game can get quite repetitive if you're trying to strive for multiple endings. Ib has lots of different endings, and variations of those endings, but it's usually really tedious to get them. This has to do with the fact that the system they use to determine your ending usually requires analyzing decisions you've made pretty early in the game, as well as mid-way. So it can get quite hectic hopping around between saves, and replaying the same puzzles over and over again without an option to skip them, just for the sake of trying different choices. The True Gallery returns to Ib, and while there is one thing I won't necessarily spoil, I will say there are some "collectibles" that are very infuriating to locate without the walk through back on the original homepage at vpg translations. Some collectibles are even locked away without any way to backtrack and grab them. (Especially one in the blue room and brown room). Overall though, still absolutely love Ib, and I'm so happy to see it got a remake along with all of its other rpg horror cousins. Very much worth while for new players and old players alike!

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't know about this remake until I stumbled on a random announcement on twitter about an English patch that just came out for it. I don't think I've purchased a game so quickly before.A remake of one of the classic staples of the Japanese RPG Maker Horror line up. But not in a bad way. Ib has been my favorite of this line for a very long time and this remake did not disappoint. The art and graphics are updated, most of the music is the same and some new features have been added! What surprised, yet delighted me was that there were new puzzles for old fans to try out. Some puzzles have been replaced, removed, added or revamped but not in a bad way. It keeps things interesting for older fans. A lot of room layouts have changed quite a bit as well.Everything has a nice glow up graphically and I really enjoy the 'talk to your partner' button. They have something new to say in every room and sometimes multiple things to say in a room depending on where you stand or what you've done in said room. It's a really nice touch.If I had any complaints, it would be the new health meter and the change in Mary's theme. I did like the original health meter and watching your rose lose petals instead of the new means where thorns disappear and the flower fades in color. But that's -hardly- a complaint and I'm kind of reaching when I call that a complaint. It is a shame Mary's theme changed as I much prefer the original, however I'm sure there's a reason for this. (Whether it be due to copyright or what may you)The extra bit of 'finding' the paintings and the requirements to consider them 'found' is a pretty neat addition and you may have to play through the game a couple of times to get them all as some depend on how you let an event play out. I thought I had gotten all of the base game paintings only to find that I missed two and one was due to how I let a event go.I can't recommend Ib enough. Both the original and this version. Considering the original game recently turned 10 years old, its a good time for this game to appear! Remakes don't always live up to the original. But this one certainly does and more.
